ECLIPSES for the YEAR 1832.
I. Of the Moon, on the 13th of the second month of February, in the afternoon; partly visible.
The moon rises 3 1/2 days after 12 P.M. (M. West.) It rises about the same time as the sun, in north latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12 Greenwich, 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12. These times are 6 1/2 hours before and after midnight respectively; consequently invisible here. It will be visible in the northwestern parts of the United States, in the northern parts of the United States, in the northern parts of New-Hampshire, &c.
II. Of the Sun, on the 13th of the Third Month (March) about half an hour after midnight; consequently invisible here. It will be visible in the northern parts of the United States, in the northern parts of New-Hampshire, in the northern parts of Maine, in the northern parts of New-England, &c.
III. Of the Moon, on the 11th of the Eighth Month (August), about 11 1/2 hours in the morning; too visible in the United States, but invisible in the northern parts of the United States, in the northern parts of New-Hampshire, &c.
IV. Of the Sun, on the 23d of the Ninth Month (September), about midnight; consequently invisible here. It will be visible in the northern parts of the United States, in the northern parts of New-Hampshire, in the southern parts of Pennsylvania.
The Sun rises, at this latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12. The Moon rises, at this latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12.
The Sun sets, at this latitude, at 9 1/4 8 1/2 7 1/2. The Moon sets, at this latitude, at 9 1/4 8 1/2 7 1/2.
The Sun is in the zenith, at 12 noon, at this latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12. The Moon is in the zenith, at this latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12.
The Sun is in the meridian, at 6 P.M., at this latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12. The Moon is in this latitude, at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12.
At Baltimore, 3 1/2 minutes after the Sun rises at 3 3/4 2 7/12 2 11/12. (These places respectively it will be sensible to find the Sun's rising and setting times at Baltimore, nearly 31/2 degrees south of London, nearly 31/2 degrees north of London.)

FROM the flattering reception that the
"AMERICAN REPOSITORY for 1795," met with
from the Public, the Editor has been encouraged
to expect his intimate will continue to render this for
1796 that more deferring of their patronage.
With this view he has not only enriched the
little Volume with an entire new text of vig-
nettes, but he has likewise enlarged the size by
such an addition of new and interesting matter,
as to furnish a competent AMBULANT READER for
the exhibition of the year.
In composing the great variety of life
that enter into this compilation, it may be easily
supposed that he has met with considerable diffi-
culty in procuring satisfactory information; but
as he has spared no pains in his endeavours, he
hopes that the few scraps which may remain to
the reader will be noticed as a grain of allowance.
Even information useful in rendering
the compilations of future years more full or
correct will be received with pleasure. The re-
gulations for transacting business at all the dif-
ferent banks, the times of receiving or closing
the mail, and the details of the various
post-towns; and the expences of government in
all the different States, are among the articles
with which the Editor is ambitious of improving
this annual Compendium; and communications
on all, or every of these topics will be gratefully
acknowledged.
The eclipses of this year are all noted in
the Calendar, against the days on which they
will occur: the only one, that of the sun, visible
at Philadelphia, will happen thirty-six minutes
before setting, on the memorable 4th of July,
about the time when the Declaration of Independence
will be read. The greatest obscuration will be 1 1/2
degrees on the sun's fourth limb.—Such an occurrence on a
feastive day, in the dark ages of superstition,
would have occasioned no final inquisition; but
at this critical period, the people of Philadelphia
contemplating the regular return of a natural
event.—It may indeed suggest a wish; and it is
not unworthy the Christian and patriot to cherish
such a wish: "That the independence, liberty and
liberality of the United States may not be
scoured; but continue to shine, until solar and
lunar eclipses, and all the vicissitudes of time
shall be no more."

The Explanation of the Calendar.
THE first column contains the day of the
month, the flood the day of the week, the flood
the festival and other remarkable days; the fourth
the rising and setting of the sun; the fifth the sun's
declination in degrees and minutes, calculated to
the nearest degree in Philadelphia; the sixth the moon's
fouthing; and the seventh the time of sunset
at Philadelphia, computed as the mean between
morning and evening flood, now enough for common use; the morning flood being really twelve
minutes earlier and that of the evening as much
later than the ordinary.
The second column contains an ephemeris of the moon's
place, and the periods when albedo is on the meridian. The time of albedo's passage over the meridian is given for the first six months above the pole, and for the last six below it, five days in each month.
At the days end at midnight, the fouthing of the
moon after that hour is to be fought for against the
following day.

All captains or masters of vessels, coming from beyond sea,

their arrival, and shall present themselves with their corres-
pondent certificate of health from the resident physician; and until they re-
solve such certificate, they shall not land and anchor in the harbor,
to be received into the port, unless they pay within the penalty of
500 dollars for every such offense.
After landing, the captain or master shall send a
letter to the resident physician, and while the physician is pre-
senting his official examination, the captain or master, every-
body of the crew, and passengers, shall be despatched or
qualified; he shall insure all individuals requesting the
examination with a certificate of health, and every person,
or, if any person denies the physician or other person offic-
ial, for every such offense he shall pay 10 dollars.
As the physician is present, and the certificate (if exempted) shall
be sent by sea before the captain has obtained a certificate,

January 1800. – City of Washington
Wednesday January 1st. At plenary Day – With
appearance of Snow – Mr. Foster called and
sent a letter from Genl. Thomson to
Wilson to take to Mr. Vernon at St. Lawrence
inclusively a letter from W. Machague at Philadelphia
with an express to put in the Canal at Baltimore which
had been in Philadelphia some months for collection.
I saw in the evening wrote to W. Machague
to obtain leave to send a few letters. – Sunday
January 4th – I was five clear Day – I
sent out to go to our farm – went as far as Georg
town & found the roads so bad we returned. –
Before we set out rented a room in our former
house on Square 33 – the Mr. & the
rate of $11.00 annum – she to quit it when ever
we came out the whole. – Have obtained
notice that he could not have his half of it
after the present quarter (from Christmas Day
till the 25 March) at the same rate as heretofore
sent her up to the farm in the afternoon from her house.
City of Washington - Territory of
Columbia - State of Maryland. -
Mr. President
Respctf to Mr. Thomson
Tuesday, Dec. 2nd - Mr. T. Potter called here & brought
a letter to Dr. In from Col. Lee - mentioning that
Mr. Washington has consented to give up the keys
of his late house to be placed on a monument
intended to be erected by the Congress in the Capitol
& requesting information respecting the General's
two houses building near the Capitol, the money
paid to the undertaker from having all gone
thru my husband's hands, he having intermingled
them as a friend.
Saturday - 1st - Some men from but two cars October
the wind over - Blake found the remainder of the
day - ordered the baggage to go to the Capitol
when Mr. Scott sent for Dr. In to go to the Commanding
office. - Part of the Load of hay arrived from
$25.000 - as soon as it was loaded - went to bed
Mr. T. Potter, who with her daughter Eleanor were very
rich. - Went after Dinner to the General's Houses
one of which is nearly finished - they are divided into
as to let as one or two houses. - Went thence
to the Capitol, where we stood for some time
to see fire in a room where they were playing the
band - while Dr. In laid out an oval round
which is taken the communication to the Gallery
of the Senate Room.— On our return Dr. S. received
a letter from an old acquaintance (W.B. Gardner of
Dover) wishing to know if he could meet with encouragement here as a Minister of Labor in a School.—
The City is yet too young for a minister to live in
too near Georgetown for an school at present.—
Sunday 5th Mr. R. Forrest called while after breakfast—
— said till our manager came from the same
with whom Dr S. continued conversing till near dinner time.—
— after dinner Dr. said once more to myself
Law & Business & Money & went to see Mr. Betsy
from there Willarding Laird, Durston & Mason
and D. Washington who had all called to see Mr B.
on his return from Annapolis where he had been
as Senator in the State legislature.— Since
they were professing to go to the great Falls, I sent
notes from Gettysburg to see what state the works are
in to know what is necessary to be done first
as the Potomac Company obtained a loan from
the State and they mean to proceed with the Canal
locks as fast as possible.— The Commissioners
of the City of Washington also obtained a loan from
the State to the amount of fifty thousand Dollars.—
Monday 6th. gloomy and morning— Snowed for
about three hours in the middle of the day—
went after breakfast to visit Mr. Deblers— on the
way stopped at the Capitol to get old Elephant
to put a glass into an oval picture frame.—
Saw at Mr. B.— her mother & sister— Mr. J. Philip Dutton
at three o'clock returned to dinner time
in the afternoon copied a little piece from Joseph
Walthamson, Gothic ornaments of the Cathedral of
York.— many of which are very curious & many
very beautiful.— I attended the Commissioners
of the Department in the afternoon with
Genl. Marshall M.B. to request him to propose
to the Congress to pass a secret vote that all Washington
tennis be laid in the same tomb with the
general and write on it in his respect to the
removal of the Empire to which she had consented.
Write to Mr. Washington respecting his request
to obtain a secret part of the late Genl. Blenker
he wishes to paint a whole length picture of him
also to stop Genl. Washington (printer) respecting a
vacancy which he thought might exist in Gardner
Tuesday 7th. after breakfast found Mr. King a man
quite sick— found him quite well only pretty with
violent letters— Mr. Johnson Smith was there, he
271
mentioned that Mr. Shaw the President's Secretary
had been at his father's house some days in conversation
from the former. I was much pleased with the City
Mayor Jackson also had been there & thought there
was no doubt but that Congress would adjourn to
some hour. -- The Committee received a letter from
the Secretary of the Navy (Walden) mentioning that the
President's time being occupied in the Senate was now
conspicuous that he intends commencing his furniture here
in June. -- The Committee were willing to take a look
at the Capitol House, which begins to make a handsome
appearance. -- On our return we met Mr. John Grant
who with Mr. J. P. King served as clerk in the office.
In the evening Mr. Lincoln wrote from Mr. King's
requesting him to send for his brother's personal
praise & congratulations of his important victory (Battle
of Lee's Mills). -- Mr. King stated his intention to
Wednesday -- 8th Mr. Lincoln called before we came down
stairs to see if Mr. Lincoln would go to Mr. Vernon with him
He stated that Mr. Lincoln got an answer from Mr. King
as he had invited them to dinner -- Mr. King was sick
Therefore they could not come. -- Mr. Lincoln
stated that while they were preparing to set off --
Mr. Wm. Dennett came to get a deed acknowledged
to Mr. Lincoln having the power of a magistrate in the City --
about noon Mr. Lincoln & I went off -- I went
to Mr. Lincoln's office to inquire if he would
allow me to get another glass, as I broke one
he put in before, with a touch, as soon as I
brought it home. -- Employed myself in copying
from the Official documents -- and entering pieces requesting
General Washington out of our Newspapers to
participate together in a Work. -- The rest of the day came
Thursday, 9th -- a very fine day. Clear & Cold. The
temperature frozen over. -- Mr. Lincoln walked
up from his house, invited us to go dinner with him
to dinner, which we declined being engaged in Work.
We came up again in the afternoon with his wife
and tea. I spent the Evening with them -- Mr. Lincoln
told them home -- they reside beyond the
Capitol about a mile 3/4 from us. -- Mr. Lincoln
spent some days in Georgia from lately where he
heard a great deal of the impossibility of accom-
modating the Congress in the vicinity of the Capitol
but they spend as they wish -- We hope differently.
Friday 10th it will very likely to know.
I spent the afternoon with Mr. Lincoln. -- Engaged
to send the carriage for her the next day &c &c
to go with her to the Capitol the General Washington
letter in 200000000000000000000000000000000
Saturday 11th a very fine day & the roads very good.
Mr. Peter intended the could not ride with us being
being obliged to go to see Mr. Hyltett who is every day
theman I go went to George Town called on Mr. Mason
& Mr. Hyltett who were with him -- Called at Mr. Johnson
who had rode out with Mr. Mason -- saw Mr. Johnson
Mr. Johnson died 8th of July 1817 -- Mr. Johnson
is gone in Lexington this morning to Mr. Colvin adjoining
to the house in occupation -- drank tea at Mr. Colvin
about one hour after our return I came home from
Mr. Vernon -- I came up with Mr. Greenbough and
dined in Alexandria at Mr. Colvin's --
Sunday 12th -- a very fine day as pleasant as a spring day
after breakfast Mr. Peter called & mentioned that his
wife & children are there for 3000 the carriage for her
& I accompanied him to the Capitol, the grounds
and Mr. Lewis house -- the latter being locked we entered
by the kitchen Window & went all over it -- It is a very
pleasant roomy house but the oval drawing room is
spired by the Corners of the ceiling & twin Pithos which
decoration the shape of the room -- Mr. Peter dinner
with us & returned home early in the afternoon some
of her children not being well -- In the evening Dr
Write to Mr. Gardner including his letter to Mr. Mason from
the painted balls requesting a vacuum in a school
Monday 13th -- a very beautiful day -- Went to
visit Mr. Mason -- with a letter from Mason to Mr. Colvin
requesting a supply of fertilizer for Mr. Washington -- Mr.
Colvin with the old former friends has built a very excellent
log house eight stones high on the Eastern Branch
and carries on the factory to a large extent --
about two o'clock Dr. L came from the office -- Mr.
Washington & Mr. Colvin came with him, the latter having
to Dinner -- In the Evening Mr. Washington came in
& mentioned that he did not think Mr. Blodgett's two
houses (one of which we were to have the refusal of) would
go on, as his son had since he went to Philad. become
on Washington's fortress of the money he had received
from selling Wood, & which he had meant to appropriate
to purchasing Planting &c -- Mr. Mason was employed
to make the windows Sashes &c -- & besides them a
small pine table & a pair of chairs &c &c &c -- I wrote a letter to Mr. Blodgett requesting him to purchase
for me a piano & the carpet & the music of the house
&c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c & &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c < &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c -- After breakfast
Mr. Dancy with his aunt Miss Lynn & three of her
children came to dine as frequenters to accompany
them to the Capitol &c -- Mr. Broome &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c >
with them returned about one o'clock -- They went
home -- We with my husband after breakfast went to
Dinner at Mr. Washington's (Nancy went) living in Gray
Town -- And there besides us Mr. St. Simon, Mr.
Whitworth, Miss Brown from the City, Mr. Farman
& two Mr. Johns -- Saw there a Miss Thomas from
Annapolis who won a visit to Mr. Washington, a pleasant
girl -- I came to the two Washingtons with
their two children & Miss Cuttle -- They live about nine
blocks from the moon house, the hill lying very steep
& bad in George Town -- They had in Federal Street
young Ladies around till one of the Ladies brought
in conversation with Mr. Washington respecting Mr. Blagheple
he said he meant to contract in a few days with Mr
Warburger for lumber to the amount of $10000 -- I that
hope the ladies will go on, even if Mr. Hardeman
is refractory.
Wednesday 15th
Another Spring Day -- While we
were preparing to go the farm Mr. Wil. Peter Wilkerson
called -- Mr. Wilkerson brought a note from his brother in town
Mr. K. Crawford to Dr. T. for the two Chinese girls he
had promised Judge Washington some time ago -- He
gave them back a note to Mrs. Brownes for them, telling
got them from her in exchange for common ones of
equal size -- and now out of the farm --
about two o'clock arrived at the farm where we
have not been since the 26 Novr 1809 -- Morning
Mr. Wilkerson's Grape Vines --
Thursday 16th -- A beautiful day -- Mr. Diggins, upon
of 70 years of age walked from his farm, at last a
nucle a half, to garden -- Threw a Negro Lad of him
named the & 10 Grammer besides clothing -- The
walker home the we offered him a horse or the
courage -- I passed some of the pieces respecting
Genl Washington in a book -- and worked at a small
piece in Latin which has been a German long time and
after walked to the new piece of post trail home
refusing to enclose the new orchard which Dr --
had this year to plant, with trees of his own graft
ings from the best fruits he could collect --
Friday 17th a pleasant morning, green oaks about from
Dr -- began to plant the orchard -- In the afternoon
went to visit Mr. Diggins to whom we had sent in the morning -- Begun to rain before we
set off -- we returned in a storm of rain from --
now there the Wolf Blakes, from the Eastern three
gentlemen to Mr. Diggins -- very beautiful fishermen
girls apparently -- There was also Mr. Chamberlain
a visitor to them -- This had been in the morning
see the bridge at the bottom Falls of Potomack --
274
Saturday 18th a very windy night -- Clear cold day.
Write a letter to Col Thomson to take up my
pages in planting trees -- Read 8 watches in the bed
Sunday 19 -- a cold windy day -- I wrote to Will
Brady Thomson I have a long letter in answer to me
received from him the latter of the 17th -- I am the
tenant of 25 -- engaged with Mr R. H. Smith during the
part of 1876 probably from to make a profit I am sure
on the ground of 2000 pounds of wheat sold -- Read
"Peter Sheridan's Patriot Chief" -- "Guns up" -- "Inバー
Leviathan in America"
Monday 20th very hot day -- More pretty early
I after breakfast set off for town -- found the roads
about half the day now bad -- I got home about
seven o'clock -- I wrote with the receipt of that
Thursday 22nd January 1877 January 22nd I paid for my
Washington Houses --
Tuesday 21 -- I got up very early in the morning
to visit Raleigh for his account of the money to be
returned for the same Houses, which he enclosed with
his own to Col. Dear -- The Executive meeting at this
time at Mr. Warren -- Sent a letter Thursday 22 to
Mr. Law, who returned yesterday from Mr. Warren --
Dr. L. was at the Office in the morning, on the evening
he wrote to Mr. Manry, American Consul at Liverpool
respecting a boat of Wedgwood Ware, if some things
& books, which are sent to him for, thru our friend
W. Lin in March 1799 & which have not yet arrived
Write also to Mr. Chorley, on whom his father in law
had one months wages empowered him to draw for a
thousand pounds sterling, acknowledging his letter mentioning
that his bills would be paid & expecting his desire
to have the next remittance sent out in 1000 pounds --
And these letters will go to his cousin Jane Thornton
at Lancaster, Engls. to Mr. H. Smith to be forwarded by
the Chicago journal from Baltimore --
Wednesday 22 -- Cold & windy -- I left the office
all the morning -- In the afternoon went for up to the
same to settle a house, as he intended to go the night
away to Mr. Biggs at Barabanton -- He began a letter
to Dr. Canton & was interrupted by a visit from Mr. Jason
Murphy, who had not come from Mr. Fairfords in Virginia
to whom he was about selling City Lots & wished to know
something concerning Divisions & other ye -- Having arrived
in the part of England where Dr. L. was domiciled
they had a great deal of conversation respecting old
regiments, he said pretty late --
Thursday 23 -- A beautiful day -- Mr. Potter called
as Dr. L. was preparing to set out with Mr. Brent to
278 W. Biggs & mentioned that he thought he was in
Alexandria -- Very therefore declined going -- but agreed
to go by Mr P. S. Stephens -- stopped out about Noon after
D. C. finished his letter to H. Dunton & wrote me to his
letter in law -- after dinner Mama of I went to
Spence's town to a few stores, and then to see Mr Berry.
Said there Mr Nicholas King -- engaged in drawings of
calculations respecting the Locks of at the Great Falls
afterwards. Mr Laird & Mr J. Mason came in they with Mr
Dunring are appointed by the Potomac Company as a
Board to set in Spence Town to attend to their business --
Mr King being now as if leaving Oakland offered him a
seat in an carriage which he accepted. -- I got home
safe -- the night very dark.
Thursday 24th -- Not very cold -- neither pleasant -- Just
to ask Mr Dunring to accompany us to Williamsburg --
plan for returning sent him to the Capitol to inquire
if the gate bespoke of the Blacksmith there was
one of to take home Mr Kearneys, Books of Gothic
monuments -- After dinner went to George -- met
with up Mr Brown her Aunt of little Maria Yount
threw in old Lands -- drank tea there of raw
a handsome set of curtains -- looking glasses of things
and just received from Scotland -- and the first time
by little Richmond -- I suppose to the place of the
house, not my husband here -- Mr Julia Houser, he
had just come from Mr Stephens of was on his way to
meet Mr John Taylor at the Union Tavern, who had
written a letter to request him to ride in, as he was obliged
to leave town very early in the morning for Annapolis.
D. C. came home about 9 o'clock --
Saturday 26th -- Very hot & windy -- Mr R. Forrest
called and as he wished to stay till the Northern Mail
came he prevailed him to dinner, D. C. went about
town to all sorts, to ask his opinion concerning some
land in Baltimore County, Virginia which Mr Stephens
offered for half his improved House -- (which he
desired him not to accept of) -- He said dinner then fixed
not return till evening -- Late the newspapers printed &
Sunday 27th -- Old P. S. -- Before we were up received
an invitation to take a family dinner with Mr Forrest.
He left about noon, called to see Mr Laird -- Mr Laird had
gone with James Rogers to Mr Stephens -- but there a
while, invited her to come & spend the night with us
with her fine little daughter Eliza -- but she declined
being too much engaged in preparing furniture for
their house, to go out. -- Went home to Williamsburg
nothing particular occurred, returned home about seven
in the morning -- Read aloud in an European Magazine
the D. C. fell asleep -- Went to bed earlier than usual.
Monday 27th -- A blinder day -- rained a little --
What to do -- Step in the pretty avenue to look for
some blacks Charity -- a few little ones -- there are
276
too few inhabitants for any enterprise to be carried
on extensively. I think there is one Mrs King
who has been very ill in Chelsea and I have
not what I call in a few hours — she is much to
be filled having no private relation or intimate to
be with her. — I find the afternoon one
from with the Kingingham filters (famous in this
country) to Mr Fitching, who is going to Rochester
to make the forts the produce of these are three
years old, & then sell them to or buy them 18000
as they may agree. The notice to Mr Colvin
who applied for the House of Commons & by his consent
sent home some books (many calendars) borrowed
of Mr Cyles — over the Eastern Branch of Portsmouth
begun a letter to Major Brooke commanding
at Fort Niagara. — Mr Forrest called on his
return from Gibraltar. — Their pretty lady —
Dr. D. at the office in the morning — Mr. Tompkins came in the afternoon, drank tea with
us yet pretty late — He has begun a house adjourned
the one we occupy on 1st of 25th and means to
have it made to carry by the time Congress meets
July 4th at the office with Mr White — Mr. Spalding called — I came home about noon with Mr Colvin
and two strangers Mr Warren & Mr Spalding. During the
later brought a letter of introduction from Mr Bellamy
who was here in the summer of 1796 — He is the
gentleman, who tries to secure you to Lafayette from
his imprisonment in Germany — The new line is Philadelphia
you lately married to Miss B. Nixon — These gentlemen were
on their way to Charleston — I did not make anything
with Colvin omitted to dine with them at his house which
I declined. He went after to dinner to Mr. Colvin who was too
busy to attend the Office — I had some letter to communicate
to General Burnside at Fort Washington — Mr. Colvin
is going to bring this
day late the 18th of the gentlemen meet with Mr. Thomas
Colvin, to a bill in George Town — Women engage
in making some of their clothes from Dutch Roman who came
in their place to replace Daughter from Charleston we have some ladies
married since June up to a Captain & one in the
City — I was employed in altering & making articles on
a map to draw the distances from the Capital & Presidents
House after one which Dr. D. had done at the Office — By
coming I was sitting on a chair —
Mr. Colvin called a little table & Dr. D. sat there.
Thursday
30th — Very cold. Snow in the House last night —
Mr. White called before me and I asked him
to the Office — Mr. Forrest called
after dinner. Dr. D. began a letter to the President Secretary
of the Navy, in answer to one from him requesting him
to name his colleagues to lay out a garden for their residence
on their in the Presidents House — This is a difficult
work without they had large funds to make every
thing agree with the President — Mr. D. was interrupted by Mr.
Colvin — Lieutenant — who want to be employed on the
President's House — and afterwards Mr. Colvin.

Friday Feb 17
1861
Dr. Stanton went from Willets after dinner to Mr.
Pollock's -- and came home about nine o'clock. --
After breakfast Mr. Whittier called on his
way to Gen. Grant's home returned about two o'clock
and dined with us -- In the morning Dr S
was engaged in working at his plan. The captain
afternoon went with Mr Fitzhugh, to both our
houses to take away Wilts chariot from
the carriage maker where it had been to be
repaired & the night before the carriage being
painted & nearly finished) some one got into
the shack & cut the linging & took much of
the carriage -- He has a blacksmith taken
upon suspension -- While they were gone Mr
Marshall Fitzhugh came here to inquire for his
brother -- he sat some time & then went to his
place where we heard they were -- They
are towards went from here to Williamsburg to
look -- After breakfast Dr S called on Mr O'Kelly
who was passing -- they walked together to the
Capital & thence with Mr George Calvert to
Mr Law's -- saw there young Nicholson
& Young Lieutenant (N. Hayes) -- In the
afternoon Mr Marbury called with Capt
Tongey who brought a letter from Mr. Davis.

Saturday Feb 18
1861
While they were here Mr Fitzhugh called on
his way home -- and Mr. Davis
returned to Mr. O'Kelly's & left him Mr. Marshall
in answer to the one he wrote
from some time since -- In the morning he
came from the farm & brought butter & eggs & chickens
& made which is my part of altogether not worth
more than four dollars. --
Dr. S myself on his plan of the Capital -- about
seven times either in Mr Nicholas King who was passing
to draw his work & with his family -- Mr. King's
father -- in the afternoon Mr. White came & took
his visit once more --
Dr. S. at the office in the morning -- after dinner
Mr. King's father going by he called him in the board
to tea -- Mr. Brady, her aunt, & two children
came in a night -- Mr. Forrest called in the
morning -- invited him and his wife to dinner tomorrow
after Mr. Hayes & Mr. Duncan were gone & as he
had just got orders to work & send up -- a sleepless night
on his return we looked out to see who were
in it -- there were six young ladies & one gentleman
turn out came in under a little while -- they
were the Misses Pollock, their brother, Nicholas
& brother-in-law, Joseph & William Duncan -- came in
afterwards Mr. Robert & Mr. B. Stewart
to write to Mr. Whittier respecting (Elboui) by

I wrote to W. Taylor at Minneapolis -- by Mr
The Governor who is sent on public business by the

in Georgia Town which is occupied by W. Simmons
Turner Keeper -- that he may write to his Brother
in Savannah respecting it, as it belongs to his

About noon the Manager came down -- The hay just
gone & the Storm will only last about a month --
We have twenty three horses -- 17 at this time at
the Farm -- one but to Wilburant -- one sent to Wil
though to keep on Charles -- 15 from men here to be
sent to Wilburant House -- Driver now at the Farm
to be sent to Wilburant in Virginia town --
a p carrying horses here, & one of the English horses
a young Jack W. Young has taken -- three horses at
the Farms -- I hope we shall have more provisions
this year --
W. Davis called -- showed us a copy of a letter written

Mr. Law is fixed in his new house his quite pleased
with it -- I went with him to visit on Captain

After breakfast we walked with Dr. Scott to the grounds
behind the President's House, which he is going
to have enclosed & laid out for a garden -- it is
at present in great confusion, having on of the
brick kilns, pits to contain water used by the
bush mechanics, rubbish &c &c -- The Commissioners
have agreed to have a few hands employed on this
&c &c -- is going to direct it, for he says if he goes
into the grounds it will not be done at all --
Which I would let it be -- Found
Dr Scotts house -- We left Dr Scott

(who had been riding toward the City of public
entertainment) to do the plan of the Capitol --
They were Mr. & Mrs. Scott from the Easton House

went when the Company went to the President's

Set out after breakfast to come to town at 10
in the morning English time.— We forgot
to bring our keys, and had to stop on the road about
3 Miles from the farm while the servant went
back for them. We are so secure from the white
Devil as we are in the house at Grand Terrestre.
Got home about eleven o'clock.— I received
2 letters from Washington with the Bills, insurance
of the things we sent for Liverpool in March
1809.— he had wanted for an opportunity to deliver
our papers.— They arrived in the morning.— They
brought down the Washington Gazette with him, which
had been up to the 1st of October. He is going home again.—
We found nothing about dinner time, and to the office
to get 4 things to day, of this lot on 18th 25th which he
is going to build.— We went out when I found him
to be neither with us nor the President. I thought
he would have gone to the office, but he returned to town.
He was in the office at 10 o'clock in the morning.
We found him to breakfast, borrowed a dollar to
go to Washington to begin organizing this money
to be sent to the office.— I returned on invitation
to town at 10 o'clock to bring some papers and
money— though it was for tomorrow but I had not
time to go to the office.
May
have gone at any rate.— After dinner time I
came with Colby to the office, neither
of them to dinner, but they declined to stay
to see a few messengers. I looked who was in.— I
sent one of them forward to get with his office last night, if
not them a bill from some letter and some money.—
I went to the office to write— came when I
found it to be.— I left Washington in the
evening at 8 o'clock in the evening, going to bed
at 10 o'clock in the evening, wishing to see the
President and the President's family, but
found them not in bed, and I went out without
seeing them.

general to Captain Taylor where to bring up the papers
to write to Mr. Kincaid.— As I am not always

it was to day not yesterday, that I may, enter

May 8
When I went out after dinner went to see Mr. Sumner
had to try. I came after breakfast some time
to breakfast about the time -- Sir junior Select as
we were about leaving Sumner's, Mr. Knapp
sent up word that there were some things landed
at the Wharf near their house -- Being a fine
even light night I did get a cart and went to
have them brought up -- Sumner & I came home
at ten o'clock -- I began to not a light funk of fire
with me -- While the things came from them
made disappointments in the neighborhood here I think
they are dear -- the place it is pretty but not
such as I expected, as they were not limited in the
price -- the houses & forches all pretty --
all Dallan called -- from Cocke's died -- I went to
the office returned about one o'clock. I find from Mr.
Jefferson a short pamphlet, an appendix to the Notes
on Virginia, respecting the authority of the Senate
of the Senate Chief Judge -- I came down from
the farm brought the cart with a little wood, some
valuable books -- We have five consulated people about
the same time all bill babies -- I got some
inoculating matter from Dr. May and inoculated
for (a negro man) William & Betty brown children
and Mrs. Luig's child -- I hope nearly 10 months old.
Wednesday 10
10 o'clock in the morning left
Dr. S. went to the Capitol in the carriage which
was going to the blacksmiths to be harnessed --
turned to him -- Mr. Drummond asked to consult
about Burke's funeral -- mentioned that he had read
a subscription for his widow, and that they would
have his remains interred to the poor house --
desired to go to Genessee -- I went out
with Mr. S. later & invited us to dinner -- I
returned, Jefferson & I went to Genessee & left him
driving -- we returned going to dinner and did not
go to the Genessee house to be seen as we
wanted to set off for Charleston in the morning --
Mr. R. Forrest called -- took him a letter from
Jefferson to go home as it rains & I was very sick --
I came about nine o'clock -- besides the English
words which pass in his leaving, Jefferson felt down
from them him off in a very dangerous manner, but
he was fortunately not hurt -- He wanted to know
into Mr. Jefferson's yard, and the old he asked Jefferson
for him that of his blue eyes, & so long banking together
constitute were the causes of their falling.
When we rose thought we should not have been
able to take our intended journey, but it began to
clear up, we had breakfast & got off about ten o'clock
called for Mr. Forrest who accompanied us on
horseback -- We crossed the eastern branch river
on the other side of which are many beautiful
George town, Alexandria Va. — The road in general
very good — two pretty carts on the road near the turn
at 1000 Pigs & 1000 chickens — arrived about three
o'clock at Mr. Branford's, Mr. Trumbull father's house
on an eminence that overlooks the town which
is a neat pretty little place — very house has a large
garden, if the number of hens & winging chickens
are planted about, with the general appearance gives it
a very pleasant appearance. — It is the place where
the Court are held — but is nothing rather than me
measuring — they are just beginning a new courthouse
which is to be larger & handsome — The women
brave of sentiment which is only necessary for bold
hearts & small craft has a romantic grand appearance
& around just as the family were at dinner — in
the afternoon we reached again with Mr. Trumbull
& Mr. Branford — Mr. Trumbull Branford got out about nine
o'clock to go to a stable about four miles from Martinsville
to include to have accomplished them, but had
the roads were very bad for a carriage — We wished
to purchase a negro boy was no reason for taking
this trip — Mr. Trumbull another night to travel
with us joins Mr. Branford — went to his house
— this is found from Judge Campbell — the best belongs
to a fine negro man who is doing very well — he
was
the house & lot in which he lives — maintains a large
family himself and is generally respected —
the gentleman returned just after we had left him
& dinner — We purchased a negro man for $1000
Walker on the night's ride to Mr. B's house which was
very little to Mr. Trumbull's satisfaction —
This early upon breakfast as we were about to leave
off Bishop Clappett arrived — he came intending
to ride with Mr. Branford to our city where is going
to settle, but Mr. Bishop refused going as Mr. Trumbull
was not now with us — Mr. Bishop left Mr. Branford
upon promise with us to dinner tomorrow The Bishop & Mr.
Trumbull & myself at dinner together then is the
best testimony I can give of the gentleman's
principles & character — but I was obliged to leave
the Bishop's intention to look at them — and go to
myself & Mr. Trumbull to dinner — got home about
one o'clock — It was very warm weather — I am
very poorly and obliged to go to bed immediately
after tea — Mr. Trumbull & Mr. Bishop Whittier
called — I played for them some time — In
the afternoon sent for to town — to the mills must
visit Mr. Trumbull to dinner — — this morning
we were about to visit the mills with us —

June 1st
we ordered the baggage. I got out about ten o'clock.
We found the roads very bad, great part of the way
it continued dropping, and when we got within about
2 1/2 miles of the house, it rained in torrents and the
wind blew very hard. -- It is about nine or ten miles
from the City. -- We found W. Litchfield sick in bed
& W. S. had just before got out for home with him
due to the weather. -- W Jackson returned and
with Thomas Litchfield went to City. I addressed to buy the
road by North Brick street -- we got out immediately
after dinner (the temperature at that time was night)
we have the roads well cut to better this morning)
a boy doing for J. Richardson more -- I left me get
within half a mile of the house we had a dreadful
ride, not only from the road being bad, but having
to pass the fields which part of the way the branches
of the trees being full of rain in breaking up the
baggage cut us very nearly altogether we had a disagreeable
ride, but got home in good time. --

home about dark. -- The men while worked very
badly and made more dirt than ever seen by
white working only. -- I got a letter from W. Dinsley
to go to W. Dinsley to see the work his men
had done -- Present two other men who worked
the whole night & did it over again -- We would
have preferred remaining with the City water rather
than have had so much trouble and dirt. --
We have found that the President is wrong. -- D. S.
went to the Office. -- He went about one o'clock
to George Town to wait on the President -- brought
home 2 horses to dinner -- those horses he had orders
to turn out was made to leave in honor. -- At
White came in to leave the horses. -- The President
intended turning to receive an address from the inhabitants
of Georgia from the Governor Town. -- D. S.
went out after dinner returned home with W. Cannon
iningham -- W. Litchfield came to stay all night. --
D. S. went to the Office. -- W. Litchfield called --
invited him this night to tea. -- W. Kinsey has written
to invite them also. -- W. Litchfield came to
dinner -- While we were at table D. S. called to
W. Kinsey -- W. Kinsey dropped came early. -- The President
came in about three o'clock. D. S. had a
horse got ready & with some thing gentlemen received
him to the Capitol. -- He slept first at
his house of the Treasury Office. -- He travels in
a horseless car -- and is going to lodge at Camer
lidge Tavern in the Capitol Hall. --

Mr. Johnston's speech being continued in time when

D. I. went to the office — a man came from the

the United States at Mr. Langhorne's Tavern.

The President went away from the dinner

sent for to look after the two Jennies. — Mr. Stewart

Wednesday — Mr. Hunt walked 1000 bars and

they came — He went away & returned at night
Mr. Stewart & Mr. Hinchliffe came — Miss Hinchliffe
was not home in our carriage — I had come home
late — I dined with a large party at Mr. Hinchliffe's
residence opposite the bank of Alexandria — Mr. Hinchliffe
stayed all night.
Wednesday 1000
after breakfast Mr. Hinchliffe & I went out — We
went to George Town — returned about twelve o'clock
to the office after a sleeping found — Mr. Hinchliffe
& Miss Hinchliffe came in the evening.
We went to the office — Mr. Hinchliffe called —
Mr. Smith called — Mr. Hinchliffe & Mr. House called —
Miss Hinchliffe came down with words — supposed to go
the same dinner one block by the time we returned
very sleepy with the appearance of rain — Miss
Hinchliffe & I went to night prayers at church of the
Methodist on my paper table —
Wednesday 1000
Mr. Hinchliffe came up twenty minutes after Mr. Hinchliffe
about a manager — but another to Mr. Hinchliffe found
all day in the office for the office — When
he returned he informed us that two horses in the
city were burnt down last night — two of the best
in the city — Mr. Hinchliffe came in the evening
to see the Buckingham horses which has a fatal
on the shoulder, wing to its being about while at
White Sulphur — Suppall all day, waiting in the
office early & got to town before ten o'clock.
The horses are quite destroyed — I was a temporary
recommendation for the War Office — the horses
not finished & inhabited by the men who built them
are dying at the time of the fire & obliged to be moved
out — This is the third fire we have had in the
city in one year at the same time.

another few days -- The weather has been delightful
for some time past -- Poor Mellett had the morning --
He is a great loss both as a public & private man --
He leaves a wife & seven children. -- Mr. Fordert

The new manager went up to the farm to see it to

general instructions at his farm in Virginia. --

came -- Mr. Betts went out & returned to dinner --
Dr. J went all the way & did not return till Evening

Mr. D. M. Ray & Lewis came, they walked so that we

a little -- Mr. Bowen went before tea -- Mr. D. M. Bowen
went in our carriage -- Went to bed a little earlier
than common --

Mr. Wells painted a little -- Mr. Betts went to town
in the Evening & called an author which Mr. Mellett
was present to & Mr. Wells went home --
Mr. Betts got up in the office of me he recollected
called from & composed by a black man
in New England -- Went to bed about eleven --
Dr. J went to the office -- Mr. Bledgett to town -- Mr.
Fult returned about 10 o'clock -- Mr. Wells came
to office -- No man came to go to the farm --

Tuesday June 17th 1805
Set off from Washington about eleven o’clock
in an horse carrying to Washington landing
around at Mc Dallton in Alexandria about
one — Mr Rigaud Mry Stephens waited on
us — We dined at Mc Dallton called at the Treasury
and set out about 4 o’clock with our companion
of Voyage (2d day’s leave) arrived at Baltimore
con sidered about 16 miles a little after four o’clock
passed over the bridge (had had 2 good butter) passed through Baltimore
which is Stafford Court House about 28 miles
from Baltimore about eleven — passed the Potomac
on the Potomac branch, which has some fine bright
water in it, some good mills situated on the top
of a rocky mountain looking over — continued on to Frederickburg
a very pleasant looking place with neat
houses & gardens — The day being pleasant
and horses able to continue on we went 20
miles further, in all 47 miles and came to
an comfortable, dry House — Here we
leave the Stage at all business for an comfortable
lodging & poor fare — Thursday 19th started
about 8 o’clock ride from Williamsburg, a bridge
being broken down, obliged to go by new market
much out of our road intended to breakfast there
371
but the appearance of this place being too
uncomfortable only suited on horses, I took
some middle Strackers -- an extremely hot
day this: I suppose cannot go right for 5
hours in sun & about 5 o'clock reached the
Walthamshp, having missed the road & gone
many miles out of the way. -- We are now at
our place in Lower St. Virginia at a farm
house tavern in the Virginia style -- The people
seemed to belong but every thing dirty, their
armoury of flintlock & halfhacked blacks &
Wood with all kinds disagreeable noises. --
The post was all built by the front of the
winter -- 2 miles off there is mills belonging to
Mr Brackenr.
I can't find time to write, for when we arrive
at the different stages I am either so sleepy or
so hungry, that I can think of nothing but to
stop and take these crowding wants.
Sunday the 21st I got from Washington at 10 o'clock
from I reached Mr. Brackenr's about 1 o'clock
in the afternoon -- I had not been there
since I left Mr. Brackenr's -- I wrote a letter
to Mr. Madison -- Between these last articles
place there was a vein of red earth like the
orange beauty soil -- This is in the bottom of
the Lynchland -- about 2 miles from Mr. Brackenr's
which is first house to Mr. Madison -- We passed
a very pretty looking lawn with a
nice garden containing a peach tree & a grape
tree which I planted from the carriage to both
25 & 75 -- I came on the light horse & 50
6 -- This is on the road to leave our horse behind
part in his gig, then, I his own carriage returned
we arrived at Washington town about dark -- I
in some grieve if my asking for apple smiths
we waited very late for supper, & the everyone
had little or no appetite -- This is a very nice
& well kept house, Washington town quite pretty
& lady like. -- The house is within 2 a mile
of Centerville -- I about 16 from Hills --
Saturday 22 -- Bradford Jones now about one
mile, the house of which appear to be pretty &
since of the fields of corn very luxuriant, but
in general the corn has remained somewhat
smaller than I expected & much to the Southern
people we stopped at a house on the road for
breakfast for a few little boys around
Bingham, who was ill in fact -- left him better
to the journeying till about 10 o'clock over a
very level road we arrived at Brentwood
about 18 miles from the last place
Court House where after making a hearty meal
at Stephens' (being Stephens' house) for it is
the only tavern here we are now about to
go off again -- The weather is of tremendous
degree -- we have had a light shower of
little thunder while here -- Left this place
immediately after dinner & passed by Mr J. Rand

Sunday 30. — Rain fell about 7 o'clock —
cleared up with a pleasant breeze. —
Wind at Genl. Mills about 4 miles distant.
The house is pleasantly shaded but the ground
round it very poor. — We rode to Lake town
about 1 1/2 miles, returned to Genl. Mills
State came up with us at 2 o'clock this morning
Monday 31st. — Rode to Lake town in the
morning, pretty situated — built of wood except the
boat house & one or two private houses —
It is not a neat dwelling town, few of the houses
being finished & many going to decay. —
Called at Genl. Mills — took a return train
with us to Col. LaFay. —
Col. LaFay took this town
on his way to the Armory — We camped at Fort
Taylor from Lake town stopped here — Salubrious
and the neighborhood is not considered as healthy as
formerly, which they attribute to a large sale
and belonging to Judge King's mill.
Tuesday 2d Rise with the line, & left Col. LaFay
hostelable mansion, breakfasted at Col. Mills &
parted in with our companions at 8 o'clock — to
within 4 or 5 miles of Genl Mills where we had a pleasant
outing & returned very pleasantly together
a comfortable feeling — which added to the latitude
afforded my spirits all the afternoon.

to go to Col. Mills & returned at 11 o'clock
to Genl Mills. — I left Genl Mills at 11 o'clock

gement passed on the Col. & Genl. & Bishop & became

Genl Washington at Cambridge waited only a very

The Country notwithstanding the ideas we entertained of it is considerably healthy — the people
do not get an evening, & I suppose themselves to be the
people of France without suffering any inconvenience
The weather has been most constantly with the Americans
the day has been miserable — I went to drink with them
at a family not working for him, & he does not come
in time — an American's wages here are from
20 to 300 $ per annum —
A quiet with some Rain this afternoon —
Lieut. G. McClelland returned from the Union
where they had as he says most excellent ball
plantations, paid at each — & afterwards to the cavalry
manufactury — He was to have accompanied the
Ladies back to their home, but as I could not go
and as he thought it necessary that
one should stay after a great deal of difficulty
& something being required all to stay at home,
suppose
they will not go a thousand miles off & I think
very uncomfortable at being the cause of breaking
their long projected plan of amusement.
I am sorry I do not find the Ladies, and the Genl
Wadsworth to go, more contrary to my expectation, as I
have seen here — they were afraid of venturing
on their home, with some in the Country but
unimportant might happen to them and were doubt
if they would go in their private coaches — I
was not well & I do not intend to go further
Wednesday 5th — I did not eat well & laid this
morning — I did not go to bed this night before I came
from there — I have been very much all day —
but I expect to be that I am sure I will be a little
more comfortable in Charleston this Summer —
They take no pains here to get fine fruit, they say the orders are so
uncertain that they do not think it worth their
while to plant orchards — but it would be better
to have it only once in 2 or 3 years than never —
But though it is said that the Age will see the
South built prairie for — or something like this —
over the mountains about 60 or 80 miles from here
the trees did not threaten at all this Spring —
they left to carry the Line has been fine prairie —
Dr. J. returned about 2 o'clock much fatigued —
Saturday 6th. I rode to Boston three hours & I left
the City to go to the ferry & I left the ferry
to go to the ferry & I left the ferry to go to the ferry
& I left the ferry to go to the ferry & I left
from thirteen to fifteen lighting within our own
town. Our ship Peggy S. Bush annexed and
hurts 2 more fisher ribbons.
There is a man bringing over Col. Burt who makes
a great project, to buy his ships about this
time at $12 or $15 a head, he keeps them
up, takes profits, stores them in the harbor
& again on the opening of their takes them to
market & sells them at 70 or 75 for prime
meat thus paying the prime cost of food by
the mail & which he sells to the public
& buys it in worth & a dollar is formed
& my letter was too late for the post.

under Col. Burt's command I went to
the office of Governor Davis & to the
office of Judge Duffey, Mr. Henderson & Campbell
and Lee. — a strong part of our military
town stood up & was very warm.
Monday 5th very warm but a fine air —
12 o'clock I left the office of Judge Duffey his
room & leave who arrived last night & sat

Duffey — I left Judge Duffey's office to visit
the gentlemen & go down to the neighborhood —
Mr. Duffey & Col. Burt said I should think it more

— a guest & 8 women from Grinnell

other side of the river, 1 mile on this side of Fortin River
Branties are to be seen — We stopped at
Reed's, instead of blacks to breakfast where
they had a little boy very ill — Dr. Strickler
overtook us a few miles from blacks having
come out of their route to do us — They rode
on with us to me Strickler's, Daniels was wounded
in the left of road having no accommodation
at Strickler's they did not like the favor to give us
some bacon, eggs & sundry things — 18000 Strickler
would much to persuade us to go to Salem with
them but they said we would have to go to
them in 3 or 4 days they at this place 2 miles
from Salem & 27 1/2 Miles Strickler's there are many
persons of Brattles & Strickler's
Rode till 10 o'clock in the night to Mr Strickler's
the latter in travelling as a favor I was not
much pleased at our arrival — We had a bed
at the head of the house, the room being occupied
previously to our arrival — We started in a quarter
diminish nothing himself, & gives nothing to ladies

for strong drink — and in some parts they could

Friday 18 — Continued to breakfast at Hartwick
but they were so long preparing they are not off
about six o'clock I went to Hunter's
family (Mrs. and Mr. Bradford) arrived while we
were here. We were detained
for nearly 3 hours before we could get our
breakfast — It requires much patience to have
to deal with the hospitable house of entertaining
the as do it in a great hurry. —
Travelled tonight 22 miles further about 6 o'clock
There is a natural spring near the face of
the country carries much from what we have
passed this — there is no clay & there is
shofer. — The crossed twin bridges, the last
called tremblone bridges — the bridge throug
the country are very high, the trees are low
& muddy, rising I suppose with the grasses —
the trees on the banks are Beech, Willows
Tyranums Elms & Maples entwined by
grape & other vines. — I preferred to have
not better fare — a very indifferent supper
from the family here that we met before at
Mr Hunter's — they are named Hall & Lin at
Tartown 115 miles from Petersburg.
There are Cabalities here & there all the way
about 3 miles from this there are also round
houses welcome stores of various ages which are
much overcrowded & break off in laminar.
The country between this & Hunter's is better
& sandy — We enter Rockingham Co. a small
distance beyond a bridge which is about 3 miles
from this order of Hunter's — 18th of 21st June 1818
the spring water was warm & bad — two miles further
at Kinsey's fine cold well water. — Mrs. W.
Broadfort, daughter to Mr. Hunter's, who has
never published says that many friends have
been found & that one man executed a pistol shot
he does not think them real friends — Mrs. W.
is a pretty woman & seems to be clever — The
straw is little & scarce & that I quite
old my girl says there is more yesterday
late the willow grass — Had a comfortable
room & bed but we did not rest well
the house is pleasantly shaded & cool
The weather was very disagreeable to day
Saturday 19th — 18th of 21st month returning & very
slack without visiting the spring, as it was very out of
our way — had a very pleasant ride for about
7 miles. — had a level country with several dams
& pretty ladies houses on the road side — We
passed a run & mill called Brown's mill —
We entered Caswell Ct. a few miles on this
side of Long's - I reached Caswell Ct House a
little further in the evening - The Landlady resembled

"There's a train - let down" -

trees - Propped Mr Williams about 4 miles
on this side of Long's - Did not know it or

Saturday 22d August - set out about
10 o'clock on a third expedition to baltimore
at Alexandria saw Mr. Button & went to
his house intending to stay only a moment
but as they were going to dinner we found
we were detained so long that it was our
delight before we reached Baltimore. The
bridge is incompatible from the effects of the
late weather - The bridge at Cincinnati is
quite destroyed - The stage now travelling
that route has injured Baltimore so much
that the Tanner is now very indifferent and
will probably be totally deserted.
January 23d - Weather pleasant - remained
Ouachita at 2 after nine - Detained by
Johns going after a horse to find grease in
for the wheels. - Hoped at Washington to have
to find the horses - passed again and got to
Indianola being about one mile. The bridge
begins destroyed here we had to go down to
Louis's ferry. The water was so high as to
disturb some horses & a steam vessel on Missouri
State at the ferry, a large tree was
laying over the wall and the water had been
over them half way up a large cornet tree.
The river has not been so high for 20 or 30
years before. - We had a tolerable supper
but no dancing -
Wednesday 24th - Sunday night - Detained by
company refusing to be done with the crowded
ship to Kentucky river line and did not get off
the ship till Tuesday evening - Hoped at Louisville
to find the horses - passed by Mr. Button's
building but found it empty. The different
stores filling place.
Thursday 25th - Weather very cool & pleasant
and before the sun rose to go to our comfortable
lodging - 9 o'clock went to bed at
Williams - Missouri State stopped at
Indianola - Missouri State stopped at
Indianola - Missouri State stopped at
Indianola - Missouri State
stopped at Indianola -
Adams to Shields (state 12 September 1818)
very kind & good & as only stopped here before
we leave - Beyond Jones Run at Centerville
in the neighborhood of which the land resembles
of the country and beautiful. - As the train
a little above bay of five years old building
days to run about the whole of a station building
get to Mr. Wilson's at Cumberland 5 hours
after dark - the roads very fine on travelled
30 miles to Day - Williams is a very good
town - we had a good supper & returned
to our hotel in the evening
Thursday Sept 27 - Weather fine - Roads good
and comfortable - Andersons to enable to breakfast
Williams a small butter house being too near
the last stage - there is a poor place
to pass it.
Friday Sept 28 - Roads good to spring
town & Williams - Myself the road here had
to turn back about a mile - Dinner at Mr.
Williams - a good dinner - there was an
early meeting of the Volunteers to hear their general
there was a camp meeting a few days ago near
here - about two thousand people in camp -
now in better condition than any I have seen
the leaders volunteers have been raised in this country
every where soldiers are mounted and infantry
infantries - arrived after dark at the widow
towns - Roads good - on travelled about 43
miles today.
Saturday Sept 29 - Roads good - Centerville
towns - road rough to Charleston & Towns
the house here was built by Mr. Scott & pretty
good - got some good produce & handsome
grain & potatoes on the way but generally
very poor & poor for anything - the time
very troublesome - have thrown & broken all
time - have tolerable spirits for the time
with the ball game - we did not stop at
Charleston, passed by & go on down to Norfolk
towns after crossing the Hunter river - In a
little town, the carriage breaking - We intended
to go by Bradsville, but heard the road was
dangerous to Norfolk & House, therefore
purposed the latter place, the Charleston it is
a hill in part of some of the road good sometimes
rough - We camped in the river on a high hill
about 2 a mile from the St. James - yesterday
& today many hot - & many people with us
at St. James, while we did not reach the
after dark, the road did not travel as far as
yesterday - but the miles are long & exceedingly
long - many raised from Orange & Prince, to
an agreeable young man - P. I. S. out of town
with him.

Saturday 29 — Though hot — came 9 miles
to Washington where we left — long time for

to sitting room & Dress & to will have
to sit at the 6th House — Roads
rough & impassable — 11000 at Manassas
a decent house to find the Ladies — great
quantities of pumpkins here, but none very fine
they were distilling — poor roads with hardly
rough — Night at Williams as there had to
go on to Danville — 20000 men obliged to

Sunday 30th July — a surprise at Danville
now near there we found last year — the
town burnt down, another night by Wilkinson
the proprietor of the one that was burnt down
rebuilt it — the 6th Inn better now the bridge
& mills — Night at Brandy where the
Ladies — We have to work at almost all the
places to have the order right out — they are
impatient people — Roads rough yet
to Harris' about sunset — We returned
at home & the daughters agreed after much
hurrying I leave to Danville — We eat out
of our own pockets — she had not even milked
& I believe nothing but bread in the house
our father came at last with a young
man who seemed to be her sweetheart — They
set up great part of the night, slept all in one
room while we occupied the other.
Monday 31 — Foggy — We travelled over
impassable roads to-day two miles to Poppy's
place in 2d regiment 60000, corn had made
up with 12000 miles — 2nd Clothes
Routes bad, came by Saunders' Bridge, stopped
at Richmond to ask for leave, as we had
to leave every 10th — We found him somewhat better
state of his Principals & a very active man
to feed on horses — Drive on as fast as the roads
will permit to Adams' late Office at the
best road, expecting to find a quite fresh horse
but the roads were full of horses of all sizes
we only took some milk punch as it was too late to
eat supper — We had a bad nights rest —
Saturday 1st July — Weather very hot — roads
more bad than good — Got to Pickens' sixteen
miles & very long since breakfasted — I went
to a miserable breakfast here — The
road with the expectation of two or three laying
thick very good for 10 miles to the postion
which we crossed just at dusk — 11000 at
Williams — Joseph Letcher & 10000 Benjamin Fine
just returned from Richmond Springs beyond
Morgan town — They are wounded & sick, Americans
with us was a mistake with the determination

Friday 10th very hot. — We set off to go to
Omaha after breakfast — Mr. Steers was so
grieved as to give us a harm to take to the
field road, and I did not buy one in Salish bay.
Stopp'd in town to buy some sugar — and my

about 5 o'clock. — We Staid at Mr. Cansdale.
Saturday 5th very hot — clouds, appearance of
gentleman writing letters — Mr. Nicholson 2000
weight and 6000 waggs 9th and 10th 4 o'clock
in the evening to a young man there is a cannon
Bought a figure from him for Godd, and leave

Sunday 11th set off from Omahd intending to go

to Aberdeen which 30 M. which I went to
Omaha stopped at Mr. Berenger's stable we found it not

guiding thus a road which never before has
been trod in the north west of
Nebraska, at last we found an over which two

were glad, after having a 20th of miles all
day the ultimate purpose to get into almost
any house — We found this house 800 better
order than last year — they gave us food and
supper 8 o'clock — we went to bed about 10 o'clock.
Monday 12th the road from Omahd to
Aberdeen is very bad, we found 5 o'clock in the
morning late 5 o'clock in the evening to go a distance of
40 miles only — this is almost impossible to horses
from the plains lay me to another, and finally
between we go backwards instead of going forwards
sometimes — It is impossible for strangers to find the
roads without a guide with all the direction
that can be given.

January 1842
This year commences authentically at length
the matter -- a beautiful bright day
to all the people are gay & thriving -- the
president stands upon platform -- Many not
able to gain entrance, & those that do in fear
of being crowded to death -- or by losing a limb
Mr. & Mrs. Adams -- Mr. Madison is gone --
the Secretary & many private families received
Company -- & provided ample refreshments --
I hope this will be a prosperous year -- & the
prospect in some respects is a little gloomy, as
it is said we have an empty Treasury to pay with
& it is very uncertain when the Currency will be
regulated -- the President's Board of Exchequer Bill
not being yet acted upon -- & any one can say
it will -- the United States will hazard by both of
Compromise & they will probably return the compliments
& vote his project.

April 25th
On Sunday last died Judge Baldwin
brother to Mr Thompson I went there on Tuesday
and the Wednesday afternoon
the remains with
his wife & her Sister (Mrs Worthill) came to examine that
burial -- & as so many persons came there (Mrs Wilson
Mr. Jones & daughter) besides all expected I thought it

Wednesday June 5th 1844 --
My old friend Mr S. Harrildson, the was struck with
apoplexy this morning about 5 o'clock --
On Thursday night he departed this life -- to the great
respect of relatives & friends & acquaintances & He was
universally & deservedly esteemed by all who had any
interection with him --
Monday 6th -- I yesterday attended the funeral of my
lamented friend Mr Rock Brick Church -- where he
was departed in a shout by the side of her two beloved
Daugther -- in the presence of a respectful & respectable
assemblage of friends & relatives -- Now solemn are
their warnings to those who must soon follow him
to the dark tomb -- & to judgment! -- the
judgment will be judged mercifully for he was charitable
generous hospitable -- a good wife and other & friend --
June 21st Friday -- I have just returned from the
funeral of J. D. Miller only for Walter Jones Miller
only six years old -- He spoke of him much
disturbed at this loss, he was a fine promising boy
was ill upwards of a fortnight -- I suffered much
they have three girls -- I give you for my friends!

August 20th. Theodor Talbot arrived from his
expedition of 15 months, (with the regiment)
to explore through the territory of Oregon &c
They went to California &c and endured many hardships
&c many risks of their lives from Cold hunger
thirst &c Indians -- The has returned in better
health & good spirits -- and notwithstanding all
his pains by land & sea & by water is very much
gratified by his trip --
Tuesday Nov 19 -- I went to the Alabama &c Ford &c
Saturday morning -- I have given up house
keeping &c let the House to Mrs Talbot remain
with her this winter -- what the Spring will
produce -- who knows -- whether I have done
right or wrong I can't tell -- but I am at any
rate relieved from the trouble of providing --
Maria &c Willy I have let go to themselves
I gave them some articles to begin house keeping

is long a subject of discussion thru the Nation
passed -- by a large majority in the House of
Representatives -- &c in the Senate the night
before -- 27th Feb -- It was generally supposed

March 4th -- inauguration of the new president
James Knox Polk -- Unfortunately stormed
all day -- but not withstanding crowded filled
the streets -- throngs of Hotemen flooded
to see the light! -- The procession was
not very imposing -- but the crowd at the Capitol
(it is said) was immense -- There was
two Bally -- one at the Theatre the other at
Carnegie -- the latter 10 1/2 tickets the other 5 1/2 --
Thursday 6th Sent night between 8 & 9 o'clock a fine
take out in the Theatre, which consumed 4 1/2 several
hours wear it -- Fortunately the persons in it, all
escaped without -- 300 armed house in 15th Street was
seized by unarmed spectators -- the Theater was burnt
off was a most awful &c rapid conflagration --

May 17th Theodor Talbot set off this morning to
company Capt Fremont on another
expedition to Oregon &c. &c.
Capt J. went yesterday.
May 28th Wednesday -- another Era of painful
one has commenced -- I have this day
conveyed to D. Miller my House lot for an
annuity of 600 $ -- very 10 p. C in 600 $ --
I have been induced to do this on finding myself
to my regret that I have only a life Estate in it
& the property generally -- on my decease
it would go to the colonization Society -- if my
present earnest desire is to secure some part to
Mr J. & children -- D M expresses care if my
death before two years from date to pay 1000 $ to
me I may direct -- Is it not wonderful
that I have lived so many years -- blind to this
fact -- & that it came out from God's hand by chance
he says he told me so before -- I suppose he did but
I either don't understand or forget it!
It has indeed given me the heartache -- & as per his
to leave this here.
June 8th
General Andrew Jackson died aged 79 years
27th a procession & oration by Mr Bancroft
(Chief Mag) in honor of Gen Jackson --
This day July 4th -- a very cool day & quiet one
principal display in provisions was of
the Union Sunday school children --
there were many small parties in different
places -- I find within the house -- we
did not go out till evening -- taken with I
called to see Mrs Newman who had just
returned from the Daughtry's (Mrs Jackson)
near Tenterfield -- It is the anniversary of
my beloved mother's death when I do not feel
inclined to join in any party or battle
of the sad accidents occurred from the war kits
last year -- Mr Keeney's (carpenter) father
a colored man and died from wounds received --
several other killed --
Mr Talbot & I have separated after living
together about six years -- It has all this
been a most painful trial to me -- and since
I left the House I have been destitute and
not knowing whether I have done right or wrong
& from the pain of quitting for even my old
residence of so many years & home --
I only pray you that if I had done what was
right (what at I was advised to do) I might have
remitted it, & if wrong that I might be forgiven.
On Tuesday over the Sale -- & almost all the articles
were sacrificed -- as I feared they would be --
I stood at Mrs Talbott's & Mullins at the interval
of my quitting the House & coming to Kalerama
my new home -- where I hope & expect to meet
with kindness & a quiet Home -- God grant it! --
I acknowledge that I have regretted quitting with
Mrs T. & Mary (who have been very kind in respecting
me in my preparations) & think sometimes that
I might have made some arrangement more to their
convenience & advantage -- but perhaps all is for the
best -- I will try to think so!
Prayer -- present preparation -- must be
any occupation
Sept 5th 1845
I thought of I told the House to Mr T.
what I might have done, I should not be
satisfied with the offer no longer made -- but I
feel I have done my duty -- for the satisfaction
very comfortless & more varied, still I feel
that they were more convenient to me -- that
our sentiments were more alike -- in that
I feel that I ought to have considered them
as relating -- I must part with them --
This difficult it is to know right from wrong
& to satisfy all our feelings -- to make all
things work together for good!
Sept. I found that I might find it dull here
particularly of winter evenings -- enjoying

Sunday 1.1838 - On returning from church
from Capt. Pennock he has arrived from Norfolk
after an absence of 18 Months - Now Virginia
has now established her - & will only form
one thing - & that is not what will follow
either it that we cannot do our Justice! -
I have ceased to imagine how things would
be fitted to have been placed with Captain
and family removed to the Bay - & I am quite sure
that in part of this Establishment, neither of which
he does not play - & that the death of Gen. Henry
but a step to another kind of quality - this is entirely
between myself and myself - & I hope that life than I
have had latterly - which sometimes found its source
in also an injury to my husband - Yet now it
must be gone.
Wednesday 19th Oct. Ruth J. Benson was married
this Evening to Commander John Spaine by the
Rev. Mr. Smith - Baron Bradt Garrett was the
only stranger & they were invited because they
were living in part of the house - Mr. Spaine has
been here - & is an old acquaintance
The bride looked very pretty & conducted herself very
brilliantly. - Thursday - They went this afternoon
on their way to Portland- Maine - after this I am to
rende.
Friday 21st - Baron Garrett & family (who I fear abandon)
went to the City - having occupied the west end of
the house for six Months - They are very amiable
people - He is the principal minister -
Saturday 22nd Nov. another friend departed - Samuel
Harper Smith - He died early this Evening
after an absence of three Months -
Monday 24th Went to the House & attended the funeral to
Curtis Creek Church - where his family remains
was deposited in a vault - with his Wife & two
daughters. - Rev. Mr. Spaine officiated.
On our return the Stock in which Mr Smith's family
(son, sister & grandchildren & wife & Boy) were owned
by the corporation of the County & they are all
bought - but not seriously.
1846 - June - Another change! I thought I was
probably settled here for life - but
Kalamazoo is sold! - & in left a lot or
part of it - for the City -
Col. & Maj. Beaulieu have occupied the part
of the House where Mr. Garrett once this Summer
Mr. Spaine minister from Belgium - They have one
children & are very agreeable Couple - They go
to the City in Oct.

1846
Sept. 2d - Gun rejoicing & cannon firing in
Alexandria to celebrate the re-occupation of
the County & town to the State of Virginia -
Is that this District of Columbia is all on
the Maryland side of the Potomac.

When I took Mr Miller & family to live with me
I felt that I would be a comfort & necessity to us
& I had no reason to be displeased with them, on
the contrary -- but I found it too much trouble
to provide for them, or rather I thought it difficult
to satisfy a gentleman -- & besides Mr. Miller's family
was increasing -- another reason that operated on my
mind, which I own was pride, was I found that though
all the trouble they took in keeping house for
me, it came directed to me at Mr Miller's, --
I shall never forget Mr. Miller's kindness in many
instances -- I then thought that if only Lady in question
with me I should be better satisfied & preferred to
Mr. J. H. Green & live with me -- & I thought as they
were alone & I alone without relatives here we could
live together very comfortably & without any being
so anxious about my table &c -- but difficulties
arose with the servants -- I then proposed their
keeping house & my living with them for the rent
& they managed our settle -- I except for some little
jealousies on both parts I think we could have done
very well -- but circumstances induced me to
sell my house -- & an farther -- St. Katherine
& Mrs. Tabbert to a house -- near Mr. Larmond --
where they are living very comfortably --

3. Not agreeing & even urging my Husband to go

after his property in Florida -
4. My consenting to the sale of Estate in
Lancaster England - which I deeply regret -
5. My Husband not engaging with Chaucer for
Livingston in Steam Boats which he could have
done at our time -
6. my changing my Farm for a House in George Town
expecting that property would be valued by them
when the Canal was finished - it is not finished yet!

ground to which all persons present have a right to claim
their share.
Never offer the ear of your equal by reproachful
language, let your remarks be seasoned with friendly
admirements.

A certain and never failing cure for an habitual blood-
ing at the Nose.
Make a strong Tea of a very common weed or flower,
called Yarrow—take a wine glass full of it every hour,
the first day and every two hours in the day, so long as
it may be required. Two or three days use
of this remedy has never failed in a single instance to
have the desired effect.—UNIVERSAL.

The following article is worthy the consideration of
persons suffering under the disease of
CONSUMPTION.
Completely to restore the diseased, I will not pos-
sibly deny the following remedy is capable of doing;
but I will venture to affirm, that a temperate mode of
living, (avoiding spirits figures wholly) wearing the
flannel next the skin, and taking every morning a pint
of strong coffee, mixed with a pint of water, and ex-
pressed juice of green mohawm, the complaint will
naturally be relieved, but the individual shall procure in
himself a LEMENT OF DUTY beyond what his form
could possibly expect from it. For myself, it is a
witness of the beneficial effects of this agreeable and
though innocent, yet powerful application. Four weeks
use of the hourglass and mild relieved the pains of my
breast; gave me to breathe deep, long and free;
strengthened and harmonized my voice; and restored
me to a state of better health than I had enjoyed for
many years.
COOPER'S POINT, (N. J.) 20th August.
Respected Friend,
I perceive in the report of deaths in your paper, that
numbers have died of the CHOLERA MORBUS,
and many of my friends the last. Dr. John Redman, did near
fifty years' practice before he took up the profession, and
often succeeded when all others failed. Which was, to
take a little fresh lime juice, loaf sugar and spirits or
brandy (the latter being the third into which he
pointed the cooling water, take it in a glass as hot as
possible, after every spell of puking. He said the acid
of the lime curried the saline on the coat of the stu-
ment and made it pass out of the body, which caused
it to be discharged. However, I have practiced
it since the above time in my family, recommended it
to others, and have not known it to fail in any case. If
it relieves one person, it compensates for my troubles.
JOSEPH COOPER.
