The complaint of a gentleman who had to marry a whole
family.
If polygamy was allowed in this country, I am sure
I might maintain a seraglio of wives at less expense,
than I have brought upon myself by marrying one woman.
But I say, Alas! if I had only kept one
wife, like a polygamist, I would have divided myself
and multiplied herself into as many bodies as she possessed.
I must know I took a woman of small fortune, and
made her my own flesh and blood; but I never thought
that her relations would likewise furnish me with a
668
full ceremony as a colonel of fife. I had scarce
brought her home, before I was obliged to marry her
mother; then I was prevailed upon to marry two of my
sisters; after that I married her aunt, then her cousin.
In short I am now married to a whole line of
of them. I do not understand matters, which I say
I am married to them all for they claim as much right
to every thing that is mine, as the person whom the world
calls my wife. They all live in their own houses,
every one in the same room as their command, except my
bed-chamber; they borrow money of me: and since I
have the whole family quartered upon me, what signification does it there take upon my name—my wife
here since, and there quartered round me?
I never sit down to table without the lamentable prospect of seeing as much victual consumed, as would
distend a horse. I have no money to spare, spending at my expense! And then there is such a variety of
provisions! for cousin Biddy likes one dish, my aunt
Hechel is fond of another; sister Melly cannot abide
this, and mother could not tolerate it, though I know
they are all of them uniform in liking the best of every
thing in season. Bridalts I could entertain a set of
jolly ropers at a less than I could in light of a
foot for the year. One of these drinks nothing but Lisbon— with another nothing goes down but Rhine and
Spain—a third swallows me an ocean of Bristol milk,
with which little remorse I have been drinking
my old friend the King of dry Mountain; while the
other thinks nothing helps digestion as well as Maestria. It was but last week, that my wife expressed a
desire of seeing some of her relatives in Florence, my
gentlemanly relations had a military language for it; but
with much ado I at last prevailed on them to compound
with me for a chest of Florence.
This is the instance that my house cannot be a very
small one, for I assure you there are as many beds in
it, as in a country inn. Yet I have scarce room enough
to turn myself about in it: for one apartment is taken
up with this relation, another by that and the most
distinct cousin must have more respect shown her than
to clip her up in a garter with the maid servants; so
that poor I have no more room in my own house than
a footman. Once, indeed, I was quite exhausted, and
left them off, and took a little box in the neighborhood of
town scarce big enough to hold my own family. But
since that time I have almost always found it difficult
and rather than not to under the same roof with their
relations, they consented to let me with their own
money in a way. At another time, thinking to clear
myself out of the house, I took my wife, my sister,
and mother, and sent them to her people in the country
for a month. But what would I do! there was no getting
her out the left behind, my wife had made up to them
the sum of fifty pounds, which I had given her for
particular employment during her absence. One was so
picky with nuts, another to preserve sweetmeats, another
to make money, and money with which they executed with
the greatest precision the great principles of their
party and waste more than they save, for the satisfaction of
eating things at home. At this my wife returned
to me, and all the rest of them, and the importation
of the new country fresh out of the country, who
never knew before were the least related to her; but
they have been so kind as to claim kindred with me by
blood.
You must know, that upon my marriage I was indis-
cernible enough to set up my character; and since my family
has increased so prodigiously, this has given them a pre-
tence to act like a great and ancient public personages.
This also furnished them with a pretext for running about to public divisions, where I am forced to

The art of dying consists of three operations, viz:
fully to cleanse the substance which is to be dyed, and
to remove all other matters which might spoil it, it
being dyed, and 3, to prepare the bath of color in which it is to
be immersed, and to work it accordingly to the rule of
the art.
TO DYE BLUE.
A vat, with caustic alkali, may be made thus: to
prepare Indigo will suffice, solt 1 1/2 lb. of tart salt,
and 218. of lime, break up the Indigo into 2 pints of water,
boll them two hours, thus put them to a boil 10
galls. of water, to which add 1 1/4 lb. of green vitriol (Cop-
perash) and as much red arsenic. Stir is frequently when
a green froth has arisen; it is ready—
Grind a pound of Indigo in Urine fresh or stale; add
it to about forty Galls. of Urine stir it with a rake till
the green scum rises and the Indigo appears dissolved,
tip the cloth in this till the vat be exhausted—
MRS. GRAHAM'S RECIPE FOR DURABLE DYE.
To dye Scarlet.
One pound of indigo (gathered from the garden)
will dye 2 lbs. of wool, the wool must be washed
clean, then boiled about fifteen minutes in strong alum
water—the madder is to be boiled in thin brant water
(the best being the water strained from the source); the
wool stripped from the alum water and put into alum
water must be boiled fifteen or twenty minutes, and wash-
ed out in soft soap such as it is cool—by leaving out
the alum it dyes a good brown color—
To make a Crimson color.
Two quarts of the juice of pokew berries, when they
are quite ripe, and one gallon of strong cider vinegar
made from the white crab-apples, steeped by day and
water which must be washed very clean with hard soap.
The cloth when wrong dry, is to be put into a copper ves-
sel form an inch thick, tie it out the wool and let it drip a
while in the steam, then put it in the bath. The vessel must be free
from grease of any kind.
To make on Dressage color.
Take a quantity of true mercurial, gathered in the steam,
and bruise it well in a wooden mortar. On layers of iron-
net and wool alternately pour rain water, or soft water
from a spout, so that they are covered, and stand
24 hours—then have another strong leather of cloth, and
wash it out and put it immediately in the sun to dry,
alum or cedar may be used by using hard soap instead of
soft—these colors brightens by washing.

Pokeberry Dye.

three fourths of a pint of pokeberry juice with a pint of
rain water about one quarter of an hour—He then took two
pieces of flannel and wringing them out and 2 hours
later he separated with about quarter of an hour
and rinsed them in cold water ; he then dipped the flan-
nel No. 1, into a pot of juice and when it was quartered
he fixed in the piece suitably to the color of the juice
itself. He then dipped the Flannel No. 2, in the juice
and washing his hands, which he had been washing before,
and time, the color of the color change to a bright veil-
low—He then threw a wine glass full of lime water into
the pot where No. 2 was simmering which turned both
juice and flannel to a bright yellow. Then he had that
Allium fixed the crimson and lime water the yellow color.
Domestic Encyclopedia.
To dye Cotton a deep Purple.
You must first dye the cotton a bright yellow with cop-
perras and lye, boil a strong decoction of maple bark, add
to that a little copperas ; throw in the cotton and boil it
well, then hang it in the sun for a week or ten days
and you please ; until the cotton is dark enough.
When it is thoroughly dried you must wash it in cold
water, and the next day boil it in greasy pot liquor.
One tea cup full of copperas, and one tea cup full dye
two pounds of cotton. The above dye, if a larger por-
tion of copperas is added, will dye a beautiful black.

January 1st 1812 Wednesday.
I was awakened very early in the morning. Found a man
from one of the ships, which arrived last night, speaking
to me for a physician who had him. He continued all day
sleeping & at intervals vomiting, what appears to be pure bile
in the morning he took some calomel & saltp. -- He had a
violent headache during the day.
On Thursday -- Many of our friends called about to inquire
after Dr. S. He was well enough to go down this morning.
He was not so well in the evening -- but went to bed. Joseph
Brandeis called by, upon business -- received a note from
Mr. H. Smith who was to have dinner here yesterday, but on
account of spending that ill declined coming.

Monday 9th. Lt. Bedford came home at dinner time in
great distress having just received intelligence of the death
of his wife in Ohio. Bed.
U.S. writing a letter to Mr. Monroe in case to one from him
refuting the patent office
Tuesday 10th. Sent to Genl. Porter. Took off 7000
3d 7th forwarded 6000 B to one man in the South & 1000
Wednesday 11th. Rain cleared up. -- 6000 B went to the office
U.S. sent his letter by delivery when she went to market. --
We went to the Evening News -- Mr. Butler with us --
Mr. Young was injured this afternoon -- Did not expect she would
be heard till tomorrow
Thursday 12th. A day spent & prayer by proclamation --
8000 B moving -- 100000 B went to bed & stayed. -- called on Mrs.
Delaney & Saffry. -- No particular here in the house.
Friday 13th. Snow -- Young Mr. Kinsey called on U.S. with

15th February - I had a very bad night
being disturbed by some sounds
getting on the chimney, whose sounds
had been continued by
lightning some time ago, & the bricks
falling from the chimney's front.
Two bricks were on the roof at
the time. -- It is a most
exceeding thing where they
could come from --
Had to pray John Saunders
to go to guard the Well -- where he
had a brush of guns to do general duty
which I was to have the half --
Mama very poorly to day. --
17th -- Col. Bancroft brought the adjt. out
thrice for the Well -- said to have no
improvement
to go to Forest and to Mr. Saunders --
Monday 18th -- Mr. H. Smith went down this
afternoon to have him call us
over Friday morning.
Wednesday 19th -- Bought a carriage horse
for 758 --
Tuesday 20th -- William Lambert killed with
21 -- Running dog -- Sale of the horses
prolonged till tomorrow --
22nd -- came in the morning cleared off --
Horses not sold -- Williams now
unbranched -- I am not sure he has
1 sent George to a blind man in
townsman -- sold 2 horses -- but they
returned without them -- I am now
entirely to day -- 11 am for husband --
the horses were purchased --
Mr. Saunders went postillion --
Mr. Torrant brought a christened --
young soldier with 2d. of present -- but said not
what he was to stay with me except --
Thursday 23d -- Illumination last night --
George to go to the canal -- Mr. Duncan
called yesterday afternoon -- brought
me 300 -- I have had some strong
lady of 3d. sisters --
1785
Thursday 25th. To day (by some of his old
Journal) would have been my
dear husband's birth day, tho he
used to think it was the 27th
from his journal. - British black
from this journal. - Sunday will come
be a day of deep feeling - I never
can forget the day he was buried.
Oh my God - support me, I have
never asked one!

Thursday - Last night a great gust
of wind came up and rain, wind, and thunder
lightning - Mr. Smith was
with me - He talked about two
hours from 9 to eleven -
Yesterday George Bradford sat up
for the last minute - I am
so sorry for him - For his own sake
as well as mine -
Mr. Wilkins went to see the Musical

Wednesday 15 - This go - our best

Thursday 26th - Mr. K. Mason
did not bring any - I am sorry for

he went to bed - He was only
talked to Saturday I was not better
as his wife & daughter were at church
the room only 30 of us - I hope - the
daughter was to have been married

so sorry - God be praised - He
has never been in the life of man
or in any man's mind what is to happen
from moment to moment -
how can we say that we will do

never come to us? - Oh how I
feel for poor Mrs. Mason & the family
God be day with you - I am

that it is said the died of

3d July - I walked early this

was very ill - On Sunday
Mr. Mason left from the Engine
at the Church in Gospel tune and
either broke or deteriorated her health
she was carried to her house on a
lorry in a suffering and guilty
state. The situation is very precarious -
Mr. L. Knapshen has left my district.
4th July - Friday - a fine and day
in after Noon - The great event
of establishing first Class Rule Grounds for the Ohio & Chesapeake
Canal is now in operation
The president of the U.S. & the Commissioners of the City, Genl. Mc
Alexander are at the ground near
the Little Falls of Potomac where
the work is in a state of great interest &
progression - as it is the commencement
of a great work in which every
individual is entitled - and when
it is hoped & expected will have many
from time to time during the year of
property & improving settlers from all
quarters - The president is to dig
the first that fall - & in consequence
of that useful employment there
will be no Company room at his
town - Many think he might
have had a Dancing room in the town
I have let the President go to the
town - or where they please & I
am very poorly at home - and the
City is now quiet except for the crackers
in the Bowls -
I feel most deeply this Day!
My poor husband would have been
grateful to see it - but when it is
supposed to happen I hope - in
the Morning of his Life - in the Prison
of his Body
July 29th Tuesday - This day
Mr. R. Miller & Mr. Charles F. King
appeared the present possession left
by my dear husband - I doubt I
could dispossess him of any property
to pay debts - I trust he has given up
his microscope - matches &c &c - I
believe I am to visit Mr. Thompson -
How much pleasure it would have
given me to have made presents
to all these kind gentlemen - but
money must be had - I cannot
tell even though this does not
give any comfort to Mrs. King! -
July 1st Tuesday - Another busy

he would send through Jefferson

steps at Mr. Raymond's Little -

calculates on the receipt from him

Arthur said here is the train — but

Monday 20th. Noon — Meeting for
York City Volunteers will not be held
returned to Genl. Wm. Forrest came
back from Richmond called after Genl.
Tuesday 21st — I went to the City Jail
& found Mr. Foley a clerk in the City Jail
for one week for 2000 — to be paid
to my credit — would be an article of
the King's pleasure to Genl. — after dinner
went to Mr. Jackson.
Wednesday 22d. Dawn — George Brentford
came — the door not within my possession
right to the Governor's hands.
Debate to Mr. Calhoun — Jackson
to the President — Mr. T. Calhoun — 3d. Genl.
Brentford called in the room.
Thursday 23d. very warm. Genl. Brentford
only Mr. Calhoun very ill
We went up to Genl. Brentford's house. Genl.
Brentford told us that he had been a servant to Mr. Jackson.
Friday 24th. Noon last night — Genl. Brentford
called — yesterday's vote (Jackson) — Genl.

Baltimore Aug 5th 1839
My Dear Madam
In the year 1839
you conveyed to Fielder Burck
the house last 9 lots 74, 230, 6, it
was at law your late mistress
now it seems by reason of some
defect in the conveyance that some
legal title to this part of lot remains
to your late husband Dr. Thurston
& the owners of the property desire a
new deed from you as Executrix.
I have examined the matter
particularly & consider no objection to your execution such
a deed which will be granted
to you by Mr. Tester & agent. I
Therefore hesitate not to advise
you to execute the same
Very Truly yours
J H Smith
Mr. A M. Thurston
of Mr. Thurston entitled at all the
expenses of the conveyance
1829
Sept 1st Tuesday I saw Mr. Graham at
Mr's Jones - He had been to the launch of
a steam boat - at Broadway street - The
president arrived from the City Lodge where he
had been for his health at the time - and
there was two ships - I went to the
15th Washington - 8 paid off - there
now I have only one Brick - I did not let out
that is a large draw - called on Mr. Graham
at Mr's Graham & Thompson - returned
to Mr's Jones - Mr. Graham called at 11
o'clock in the morning gave him some wine - I went
to the City Lodge - very warm - Mr. Graham called
gave him the bill of 256.50 - I think - to be
repaided this is the 15th of the month
Mr. Graham with us - I went to Mr. Thompson to
ask him about giving a release from the
prisonity mentioned to him as bad men - I am
only one branch - drank ten at Mr's Thompson -
Thursday 3rd quite cool. The 6th - Mr. Graham
brought me back the bill to receive - I went
to inquire after Mr. Graham who only went as far
as City Lodge - He was too sick to distinguished to go to
Boston - Washington came with words to go -
took Mr. Graham with us to City Lodge - only
from Washington came at home - Eat some fruit &
returned early - Washington myself called - I
have given him the wrong note -

Wednesday Jan 16th - Good Rain - almost all day
Bad day prevailing by night - Snowy
Thursday 17th Fine day - I walked to Mr. Benjamin
's Benchings - Mr. Smith was called - Mr. Smith
's name came - had a search - waiting for Mr.
Smith was attending the sale of Mr. Dibbs' estate -
Mr. Dibbs came at from the East Town
at 10 o'clock - he died here - I do not quite - do
witness a letter to Mr. Collyman - I find one from Collyman
about Kasten - quite disagreeable between the people.
Mr. Dibbs came to him - quite a breathing day -
sent a note to Mr. Struthers about 2 o'clock
Friday 18th Fine day - Rachel came over and told
that Mr. Dibbs Smith had all gone by Thursday to Louisville
to purchase some land myself saying that Collyman was ill -
Dr. Smith went to Louisville - Collyman died that night
Wednesday after dinner with me over to bed at Mr. Collyman's
funeral - Mark returned brought word that
Collyman's body had died at 4 o'clock this morning -
Col. Smith is in Louisville Indiana - Martin has disposed
of Collyman's estate with him - from 10 o'clock - this
is indeed a bad hard trial -
Saturday 19th Fine day - Genl. Cattinngs & M. Thomson
called - Mr. Thomson at the sale
I wrote to Mr Smith that we could not spend the day
with the Townsman on Saturday Mr. Smith would come home
if I did not wish to be absent - Went to Col. Dibbs
's house and my letter to Mr. Collyman - returned to meet Mr.
Smith at his office at Liberty - Read - Townsman
Saturday 20th Fine day - walked to Liberty - Martin
went out of Town - I opposed the Board not wishing to go
on to Collyman's estate if Mr. Collyman's family - Mr. Smith
was glad to go home with me - Mr. Collyman called - he
went home with me at 7 o'clock - They are not coming for a week

Thursday 20thandy— Rain last night— Got on the
flourins— Got came with potatoes— Sunday 21st—
Miss Potter Gardiens called— Col. 12 came to my house
and said not take up his note & I wrote to the Bank
and he ported it— George 8 Arthur giving me orders
with biggin from to Mr. Hunter & sent off—
Wednesday 22nd 1838— George coming Arkansas &
Mr. Baker called & told me— Mama not well
Wednesday 23rd Sunday 24th— Col. 12 called & said
George then Mr. Hunter planted & Mr. Baker on Kentucky—
Order to the Barrackers to give James to Capt. Brown
Friday 25th Sunday 26th— Mr. Dickson & daughter called
to Solomon 12— Mr. Baker called about horses—
Col. 12 called, had seen Judge Chase about money in a
letter appointment— Mr. Forrest came over
to see to him about the appearance— He thinks it may
convenient to be so very stout in my case—
Did not go out— Mrs Jones asked me to go out here
to your house—
Saturday 27th Sunday 28th— Mama had a fall on the back
part of her back but she is here— I went to the bank to
see her— Mr. Jackson called. I had to go to the Interimion to
the Mexican soldiers— After dinner Mama had a
fall— I had ordered the carriage before 10 o’ clock to
the door. I went to Mr. Graham to get the horse & got
of Capt. David Wells Traders in Missouri—
Sunday 29th Sunday 30th— Mama very poorly— I came over
without help— I leave from 12 o’ clock— Mr. Brown— Smiths
Mr. Jones & Baker— W.B. Vanderbilt— Lady of company
not called—
Monday 26th Monday 27th— Rain last night— Col. 12
called— We leave town— came in Friday last—
Col. 12 called after dinner on his way to the Bank & left
me in the house— called in the afternoon— Rain—

Monday 30th July — Mr. Potter called the Lords
very lively — Judge Washington died in Philadelphia —
a few days ago — George Kirk the bearer to Mr.
Washington brought it — against this day of Lightning
Thunder Ram & Sword
Sunday April 2d June 1812 — Maj. Anderson came to
Washington to the Congress for the bearer — which he returned
from after with the money for Ram — Sword & Sword
they are for Mr. Potter (the bearer) from bearer
Washington — returned 8 days after — I am
wanting to pay him — & expect that Mr Washington
will send in the said bearer
Wednesday April 2d June 1812 — The Ambulance to Norfolk
came before me with the Ambulance to Norfolk
to stand at breakfast — I must to Mr. Potter to answer
your part — He intends time pay Mr Potter died soon
after he left Philadelphia — in the way down
which I bought wood from the carrier — the last bearer —
Sam Smith — & I believe he is gone — Mr. Potter called
came in an opinion for the bearer of the Congress
for Washington to take the boat yesterday & 2d — he left the bearer
& returned — & he went in the Ambulance — from Mr Potter to the
Carriage — & returned to the carrier
Thursday 5th — Board — Washington came to the Congress
to take the bearer to Philadelphia to answer the
case amounted to upwards of 20000 — I am very
pleased — & I am very much obliged to you for your
opinion — & I am very much obliged to Mr Potter for his
opinion — & I am very much obliged to the bearer of the Congress
for Washington to take the boat yesterday & 2d — he left the bearer
& returned — & he went in the Ambulance — from Mr Potter to the
carriage — & returned to the bearer

1830
Friday 1st Jan. a Beautiful Day
clean'd & a little cold -- Mr Smith &
Mr Cleston called -- & Mr Harman and his
children -- Mr Torrey this my last tea with him.
Saturday 2d fine day -- There was as usual
a great crowd at the president's yesterday --
We passed the Penilla & a medal I gave
her to Genl Washington -- I said a gentleman
would give ten dollars for me -- I gave her
an offer to day -- McBrady got the first --
Manass I rode out -- took Mr Smith with us --
Mr Torrey -- the murder as to him -- I declined --
I walked to Mr Smith -- Julia Harthe Smith --
Mr Sanford called -- She is not well -- Did not
stay long -- Mr Jones here -- Reading the
Museum -- Mr & the Mrs Jones went back
early -- to Mr Talbott's party --
Sunday 3d fine day -- Walked to Mr Smith's to
church -- Bishop Chase preached -- Mr Jones
up to Mr Sanford -- to show him a junior about her
brother in the Telegraph -- Mr had been here --
We went in at Mr Tompkins -- The brother
is absent -- came up to Mr Tompkins --
Monday 4th Col -- Mr Sanford went with
me to visit Mr Peltz & Adams -- afterwards called
at Mr Smith's & Col Peltz -- Mr Smith father
called in the evening -- Read Mr Garret's opinion
Sunday 5th Winter's end -- Walked to Mr Smith's --
after dinner rode on the avenue & to Mr Smith's
not at home -- returned the car did think of
going to Mr Thompson -- Read a letter from Mr
Bransfield & Mr Kennedy -- Now different it
is to get business finished! --
Wednesday 6th Col -- Wrote to Mr Solomon, Transferred
Whitneyoff Allen & then Clark -- Mr Smith called
to me of 2 and finds 15 book relative to the post office
found all day but I do not lay -- closed in the
evening -- Mr King called -- he has just returned from
Baltic -- Since he went to Grand Christmas with Mr Smith's
family -- Thursday 7th fine day -- Mr WhitneyBrown came -- smiles
at the King to dinner -- Mr Smith came & informed us there to be
ridiculous on the American book trip -- I have & must & I
pland -- I want -- or rather want to be so --
Friday 8th fine day -- Mr Davis -- Smith's King called
I was planting flowers for Mr Smith's bishop of
one while there is becoming a successful work in the
city from the Church -- Rose after dinner -- Col Peltz
& Thompson -- they said they were dying for the Ball
the 9th -- Brooks of N. Orleans -- Read his papers
to Col Peltz -- I went over to Mr Smith's --

the train by Elizabeth
Town where we wished to go
but by I. Albany - thence
in a Steamboat to N.York
when after a pleasant sail
in a fine Boat we arrived
about 2 after Eleven
Mr B. went out of trains
a little & I stood in
Boris here hospitality &
went to Elizabeth town
fast in a Steam ferry boat
then in car & thus walked
The King of an Island
very pretty country round with
a river of Spaldingth. Parked
they go by the turn in a few minutes
to a bridge if you find them
also in one place called
Bellamont at a distance a view
of a light house at Newcastle
which is fort independence &c
a distant view of a mountain
called Argyll mountains
the country to the North East
some thing like the region of hills
on which Hard, Maiden hill
&c. -- It is a pleasant summer
residence & convenient agreeable
to their climate and to their country

& the water like a looking glass
& looking the houses & hills very
distinctly -- went six before we
returned -- Saw the Carriageway
on the bridge, leading to portland
while on laid on one bay on the

a crowd at the Depot & they said
a poor man had been run over &
Mr. Pennant I went to call on
Mr. Tavern -- The officer informed
he could not make a glass of Irish punch
for Ruth.
Sunday went to Church --
Mr. Lambert preached a good
sermon at 11 am on occasion of the
death of Mr. Pennant's brother at
Cape May in bringing it to his sister
who was removed by a boat from
her home -- Mr. Tavern & Delaney went
with me to Bishop's -- to Mr. Bushing
at the family house with some
good pictures, at supper on

was there -- on with the mail
bills to do the four pounds of
different objects -- a very pleasant
row home & back --

Ye firing elements combine,
Spume your most terrific forms,
Afflail the firmest hearts, yet mine,

Can mock your rage ye tempests blow!
Rise threatening, rise, ye whirling waves,
In liquid mountains dark and deep,

To furious flames indeed, my heart,

Lines by Robert Southey
The days of infancy are all a dream,
Those fair, but oh! how short they seem
For Life's sweet opening spring;
The days of youth and man
The morning sun to the distant plains
The bidding clouds they bring,
It is Life's burning Summer time.
Many hard, maligned in it, without fault
Reasons of learning, respect, parentage
Succeed, as Autumn follows Summer's prime
And thus is that calm year by
And what remains the languid bye
The failing flame, the soul direct,
The Winter's gathering, withering blast
Lives its final season—for it is the last.—

The Mother's Farewell to her widow'd Daughter.
Go, dearest one, my selfish love
Shall never part the cheek
Not even mother's feet for thee
While I on widow's speech
With human's on child'sness check
The humming tears that start
That then not turn from me to deth
Within another heart!
I think on earlier brighter days
When first my lips were first
Upon thy babe's brow, whilst thou
Lay helpless in my breast;
In fancy still I see those eyes
Upheld in one fire
I hear thy lapping tones I mark
With thy tiny childish grace.
Even then I knew it would be thus,
I thought then in that hour
Another world its perfume steal
When I had passed the grave,
And yet I will not breathe a sigh
Now can I dare refuse
The scream that thy mother feels
Was suffered once by mine
A Mother's love! oh! then knowest not
How much of feeling lies
In those sweet words, the hopes of years
The daily strengthening ties
It loves to see yet the infant drawns
Its earliest vital breath
And dies but when the mother's heart
Chills in the grasp of Death.
Will he in whose fond arms thy sick
Prune all of earthly things,
Be feel a love returning, deep,
And free from self as this!
Am no husband's tenderness
My gentle heart may prove?
But never, never with them meet
Again a mother's love!
My love for thee must ever be
Find as in years gone by
While to thy heart I shall be like
A dream of memory.
Dearest farewell, many angel hosts
Thy visits on the keep,
Now can I speak that painful word
Farewell, I yet not weep!

June 19 Mrs. Doria called sweet to church
long gone young all day I did not
go out of the house at the risk of
being at the risk of my life
Mon 26 Trouble every where. Times awful
up to this time I am not part of the money
more here is coming -- Brooks from
June 18th -- Mr. Bryan in the house
June 19th
Tues 21 Mary Elizabeth called -- to Maria
chair died not long after all the things
her children had to offer to her come
Wednesday 22 -- Sister to Mary
18th June 22 -- Sister to Mary
belonging to Mrs. Smith --
July 12th -- I am going to Mrs. Smith's
Cap. J. Mc. Tubman here --
Thurs 23 I expect Mrs. Smith to go with me
to Mrs. Smith's -- went there to
see my children -- went there to
see my brother -- stand all day -- I think I
have had to get on a charge for if
Mr. Smith comes home with his first think
24 I hope gone to bed -- I think I
look like sleeping -- Dr. Miller writes
for bringing package from Alex --
Reliable -- Mrs. Smith and Bestman
visited -- walked on the Sabbath in
the house --
Sat 28 I told Elizabeth the funeral to go from
prison to her home -- I was exceedingly
angry by Judah in taking down
the flag -- I am going to Mrs. Smith's
to see her -- I am going to the country --

Mr Hon. H. Drummond
Chargé d'Affaires
Imperial Jnt. Embassy
My dear Mr Drummond:
I have just received the beautiful
card which His Majesty the Cumber has to
graciously entertained upon me and I beg you
to express to His Majesty my most grateful
thanks for this great favour. That His Majesty
should have included me among the recipients
of honors bestowed upon the officials of
the Bedford and Durham in connection
with the proceedings of July 4, 1918 will
always be a source of delectation to me.
I fully realize that my heart in the most
interesting event was relatively a minor
one, but I am sure that words fail
me to express the deep pleasure it gives
25
my husband and myself to be privileged to
entertain your Ambassador Viscount Selim
and Lieutenant Selim and their suite at
our home in 1911 and to see the love of our
commercial allies and the people of our
vicinity the opportunity of meeting this
distinguished representative of one of the
great Powers of the world.
The souvenir which Viscount Selim,
in the name of the son of Munjira Nasabanna,
presented to the room of Fairhaven, is now
shornific in the Public library and our
people regard it as one of their most cherished
possessions, and, as well, as a token of
mutual respect, love, and esteem between
the respective countries which can never
be broken and which trust will last
ever to mankind.
With again my most grateful thanks,
believe me,
Very sincerely yours
Hughelbert Prince Hamilton

Received from Washington the letter written to me
by sir Cecil Churchill Rice, the British ambassador
at Washington, dated Dec 5, 1915, -- 7 months after
the Lusitania was sunk. In it he defends the
U.S. for not entering the war.
This letter is most important historically --
it shows that the real sentiment of the English
people was not against the U.S for not
entering the war.
copy of letter:-
Personal. British Embassy, Washington
5 Dec. 1915
My dear Sir Judkin:-
I am very grateful for your letter. My
webb and I enjoyed our evening amicably,
gratifying ourselves to your great kindness and
sympathy, of which we are all the more
convinced at it is not in words.
I am glad your disappointed guest had
a chance of seeing you. He enjoyed it
81
greatly.
I hear Sydney Brooke and some others are saying
things about English sentiment towards America
when a Nation is at war I have noticed it is
always at odds with all the Nations with
which it is not at war. I suppose this is
one of the effects of the state of mind.
This was the feeling in France in 1877 towards
England, although England sympathized
entirely with France. It is a common rule,
and I suppose will turn true to the
end of time.
However, the evident fact remains that the
Allies have received sympathy, arms, money
and charity from this country, and this was
all any foreign power could expect. If
they express disappointment at America
not joining the war, it is an evident evidence
of a desire for something which is solely
in the consciousness of the American people
to decide, and in the case of France the
English people had the same decision
to make, and decided in peace.
I do not believe that any sensible person in
England thought or even wished that the
82
United States should go to war. But some
sentimental people had expected it and
brief disappointment, made a row. I do not
think there are many such.
I think Harney is coming again and we
must have another meeting.
Very sincerely,
Cecil King. Rice.

My dear Catherine:
Christmas Eve.
The sun has set but I can not let it
rise again before trying to tell you how deeply your
gift has touched me. Returning from a brief walk
this afternoon we found it awaiting us,
delivered through the courtesy of Mr. Amory
I embrace my hands briefly, humbled as I
looked thru water glasses, but when I read
the beautiful message, I can only say
that the tears rose to my cheeks and gathered
to my eyes as I thought of the "deep that
cut me more".
And as I said I felt that dear Annie
was hovering over me with a smile of
pleasure in her face.
She was, as you know, the idol of our
101
little, and what would we get and neither one of us
utter despair in the deep feeling and conviction
that she has not really left us, but that we
merely lack some cause or source of seeing her,
and that she is constantly by our side.
Here are the feelings the message brings
to me. It is well done and we shall always
look upon it as one of our most beautiful
homilies.
As to your second thought of me, I can only
say it has deeply touched me and that
you hold us in a bond of sympathy and
obligation which time can never break.
With our heartfelt wish that the new year
may bring you every happiness, and with
much love to you and yours, believe me,
affectionately yours,
Charles S. Hamlin

market operation, deliberately designed to put up prices. He
explained Dr. Miller's proposition that the most his bank could do

has been the policy of his Directors, thus making credit easier,

stock market was caused by prior Federal reserve policy; that a
state of mental depression has set in which exaggerates the real

December 20, Saturday. Preliminary Conference with Open Market Committee.
Present: Governor Harrison, Governor Rancher, Governor Young,
Deputy Governor Burgess, and Deputy Governor McKay of Chicago. Ogden Mills
also was present.
Governor Harrison went over again, as yesterday, the history of the
collapse of the merger of the four New York banks and the closing of the
Bank of the United States. He said that arrangements were practically
completed to raise 30 million dollars, or guarantee that amount for the
Bank of the United States, but that everthing hinged on the admission into
the clearing system of the Manufacturers' Trust Company and the Peoples'
Trust Company; that the Admission Committee of the Clearing House refused
to admit the Manufacturers Trust Company; that they placed a value on the
Company far below its real value; that the Manufacturers' Trust Company
and the Peoples Trust were now in good condition, and he did not worry
about them unless some new withdrawals should occur, which he did not
anticipate. He said that the reports of the New York state examiner as
to the Bank of the United States gave no reason to suspect its solvency,
although the Federal Reserve Bank did not like the management, and had done
its best to secure a new management by merging it with the other three banks.
Governor Harrison then took up his trip abroad. He said the central
banks wanted to come over, but he consulted with Governor Meyer, Mr. Mills,
and Mr. Cotton of the State Department, and they all felt that it would
be better for him to go there. (Governor Meyer never reported this to the
Board.) He said that France had done all it could to popularize foreign
investments, and had reduced the taxation on foreign bonds until it was
the same as domestic bonds; that this change had been so recent that it
had not had a fair trial.
Governor Harrison said he told the Bank of France that the Federal
Reserve Bank of New York would do all it could to arrange for the exportation
of long-time capital, but that the Bank of France must also do its share;
that he had a very satisfactory interview with Tardieu, and told him that
future participation of the United States in furnishing foreign capital,
depended on the attitude of France. Tardieu agreed, and said that France
would do all it could; that it would like to make a loan to Italy, but the
French people would only subscribe to loans for countries with whom they
were in sympathy, and that these were second class loans. He pointed out
the difficulty of getting political Governments to meet economic crises.
Governor Harrison said the English dole was once the question of
insurance, but had now become a pure gift; that England was almost destroyed
by taxation; that its difficulties were greater than any other country.
2.
Referring to France, Governor Harrison said there was now an
economic crisis there which began only a few weeks ago; that the importation
of gold into France was accompanied by an equivalent increase of currency,
and that much currency was being hoarded; that some claimed that this
increased currency was caused by increased prices, but there was some doubt
as to this; that the only way for a Frenchman to get Bank of France notes
was to present gold; that prices were now advancing very rapidly; that
wholesale prices also increased until about six weeks ago; that the stabilization
of the franc necessitated an increase of prices which were then below
the gold equivalents of other countries; that retail prices reached their
peak about January, 1929, and then fell through April 1930, but that from
April, 1930, there had been a steady increase of prices, which caused an
economic crisis, and that luxury business is practically suspended; that
one dressmaker offered a friend of his one of the best dresses in her
establishment for an equivalent in France of $40, she was so eager to sell
at any cost!
Governor Harrison said there was really no fear in France of war with
Italy; that no one thought of Italy, but everyone feared Germany; that
Mussolini's speeches were purely for home consumption; that a friend of
Mussolini's told him that Mussolini remembered Harrison's statement last

Parenthetically Governor Harrison told Governor Young that the offer
of the clearing house banks to loan up to 50% of the deposits of the Bank
of the United States cleared the situation very much, but the rate charged —
5% — somewhat dampened the enthusiasm.
Governor Harrison then spoke of Germany. He said that the people
generally believed that the Young plan was the cause of their depression;
that unemployment was increasing very rapidly, and that a socialistic
movement was threatened which might imperil the capitalistic system; that
the party in Germany led by Hugner was not organised, and that he had no
real plan, but that he was supported by the intellectualists and by those
living on fixed incomes.
Governor Harrison said that in Berlin he dined with Luther and 7 or 8
other prominent men; that they were determined to go to the limit along
the lines of the Young plan; that they did not doubt German's capacity to
pay, but the difficulty was in transferring the payments; that there was danger that Germany might be forced by public clamor to ask for a moratorium which, however, they knew would not be needed for two years or so in any event; that Germany did not need new long-time money, but wished to fund her short-time obligations which may be called at any moment; that the last loan had been very helpful, and capital was slowly returning to Germany; that Brusning did a good job.
Governor Harrison also said that what Germany really wanted was cooperation with the United States in financing countries of Eastern Europe such as Romania, and even South America; that the Germans were angry with France for withdrawing money from Germany, but Governor Harrison pointed out that these withdrawals relatively were so small that they could not explain Germany's loss of capital; that the real trouble was the export of German capital because of fear of Hyner and his policies; that Germany has 6 billion marks in short term currency, or a net of about 5 billions; that the income from Germany's agriculture far exceeded that of industry, but that agricultural mortgages ran up to 8 or 9%, and that agricultural income had very seriously declined.
He said that Mussolini said that Germany was in direct contact with Russia.
Governor Harrison said the object of the central Bank conferences was to discuss world difficulties; that while the Bank of France was glad to help England, yet the Bank of France and the Bank of England had not yet got completely together; that to obtain money from France England would have to issue bonds payable in France, which she was not willing to do.
Governor Harrison said that the Bank of England had been very stupid; that she had plenty of gold more than a year ago, but the coin was of greater fineness than that of other countries; that she paid out coin which France would not accept, but insisted on bars; that this caused a backing up in the Mints, which made great delay.

Governor Harrison opened the Conference in the morning, by
stating the seriousness of present conditions. He said that the
deflation in two years was 6 billions in credit, and also 6 billions
in loans "for others." He said that prices were still falling, and
that banks were afraid to loan from their desire to remain liquid.
He stated that he had had a conference with Senator Glass,
suggesting an amendment to the Act, so as to provide that Federal
reserve notes may be issued against any collateral which Federal
reserve banks are authorized to acquire, - meaning specifically
Government securities. He said that the free gold was now down to
between 400 and 500 millions, although the excess reserves were
over a billion, and that the necessity of using these excess reserves
in place of commercial paper as collateral for Federal reserve notes
was becoming a menace to the System.
He said that if the Reconstruction Finance Act should be passed
quickly, and an amendment as to Federal reserve notes such as the
above, he thought there would be a very fair chance that the tide
could be turned. He said that, in his opinion, it might be necessary
to buy a further large amount of Government securities, - not, however,
just at this present time, but possibly in the near future. He said
there were two views which could be held:
1. The Federal reserve banks to take a bold course, and
try to prevent further withdrawals of deposits
by the purchase of Government securities, and
the use of the new Act and amendment above
suggested.
2. That the Federal reserve banks should maintain
themselves in a liquid condition in order to be
able to meet the withdrawals of deposits,
assuming that they are to go on indefinitely at
the present rate, - that is, 25% per year.
He said that, in his opinion, the bold course to
take.
He also spoke of the bond pool formed in New York which bought
in January enough to keep prices stable. He added that if the above
provisions were enacted into law, the pool would undoubtedly buy enough
to put up prices, - perhaps even to par.
2. Governor McDougall suggested that, in his opinion, we should
gradually dispose of Government securities bought within the last
two months; that we had bought now more than any one dreamed would
be bought during the last two years; that he thought it was the
duty of the Federal reserve banks to be liquid, in order to meet
the steady withdrawal of deposits from member banks.
Governor Seay agreed with Governor McDougall, assuming the
Federal Reserve Act to remain as it is.
Governor Harrison said that he contemplated only the purchase
of Government securities in large amounts if such should be deemed
necessary following the correction of the railroad wage situation
and the passage of the Act and amendment above suggested, but that
he was fearful an emergency might arise within two or three weeks
requiring such purchases.
The Conference unanimously passed a resolution that in order
to expedite the operation of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation,
the assistance of the operating facilities and services of the
Federal reserve banks should be available to the Corporation, on
the understanding that the Corporation should reimburse the Federal
reserve banks for these services in such manner as may be agreed upon.
In the afternoon, Ogden Mills came before the Conference,
explaining Treasury policy. He stated that President Hoover has
informed Congress that about 2 billions of bonds or securities may
be necessary to meet the deficit for the fiscal year ending June 30,
1932; that after that date, the administration will make no further
issue of bonds, but will rely on taxation to balance the budget.
C.S.H. asked him if such a statement as to future policy was
essential to the Treasury plan, and Mr. Mills stated that it was.
Mr. Mills further asked the Board to establish a lower rate on paper
secured by Government securities, in order to assist in placing them,
stating that the emergency was as great as during the war, and that
the Federal Reserve should cooperate.
No action was taken by the Board.

Senator Glass telephoned to C.S.H.
He said he wished to know if there was any doubt about the power of
the Federal reserve bank to refuse discounts; that a very prominent banker
had told him that neither the Board nor banks had such power, but he felt
that the word "may" in Section 13 unquestionably gave the power.
C.S.H. told him that he, personally, and also Dr. Miller, construed
the word "may" to give discretion to the Federal reserve bank to refuse
discounts where the privilege had been abused, but while he remembered no
formal ruling of the Board to this effect, he was very sure that there was
no question about this; that Mr. Wyatt, the General Counsel, and Newton D.
Baker, had so advised the Board.
C.S.H. said that this power has, from time to time, been denied, and
Senator Glass asked, "By whom?" C.S.H. said that Mr. McFarrah, by letter
of May 1, 1929, speaking for the directors of the Federal Reserve Bank of
New York, denied the power of the bank, or the Board, even to examine into
customers security loans, or to refuse discounts because of the undue
increase of such loans, even though the bank might be borrowing frequently
or continuously.
Senator Glass asked if any Federal reserve bank had ever refused
discounts for this reason.
C.S.H. replied that he thought the Federal Reserve Bank of New York had
threatened banks which were out of line, -- that is borrowing more than the
average bank of their size in the community, or were borrowing for profit, --
that they must cease under penalty of refusal, but that if all banks were
expanding at the same time, C.S.H. understands that the New York Bank
would not undertake to stop this expansion except through increases in the
discount rate; that the New York Bank even disagreed with the Board as to
the public warning which it gave, stating that it was not the proper way
to meet the situation, which should be met by increases in discount rates.
Senator Glass then asked whether the Federal reserve bank has power
to fix the rate on 15-day member bank collateral notes, without the
final approval of the Board, and C.S.H. said No. C.S.H. again emphasized
the necessity of Section 3 of the Glass bill, but suggested that where the
absolute prohibition is set down in Section 3, it might be well to add a
qualifying clause "except as provided in this mandatory Act."
C.S.H. said he understood clearly that the Committee intended to permit
a reasonable amount of speculative loans, and, in fact, Section 8 of the
Glass bill made it the duty of the Board to fix the percentage of these loans,

July 12, Saturday
About noon, I called up Senator Glass, and during our talk incidentally
I referred to the provision in the relief bill giving the Reconstruction
Finance Corporation the right to make loans direct to individuals, etc. without
the intervention of any bank. I told Glass that I agreed with President
Hoover that this was most objectionable and should be defeated. I then said
to Glass, that if Garner had suggested as a substitute giving such power to
the Federal Reserve System, I should be inclined to say that I personally
would favor it, as practically every central bank in the world had this
power, and I knew it was largely exercised by the Bank of France. Glass
did not seem to be much taken with this suggestion, and the conversation was
terminated.
About 12:30, Glass called up again, and said he had been thinking over
our talk, and asked me personally to draw for his confidential information
an amendment giving such power to the Federal Reserve System. I told him,
of course, that I would be glad to do this, but pointed out that it was
purely personal to myself and to him, as I had never discussed this in any
way with the Board.
I then told Dr. Miller about this. While he did not express any
opinion on the merits of the proposition, he told me there was no reason in
the world why I should not comply with Senator Glass' request, on the understanding
that it was personal and confidential and had nothing to do with
the Board.
July 11, Monday
Senator Glass introduced the above amendment to the emergency relief
bill - H.R. 9642.
July 12, Tuesday
Governor Meyer told the Board about this amendment introduced by
Senator Glass. I then explained to the Board my connection with the matter.
Governor Meyer was quite severe in his criticism of my having suggested this
amendment without consultation with the Board. I replied at once that I
had suggested nothing; that the amendment grew out of a personal talk between
Senator Glass and myself over the telephone, in which I suggested that I
agreed with President Hoover in his opposition to giving such power to the
Reconstruction Finance Corporation, and then I added, somewhat jocosely,
that if Mr. Garner had had the sense to suggest that this power be given
to the Federal Reserve System, I thought I should be inclined to approve
it, as I knew that practically every central bank in the world had this
power. I told the Board that Senator Glass did not seem to take any
interest in this matter, but that 15 minutes later he called me up and
said that he would like to have me draw an amendment along these lines.
I told him that I of course would do this with pleasure, on the understanding that it was purely personal and confidential between him and
myself, and had nothing to do with the Federal Reserve Board, which had
never considered the matter.
I told the Board that personally I approved this amendment, as I
believed there were many people in the United States with ample collateral
who could not obtain loans from member banks, and I stated a conversation
I had with Mr. DuBois, who told me that Henry W. Robinson of Los Angeles
told him that in his district there were many such cases.
Governor Mayer then said that evidently this amendment was put in
by Glass on the strength of Mr. DuBois's statement. I said that I had
never mentioned this statement to Glass; that I had just stated it in
reply to a statement just made by Mr. Jones that everyone entitled to
credit in the United States could easily procure it, -- which I could not
accept.
I also told the Board that I had sent Senator Glass a list of
central banks having this power, which I obtained from Mr. Miller, but
that as sent it merely gave the name of the finance journal from which it
was taken.
A long discussion followed on to the merits, and Jones was bitterly
opposed, and the Committee also, although not quite so positive about
the matter. Miller said that in normal times he could see much that might
be said for this amendment, in that it might make our Federal reserve
policy more effective, but he feared that at the present time it might
cause a rush on the Federal reserve banks.
Governor Mayer finally became a little less positive as to his
objections to the amendment on the merits, but finally said that his
principal objection was that such an important matter should not be sprung
at the last moment without any opportunity for hearing or decision.
Governor Mayer then asked the opinion of the Board as to its merits and
as to the expediency of having it enacted at the present time. C.S.R. voted
Yes, Dr. Miller, Jones and the Committee voted No. I think Governor Mayer
did not vote, but if he did it was without doubt in the negative.
The question arose as to what course to take to indicate the feeling
of the Board toward this amendment. All agreed that it was too late to
write anything, and that whatever was to be done must be done over the
telephones. Finally Governor Mayer asked Miller to telephone President Hoover
and express the views of the Board as above indicated. The Board then
adjourned.
At 1200 p.m. Dr. Miller came to my office, and said that he had
talked with the President who seemed very tired, and told him that the
Board should communicate with Glass. This was all Dr. Miller said as
to his conversation. He then repeated to me what he had said in the
morning -- that in normal times this night be a wise move, but he feared
at the present time it was not opportune, and he suggested to me that I
call up Glass and tell him how the Board felt about it. I asked him to
remain, and called up Senator Glass, and finally got him over the
telephone. I told him that the Board felt very much disturbed over the
amendment, and some of them criticized me for having suggested or drum
it, but that I had explained to the Board that the matter was a purely
personal one between him (Glass) and me, and that I had not suggested
it in any way or shape.
Glass replied that that was absolutely correct; that he assumed
all responsibility for the amendment, and that he thoroughly believed
in it. I then said to him that I wanted to express in Dr. Miller's
presence the fact that I had never, directly or indirectly, suggested
this amendment, or any amendment, to him, and he repeated what I had
stated above. I repeated the same to Dr. Miller. I then reminded
Dr. Miller that on Saturday noon he told me there was no possible reason
why I should not comply with Glass' request. He said this was absolutely
so, and that he believed that any member had a right to have a confidential
talk on any subject with a member of Congress, especially with Mr. Glass,
and he said that it was unfortunate that this particular talk had resulted
as it had. He then talked with Glass of some length over the telephone,
which conversation I could not hear, but evidently Glass had made up his
mind that this amendment was wise, and that he should press it. Miller
made the suggestion to him that these lessons would be dollar for dollar,
while a loan to a member bank would require only the lawful reserve to
be deposited by the bank. Apparently Glass had said that he thought
this amendment would do more good than pouring millions of money into
the market by buying Government securities.
Considerable discussion was had, and Miller said he would be glad
to talk with him about it later, but that he evidently had made up his
mind.
I then talked again with Glass over the telephone, and he told me
that the Senate Committee had unanimously endorsed this amendment; that
he believed in it, and that he should do his best to secure its passage.
As to Governor Meyer's statement that I should have consulted with

July 14, 1932.
The Governors met with the Board in an open market conference
this morning. Governor Mayor gave a resume of the situation, saying
that the open market policy had been effective, and expressing the
opinion that it would be very ill-advised and dangerous to stop it;
that we ought to go on, as the operations from now on would have
much more force than they could before, because of gold experts. Governor
Harrison then addressed the meeting, showing the good effect of open
market operations up to the present date, and expressing the firm
belief that we should continue keeping the excess reserve at about
200 million dollars.
Governor Halseygal expressed the opinion that we should stop
buying, and C.S.R. pointed out to him that he originally voted for the
major operation, -- 200 millions on April 12th -- and asked him whether
he did not believe it would be dangerous to stop completely now. He
said he could see that there might be some danger from it.
Governor Calhoun thought it was not necessary to keep up the
amount to 260 millions excess reserves, but that it would be all right
to go on keeping the reserves at about their present status -- a little
over 200 millions.
Governor Young suggested that while he was originally opposed to
the operation and might vote to discontinue if that were the sentiment
of the conference, yet otherwise he believed it would be wise to proceed
and buy a little each week so that the public would not see or feel we
had discontinued our open market policy.
Secretary Hills addressed the meeting, expressing the firm belief
that to stop purchases now would be disastrous.
Governor Mayor, in his opening address, spoke of the proposed
amendment offered by Senator Glass permitting direct loans to individuals,
etc. He said that all over the country bank presidents are stating
that everyone entitled to credit can get it. He said this was pure
"bull" -- that he knew, and everyone knew, that all over the country
people who were entitled to credit -- with satisfactory collateral for
business purposes -- were unable to procure it from the banks. Secretary
Hills stated that only this morning he had not two gentlemen who stated
positively that credit was not available even to nonborrowers who had
good collateral. He said that one representative of the Southern Pacific
Railroad told him he had made an examination all along their lines of
customers who furnished them freight, and that he was satisfied that
many of these customers wanted to go on and manufacture, were good
reins with satisfactory collateral, yet were not able to obtain credit.
In the afternoon, discussion as to the open market policy was
resumed, and there were some expressions of opinion on the proposed
draft of regulations under the new Glass amendment.
C.S.R. heard today, indirectly, that Mr. Merrill who was down
at the Senate when the Glass amendment was introduced, called it to the
attention of Mr. Ballantine, the Under-Secretary of the Treasury, who
bitterly opposed it, and did all in his power to defeat it in the Senate
and in the House, but that when Oglesbills returned from Boston he
quickly reversed this procedure and did, and is now doing, all he can
to secure its passage.
After the morning meeting, Governor Harrison told me that he
thoroughly favored the proposed Glass amendment, but that he would go
even farther, -- he would not have the condition imposed that the borrower
must first try to obtain a loan from a member bank. He seemed to be
almost enthusiastic about it.
Governor Young told me that at first he was opposed to it, but
that on further examination he was inclined to think that it would be a
very wise measure to adopt. In the afternoon session, Governor Mayor
announced that the President would be very glad to meet the Governors
this evening. Nothing was said about the Federal Reserve Board members.
After talking the matter over, the Governors felt that it might be very
embarrassing if the public were to know that the Governors all went to
the President, and might create a false impression, and therefore
Governor Mayor said he would tell the President that he felt they had
better not come.

Butler, Dr. Nicholas Murray
Mr. Sherman, one of trustees of Carnegie Endowment told C.S.H.
that Dr. Butler persuaded Briand to drop the phrase
"outlawry of war" and substitute the repudiation of war as
a national policy; that Dr. Butler was entitled to the
credit for the anti-war treaty.
Dr. Butler verified the above and said Briand was terribly chagrined
that so little notice was taken in U.S. of his peace offer;
that he (Dr. B.) went west and delivered 30 addresses
advocating acceptance of the offer; that he tried to interest
Butler, Dr. Nicholas Murray (Cont'd.)
the State Department but Kellogg said it was a pacifist proposition;
that he and Shotwell prepared the draft of a treaty but the
State Department would not take it up but suggested that he
(Dr. Butler) press it as an individual; that he condensed the
treaty into two clauses and gave it to Briand who in an address
adopted it as his own; that the State Department then took it up
as if it were its own suggestion.
Dec. 6, 1928. 96, 97
Dr. Butler took C.S.H. to luncheon at the Century Club.
He was very bitter at Coolidge's armistice day address saying it put
our country back for years.
Dr. Butler said Hoover was a man of no intelligence; that his course
as food administration in permitting shipments of lard to Belgium
firms knowing full well that it was en route for Germany, made
him doubt his patriotism and even his honesty; that he had said
to a friend of his (Dr. B.) that he would tell those damned
Wall Street bankers where to get off.
Dr. Butler said Hoover was furtive and indirect, that he could do
nothing frankly or directly.
He also said Vare was pulled over to Hoover in the Convention by
Senator Moses who was on the Committee on Elections, who was
said to have intimated to Vare that if he wished to secure his
seat he had better come over to Hoover. He said Sec. Mellon's
political power was gone; that Gov. Fisher was the boss of
Pennsylvania.
He said Coolidge was not friendly to Hoover; that Coolidge had been
firm in the resolution that neither Dawes nor Lowden should be
nominated.
Dr. Butler said he voted for Gov. Smith and hardly knew more than
four Republicans among his close friends who voted for Hoover;
that Gov. Smith probably had no political future; that Tammany,
outside of Manhattan, was treacherous to Smith; that they felt
that they had gotten little or nothing from Smith and would get
less from him as President; that the Jews also were against him.

Butler, Dr. Nicholas Murray (Cont'd.)
Charles R. Crane told Senator Bruce that Dr. Butler told him that
when Belgian relief affairs were wound up, there were 2 millions
left over, which the Red Cross asked for to continue its
relief work; that Hoover had never turned this in nor accounted
for it, but that he had used it to pay Secretaries to work up
propaganda for himself; that when John Barton Payne was going
away he asked Hoover to take charge of Red Cross relief; that
when he returned the letter heads were changed to "Hoover Relief";
that Crane said he introduced Hoover to Wilson and asked for his
appointment as Food Conservator; that, later, Hoover said there
was room in Washington for an independent newspaper; that he
could buy one for $200,000; that he asked him to contribute and
that he (Crane) gave $25,000; that he sent his secretary to
Washington to see the operation of the paper; that he stayed in
Washington a month and reported that it was being used to boom
Hoover; that he wrote Hoover as to this and that Hoover returned
the money; that Frank Kent (Baltimore Sun) had always been strong
Democrat but that, at first, he began to side with Senator
Couzens against Sec. Mellon, and later did all he could to help
Hoover; that everyone believes he was paid by Couzens and Hoover.

C.S.H. gives Miss Eyer, in Boston, a letter from Clephane.
She says she would like to have me talk freely with Clephane
as to the advisability of preparing a memorandum as to her
past experiences with her nephew.
C.S.H. and Clephans lunch together at Cosmos Club. C.S.H. told
him what Dr. Ruffin said as to Miss Myer's condition.
Clephane said he had no doubt but that, although in a neuritic
condition, she was competent to make a will.
He agreed with C.S.H. as to advisability of Gertrude's preparing
a statement as to her nephew and his father, and said he
would see to this.
He agreed with C.S.H. that the nephew might contest Gertrude's
will.
Clephane said that after Gertrude had executed her last will
(She told C.S.H. it was her third will, she wrote on it that
she had made no bequest to any of her family because they
were already comfortably provided for, and that he had this
witnessed by the same witnesses.
Clephane said her gift to the Cathedral was not an outright
gift but was specifically stated to be for the erection of
a Chapel in which she and Walden were to be buried.
1928. 102
Gertrude said Clephane had advised her to tell Dr. Ruffin as to
her will and ask him if he would accept an honorarium of say
$500 in lieu of compensation as executor; that he thought
$1000 might be better.
C.S.H. said if she desired he would speak to Clephane about this.
At first she thought I had better not as he had already advised
her and that she had not told him that I originally had suggested
this.
Later, however, in Bertie's presence, she asked me to speak to
Clephane about it and even suggested that I speak to Dr. Ruffin

Crop marketing paper
Miller presented a proposed letter to F.R. banks stating Board
would approve a seasonal crop marketing rate from 1/2 to 1%
below rates on other classes to continue to end of normal

out of the movement and marketing of crops.

Said Jefferson, Lincoln, and Wilson were the three great

Gov. Norman said gold standard was in peril in near future;
that the purpose of a gold standard originally was to
protect the exchanges; that recently, however, European and
South American countries had obtained gold for capital
and not for exchange purposes, - e.g. France, Brazil,
Argentina; that it was a strain on gold even when used to
maintain a central banks reserves; that while he believed
a much lower ratio would be safe, his people did not feel
so, and any appreciable decline in gold reserves was
reflected at once in the country's exchange, and the
country must increase discount rates to protect its gold
although no increase was necessary from the commercial
standpoint; that he feared trouble if countries need gold
for other than its real purpose, - settling of balances
with other countries.
He said prices were now adjusted on an international world level
and that any pronounced fall would be most injurious.

Grant, Catherine (Cont'd.)
Bertie and I are feeling really blue at Catherine's moving up
to Boston and especially so as she says she will probably be
in Mahant next summer. We have seen her, almost every day
in the summer for many years, and she has been absolutely
devoted to us. Her coming over with her children to bathe
has meant much to Bertie, and we both have a feeling of deep
affection for her as if she was one of our family, - a sister
or even a daughter.

Sept. 20, 1928. 30
Catherine dined with us, with Mrs. Stanley McCormick and others.
Alexander Grant said he had a cold and could not come.
On leaving she said she hoped I would write her some more of my
delightful gossip letters, giving all the news from Washington,
and I said I would but that when she wrote me she must drop
"Mr." and substitute "Charlie" or even "grandfather" if she
preferred that. This she said she would do.
She spoke of her deep love and affection for Bertie and said whenever
Bertie came to Boston she must stay with her.
She also said it was within the bounds of possibility that she might
be back in Fairhaven, or possibly in Mattapoisett next summer.

Oct. 29, 1928. 63
While Catherine was dressing for supper, I had a talk with
Alexander about brokers loans. He always addressed me as
Mr. Hamlin and I finally told him his father and I had used
their Christian names for 30 or 40 years; that for many
years I had called him Alexander; that Bertie and I looked
on Catherine and himself as one of our family and as a
younger brother and sister; that I really wished, at least in
the bosom of the family, he would drop the "Sir," and call
me Charlie. He seemed very much pleased and said, -- would
you consider it respectful? I said yes, and when I left he
addressed me as "Charlie."
Oct. 29, 1928. 63
C.S.H. told Alexander that we considered him one of the luckiest
men in the world in having Catherine.
Later I told Catherine of my talk with Alexander and she was
very much pleased. During our walk she told me how she
admired and loved Bertie, and that she felt as if she were
a younger sister to us both. She finally said she expected
a bread and butter letter right away.

Catherine dined with us and asked me to come to her a week from
Monday when I returned from my last visit to Mattapoisett
for the season. She asked me to telephone her from Boston,

Hale, Rachel (Cont'd.)
C.S.H. started to write Rachel when something seemed to say
to him that she was at her house in Washington.
I called her up and found she was there but was resting.
Later I called up again and she had returned unexpectedly and would
have called me up before (she arrived on Thursday) but her house
was in such utter confusion that there was not a room in which she
could receive any one. She begged me to come right over, which
I did.
We had a delightful talk of nearly 1 1/2 hours, and I told her in detail
everything Gertrude had said to me during the summer.
She said my letters were perfectly fascinating, --that she had never
read such charming letters, that Mary also was entranced with them,
and would often meet her at the door, when she was returning after
a call, and explain in great excitement, --another "Chronicle" has
come; that they would both run up to read it with avidity.
She said she told Mrs. Rogers about my letter describing Gertrude's
visit, and had finally destroyed it lest some one might come across
it unawares.
She spoke of Gertrude's nephew and said he was a bad lot.
She said Major Leonard told her that Gertrude had between $30,000 and
$40,000 per year.
She spoke of her own income saying she could not tell exactly what it
was, she was so stupid about such matters, but she rather implied
it was not much more than that.
She said Gertrude was simply able to take a house for the summer and ought
not to expect that her friends should entertain her for long visits.
She agreed with C.S.H. that Gertrude was crazy to marry if she could get
a husband who suited her.
C.S.H. said he would call up Rachel when he returned on Wednesday and
she said she might ask us both to dinner, if her house painting was
finished.

C.S.H. called up Rachel and had a fine talk with her. I told her I
fearred Gertrude was angry with me because of my frankness in
answering her questions, but Rachel said I ought to call her up as
she was most friendly to and appreciative of Bertie and myself.

Oct. 7, 1928. 44
Rachel telephones at 8:45 a.m. asking me to come to dinner at 7:30 to meet Mr. and Mrs. Horace Washington. She said not to wear even a dinner jacket as Mr. Washington had none with him.
C.S.H. went to Rachel's a little before 7:30 and met her coming down the stairs from her room winding an alarm clock. C.S.H. said that he knew this clock was prepared because of the long dinner Bertie and I once had at her house, when, no clock being visible, we stayed very late. She seemed almost embarrassed at this witticism but said it was not on my account that she wanted the clock.
C.S.H. had on his heavy winter cut away suit (his other being at Mattapoisett) and as it was a very hot evening he felt almost suffocated.
To his surprise, Mr. Washington arrived dressed in a dinner jacket, which Rachel had said he did not have with him. Soon after, Major and Mrs. Leonard appeared, the Major in a dinner jacket also!
Rachel meekly apologized for having insisted that I should not dress and the incident afforded much humor.
We had a most interesting dinner. Rachel put me vis a vis to her. During the dinner Mary Hale came in dressed for another dinner, and she really looked most charming and attractive; her dress was most becoming and beautiful. She is really getting to be more like her mother every day, and bids fair to be a very beautiful woman. She is also a girl of good sense and has a good mind. The man who gets her will be lucky indeed!

Hale, Rachel (Cont'd.)
C.S.H. calls on Rachel and we had a long talk together.
She said she had been feeling wretchedly for some time, and had lost
all the weight she had gained during the summer; that her regular
Doctor, Dr. Liner, was away; that her new Doctor had ordered her
to stay in bed every day until lunch, which she said she was
doing; that he also said she must go to Garfield Hospital to have
another gall bladder test, -- which she certainly would not do,
at least not until her regular Doctor returned.
She did not seem at all disturbed because Gertrude spoke to me.
She thanked me for my most kind letter offering to come and read to
her, and seemed very much pleased with it. (In it, C.S.H. said
Bertie and he considered her the closest and dearest friend we had.)
Nov. 16, 1928, 78
Rachel told C.S.H. she had purchased an old Manorial estate called
"His Lordship's Kindness" about 3/4 of an hour distant from
Washington, not far from Ellen Leonard's place.
She said she had already paid down $15,000 on it; that the sale required
an order of the court which had only recently been issued. C.S.H.
asked if she had an Attorney to represent her and she said No, but
that the Maryland Trust Co. was looking up the title. She said
she was worried at the delay in getting the title, and wished to
be able to say, from time to time, if in any doubt that she
must consult some one as her adviser, and would like to be permitted
to say that C.S.H. was her adviser.
C.S.H. at once said she could use his name in any way, and at any time
she saw fit, and this pleased her very much.
She said she wanted to drive us down to see the place as soon as Bertie
returned to Washington.
She asked me surely to call again on my return next week.
C.S.H. apologized for his somewhat hysterical letter to her about her
health, but she said, on the contrary, it was a most delightful
letter to her.

Hale, Rachel (Cont'd.)
She said Gertrude told her the other day that she was going to
sell two tables owned by Walden; that she asked the price
she wanted for them and she said $50 each; that she went
around to see them in an antique shop and the man said the
price was $100 each, which she (Rachel) paid.
She said Gertrude made her very angry by saying, "You can have these
for $50 each, but I have no doubt you will sell them later at
a handsome profit!"
C.S.H. asked Rachel what reply she made to this, and she said she
merely gave her a soft answer.
C.S.H. said she ought to have slapped Gertrude's face and Mary Hale
agreed enthusiastically.
Rachel asked me what I would have said to Gertrude if she had said
that to me, and I said I would have said to her, "No woman
who wears a wig can speak to me in that fashion."
Both Rachel and Mary laughed at this.
Rachel said Gertrude once told her that her hair under her wig
was very white.

Gertrude told C.S.H. that in her will she had provided that of

Gertrude seemed angry with Rachel at dinner. She said some time

down on a bench to rest; that later Rachel said that she

who looked like Gertrude, just as she was driving off in
her motor, but that she was so tired she really did not
have the strength to drive around to see if it was Gertrude

Gertrude evidently had not seen Rachel on that occasion, but she
told C.S.H. that Rachel evidently had a guilty conscience,
and she evidently was very angry at Rachel's remark.
She said that Rachel, tired as she was, had strength enough to take
her old friend, Mr. Appleton, that very afternoon to her
new home in Maryland.

Hale, Rachel (Cont'd.)

Nov. 23, 1928, 85
Gertrude also said that although Rachel and she were very close

C.S.H. vigorously dissented at this statement.
Nov. 23, 1928, 85, 86
Gertrude said that Mrs. Warder had said many times to her that
Rachel was beautiful and fine in all things, - but -
She gave C.S.H. to understand that Mrs. Warder felt that there was
something lacking in Rachel's character.
This, to C.S.H., is utter nonsense. That Rachel should have so long
and so patiently put up with Gertrude's inconsistencies,
prevarications and petty jealousies, would be proof enough, for
any reasonable person, of her character and loyalty.
When C.S.H. thinks of her care for Gertrude and the devotion she
showed to Miss Loring, not to speak of her kindness and
sweetness to Bertie and himself, such twaddle as the above
fairly makes his blood boil.
Nov. 23, 1928, 86
Gertrude also said that when Walden died and Rachel went down from
Bar Harbor to her at Eastern Point, Rachel said she came down
as much for Walden's sake as for hers. This, however, did not
seem to disturb Gertrude for she said she always hoped Walden
would fall in love with Rachel and that she would accept him,
but that while Walden was a great friend of Rachel's, he never
was in love with her.
C.S.H. thinks this also is utter rubbish as he firmly believes Walden
worshipped Rachel and that it was not his fault that they never
became engaged. On the other hand, good and fine as Walden
was, C.S.H. could not conceive of such a thing as Rachel, with
all her charm and beauty, falling in love with him.

Hale, Rachel (Cont'd.)
Gertrude also said that when Rachel's son, Eugene, was ill at
St. Paul's School with measles, Rachel called her up and
asked her whether she thought she ought to go to Concord
to take care of him; that Rachel said Mary thought she ought
to go, but as it was merely a simple case of measles she
feared she would merely be in the way.
Gertrude did not say what advice she gave Rachel, but merely said
Rachel did not go at once, and that later scarlet fever
set in, and that then Rachel went at once to Concord but
that Eugene died.
Gertrude did not, of course, say that Rachel had been derelict in
her duty towards her child. C.S.H. fears that she hoped
it would leave that impression on his mind.
At first C.S.H. could not understand Gertrude's reason for these
vitriolic attacks as she seemed outwardly calm and sober,
but finally she said she merely wished to give C.S.H. an
inkling as to Rachel's character.
It seems clear to C.S.H. that Gertrude is morbidly jealous and thinking
that C.S.H. admires Rachel greatly is determined to break up
the friendship by such vile slanders as the above.
Rachel has been a loyal friend to Gertrude, often under trying
circumstances, and such contemptible innuendos stamps
Gertrude's character most clearly.
Gertrude has often told C.S.H. that she considered Rachel as her
dearest friend! Heaven save one from such friends!
