July 4th— How pleasing is it to receive even the least testimony of gratitude from a slave, for my part I think I have
so much injured that I never feel as if I had a claim to their affection or voluntary good offices— Just now I gave
harry the key of the milk house to get out some butter to drop Tabby's rabbit for her, it being one of the
dog had caught a bright day, I after wards, as it was the conclusion of harvest I had worked hard all
day, sent him tea biscuit & butter for their supper, aiders as I gave them to harry, now with Tabby's
rabbits you will have a nice supper, she went out with this message, but when she delivered it, it shant be fixed, said Tabby,
no, no, added the other, we wont eat it but save it for your son, as it is a rarity—
It has most sweet with this rabbit taste to me, thus reasoned with the good will of
these poor slaves.—
During the last week or two, I have had my feelings almost agitated at the sight of the suffering of one of these unfortunate
creatures— Lizzie, a fine, good natured, active young Man, had been hewed by Mr Smith most of last winter; in the spring his master died
to be used as for sale by the executor. He solicited Mr Smith to buy him, but the interest seconded his request, my excellent hus-
band would not sacrifice his principles, which were all adverse to slavery.— He was bought
by Major Beans; but was so discontented with his
situation that in a few months he again came
to Mr Smith with the same request, this
was again denied. The poor fellow, separated
from all those whom he loved, with
a cruel master, was so mistaken, that
he ran away. After concealing himself about
a week in the woods, he at last ventured
here, I again besought Mr Smith to lay him.
His eyes were sent in his head, his cheeks
were hollow, I he looked almost worn
out with watering & hunger. I felt
extremely affected, I to persuade him, seemed
in clearly the dictate of humanity, that Mr
Smith consented in case his master would
part with him promising him at the
same time to set him free at 35 pounds
in case he behaved well. Pepy was always
so said he would leave nothing undone to please
Mr Smith. He did persuasion to
remain here until Mr S. could write to his
master & get a to answer; believing him, however
that he would run the risk of being taken
as his master would learn from the letter
where he was. This will he was willing
to run.
He was here two weeks, 2 rop pay 2 safety that
he was singing from morning to night, his feet
often stepping company with his voice. He was
so obliging, a quiet demeanor, so affectate I loved
to the children, that I became quite attached to
him. I don't think Major Beans called on me,
he was alone, & unarmed, so that his appearance
reappeared one as to his profession -- He told me
he & Mr Smith had not yet agreed about the
price, but that he thought they would & that
he intended to return to the City for that purpose,
but that mean while he would to talk to safety,
I was so free from suspicion that I directed
him to the spot where he was at work & he
rode off -- not long after safety came running
to the door. Our hands clashed 2 carried out & came
come Mysteries, safety begs you will come, they
have got him bound to a tree! I was the
way the streets, but I encountered a lot I saw
him at a distance, found a conductor along
several men. I stopped, but asked as bad
as I could to Major Beans to come to me,
he saw me, I changed my signal, -- I was quite
out of breath when he came, but after
recovering myself, Sir said I, it is your interest
& not your humanity that I address --
you may take for granted that you will not be able
to keep him, he has solemnly declared he
will not live with you & that if he cannot
escape, he will take his own life, -- & salt
in his aversion to being your slave, & in his
own hatreds, I make no doubt but he will --
I then you will have the power to offer
to your slave to -- You smile sir, as if such
a thing had never happened, but within a year
I know several instances, of it was but last
week that Genl. Osborne's man threw himself
overboard, to save himself from punishment,
& it is not a great while since, a poor old
man, when his son was torn from him
to be sold, in distress, hung himself in my
house -- And her son escaped from the hands
of the purchaser, threw himself into the river,
thus did you see what I say is founded on
experience. Or as he said he, it was
not in that account I smiled, for I have known
many instances of the kindyer opinion, but
I will not suppose I mean to set him down
to the Georgia negro-buyers & thus he may
escape. This is treason & being himself an
son of the President, and in it respectable
sir, that for the sake of a hundred more dollars
than Mrs. will give you, that you will sacrifice
the happiness, perhaps the life of a fellow creature!!
I continued to talk & urged every motive interest
& humanity could suggest -- but all in vain &
the poor wretch was taken away -- I remained
in tears & with determination never to own a
slave, except in cases in which humanity might
be served -- As to slave, here have a great
deal of heavy soldiers Georgia & seem to consider

originally torn from their native soil. -- As we were
travelling one summer, the carrier broke & we
found shelter in a little log hut in the woods,
the only inhabitants was an old woman, a little
dog about 30 lbs. & 2 a pig -- Julia was
afford of the pig & cried, "What you cry for
said the child, don't be afraid, pig ain't
negro-buyer, no negro buyers take you, I don't
any --
Nothing -- to prevent them from obtaining
ground of so unpardonable a character & likewise a dishonor
that we were obliged to part with her. On one occasion
in which she was instructed strongly suspected, stole her
alone & endeavored to draw from her a confession
of the fact -- She distinctly maintained her innocence
& when I alleged my strong reasons for doubting
"which Madame said she have done, I wish any nothing
"more, but that God, who made you & made me
liberties, & the time will come when you as well
as me will meet before him. Here indeed we
are very different; you are a pretty lady, that dress
you with a machine, I have done to need a pretty lady
in a few years, crowded with caps & bows not one letter
is but when one dies & you must die on well in me,
I am quite dissatisfied with her that your office will be a
little longer than mine. Then when that time
comes you will know I am innocent, -- that God
saved the prince her arms & eyes forwards, that God did
it wider as both -- because that I am innocent. These were
her words as nearly as I can recollect.
Her character is yet one had proof beyond doubt
that she was guilty of the theft laid to her charge.
She is a most extraordinary woman, amplying the
character of virtue divine with a proud intellectual
value would have triumphed over her has the most
humane & tender disposition. She has a most
refinement bordering of mind, great activity & vigour
of body, very inventive, full of experiments, a
difficulty, full of ardor and in any undertaking she
could do any kind of work, either men or women,
her soul was not the soul of a slave.

Seventeenth of September, in a hospital, into which
rapidly does time pass & thus few visitors dare to leave behind.
I am not able to get in contact with them, I seem to have done
nothing. The happiness of a family in every day adds, every day
to home is to be put in order the two principal
to clothing made a model. -- From it then require to
whole of life to support life, few are exempt from
the necessity -- at times how inconvenient it has been sometimes
to these domestic arrangements cause it with difficulty
I seem to admit my mind to this kind of existence a woman
it not for the animal spirits a constitutional good
humour & contentment with which I am endowed often
would this contrast between my duties & melancholy
make me quite miserable -- This evening I have
enjoyed a most pleasant portion of placidity
& cheerfulness; few days have occurred in which I have
not felt an almost to discharge to duties in which
I have not enjoyed the greatest temperature of mind,
but this sunshine has been more & then overlanded in
moments when have occurred when my mind has refused
to be trained to the memory of family business & has
found to secure in to the regimen of intellectual existence,
feel within me an activity & self-possession thought,
an elevation of soul, a overflowing of imagination,
which quite unfit me for the lively duties of
my humble situation. The limited circle which
it is prescribed for woman to tread, seems like
that of the house chained to the wall, while
the unlimited sphere of man is like that of the
front course, who overlooks every obstacle,
I am no bands opposed to the expansion & exercise
of his powers.— So how at each moment, obliged
to explore this scene, to try other paths, to give
full scope to that active & venturesome power that
feels within me, to break through the narrow of
the little cage that confines me, to extend my
vision & rise far beyond the mere possibility
of what I now see. But I am a woman, and society
says, thus far & no farther shall then come.—
Why then has nature given me a mind so
active & ingenious, an imagination so untrammeled
& free, qualities are not necessary to the discharge
of female duties? But why this agony, it
cannot charge my destiny as rather my own, I must
see a woman! I have only to try to describe
my duties faithfully.— How delightful would
be even table & quiet full scope to the powers
of mind, to plunge into all the actions, the sensations
the strong contradictions of life—to meet with certain
stars & objects that would call forth exercise
all the noblest qualities of the soul.— But
what to what end and how are these thoughts, I cannot
say, that mountains about me rise and spread in
horridness in this wild valley at its foot—
well, the valley has its charms & when I do not raise my
eyes to the summit of the mountain, I am befoged entirely
in calling the flowers that are scattered in my path.
I have often said & said with truth, & at this moment
say, I never knew any woman so happy as myself. But
what to a reflecting mind is the happiness which human
life can afford; Its comforts, its joys, its splendours, are
often mitigated, or magnified, that the immortal soul
turns with disgust from them, finding them a spectacle
for its desire to an individual & more individual existence.— I have every thing which this
world can give, it is impossible in this life for
me to have more source of happiness, a yet I
feel within me the capacity of being happier.—
Does not this speak the soul to be of higher origin
than the body, does not this prove that it is destined
to a distinct existence.— If we believe in the
goodness of God, it does prove this—in this case
is found whatever is necessary for the well-being
& enjoyment of the body, but can the soul find
in the whole world of human life, objects that
can satisfy its desires, objects that can exercise
its faculties? The labour of the body can obtain
the sustenance clothing & shelter necessary to the
preservation of animal life, but the most active
& entertaining soul cannot desired objects vast enough
to exercise all its abilities, or give scope to all its
energies. These are the reasons why I am
content with my present situation, I
have not the power to acquire
more, I have not the desire to acquire
more, I have not the means of acquiring
more, I have not the opportunity of acquiring
more, I have not the inclination to acquire
more, I have not the ability to acquire
more, I have not the desire to acquire
and cannot be fostered beyond the narrow limits of this
little garden. Without the support of this small
but most important garden, I would not have been
able to pursue the work of my life, which is the
description of plants for the Royal Gardens at Kew.
Poor indeed would life be, even to the richest
in its enjoyments, if it was not connected with
the life to come. The seed which the farmer
holds in his hand is small in quantity &
of little value; it is for the sake of it produced
that he labours his labour & experiences anxiety.
Thus the circumstances of life are in themselves
but of little moment, but on their cultivation depends
the harvest we shall reap in futurity. I
think of this, & of the husbandman labouring
the winter or the summer in order to obtain his small & precarious
harvest, state not I cheerfully discharge the duties
of this life, in order to gain a hoped immortality.
As one of the ancient writers has observed, life
is a stage, on which our parts are given to
us, & it is not he who acts with the highest character
but he who acts with the lowest that defains
the affrontation of the Manager.
Oh my children remember this, & however humble,
the part allotted, endeavour not
only to act it well, but to act it willingly -- A willing
mind makes labour easy & a cheerful heart makes duty
pleasant. -- seldom have I to struggle with discontent,
or despondion of spirit, & when I find myself enjoying
a questionary the pleasure & duties of life, generally
check this habit of the soul, which is indulged, leads
inevitable to discontent. -- I have been thinking
this morning, that it would amuse, & perhaps
interest me, to read a brief diary of my
unseasonable occupation, state of mind, a state of the
weather. -- I know not if I shall find either method
& leave to pursue this, however I will make
the attempt -- This little record may instruct me
to do better, when I think it will be read by
my dear daughter. -- The weather for a few days
past has been so oppressively warm, that it
has interfered me for every creation. Now have
to order men, necessitise with a long continued
strength, we have had scarcely any thunder or
rain to clothe summer & many streams & things
are dry, so that all the mills for many miles
round are stopped & the flour I have been able
to obtain has been from a windmill.
The weather oppressively hot. -- None at breakfast after 8 o'clock found
it necessary to get up and neglected their usual part in the morning
while at breakfast, received my temper by reflecting that I should

James and I went to town -- I went the whole distance in

The rest of the evening passed while Mrs Smith

The day was dark & cloudy & had a few little

After breakfast I collected the children's

29 A stormy day - The first we have had since May! I was

In nature all they shows & forms

Sidney July 1st 1830
Thursday
A very warm day I spent my
morning in reading, writing
& reading Lady Morgan's France.
The Ball finished paid us a short
visit in the afternoon, and the
two Mrs Blackford's spent the
evening with us. Young Mrs B-
played & sang a great deal for
which I had quite a pleasant evening.
Friday
We all went to the city, Miss
Ann & Julia spent the day with
Mrs Gilles. I went to see E Smith
& Mrs Howell. I was very glad
to see Kitty, after so long an
absence. I spent most of the morn-
ing with her. I received a letter
from E. Boyd -- we had no
company -- a very warm day.
Saturday
I served nearly all the morning.
I read "Lady Morgan" in the afternoon. We company
Sunday 24th July
We went to church as usual, but
had a very indifferent sermon.
Mr Smith walked to and from
towns with us after church;
where we saw Mrs. Bemford
Louisa -- we received a letter
from Mama saying that she
would probably be with us
in the afternoon -- the carriage
went in for her immediately
after dinner. Mr Smith rose
but I spent the afternoon &
evening with us -- Mama and
Susan got home about six.
We were all very glad to
see them home again, cousin
Julia was better. A very pleasant
day -- The moon is ten 85 --
Monday
I was very busy all the morning
breaking ads. -- In the afternoon
I read "Lady Morgan" and took
a very pleasant walk -- Capt. and
Mrs Doug. L., Miss Mann and
James spent the evening with us.
The city was very quiet, there
was less dinners, a ball and a
fallen queen.
Tuesday
Mrs. Thornton & Mrs. Berdican spent
the day with us -- we read aloud
"The Rivels" quite an interesting
tale -- it was quite warm, but
we had a very pleasant day.
Wednesday
I read nearly all the morning
finished Lady Morgan's France
it is quite an interesting work.
Then wrote in my "Journal" --
Thursday
I commenced Nipps Ancient
History, & read it for two hours,
& then read the Memoirs of
Madame Montenton until
diviner time - Esther & Catherine
Smith rode out in the after-
noon; Mr Wood & Mr Kend
spent the evening with.
Friday
I finished Madame de Monte-
non, which I liked very much
after dinner read "The Wild
Irish Girl," along to Mama, I
also finished that, it is very
interesting - no company.
Saturday
I went into Miss Stewart's to
spend a few days - we took a
ride in the afternoon, had
no company in the evening -
Tuesday - 11th
I went with Mr F. to St. Johns
church - Mama went home
with Mrs Bemford to dine, &
Louisa stayed with us. In the
afternoon we went up to Rab-
orama, Mama returned with
us & stayed all night.
Monday
I wrote a letter to C. Boyd, after
breakfast - at twelve Mrs J.
Mann & I went to Miss Scaturs,
they all seem very glad that
Julia has returned home -
I spent the day with her in
the afternoon she returned
with me to Miss Towns -
where we found Louisa, We
spent the evening with us.
Tuesday
Quite a rainy morning, I was busy
sewing all the morning making
a new dress - we rode in the
afternoon - In the evening Mr
F. & I went to see the Shipes Chris-
and the Whips Dickens. Mr
Smith came to see us, and
brought me a letter from
Rosa Wait.
Wednesday
I saved a seed cloud during
the morning - Esther & Catherine
Smith came to see me in
the afternoon - after they
went, we took a ride; Mr
King spent the evening with us.
Thursday
Soon after breakfast I went
to see Kitty (the family are
all coming into the City -)
and Miss Forest, served a
meal until dinner - finished
it reading a very pretty
little book, Emma Mathews -
We went to Haines' in the
afternoon, I had an uncon-
tinuous pleasant visit there.
Friday
A very oppressively warm
day - I returned home in
the afternoon - We had no
company.
Saturday
Mr Wood came to see us
while we were at breakfast - he came to say
Yankee, as he is going
to New England. James
Boniford came home with
Beyond its doors - he said
to us in the afternoon.
Sunday - 18th -
As the weather was so
very warm I came out
for in to church - he we
went - we heard old Dr
Batch preach - after church
we went to Mrs Thomson's
& Mrs Howell's - The girls
wanted me to stay with them
very much. We had no
Company I fasted a long night - 15th
Monday
Very busy during all the morning. I had the Duchess de la
Pallière aboard to remain in
the afternoon; the weather
still continued very warm.
Tuesday
I sewed & read "Raphael"; before
sunrise. In the afternoon I
practised & read "Divergent"
Manus & Susan rode down
to the Mary Road & brought
Mrs Colston & Mrs Tucker home
with us - the Thermometer has
been very high 88 - in the Shade -
Wednesday
I went into the City with Pope,
& spent the day with Hattly & Sister
Hattly & Mrs R. Howell brought
me home (in the carriage) in
the afternoon - they stayed to
tea with - I spent a very pleasant day.
Mrs Ellison came to visit us.
Thursday
I read Haggard's "The King" nearly all
the morning - Mama & the ladies
rode in the afternoon - I read "Dev-
erness" - In the evening I played
backgammon with Hazard.
Friday
I sewed Ladies' Kuffs during the
morning - I read "Divergent", in the afternoon I received a note from Hattly
begging me to come in.
Saturday
Went into the City in the morning
to stay with Hattly until Sunday afternoon - We spent our morning,
very pleasantly serving & conversing
& took a very pleasant walk after
dusk. Sunday - 25 July
Helen and myself went to St Johns
church -- we found it very warm --
This has been a very long warm
spell -- we have heard of a
number of deaths occasioned
by the heat. I received a long
letter from E. Boyd. We took a
very pleasant walk in the evening.
Monday
I went to see the Randolphs in
the morning -- Mama came for
me in the evening & I returned
home after having had a most
agreeable visit.
Tuesday
I copied several things for
Mama & wrote in my journal
which occupied me until
dinner. Mr. & Mrs. Agg paid as
a visit in the afternoon, but
did not stay to tea -- Mr & Mrs
Ingham, Mr & Mrs Clarke and
Mr H. Smith spent the after-
noon & evening with us. Mr
S. stayed very late.
Wednesday
I was busy serving & reading
Rapel until dinner -- Mrs
Thomson, her mother & Mr
Higgins spent the afternoon and
evening with us -- Mr H. was
quite agreeable -- he asked me
if I would come & sit for him
as he wished to take my life --
I made it a present to him --
of course accepted his offer --
Thursday
I was busy serving & reading all
the morning --
Friday
Mama, Sister & myself went to
the City in the morning - just
as we were going, George &
James Bonfort came to spend
the day - I went to see Helen
& at twelve o'clock went to Mr
King's to sit - In the afternoon
Saban played a good deal
for George & James - just as
we sat down to tea, all the
Doughty's came over & spent
the evening - we had a very
agreeable evening.
Saturday
I slept & read all the morn-
ing - In the afternoon we took
a ride & then went to Mrs
Agg's where we spent a very
pleasant evening - I had a
very lightful ride home by
moonlight -
Sunday - 1st August.
They all went to church
except me as it was my turn
to stay home - there was a
thunder gath in the afternoon
& a great deal of rain for a
short time. Mr Ellison spent
the evening with us.
Monday
Sister A. & Sister went to the
City - I made cake - then sewed
2nd Mad Hassel until dinner - read
"Vicilia" in the afternoon - it
rained all the afternoon & evening.
Tuesday
It rained nearly all day - I went
to Rose Wait - Mama rode into
the City in the afternoon and
brought the two Misses Randolph
out to spend a few days with us.
Mr & Mrs Agg & Mrs Delanti spent
the evening with us -
Wednesday
I went into the City to sit to
Mr King - I sat from nine o-
lock until half past one - then
went to see Mrs Hamilton and
Hetty & Helen. When I returned
to home, I found that we
had all been invited to
spend the evening at Mrs
Doughty's - Martha took the
Wiper handship to ride after
dinner & then went to Mrs De
we all went except Papa and
Susan - Mr & Mrs Agg, Mrs
Delan the, Mrs Blackford,
Mr Flah & Mr Stone were
there - we had a good deal
of music & quite a pleasant
evening. Mrs Blackford is
a very agreeable woman.
Thursday
I served tea at about 11 o'clock
in the morning. Mrs Thornton
& her mother came out and
spent the afternoon & evening
Col: Beechey & his daughter Mrs
Wharton, Mrs Lennard & Miss
Elgar also came out, but did
not stay to tea -
Friday
I made cake in the morning.
Martha took the Wiper hand-
ship to ride in the afternoon -
we had no company.
Saturday
I went in the morning to the
City to sit. I found it very
agreeable at Mr Kings, he is a
very entertaining man - I stayed
with him until one o clock -
then went to Mrs Neville's, to
see the girls - the Misses Randall
returned home in the
afternoon -- we had no company.
Monday 8th.
As I was not quite well I
did not go to church -- Maria
went to see poor Mrs Ransom
in the afternoon.
Tuesday
I was busy sewing until two
o'clock, then Mad Russell's
History stood to arrange.
Monday, Papa & Susan went
to see Mrs Ingham in the after-
noon; Julia went over to Mrs
Doughty's & stayed to tea -- when
the returned home at nine
Mrs Doughty, Miss Maria the
two young gentlemen, Mr
Hoad & Mr Ellison accompanied
her & stayed with us
until near eleven.
Tuesday
A very pleasant city day, I
went to the City again to sit
I sat in from nine until one --
the City was particularly agreeable
I then went to see Mrs Hunter
for a short time -- after which
I went to Mrs Newell's -- When
Papa called for me, I was
surprised to see Uncle John
from Philadelphia in the door-
frame -- as there was no room
for me, I stayed with the girls.
late in the afternoon Helen &
I took a walk; Betty & the boys
went in the evening to a
concert, Helen & I were too
much fatigued with our
walk -- Wednesday
We spent our morning very
pleasantly in sewing & convers-
ing -- Papa called for me at
three & returned home, the
girls wanted me very much
to stay longer with them.
On my return home, I found
Miss L. English on a visit to
us. Uncle John has been very
ill, I is still very unwell.
In the afternoon, Miss Lydia,
Susan & I took a walk and
had a chat visit at Mr
Doughty's - Thursday
I was busy most of the morn-
ing making cake - Betty &
the captain rode out to sea
in the afternoon -
Friday
I was very busy seeing all the morn-
ing - spent the practiced afternoon
I worked in my watch guard in the
evening - Susan & myself went ashore
dinner to see Mrs Dunn out but did
not stay to tea.
Saturday
I went & read in the morning -
George Burford came in the afternoon
& stayed all night, he brought
me a note from Louisa, begging
me to come & stay a week with her
on Ruggles & the Boulevard, spent
the evening with us.
Sunday 15th August
We went to our church as usual & heard Mr Bolton preach.
after church we went to Mrs
Thomson's - Young Mrs Blackford
paid us a short visit in the
afternoon - James Doughty spent the
evening with us.
Monday
I was busy until 11 o'clock
making cake - at which time it
commenced raining & ran it
all the afternoon we had no
company of course.
Tuesday
It rained nearly all the morning -
we had a long visit from old Mr
Burchnidge - Used all the morning
In the afternoon Mr English came
for Miss Lydia, we were all very
happy is part with her.
Wednesday
A very fine day. The rain has made
a great change in the weather. It is
quite cool now & very much like
Autumn. Jason & I went over in the
morning to Mrs Dougltys, we had
quite a pleasant visit. We invited
them to spend the evening with us
which they all did, also the Misses
Queen, Mrs Hard & Mrs Ellison.
Thursday
I went to the City in the morning.
I first went to the Hattys & Helen, then
Mrs Thornton, Ben King, did some
shopping, & spent the rest of the
morning very agreeably at Mrs
Leaton's -- Mr & Mrs Clarke, Mrs
Thompson, Mrs Williams & De Colliis
spent the afternoon with us.
In the evening I began to work a purse.
Friday
Mama went to the City in the morn-
ing. I went to E. Boyd. I read
"Franklin," in the afternoon -- no
company -- Saturday
Susan & myself went to the City in
the morning -- I went to Mr. Thig's
& sat for an hour -- we spent
most of the morning with Kitty.
Susan did not return home, but
agreed to stay at Mrs. Russell's
until Monday -- Mrs. Thorton
& her mother spent the afternoon
with us.
Sunday 22nd
We all went to church as usual,
& heard Mr. Colton preach -- Col. & Mrs
Bourne and family spent the afternoon
& evening with us. I was very glad to
see Louise - George is going to
the West next week -
Monday
Holly brought Susan home and
spent the day with us. The
Captain came out in the after-
noon, they left us before dark -
Tuesday
I was very busy all the morning
making coke - Julie Sexton came
out with Papa to spend some
days with us. Bayard went to
Halorama to George & stayed all
night - Mr Ellison spent the
evening with us. Mrs Agg & Mrs
Blackford paid us a short visit
in the afternoon -
Wednesday
Julie Sexton played & sang a good
deal, then wrote a letter while I
copied music - Some effort divine
Mr Ellison came for Julie to take
a ride on horseback, (as had been
agreed the night before) Bayard
accompanied them - they returned
home just before dark - Julie
sung & played a great deal for
us after that -
Thursday
About twelve o'clock Mrs Sexton
sent out a servant & gig for Julie -
We were very sorry to part with
her & her going was very un-
expected. Matron, Sister Jennie & Julia
sat the evening with Mrs Houston -
Miss F. Flanagan & her brother Randall
& Mrs Thomas, rode out soon after
divine & spent the afternoon -
Friday
I was busy during most of the morn-
ing - Matron & Uncle John rode in the
afternoon, Susan, Bayard & Julie
spent the evening at Mrs Agg's -
Mr Stand, Mr Ellison & James
Doughty spent the evening
with us. I read "Ivanhoe", all
the afternoon.
Saturday
Body most of the morning during
Mama's Uncle took a ride. I
finished reading "Ivanhoe" --
& found it extremely entertaining
our company.
Sunday 25th
They all went to church but
myself -- as it was her turn to
remain at home -- (Capt. & J.
Doughty spent the evening
with us. (Monday)
I read a little of Stasell, trans-
lated some punch & served
in the morning -- read aloud
the "Betrushed"; in the afternoon
Tuesday
I wrote for two hours, then served
until dinner -- Mrs Thomson, her
husband & Miss Brown spent the
afternoon & part of the evening
with us. Julia went to Georgetown
to spend a few days with Miss
L. English --
Wednesday (26th September)
Susan & I went to the City in
the morning -- I went to see F.
Hagner, L. Smith & D. Boths, and
Helen -- Susan spent most of the
morning at Mrs Howell's --
I read the "Betrushed", in the after-
noon -- (Mr Ellison spent the m-
orning with us.
Thursday
Mama & Uncle went to the
City -- They went to Mr Thurgs.
Julia knew my likeness immediately & thought it a very excellent one -- Mr. King presented it to me and as it was finished he brought it home. Uncle was very much pleased with Mr. King & his paintings. Julia returned home -- I was occupied all the morning copying music. I read the "Barkeret" -- in the afternoon.
Friday I was very busy during all the morning -- after dinner, myself, my sister Anna, Julia & myself rode over to see Mrs. Magy & Mrs. Ingham -- but they had all left the country & returned to the City -- after I finished the "Barkeret" -- I found it much more interesting than I expected.
Saturday Uncle & I went to the City -- we went with Papa to Georgetown -- on our return I went to see Betty & Helen & stayed with them until three o'clock -- when I went to see Mrs. Houston for a short time -- after dinner I went to see Miss Queen & old Mrs. Williams. I commenced reading the "Mechanics of the Prince's Sham Battle".
Sunday -- 6th We all went up to Rockbridge Church, where we heard Mr. Breckenridge preach a funeral sermon -- the Church was quite crowded -- a number of the gentlemen had to stand.
De Jones, who is an old acquaintance of Buck's, arrived with us.
Monday
I saved part of the morning & then read the Prince's Lamballie -- This great revolution in France has excited a great deal of excitement throughout our country -- Bayard read us a long account of it in the evening -- It is supposed the present King will abdicite his Throne -- We are all very anxious to hear further accounts from Paris. -- X
Tuesday
Sister & Julia went to the City I was very busy during until two, after which I read the
Prince's Lamballie -- in the afternoon I find it -- it is extremely interesting & I am very much pleased with it. It carried very distinctly all the afternoon & evening.
Wednesday
I read all the morning Russell's Ancient History -- It was very interesting. I read all the afternoon after -- I read of the celebrated battle of Marathon -- Thermopylae -- Salamis -- Platæa & Mycale -- in all of which the Persians conquered the Persians -- we had another rainstorm, it commenced at three & rained in torrents until sunset -- then rained gently all night.
Thursday
I spent most of the morning in
reading Haysells History - the
port I am now reading is ex-
ternally interesting. In the
afternoon Mama, Uncle, Susan
& myself took a delightful ride
and Ellison spent the evening
with us. Friday
Mama & myself went to the City,
we went to see Mrs Bishop, Mrs
Clarke, Mrs Seaton & Mrs Thorton
& Mrs Newell - I received a
long letter from Rose Wait. Miss
Buean her cousin, James Dougherty
& James William spent the evening
with us - Saturday
I was busy all the morning do-
ing Stockings, that most delightful
occupation - In the afternoon I
commenced reading the "Memoirs
of Madame Genlis" there is two
other volumes - Mr Ruggles and
Mr Boulware spent the afternoon
writing with us - I did not go
down until tea time.
Sunday 12th
Mama was very well I did not
go to church, Sister A. J. & myself
went. William Ellis & Frank
Taylor came out while we were
at dinner & spent the afternoon -
Mr Strastou & Mr Bochran also
came out. After tea I read aloud
the book of "Get" to Mama.
Monday
I read "Madame Genlis Memoirs"
aloud to Mama most of the morn-
ing - Catherine Smith & D. Batts came
in to tea as for a short time in the
afternoon - I read & served in the
evening.
Tuesday
I read Madame Feuilis aloud to
Beame until one o'clock - then
stood until dinner, in the after-
noon I evening I read Mad Feuilis.
Wednesday
A very fine day, at length I went to
pay my long intended visit to Hakan
I went for a few minutes to see
Helen before I went to H. I was
very much surprised when she
told me that Lloyd had re-
turned home. Louise seemed
very glad to see me, we spent
our morning in reading & sewing.
In the afternoon Mrs B. Louise
& myself went to the City, we
spent the evening at Mrs Stan-
blocks - we spent quite an agreeable
evening, Dr. Hall was there, he
lent me the Romance of the City,
by Steele -
Thursday (The next)
I practiced after breakfast for an
hour, then read to Mrs B. for
some time Romance of History -
We spent the evening at Mrs W.
Jones's by invitation, there was
a good deal of company, I we-
spent a very merry & pleasant eve-
ning.
Friday
There has been such a change
in the, & it is so cold, we can
scarcely keep ourselves warm -
After breakfast Louise & I took
a walk & went to the Mill to be
weighed, I was very much aston-
ished when I found that I
weighed 110! - we then went to
see Miss Davis; she lent us some
very pretty music. I practiced after
dinner I went aloud in the
evening - We are very much
pleased with the Romance of
History -
Saturday
In the morning I practiced, sun-
ed & read aloud, we took a
long walk in the afternoon -
as we had no company we
read aloud in the evening.
Sunday 19th
Mrs B. Louise & myself went to
Dr Lannie's church; after which
we went to Mrs Thoutou's, I
saw mama & the girls. Bayard
returned to Helena with us.
In the afternoon Mrs B. Louise
Benita, Bayard, Henry & myself
walked down to the river & jump-
ed we returned home to tea.
Monday
Bayard left us after breakfast -
I practiced, sewed & read aloud in
the morning - In the afternoon
we went down to Mrs Lull's we
stayed to tea but returned before nine
o'clock - we have had fine sunshine
today
I applied myself for some time
Louis & I took a long delightful
ramble in the woods - The Misses
Van Bliks came up about one
o'clock & spent the afternoon &
evening - from office dinner
Helen & Lady walked up, Mrs
Hall & Mechlin & Bayard also
came & spent the evening. We all
walked in the garden & gathered
beautiful bouquets, then returned
to the drawing room & had some
music - after tea Louise & I
played cottillions & we danced
we then played some very amusing
games - away over dinner
to enjoy themselves & I cannot
spend a delightful evening.
Wednesday
I still continue very cold I spent
the morning in enjoying music &
reading aloud to Miss Bonford
immediately after dinner Louise
& I went down to Mrs Jessup's, when
we spent the afternoon, Mrs B-2
& Mr Lear came there just about
dark & stayed there a short time,
then we went to see Mrs Thorton.
I felt very much fatigued when
we returned home with our
long walk.
Thursday
I espied music most of the
morning. Mrs Lanch came to
see Mrs Bonford & Mrs Stagg
Miss Mechlin. Bayard came
up to dinner -- soon after which we
went to see the Houses. The event
the walk is quite short; we
spent a very pleasant evening.
Friday
It rained all day. Louise & I did
not like it much as we had
intended to pay several visits
that morning. I served, copied
music & read aloud in the morn-
ing; I read all the evening.
Saturday
A very damp, cloudy day, it rained
mostly all the time, we had no
company of course -- I read aloud
all the afternoon & evening.
Sunday 26th
We went to church in the morn-
ing, & to Mrs Thorton's, where I
saw Warren & the girls. In the
afternoon I returned home, after
being about twelve days, and
having had a delightful visit.
Mrs Bonford, Louise & Ruth returned
with me, they stayed to tea.
Monday
I was busy writing & sewing all
the morning. Mrs Ellison spent
the evening with us.
Tuesday
I was sleeping all the morn-
ing in espying music.
Immediately after dinner
Mr Ellison & James Doughty
came to walk with us.
We went up to Mrs Houghton's
The Ladies had all gone
out - Mr Ellison was in
very fine spirits, in fact
we were all very gay. in
our walk we met with a
very pretty little spring, near
which was a rustic seat on
which we rested ourselves
while we drank from the
limpid stream. It would
have been very romantic
had we been in nine pensive
mood - We returned home to
tea, after having had a very
agreeable walk.
Wednesday
Susan & I went to the City in
the morning. We went to see
Mrs Lamb from Boston - Esther
Smith, Mrs Thorne, Misses
Thorn & The Merrills. Mr & Mrs
Browning & Miss Benson
came out in the morning. I
received a long letter from E.P.
B--
Thursday
Mama, Uncle & Julia went to
the City. I read & served most
of the morning - Mrs Beale paid
us quite a long visit. Directly
after dinner the two Mrs
Yosts & Mr L. Hardell came
out. They stayed until after
my clock - we had a very
pleasant evening.
Friday Oct 8th
I commenced making a pair
of cordets I was very busy
during all the morning
In the afternoon we took a
very pleasant walk. Mr
Ruggles & Mr Word spent
the evening with us.
Saturday
I finished my ensets at
three o'clock. In the after-
noon took a short walk &
was here 7 o'clock. No company
Sunday 3rd
We all went to church at usual
& heard the Colton preach a very
good sermon. after church we
went to Mrs Thornson's.
Monday
Mrs Deane came down to see her
as -- We commenced the quilting
of the breakfast & were all very busy
at it all the morning. Mrs Laph
& her brother Mr Elliot paid us
a short visit in the afternoon
Mr & Mrs Smith & Miss Ryan
spent the evening with us.
Tuesday
Sister Ann & I went to the City. we
went to see Mrs Gillis, Mrs Thom-
son & the Newells. I letty was
very busy preparing to go to Phila-
delphia. No company
Wednesday
We were busy quilting all the
morning & evening. It is very
pleasant work I think.
Thursday
A very fine day. We were occupied
again the whole day quilting.
Friday
A very rainy day, we had a fine
time for work & began another
quilt. Mama read aloud to us
Saturday
It rained all the morning
but cleared up before dinner.
we had a visit from old Mr
Brackenridge. - we quitted all
the morning. I read Madame
de Genlis in the afternoon, &
finished it after tea; it is a
book with which I am very
much pleased. - I found it
interesting & very amusing.
(Sunday 10th)
We all went in to church and
heard a Mr Smith (from Phila-
delphia) preach. - if he is generally liked, it is probable he will
be called - he is quite a young man,
we were all very much pleased
with him. After church I returned
home with Helen - Hettys does not
seem well at all - she intends going
next week - Helen & the captain.
came out with me in the afternoon in their
carriage - they could not stay to
tea - Mama & the girls went in
to the City to hear Mr Blagden -
Mr Ellison James Toughey spent
the evening with us. Mr E. Trill as
of Mrs Abraham Bradley's death -
(Monday)
I was busy quilting until two. Mama
visited Mrs Julia's Bayard went in to
Mrs Bradley's funeral - It was after
five when they returned & just
then Mrs St. Smith's carriage drove
up to the door - They stayed but a
very short time I wrote a very long letter to
Rose Whit (Tuesday)
We began another quilting & as it was
a rainy day, we were not interrupted & quitted all the morning and
evening. (Wednesday)
Another rainy day! There seems an
end to the rain - I have a read.
"Old Mortality," aloud to us
while we worked.
Thursday
Still raining, stifling! - however
even as we were very much
interested in "Old Mortality,"
& our work. The time passed
very pleasantly.
Friday
A dear day at last! Mama
& Julia went to the City.
We had a long visit from Mr
Wood - Esther Smith sent us
out "Blarence" - a new novel by
Mrs Settgenie - we commenced
reading it after tea.
Saturday
A most delightful day. I went to
the City. I went to see Louise
& her cousin Miss Baldwin
who has lately arrived from New
Haven - she appears to be a very
pleasing girl & I think I shall like
her very much - when I left Helena
I did a little shopping & spent
the rest of the morning with Aunt
Shannon. We read "Blarence," about
in the evening.
Sunday 27th.
William was so sick, he was not able
to drive - We then for all walked
up to Rock buck church. Where we
heard the Ash preach a very interest-
ing sermon - the day was very
damp & unpleasant & of course our
walk was not very pleasant. I wrote
in my journal all the afternoon.
Mr Ellison spent the evening with us.
Monday
Another dismal rainy day. I worked
& practiced in the morning & read
"Blarence" aloud in the evening.
Received a long note from Helen.
Thursday
A bright, brilliant day! which
I was very glad to see. For an
hour & a half after breakfast I
practiced - then sewed, wrote &
read until dinner - I finished
the second volume of Horsell's
Ancient History". After dinner we
went out to see Mrs Hand, who has
lately returned from New England
she has a very fine baby & is very
well - we returned home to tea
after which I read "Coleraine"
aloud, we finished it. I like
it very much indeed, the inter-
est is kept up throughout - and
though rather romantic for
the present day. I like it very
much & think on the whole it
is a very well written book.
Wednesday
A very stormy day. I cleaned up in
the afternoon - I commenced reading
"Patience", a novel by Miss
Edgeworth - I read aloud all
the evening.
Thursday
A very fine day - Bagard went
to the Races - Mrs Agg. Mrs
Blackford & Mr Ellison spent
the evening with us. Mr & Mrs
Hand paid us a short visit
in the afternoon.
Friday
I was busy most of the morning
clean stocking. I read "Patience"
aloud in the afternoon & evening.
Saturday
The weather still continues
very fine - for a wonder! I went
to the bits & spent the morning
with Helen - very pleasantly.
In the evening I saw read aloud
"Patience" -
Sunday 24th
They all went to church as usual, it was my turn to stay at
home. Mrs. Bedford, Miss Baldwin came in the
afternoon & stayed to tea - Miss
B. is quite pretty & very pleasing.
Monday
I was busy serving first of the
morning duties & then Susan
went to the City. I read aloud
in the afternoon. Captain and
James Dougkty spent the eve-
ning with us.
Tuesday
Susan & I in the morning went
over to see old Mrs Williams
& paid her quite a long visit.
De Bollins & one more clergyman
Mr Smith, Mr. Bernard & Mr
R. Smith spent the afternoon
& part of the evening with us.
Wednesday
A very fine day, I went in, to stay
a day or two with Helen -- In
the morning I went to see Julia
Seaton & G. Hindsley. In the
afternoon Helen & I went to see
the Randolphs we returned home
to tea. (Thursday 28th)
The City was in a great hustle
& confusion, occasioned by
the celebration of the late
French revolution. All the
military of the City & George Town
turned out -- there was a very
long procession -- in which a
great number of the citizens
heads of department, President,
Diplomatics & we joined --
Mr W. Jones delivered an Oration
from the Eastern Portico of the
Capitol -- there was a Ball in the
evening.
Helen, Mr L. Hewell & myself
took a delightful walk in the
afternoon. Friday
Helen & I went on the Avenue
in the morning & went to see
Mrs Stone &c returned
home with Papa. At sun-
set Susan, Julia, Bayard
& myself rode up to Mrs Aggs
young Mrs Blackford gave
us home very sweet music
We spent a very agreeable eve-
ning -- on our return home
we met Mrs Ellison & James
Doughty, who had been at
our house & came up to
walk home with us -- we
had a very merry walk home.
Saturday
I was reading "Paternage," nearly
all the morning -- I finished
it, & like it very much -- Sister
Ann, Susan, Bayard & myself
spent the evening at Mrs
McKinnis. I received a letter
from Rose Wilt yesterday.
Sunday 31st
We all came into church as
usual & heard Mr Smiths
preach -- after church we went
to Mrs Thornton's where I saw
Louise -- Mr Ellison spent the
evening with us.
Monday 1st November
We came out into the city as
we about leaving the house
cleaned -- she said all night
with Mrs Thornton. We were
busy all the morning preparing
for moving -- no company --
Tuesday-
Susan went in to assist
Mama - I served I read all
day - Mr Ellison spent the
evening with us-
Wednesday
A dismal rainy day - we were
all very busy moving - Bayard
spent the evening with Mrs
Ellison. Thursday
We were all in great con-
fusion & very busy as it
was the last day of our
moving - Papa, Uncle and
Bayard went in in the
morning, I did the Ann, Julia
& myself went in in the
afternoon - I really felt very
pry to leave the country -
we got in just at sunset, I
found the house all fixed
very nicely - Helen was there
& I went to ask us all to come
there & spend the evening - but
Mama was too much fat-
igued - Susan, Bayard and
myself however went in -
Papa dined at the President's -
the dinner was very open -
did I about 40 persons sat
down to table, they were
3 hours at table.
Friday
A very fine day - We received
a very early visit from Mr
Lyon, who had just arrived
in the city - Helen came in
after dinner to ask me to
walk. Lloyd & Bayard accom-
panied us -- we had a very
pleasant walk -- Mrs Thir-
ton, Mrs Berstein, Helen
& me Lynn & me King spent
the evening with us.
Saturday
Another delightful full day --
Susan, Helen & myself went
a short swing about one o'clock --
Mr Wood came to see us in
the afternoon & Mr Ellison
in the evening.
Sunday
Susan, Helen, Lloyd & myself
walked down to hear Mr
John's preach in the morn-
ing -- I received a letter from
Ketty -- In the afternoon we
went to our own church -- Gen
& Mrs Macomb came from
from church with us & said
to us --
Monday
A very cloudy day -- we were
very busy during all day -- Mrs
Ferstond & Julie paid us quite a
long visit -- Mrs Branch had
a large party but as the evening
was so bad we did not go.
Tuesday
Another very disagreeable day,
I was busy writing most of the
morning -- I had sketches of a
naval life -- all the afternoon --
Wednesday
Bayard & myself walked out to
Holocoma in the morning, and
had a very pleasant visit
In the afternoon I walked
with Helen - Mama, Susan,
Bayard & myself spent the
evening with Mrs Johnston -
was gone 2 family & the King
went there & we had a very
happy & pleasant evening --
Thursday
I was very much occupied
all the morning drawing - Mr
King, Helen & Mrs Wood spent
the evening with us.
Friday
A dismal rainy day! I spent
the whole morning & afternoon
on my desk which I finished.
Saturday
Miss Lydia English spent the
morning with us -- I went
to the church with
other visitors came, when I
did not see -- Mr Ellison &
James Doughty came in the
afternoon & stayed to tea but
could not spend the evening
Mama, Papa, Bayard & myself
went to a party at Mrs Smith-
Ogle Taylor's -- it was most large
part brilliant & pleasant.
Tuesday 14th --
Mama, Julia & myself went
down to the Mission Church
& heard an excellent sermon
from Mr Patfey -- after church
we went to see Mrs Scantlin
& Mrs Taylor. In the afternoon
I went over to see Helen --
they expected Kitty & were all
very much delighted when they
see the Stage drive up to the
door -- Helly insisted on my
spending the evening with her.
Monday
I was busy all the morning
making cake -- bed -- and Born-
ford, Lucy, Louise, Ruth, Helen,
and Mr Hagan & I have spent
the evening with us -- We
had a very gay & agreeable eve-
ning -- Mr Lyon also spent the
evening, he told us that he
intended to leave Washing ton
the next day -- as I was very
anxious, I sent him to take a letter to Mr
Wit for me -- I sat up after
the family had all retired
to rest & wrote quite a long
letter --
Tuesday
A very delightful day -- Uncle
was so much more that he
had to keep his room -- Mr
Lyon came to bed as far well.
I went shopping with Helly &
Helen -- Sister Ann, Susan, Bay-
ard & myself went down & spent
the evening with Mrs Gillis
& her little -- the both very
well & seems very happy --
We had quite a pleasant
evening, Mr Ellison who we
sent rode home with us.
Wednesday
The weather is now delightful
but it is too warm for it to
last long, I am afraid -- Uncle
still keeps his room & the doctor
attends him --
Monday November 22nd
Admiral rising day - Helen
came in & spent most of the
morning with us. Her compa-
ny with us in the evening.
Tuesday
I was very busy during all the
morning. I hope this rainy
weather will not last long.
it rained almost incessantly
all day - Mrs Hillis and Mrs
Thorton came to see us. Mr
King spent the evening with
us.
Wednesday
Another rainy day - Helen
spent most of the morning with
us, Dolly butts the afternoon and
Thursday
Mr R. & Mr Z. Hewitt spent the
evening.
Friday
Busy writing from the Histori-
cal Summary most of the morn-
ing - after dinner Susan & myself
talked with Papa - I was
the first time had been out
of the house for a week - On
our return home Helen, Mrs
Ellison & James Boughty there
was Thornton & his mother came
soon after & they all spent the
evening with us - it was very
agreeable.
Saturday
We were very much surprised
with a visit from Miss B. Belt
a very old friend of ours - there
was a great deal of company
during the morning - Mr &
Mrs Island, & Mr & Mrs Gunley
came in after tea. I received
a letter from Mrs Wat.
Saturday
Mrs B. Belt stayed with us
until after dinner - Mrs Gillespie
spent the day with us. Hettie
came in after dinner - Mr
King spent part of the evening
with us.
Sunday
Another dismal day! I never
knew any weather like this.
We all went to church and
heard Mr Smith preach.
Mama & the girls went in
the afternoon but I did not.
Helen came & stayed most of
the evening.
Monday
It rained heavily all day. I was
bush all the morning making
cake - Mr Wood & Mr Bulfinch
came in after tea.
Tuesday
It rained heavily all the morn-
ing. I went & served until din-
ner -
Wednesday
I was very busy serving in my
silk dress all the morning. In
the afternoon I took a short walk
with Hettie -
Thursday
A very fine day. Helen and
I took a very long & pleasant
walk in the afternoon - on my
return home, I found Mr Ellin-
son James Dougley at our
house - they came to walk
with us but as soon I u
were at home they stayed
with Mama and spent the
evening as did Mrs and
Sawed also - Sister A. Susan
spent the day at Mrs Houston's.
Friday
I was out most of the morn-
ing visiting & shopping - Mrs
Houston, Miss Brodie, Mrs
Temple & Mr Ellison
spent the evening with us
it was very agreeable, and I
appeared to be a very sweet woman.
Saturday
I was busy during until two
when we all went to our
new museum, accompanied
by Mrs Houston, Mr Hewett
& Mr Wood. We were quite
surprised to find that in so
short a time, they had formed
so good & interesting a
collection. In the after-
noon Helen & I took a walk.
I returned home with her
& spent the evening - it was
as usual very agreeable time.
Sunday 6th.
The girls, Helen & myself
went to Mr John's church
the day was very unpleasant
& I did not go out in the
afternoon - Bapt. Dougherty &
James came in, but did
not stay long after tea - I
read "Beck's Remains," & the
Bible all the evening.
Monday
When we arose in the
morning, we found it was
snowing quite fast -- it did
not however remain long
on the ground, as it was very
wet from previous rain --
it is the first snow we have
had -- In the afternoon it
cleared up very brilliant
& bright -- but quite cold.
I wrote a letter to E. Boyd,
and copied some for Papa.
I went abroad in the evening.
Tuesday
Went abroad in most of the
morning. In the afternoon
When I walked -- She
spent the evening with us
as did, also Mr King, Mr
H. Smith & W. Eliot.
Wednesday
A very rainy day -- I served all
the morning on my place in
fine dress -- I went abroad in
the evening. + 8th
Thursday
A very fine day -- I served all
the morning on my dress -- In
the afternoon Bayard & I went
to see E. Smith -- Mrs Stanton
& Mrs Smith, Mrs Graham
& Bolly balls spent the evening
Friday
I served until one o'clock --
When I went with Papa &
Maria to pay some visits --
Mr Hillbach brought our
piano home -- we were
all delighted again to have
it, it seems to be in excellent
order -- Susan, H.B. & I walked
in the afternoon -- I spent the
evening at Mrs Hewell's --
Saturday
I sweated most of the morn-
ing, finished my new deck
In the afternoon read the
new number of the "Museum".
Miss Lydia English & Mr Wood
spent the evening with us
Sunday 12th.
A very pleasant day. Mama
Julie, Beyond myself went
to the Unitarian Church,
Mr Palfrey gave us an ex-
cellent sermon - after ser-
vice we went to see Mrs
Seaton. I wrote in my
journal & read all the
afternoon, the rest went
to church. Mama & myself
spent the evening at Mrs Thra-
wn'd, as she sent for us. No
ling was there.
Monday
I was damp & cloudy day. I wrote
until one o'clock then went
with Mama to pay some visits in
Genessee town. It rained all the
afternoon I practiced until
near dark. Lloyd Russell spent
part of the evening with us. after
which we read aloud "Maurice
& Berthea" - it is very interesting
Tuesday
A dismal rainy day! I was very
much occupied in doing all
the morning - Mr Ellison paid
us a long visit - Mr Taylor and
his son spent part of the evening
with us
Wednesday
A clear cold day! Mama, Julia
& myself, went up to Holorama
and spent most of the morn-
ing - James Doughty came up
to see us after dinner, as we
were going to walk went with
us. Helen also went - we had
a very pleasant walk - Mr H.
Smith & Mr Boulware spent
the evening with us.
Thursday
I went into Mr Russell's
about twelve - I was detain-
ed there by a violent storm
- all day.
Friday
I was out shopping, visiting
most of the morning - In
the afternoon went to see
the hand of Mr's Hettle -
Helen & Lloyd spent the
evening with us.
Saturday
I was busy during most of the
morning - In the afternoon I
practiced - Mrs Swerden, Mr
Baggles, Dr Collins, Mr Ellison
& Mr Wood spent the evening
with us - I had a dreadful
tooth-ache all the evening
therefore did not enjoy myself
very much -
Tuesday 19th.
A dismal rainy day, I did
not go to church but read
& wrote all the morning -
I spent the evening with
Mrs. Bemford at Mrs. Thomas'
house - Monday
I immediately after breakfast
sister Anna & Helen went with
me to Dr Gannell's to have
two teeth extracted -- I gave
me a great deal of pain --

Observations on, & reflections upon Philosophy.
From the earliest ages Greece has been distinguished by its pursuit of
learning & wisdom. It has ever afforded a permanent argument to philosophy.
The philosopher were all bound in idle speculation, which excused the
recurring passion & served to display their ingenuity & acuteness, or vague
impatience about the origin of creation. Researches of this kind produced
but little benefit to individuals & none to the community. From this general
remains, Socrates should be excused where were a part conducted from him
to the office of chief magistrates & legislators. His excellent code of laws were
adopted by the Athenians & entitled them to their lasting gratitude.
About the same time with Socrates, two Thales, the founders of the Ionian
school, which were burdened with investigating the nature & origin of things
attending little to their subjects which more immediately concern the
happiness of human life. The merit of correcting this error & introducing
a Philosophical calculation to improve the mind & enlighten the social
relations is entirely to be assigned to Socrates.
This eminent wise, a good man was born in a village near
Athens, about 400 yrs before Christ. His parent were poor & Socrates
his father was a stonemason & left his son little besides his art, & by
he had for some time to gain his subsistence. Into a wealthy
Athenian, remarking the strong propensity to study discovered by this
generously took him under his patronage & gave him the instruction
of his children -- In this situation he enjoyed the advantage of
attending the lectures of the worst philosopher, by which his thirst
for wisdom was so increased that he sustained every idea of emoluments
& indeed himself to the pursuit of wisdom -- with every advantage
which learning could secure he appeared at Athens as a good Athens
a true philosopher. He distinguished himself in several military
engagements by his temperance & sobriety & at several times in the
field of battle saved the life of Archimedes & Zenonikon -- About
the age of 60 he first served for country in a civil capacity
when he was chosen a member of the senate of five hundred;
here he uniformly opposed every species of injustice & centralism
only to at the expense of his life vindicated the rights of the
citizen -- But it is as a philosopher & moralist that Socrates
is most distinguished -- Having seen with regret how much the
Athenian youth were misled & thus principally corrupted by
philosophers who spent all their time in idle declamation
& by Sophists who taught the art of false eloquence & deceitful
reasoning, Socrates formed the generous design of instituting
a more useful mode of instruction. He justly conceived the end
of true philosophy to be, not to make an intellectual Fable
of superior learning & ability in subtle Speculations or ingenious
conjectures,
but to free mankind from Prometheus ignorance, to correct their views, to inspire
them with a love of virtue & thus to conduct them in the path of wisdom
to true felicity; he therefore appointed the character of moral philosopher, &
considering the whole city of Athens as his school, he seized every occasion
of communicating moral wisdom to his fellow citizens. It was his custom
in the mornings to visit the places of public exercise & walking, where
every one used to appear among crowds in markets & courts, then spending
all the time in the most frequentable parts of the city. Sometimes he addressed
an audience about him in the Gymnasion (a pleasant meadow on the borders
of the river Hippus) where he delivered his Discourses from a chair, while his
audience were seated around him. At other places he conversed in a
less formal way with his fellow citizens whether he met them, or with his
friends at their meals, or in their houses of amusement. Thus making
every place where is afforded, the School of virtue. He never assumed
the air of a mover of great intellect, but communicating useful instruction
with all the ease & pleasure of polite conversation --
Avoiding scientific or metaphysical Disquisitions, the great object of
all his Discourses was to lead men to an acquaintance with themselves,
to convince them of folly & vice & to inspire the love & practice of virtue.
Cicero, then justly said of Socrates that he was the first who called
Sown Philosophy from the heaven to earth & introduced her into the
public walks & domestic retirement of men. The moral lessons which
Socrates taught, he diligently practised. Thus his whole life this good
man ever discovered a mind superior to the all actions of wealth &
power.
Contrary to the general practice of the prosecutors of his time, he prosecuted

A faith, which teaches man that God is an ever present authority,

I have had a solitary, but delightful walk. The late cold weather has greatly
changed the appearance of the country & the verdure of every tree & the
rich coloring of autumn have changed for myself how. The after
noon was cool but clear. I had walked in the valley of a stream,
the following lines occurred. Thanks to a kind Providence, the actual
they desire is imaginary, suggested by the scenery & not by my own
feelings.-
That thou not even some rude & desert coast,
Or bare and waveless tribes upon the rugged rocks,
Where never end or expand where ever the green leaves
Whithering on the blast, the unpolying rock and valley?
That thou had seen more state
So chill so dreary, so solemn am I.
The kindly, gleam of friendship sheds its rays.
The gentle warmth of love has long expired
And with it dies artifice, its tender flowers
Werde my stream of life no longer bloom
But miffed by disappointment freezing blast
Die withered on the ground.

As Idleness is the parent of every vice, & as vice is the cause of most
of that wantchessness we meet with in society, no means to relieve the
misery of others can be more effectual than affording them an honest
mode of subsistence. Education affords the sweetest method of attaining
this end. But as poverty prevents a numerous class of citizens from
giving this advantage to their children, schools have been established
where the poor could be instructed without expense, & receive
trades, which would yield them an honest livelihood.
As there is no part of the community, so exposed to need &
misery as the female sex, it should be the first earnest care
of benevolence, to protect their weakness & relieve their necessities,
as habits of industry, are best adapted to promote this end
a small association of young ladies have taken under their
care, the female children of poor parents, but as their limited
resources, after giving a plain education will not allow them
to give these children, trades, by which they may gain a
future subsistence, they are induced to apply to the benevolence
of others.

For some days past the character which for a long time, I have so minutely
intensely enjoyed, has been disturbed. My spirits have been unanswerable, which
should attribute it to bodily indisposition, but in truth I cannot say this
is the only cause, I have found with all my endeavours to the contrary,
that I am still too dependent on others for my happiness. The convention
of three or four friends has thus entirely been almost the only source
of pleasure or consolation; it has been expensive & valuable; & when by
any accident it is cloven I feel lost & defeated. This might not be
the case, with my own mind & my own heart. I should lay up
stores of enjoyment, to which I could always resort when alone.
For these many months past, my thoughts have been perplexed
& doubtful, which increased by reflection, these doubts render
my understanding a blasted, my heart, I sought for truth, but in
obtaining new light, I was involved in theodoric darkness. There now
are those unshaken hopes, that humble trust, that fervent love,
which used to animate devotion! Hope, when I need, I have
no longer realise the presence of my heavenly Father, but instead
I feel surrounded by falsehoods, I feel like a felon &
unsignificant being, toying upon a tumultuous ocean, without
the night of any horizon. I doubt not indeed, the government of
God, but I feel that intimate a constant persuasion quit, which used
to persuade my mind, which connected every present event, with
the idea of divine government. Such evil, but no benefit, was
produced by the memories into which I had entered. I determined to
change the current of thought, after a few vigorous & indiscernible
succeeds. I have entered a different course of reading, in stead
of history, or controversial disquisitions, confine myself to moral
& religious subjects. I already feel the good effects of this plan.
The motto which observes my views of filantropy are drawing

It is the nearest basis on which virtue can rest. Who, that constant
& believes it feels, that the creator a governor of the world, is ever prone
& takes cognizance of each word, thought, action, use, that forms

Who, that believes each occurrence of his life, to be the design of

Why do I perpetually perplex myself with those questions which I cannot even
— understand, or find which history does not explain? The Christian religion
contains a system of morals calculated to produce individual & general
virtue; virtue whose effusion is happiness. About this there can be no
doubt, this system is more perfect than any other known to me; nor
therefore deduces that I should adopt it. To say that there is no
other as perfect, is asserting that which I did not know, I am for
instance but little acquainted with the real state of China, one of
the most populous countries on the globe. All I have to do is to
choose the best, & to make that the rule of my life.
There is no duty relative to God, to others, or to myself, which
revealed religion does not teach, to study it therefore & to regulate

to give me eternal happiness, if it is in this way only,

The difference in human characters, is not confined to the
the prominent features or leading dispositions of an individual,
but extends itself to the minutest aspects of circumstances.
Two men, magnanimous the same salutation from a third,
to one it may seem, frank & affectionate to the other
distant & indifferent. Two men may contemplate the
same object, one with emotions of delight, the other with
those of disgust. Our perceptions of beauty & deformity, are
not always the result of different objects, but of different
dispositions in the view of the same object. It is impossible
for one man, to determine by his own experience what will
give pain or pleasure to another. It is impossible therefore
for any individual, to give a true picture of another. I was
led to these reflections, by the difference found in the
character of Johnson, when described by Foxwell, & when
delimited by himself. I cannot help wishing that he
had been his own historian. He alone knew, the motives which
decided his conduct, the feelings which impelled to action.
To judge man from appearances in our only mode, yet is
it possible to err so & mistake? Is the motive, which
decides an action to be esthetic or criminal.
Johnson -- "For the only method, by which religious truth can be established,
is by Martyrdom. I am afraid there is no other way of ascertaining the
truth, but by persecution on one hand, & enduring it on the other."
So said Johnson: even his great mind, unaltered free from prejudice,
& his attachment to the established church, leads him to renounce those
who differ from it. He would, forbid freedom of thought, but he would
restrain & even forbid the freedom of expression. He affirms of the
exercise of civil authority over the religion of men, & would oppose
to human favor, that judgment, which surely should be left to
God. When there are such infinite differences among in the opinions
of men, is it possible that one man, should require all to conform to his notions of truth, & prevent them from conformity?
Why need there be persecution to ascertain truth? Would it
not be better for every one to know what he desires to be truth?
and must not the breed of suffering, frequently perpetuate error?
If the civil authority, had been able to silence the reformers, we
had still been involved in the superstitions of the church of Rome.
That many, error, & corruption have entered into the present
Christian church, must be allowed, & if freedom of enquiry & enquiry

The more intimately we are acquainted with the history of men, the more apparent
appears the distribution of happiness, learning, genius, fame, power & wealth.
This desired & reverenced by mankind, cannot confer happiness on the recipient.
There is an art in being happy, which the poor & the humble, & sometimes
the rich, with excuse, & which the wise & the wealthy can never acquire.
In reading the works of Johnson, who, would not believe that his strength
of mind, might contrive & devise to own power, that his religious faith
would have raised him above the little idea of life, & have illuminated
all its gloomy scenes! that his extensive stores of knowledge, would
not have afforded him ample means of diversifying all his hours?
Yet, he was a melancholy, depressed being, frequently discontented
with life & yet afraid of death— Hope was often a burden, yet he
struggled with honor from the moment that he could not live from it.
The loss of a beloved wife, broke the dearest tie which held
him to the world, & he had to seek among strangers, that society
which he could not find at home. Friends, companions, & fame
were left him, but a melancholy disposition & diseased body, allowed
him not their enjoyment.—
Lemmanson, with more than Johnson's advantages was not much
happier. I have just finished a short but interesting sketch of his
life. He had all the desirable ages of education, which the most liberal
plant & the best teachers could afford him. He was distinguished at
the university by his audacious zeal in study. After he left it, he pursued
his studies with such intensity, that he improved his health, a
blessing which in after life was necessarily restored to him.
He married a woman of distinguished excellence & character, who
made him the father of a daughter & son. He was affluent, beloved
& respected & admired. The town in which he lived, afforded
him all the advantages of various extensive society, & his mind
not possessing a full scope for its powers, preyed upon itself.
The loss of his wife, of a lovely daughter, & the derangement of his own
mind completed the catalogue of his domestic misfortunes. He became
moribund, & feeble; the energies of the mind were exhausted, &
life to him, became a wearying & cheerless, painful journey.
The care of his friends & physicians restored him in a perfect degree,
to his former enjoyment, & the choice which he made, of emigration
in a second marriage, afforded a companion, whose understanding
& improvement, enabled her to participate in his literary
labours, whose amiable disposition, cheered the path of life, &
whose tender affection, supported & supported him under all its
troubles. Still he was often misled by gloom & discontent. The health
forbade invincibility of mind, & each was the more anxious to which he
was reduced, that he was constantly harried with the fear of poverty
& disgrace. If at intervals his reason was undermined, it returned
light, derived only to declare to him his approaching dissolution.
Of all the miseries incident to human life, surely the loss of reason
must be the greatest. How humbling is it to the finder of man, to
behold a strong & injurious mind, thus laid in mind! Of the
physicians, which distinguished the lot of Lemmerman, failed in
making him happy, what is there left for us to hope? I never
read of the weak-witted & errors, of men distinguished for their talents
& virtue, without a degree of despondancy. If such men, I assert,
possessed of extensive knowledge & strength of mind, cannot gain
an independence of the little casualties of life, & preserve the resources
& security of mind amidst its little selfishities, what can avail
my feeble efforts? If such men have suffered, who can be free from
suffering? Whatever superiority of intellect, one man may have over
his fellow creatures, the his social wants, his bodily infirmities,
or the caprices of his temper, generally bring him on a level with
the rest of mankind. Lemmerman was born in 1729 at Kings
town in the canton of Bern, & died in 1795.

conmoded by anxiety, 2 soothed by tenderness, the beloved has now
arrived, which is to unite me to the chosen friend
of my heart.— The passions of imagination are to be cast away
for realities. 2 my intellect hopes to be realized.
Let me at this interesting moment, take an impartial
view of human life, 2 let me listen to the voice of ca-
refence, which loudly declares, that human happiness
has ever been & must ever be imperfect. Let me not
then blindly 2 foolishly expect an exemption from those
ills which are the portion of man. I am entering on
new & untriedden path, let me not expect it strenuous
only with flowers, but rather prepare to encounter difficulties
& to meet with disappointments.— The change I
am about to make, is an important 2 momentous one.
New cares & new duties, as well as new pleasures lie before
me. To perform these duties, various in their nature, 2 im-
portant in their nature, is to be the future aspect of my life.
I am no longer to live for myself, the happiness & the
virtue of others is committed to my charge.—
Gracious God! at this moment do I realize that superior
intending power, I acknowledge my entire dependence on thee.
I pray not for riches or for length of days. But I pray for a cheerful
desperation to thy will, & thy grace to enable me, to devote that
life which thou hast given me, to thy glory & to the good of my fellow-
creatures.

Prone to admit the ever changeful scene,
which Nature opens to the observant eye,
I tread delighted the expanse of green
or page with reptiles on the stony sky;
to trace the murmuring streams retires there,
and Switches slay its side, to leave them,
to stretch, catch the torrent distant roar,
and turning clothe with forest foliage dare.
Amid their wilds, we wind our dreary way,
and find our feet waste from human ken.
Beneath the luscious rocks an immense stream
and thoughtful man in wild entangled Glen.
Behold ye Whirling Steam in patient course!
Veak the wild tumult of the waters roar!
be, aged trees brave with inspection free,
Resistless dashed upa the rocky shore!
Succeeding ages still their waters flow,
Then who succeeding ages shall remain,
While a few years shall chill the fervent flame
When adown animates the youthful vein.
The weeks the outskirt land of time shall feel,
and Queen's self in years shall slide away,
Clarity or even state stamp the fact,
has given the promise of immortal day.

One week has this day closed, since I was united to my excellent
husband. Each day of this week, has been marked by events & new enjoy
ment. The animalist & glowing tenderness of love, the kindness of affection,
the mutual notes of friendship, the attentions of general acquaintance, have
all combined, to give value to the passing hours. To be the object,
on which trepidation & love have lavished all their cares, is to be
happy. Happily indeed have I been, not the slightest, not the most
transient cloud, has darkened the sunshine of my felicity. I left
ear & valued friends, & not without regret, & I had with me a
friend, who could compensate for the loss of every human relation.

This little being in the most wretched situation, deprived of liberty, and exposed to every hardship, and danger, which the most hardened criminal, or the most vicious animal, could not inflict upon it. I was much pleased with the reflection of the woman's tale, and with the genuine tenderness she displayed. It on further acquaintance I find no doubt, I doubt nothing but in preference to others, I should be sure, about judging her children out, to arrive at finding the most obvious evidence of her affection for them. I would make a trial of her opinion. After I departed the woman walked awhile during time with Mrs. H. The air was clear & clean & the prospects around me seemed beautiful. In our walk I met at several places, made acquaintance with the Indians as my guide, as the other quarter of nature we never much observed, he conversed for an hour while with a woman who had a son who did not seem happy, he went thro' a garden of large extent, examined the principle of the manufacture, explained with familiarity with the persons employed, who seemed most intelligently to give me all the information they could. After dinner we went to George Town & found the tavern in disarray, returned to our apartment where a cheerful fire awaited me. While Charles was frequently tea, I sat beside my husband & read to him part of the Traveller's. Simplicity but tender conversation gave way to several hours when the table was removed & till my watch was read & dinner appeared & while still in this agreeable scene, we realized the joys of mutual love & conference we talked of, I believe, of the most intimate conversation which mankind can give, of many years eternal comfort & peace, as to poverty, the causes of the great, the most humble, as to personal resources, but we always remarked that family, in neglect could not define, as to happiness, within our own hearts we possessed an inexhaustible store of felicity, secure against all the storms of adversity. The honest & most animated kindness flowed in our hearts & filled our eyes with tears. Another day passed, and another day passed, bitter of experience, may I ever remember that then at the source of every blessing!
It is, in one word, peace.

Directions for the cultivation of the Muskmelon.
At first two smooth, or seed-leaves appear above ground, then
two rough or vine leaves, afterwards in the middle of these, the
third leaf rough & leaf-like appears, as soon as it dies off, it
must be taken off; for if left it would become the main
stock of the vine & ruin a great length, whereas if on its
first appearance it be taken off, instead of one, the plant
will shoot forth two lateral branches; the third leafy &
which appears on each of these, must be likewise destroyed,
This method will prevent a great extension of the vine,
The fruit will thus derive all that nourishment from
the plants, which would in the other case be expended
on the stalk & leaves. — When the fruit is the
size of an egg, the best should be selected & the root
cut off; when it is more than half grown, a stick,
stone or piece of wood, should be put under each
Melon & each day the melon should be turned, but
with great care, lest it should be broken from the

The descent to greatness, however steep & dangerous, may
entertain and active spirit with the consciousness & exercise
of its own powers; but the possession of a throne could never
yet afford a lasting satisfaction to an ambitious mind.
This melancholy truth was felt & acknowledged
by Severus. Fortune & merit had, from an humble
station, elevated him to the first place among mankind.
"He had been all things," as he said himself, "and all
"was of little value." Distracted with the care, not
of acquiring, but of preserving an empire, oppressed
with age & infirmities, harassed of Time, &bettled
with power, all his precepts of life were closed.
The desire of perpetuating the greatness of his
family was the only remaining spark of his ambition & paternal tenderness.
