The religious system of the Germans (of the wild ignorance
of sacrifice can deserve that name) was dictated by their
wants, their fears, & their ignorance. They adored the
great visible objects of nature, the Sun & the moon,
the fire & the Earth, together with three imaginary
Deities, who were supposed to preside over the most
important occupations of human life. They were persuaded,
that by some miraculous arts of divination
they could discover the will of the superior
beings, & that human sacrifices, were the most
precious & acceptable offerings to their alters. Some
offerings has been hastily bestowed on the sublime
notion entertained by the people of the Deities
that they neither confined within the walls of
Temples, nor represented by any human figures;
but when we recollect that the Germans were unshil-
-led in architecture & totally unacquainted with the art
of sculpture, we shall readily assign the true reason,
as from a want of ingenuity. The only Temples
in Germany were dark & ancient graves, consecrated
by the reverence of succeeding generations.
Their secret gloom, the imagined residence of
an invisible power, by presenting no distinct object
of fear or worship, impregnated the mind
with a still deeper horror; & the priests, rude
& illiterate as they were, had been taught by
superstition the use of every artifice that could
preserve & fortify impressions so well suited to
their own interests.
The same ignorance, which renders barbarians
incapable of conceiving or embracing the useful
restraints of laws, empowers them naked & unarmed
to the blind terror of superstition. The German
Priests improving this favorable temper of their
countrymen, had assumed a jurisdiction over
temporal concerns, which the magistrate could not
venture to exercise; and the haughty warrior
faintly submitted to the lash of correction, when
it was inflicted not by any human power,
but by the immediate order of the God of war.
The defects of civil policy were sometimes supplied
by the interposition of ecclesiastical authority.
The latter was constantly excited to maintain silence &
quietness in popular assemblies & was sometimes extended
to a more enlarged concern for the national welfare.
But the influence of Religion was far more powerful
to inflame, than to moderate the furious
passions of the Germans. Interest & fanaticism often
prompted its ministers to sanctify the most daring
& unjust enterprises, by the approbation of heaven
& the assurance of full success. The consecrated
standard long reverend in the groves of superstition
was placed in the front of the battle, & the
hostile army was destined with dire execrations
to the Gods of War & Thunder. In the faith of
soldiers (a faith not the Germans) cowardice was
the most un pardonable of sins. A brave man
was the worthy favorite of their martial Deities; the
witch who had lost his shield in battle, was
alike banished from the religious & civil assemblies
of his countryman. Some tribes of the north seem
to have embraced the doctrine of transmigration,
others embraced a prophetic paradox of immortal Death
& enfeud. All agreed that a life spent in armed
& glorious death in battle, were the best preparations
for a happy futurity, either in this or
another world. The immortality so vainly promised
by the priests was in some degree conferred by
the swords. That singular order of men has most
deservedly attracted the notice of all who have attempted
to investigate the antiquities of the Celtic
Scandinavians & the Germans.

arbres, à la vue du soleil levant ; c'est pour

retentir les déserts de ses terribles rugissements.
Lui, ô mon ame ! le Dieu créateur et conser-
vateur. Que le cantique des hommes s'élève vers
toi, Seigneur, avant eux des autres créatures ;
que l'homme te loue pendant que les
oiseaux sonnent, encore sur les sommets
et dans les bocages. Que mes chants solitaires
préviennent dès la naissance du
crépuscule, et invite tout ce qui existe
à louer le Créateur ! Oh ! que la création
est magnifique ! tu nous y développe
gracieusement les vues de la sagesse
et de ta bonté. Chacun de mes sens
puise des transports dans cette mer

à mon âme ravie. Comment pourrai-
t-elle te balbutier ses louanges ?
Que est-ce que tu obliges, ô Tout-
Puissant ! de sortir du silence sacré
qui environnoit ton hôte, d'appeler des
êtres du néant, et de tirer de la nuit
cet univers immense ? Ce fut ta bonté infinie

nie, et que toutes les créatures que j'étoient

Thus is hardly a principle of the
human mind more extensive in its
influence; & none more necessary or
useful than gratitude. Accustomed
as we are to appropriate the word to signify, almost exclusively, a disposition to
reciprocate favours between individuals,
we will hear with surprise -- that it
is the only true foundation of our duty
towards our Creator & towards our fellow-men -- that it is essential to the existence of
our Society -- & is the source of patriotism
of filial & paternal affection, & friendship.
Thus useful, it is assisted in its operations
by the auxiliary & kindred passions of love,
pity & interest. Although the idea of
the great importance & extended utility of
gratitude presented itself almost as soon as
I had turned my thoughts to the subject,
I was happy to find in Ciceronian sentiments
perfectly coincident with my own.
I could wish (says that illustrious author

-itude. For it is not only itself the greatest
virtue, but also the parent of all others.
What is filial affection, but a grateful
disposition towards parents? Who are good
or useful citizens but those who bear in
mind the benefits of their country? Who are

of the favours of the Gods, offer up to them in
return their grateful yet suitable acknowledgements? What pleasure could there be

It must be self evident that the
adoration which is prompted by inter-
-est or fear cannot be acceptable to
the Deity. "My Son give me thy heart"
is, according to Solomon, his language.
Those therefore err who attempt to
work upon the minds of men by repre-
senting the Almighty - as an unjust
judge condemning to everlasting anguish
those who neglect his ordinances, and
rewarding with endless enjoyments
those who regard them - as that being
who rides upon the whirlwind, and
is heard amidst the thunder and
tempest. Such inducements to religion
are the inducements of interest & fear, &
surely there is no occasion for these.
When we consider that he, who hath
endowed us with lofty faculties, with
the ability to distinguish between
good & evil, & with interminable des-
-tinies, might with equal facility
have made us less than the worm
which perishes under our feet: that
he, who hath placed us in a world affording
abundantly all that is necessary for our
subsistence & happiness, who has spread
abroad on every side the fruitful field
and tilling stream, the verdant lawn
and stately forest, might have cast
our lots in aightful waste amidst
eternal darkness & winter. When we
consider that to God, the author of our
existence, the guardian of our infancy
and protector of our mature years, we
owe the light & warmth of the Sun by
day, & the moon & stars which adorn
the night, the fertilizing showers of
spring, the cooling breezes of summer
& every blessing we enjoy. What
is the man whose bosom is not filled
with grateful emotions, prompting him
to yield in return every thing he can, his
love and veneration to the author of
every good & perfect gift.
Nature has given to man,
neither the acute ness of smell
or hearing, nor the fleetness, nor the
weapons of defence, nor the strength
which she has given to other animals. Helvetius has asserted
that this defective construction
of the human frame is the source
of all our excellence. And he
is no doubt right: not only because
the human capacity as well
as that of other animals is measured
in proportion to the emergency: but
more especially because, conscious
of the insufficiency of his unaided
exertions either for his support or
defence, man is compelled to seek
assistance from his fellows. The
foundations of society are laid in
our necessities: & most of our im-
provements spring from society.
The boasted endowments of speech &
reason are not inherent in man,
but acquired from intercourse with
his fellow men. "We have instances
(says Rattel) of persons, who, having
grown up to manhood among the bears
of the forest, enjoyed not the use of
speech or of reason, but were, like the
brute beasts possessed only of sen-
sitive faculties." Society, thus im-
portant, and arising from the necessity
of mankind for mutual assistance,
could never exist without gratitude
which implies an interchange of
favour. To judge of the import-
ance of gratitude in Society,
we need only imagine to ourselves
the wretched condition of a com-
munity where no man either re-
membered or returned the
the obligations he had received.
Gratitude creates obligations
in proportion to the benefits received.
Most love, most veneration, most
attention is due where we have received
most favours. Thus our duty to God com-
prises as being our first & greatest
benefactor. Then comes our duty to
our Country, our Parents, our Friends,
our Relations, our fellow citizens,
& last of all the whole human fam-
ily. Man is a being so constituted
that he seldom looks to second causes
or to what is without the range of his
sensitive faculties; & hence it is, that
seeing most of the benefits he enjoys
to come from his country or his
parents, his patriotism & his filial
affections are usually stronger
than his love of the Duty, which
he does not consider as the ultimate
source of all good. We can never
love, either that Country, or that
parent, or that friend, or that man
who has done little for our good
& much for our injury. And
in proportion to the goodness of the
government under which we live
to the parental attentions we
have received, to the love of our
brother or our friend, so will be
the ardour of our patriotism, &
the strength of our filial & fraternal
affection, & friendship. For these
affections are, as we have said,
founded in gratitude & gratitude
increased with the increase of
the favours confended.
I have but entered upon my
subject. But it is an old saying that
we never know our weaknesses till
experiment discovers them nor was
I aware of my incompetency to write
an essay on gratitude suited to
a Ladies portfolio until I had attempted
it. I shall cast that dry remark
upon a title topic with the observation of Cicero that "There is no Duty
more necessary than gratitude."

Thing, like a gem, on the brow of the sky;

Look to the waters!— asleep on their breast,
Seems not the ship like an island of rest?
Bright and alone on the shadowy main
Like a heart— cherished home on some desolate plain.
Who— as she smiles in the silvery light,
Spreading her wings on the bosom of night,
More on the deep, as the moon in the sky.
Or phantom of beauty— could deem, with sighs,
That so lovely a thing is the mansion of sin,
And souls that are omitted lie bursting within?
Who— as he watches her silently gliding
Remembers that wave after wave is devoting
Bodies that scream and guilt could not sever,
Hearts that are parted and broken for ever?
Or deems that he watches, affront on the wave
The death bed of hope, or the young spirit's grave?
Like a rebel at sea, amid sunshine and song!

Gaily we glide, in the grace of the world,
With steamers afloat and with canvas unfurled;
All glad of, and gay, to wandering eyes,
Yet chartered by sorrow, and freighted with sighs—
Fading and false is the aspect it wears,
As the miles we put on part to our own loss;
And the withering thoughts which the world cannot know
Like heart— broken spirits, lie burning below;
Whilst the vessel drives on to that desolate shore
Where the dreams of our childhood are vanquished and dies!

O! let the soul its slumber break,
Thro' use its senses and awake,
To see how soon
Life, with its glories, glides away
And the stern footstep of decay
Comes stealing on
Your pleasure, like the passing wind,
Blows by, and leaves us nought behind
But sorrow at last;
How still our present happiness
Seems, to the wayward fancy, less,
Than what is past.
And while we oye the rolling tide,
Down which our flying minutes glide
Twixt so fast;
Let us the present hour employ,
And deem each future dream of joy
Already past.
Let no vain hope deceive the mind
No hap join let us hope to find
Somewhat than to-day.
Our golden dreams of yore have bright,
Like them the present shall delight
Like them decay.
Our lives like hastening streams must be,
That into one engulfing sea
Are doomed to fall:
The Sea of Death, whose waves roll on,
Viking and Kingdom, crown and Throne,
And swallow all.
Like the river's leadly tide,
Like the humble violet's slide
To that sad wave;
Death levels poverty and pride,
And rich and poor sleep side by side
Within the grave.
Our birth is but a startling place,
Death is the warning of the river,
And death the goal:
There all our steps at last are brought
That path alone, of all unsought,
Is found of all.
Gay, then, how poor and little worth,
Is all those glittering tops of earth
That lurk as here;
Dreams of fast in that death must break,
Has! before it hide as wake,
Ye disappear.
Long ere the damps of death can blight
The cheek's pure glow of red and white
Hath passed away:
Youth smiled, and all was heavenly fair;
He came, and laid his finger there,
And where are they?
Where is the strength that mocked decay,
The step that rose so light and gay,
The heart's blithe tone?
The strength is gone, the step is slow,
And joy grows weary of and woe
When age come on.

The Heirship's Complaint.
Why tell me with officious zeal,
That I am young, and rich, and fair,
And wonder how my soul can feel,
The pangs of sorrow and of care?
Why dost thou court the golden store,
The sparkling jewels that are mine,
And name the suitors 'er and o'er
Who breathe theirincesse at my shrine?
Know that I scorn the sordid train
Whose loveless vows are bought & sold,
Know that the heart I sigh to gain
Despises, spurns, my worthless gold.
I love — I dare not breathe his name,
The son of genius, of mind;
He climbs the sleepy path of fame,
Content to leave the crowd behind.
Wind while in halls illuminated bright,
I hear the same false flatteries o'er,
The patient wastes the midnight light
In studious toil, in learned love.
Seldom he seeks the giddy throng,
And then he stands retired, apart,
And views the dance, & hears the song,
With listless look & joggle heart.
He turns from Love's all speaking eye,
His mind to fame, to science clings,
Throned in a world of visions high,
Of deep, & vast imaginings.
My vaunted wealth, my flattered face,
The praise of coxcombs may employ;
But he regards that drops as base,
He holds that beauty as a toy.
Yet must I still reluctant wear
These flashing gems, these robes of state,
And nightly must submit to share
The futile vanities I hate.
Oh! never shall the world deride
My passion with unfeeling jest,
While smiles of more than Spartan pride
Can hide the tortures of my breast.
My tears flow fast—Now judge if gold
Can banish anguish from its shrine,
And say if ever tale was told
So sad, so sorrowful as mine.

Solomon, and the Queen of Sheba.
The Rabbins tell of an ingenious
invention, which in the Talmud
is attributed to Solomon; and the
story shows that there are some plea-
sing tales in that immense compila-
tion.
The power of the Monarch
had spread his wisdom to the remotest parts of the known world.
Queen Sheba, attracted by the splendour of his reputation, visited this
poetical King at his own court; there
one day to exercise the sagacity of the
monarch, she presented herself at
the foot of the Throne; in each hand
she held a wreath; the one was
conspicuous of natural, & the other
of artificial flowers. Art, in the
labour of the mimetic wreath,
had exquisitely imitated the lively
hue of nature; so that at the dis-
stance it was held by the Queen for
the inspection of the King, it was
deemed impossible for him to decide,
as her question implied, which
wreath was the production of na-
ture, & which the work of art.

his pride. The son of David,
he who had written treatises on

wledge himself outwitted by a wo-

"Write a few lines, 'tis all task"
"Fill but a single page."
Laura, 'tis an easy task
For youth — but not for age.
Know you not that Spring has flown
That all its lovely bloom has gone?
Know you not that Summer's past
And Autumn breathes its chilling blast?
When in you walk and look around,
Withered leaves beset the ground;
Tasted is the lovely green,
And when sunset clothe the scene.
This you know, no hope to find meet;
Violetts springing round your feet;
This you know — no hope to find,
Luscious fruit of summer kind.
Know you not the life of man,
Refashioned on the selfsame plan?
That on its youthful, venial hour,
Sportive Fancy strews her flowers;
That young affections of the heart,
Their genial power to mind impart?
Then, the thoughts as freely rise,
To warling birds in summer skies,
When this inspiring warmth has fled,
Our thoughts are chilled, our fancy dead.
Then vain dear girl what you require,
Fancy denies her kindling fire.
I feel the approach of Autumn roll,
Its chilling influence on my soul.
Well be it so — I'll not repine,
While Autumn richer store is sowed;
The richest store kind heaven sends,
Domestic love, and faithful friends.
— Louisa, when your spring is flown,
Your summer days and joys are gone,
When cold autumn days shall come,
Be yours as dear and calm a home,
A husband suited to your mind
Is true, so tender, and so kind
That when your youth has passed away,
And your maturing decay,
This love like some bright evergreen,
Shall screen, and cheer life's winter scene.
Louisa, round your cheerful hearth
May you enjoy as harmless youth
With objects to your heart as dear
As those you've often met with, here.
And when from us you're far away
Sometimes recall the cheerful day
When gathered round the quilling flame
Our hopes, our fears, our tasks, the same.
The years may pass, and sorrows come,
Do not forget the evening hour
When Sidney's neighbours used to meet,
And pass their time in converse sweet.
No yet forget, how oft you've stayed
On sunny hills, — through forest shade
How happy with your friends you've been
While summer smiled upon the scene.
How often plucked its glowing rose
To twine around your youthful brows.
That youthful brow so smooth and fair!
Unfavored yet by pain or care,
And must it bear the deep impress,
Of dimming age, and dark distress?
That fragrant rose, without a thorn
Sparkling in the dew of morn;
Must it then wither drop and die,
Beneath a cold and flowering sky?
That sunny hill, that woodland shade,
In Nature's loveliest hues arrayed;
How bright they seem! as if decay
Could never wear their charms away.
Those evenings cloaked with social mist
Those cheering friends around the hearth
Those devout joys I wish for you
These - these, alas must vanish too!
Since charms and joys, which spring from earth
Return to whence they take their birth.
— Yet sigh not at the sad presage
Since there's a charm to brighten age
Since there are joys which in decay,
But last when Time has past away.
Then let me dear Louisa say
Forget not these when far away,
When to kind heaven your prayer ascends
Remember then your Sidney friends.

To my dear Mother
With the first Viollets of the Spring 1823.
With what delight in childhood's hour
I've watched the Spring's advancing foot,
With her who loved to mark and trace
Sweet nature's every charm and grace—
Each leaf and every bud that burst
Bore hail and every bud that burst
Were hail with rapture as the first
But to the viollets humble shade
Were our first visits always made,
Searching the earliest bud to find
To shield it from the stormy wind
That soon it might rise and bloom
And yield to the its sweet perfume.
But sometimes to our surprise
A flower unnoticed would arise
The one we thought would soonest blow
Had still to bear the frost and snow.
Oh with what fond and eager haste
The first flower on thy breast was placed,
That breast where all the virtues meet
And blest religion finds her seat.
But she who loved the opening spring
And loved to see its flowers to bring
She whom we loved is now no more
Our earthly hopes for her are over.
Oh! can we ever cease to sigh
For those sweet hours, alas, gone by.
Those days of pleasure and of joy
And happiness without alloy
Oh no! in memory they dwell
To be "remember'd oft and well"
Time can her image nier efface
But death for her remembrance trace.
Let the sweet humble widow's fate
Be emblematic of her state.
Perhaps you did not think that she,
The youngest of our little band,
That she the first would gather, be
By your heavenly Father's hand.
Yes she has first been called away
To the bright realms of endless day
Like the fair flower, this left below
The stormy wind and winter's snow,
Removed to that celestial home
Where earthly blisses can never come
She has exchanged a world of light
For one of glory and of light
And on her Heavenly Father's breast,
Her soul enjoys eternal rest.
The sentiment of filial and sisterly affection
Which animates these simple lines, I know will
be sufficient to recommend them to my sweet home,
because in her bosom are the same chords of
love, that will vibrate with the touch of sympathy.
Long, long may you enjoy all the delight
which flows from these affections, and be spared
the anguish which arises from bereavement.
But when it last the swearing stroke shall
come, may you be sustained by that hope
which looks beyond the tomb.
J.B.

The strong hold of Friendship is lasting,
And firm as a rock in the Heart;
But Love is delusive swaying,
And owns all its beauty to art.
Tho' it beams like a brilliant Lightning,
It shines over its own distant tomb,
Like the flash of the Heaven's redlightning,
Encircling the darkness and gloom.
Let me claim then a spot in your bosom
To Friendship and Memory dear;
Where the buds of remembrance may blossom,
Their fragrance embalmed with a tear.
The pleasures of life are but fleeting,
They pass like the rays of Spring,
And the heart that with anguish is beating
May soon throb with agony's string.
Let me hail then the joys which have broken
The dark recollections of sorrow,
But this record, alas! is the token
Of long desperation tomorrow.
January—Oh! it flames as if parting,

Of the Sunshine whose Splendor has fled,

"Praise be to him who invented Sleep." Sancho Panza
When baling Sleep its soothing influence sheds,
And lulls in blissful dreams our aching heads,
No longer then by toil or pain oppress
We sink in sweet repose and quiet rest.
For then removed from every anxious care,
We breathe in brighter worlds a purer air,
Range fancy's fairy realms on wing sublime
Free and unfetter'd by the lapse of time.
Mute, in peaceful slumber, long and deep,
The sage-the Shepherd-and their Sovereign sleep,
No longer then the Ambition and the Brave
Pant for the Victor's laurel or the grave-
Een Hated sleeps! yet guiltless of the blow
Which waking dooms to death his hapless foe,
And hopeless Love-forgets its dark despair
In vision roos and wins the beautious fair.
Come sweet sleep! thy powerful aid impart
To soothe the sick, and cheer the sinking heart,
For soon Life's fitful fever will be o'er.
And eyes that weep, will close to weep no more;
Then shall the Spirit wing its upward flight.
Beyond the Stars which girt the brow of Night,
To worlds of light in living verdure dress,
The abodes of peace—the mansions of the blest.
March 15. 1829.

There may be a certain self-surrender of propriety, given on
relations of what is now called taste (an idol that
has misruined our styles;) but Dante and Ariosto
were ambitious of conveying to the minds of others
the impressions on their own, with force and persua-
siveness, and to affect this they could not
refuse to stoop to the meanest images.
Indeed, in spite of all his romance, Ariosto is the poet of
Nature; his images, and he abounds in them beyond almost
any other writer, are from things which seem all to
have come under his own observation. They have all the
simplicity and spirit of proof impressions. They are not
refined from ancient and improved artists, which by
transformation through various hands have lost
the most delicate features of the model,
but they are original drawings by a most original
master. Hence the mighty mixture of the new
and magnificent which they sometimes present,
because it is only by exhibiting natural objects
in unnatural proportions that this can be kept
out of sight. Hence, again, the distinctness of their
images, which when they are introduced for the
purpose of occasion to make use of a lion or a
bear (and what poet has not?) he exhibits them
them in a circus or a cage, or with a rascal about
their necks, more frequently than amidst their
natural haunts; because in the one situation
he had probably seen them with his own eyes,

on trust, if he would describe a stream of blood

Chinese method of propagating various kinds
of fruit-trees:
They strip a ring of bark, about an inch
in width from a bearing branch; surround
the place with a ball of fat earth or loam,
and fast to the branch with a piece of mat-
ting; over this they suspend a pot or horn,
full water having a small hole in the bot-
tom, just sufficient to let the water drop,
in order to keep the earth constantly moist;
the branch throws new roots into the earth
at above the place where the ring was
stripped off. The operation is performed in
the spring, and the branch is drawn off and
put into the ground at the fall of the leaf:
the following year it bears fruit.

of Green House Plants —
Geraniums, are very culture, requiring
a sort of loam with a little peat must
have little water when not in flower
They require more light than ever
green plants with coriaceous leaves & woody
stems, such as the myrtle & camellia, when
they grow large & strong, they should be
cut down, or cut off, for the smaller the plant
in general, the more vigorous the flowering
leaves — The seeds should be sown in
soil of light earth, no sooner as germination
is over they come up a seedling, for seed
may be transplanted into soil of the smaller
size. Seedlings from seeds sown early
in the season will flower the succeeding
autumn, & none will be later than one
year in showing their flowers. To obtain
new sets another way is to put plants home
where they will be influenced by other plants
in flower, produce to same effect.
All those which have not fallen
away or other their roots are propagated
by cuttings of the wood taken off at a
point where the it is beginning to refer
all the thick wood tends to dry up great
difficulty is that one plant will half
with stand above ground — Cuttings from
the root may be taken off at any time
during the Summer season & if the
Summer pots or tubs they are planted
are plunged in a hot bed, they will
become handsome plants in 2 or 3 months
time. Many gardeners plant their cuttings
in the open ground in a shady border
& take them up & pot them in autumn.
In some gardens a number of cuttings
of the hardier kinds are every spring planted
in open borders, where they make a
fine show during summer & though they
are killed by the first frost it is easy
to plant them in the spring. Old
plants, unfit for the green house, may
whenever be planted in open ground &
produce a favourite display of flowers
before they perish.

Mode for cultivating early Potatoes.
We take up all intended for seed next
year before they are ripe, just when
the outer skin feels off, and before
the stalk or stem begins to wither; they
are then laid upon a gravel walk,
fully exposed to the sun, for a month
or six weeks, when they becomes quite
green and soft, as if roasted, and often
much shi p pedled; they are then
put away, and protected as other pota-
toes are. In February we examine them,
when we generally find every eye full
of long sprouts fit to be planted; they
are then cut as described by R.W.; but
less economically, as we seldom make
more than two sets from each tuber,
— the eye, or tip part, and the root or
bottom part. We plant them as descri-
bed by him, the eyes upwards in
both parts; and we observe, as des-
cribed by him, that the potatoes from
the eye or tip sets are earthen by a
fortnight, and that those planted in
the common ground. And let me
observe, in by no means the warm-
est or richest part of our country, the
writer had a dish of ripe potatoes at
dinner last Whitsunday the 14th of
May, and the same every day since,
from successiveal crops, until the
20th of July, when the common
potatoes come in use.
You will perhaps wish to know how
we secure the successiveal crops of
the same variety. In February 1818, the
writer purchased the above variety
from town, &, they were planted the
latter end of March; although
treated as the other potatoes, they
were three weeks or a month earlier
than the general crops. Before they
were ripe, as before described, every
other row was taken up, and the potatoes
exposed to the influence of the
scorching sun; the other rows were
left until ripe, and were laid up
with those taken of unripe, care
being taken to keep each sort separate.
In December they were examined.
Every eye of those taken up unripe
had a sprout almost an inch long, yet
the tuber itself quite soft, was as
hard and all wrinkles had dis-
appeared; while those left to grow
ripe, were as hard as when laid up,
showing no appearance of vegetation.
In February they were again examined.
Those taken of unripe were covered
with sprouts from six to eight
inches long; those taken up ripe began to show sprouts. Each sort was
then cut harrasline fashion, and
planted the same day in alternate
rows of ripe and unripe; and also the
tops and bottoms of both sorts were
set separately in alternate rows. In
the beginning of April, every plant
from the unripe sorts was earlier
than the others; the plants from
the ripe set were only beginning
to appear; the eye sets of those
were evidently earlier than the
bottoms. When planted on litter and
stable dung, they were all covered
with earth, about two or three
inches deep, and were not earthe'd
up, as is usually the case.
Brevity being essential to render
your miscellaneous interesting, I will
not at present enter into further details,
but state to you how they were taken
up. The early potatoes last earthe'd
up, grew close round the stalk or stem,
like eggs in a nest, and at near
the surface, that they may readily
be picked off with the finger,
leaving the stalk or stem standing
uninjured, to produce more potatoes
from the runners. From the eye set
of the unripe tubers we had a full
supply every day for a fortnight,
when those from the bottom set of the
unripe seed came into use for another
fortnight; at that time potatoes from
the eye or top sets from the ripe seed
came into use, and were succeeded
by potatoes from the bottom sets of
the ripe seed. Those kept for seed or
for the table, were earthed up as usual,
and each row produced almost as large
a crop as any two of the rows not earthed
up—the luxury of an early potato
being a greater object than the quantity.
The writer has this day examined
the potatoes preserved for seed (taken
up unripe) of the three varieties
laid in the garden-house, northern
aspect, upon a stone floor, and the
spouts from the eye, on the eye
end of all are nearly an inch
long, vigorous and strong.
By earthing up the potatoes, they
become three weeks later earlier . I
could add much more, but fear-
ful that I shall exhaust your
patience, as well as that of your
readers, I will now conclude.

it has been supposed, in most countries,
that the best and most effectual method, either for
stimulating or for the milk, is to make
the calf suck the mother's milk; it is not so
certainly, that the following is the preferred
method. The calf can drink. When it is three
days old, two-thirds of oatmeal (spurry,
corn meal as good) is made into a paste, and
fed for a minute. It is then left to suck it
until it has drunk as much as it can, which is
one or two quarts of milk that has stood twelve
hours. Then it is given a second time, stir the whole,
and give it to the calf to drink. This method is
designed to make the calf drink by preventing the
fetus from being irritated by the milk, thus
help, and will grow incomparably fatter than by
the other method. This method is not only a
theoretical truth, but its success is not doubted.
The economical advantages that result from it
are striking. According to the old method,
a calf finished at the age of three months is to
suck for three weeks, and times intended for
grazing are left empty. This is supposing
the cow gives only a moderate quantity of milk.
The value of the milk in these three weeks to the
mother is the value of the calf. If, in the new method, we
consider the calf according to this new method, we
consider it as having received only three
quarts of oat-meal, at most, and the elementary
milk.
M. Schune adds, that he has practiced this
method himself, and that his calves have been
always as healthy, and as strong as the others,
and not subject to disease. The only alterations
he has made in the method, is to prevent them
to suck at all, but give them the pure milk of the
mother, and the same quantity every day; because,
he has observed, that the separation of the
mother from the calf is more painful to the mother than when the
calf is taken from her at the time of birth. He
makes no exception, only when the cow calves

mother, and the cow is more easily milked, if

friends, though still of diametrically opposed sentiments, diametrically
opposed; to this I must repeat, that no one can be
personally acquainted with Mr Jefferson & cannot have
known Jefferson. The value of the testimony thus given in Mr Jefferson's
favour, will be more sensibly felt by the knowledge of Judge
B----n's opinion on his political opinions. On
an occasion when he had the company of a bar dinner at his
table, along with other company, some of them ladies, as
usual when the wine was circulating after dinner, toasts were
given, a young lady whose called upon for a toast
gave "Mr Giles," Judge B. looked astonished, & almost angrily
declared, while he struck the table violently with his hand,
"You had better give the devil next!!"
If this man did full justice to Mr Jefferson, whose
political character he looked upon in the same light as
that of Mr Giles --
Although Mr Jefferson has been called a visionary man
& certainly did owe to the science & philosophy on the perfectness
ability of man, yet he was likewise an essentially practical man,
& like Franklin studied the most minute circumstances that
surrounding him influenced the welfare, & comfort & improvement of social life. Among other customs which he thought
did more harm than good, was the futilely wearing mourning
for deceased relatives, & making very expensive funerals.
Could these observances be confined to the rich, they would
be, he said, comparable to harpies, but as such a limitation was impossible, the only way to check the evil, was
in the wealthy class renouncing these expensive shows &
forms of grief, the consideration which is the former
shape, now not only inconvenient, but often ruinous.
On this point, he informed me, except by example, when
he lost his almost idolized daughter Mrs E. —, hardly a death-
day as he felt this bereavement, neither he or any of his family
but on mourning, neither did he make any change in
his usual habits, but continued his dinner parties & received company as usual, considering them as portions of his public duty,
to receive & entertain members of Congress & other official characters. In this he went too far, & miscalculated the common feeling
of humanity, which on such an occasion would have afforded
rather than condemned his excluding himself from for a
whole from society; he had not sufficient faith in the sympathies of human nature & impeded to it an undeserved
degree of self-interest, when he believed it his duty
to enrich the poor, private, in the public man. At the time, persons
said, "what a vile Mr Jefferson is". But it was not otherwise, as
those who saw him watching over the declining life of this beloved child, might have told them. During Jefferson's mother's lifetime he
had with her, with him at Monticello, where he devoted himself exclusively to her. She preferred less to be buried
more easily in the open air, & was daily drawn for hours together through the grounds in a low garden-chair, he never
allowed any one to draw this chair but himself. Daily did
he die. Death did he guard for his lovely & beloved child. Mr Jefferson was no stoic.
As the close of his official life drew towards a close, he
looked brighter & happier, could it be otherwise, even allowing him to
be an ambitious man, for had he not gained the goal & won the
prize, the ambition of an American citizen could obtain. He was
urged by his friends to some matter more than another election,
but positively declined, "he longed," as he expressed himself in
a letter to his daughter, "to be longed for for the privacy & tranquility
of home." To this home he looked as a secure & peaceful
haven where he might repose after the exertions of a period of
a stormy voyage. He tranquilly calculates on Mr Madison as
his successor, consequently on a continuance of the same policy
that had governed his own administration. For this excellent
man Mr Jefferson felt not only the esteem & confidence of the most
perfect friend's help, but an almost paternal affection & was as ambitious for him, as he had ever been for himself.
There are few, if any instances of a friendship so perfect, so
unselfish as that which united these two great men. In
a letter to a friend Mr Madison gives the following account of
the commencement & growth of this friendship.
I was a stranger to Mr Jefferson till the year 1796 when
he took his seat in the first legislature under the constitution of
Virginia, then newly framed being myself at the time myself
a member of that body, & for the first time a member of any
public body. The acquaintance then made with him was very
slight, the distance between our ages being considerable &
other distances much more so. During part of the time whilst
he was governor of Virginia the State, I had a seat in the
council associated with him. Our acquaintance then became
intimatele & a friendship was formed, which was for life &
which was never interrupted in the slightest degree, for
a moment.
It is wonder then that Mr Jefferson looked forward with
satisfaction to the close of his political life, under believing
as he confidently did that Mr Madison would fill the place
he vacated, & would carry out those principles & measures
which he sincerely thought would best promote his country's
good.
In the morning of Mr Madison's inauguration, he asked
Mr Jefferson to ride in his carriage with him to the Capitol,
but thus he declined, & in answer to a friend who enquired
if from delay he had not accompanied his friend
he smiled & replied, "I wished not to divide with him the
honors of the day. I preferred one better to see them all bestowed on
him." A large procession of citizens, some in carriages, &c
on horse backs &c still larger on foot, followed Mr Madison along
Pennsylvania avenue to the Capitol. Among those on horseback
was Mr Jefferson, &c &c unattended by even a servant, un-
interrupcted in any way by any citizen. Arrived at the Capitol
he dismounted &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &c &
It was the design, as was generally understood, after paying this
respect to the new President, that citizens should go to the President's
House to pay a forcible visit to Mr Jefferson, but to the surprise
of every one, he himself, was among the visitors at Mr Madison's.
A lady who was on terms of intimacy with the ex-President
& could therefore take that liberty, after telling him that the
present company & citizens generally deemed to impose
this last opportunity of assuring their respect by visiting on
him, added her hopes that he would be at home to receive
them. Unrefreshed her presence at every hour have been to
disappoint our former supporters to my friends, & multiplied his to
leave this opportunity of joining with my fellow citizens in their
demonstration "This day should be cautiously my friend's" re-
plies he, "I am too happy to be here, to remain at home."
"But indeed Sir you must receive us, you would not let
all these ladies -- all your friends find an empty house, for
at any rate we are determined to go, & to show that even
on this glad occasion, the regret we feel on leaving you."
The countenance expressed emotion, he made no reply, but bowed
expressively. The lady had no positive information to give those
who had requested her to inquire whether Mr Jefferson would receive
company, but watching his motions, found that after a little
while he had left the orderly stilled through the crowd --
left the room. This she communicated to the company, who
with one accord determined to follow him to the President's
house. It was evident that he had not expected this attention from his friends & fellow citizens, as his whole interior-hall
had gone forth to witness the ceremonies of the day -- he was alone --
not therefore the less happy, for not one of the eager crowd
that followed Mr Madison, was as anxious as himself, to show
every possible mark of respect to the new President.
How memorable was this last interview! -- Every one present seemed
to feel it so, & each in turn shook hands with him, their coun-
tenance expressed more forcibly than their words the respect
they felt on leaving one who had been the uniform friend of
the city & the citizens with whom had lived on terms of hospita-
lity & kindness.
In the evening there was an Inauguration Ball.
Mr Jefferson was among the first that entered the Ball-
room; he came before the President's arrival -- "Am I too early?"
he said to a friend, "You must tell me how to behave -- for it
is more than forty years since I have been to a ball."
On the course of the evening, some one remarked
to him, "you look so happy & satisfied Mr Jefferson, that you
won't the President's appointment; & Mr Madison looks so serious
not to say, sad, that a spectator might imagine that you were
the one coming in, & be the one going out of office."
"There's good reason for my happiness & his sorrow looks,"
replied Mr Jefferson, "Shane got the barther off my shoulders,
while he has now got it on his."
Thus closed Mr Jefferson's eight years residence in
Washington. The constant interest he had taken in the improve-
ment of the city -- the frank hospitality he had extended to
the citizens, made his departure the subject of general regret.

Yesterday mail brought me my beloved, your letter of Thursday
and Sunday and Sunday brought me the packet of newspapers
and the mail before, Do not suppose your grief to grow

for them, If I set you an example of fortitude & concord

always strong them there in both I will be here your
reply to my mother & it doubles my pleasure that she
is so sensible of it. Your letter brought the first account
of the death of Mr. H. The surprise was felt by those who
knew the quantity of persons he surrounded in being.
Let long letters on Sunday morning in this letter for yours
which he promised to deliver out that evening on the
addition of his conversation it will tell you all that has occurred here
The examinations are going on these of a day to
make it a point to show your attention, the intensity
of feeling in them in the President's, is that we have
but few moments in the day for the ordinary business of the Board, which is very considerable & much of it, apparently of little, is really of material importance.
I was in great hopes that when I should be able to write you on Thursday evening but I fear it may be a day
latter. By the arrival of Mr. Johnson we have a board of 5 visitors & something may be taken up which otherwise might not have been. You may be sure that no effort will be omitted on my part to secure his conclusion. Mr. Danvers of course is jealous in his efforts also, indeed, the feeling is sufficiently operative in all, at all events I wish you to give notice to the post office to send me nothing more for me. I have not forgotten the books, Mr. Tucker promised to bring them to day. They are not all of them well in the family to which he belongs, but none are useless indispensable. The child has a cough which is thought to be the commencement of the whooping one. I have my calls on the tail still to make, we purpose to drink tea this evening with Mr. Tucker & shall endeavour to give Mr. Danvers lessons at least, but our inclement situation will be an apology if it should be prevented. I have seen very early for the sake of this letter which is written by candle light & in haste.
Ed. Ogle you deserves young
J. Madison

smiles of the moon fall gently on the shadowy waves
below -- and infuse my spirits with the meditative
broom. I came at the midnight hour when all is
dark around and all is silent there -- and when the
Whip-poor-will is heard -- or Chanticleer's more cheer-
ing voice comes early from the night bounding bower --
gone with rupture on the setting sun -- I watch his
golden beams as they sink a hill on the wood -- ascend

they foam and dash against the rocky shore -- I
wander where the forest rises in all its grand and
impressive majesty -- and dear is the night wing
of the winds as they whistle round some isolated
tailing -- I love the thunder's tone -- and the
lightning's flash amid the sleeping gloom -- and
pray where the cateract whirled through the unuttered
voice of nature in agony, mine are the autumnal
thins, the withered leaf -- the fatigued hunter's justice
in decay -- I am the soul of song -- I am music
over the most enduring charm -- and I pour from
the father and the father's spirit which often and with the
heart -- and love for owns my influence -- I not only
create its enthusiasm -- but give it constancy to its reflec-
tions emotion -- If genius too, I am the chosen com-
fiance -- not only the lover and the poet are mine --
but I dwell in the clopine hills where wisdom and
sincerity hold their court -- and there I have my mystic
gods and their virtues. To destiny also, I give an
energy and zeal -- I am not a dark and gloomy power,
but a magnificent of noble and strong, pensive man --
born to captivate but the feeling heart!

The Rainbow at Purning.
'Twas evening, once the setting sun
Boke from the cloudy West,
Athwart the misty sky it shone
And gladdened all the East;
There, on the clouds which dense and low
Stung up the humid sky,
A beautiful majestic bow
Of nebeys met the eye.
The thunder seals were harn'd no more
The lightnings ceased to glow,
The winds had rushed its assistant rear
Along the vale below—
Nature, just bursting from her chain
Of winter, fresh & fair,
Set on her robes of liveliest green,
And fragrant was the air.
So may this life of toil and storm,
At evening passed me by:
So may my sun break out, anasform
To rainbow in my sky.—
May gratitude and love and praise,
Thin fragrancy impart,
To cheer the errings of my days
And fill my haptur'd heart.
And when life's latest beams recede
From earth and time away,
May glory, bless and blest endure,
In bright suffulgency:
Then, as the colors of your rocks,
Are blended in all in one;
May I with Christ's triumphant breath
Compose an everlasting arch
To rainbow round his throne.

when the rapid pulse throbs wildly with the
vague delight which fills the empty heart,
and when it may be truly said that nothing is, but what is not.

the sufferings he suffered, or to arrest the waves

to restrain the blasphemies of the profane

with the hope of better fortune, and however
oppress our consciences with intimations of experience;
but the time comes at last in which life has no
more to promise, in which happiness can be
drawn only from recollection, and virtue will
be all that we can recollect with pleasure.

"My Brother and Strangers! Your goodness to me always finds as strongly in the afflictions that are inflicted upon me as on the Blessings wherewith I have been continually blessed. May I enjoy thy blessings with a thankful and a grateful heart, yet ever be ready to repay them when it shall be thy part to require me of them! and when they are fulfilled to provide me with affliction, may I always receive them with patience and humility; remembering that they are sent by an indulgent Father who promises them for my good, and who will assist and support me under them!
May I never indulge the least suspicion or discontented thoughts, but keeping my attention on those divine joys which I have been blessed with for time and eternity. For these, may I ever be ready to resign what I must lose and value, when they cannot be had to require it of me, and by a patient perseverance to regain my will to shine in all the brightness of the world, may I at length, like thy infinite mercy, arrive at that Eternal Kingdom, where true will reign and sincere thoughts imperfect obedience, with everlasting and unchangeable felicity!"

New Brunswick Nov 1st 1800
I received your dutiful & affectionate
Letter some time since, and would have answered it long before
this, but was waiting to accompany it, with a sum of money, to
make up what, I intended giving you at your Marriage, but
I have hitherto been disappointed, in receiving, what has been
long promised me -- so favorable an opportunity as Mr. Schurmann
presenting, I could not refrain dropping Your line --
It gives me great pleasure in hearing by your
Letters to your Sisters that you enjoy Health & seem so well
satisfied with your situation, -- that you have had attention
paid you by several respectable inhabitants & that Mr. Smith
is like to succeed in this business -- May a Gracious God
continue to bless You both & give you gratefull Hearts in
the receipt of His manifold favors -- May the Religion You
profess, & a firm & unshaken trust & reliance on the Hope
Jesus our adorable Lord & Saviour ever be your Support &
Refuge. & may the blessed Spirit of God lead you in the
ways of truth & Righteousness, this will enable you to bear
up & to let right under all the trials of life, & if you have
in a fair better State beyond the grave -- Your Education
your short experience has no doubt frequently led you to contemplate
this Life as a State of Probation, & that we are but in the infancy
& due Existence – There is a Glorious prize still before us, & We are directed by the
unerring Word of divine Inspiration – By our Beloved Lord – to strive to enter in at the first Gate – to
strive the good fight of faith – to lay aside every weight – & the Sin that most easily begets – to run the
tree that is set before us looking to Jesus as the Author & Finisher of our Faith –
If We sell our Faces & Remain Hard – We must expect to
encounter difficulties, Losses & Tributes – Our Beloved Lord never
promised His children great temporal Happiness & prosperity,
but on the other hand warned them by telling them “in
“the World You shall have tribulation but He of good cheer
I have overcome the World” Yet blessed be God even in this
World the true children of God enjoy the blessings of Life
with abundantly more relish & satisfaction than the World
The receives all the Mercies He enjoys as coming from the
hands of a kind & beneficent Parent – His heart overflows
with Gratitude & Love & even the afflictions that beset
Him, when sanctified He counts among His greatest
Mercies – I am happy to hear that you have a Church
& Regular Worship on the Sabbath, I trust You will not fail
to frequent it – Your Sisters write You by this Opportunity
as customary – I have long Christies, gives you all the
Information in this place affords – to them I refer you
to Mr Smith to put me down as a subscriber to His Pastor
Altho You know I am not a Friend to His Politics –
You may expect to hear from me in a short time
when I intend enclosing You some Money –
Your Mama joins me in Love to You & Mr Smith
wishing You both Health & Happiness
I am My dear daughter
Your Affectionate Father
John Bayard
P.S. Enclosed You have a Bank Note & please to receive on it $100
My dear Daughter
New Brunswick July 27th 1821
In my letter of June 27th to your
Sister Maria, in answer to hers of June 21st. I promised my
next should be to you - I have before me your affectionate
letter of June 12th. It certainly gives me great pleasure
to hear that Mr Smith is succeeding so well in Business
& that both He and You are respected & taken so much notice
of by the Inhabitants, may these blessings be continued
to you both - And may You have gratefullness in the
receipt thereof, to God your bountiful Benefactor -
When the Mercies of God & the bounties of His Providence
are received with humility & gratitude and more especially
when they are multiplied & flow to us thro the channels of
covenant Love from our Blessed Lord & Saviour
Jesus Christ, then indeed they are sweet & comfortable
But alas! how apt are we to receive the Gift & forget the giver
temporal prosperity, has a natural tendency (unless sanctified)
to lead us to a forgetfulness of our Dependance on God
& hence it is that Our Religious leaders, in Their excellent
Discourses to Their disciples frequently warns them of the
Danger of worldly prosperity & exhails them to avoid a
too great Anxiety after Worldly Riches & Honours - At the same
time He sets us before them, the prospect of more durable Riches
& Honor, in the World to Come - Indeed the whole design of the Gospel of
Jesus is, to show us our Lot of perishing Earth by Nature - the
Way of recovery thro' Him as our Great Attestation - the necessity
& Truth in Him - Wholeness of Life - a Weaning off to this
World, considering our enjoyment, here as short and doubtful
Uncertain - An earnest desire after Eternal Life & the
Enjoyment of Him forever - And Oh! my dear Daughter
Hoping thrice happy are they - that are thus pursuing the
great end for Which they came into the World. -
Your Sister Jane Spivacum will write you by this
Opportunity - it will no doubt give both You & Maria
Pleasure to see Judge Patterson. He will tell you all the
Occasions of your Town - Your Brother Nicolas, Nancy &
their Child live in this Place - His affairs are not yet settled
& He is as yet unfixed as to his future pursuits -
Johannat Rodgers is with us, it is uncertain whether
He will continue thro' the Winter - a return at the close
of Warm Weather - Your Mama is well & joins me in
Love to Mr Smith - Maria - Yourself to You.
I am my dear Daughter
Your sincerely affectionate father
John Spivacum

I received your letter yesterday, I answer it im
mediately, in hopes it will reach you before 2 o'clock
to 13- for I am anxious the business may be adjusted as
soon as possible - If I only were concurred, I would
patiently wait as much longer as my friends desired.
But every letter I receive from the family of my
dear & unhappy friend Jublet, makes me more anxious
to dispense of my mess - Since Mrs death, my
interecourse has been regular & frequent. Jublet has never
been able to unite herself, but I hear almost weekly
from Mary or Anna & I have procured the place
of private governess in the family of my friend Mrs Burnside
for Mary. She pretends to teach nothing but French English
& needle work - for that, she is to receive 100 dollars a
year & be exempt from any expense her board, washing &c &c.
I hope to procure an equally eligible place for Anna -
on the same terms - Their ignorance of French drawing,
music &c &c makes it difficult to procure any places of
parfaititude & I am I feel anxious lest they should be found
unequal to the tasks they have undertaken - Jublet's health
is untatched - her nervous system sadly disordered - yet she has
opened her school & has a few scholars - She is to accompany Mary
here & I expect her next week - Her daughter have persuaded her

Sunday - May 11 - 1828
Your letter dear Maria, which I received
on Friday, was an unexpected pleasure; for I imagined
you would be so much fatigued & so much engaged
while in Baltimore that you would not be able to
find time to write. That amid so many engagements
you did find time, makes it the more acceptable
as it furnishes a new proof of your affection
I felt very anxious about Dear Bayard -
though it probable he would have a return
of his fever - I hope it prove only an intermittent
which the very disagreeable is no way dangerous
& will not be increased by his travellers.
For months I was anticipating of our visit
& promising myself benefit as well as pleasure.
It was a kind of spectacle to which I looked forward
when I expected I should be rescued from the
langour, rather the apathy of disuse & restlessness to
an interest in life - when my habits, as well as
feelings would change - Well, this event has come &
it is gone - a new appears like a dream - I can
scarcely believe you have been here so short does
your visit seem. It proved a stimulus quite
it lasted but now the same animation has returned
& the stream of life flows sluggishly along & will
do so until some one it receives some new impetus
or till it ceases to flow at all -
The morning after your visit, I passed out
from Doughty. Her health is as much impaired
as mine -- Her complaints being more continued
the less violent and more subservient to the truth,
she seems to think of nothing else but the remedies
the remedies or their effects & by them forever her
mind on the ravages of disease & death -- In
reassure them -- for her she that fillet of animal
spirit which Van Brady & myself are
about by brutal nature -- Just, she acknowledges
the helping, there is a higher one for
which I am still more grateful -- an enthusiastic
which can separate itself from an infirm
body & give to engagements of a nobler &
prince ordinary nature, than mere animal spirits
affirmed -- Here alone with my sister & my
brother, from a brother, if not quite a brother, are
many I deeply endeavored but the fact is, when
my mind is thoroughly engaged -- I become incapable
& those of consequence to anyone's sensations should
interfer with me at other times -- after Bayard
gone I shall enjoy this freedom of sightful solitude
until time I shall be a little in a battle --
I slept all preparations for the departure, within
the last week & since you left us have
been occupied in getting the summer clothes
out -- Van Brady was very useful in supplying
it not seeing you again -- every morning until
week she expected you to every morning was disapproving
the is quite fancifully with you & says she never
met with any one that in so short a time she
could so much --
I told her you will receive all these kind sentiments --
which have more pleasure than ever in writing them
to your dear father of you to one who will feel
an interest in learning -- I have looked at the subject
of your words -- I could send you a large
number of our beautiful views -- indeed I shall
write for every day while I contemplate the immense
beauty of the scenery around. The recent breezes
have in full strength & the avenue & yard, have formed
a richer colour -- I cannot help reflecting while
gazing on the bright verdure & green the immense cost
that millions of terminating, your ability did not commence
with the front of May -- And the dear little girls
they too would have had more pleasure in instead
of it a chat at home & a merry day would have
costed this glorious & delicious season -- I have long

to take -- George Bradford has been gone from home
for two months to the two Government to draw the Papacy

Scott came yesterday morning & will stay until tomorrow
to complete his duties to them -- I think of your two

I cannot understand dear Mama whether I have an answer to your last letter, or not. But it is of no consequence -
an answer never to wait for answers but write to each other whenever we can - I should have written
some weeks ago but have neglected it because I sometimes intend to mention it at other times incompatible with writing. My mind remains as much better as it can ever be without me -
the office has been changed in its functions and mind I think was never in so healthy a state - actions, thoughts & cheerful - I never more fully enjoyed an office -
which must be best for myself and for others - I pass the largest portion of my time alone in my chamber reading, writing & contemplating the various beauties of nature which
are lavished upon her children - on the choldest
thick in my mind after I have enjoyed a holiday
from work or from any other kind of labour - I feel as much as ever from the united hands of a moment's
breathing to hasten rail & launch on the ocean of eternity. This freedom of the soul from slavery
has in strong emotions is delightful - some imagine that the effects of confidence & quietude
are more considerable than any kind of agitation & excitement would be - among a principal description -
but now I am so contented with being contented, that I would not exchange the present danger for the crowded
refugees I have ever known. I do not think the imagination to become the means of misfortune in which I have complained - Oh no my heart is constantly in the
hands of God to protect me from all danger & to enable me to live as long as I wish & I pray no longer for
the life that is passing away from me - I am with reluctance I leave out any other sentiment
of my chamber letters to pray or converse a minute
yet I do not neglect intimacy, these social duties
visit Mrs Thornton often in the evening, which is a
day in the winter with us. Mrs Bradford's visit
to Washington led me into more society than usual.
She & Fanny passed a social day with us, which I greatly
enjoyed. I could scarcely realize any time, much less
a year had intervened since we had been passed a
day together -- The season was the same -- the same pleasant
truths -- we sat in the same places & talked of
the same friends -- How wonderfully well Mrs B. looks for
a woman of her age & what spirit & activity -- Sue
and Fanny, made hardly any appearance. To pass away the
long manner, I read them the little MSS. I had got to
you -- The deserted Child, Whether Mrs Bradford's tears
were as much at her command as her smiles I knew
not, but whether voluntary or not, my narrative required
her a fancy of some kind more than once -- He & she
--- motions of excellent taste & beautiful time & I
did not flatter me half so much as their time & un-
interrupted attention -- I know of fewer pleasures that
satisfy that of exciting this kind of interest & attention
The Prairie sheltered by a hundred indifferent people
or paragraphs would not equal it -- No praise can give
me pleasure, unless bestowed either by good judgment on dear friends --
& the latter is for the sweetest -- Your dinner, we were
joined by some of your friends -- acquaintances I mean -- Mrs &
two sisters Rushie, Mrs Johnson, Bradford, Clarke & a dozen
more -- making a social & agreeable little party
Mrs Bradford seemed pleased. Mrs Bradford asked us all to
her house the next after noon -- We went -- the weather very
delightful -- Kalorama lovely in her flower garden in all
its pride & glory -- It was a charming afternoon -- 2 charming
girls -- Mrs Johnson then invited us -- It was an evening
pretty, very large & crowded in eleven rooms -- Mrs Rush after
wards gave a larger party to Mrs Brown (Mrs B's daughter)
& Mrs Bradford -- it was elegant & agreeable -- I suppose social
at the Mayo all the evening -- I suppose social
evening for water Mrs B -- at Mrs Brown's -- So you see how
I returned with increased delirium to the solitude of our dear
room -- which I have since seldom been tempted to
leave -- Mrs Brown I have seen more of, & in
a more social manner than I ever have before -- as
I called it, to Sister -- we have had quite sentimental
discussions -- exchanging tales, visits, notes, verses & comparisons of other friends -- all about flowers -- I expected out

one. -- Could do odd -- an absolute original! The first
rainy day I can find time I mean to draw her portrait &
record some of her sayings & phrases -- to add to my
collection of original pictures -- I like her very much
that shall see little of her, for she is now in for it -- she
is very busy in the office & business of company -- She has her
time to eat or sleep. she says -- I went out one morning visiting with, to
see her list of visitors to be returned already amounted to 500 --
talk who calls on her -- she is obliged to invite to her parties -- as, Mr L.
of your city, who preached for us said -- "Is the Lord a hard master in
his work, & rudgery -- no I tell you, his yoke is easy & his burden light --
It is the world that is a hard master & let you do what you
will, slave yourself to death, give health, give fortune, give in
all your time & I will give you pleasure here -- and though in
the hard & exacting world, I will not be shy silence --

This world is a seducing world my dear sister, I
can make no excuse for it, since it has interfered with
my writing to you -- but believe me, it has no power
of making me forget you -- Every day, every night when I
lie down at every morning when I rise, the image of my sister
my dearest friends, mingle with my thoughts -- when ever I have
any peculiar pleasure, a spontaneous desire blends with
my enjoyment, that you could participate in it with me
and when sorrow or sadness of heart, my feelings & thoughts
become united I have poured out my feelings & thoughts
into your sympathetic bosom -- Think not these are mere
words -- no -- the thought of you mingling with all
my trials & sufferings would fill me with joy -- If these
thoughts could arrange themselves without them many long
chapters would have been written for me -- I have
written 20 sheets of letters for you -- I wish you could
see my letters to Bayard -- they are perfect journals
from them you might form some idea of the business
we had, with the exception of one part of our occupation
the office duties, which are an endeavour to perform,
but of course I know it would be to you -- But your salary
is to be doubled by the world as to neglect her matrimonial
obligation -- It will indeed far short not only of the requirements
of the Gospel -- but, far below my own desires & determinations --
not a day passes, in which I have not omitted to
do it -- I am not forgetting, as any one might imagine
the journal of my present mode of life -- I do not believe

Dear man! what shall we do, if either of us one very
many ill -- how painful will separation then be! when our
last sickness comes -- & come it must, what consolation
would it be to receive the last human support, from those
we have loved from birth & through life -- alas, I fear
at times this consolation will not be ours -- in truth I often
fear we never shall meet again -- well, -- what then? Say
to myself -- It will only make a little longer interval, between
our communications & will be followed by a communion, a
thousand times more perfect & more satisfying to affection,
than any we can henceforth expect to enjoy on earth -- For
unrespect, very improper in the communion we now have --
what have I known of the state of your mind or feelings,
since I saw you, it is now a year ago. -- How many sad hours, how
many corroding years, & how many enjoyments too, have we
mutually had, as entirely unknown to each other, as if we
separated by death. -- In this manner I try to reconcile myself
to circumstances beyond our control -- that when my heart
is full, either of sadness, or tenderness, or joy, it will serve
for my sister! -- Dearest, dearest friends -- would that I could at
such moments feel myself prepared in your arms -- feel my
lean merges with yours -- Do you remember the last bitter
day I passed with you? The mine on the road between
Haston & Brunswick -- the ground covered with snow, the sky
cloudy -- the air cold -- but what were these things to us? we
felt no cold -- our hearts were too warm -- our hands were
clasped in each other & our spirits were as closely united
from morning on each succeeding morning to the hour of
each other -- & so I have -- The 20 of this last month, with long
be remembered by many, on account of the tremendous snow
storm, which was so wide spread in its desolation --
where were you that day? -- It was the sweetest &
most interesting birth-days I ever passed! -- Cold & temper-
tuous as it was without doors, it was beam & bright with
joy -- Not expecting any interruption, I had gathered the girls
around me & round a blazing fire & more comfortable
seated with our backs & our backs, looking from time to
time at the drawing snow & listening to the loud blast, when
a carriage drove to the door -- it was opened, & our interesting
friend, Mrs W entined -- Always

Merriment, dear Maria, would not be
engagement to us -- Therefore I will not wish you a merry
Christmas but most sincerely hope this anniversary of our former
happy holiday may find you in possession of substantial, rational
tranquil happiness -- or, what is the highest degree of felicity
we can possess on earth, a contented mind. Contentment
founded upon a full persuasion of the government of a good
& merciful God, whose dispensations, whether in accordance or
in opposition to our desires, we feel to be best for us, -- This
conviction can give us a contented mind even in affliction.

Should I ever have a sufficient sum at my own
disposal, & it be not required for the absolute comfort of my
family, I shall certainly appropriate it to building & furnishing
a spare chamber & thus save myself the uncomfortable
feelings I have when my friends visit Washington. It
is really painful to me to have them staying at public
houses. Had I had the means I should have entertained some
mode of making the dining room this winter so double
duty -- for although this cold weather we do not eat in it when
alone, yet we should be obliged to so move friends staying
with us but the necessities for such an arrangement are wanting &
as necessarily has no law, I endeavour to submit without complaint
to this & many other of the inconveniences of a narrow income --
However, the discomfort & anxiety of living beyond one's
means, which in all conditions would to me be most annoying
wealth is becoming every day more & more essential to
social intercourse in our city. Elegance & luxury of every kind
seem now a days as essential as convenience & comfort used to
be, & as these essential are totally those of my command, all
that remains is to relinquish society, & this I can now most
willingly do, except where attention to friends must be sacrificed.
The society in which I most delight, -- Books, -- Thanks fortune and
folly at my command a are every day more & more enjoyed,

Feb 7-24, 1839-
I have my dear Maria, taken so little note of the
lapse of days & weeks, that I really felt astonished on
looking at the date of your last letter, for find that
almost a month has intervened since I received it- The
first of Feburary had this interval been marked by
any new or interesting incidents, like land marks they would
have reminded me of the progress of my journey. I
should have counted days, as one count mile stones
seen journeying along the high road- But one day
apart is little from the preceding, & all, are so alike,
& smooth & unbroken that I pass them over, as
if tranckion does an even rail through a level country,
unconscious of the distance. The last few days,
however form an exception, as they afforded objects
& agreeable excitement- One evening at Mr Smith's
particular request, I consented to go into Mr Smith's
house to meet Mr & Mrs Combe
Mr Abbot & others of the same descent- Anna
Johns likewise went- We effected a small
select company of other, good & literary folks, but
to our surprise found an amusement of more than
hundreds- However, one may be alone in a crowd
I felt very much so while engaged in a most agreeable
conversation with Mrs Abbot- Besides time, I met
Mr George Boyd, who during the evening entertained
myself almost entirely to our party- Judge Story, & three
or four old acquaintances whom I had not seen for
long time, I was likewise glad to meet, & on the
whole passed a most pleasant evening, the first
have passed in company for more than two, & believe
that I had nothing that could be called
68200
communicate with them. I asked the Board of Mr. Albee
to deliver to him a family surgeon with as much
money as he could get. His agreement came down
to the day I had enjoyed John's services for
the memory, I recommend to him, an excellent
establishment in the pleasant style of an English
communion. He has about 200 soldiers in his
own hospital, and I am satisfied that his army
is in perfect order. He has also established
the most perfect system of administration
— particularly, at the army-vie, he is a school — the entire work of
the army is carried on methodically and efficiently
under His English officers, accompanied by
the Catholic Female Seminary, a very large building
affiliated to the University. Here every thing was
in a larger degree Christian than in any other
part of the United States. The only thing I have
not seen in a military establishment — but I
have not felt any desire to see, is the army surgeon
who sees the officer & rear from him. From my
experience with his military examination
system, Colonel Rebecca, the man who is at the head
of the establishment, is one of the most interesting
persons I have ever met. He had discharged
more than 1000 men before me, none of whom
had been in the army, and he makes our intended visit
to Fort Washington a matter of pleasure. It was the chief pleasure
of the morning to see the soldiers' examinations. I am not
so English as my brethren — I am the chief pleasure
in your own in your children's plans of living, have
an abundant store of interesting material. Nothing that belongs to
you will be indispensable to me -- you cannot be too minute
in your details.
