New Brunswick, N.J.
I can scarcely believe that a whole week has passed
since I wrote you my last letter. x x x
On Wednesday evening last, we were just seated at our tea-table,
when the door was opened & Brother S & Sister entered. I felt
most truly rejoiced to see them. They passed the next day with
us, & left this on Friday morning. They spent the day in look-
ing about them, & will give you a truer idea of our situation,
than I have been able to in my letters. Mr, & Mrs, Huges left
this on Wednesday; the two preceding days, Mrs H. was well
enough to dine & sup below stairs, & these interviews made me
regret not having visited her in her room. She is a woman,
plain both in manners & appearance, very social & talkative, &
is what you would call a good kind of a woman. To me she was
extremely friendly, & one evening after tea came in my room &
sat more than an hour. She is to stay at George-town this win-
ter, & I have promised to visit her. I not only got over my
prejudice against Mr H, but before he left us, used to feel con-
siderable pleasure in talking & listening to him. He is very
communicative & seems to like talking as well as he does eating,
which is not a little. He is a moderate federalist, & he & Mr
Smith talked by the hour, of political affairs & political men.
As for Mr Myers, who is still here, he seems to be out of humour,
& since Mr S, has been unable to converse, he every day gets up
from the table, turns his back to the company & either ruminates
over his own cares, or pores over a book. Cap. Memmenger, a
Benjamin Huger, Representative from South Carolina
2.
clever good natured man, who has been here several weeks, is to
leave us to-day, & altho' he is not very entertaining, he has
been so friendly & attentive, that I shall feel sorry to lose
this member of our little society. Cap. Babcock, an old gen-
tleman from Boston has been here three days. While sister was
here, they found they were mutually acquainted with many per-
sons, & this seemed to make them acquainted with each other, he
attached himself exclusively to our party & since they have
left us, behaves in the same way to us. He is blunt & honest
in his manners, but at the same time very affectionate, & gen-
erally when I enter the room, he takes my hand, & shaking it,
asks, "Well, how goes it Mrs Smith?" He asked Mr. S. if he in-
tended settling here, what was his business? and on being
told, "well said he, "consider me as a subscriber, & give me one
or two subscription papers & I shall get you some subscribers
in Boston." He spoke of visiting Mrs Faithch (?) & I told him,
Mr Bradford had spoken to me very highly of this lady & wished
me to be known to her. Last night when he came home, he
stretched out his hand, made me sit on the chair next him, "well,
said he, I have said a good word for you, & Mama Falton will
come & see you soon." In my last letter, I mentioned the name
of Mr. Law. Since then, he has often called in, & talked a
great deal with Mr S. He is a man well informed on every sub-
ject, remarkably free & communicative, & of much the same poli-
tical opinions with Mr S. He subscribed to his paper, asked
for a subscription paper, offered us his books, & told Mr S to
3.
let him know whenever it was possible for him to serve him.
The first time he ever spoke to me he saw me at the window;
"Good morning Mrs Smith, are there any books or anything else
which I can send you for your amusement? Do not be uneasy about
the vessel Mrs. Smith, if you do loose a little, why you are young
people, & every one will be the more willing to assist you.
Well Mrs. Smith, your house will be soon done, I have been push-
ing Moffet on, & this morning paid him 1200 dolts, so he need
not wait for money." After a few more such abrupt speeches, he
bid me a good morning & went away. He is a most singular man.
Friday afternoon Mrs. Law, & the two Miss Tincy's called on me.
Mrs. Law met me with a sweet & facinating smile, apologised for
not having called sooner, but hoped now by sociability to make
up for it. We were to be her neighbors, & she wished that
this winter we might see each other without ceremony. She was
averse to form & never observed it. She is a lovely woman.
Her soft voice, her benevolent countenance, her affectionate
manners, must make every one her friend at first sight. She is
not as large as Mrs White, but otherwise like her. Yes, with
this woman, I will if possible be social & intimatetimate. She had
with her a lovely little girl of four years old, her only child.
If all be as I wish, she shall be my Mary Ann. The Miss Tincy's
are plain looking girls, & said nothing more than that their
Mama proposed calling on me soon. Mrs Law asked us to take a
family dinner with her to-day, but Mr S's tooth-ache prevented
our accepting the invitation. Mr. English sat a whole morning
4.
with us & seemed quite like an old friend. Yesterday Miss
---------------- whom I often met last winter at Mrs Bethune's,
Mrs Bell, the lady with whom she lives & Miss Bell called. Mr
Bell is a very wealthy & respectable man, & what is uncommon
here, they are professors of religion. They sat more than
an hour with me, asked us to their house, & offer'd us seats in
their pew. Told me Mr Balch, their clergyman, knew my family
& intended calling on me. I did not expect a single person to
call on me. Mr Smith's vessel has at last arrived at Alex-
andria. Last night & all this morning there has been a most
violent storm of wind & rain, but I trust our little property
will arrive safely. The carpenter work is almost finished &
two rooms are plastered. In two or three weeks more, I trust
I shall write to you from our own house. Let me end, as I began
my letter, by entreat ing you to write to us. Tell me a great
deal about my dear children & tell Mary Ann to begin her letter
a month before Mr S sets off, so that it may be a very long one.
My most affectionate regards to all my dear friends, -they are
oftener thought of than ever, and do not forget to remember me
to Betsy & Sally. Tell Betsy that if John comes here he will
soon make a fortune. If you go a hundred yrds, each one pays
a qr of dollar a seat for going & returning. U And this winter
no one will be able to walk. On reading these last lines to
Mr S he thinks I am wrong in promising a fortune, for on inquiry
he has found the backs did not make much. I will let her know
more on this subject. Adieu, -my paper is too full already.

Washington. Sunday Oct. 19. 1850.
I can scarcely believe that a whole week has passed since I wrote
you my last letter. This is the third time I have written from this
place, & I have at yet received no answer to my first letter. I cannot
avoid some apprehension I begin to fear that some one of the family
is ill. Oh, my dear sisters do be punctual in writing, you cannot
conceive how the value of a letter is increased by our seifer attempts
from all our friends, & being as we are in a land of strangers. The last
week, Mrs S. had a letter from Mary & John, I welcomed them most
sincerely, but still I felt sadly disappointed that first after first
arrived without any intelligence from Brant. Since this day week,
my good husband, has not been an hour free from a violent toothache
It keeps him awake, almost the whole night & incapacitates him for
business or society through the day. In attempting to extract it the dentist
had it, & in endeavouring to get out the broken parts, he said he has
eructated the gum, so much, that his whole head is affected. -- He suffers
so much pain, that it produces a slight fever. The indisposition, has so
depressed my spirits, that for this day or two, I have been quite
good for nothing. I find it impossible to fix my mind sufficiently
for reading or writing. On wednesday evening last, we were just
seated at our tea-table, when the door was opened & brothers
& Sister entered. I felt most truly rejoiced to see them. They
passed the next day with us, I left this on Friday morning.
They spent the day in looking about them, I will give you a
truer idea of our situation than I have been able to in my
letters. Mrs & Mrs Nugee left this on Wednesday, the two preceding
days, Mrs H. was well enough to dine & sup below stairs, & these
interviews made me regret not having invited her in her room.
She is a woman, plain both in manners & appearance, very

got over my prejudice against Mrs H; but before he left us, used

This morning Mrs P's sent her carriage for us & we went to
church, where a good sermon, was preached in a small but re-
table congregt. After church, Ch. T. & Mr Foster came home
as, & I received them same ceremony in my chamber -- Do I have
but little more to say, I will not begin another sheet. Mr Patterson was
on Friday & was quite well. Remember us to all our dear friends & bid
not to forget us -- Farewell my dear sisters. --

Many wrote me word that your little Elizabeth had
been sick for several days previous to the appearance of a
tooth, I could not but regret that she had not described to
me the symptoms, in which case I could have compared them
with Fulton. Her gums were not seared, she had no fever, breath
more than usual, but was extremely fretful & restless; her breath
was much diminished & the complaint seemed to be attended

I cannot describe to you my sensations when the next day

extremely kind, & gave my lodging a room with them, which when
they & I declined they offered me every thing their house required
could afford & gave me almost every day sent something to me.
The cottage in which I am, is a small building of one story
with four rooms, two of which I occupy, & the tenants the others.
The walls of my room are made in which time has made
many a chink, my window have no glass, (except one
for Smith has dismounted) but are protected by shutters.
I brought out, what little furniture is here & have
to find my ingenuity to work to make that little room
all my wants. The stairs serve as a dresser on which I place
bottles, cups, saucers &c are displayed to the most advantage. The
chimney in my mud walls serves as a book case, in which
my table library is fixed to the front entrance; a post to give
about me an air of quiet room, a small bake oven, serves as a pot,
an oven for griddle & frying pan. My tea cup serves as sugar pot,
in which I steep my coffee, salt cellar a potter box &c. These
little continuance please me. I have a bench under the
noble willow which shade the front yard, where I pass most
of my time & I assure you it looks quite romantic to see
me seated on this most beautiful, with my cradle & my bed &
a small table before me. Here too when I have visitors, I
spread my tea table. There is a novelty in my situation, which
confers a degree of pleasure which compensates for every inconvenience.
As for solitude, every day trial but attaches me the more to it.
I spend my time in reading, writing & seeing & never feel lonely
or weary. Sam carried me to a most beautiful country, surrounded
by orchards, cops fields, meadows, fields & woods. Already have
I wondered this came of the most romantic scenery, where one
human fabrication reminds me of the vicinity of man. It first
I was charmed with my solitary ramble & preferred them
to having any company, but when my dear husband came
I, quickly abandoned a most sensible difference. United as we
one, not only by the most fervent affection, but by a consciousness of mutual
a similarity of taste, a powerful love action in myself. Every opinion
seemed to gain some new charm when he was with me, and I never
had a double power to please. He left me yesterday, after saying
three happy, incommensurably happy days. He left though I felt he
behind him & gave himself up to the charms of solitude &
grief, of love. The weather was very cool, & I am sometimes
afraid the whole morning in wandering thru woods, where the
silence was only interrupted by the wind mothing among the
leaves, at home he read aloud, while I seemed to enjoy myself
with fiction in the yard. All my old romance & Enthusiasm seem
to be revived & my heart responds with more than common
tenderness. -- What a transition from my situation one week

Snow is faithful - I am very happy to day, both owing I believe
to the return heat, for two days past - it has been so oppressive
that I have been good for nothing. - Maine 2 Snow in this letter
complaint of stormy weather, & he has informed us this day a
parcel of land would a whole weather storm be - I really
believe that all the country people would willingly not see the
sun again for a month, if the clouds that hid it, would but pour
down rain. - As much as I can collect we have had but
three rainy days since the first of May, 2 not a Showers in
a month, on an average 2 I have not heard thunder but
three or four times this summer - The oldest people do not recollect
but such a long continued drought, streams & springs are very
often failing & few mills can grind, so that in some parts
of the country people have had to go 15 to 20 or 30 miles to
mill - There is much distress around us from this circumstance,
at the corn meal we have used for some time past, we obtained
from a windmill & wheat flour is absolutely tough, we have
given up selling a barrel. Many families have had to
use hominy instead of bread 2 yesterday I sent three cents to buy a
little meal, & the children were crying for this breakfast & I do
not as I send to give them; another of my neighbors came for a bottle
of hay, could get no meal. - The crops of wheat 2 rye have
been abundant, but the product of corn, & melancholy.
By this time Maine is again at Brunswick, I expect your
letters were received at the same time, I must in this instance
make one answer do for both. Had I written to you the day after
I received it I could have written with more pleasure to myself
for the weather was then, truly delightful, & I felt at the animation
of the sun & electric air so refreshing. - You my dear sister, consider
the little lessons a succession of incidents had left you, I can make
no such excuse for my silence, for I have passed the summer free
from all the intimisions of society 2 have enjoyed the charms
of solitude in most abundance & perfection, that could admit
into a book as big as Timon's was original, in its progress
to fact I had no idea could have been so contented on
such fatal occasions till I have written three miles of only, 2
never go there except on business - My time has passed very
pleasantly not from the circumstances with which it is surrounded
but from the happy state of mind I have enjoyed. I never
have been free from all kind of care. The children are healthy
& gay, & I have myself perfectly well, 2 I have for an
unlettered servant woman, 2 Mrs. Has set your eleven years
to which -- we have made several small improvements, which by

Betsy Johnson & Mr Smith have gone to take a
long walk to a mile at least 5 miles from hence, so
after finishing the childrens lessons I supposed devoting a long
morning to letter writing; but the morning has almost gone
making my butter, attending my poultry, entertaining my young
gardener, you do know it has done me the honor I desired
for my hero- But I am anxious to answer my dear sister
for my hero, 2 The many other things yet remain of my days
work, this hour shall be appropriated to her - I really rejoice
that she could have intireed her welcome to stranger met,
you would visit us more frequently. I particulate in
all your Pleasures, but in none so fully as those
you derive from your children - I think Mary Ann has
been very diligent in her studies; she has need a great
deal 2 I rejoice in her taste for books, she does not resemble
Margaret, but suffers weakness of which to those circumstances
- But tell, that her Papa used often to reproach
me for giving too much of my time to reading an
used to promise great things for her what an excellent
house keeper she should be at 15, what fine, middling
pies, basters & wagons she should make, saying that
woman could never be a great woman in her profession, or
cooking was one of the greatest accomplishments an
woman could have - are his prophetic fulfilled, 2 does
Mary take this part of family business? Many and
many has commended Beaufort to me, Aunt Maria must
be a better to visit us at Washington. If we had a
large house here I really cannot conceive any thing
which would give me more delight than to
have Mary, Sally & Jane, with the young gentlemen
here. - What charming walking & riding to which would
we not have - provided we had a carriage. - well
who knows but some of these days we may have a
little richer & have a larger estate & carriage in
the bargain - this is better The last will come first, I
am so well I do not think I am not able to take long walks as I used to

Day after day, a week after week I earnestly asked
to write to you, I cannot overlook the necessity
for several letters of my having written a note, but
since I have not been able. The complaint I mentioned
in my last has continued so that I could take no
more time in the want of excuse or justification. I am
about full habit and induced other complaints which
have disabled me from any action whatever. I found
that to me is no amusement, except in of chiefly
a good deal of hypnotical affection. I made a
great exertion to write. Many a very miserable
letter in order to prevent the feeling away at my
place. I am growing very uncomfortably in points of
life which remains entirely in painful pain. Whenever
I have been at all able, I have been obliged to
give their lessons, the frequently while they were reading.
I have fallen fast asleep for this drowning, comes
over me as regularly about noon or ever the noon and
ten I always feel the better for company a hour
either to weather God a good deal. Since battling cannot
stay with me as the difficulty opens on the business
but ride out on downcast Ohio or leave a meal
to pass part of the morning – always spends Sunday
with me – Mrs. Thorton & Mrs. Baudreau, Mrs. L. Mrs.
Luella, Mrs. Castis, & now Mrs. Duff with her daughter,
& several other ladies & a number of gentlemen have
come out to spend the day or afternoon without
restation – among the gentlemen I have made a new
& most agreeable acquaintance. Mr. Warden, excellent
at Paris – He is a young man of great taste, intellect
& literary, & quite in the literary circle of Paris. Intellectuals
with the members of the National Institute, & a
the men of science – He is the particular acquaintance
of Mrs. D. Arthly of Helen, Mrs. Williams, of Van Kempton
& Baron Hamoldt (very acquaintances) & almost
an inmate at the Dickinson. In his manner he
has all the simplicity of which I do not wonder
that him for the literary man he is the comes
close to Breckfast's dinner, & tea time and so much
at once in the cathedral. That he is a reader, I doubt if
no debt for a takes to go to where he seems very poor
(particularly S he) I wander in the woods, to gather flowers
& give them lessons in botany, with which I am
not highly delighted - The accidental company, which
was at the moment, but to tell the truth I feel
the want of a companion in the house, for the time
is at time only at his meals; a after keeping the
children occupied all the morning & part of the afternoon
I let them take occasional plays, when natural
am glad for a little while to be relieved from
their perpetual questions & little about what I
know what more Sarah's danger & my wishes
I could determine whether to take to Botany. I
suppose that after our absence this summer, she will
write to you with you on the autumnal winter.
But as I have to do to give her to pass the winter
here, I feel a difficulty in asking her to come
on shore as she would be real quite the only lodging I
should have found in the harbour, unless every
night a bed must be made with arms & Bayonet
in it as companions -- for the two little bed rooms
of stairs are full of one they is another who had
to buy from the editor. I suppose a general chat or
answer to any one confinement or account of Bayonet
for the month past he has had a terrible examination
on his face, which has made him so foolish
that he requires the attention of every one in
the house to turn & as at night he might have
so much awake I have often made enough, let him
sleep the Regiments of the night 2 sat by him outside
one or two octobers the examination seemed like
hours to every party of his body -- But I am not
doing, or from Sarah's case I found it prevented from
fever & General complaints during lectures -- He is
perfectly healthy, quiet, fat, & in every way put me his
favorite -- he begins to sleep alone, & at times when his
face does not show, he is thoughtful as even this landscape
truth is almost out to give is much puzzled, but he
has not the least favor, & cats his marked statement with his
little as healthy as ever. This is at present his only wish.
But once your little angel was taken from me, I have
never regretted that mine would be separate from me of
some time that reason required me -- But perhaps these
melancholy images are only the offspring of theological
debility -- For with all his want of intellect & desire of
reason we are often able very independent on these matters
of day, & when they are out of repair, your noble
philanthropist repairs with them. Do not let Maria know
of this compulsory letter; indeed leave almost entirely
to send it to you -- What night I loved or would love
is many a noble great bishop, what night I love to
complain of a noble independence -- Let me rather speak
of my dearest sister, my tender friend, of those bishops, of
the goodness of my dearest father, when I would recount
the memories of my god, my eyes are blinded by tears of
patience -- These dear these precious children, they are
a source of unmerited felicity & comfort. I wish I could
tell you of all this tender & pleasant affection to me
from some of the children of my family -- Their great
intelligence, this general benevolence & goodness -- Their
touching delicacy, & their affection, their anxiety to
acquire knowledge -- While I have been writing this
letter they have been quietly working & studying -- They are
my mama, my wife not intolerable, you understand, I am
not quite sure I am in love with every book -- And often when
not well, they will not trouble yourself dear mother
we will not let our own name & our own bodies be needed
for a little, you say my son on the subject -- I never saw
so young a child as Joseph so deeply impressed with religious
sentiments -- His greatest delight is to read & learn by heart their
sayings, no book of entertainment gives him really the
delight that reading the Bible and Shakespeare gives him -- He has literally
worn them out. He repeats them with enthusiasm
& continual quoting & applying passages to the circumstances of the day. Boy after the boys me & so does John
& need about our summer to know & the they have

that she will not perhaps for years wander from
her home. But to me it is a melancholy one, so

a stranger here, as the first year I came - It seems
strange that to a heart so easily attached as mine,

not found one whom it could unite with

sentiment, & we are separated by our family duties,

cloche work & I find that constant employment, so arranged

while the rain beats against the windows & the winds
roar amongst the trees to sit silent a solitary listening
to this music of the elements. At such moments
the mind wanders over the past & finds a moun tain
pleasure in pondering on days forever gone. A bright
sunny day dissipates the thoughts, quickens the anim al
spirits, & leads the busy fancy thro' scenes of
future life; in which the mind, animated by the
society of nature delights to exhastiate, instead

murkly with eternity. It is when the soul is suddenly

I am exceedingly sorry my dear Margaret that
you so impatiently ask me to mention our alarm and apprehension to
you. It shall be a lesson to me in future. It is not right to cast
the piece of our friends after us over such a distance. God in
the time I was writing forgetting that circumstances should not
be I should have told you and communicated all my fears. For many
days we were indeed extremely gloomy. I heard of various
accidents and deaths and symptoms of insanity in our own
family brought it all home to me. This did not last long. I
have been greatly distressed and I have been able to write, and moved to her own home. On the 1st
of May, I was greatly distressed on a new scene in connection with
the family. I hope they will do well. The man, who has married Hannah, is
a comforter & joiner by trade. He appears already capable. Smithson
had united labour. I think will be sufficient for a comfortable
support if they are favored with health. It would very strange
to part with Sally. I thought I should have told you more, but
for some time past she has been quite satisfied by her own
comments so that I have no need to speak of the charge. I am very
much favored with the women I have got, and if they come
to me as they have begun I shall not wish to look further.
So you have so often sympathized in the sorrows of my dear
Fanny, I am certain you will also rejoice in any good that may
come her. At this moment she is quite healthy, her father
her and earthly stay, where she almost gave up at last has
returned in the last instalment in death and aged. I was the
only from the dead. She is entirely reconciled, and I have
the satisfaction of seeing once more well & cheerful. I get it
only as a gleam of sunshine thru a dark and stormy cloud.
For her brother is out of employ -- and greatly in debt from
the expense of his captivity, and therefore utterly unable to do
any thing for her or Antoinette, much as he wishes to provide
for them. Fanny has at last an asylum with me but she
will not seek a place. Do you know whether Mr. Brown
can get a friend for her? If she has not would you be
good enough to mention Antoinette to him. Her manners are altogether
polite and agreeable, and she is very well qualified to make a
brilliant & useful inmate in a family. They were very much
afflicted to her at Windsor and I believe she gave entire satisfaction
to all particulars. She does not understand music nor piano
which probably would be against her, but she could certainly
talk her own language, and with the help of books, all the
essential branches of education -- If Mr. Brown should
die I do not know of any other place, where she would be
to meet with kindness and consideration they would be
comfortable about the place. Preferring one of your merits &
perpetuity. I do not expect to apply to you, my dear Margaret, because I know the pleasure it gives you to depend on the unfortunate
and Fanny says she would rather give an obligation to you than any
other -- I am not afraid that Antoinette would get to
judging our actions. She is an amiable young woman, and I am
surprised would render herself acceptable. She has real tenderness
but no that extreme of sensibility which however interesting
it is a source of sorrow to the father. and if in all events
limited to this, is good sense and a knowledge of the world and
before her late afflictions. The most charming society of women.
I am told she is a good deal altered -- but further in matters
there she would regain her native spiritfulness -- Let me hear
from you soon
How are all your dear children? Jane has got the
shaking seriously. Elizabeth does not yet know the one cause
of her illness. I hope they will have it removed as soon as
possible. I give Jane Antoinette were in small way
from the day -- and I do with a great deal of

December 10th 1817.
A variety of little matters, in a different
way has so occupied my time, since I received your letter my
dear Harpster, that I have not been able to devote that
quiet hour to you which is essential to the execution of
philosophy converse. By this time I suppose you are quite
blind in the city -- and have completed your winter prepara-
tions. I hope you will pass an agreeable season -- but so
gay I presume as the Lord's Short -- will hardly
be in time be in time for general society -- but you may
easily compensate to her -- any loss sustained in that way --
indeed from what you say, if her present views retirement
will be the most acceptable. A heart that is occupied with
a new affection touched by grief -- and awakened to religion can
not find enjoyment in gay errands. This has been an interesting season to me -- I sincerely hope it may continue in her
lasting happiness. It will be delightful to you to have settled
near you -- and see her united to an amiable and deserving
young man. Her entering the family just at this moment
must endear her greatly to the parents -- She will fill up
the place in their hearts and be adopted as a daughter.
-- It would gratify Mary exceedingly to be with you again --
but at present -- I can not say when, nor how -- Robert's
Bayard returns in safety, and makes a prosperous voyage he
may complete his much wished for excursion to Washington &
take Mary with him. But this is all uncertain. As to
Gov. Ro. he says it is impossible for him to leave home
for another he has so much to do in his office.
I regret it exceedingly - for I am sure he would enjoy it
and he really wants some recreation - he rarely denies anything
to his family - and as rarely indulges himself.
Brother Samuel is appointed by the Committee of the
Bible Society to go to U. S. Edition borough - for certain
favour to the U. S. I hope he will be successful. It is not
quite so unpleasant as begging for money directly. I think he
is a suitable agent - for he has great zeal in the cause and
great activity & perseverance. I imagine you will not find
the collision of political sentiment so sharp as it was when you
were here - there is a very great change, generally characterized
the present President has conciliated the good opinion of many
by the gentleness and candor of his manners while on his tour
and has pleased in his late appointments. Every one I have
heard speak on the subject think that Mr. Dick & Biblical
hom do honour to the Presidents judgment and to their
country. That will be the effect of the refusal of the inter-
nal taxes on Mr Smith's office? Will it be absolute? or shall
continued in case of contingencies? I hope if this place is
disposed of - that will be some other opening for him.
I am now looking for heavy - by the next stage that
comes in - Elizabeth is to remain in D.C. with her cousin
June Stevens, this winter. She has commenced taking lessons in
drawing - of a teacher that is very much celebrated - Mrs Johnson
profits from her - objection - and recommends him highly. If C. has
as much taste as you had she might make great improvements
this winter - I hope she will acquire so much that she can
hereafter prosecute it at home, with more pleasure & advantage.
Do your girls go to Dix's Stone this Winter? Does their
improve in music? - As to their dress - I do not think
you need to make any change. I do not think otherwise
expect it - perhaps not notice it. If I did, the excuse you
give is quite sufficient.
I expect to pass a few days with our friend at
prisonation toward the close of this week. I have not seen
sister since the painful scene of Susan's death. I will receive
many affecting recollections. but I hope it will be a salutary
sorrow.
I do not know what to make of the strange
accounts you give of Littledon. I hope you will see more of
him now you are in town - so as to form more accurate
judgment. Have you said anything to Mr Baldock about him?
Does he consider his late poem as proceeding from religious
impressions? I long to know something more about him.
He writes very seldom to us, and when he does it is in a way
that affords no weight into his sentiments or feelings. His
other validity that he is living - and that is all.
We have had the pleasure of hearing from King.
He arrived at Eutawja on the 23d of Sept. and was obliged to
perform guarentine - he appears well - and in good spirits
but does not say when he will return. We now begin to
look for him and hope he will be with us by Christmas.
Have you seen an account of James D. Bayard's death
in the Baltimore paper? God fellow of years he has suffered
pitifully without any kind friend to look his last hour.
But death is the best thing that could have befallen him -
for there was no rational ground of hope - of his reformation.

I want to send you a pair of shoes, that I hope founded at home - as a small remembrance of us - but I am afraid they are not presentable - not fit to go as a gentleman. I will consider about it.

x x x But here we are, -& for myself, gratefully
do I acknowledge never was I more happy. Happy in being per-
fectly tranquil & content, living by the day, without regret
for the past, or anxiety for the future. "Give me my daily
bread", is all I ask or desire, & gladly leave all beyond in
the hands of the great disperser of all things, without ex-
pending even a thought or hope on what may be decreed, certain
that be it joy or sorrow, sickness or health, poverty or riches,
it will be that which is wisest, -best. Amid my doubts and dark-
nesses, never has my belief & trust, in an all directing &
special Providence, been weakened or clouded. God reigns! thy
kingdom come & thy will be done on earth, as it is in Heaven,
I can say with my whole heart & soul. Would that all the
other points of Faith, were as obvious & soul convincing.
In your last letter you say, "Poor Christianity, what has it
done to arouse so much enmity"? & I tell you my sister what
it does, (at least that system taught in our churches) it re-
quires us to sacrifice our reason, that best & distinguishing
& brightest gift of the creator to his creatures. It opposes
itself to that instinctive, moral sense of justice implanted by
the creator in the hearts of his creatures. Our natural
powers of intelligence & our natural feelings, (& is not nature
God's ordinance?) are opposed to such doctrines as the Trinity.
Election, -an eternity of infinite sufferings, for frailties,
2.
shortcomings, & sins of a momentary existence, what do I say,
even more than that, an eternity of infinite suffering, for an
impossible obedience, for not believing, what we can not believe
even when we know it, for not believing, even what is not known,
as certainly the scheme of salvation of Jesus, is not known to
a millionth part of mankind. And while suffering infinitely
& eternally for these short-lived sins & this irresistible un-
belief, no reward is allowed to the most self-sacrificing duty
& morality, but the man whose whole life has been passed in
loving & benefitting his fellow creatures even to the sacrifice
of his own ease & enjoyment, is doomed to eternal punishment
if he did not believe what he could not believe. Such are
some of the reasons why wise & good men reject the Christian
religion while they are the devout & sincere disciples of
natural religion. Mr Jefferson believed in the same God that
Christians believe in, he believed in the immortality of the
soul, he believed that Jesus Christ was the greatest reformer
& the best man that ever lived, -that his religion was the
most pure & sublime ever before taught to man, namely, that God
is a spirit, to be worshipped in spirit & in truth, the father
of all his creatures, to whom he has impartially given all
things necessary for their well being, here & hereafter. He be-
lieved that the system of church morality is the most perfect
ever given to man, & by it was his life & his temper governed.
Had he ignorantly rejected the Christian doctrines, he would
deserve blame, had he rejected them in order to escape from

their moral restraints, he would be guilty, but contrary from
this, He deeply, thoroughly, laboriously studied the scriptures.
Part of them he extolled & admired, for their wisdom, sublimity
& beauty, but in other parts, discovered matter which to his
mind brought the conviction that they were not divinely inspired
writings & therefore not more obligatory or sacred than the
works of Plato or other wise & good men. That he did not
neglect Christianity in order to escape its moral restraints
his life is a proof, those that say otherwise did not know
him, but have formed their opinions from political-party re-
presentations. I am sure my dear sister, did you know all I
know of this good & great man, you would think as I do. I
hope Dr Green will not be unjust, but can he be otherwise?

ments be impartial.

Yesterday I came home in a great hurry
to get a mouthful of dinner & to finish a flower
of fate, to return a quickly as possible to my sale
where Mrs Smith handed me your dear letter. I have
only read it hastily over -- but attentive enough
to remember among the numerous gentlemen I meet
to inquire for an opportunity to send you for clothing
of the housewife rose which Mary Ann Archer
(fortunately I have met with one -- just learned) the
brother of our neighbour goes to Denver & has kindly
and taken to carry a little parcel for me. He
will leave it at the steam boat tavern, where you
will please send it for me. If it is possible, I
will leave it at your door. After being all day
at the sale, Anna & I passed the evening with the
Mr Elgers, her husband & some other friends, at Mrs Larned's
and a father remained at the sale, until 11 o'clock
at night. In thought against my own judgment, I
yielded to the wishes of the majority, to continue
the sale through the evening. By way of refreshment
I purchased a room in the avenue -- I think the
public situation with from beneficial, judging
by the crowds that came -- many however from
more curiosity to see what had corporalized so
many ladies in one shape & in the evening after
the tea it was lighted up there was an absolute
throng, not to any men, about the door. But our Pastor
& three or four of the clerks stood dancing the evening
to protect our ladies -- If we took in a 100 dollars
we shall be quite proud & it will make at 500
dollars for the year.

you should have seen us, how comfortable we looked in
our indistinct. Virginia & Anna, doing their canvas work in
frames; Ann & S. doing mine on our hands, each with
a little table before us, covered with wares-ticks of every shade
& colour. Mrs. Barrel & Julia working needle - all united
round a blazing fire - while without doors was old &
leaving. The bell rings - it is New Clay, who feeling at
home, sat down among us without interrupting us - The bell
rings - some ladies you do not know, - who put up a little
out, but they did not stay long - some shade of colour
was wanting - the shop was distant, but the difficulty was
surmounted by Mrs. Clay, telling the girls to take her carriage
as the would not wait - as the they returned - Virginia &
Anna, ran up stairs for bare necks & cloaks & just as they
got down, Mrs. Barryan entered, bringing into him a
very handsome young man, whom he introduced, but
funding the girls on the wing, he handed them into the
carrage, jumped in with them, & left the handsome
stranger find his way on foot - (a love-tender partner
of Virginia's, as we afterwards found) Mrs. Clay took up one
of the girls' waist & our needles were resumed - when
the bell again rings, & Mrs Calhoun comes in - It seemed
so quite like old times to have him & Mrs Clay together
opposite us - they have long been, not only by distance, but still
more by politics - I dare say he sat near an hour & we had
a talk of old times, as well as present times, but said
not a word of the future - whose collisions of interest may
again separate two once friends. After he went, Catherine
Smith came in, to show us a screen she had just finished
the canvas was worked out while we sat & the threads after
words drew out - which has a beautiful effect - It was the
finest specimen of the world's work & I have seen & our
redactions of admirations were not stopped - This work is
becoming quite a mania here - even friends not meet
but I cannot wait after a pullman - or countatches a train
attended the girls with my fine bunch of flowers done
at fresco. I composed the flowers as I proceeded - one after the
other, filling them in on route. - I am an almost helpless
critic when their work is worth inventing - Virginia, Anna & Anna
are all working alterations for Mrs Clay & I am Irving has largely finished
the bowl, they are present quantities of work, & I am made
for a me are thus helping her to use them. She does the
filing up - the girls only do the flowers, for which they have
gone to seats for some peculiar colour. But when once in the
carrage I imagine Mrs C. was perfectly fixed with us, they
told the opportunity to make some other calls & it was
almost three o'clock when they came back, so I could not
but ask my cousin Barryan, to stay to dinner & soon after Barryard
came in & brought George Brougham, on the other door, to dinner
too - Uncle, & myself - one more old friends & relations, it
was only adding 2 more plates & another loaf of tea table.
Mr Barryan, in twitted to Virginia - he has expert ear & tongue
for no one else - whether it is love - or situation & however not
for an Virginian in quite 400, heavy men distinguished them
others by being in her train & self-love is often
the cause of the devoted admiration they suffer for
great bodies. But Virginia, is worthy of admiration for
herself alone - she really looks beautifully. The latter part
of last evening she went to a party at Mrs Webster's - Anna
& I sat up until after 11 for her & when she came home
her father, her almost idolizing father, with her looked not
only lovely, but splendid, & so splendid were her eyes & so radiant
her countenance & so brilliant her complexion - I cannot else have
been greatly admired - for her Southern, looked so plain & so distinctly
unable. The Diary of this day, will give you some idea
of most of our days, though it is seldom our masters are as
interesting as agreeable - too generally they are common place
& indifferent, & I would prefer being alone with my family
2 hours, by for parties - I could not stand them - I went to
two - but love my own fine ride two much to go to any
more. Anna, is almost an even. She has been likewise only
to her or three this month - Attempt we have invitations to
meet, if not all that were given - Julia, is the only individual
in the family, that really likes to go out - Ann, is
very much engaged in her various occupations & the motions
& duties they render necessary, & I have several industriious
families to visit. The one in which I take most concern is
that of a young woman in the last stage of consumption -- both
she & her mother are destitute widows. Her invalid, is young
& very pleasing in her appearance -- I love to eat with her --
There is a great deal of suffering & distress, this week
among the labouring class, & how society is to give form
a system that will give permanency, or even regular relief
to a class, who depend on daily labour & never make provision
for a day beyond -- I know not -- The very remedies
provided by benevolence, seem to increase the evil by making
them their still more imprudent, what is to be done?
Employment would do -- But Houses of Industry, require not
only great capital -- but great, very great perseverance, zeal
& enterprise on the administrators' part. There are other forces, still
more to be felted -- sudden reverses, such as dismember from
office produce -- In one day, reduced from confidence to
fervor, we are acquainted with Elgar -- The blow to them
was quite unexpected -- Occasioned by some disagreement with
the President. -- The family will leave the city in the spring
& I believe, return to a little farm in Ohio -- How little could
with the girls be for a farm in Ohio -- where female servants

To my dear Sister your letter has found me
rested & home in safety, health & spirits Both
Anna Maria & myself feel surprisingly better for our most
delightful excursion Not one untoward incident occurred
to mar our enjoyment Even the elements seemed pro-
fusive & enabled us to travel with pleasure as well
as safety. But the circumstances which has made the
deeper & most gratifying impression on the kindness of
our friends this excited my expectations & excited the
most tender & grateful feelings At Germantown I expected
to be received & to feel as in a stranger It was the first time
I had ever been in Philadelphia family & had no regret to
look for more than felicities But 5 hours left
this charming relation with awakened sentiments of
admiration affection which I must with never be exhausted
& Anna has become well acquainted with these ladies
a with Theodore Brooks whom she likes very much
In Mrs Ashley's family I had an opportunity of
more social & familiar intercourse with our Smith connec-
tions than I ever before had With the Thirteenth
family we got quite intimate we liked them uncom-
monly well Mary & Anna Brick & Betty Summatt
were great part of the time in the house with us
Mrs Summatt I always liked but never so well as they
intimate intercourse I promise myself much satisfaction
in keeping up this intimacy as she & her sister is at Baltimore

Once more dear sister do I date my
letter from dear Sidney -- How much more like home
can it feel than the city of Sydney, the society is
now changing -- here, my friends they know a friend is killed,
a friend is dead fast & unchangeable, & being separated
with the severest recollections of many, many
years I feel united to them by the closest bonds of
sympathy, I have with them a companionship which
if I did not feel, I never should imagine exist between
the heart & inexorable nature -- But for the first
week I felt sad & lonely without Anna, whom I left
at Kalarama -- but because of her absence, but the occasion
of that absence -- I went for Julia & when she came was
saved from that childish & disloyal feeling -- Her situation
awakened a more than usual degree of tenderness --
indeed we both felt, we had never loved each other
so perfectly before -- She was so full of activity, so
crazy to spend me, that I could not make her sit
quiet, & Mrs. Drake who was with me, advised me
not to restrain her from her usual exercise -- The first
week she was so perfectly well as she was happy, but
one day when I let her ride into the city she went
about all the morning in the hot sun -- stuck with some
other independent foolish consequences which disapponted
my fond hopes of having a grand manner -- She was taken
ill the evening day -- but soon recovered -- I would not however
allow her to leave me until a day or two after I am so sorry
Anna is now better than she has been for
many months. The air is perfumed with the
scent of thousands of flowers in the unending foliage
of trees, & it seems to me most perfect a healthy
& balgamic quality, peculiarly calculated to benefit
the lungs. Still, she is very delicate & feeble, a little
too much excitement of pleasure or occupation or exercise
brings on fever & a sinking or fretfulness of strength.

I regret my dear Hazard that I have not been able
to write to you for so long a time -- and fear you will think me remiss yet I
think you must from long experience felt that confidence in my sympathy -- which will
cause you to think I never could night you lose your son especially in your present
circumstances -- But I have been much indebted -- Washington has been possessing
a pretty powerful sense of treatment -- as the complaint seemed so many times --
which has affected my whole frame -- yet has not exalted the malady the is assisted
the febrile symptoms. sometimes I feel distressed but I should have the same
obvious satisfaction of former years but yesterday -- and today I am in better order.
It is not always an easy attainment to live by the day. Many will make flight
into futility and bring back unworthy apprehensions. Except of myself I trust I
shall do well. At last I will enjoy present comfort which divine providence
has so graciously bestowed beyond all expectation.
It is more than twenty days since the date of your last -- Dear Anna was
thus more comfortable -- and not hearing either from you or from Hazard unless
we hope the remission of painful symptoms is still continued -- and that the
same such warm expressions are still continued to you. What proofs of goodness
are there bunched mitigations of suffering! At a distance we think only of
what is painful and distressing -- but when with a patient we see how many
real pleasure and gratifications -- thus the gloom and sadness as position
habits itself as health itself can ever taste. The comforts of devotion -- the
tenderness of friendship are related in a manner known only to the sufferer
and then the minor gifts of kindness -- the visits of friends -- of a physician
from the apriority of something afford so much satisfaction that pain is
often bequited by its potency, and a sweet feeling is diffused over the sorrows
of disease in the being the object of so much love and care. I must afford you
my dear sister suchlib gratification that you are in circumstances to command all
that comfort for your beloved child -- and that her complaint alone will
mitigatome. I feel very anxious to hear from you -- and from Regard that
has prevented him from writing. He is thus letter in debt to me, and I was deeply
interested in not hearing from me. He did not know how much I needed his prompt
attention -- when you can him inquire if he has not written I think probably he has
written by a private opportunity and that the letter is bad. Every day I have been
expecting he would bring me some mission.
Being shut up in my room -- I have not much to say -- you know there
is a sort of stagnation of mind when cut off from society -- I have omitted only
a few friends -- and when at all interested in conversation have always suffered
from Monday I had quite a leave -- or rather succession, and gentlemen too. I find myself
a venerable elogeeman (real existence) an agent for Belongings. I made an earnest
pleasure visit. He talks as a great and about the prosperity and prosperity of the
Besa Cove settlement -- and appears to think that humanity has every thing
to hope from the appearance of success in all their plans. Before he went
he made a most sweet and soothing address from some corner in the 45th Psalm
where God's care of the kiddos & fatherly is spoken of -- and in an art of liberal
portion recommended as to that case. It was really astonishing! -- I have called
soon after -- and was very kind and cheerful. I had a few female friends also
so that it was quite a legal day in my calendar -- but since then I have had to
practice abstinence --
You speak of Miss Jane -- I believe she is a relation of the Governor
and if the Governor has I wonder not that you love her. I am sure you do
debates with Mrs B. and I am also certain I should admire your wife Jane.
My body is in a very bad state this summer and always came most kindly
to die me -- without waiting for any return. My fortune Mr. Paul has him in
a fluctuating state of health all summer travelling from place to place -- and rarely
led by -- always making addresses -- and effecting at all establishments where he can
promote the cause of religion or mission. He is in hopes he shall get in October
go out to China -- and will make the attempt if strength permits -- he has been
die on the passage. There are different opinions respecting his complaint -- some think

but rather more variable in its progress -- and termination. He is at times so sick that
life is despised of and gladly dies. His friends, then he remains and travels

I have just read a letter from Maria in which she informs me she expects to
leave for Washington near to you -- where she can be with you occasionally
on your circumstances will admit. I hope you will derive mutual comfort &

My dear Son, You do not write me as often as
you ought. In your next you must assign some
reason for this neglect. Possibly I have not
received all your letters. Nothing will improve
you so much in Epistolary writing as practice. Take
great pains with your letters. Avoid vulgar
phrases. Study to have your ideas pertinent &
correct, & clothe them in an easy & grammatical
dress. Pay attention to your spelling, pointing,
the use of capitals, & to your hand writing. After a
little practice these things will become natural & you will thus acquire a habit of writing correctly & well. General Washington
was a remarkable instance of what I have now
recommended to you. His letters are a perfect
model for Epistolary writers. They are written
with a great uniformity in respect to the hand
writing & disposition of the several parts of the
letter. I will show you some of his letters when
I have the pleasure of seeing you next vacation; & when I shall expect to find you much
improved in your natural disposition, my dear
son, renders it proper for me earnestly to recommend to you to attend to one thing at a time.
It is impossible that you can do two things well
at the same time, & I would, therefore, never have
you attempt it. - Never undertake to do what might
not to be done; & then, whatever you undertake
endeavour to do it in the best manner.
It is said of Mr. DeWitt, a celebrated States-
man in Holland, "who was born to success in the
year 1672, did the whole business of the republic,
I yet had time left to go to assemblies in the
evening, & sup in company. Being asked how
he could possibly find time to go through so
much business & yet amase him self in the even-
ings as he did? he answered, there was nothing
to do but, for that it was only doing one thing
at a time, & never putting off anything till to-
morrow that could be done today. The study
I am dissipated attention to one object, is a fine
mark of a superior Genius; as hurry, bustle,
agitation are the never failing symptoms
of a weak & frivolous mind."

Dear Parents,
As an opportunity now
offers I take the pleasure of informing you that
I received your letter & bundles safe & give
you great thanks for them, I gave that little
book to Mrs. Blanchard & she told me to thank
you for her. Our class has joined again & we
are all together in Ruge Dictums I have read considerable
in Plutarch & I am tell you the position
of Demosthenes which is as follows, History
of THE MSSINES
Demosthenes (the father of this Demosthenes) was
a citizen of great note among the Grecians & as
Theopompus writes he was surrounded (the sword
maker) because he had a great number of ser-
vants to work in that art. When Demosthenes
was but seven years old his father died &
left him a large estate, of fifteen talents of which
his Guardians cheated him as of three quarters
of it. his Constitution was sickly and very thin
and it is said that in this respect the boys gave
him the Nickname of Batalis. This Batalis
was a weak infirm fellow & none make mention
of Batalis as a Poet who used to write wicked
songs & Lampoons & the name of Clancy they
put upon him because he was fierce & passionate.
He began to learn oratory very soon &
hearing that Callistratus an Orator was going
to speak one day, he desired his tutor to let
him see him, the tutor being well acquainted
with the Door keepers to easily found a
place for the Boy, who admired Calli, too,
very much & resolved to imitate him,
he had a very odd place for studying, he had
a study built on purpose for him under
ground & there he used to shave himself
that he might be in no condition to go a
broad. he was no great warrior, for often times
he got beat off and especially by Alexander
who order'd (after he conquerd Demosthenes)
twelve of the Orators, of whom Demosthenes
was one but after wards he said he would be
content with eight only, an ambassador was
sent to demand pardon which was readily given
by Alexander. sometime after Aristophanes
came to Athens who was a great seducer he
had a silver cup of a certain king with
which he tried to seduce Demosthenes & setting
it on the table as he dined with Demosthenes
Demosthenes ey'd it with attention
asked him how much he would give him for it
he said five talents which he took & gave him
the cup & the next night he was seized with
a Quinsey & could not speak, & as he went
into the senate house, the senate desired him
to get up & speak, but he made signs to
them that he could not speak and the people
began to ridicule him & said the Orator had
no other disease than that of a Silver Coinsey.
Soon after this he went to war with Cratinus
& the Exile Flautus
and got defeated & Demosthenes having fled, the
enemy pursued him, with Archias at their head
& overtook him at the temple of Siptane where
he begged he might have a letter and going
further into the temple he took a quill of
poison & put it into his mouth and held it there
for some time and as he proceeded out of the
temple he began to staggen and fell down dead
This concludes
my love to all the family, Yours, &c,
S.F.B.Morse.
S.F.B. Morse

Sir: I received your favor of the 2d inst.
in due course, I have delayed a reply
till I had rec'd & examined the book
you mention. It was not rec'd till Sat-
urday last & since that time I have
examined it as far as my pleasure
would allow -- I judge, not pretending, however,
to perfect exactness, that one half
of the states contained between 1200000000000000000000000000000000
of inhabitants may be found verbatim
in my geography. The portion
of descriptions of the several states
in the Union, which make the bulk of
the work, are almost wholly taken from
my book -- I am not aware, may have
made use of Carey's edition of Guthrie,
but he should know that Mr. Carey copied
my work (so far as it respected
the United States or the most of them) by
my permission, & for a stipulated
consideration. Mr. Doyle certainly could
not have been ignorant of the fact that
the Corps, under the U.S. was chiefly
copied from mine, I think it therefore
disingenuous in Mr D. entirely to omit giving
me the least credit for any assistance
derived from my work, when it is evident
he was indebted to it for so great a
part of his. He calls it an epitome
of Pinkerton's Geo. 9. It would be quite as correct to say that it was
an epitome of mine, arranged on
Pinkerton's plan. He is perhaps equally indebted to me both in propriety and
to have honorably acknowledged it in his preface. I object to the reason he assigns
in the last paragraph but one of his preface for publishing his work. I conceive that there has long been in circulation in the United States, as exact and full an abridgement of Modern Geo. 9 for schools
as Mr Doyle has furnished, though not on Pinkerton's plan, yet perhaps as useful for youth. I perceive important defects errors in Mr D.'s work, the former arising probably from an attempt to conform
to Mr Pinkerton's plan, the latter from adhering to old editions of my Geo 9. I not attending to the improvements and alterations
in the last Editions
After these few remarks, I have to thank
you Sir for your ingeniousness & disposition to
do in this case what is just & honourable If
any thing would induce me to permit the fall
of this work under existing circumstances it would
be the manner in which you have presented the
subject for new consideration. I am ready to meet
you on this fair ground. I wish not to injure
Mr Doyle he is a stranger to me. Had he merely
made an epitome of Pinkerton with might have
been done, I conceive with advantage (I hope?
don't, however, whether Mr D. has the proper talents
to execute such a work well) I should have had
no objection to it.

Dear Boys,
I cannot omit writing
you one line by Capt. Phillips
today - I hope you enter on
your studies, at the close of
vacation, with renewed pleasure;
I will determination
to make greater progress than
ever. Your behaviour the
last term, & while at home
gave us much pleasure I
has increased our affection
for you. I hope neither
of you, nor your brother Finley
will be found on either
of the bills at the close of
the term.
I have no news to write you
Grandma Beech, we hear is not
very well - Lydia will leave
us very shortly - we miss your
company very much - You must
write us frequently, & long letters
& comfort us - To hear of your
good behaviour, & of your pro-
gress in your studies, will com-
fort us more than any thing
else - Don't forget to read
your bible daily, & perform
devoutly your morning &
evening devotions - Your
Mama & Many join me
in love to you both
Regards to Mr & Mrs Blan-
chard - Your affectionate parent
J. Moser

Dear boys, We have not had the pleasure
of a line from you since you left us -- we
are quite anxious to hear how you do,
& what progress you are making in
your studies. We hope you are very
happy, & making rapid progress
in your studies. I have written
one letter to Finlay -- & one to
Edward & Richard. I hope you had
received them -- We should be glad
to hear from Cousin Hazard -- we
hope he finds himself agreeably
situated. -- Let us hear from you
all very soon & often.
I have nothing new to write
you -- Master Charles Hud, who
carries this will tell you the news
what will be most interesting to you.
Mr. Lathrop's parents have come on
from Norwich, I will take her home
on Friday, so we shall be quite alone.
Anne was married last Saturday
evening - a very good girl, Rev-
inda Brown, has come in her place.
She is all well. Mama always
send you much love. The think of
you every day, & many times in a
day - Your good behaviour will
make us happy - This is all we ask
of you in return for the expence
we are at for your education - Don't
deny us that.
It is now bed time - Give
our love to cousin Hazard - remem-
ber us also, to Mr & Mrs Blanchard.
Your affectionate
son J. Moree

Dear Son
We have the pleasure of a letter from you, which has gratified
us very much it is the only intelligence we have had from you since Mr Brax-
ton left you. I began to think that something was the matter with respect to
your health, that occasioned your long silence. You must have your letters
written and have them at Mr Phillips, as the frequently has opportunities
of finding them that you do not know of. We are all pleased to find that
you were so happy in your new situation; we thought that it was a sign that
you behaved well yourself to find you satisfied. Mr and Mrs Abbott we know
have always sustained the character of very worthy excellent people, and we
felt pleased that you was not in humble to their merits how is Erskine?
you say nothing of him in your letter. I hope he is well, give our love to
him and tell him we wish him to write us and let us know whether he is
happy in his new situation, and whether he hears frequently from home?
Do you need an Umbrella? if you do we will send you one by the first good
opportunity. Hope you will be very studious and be well fitted for Collledge by
the time you enter that you may pass your examination with honour
to yourself as well as your instructor. We are very anxious now for
that you should excel in every thing that will make you truly happy
and be useful to your fellow men. In particular by no means forget
your duty to your heavenly Father. Remember what has been said with
great truth, that he can never be faithful to others him who is not so, to his
God, and his conscience, I wish you constantly to keep in mind the first
question of a man in that excellent form of sound reason the humble
Catechism. viz What is the chief End of man? the Answer you will
readily recollect in To glorify God and enjoy him forever. Let it be evident
to your mind son that this be your chief aim in all that you do, and may you
be so happy as to enjoy him forever in the sincere prayer of your affectionate
Parent. - We have the promise of two letters a week from you, be punctual
to your engagements, that we may know what to expect from you.
We have had a letter from your Grandmother, even last week. She was not
well now in good Spirits your Uncle Grant Inarden are now at Shrewsbury,
they intend taking your Grandmother and Aunt Abby back with them to
Hartford if they can get ready to go, so as not to make it necessary
for them to return to Saginaw. - The Fourth of July is to be celebrated
here with a good deal of Parade both by Federalists & Jacobins the
former are to meet in our Meeting house their to hear an Oration which
is to be delivered by Mr. Aaron Putnam a prayer by your pastor
and on the hill at once by the monument a Standard is to be presented
to a new Company (called The Warren Washington Federalist) by
Doctor Putnam who is the president of the day, and all the gentlemen
are to dine at Petershall otherwise called Mashunk's Hall. The Ladies
are to take Part at the same place. The Jacobins are to have an
oration at the Baptist meeting house from Mr. Gleason I know nothing
more about them. The boys are forming themselves in Companies &
they have two or three companies of Drums which at some times are
enough to excite one. Grant well thinking when you have done I am
sure that my sons are better employed at Andover than beating
the streets or Docks, that they are laying in a good store of
useful knowledge against the time to come While these poor boys
many of them at least are learning what they will be glad by & by
to believe you must send this letter to your Brothers and to no other
person your Papa thinks it is not but to send you the happy news but will
send you the No. of the pamphlet as soon as they are out Wish you to
read it attentively and give us your opinion of the merits of each
particular piece especially the last piece of poetry entitled Sweet babe
I must now hasten to conclude Papa was very sick last night but is
better to day he joins me in love to you and your Brothers & cousin
Eskimee in all which Nancy joins. Remember us also with respect
to Madame Philispe & all inquiring Friends. Lydia Lathropse
is gone home, she went last week. I told you before that Anne
is married and we have a young Woman here has in her place
where Anne is Rebecca Brown a young Dear Girl, she Used to live
at Mrs Lovells. Mrs L is going to move to Boston soon, which we
are sorry for. I can think of nothing more to say to you at present
Adieu my dear Son, and believe me ever your affectionate
Mother E Bellamy
Master S.F.B. More

Charleston July 12, 1805
Dear Sir
Received your favor of the 2nd inst, on
my return from an excursion into the country to
recruit my health & spirit, which, under Providence,
has had the desired effect. I am gratified that your
Committee have agreed to take 100 copies of the Panoptist.
I have little doubt of your procuring subscribers enough
in Hampshire County to take the whole number. They
shall be delivered free of expense, at Northampton at
9d payable semiannually. We shall be obliged
by your expending your profits in the work, at the
same price, for distribution. I think the same num-
ber might easily be disposed of in Berkshire County,
with a little exertion, on the same terms. Some very favor-
able returns from that county, I have now received. Will
you undertake to negotiate with Mr Hyde for me. I
will be obliged to you to do it. He shall have all the
subscribers received from that County, if he, in behalf
of the Missionary Society in that County, will take
100, delivered at Northampton. I have received no returns from
Hampshire County, but have heard that Dr Lathrop has a num-
ber that he is friendly to the work. Opposition is silenced here,
at least for the present, by the appearance of the first number.
I had forgotten in my great haste, to say that I sent last
week 100 copies of the Panoptist to Hadley, by Dr Thom-
son, in Stage, which I hope have been received. I send with
this a number of subscription papers. I shall direct all
subscribers in Hampshire County to receive their books of your
100 – this moment, while I am writing, a subscription paper,
for 22 copies has been received from Mr Somroy, Worthington,
which I enclose, as belonging to you, & which will take a large
portion of your 100 at once. I hope you will want 100 more. I
think you will. I will write you longer soon. The heat, at
a lecture this evening
the count of 2000 prevent Badding only that we are

Charlestown. Dec 2d 1805.
My dear Sir, I am indebted to you for two letters, the last rec'd
last evening of the 27th ult. My health has been very feeble for the
last fortnight or three weeks, or I should have written you. I am
now not well. After passing through a good deal of trouble &
difficulty with the printers paper maker, I have transferred the
printing to the Panoptist to Boston, & feel relieved of a considera-
ble portion of care. I expect the work will be more punctually prin-
ted & distributed than it has been. I feel the force of your remarks,
& we shall readily do what we consistently can to adapt it to the
taste of your common readers; but if we go too far that way,
we shall lose on the other hand & defeat our main object. The
work, so far as I learn is very well rec'd this way, & subscriptions
are increasing. The deficient number you mention were
sent 10 days or a fortnight ago, & I hope before this have
been rec'd. The dilatoriness of the paper maker & printer occasion-
ed the disappointment. I hope your society will take 200 & distribute
what are not taken by subscribers. I have sent 25 sets to Mr
Hyde. I hope the Berkshire society will find it convenient for
their interest to take 50. I find I shall lose about 820 by the ex-
change I made with you, owing to the difference of printing here
& with you; as I shall dispose of the books I receive of you at
38 cents bound, but I shall not get back. I will do what I can
to have them ready against you send for them. I believe South
on Education is not yet printed, nor Henry on Meekness. When
all are ready I will write you particularly. I expect a Resident
of the College will shortly be chosen, who it will be cannot be con-
jectured. All plans are kept profusely secret. We expect they mean to
complete the revolution put in Dr H - or Prof We are perhaps. Should
the Corporation elect such a man, will any of the Senators in your
country have the firmness publicly to oppose the sanction of the Bull

My Dear Sons
I have had a few lines from Finley to day which gave
me pleasure to hear that you were all well he mentions Edward, not
being quite well a few days before but never said what was the matter
with him; have a grand best wishes too hand if this is the cause of his
not being so well he must not continue it his health is of
great importance to him, as without it, he can do nothing
to that advantage, that he otherwise would. I shall send
Finley affairs from Paris will send the 2d No of the Transplantist
and if I can find it will send the Music Book all by Mrs
Abbott, to morrow morning. You have not told me whether
you received the two bundles of papers sent you by Capt Phillips
Have you heard of the death of Young Williard of Cambridge
the late president Williard son he died of a violent fever occasioned
by going into Eaton when he was very hot in the middle of the
day he also pumped a great deal of cold water on him had
it not been for his being so very hot this be a warning to you all
not to be guilty of the like Indiscretion which may cost you
your life Dreadfull indeed would this be to all of us. Drink
you would not go into water afterer than once a week and
then either early in the morning or late in the afternoon and
not go in when hot nor stay long in the water remember
these cautions of your mama and obey them Strictly. A young
Lady of 20 years old died in Boston yesterday I very suddenly the
cut her dinner perfectly well and was dead in five minutes
after. her name was Ann Hinkley. You see my dear boys
the great uncertainty of life and of course the importance of be-
ing always prepared for death even a sudden death as we have
not what an hour may bring forth. This we are sensible of we cannot
be too soon or too well prepared for that all important moment as
this is what we are sent into this world for, the main business
of life is to prepare for death let us not then put of these most
important concerns to an uncertain tomorrow but let us in
certain attend to the concerns of our precious saving dying
souls While we feel ourselves alive "that whether we live or
may live to the Lord or whether we die we may die to the Lord
that living or dying we may be the Lord" that this may be the
happy situation of each of us is the sincere prayer of your
own affectionate parents. I had a letter from your good
Grandmama Breen yesterday from New York she was on
her way to Whitestown with your Uncle & Aunt
Madison she desired her love to you all Your Aunt Abby
is gone to Philadelphia to spend the fall & winter with Uncle
& Aunt Hazard they do not expect ever to return to
Kreussburg again which I am very glad to hear Nancy
Shepard is gone to Amherst to see her Sister Beecky Cushing
She will be home I hope by Vacation which will soon be here
I will leave this letter for Papa to finish and shall bid you
good bye for the present Your Affectionate mother
E A M
My dear boy,
Your Mamma has left me this page to
fill it with pleasure, as I am fond of writing
to those who are pleased as you seem to be with reading my letters. Mr. Abbott, who dined with us today,
gives a good account of Finley's behaviour in the family. I say he is a boarder, in general are very studious -- Hope Finley will learn to fix his
attention to his proper business, he will soon find his prospects will reward him for all his labour. If Mr Newman thinks it proper he will
furnish Edwards with a suitable piece for him to speak at exhibition -- I think it will not be best for him to go to College this fall -- to leave Rochester
alone -- He is young enough yet -- I am sorry to hear he has been unwell -- You must all take care of your healths -- & not play hard this last in
& especially take care not to go into the town -- You are warned, now in the middle of the day -- I am more than once in the week -- Your Mama has
told you what happened to young Willard who was buried yesterday -- The yellow fever is in Providence & St. Haven -- The College at U. S. is on that side
broken up for the present -- I hope the sick keep there will soon subside -- The H. M. of the Penophilist is not quite ready the last half of the flowers are not stuck off.
The paper for Andover may be sent on Saturday --
The season is very dry, melancholy in that respect but the town is very healthy at present -- Your Mama sends you
some lilies, which she has written from memory, with the wishes you all to remain up in your memories -- We send you all
dear Cousin Hutchinson, a great deal of love -- Your affectionate father J. Mosse

Charlestown August 27th 1803
Dear Sir,
In June last your brother John
called on me, in great distress to indorse a
note for him, at 90 days, for $257. His wife
at this time lay at the point of death; his goods
were all attached, & a man watching them
in his house, at his expense. I told him
that I could not be obliged for him without
security, as I had promised Mrs. Mosey, I never would be.
He said he was willing to make me secure, & the
sheriff & he made out a bill of sale of furniture
to the amount of the debt, he signed it, & the
sheriff witnessed it, & I endorsed the note. I believe
it a means of saving the life of Mrs. P. it is
so considered by others. I had hoped by this act
to have continued your brother in the Bank,
till your return.
A strong inducement to indorse
this Note; in addition to the above, was
your brother assured me repeatedly, that he had
just received a letter from you, requesting him to
get some one to assist him till your return,
& that you would be given me immediately on
your return. I had no opportunity to see you
before your departure to the east-ward.
As the Sheriff made out the Bill of sale
& you rather receipted the goods, I supposed them secure
in his hands & did not remove them - I was
induced thus to do, also an acct of the delicate state
of Mrs P. health, unwilling to do anything to disturb
her - Things remained in this state till about 10 days ago
it was intimated that your brothers affairs were growing
worse, & the goods made over to me were not safe in his
hands. I immediately called on him, & he agreed to send part
of them to me that evening, & a part on subsequent evenings
to avoid observation, till all but the bed should be
delivered - Promised me he would keep his son locked till
he left town - He however sent the things sparingly to me
about the amount of 40 or 50 dollars - & in my absence
an officer entered & seized all his goods - & last week, he
with his family left town in the night - to day his goods
remaining have been sold at auction - I am left to pay the
last of next month 257 doll. unless you will consent to take
my place, as I hope you will, as I am very illly able, to sustain
such a loss - & I became obligated, to save the life of his wife
to continue him in business, & in confident expectation
that on your return, you could pay the note - I know
the humanity & goodness of your heart & was assured by
your brother both of your ability & willingness to assist him

Charlestown Sept 3d
Dear Grandpapa,
I received your letter
dated the 22d of May. I have got through
the Junior Class in my Academic Studies,
and it will take me but one year more to
fit for College. Finley is trying to enter New
Haven College, this year.
You made one Mistake
in your last letter, that was in Richard's age
he will be 11 next June 18th day, & Thomas
Rufsel if he had lived would have been 8
next May.
Papa is now going a journey &
we are going to Andover, & the house will
be left by all except Nancy.
I expect you will receive this letter.
I am your affectionate
Grandson, Edwards Morse.
Now, sir.
We are about to set out for
Phil.a tomorrow in the stage. We meant
to have gone as far as Woodstock in
our own chaise, & to have left the
chaise at home, with you till our
return but for reasons, which
I will mention when I see you
we have thought best to go by
stage from home, & pay you our
visit on our return, 4 or 5
weeks hence – In the mean time
Oliver Brown, takes the horse
Chaise, & carries up Mrs Howard
& her infant to Woodstock, will
leave the horse & Chaise, till
I return. I wish you would be
so good as let one of the boys
take a horse of brother's, & my
horse, & carry Mr Brown to
Worcester, where he can take

My dear Secretary of War:
It is a source of deep pleasure to me to
inform you that the President of the United
States has appointed you to be a member of
the Committee of Military Affairs. I have
always been anxious to give you the
opportunity of serving in this capacity
and I am confident that you will
render the highest satisfaction to the
President and the Government of the
United States by your services.
I am, Sir,
Very respectfully
Yours,
Abraham Lincoln

see you, I regret that circumstances have

since the decease of my honoured and

affection.
Though the weather has been
extremely warm & sultry, my journey
has been evidently conducive to my health
& that of Mrs Moser. We have had a
pleasant Commencement, & a charming
visit at Mr Marsh's where we now
are.
Today is the election, with so far, as
I can learn is likely to have favorably
to the cause of Federalism. -- I have
no special news to write you. You have
probably heard of a battle between the
English & combined fleets with Spud
favorably to the English -- We have had
the last three days, a plentiful sea-
table rain -- No sickness prevails
in this part of our country -- New York
is in great distress.
My Moser joins me in affectionate
regards to yourself, brother &
sister -- Hoping soon to see you I remain
your affectionate son
Genl. J. Moser

angry with Nancy (which I like to have

will get me a son & I will be very happy
to have one for my father & mother
whch I will love & honor
