My Dear Son
We had a letter from Mr. Backus last night dated
Oct 17th at Springfield he informed us that you left him at Boston
despite the care of a lady for Hartford that he had just heard
by the Stage driver that you were safely arrived at Major Ripley at
Hartford we were pleased to hear from you thus far we are now very
determined to know how you got along from there to Mr. Marshes and to
Newhaven hope you met with no uncommon difficulty getting to
your journey's end. You will receive this letter with one from your
Dada by Dr. Green & Son of Philadelphia who will spend one day
in Newhaven you will make a point of calling on him and
Asking after H, and devoting the favour of him to remember
you to your Aunt Abby & all your Philadelphia Friends I have
just seen Mr. Blanchard he has brought letters from your
Brothers who are well will send you Richard. You must write
them on the same sheet of paper that you write us and that will
save postage What money had you remaining when you got to N.H.
let us know and let us have a particular account from time to time
of your expenses. Engage our Friends in N.H. to let you know when
there is Opportunities of writing to us by private convenience and to
save and improve it. I intend sending you some Cambrick ruffles for your
three plain shirts & 2 shirts let be worn on them when your ruffles get ragged
let them be picked of and either wear them 2, though if the shirts are
good enough let them have ruffles on if you happen to have any by
you ready for the purpose which I will endeavour shall be the case.
Your Papa is not very well to day he had a tooth extracted yesterday
afternoon he will I hope be better soon Nancy is much better but
has not got down yet Mr Gardiner Spring lodged here last night he
had not seen or heard of you on his way here from New Haven being
particular in your account of your journey when you write us over

Dear Brother:
I will now address you in a
few lines to inform you we are all well excepting

The State-Prison is done and Mama is
going to see it with us before the Prisoners are
put in it which will be on December next
the 1st day of the month. It is Vacation now
in all its Beauties, the most pleasing Vacation
to I, ever had, Richard and I both study for
all it is Vacation and that makes it seem the
more pleasant, when I left Andover all the
sch ool were well.
I hope you will be contented with
your situation at New haven seeing when you
were at Andover you wished to go there, I would
try to bear it as well as I could and not go
into College as it is like enough if there are
any bad scholars they will try to make you
as bad as themselves.
There has not been much
alteration since you have been gone only
they are paving the side of the road by our
house.
I am your affectionate
Samt Morse.

Parent J. Morse

a light bodyed coat, I think you must be very much mistaken with respect
to that dont you remember I told you I had no expectation that you
would need anything of the kind till next Mayor some your brown
coat for every day and your blue one for the Sabbath & other days when
you are under a necessity of being more drafty is quite enough for any
boy that is not a going to be an extravagant foolish fellow you will
remember that you have promised in your first letter to be an Occasional
in your last you seem to have forgotten all about it pray What does your
hurrying frontier cost you for possession & that you think you to consider and
not go driving on from one foolish Whine to another till you provoke
us to withdraw from you the means of gratifying you in anything that
may be even less objectionable than gaming. For the Government of Colliidge
allow the Students to go a gaming I hope you will never do any
thing contrary to the rules of the College whether you are in Colliidge
or not. – I have dealt very plainly with you on if you and you must
attend to what we say if you mean to make a nuisance trouble some times
to be to find fault with you but it is necessary you must be patient
answering our letters every fall the questions we ask
you are thank us when we send you things I spent up in your trunk
that went by Captain Collis some raincoats also by Esquire I went
some but you have not told me whether you have received them or
whether you got a letter from us by Dr Green with a pair of yarn socks
let us know all this & if you delivered the bundle to young Mr Marsh
that went by Captain Collis for his Father you must read my two
last letters to you before you set down to write me an answer let
your lines in your letters be very clear and fill a large sheet very fast there
sides and by doing thus you will be able to answer all my requests to you
I must now bid you detain your Papa in our well but those will be better
soon the rest of the family are all well and all join in love to you –
Remember Papa & myself Respectfully to all who inquire after us
in particular to Dr & Mr Dwight & I beg you not to go into the sick
parts of the town and wear your sleeve now the weather is cold & don't
heat yourself & then take a sudden cold by cooling or you may take the
even without going into the parts of the town most infected from Affectionate
Emil Nourse

My Dear Son
We had a letter from you dated
the next day after your arrival at New Haven which gave
us much pleasure. We were glad to find that you had no agreeable
a journey and so little difficulty in getting on we supposed
it would cost you more than we had contemplated as you
left Mr Backus so soon but it was perhaps best to do as you
did and go on in the Stage I was a little afraid of
your staying too long at Mr Marshes I hope you took care
not to give them any more trouble than you could not
possibly help and that you were particular in thanking
them when you left them for their kind attentions to
you be sure my son that you do not forget at all times to be
very gratefull to every body that treats you with any attention
and kindness whatever whether for your parents sake
or your own and take every opportunity of showing
that you are your feelings by being as polite and kind
to them as you can whenever you have opportunity always
keep in mind that excellent proverb "that those who
have Friends must show themselves Friends" - You have
received letters from us by Mr Green I presume before this I hope
you called on him while he & his son were in New Haven
and paid your respects to him & thank'd him for his
care of your letters & a pair of yarn socks which I sent you
by him. be sure and express your thanks to any person that
brings you letters or anything from your Friends or tells
you that they have seen us at any time. I wish to know if you
have received your trunk by Captain Collis and the bundle directed
to Mr Marsh when you receive the latter carry it to young Mr
Marsh and request him to send it to his father with your papers
respect, to him - Your writing Desk also went by Captain
Collis. Consult Mr Davis what kind of legs you had better
have to it and hope you had better have them made and do
young Papa think an en en gineer himself will do this for you.
as he directs. I find that your expenses run up so high that
you could not have but a few shillings over for pocket money
We shall therefore enclose you a few Dollars to prevent your
calling on Mr Beers till you have further orders from us We
expect you will attend strictly to your promise of being very
economical and spending as little as possible and it is with exertion
on our part that we shall be able to give you all such an
Education as we wish. you will receive this letter by your Cousin
Eskime who is going home to Philadelphia on his legs are so
weak that he cannot study. Eskime will hand you a bundle
containing your two Summer Coats & pantaloons which I think
will serve you next summer for every day we have made the
trousers coat slivers as much longer as we could. send also a neat
bundle of the pieces to mend with and four Cambrick ruffles all
ready to set on your shirts I wish three of them put on your
three plain shirts and keep the other in your little trunk of
patches to sew on the first of your shirts that has a ragged ruffle
let Mrs Davis know that you have this direction with respect to
them from me and she will be so kind as to see it executed should
have put them on before you went but for our hurry to have you
go with Mrs Backus. you will receive a paper of raisins & a piece
of association cake also in the bundle you need not forget you
We were much pleased with your letter and it was particular in letting
us know how you got along from place to place. We enclosed your
letter to our brothers promising it would afford them much
pleasure I hope we shall receive some letters from them to enclose to
you in this before it goes -- but if we should not have letters from them
we take it for granted they are well. They were well a week ago. -- Dear
Bapa is appointed Chaplain to the State Prison by the Governor's Council
he has in consequence an addition to his labours which you know
were very great before I am afraid it will be more than he can do
to get through with all without injuring his health. You must be very
industrious in your studies and be able to relieve him from a great many
of his cares the reason that he can get through with so much business
is that he early inbibed habits of Industry and application to
his studies which have grown up with him and makes him thus
able to be useful to his fellow men in various ways if his children
would be as useful to his fellow men in various ways as his father
and grandfather have been in their youth they must follow his example and not let their
prerious moments pass unimproved in but in early life lay upon
store a fund of good and useful knowledge now that they
have the means put into their hands lest they should not be always
thus favoured be ambitious therefore my son to excel in whatever
you undertake that is good and no doubt with the blessing of heaven
on your endeavours which I trust you will not fail to ask daily
you will succeed and be a great comfort to your parents by being a
blessing in the world. and Samll Ward is well and pleased with
Caldridge his mama says I hope you will keep up with him and know
as much as he does when you leave N'Havan -- how do you like the
place if you had not been there long enough where you devote to know
how you should be pleased to continue -- I think it a charming place and
very agreeable people indeed I hope you will be able to well as to

which for the want of those advantages which you enjoy in my

but they convey to my children and Friend the feeling I have

I hope my Dear son you will not fail to do your duty in reading

all who may ask you when you have heard from us and
how we do. I must bid you remain as ever
Papa & Nancy join me in love Your Affectionate
Mother E A Morett

Charleston Dec. 2d 1805
My dear Sir, I am indebted to you for two letters
the last one, last evening of the 27th ult. -- My health
has been very feeble for the last fortnight or
three weeks -- or I should have written you -- I
am now not well -- After passing through a
good deal of trouble & difficulty with the printer
& paper maker I have transferred the printing
of the People's Republic to Boston, I feel re-
lieved of a considerable portion of care -- I
expect the work will be more punctually printed
& distributed than it has been -- I feel the more
as you remark -- & we shall readily do what
we consistently can to adapt it to the taste
of your common readers but if we go too far
that way we shall loose on the other hand
& defeat our main object -- The work, to far
as I learn is very well wt. this way, & subscriptions
are increasing -- The Deficient numbers
you mention were sent on 10 days or a fortnight
ago, & I hope before this have been received --
The relations of the paper maker & printer
questioned the disappointment -- I hope your
Society will take your distribute, what are not
taken by subscribers I have sent 25 potts
to Mr Hyde - I hope this Berkshire Society
will find it convenient for their interest
to take 50-
I find I shall lose about 20 doll. by the
exchange I made with you, owing to the difference of
printing here with you as I shall dispose of the
books I receive of you at 38 cents bound - but I
shall not go back. I will do what I can to have
them ready against you sent for them. I believe
Dodson's Education is not yet printed nor Henry on
Meckwep - when all are ready I will write you
particularly.
I expect a President of the College will
shortly be chosen, who will be cannot be suspected
All plans are kept profoudly secret we expect they
mean to complete the revolution & put in Dr. K. or Bush
Wee perhaps - Should the Corporation elect such a
man, will any of the Senators in your county have
the firmness publickly to oppose the sanction of
the Overseers to their choice? - Will you talk with some
of them on the subject & cause others to be talked with?
A word with of the Govt. w/ not be amiss - If some gen-
tleman in the civil line w/ take up the subject
spiritedly, I am by no means certain that a suc-
cessful opposition might not be made I refer
all to you - It is a crisis - Wisdom is profitable
& necessary to direct -
This Man has been confined a week, but
is now below stairs at 10 o'clock for the first time - the papers
in affectimate regret to him for his self destruction, with
the loss of his family in your truly J. Morse
P.S. You will much oblige me by sending the balance
due for the first half year of the Pamphlet, as the money
is wanted to pay expenses. The balance is about 80 dollars
50 are rec'd from Mr Phillips.
We have inserted a part of your excellent report
It was owing to unavoidable circumstances that it was
not before inserted. I shall mention Mr
Phillip's donation in the next No.
Pres* of H.C.
Rev. Dr. Joseph Lyman

My Dear Son
It is three weeks to day since we have heard a word
from you which makes me very anxious indeed if you are and
have been well I much wonder that you are not more regular
and punctilious in writing us than you are we depend on hearing
from you at least once a fortnight by post you must write a
long letter and answer it to the post office every other Sunday
night in season to be put in the mail and come on on Monday
morning and we should get it every other Wednesday
which would be a great pleasure to us your brothers almost
every day come to the office in expectation of getting a letter from
brother Finley and are greatly disappointed to return us that
one you cannot therefore please us all by being more punctual in
your brothers are to stay home this winter to supply the place of
Prince by taking care of the cord & supplying the young boys
bringing in wood & going of commands leaving having a man
and to save paying board for them in order to enable you to
be so far from home to get your education so you see the need
of close application on your part to render us all for our attention
to you your brothers study very closely at home and devote
things as recreation and are good boys. You must write them
on the same paper you write us occasionally, I wrote you a long
letter by Mr Nichols a fortnight ago & your brother Walt
then too. hope you have received them I heard from Philadelphia
this week that Dr Green took the sick of Washington the letter to
you on to Philadelphia with him through an intable he went
return them by Mr. Thompson to you have you received them?
let me know how you come on with your studies I hope you have got
up with your class and that you will not again let them get before
you be very attentive to your studies and get your name up
for an excellent School believing you capable of it if you only have
the disposition but your advancement to be brilliant and only enough
to fit you for brilliant application to your studies. The Corporation of
Harvard College chose a President yesterday it was Judge Ames
Esq of Dedham I & Dr Dwight know this we will be glad to
hear that they have come to a choice give our kind regards to him
and Mrs D G there sons we hope they are well how is the sickness in
St. Haven? and how is Miss Millen Davis? I hope Millen has got well
when you wrote us last he had a very sore throat I hope it was not the
throat Distemper give our regards to them. Samuel Wendell Walcott
the last time I saw his Granna I don't let him beat you in learning he
studies steadily & so does Zanney Gray his Churn some of the boys are every bad
in this Collledge they have been suspended some of them for breaking Din
dows and other bad motions tricks some of the Don't are much as have en
tire this fall. how it must grieve their parents to hear such bad actions
from them your papers has not been well this fall his bilious complaints
have troubled him but he is better than been sick but am quite well at
present as is Nancy I hope you will give your brothers and sisters every
self in love to you and best wishes for your health and prosperity
I had a letter from your Grandma and Green the day your Uncle & Aunt
in that part of the Country went well she devoted her love to you
I had a letter from your Grandfather Moses held your Uncle's hands
at Doodstock wine well and sent love to you have you had a letter from
your Aunt Abby in Philadelphia? She wrote me that she should write
you by Mr Higgenson you must call once in a while to see Mrs
Morse & Ezekiel as they wish you too When you go give my regards
to them All how are your clothes done? is your washing turning out
coming done well? See that your shirts are well dried before you put
them on as it is very unhealthy to wear damp linen Who lived
on your ruffles on your shirts that I went by Erskine? Did you get
a letter from us by Mr Webster? I must hasten to conclude this letter
as your Brothers are waiting to carry it to the office Your Papa
is in Boston I hope he will bring a letter from you when he comes
back. how have you spent thanksgiving? thankfully and piously
I hope I trust you were not unmindfull of the goodness of
God to you all your life long and particularly in preserving
you through your journey to N' Haven in raising up Friends to
tentive and kind to you and your family and since you arrived and
in ordering every thing so kindly for you in preserving your life
and your health I trust while so many all around you in the
Place were you live have been called of the stage of life and have
given to render an account a solemn account at the bar of God
for all the deeds done here in the body Oh may dear Son forget
not all these mercies but ever beg of God to make you truly
thankful for his numberless mercies and give you a heart to
prove them for his Glory that this may be the case in the Daily prayer
of your Affectionate parents E D Morse & J Morse

New Haven Dec. 18. 1805.
My dear Parents,
I now take my pen to write a few lines
by post, I hope this will be acceptable to you & will
find you well. I received your long letter & socks with a
letter from Aunt Abby Beeu some time ago, and on the
16 inst. a letter by post the 1st one that I have received from
you by post; in which you mention that my brothers will
stay at home this winter & am very glad for their sake
because they wish it very much when I was at
home; I feel a great affection for them and you &
long to see you. I hope my brothers will have the
pleasure of giving this to you as they wish to get
one from me very much I am glad to hear that
the corporation have chosen a President; the sickness
in New-Haven is very much abated one of the
students died yesterday of the bilious fever his name was
William B. Peck of Norwich a relation I believe
of Mr. Lathrop of the same place, he was a member
of the Junior Class his funeral was this afternoon. I am
in very good health and have been since I have been here
I shall not go out to gun any more for I know it
makes you anxious about me. There was one of the
scholars expended a few days ago for rolling logs down
stairs his name is Shelton; I am sorry Papa & Mama
have been unwell & glad that they and Nancy have
got well give my love to Nancy & tell her I will
write her as often as time will admit & also to S.D. Lead
when you see him and tell him I will write him soon
my clothes are done up neat my washing, ironing & mend-
ing are done well: the muffles that you sent on by
Erskine have not been served on the muffles on 2 of my
skirts are very ragged and have been taken off. I have
received the letters by Mrs. Webster. Thanksgiving day
I spent as I did other thanksgiving days at Charlestown
I have got me a leaf chair like Papa's which I find very
handy to write on I gave 3 dol. for it which I think is
quite a high price, as is every thing in New Haven. My
Boots must be new soled for they are quite worn out
which I suppose will come to a great price. You mention
that you hope I shall get rep with my class, I cannot
if I study night and day for they gain upon me
every day in Homer & in Horace every student advises me
to get a room in College as soon as I possibly can. If I don't
enter till next spring I shall have to be examined again
& perhaps I may be turned by which will not be very pleasing
to me; I should like to go next term & I can with honor
it would make me a great deal happier, I did not like the
proposal when you first mentioned it. I know nothing
more to write at Present. only give my affectionate
love to my brothers & tell them must write me a long
letter soon.
This is the shortest letter I shall ever write you
So Adieu.
Yours &c. S. F. B. Morse.
Rev'd Dr. Morse.

My dear Son,
Your letter of the 18th was
received this evening & I received
our anxiety, which was great as we had
not heard from you for more than a
month before, not with standing our
defects in punctuities to write us
regularly once a fortnight by mail.
I fear my son you are too attentive to our
letters & inquiries of you -- Your Mama complains that
you are not at all particular in
answering her questions -- The next
letter you write Don't fail to read
over all our past letters to you,
& take time particularly to write
us a satisfactory answer to our
enquiries. Particularly whether
you rec'd the 5 dol. bill we sent
you by Erskine Hazard, & what
have been your expenses, & whether
you have taken any money at Ma
Beers? & how far you have
advanced in your studies. I am sorry
you should let your class get before
you. I hope you are not getting into
idle habits. The vacation will give
you a fine opportunity to get up with your
class, & even to get ahead of them,
& I hope my son, you will cheerfully
& diligently improve it for
that purpose. I remember I
used to value vacations as among
the most important seasons for improvement.
I wish you to be ambitious
to among the best scholars in your
class— I presume you may be if you
have but the inclination, I will
subsequently apply yourself to your
studies. I would not have you too
anxious to go into College. I am persuaded
you are well situated as you
are—in the Spring, I will (God willing)
come on & place you in College. If
you are studious, you need not fear
an examination. I trust you will pass
it with honours to yourself.
Your brothers are very diligent & make
good progress in their studies. They are
a comfort to us, as I hope you
will be by your good behaviour –
Don't fail to write us once a fortnight
by mail – take great pains with your
letters, with regard to the hand writing,
the grammar, pointing, spelling &c. –
give us all the information concerning
yourself, which you know will be inter-
esting to us. Your last letters were
too carelessly & inaccurately written.
Make no marks on the back side,
of your letters of the place where you
are – it is improper & boyish – Be
manly in your behaviour – very
respectful obliging to your instructor,
& the family where you live – Call frequent-
ly & sociably at Mrs Morse's & make as
many friends in N.H. as you can by your
good behaviour.
The family are all well & send love to you.
Your brother had two clothes with him
for a private conveyance. Thirty prisoners
are in our prisons. I have not preached to them
yet, but have visited most of them in their
cells. I shall expect to hear regularly & particularly from
you a fortnight from this time.

I enjoy & have enjoyed good health since I have been here. I must again inform

to me, next term for I shall have to study night & day, in the vacancy to get up
with my class; I feel very much discontented with my situation here because I fall behind
my class every day; it makes me homesick & very unhappy.

Dear Brother:
This is the first time I have had
an opportunity of writing you, and I hope now
I shall write what you shall call a long letter.
I have been down to the State Prison
since it has been finished and all the rooms
excepting the lower cells are very comfortable.
The Prisoners are all very comfortable,
and they say they have better victuals than
they could possibly expect. One of them is sick,
but he is said to be the worst of them all. I
saw all of them at work outside of the walls
of the Prison a few days ago, in the Prison
dress which I suppose you know is red & blue.
This sick Man whom I mentioned with 5 others,
would have got out of Boston Jail, if they had
not been seasonably discovered by the Jailer.
Two of them have been put in the Prison upon suspicion of having taken stolen Goods, but
the Goods were found upon another person.
and there are great hopes of their release.
Nancy is making shirts for you
and desires her love to you; she is very well and
desires to see you very much, and says when
she grows rich and has time to spare, she
will come to New-Haven and see you; she says
she thinks very much about you.
Will you write me how much
you study? what are your hours for study? how
far you have advanced in them? and whether you
cannot keep up with your class by any means
whatever?
Sam Ward has got exceedingly far
in his studies; he studies very hard indeed he
and his chum come down from Cambridge
almost every evening.
In haste Your beloved Brother
Edw Cds Morse.

My dear Son I have received three letters
from you since my last they inform us
of your great solicitude to join your
class & get into College. We have con-
sidered your request, & though we are well
satisfied with your present situation,
& consider Mr Davis as one of the best
Instructors, & as having been of great
service to you hitherto, he have
pretty much concluded to gratify your
wishes, provided you can get up with
your class (as you can easily do, with
proper application before the end of
vacation) & you can get a steady,
direct roommate older than yourself,
such as Mr Shedman can recommend. Give my regards to Mr Ash-
man if he is in New Haven, & request
him to befriend you & me in procuring
for you a suitable Church. If he
is not in town request young Mr. Dwight
to do me this favor. In conversing with
Prof. Pearson on the subject I am convinced
that after this you may derive more
advantages from being with your class
than by yourself. But my son, in order
to this, it will be indispensable necessary
for you to be steady, diligent & economical
in all your conduct punctual
in your attendance on all College
exercises. Never be absent from paddings but
from necessity, & be always in season at in
your attendance on all College exercises.
Study a proper economy in all your expenses.
Write me immediately after receiving
this & let me know when your vacation ends.
Possibly I may visit N. Haven before it
closes to make arrangements for your removal
to College -- but this is very uncertain,
you must not calculate upon it. At any rate
you must apply yourself very closely to your
studies, so that I may be able to recommend
you as qualified to join your class without
an examination. With I am sorry you do much
read.
You will present my kind regards
& Mr Davis, inform him that I have
read his letter, I am much obliged to
him for it. The family are all very
well -- Your brothers are very good boys,
attentive to their studies, & to their
other duties, I give us a great deal of
comfort -- We all think of you, very
affectionately every day -- By your
good behaviour, fail not, my son,
to give us all comfort in hearing
from -- I shall be contented with
your situation -- leave your fondness
for continual change, it is a bad
habit -- you must strive to break it,
or it will be ruinous to you -- Resolve
to be steady & manly in all your be-
haviour -- You are now in a situation of
an age to put away childish & toyish
things -- We all send you most love --
You have daily remembrance in our prayers -- pray
for me to pray for myself -- Remember your accountability to
God & to nothing to spend time -- Daily, ask his guidance
of your heart -- Read a portion of the Scriptures with
earnestness, forget not this advice -- When family entice you
to consent not -- Your affectionate parent

I have just the moment received
your letter dated Jan 15, in which I
find you approve of my desire of enter-
ing College. I can get up with my
class this vacation which ends on the 29 of
this month; I wish that you would come
on for I think that you could settle me
in College better; I believe I will let
Mr Stedman who is in town see your
letter & get me into College, I have
no doubt but he will satisfy me. I
am in great haste to study, therefore remem-
ber to my brothers & Nancy & excuse
my brevity & bad writing I must
now bid you Adieu. yours to
S. F. B. Morse.
My dear Son,
I had enjoyed my passage
in the stage for N.Haven, but the weather
being so bad I intended to travel for
this time. I intend coming about the
middle of next month, if the travelling
admit. I have written Mr Davis to
answer with Mr Davis's opinion on the subject
of your admission to College. Perhaps they will think it best for you still
to board at Mr Davis's till I come & please
you in College myself. I think myself
the best for you. If you should be join your class let me charge

your companions, the sober, studious, virtuous. Be diligent & faithful in
getting your leisures constant spiritual
in attending all College exercises - never
be absent from any of them but from
indispensable need - let me bear
a good account of you when I come to
see you. - Be prudent in all
your expenses - & by all means keep
an accurate account of what you receive
& what you expend - This I expect
from you, & shall not dispense
with it. No excuse will be
need for loosing your account.
I enclose Mr Davis' letter which
you will deliver him - We are all
very anxious to hear from you.
Your brothers are very studious, attentive
good boys, & give us a great deal
of comfort. Your affectionate father
J. Monroe

Dear Son
I am in great hopes that your Papa would be with
you before this or I should have written you before that but the
traveling is so bad that I have not when he will be able to see you
I hope you feel easy and respects going into College as your Papa
has presented that you should go in and join your Class and want
get the favour of Mr. Steidman to appoint you to get you a good
chair, that will not lead you astray in any way by bringing
travagant with Wood or Candies or anything else think you to
get a worker woman to do your Nails that will not change so
much as 4 1/2 Mr. Dozen artificer is a very extravagant piece
Mr. Ely says he did not pay so much by a great deal as that when
he Bar in at Havana he had his Washing done by the piece
so much by the shirt 8 1/2 for a pair of stockings 1/2 cent for a
handkerchief and so on. You must keep a Book and set down
your expences in every Artificial in it that we may see what
We pay our money for and to leave you to keep your own Acc
ounts that you may be able to make an estimate of the expense
of your Education and leave the value of money I beg that you would
be an Acceptant on your Brothers will not be able to join
you. one thing I hope that you would avoid and that is hav
ing any thing to do with raining to the buttons as they have a
great price for Truffles and on no Consideration dont have any skill
to pay there I am told that one way to find out who are able
& Gluttons among the Scholars is to go to the buttons and if there
is Changes on their Books against the ladies they judge them to
be very extravagant I will tell you according to the number of
changes on the buttery Books. I have never to hear of your
name on their books and make no use of Rogers or Brandt or Wine
or any thing of the kind as they cannot do you any good but much
harm and may be the consequence to you. Your papers myself are very
anxious to have you keep an account of your expenses during your
stay in Newhaven that at the end of the 4 years that you may
be able to say my whole expenses amount to so much and you will
find it very easy to do it if you will only attend to it every morning
to set down the expenses of the day when anyone arrives and
every Saturday cast it up and see how much it comes to and at
the end of every term see what the expense of the term comes to
for board tuition washing mendings shoes boots &c and how you
spend your pocket money and look up your account book and
dont look it or leave it about for other boys to see its content.
had a young man that was educated at N' Haven this week
he said the school of his expenses did not cost his father 500
for the 4 years he was in College he has been out 3 years
another who was educated last year kept an account
of his expenses were 900 now I hope you will be ambitious
that yours do not exceed the last in this way to know
is to be accurate in stating every particular if both them
had not done this they would not have been able to
have known. – I wish you to make Mr. Steepleman your
friend and he will assist you I know. – July 2d thus far
had written yesterday but hearing Mr. Ethridge was going
on by land to the Southland to tomorrow morning I thought I
could finish my letter and send it by him and it would save postage
which comes to a great deal every Quarter as you send all your
pay post I wish you would try and find private opportunities
to write by as Mr. Stedman & Mr. Simon Dwight or anyone
that would be like to know to inform you if they hear of any
person going on to Boston and write by them. – I wish you
to be careful only send not to dirt more clothes than is necessary
as working is so dear put on two clean shirts a week two thick
clothes & one pair of stockings is enough this cold weather two
in Summer & 1 pocket handkerchief. Count your clothes when you
send them to be washed & when they come back and see that
you soon done your self a hope to be on to see you next week
if the weather and roads and other things will admit of it
let me only dear son above all other things beg of you not
to follow any of the bad examples that you may see around
you either in the schools or any one else remember everyone
must be accountable to that great and all seeing God who has
with us in secret and it will be no excuse to him that we only
did as others did who blasphemed his holy name & profaned his
holy Sabbaths or was guilty of disobeying his commands in any
other way but endeavour to have a constant sense of his presence
being always with you even when no other eye beholds you &
make this resolution your own How shall I do this or that and
and sin against God?
We are extremtly anxious my Son that above all other things
you should make Religion your early choice as that is indeed
the one thing Godful that good part which shall never
be taken from you neglect not your Daily Devotions read
your Bible constantly & prayerfully and avoid as much as
possible all companions that have not the fear of God before
their eyes better be alone at any time than with such Company
never be absent from prayers at Candleight always be very
serious While attending don't let the folly and lightness of
others tempt you to be of your Guard at such Solomon Season
but keep always in Mind Your Accountability as I have been
for mentioned. – attend on all Dr Dwight's Sermons on
lectures and profit by all your Opportunities to get Wisdom
endeavour to be the better for all your Advantages as this is
the only way that you can Compressate & comfort your
Affectionate Parents Who cannot pray Daily & earnestly
that having a prince put into your hand to get Wisdom
you may have a dear heart given you from above to
prove it just to make all the advances you can both in
Human and Divine knowledge and this will rejoice our
hearts. – I must now bid you good night as it is late & my
hopes is full Your Papa & Brothers & Sisters join me in
love to you May heaven bless you my son Your Affectionate
mother E D Moon

My dear Sir, I have received no answer to my
last letter to you. I regret that the books
did not go in season to answer your purpose they were ready for Butler & your
Son in law had they called for them I have
time carefully sought opportunity to send them but have found none – They are in a box
directed to Wm. Butler at White's Bookstore.
Orders are left to forward them by the first
team to Northampton Henry on Beecher
& Goddridge on Education are not yet out
of press they will do to distribute separately
& you had better make your Vol. of such as
you have – Is Vincent yet out? – I wish
to hear from you on many subjects. – If
Gov. Strong is doubtless re-elected unless it
legal votes, or too late returning, or some other
accident prevent – The Senate will probably be equally divided – It will depend on
the House what sort of Senate & Connell
we shall have – It will be a stormy Session
I think in before us – Our Nation alas how
fallen! – What is to become of us? – I am
not refrain weeping over our University.
We intend publishing Dr. Pearson's resignation
& the Addresses of the Students in this Answer
in the No. of the Panoptist. They will interest
the public. I think, if we are not destined to
fall a prey to the artifices of the adversary,
to eat the fruit of our own labor, to be
filled with our own devices. -- My heart
is sometimes ready to sink within me, but
I hope never to be permitted to despair of
the cause in which I am engaged.
There is considerable said in the circle of
a few confidential friends of establishing
a Theological Academy at Andover, & of
placing Dr. P. at the head of it. Such a
plan appears to strike fearfully, when men-
tioned: -- I hope to have opportunity to open to you
fully the plan at Election. -- I wish you to
come down as early as you can, that we may
have time to converse much on that & many
other important subjects. -- If you are at my
house Thursday or Friday of the week before
Election it will not be too soon. -- I hope a
larger No. of our Western brethren than usual
will attend Convention this year -- I think
it an object to save the Convention if possi-
ble. We can do it if we will --
The Panegylist is the only channel through which
we can, with effect, communicate such information
to the public from time to time, as may be necessary
to our purpose. It is the only weapon of
the kind, with our Opposers, fear. It is now
formidable, & must be made more so. I hope
you will still continue & increase your exertions
& support it. If there be a falling off
in some places, let exertions be made to make
up the Deficiency in others. Mr Baker of Gran-
ville, told me at Hartford that he believed there
were between 20 & 30 Subscribers in the several
parishes in that town whose names had not
been returned, & that he w'd see about it on
his return. Pray, collect all the information you
can on the subject, so as to be able to make arrangements
for the next year. Will not your
Society consent to purchase parts of the Panegylist,
with the profits they receive on the Work?
I wish they w'd as we have 200 on hand, & we
shall need to make great exertions to pay our
Debt. Do what you can to aid us.
My family is in tolerable health. My
repeating spring complaints are upon me, & compel
me for much service. Mrs M. writes in best
affections to both your son daughter
I self with your faithful
friend

By Dr Holmes. I write you a

a line by McGuiffin Child, with Hope you

to make our house her future home), & Nancy
is spared. – Things are quiet in the Parish
& town, as respects myself – there is a
very pleasing & increasing attention to
serious things, among Christians young
people – the former seem to be awake &
lively, & fond of meeting for religious
conference – the latter are thoughtful,
& disposed to instruction. I find they
seem unwilling to have me discontinue
my Saturday evening Lectures, as I have
usually done at this season. My heart
is encouraged by these things. The Affairs
of College are still interesting. I will
tell you all about them when I see you,
as also about a contemplated Theolo-
gical Academy at Andover.
Our political affairs are in a
sad state. Gov. Long is chosen -- but
there will be a Democratic Council,
Senate, House of Representatives.
Our Legislature will consist, as it is
conjectured of 4 or 500 people -- The house
will hardly hold them all -- It will
be like the National Assembly in
France. You remain from Connecticut -- Long continues your "Steady
habits." We hope to see you early in June.
Perhaps after your visit, We may
wish to take a short journey -- We
send love to all the family.
Your affectionate Son
[Mark Twain]

support the Panoplist in Woodstock
I shall attend to Hunt Moore's

Baltimore, August 1st 1856
My dear Wife,
We arrived here yesterday to Cook's
& obtained accommodations at Lord's new house, with
the resort of the geniectest company. We are about
20 in number. General Derby his brother & his family
are among them. I know Miss Betty Malcom is here from New York the left the
family well. Abby Sands came in with us this
morning at 6 o'clock expecting to reach Sherridaville at 9 o'clock. I take the
stage at 10 for Whitehouse. They have a fine day
for travelling. Eliza Catharine are with me
they are both writing for themselves. They have both
been very good girls, & are learning to drink the
water. It will take us several days to become
acquainted with the company I am accustomed to the
place. As for myself I feel a little fatigued with
my journey, but hope here to rest & refresh myself.
I should be much happier were you with me
now. I feel lonely amidst a crowd. While travelling
the constant change of objects, employs my attention
& the exercise serves to exhilarate my spirits, but
when I am at rest distant from my books &
the scene of business my spirit flag, & I think with
desire & pleasure of home. Indeed I feel
less happy from home than I ever did & be
that in future, when a journey shall be necessary
to my health, it will be always convenient for you
& be with me. I think much of you, my dears
of the boys & of the people & pray that the health
of you all may be preserved. I am anxious
to hear from you. I am sorry I forgot to make
an arrangement for writing me before I left home.
Write you a lasty line on the subject from the
by mail. Betty Hazard's letter from Brockville
& another from Washington with a short postscript
to me & the one I wrote from Albany are all the
letters we have written before this.
I intend leaving the Springs at first
on Thursday evening next, or early Wednesday morning to
reach Baltimore on Thursday evening -- but I
write you ago before that time.
Since my arrival I have drank freely
of the waters & this morning have taken the warm
bath I meant to day to rest. I have retired to my
private room & in other respects pretty well accommodated
Dr Bradford from Albany is now at home, he will
leave the Springs tomorrow Mr Birmingham is here
from Boston with his daughter. Dr Nott will be here
tomorrow, I spend the Sabbath but days his health
will not permit him to speak. I hope it will
however -- I shall probably speak here in three
mile distant a part of the whole of the day
tomorrow morning we propose to visit the
Saratoga Springs, whose waters are said to be better
than those of this place. They are only 7 miles from
Baltimore. I am now going to call on Mr Har-
per who I learn is here & will finish my letter
on my return.
I have just had a pleasant interview with Mr
Happer, I was introduced to Mrs H. who is an invalid
& if able will visit Boston before her return to Baltimore.
I hope the boys are very attentive to your & all
my wishes. I have not been a state of enjoyment. I hope
however it has not been a sort of relaxation which will
conduce to health.
Believe me my dear to be with great sincerity your affectionate
husband Morse

My dear wife, Our Miss Hazard arrived here
last evening to our great joy They are lodged
in a good house near us. We intend leaving this
place on Tuesday afternoon, & go on from
there to-day, on Wednesday morning, to White-
town. We are all in good health & spirits –
Mr Bartlett & Eliza have a room to themselves – Mr Hamilton, of Boston a young
merchant who came on with them, is their
gallant & very agreeable & attentive I think
I am befriended by the waters – To-morrow
We think of going to Saratoga, to try the
more powerful waters of that place –
I preached this morning 3 miles from this
for Mr Bradley a spirit of wine, I returned
& preached a 2d sermon in the house
where I lodge, to about 300 people, collected from all parts of the world.
On Friday evening we were entertained
with the eloquence of a Miss Hamilton
of whom I will tell you more, when I see
you – On Saturday forenoon, we attend
a lecture of Stewart the Traveller, who
is otherwise idle in his Sentiments -- but appears
not capable of doing much harm -- His mind
appears to be a perfect chaos -- You see that
I have variety of entertainment -- I will
give much to have you present to participate
in the pleasures of the Society of our fine
people who are collected here -- I have found
Mr. Lewis Devereaux, whom we saw at
Weathersfield last year -- I am now fatigued and shall finish my letter in the
morning & tomorrow afternoon -- for
the present -- Amen.
Aug. 14th -- Evenings
We have all been to Saratoga to-day, I am
where we did not return this afternoon -- The
waters of that place are more powerful than those
of this place -- I drank freely of them -- without
much effect, other than to make me sleepy.
Miss Barthlett herself with Mr. Thomson
shall set out in the morning of tomorrow, in
stead of afternoon, as the stage starts at 9 O.C. -- It will
give us a little time at Schenectady.
I long to hear from you -- the boys but more
to see you -- My health is much improved by my
Journey - indeed I feel tiredly well I can eat
heartyily without inconvenience sleep well &
have good spirits. I hope you & the
family & people enjoy health - My regards
to the Brown & to all who ask after
me - It is late - Accept my dear, the
tenderest regards of your ever affectionate
husband & most
Love to the boys &
remember me to Nancy &
the family.

My Dear Husband
I wrote you on Sabbath but having a few lines on
Monday evening to you from Brother Arthur I thought
I would write you again and give you an Extract from
his letter respecting the Chenango turnpike though doubtless
you will have talked over the matter before this and have
known how completely you have been taken in by W.K.
"The Chenango turnpike there is but one gate on the route, the
road never will be finished. But if it was would afford no
dividend for this good reasoning there is no travelling -
Shares may be purchased at any price you choose to give - In
short my Dear Brother have nothing to do with Shares in
this turnpike there has been great Iniquity made use of by
Stockholders attempting to sell Shares at a Distance from
home they cant give them away, - thus far Arthur
now would it not be best to let W.K. know this and see if he
has honour or Common honesty enough to do something
to indemnify you for this Intolerable take in which under
the Appearance of a great deal of Religion & a sanctified
prince he has palmed upon you I am sick sick sick of this
Bicked World how much deceit is practiced in it, - let my
Dear be earnestly endeavouring after Subterfance Inconspicu-
ble The defiled & that faith not again in a better World -
I drank tea yesterday with Mr. S. Knappell. He begs to be kindly remem-
bered to you and Mr. Healey & Mr. Lowell they all think you ought
ought to spend the most of the time that you are absent at the
Springs, and give them a fair & full trial. Mr. S. R. bid me to
tell you this from her she is very desirous of it and hopes you will
oblige us all so much as to do it. She joins me in thinking this
primary importance we hope you will think so to. Perhaps
if you cannot be accommodated at the Springs to your mind
you may a few miles from it Mrs. Joy died so and preferred
it to being on the spot. Remember you cannot get there often
therefore I implore the present opportunity if you have stand but
a few days at the springs on your way to White town renew
your visit on your return and make your stay at W the shorter
but let friends tempt you to neglect this by their impertinent
queries to have you torry with them. -- The public mind this
way is greatly agitated by what has taken place yesterday
between Mr. Selfridge a lawyer & Young Charles Austin
son of Honettis. Selfridge killed Young A that him through the
heart with a pistol at one o'clock on the exchange in the
midst of a numerous concourse of people and then deliv-
ered himself up to justice. It seems, there had been a high dis-
pute between Honettis & Selfridge the latter as appears by
the newspapers had demanded satisfaction which the
for me refused to give up. Therefore ported it as a Racket
& a Liar & a Coward in the Newspapers Which the you
look up & determined to have satisfaction on P for (as the story
is here) and went on change with A Cain to be revenge'd upon
meeting P and some words ensuing (and some say a blow)
with the cane I took a loaded pistol from his pocket and
shot him through the heart & after being shot through
several times with the cane before he fell and I fetched
him a blow on the head with the pistol which brought
him to the Ground a Jury of Inquest sat immediately on
the body and brought in their verdict Willful Murder.
Was committed to Jail but the mob was so in rage that
they had like to have torn him from the Carri
Rockwood told me, the Jury had a number of high toned
Federalists among them Young P Rigerson was one I was
told. Young P was in this town yesterday morning distrib
uting tickets for his commencement among his Friends
he was 18 years old there was as many as five hundred
People invited to dine with him on Commencement day
how must his parents feel, but Mr P is most to be pitied to
have a Husband confined for Murder Shocking thought
She has three young Children and lives at Medford. I
must now bid you adieu my dear as I have one of my
Nervous head Aches my mind being Agitated gives up
love to all Friends and Accept a large More from your affectionate
son

Whitehouse Aug 1st 1861
Saturday morning
My dear wife:
In the hearty line I wrote you from
Utica on my arrival there, I promised I would write
you more deliberately from this place. I improve the license of this morning for
the purpose.
From the necessity to Utica, a day or half a
journey, we had very decent company, the weather warm
on the road, though turnpike, not good. We were much fatigued. At the Hotel, in Utica, we happily found our friends
whose names I before mentioned to receive us. It was
a really a happy meeting -- the circumstance of your absence was the only drawback on our joy. It was a source of much regret to us all that you could not
be here. -- We came up to this place in Mr Snowden's carriage; I found Sister other children, eight
of them glad to see us. Sister is in fair condition as
you are -- the children are fine. I find Mrs. S. looks
as well as I ever saw her -- Mrs. S. them, but in good health -- Mr. A. has been a little indisposed but in
fat & portly. All are very clever -- Yesterday I was
introduced to Mr Caruthers spent several hours with
him -- I am most pleased with him -- he is a modest,
informed man -- his family are in Jersey
I expect to preach for him in the morning, & for Mr
Stevenson in the afternoon -- We expect Mr. Sidney
here to-day -- his wife expects to be confined next month so
he cannot come -- Abby will return with us. It was
not convenient for Miss Battlett to visit her Aunt. She
is made very welcome & happy with our Friends here.
I have conversed with Mr. Arthur respecting the Penn-
silva, to him I Willing -- he informs me that he has
written me on the subject, that they are good for
nothing -- I have not yet taken them, I shall see
whating on my return, I intend he shall annul the
bargain & give me some other property or return
the books -- I think the hint of Lys? will be introduced
into Schools in this quarter -- B34 has sold nearly
all the 24. he had.
Jerseyfield is increasing in reputation & va-
lue -- a turnpike road runs not far from our lots. The suit
of the Ct. provided a favorable issue when he sued
The Steensbury estate sold for £3950. & there is some
fine land yet uncut -- About two lots, has been used for
furniture stock & sold at Ventnor -- more is yet due -- I
know not to what Amount -- I shall enquire of Mr. Sidney
the situation of Steensbury land in other States.
We A. says, about the body of the estate are two full time ministers.
If I can is building him a handsome house on a
fine building site, on an eminence 30 or 40 rods
from the street, surrounded by about 30 acres of good
land -- He appears to be in a prosperous way -- His eldest
son Sam. has begun the study of latin -- but W. is deaf
but whether to give him an education or to shut him in after
Yesterday We had several gentlemen, two Mr. Rensallaers
& a Mr. Schuyler to dine with him also Mr. Camptcham
& Mr. Sister Sprouden -- We sat down after 3 O'clock
till tea time -- quite in high style all things in
very good order & an excellent dinner -- My
next letter will be from Albany, as no mail will
leave this place, except the one that comes this, till the
one which we shall accompany on Wednesday next
when we propose leaving White town -- I am going
this morning with Mr. Utica, I will finish my
letter on my return --
Sabbath Morning Sept 96334
The eastern mail closes to-day -- I went to Utica & transacted
considerable business to advantage -- The Sergeant will meet me
to-morrow with Capt. Hendrick, at Mr. Sprouders. The mail closes
today & I have no letter from you, as I expected -- I am greatly
desirous to hear from you, not having heard a word from
home since I left it -- I am sorry I forgot to make
arrangements with you about writing me -- Mr. & Mrs. Hazard
& Watney arrived here last evening well -- We are all now
at Mr. Arthur's, a house full of us -- The weather is clear,
cool, & fine & we are all well -- Mr. Sidney did not come
last evening as we expected, he may be here to-day or tomorrow -- It is probable we shall not leave this place till
Friday's stage, as we contemplate an excursion together into
some of the neighboring towns, & possibly may go on to
Cazenovia, if Mr. S. does not come -- I shall write you
by next mail -- I expect to spend the next Sabbath in
Albany, & to leave it on Tuesday following -- You will have
time to write me there, after you receive this -- Don't fail to do it --
I hope to receive a letter here by next mail -- Love to the boys -- Remember
me affectionately to Mr. Brown, Mrs. Campbell &c. &c. forgetting your name in writing
to Mr. Rensallaers -- I am
Yours affec. &c. S. P. G. H. S.
1 M. to 2 Am
Utica

my Dear Husband
Charleston August 9th 1806
Yesterday I received yours of the 1st inst from
Belle town Springs was very happy to find by it that you were as
well as you never, when you consider how much fatigue you
had gone through before you set out on your journey and the
rashness with which you performed it your firmness you can
hardly wonder at your spirits flagging after you had gotten
to a resting place I was sorry to find you had determined
to leave the Springs so soon I feared your being out of employ
so long would make the time pass heavily but you should
recollect that it was Duty to your family & Friends that all
you have at this time and Duty should make you willing
to stay and give them a full and fair trial. by the
time you receive this you will have made your visit
to White town and be on your way back as far as
Auburn you will have received two letters from me at
White town Hope one of which I have written I wish
I had written one to meet you at the Springs it would
have relieved your mind while there but I did not know
till it was too late how long you would remain there or
when you would arrive there. In my last letter I gave
you Arthur's opinion of the Chevau legs transfere which
if you have not received you doubtless will have converse
with him on before you receive this I hope you will talk
with Whiting on the subject and endeavour to adjust the
matters with him as it is a miserable take in I find Arthur
are good for nothing. – Mr Racketwood informs me that
Mr & Mrs Hazard had arrived at the Springs and was to
turn, there some time for Betys health I wish you would
return there and try them a little longer I fear that you
are hurrying from them too much for to experience all that
benefit from them which we so much desire You must not
mind Abbs. prefix you to come on home but attend to
yourself it is very healthy in town & all around as far as I know
our family are well I have Finley your memorandum to
Mr. Cotton to hand to Mr. Melequet who I informed you had
the case with Prof. Mr. C. Brownsh as Mr. C is gone to Bath.
more to see about his Brothers Affairs who went around
Mr. Brown gave us a very good sermon last evening &
Colwell is to preach to morning morning & attend to the
Communion I shall not close any letter till to morning
after service when I will tell you how things went on
I expect a letter from you this evening to good bye at
Merret Sunday afternoon - thus far I had written yesterday
and agreeable to my promise I now will give you an account
of to days exercises Mr. Colwell preached and administered
the sacrament of the supper this morning his text was God
gave us his only begotten Son he gave us an excellent sermon and
good as far as it went I thank God for it I liked his address
to the Communicants before he made the first prayer at
Communion & his exhortation to them after the service to
live holy & blameless lives there was something I did not like
in the sermon which will tell you when I see you Mr. Brown
preached this afternoon a serious good sermon he & Finley
are gone to the prison - I did not get a letter from you
owing to Mr. R. calling too late last evening but when I
send this to night shall expect to have it no water for six
hours to day I called on Mr. Haffell today yesterday she & Mrs
Hendley were well & send love to you and beg you to bring the spring
with before you return not to fail on any Account but let
it be the primary Object of your Journey as they have great
faith that they will do you great good by telling you all
these things. You will give me the Credit of acting very
disinterestedly as I long much to see you but I am not
as disinterested as at first appears, his very wish to detain
you longer with me here below that prompts me
thus to advise I must hasten to conclude as any family
need me I shall write to meet you at North
Hampton if I can guess when you will be likely
to be at that place. have received a large Box
of books from Butler which are in the Barn
have recieved no letters of any consequence I think for
you to be made acquainted with those Contents till you
return Deacon Darkin & Capt. Walker are returned
they were out all day at meeting a great
many enquires are made after your health by your
people & other Friends and many good wishes pray
in attend you from them as well as your family whom
we wish to be remembered to you besides the Custodians
Maney & Mr. Brown remember me to all Friends and
believe me ever your affectionate Wife E B Mose

My dear Wife
I am impatient to receive a
Letter from you, I hope to find one in the morning
at the Post Office in Utica Eliza has no one
from Mr R. who informs us you were well 3
days after we left home; but that you were dull
after having been for so long a time accustomed
to such a family around you as we had to be left
almost alone, it is not surprising that you should
feel the change but I hope you soon recovered your
sprits, I that you have experienced the liberty
you hoped to enjoy in your comparative soli-
tude. Not an hour passes except when asleep, that I
do not think of you & the dear boys I hope they do
all they can to make you happy & that you all enjoy
health. The time now seems long since I saw you,
& I am anxious to see my return
As to myself I am made very happy by our
friends here I specked last Sabbath in the morning
& in the afternoon at New Hartford 5 miles for Mr
Rowden, I spent the night & next day with him

borow even's before he is well his wife sent

that we have had a letter from Sam Hilarion

write in much love to you -- We talk much of your

next Sabbath -- My love to the
members of the family -- I will tell my friends, who ask after

I hope will be in Charlestown when you receive

your every affectionate
husband J. Morse

Wednesday morning -- All well -- The rain this
morning may prevent getting this letter
to Utica -- I am on for the mail, with closes at 8 o'clock

My dear wife,
We arrived here safely half
past 7 O'clock have had a very pleasant
ride -- promising appearance of a fine
day tomorrow -- We hope to reach Kentucky
even to-morrow to C. P.Mo -- You will
not probably hear from us yet -- till
you see us, which we hope will be
Friday evening -- or Saturday noon --
I have partly engaged you a
girl, who passed with us in the stage
from Thompson to Pomfret by the name
of Becca Burrill -- She has the appearance
of a good girl -- I have promised
her 4/6 a week -- & to pay her passage to
now she may come on in the stage on
Saturday -- We are in the midst of a
company of soldiers -- noisy & confusing
-- I cannot add -- I expect not to
sleep much to night -- Take good care
of yourself -- I hope the people will
not complain -- Love to sister Abby,
the boys -- not forgetting Nancy & other
friends -- Believe your loving affectionate
husband J Mosse
Mr. Eliabett A. More

Dear Boston
Charleston Oct. 1. 1866
My Son, I have only time, by brother Chris
to tell you we are all well - I have
been at St Haven Cont. as I presume
Mr Lyman informed you - We came
home, 160 miles in 30 hours - My health
was never better - & I have as much
to do as I can do - I shall not
be able to visit Woodstock this fall
having rode between 11 & 12,000 miles,
the last two months - I must now
set down to business to make up for
the time of my absence - Wish you
to write us as often as you can -
Pray is Aunt Moor come to Woodstock
yet? We want much to see her - I do
hear she is comfortable with you -
We all send Duty & love as usual -
Your affectionate Son
Joseph G. Moser
Charleston

at the same prices for purchase, at which Subscriptions
to their respective Societies are supplied; and that he
may request each Sec'y to send one copy of each

which our Society may be supplied with
the same; all said specimens to be paid for
by our Society, & to be for the sole use & benefit

I suppose by this time you are in Philadelphia
& therefore I shall direct my letter there, I am very well, in
good spirits, & well contented with my situation, the term
to have next term begin & end. Mr Day (Tutor) set out
this morning I believe, for Washington & will continue there

Just now I asked Mr Twining to let me go a gaming
for this afternoon, he told me you had expressly forbidden

present. Please to give my respects to all my friends & relations who

Yale College June 7th 1807.
My dear Parents,
I hope you will excuse my not writing
you soon, when I inform you that my time is entirely
taken up with my studies. In the morning I must rise at
5 o'clock to attend prayers, immediately after recitation, then
I must breakfast, & begin to study from 8 o'clock till 11, then recite
my forenoons lesson, which takes me an hour, at 12 I must
study French till 1, which is dinner time, directly after dinner
I must recite French to Monsieur Vallee, till 2 o'clock;
then begin to study my afternoon lesson, recite it at five,
immediately after recitation I must study another French
lesson and recite at 7 in the evening, come home at 9 o'clock & study
my morning lesson till, 10, 11, & sometimes 12 o'clock & by that
time I am prepared to sleep.
Monsieur Vallee says that I make great progress
in French & will engage to teach me in 3 months so
as to read any French book. I have bought several
French books -- one, Bayard Dictionary, 2d and 3d. Semaine
1st, 25 -- Lectures Francois -- 1st, 25 -- Likewise I have bought
me a pocket edition of the Bible to, last me this college & Longman's
1. Spence Minor, a Sett of the Geography & atlas. I am greatly in
need of Dufief, would thank you to send it on as soon as
possible. You see now I have enough to do my hands as
full as can be, not 5 minutes time to take recreation
I am determined to study, & thus far have not miss'd
a single word. The students call me by the nick-name
of "Geography", almost every student is called by some nickname
or another.
I find it very necessary to have a room in college for
Mr. Pwinning's house is so far from the Colleges that I can scarcely
hear the bell at any time, I cannot at all in the morning,
I either wake 2 hours too soon, or too late, but never in the right
time I have missed prayers three times this term, but was not
noted because it is the first of the term, I must choose me a room
in college when the time comes, which will be in six weeks, I
suppose they government, will let me take my choice now, but not
take possession of it till next term, but I should rather go into it now &
then I should not miss prayers at all.
The college still remains in excellent order & harmony,
no tricks played or any disturbances. I should like to know
how Cambridge college is situated, & whether there is any
likelihood of any of the scholars coming to this college.
My Repertory has not yet been rec'd nor any
letters from home I should to receive either or all. Please excuse all
mistakes, Blots, & every thing that is incorrect as I have
no time to correct this, or to write any more, till now 11 o'clock
on the evening, so Adieu. My respects to Grandmama &
Aunt Abby & love to my Brother, Nancy, & all the family.
I hope Mary is well & will continue so.
Remember me to all who inquire after me in very great
paste, do write me soon.
Your affectionate Son
S. B. Morse
N.B. I am as well as this weather will allow me, I have my
spring combines the hard work.
P.S. Since writing this I have received Briefs, Georgia Minor o &
Testament, but no letter.

Yale College New Haven June 18th 1807
My dear Parents,
I have just rec'd your letter informing me
of my sisters death, altho' it is very afflicting to me, yet it
was not unexpected, I have been expecting this long time to
hear this news, my aunts letter raised my suspicions, &
I then thought she could not live long; I am very sorry, & will
try to give you some comfort, by applying myself to my
studies, more diligently; I intend (if possible) you shall hear
no complaints of my idleness or irregularity.
Last week I went to Mrs Beers & saw a sett
of Montaigne's plays in French in 8 vols handsome hand-
somely bound in calf & gilted -- for 2 dollars; the reason they
are so cheap is, because they are, wicked, & bad books for me to
read, I got them because they were cheap, & have exchanged them
for a handsome English edition of Gil Blas
price $4,,50 -- I am about to get a desk & bookcase
made of Cherry wood, the price to be 12 dollars, which will last me
tho' I then I can sell it for the price I gave for it, if
I was to get a desk made of stained wood it would cost
about 8 or 9 dollars, & when I am thro' college sell for
11 or 5 dollars but Cherry wood (like mahogany) is handsome
the longer it is kept. I hope you will not think
this extravagant. I will endeavor to be as economical as possible. In great haste. -- Your affectionate & obedient son
S. S. B. Morse.
(I am in good health.)

Yale College, New Haven June 30th 1807
My Dear Parents,
I have just read your letter of the 27th inst.
and now have but one moment to answer it
I shall follow my resolutions of studying hard this term
if it is only to please you, it comes quite natural to
me now to sit down & study my lessons & not leave them
till I have got them perfectly, I have nothing now to interrupt
me in my studies, as I had at home.
I will return Gracia Minerva, & the Bible as
you request, it was necessary for me to get Gracia Minerva
at the first of the term as I had none, then I could not
borrow one; the Bible you told me to get, but as you will
send me one I can return it as well as not. You wish
me to return Gil Blas & say I can get it from the Society.
I am in: I am about to take a admission from that Society
because I have not time to attend to its exercises, & the one
in the Society Library is an English one, whereas mine in Paris
it is not so much for the books contents, as its acquainting
me more thoroughly with the language; I hope you will
let me keep it as it was recommended to me by Monsieur
Vallec as a very easy book to read for beginners;
M. Vallec says that I make great progress in
the French Language, & will teach it to me in 3 months
so that by vacation I shall have a considerable
knowledge of it.
In some haste
Your affectionate Son
S.B. Morse
P.S. I am in good health

Yale College New Haven August 5th 1807.
Dear Parents,
You must excuse me for not writing you the
some time past as my time has been wholly engrossed
in my studies; I have scarcely any time for exercise, I
begin to feel the want of it very much. I hope I shall have
sufficient time in the vacation for all these things, as I have
nothing to do but to study now if I can truly say, I never stud-
yed so hard before; I begin to feel a pain in my breast &
weakness, which troubles me considerably.
To-day was the first time I declaimed in the
Chapel I was very much frightened at first but soon over-
came it; the students plainly perceive the defect in my
voice, the I think it is growing better every day, you will
be able to tell best as you have not seen me this some
time. I am very well excepting the forementioned pain
in my breast, enjoy good spirits I am more & more
delighted with the college... it is but 4 or 5 weeks now
to vacation & then I think I shall be not a little re-
joiced the scholars have drawn for choice of rooms & I
among the rest, my room mate had the first choice & I the
last, which was rather remarkable, but my choice is as
good as his, & better than the middle choice, as I have
the first room that is vacated. I have however chosen a
very good room that will suit me till next year &
then I shall, (I hope) have a better chance to get a room.
I wish you tellt Wm Walker that I expect him to come
on with me next term & shall be very much disappointed
indeed, till him not to decide till I come home for commence-
ments, for if he should decide in the negative without
hearing both sides of the question, it would disappoint me
very much; I ought to have written him but I have
not had time, Please to give my love to him, Elisha Godard &
John Bartlett, & Saml. Ward I take it for granted he is com-
ing on to this college;
Give my love particularly to my brothers, to Grand-
mother, Aunt Abby, Nancy, & in short all the family.
I hope my brothers will be at home when it's vacation here,
I would write them if I could. I am in great haste as
it is past ten o'Clock even.
Please excuse all blots & mistakes,
Yours etcetera
S F B Morse

Gale College. N.H. August 12th. 1807.
My Dear Parents
I have just rec'd your letter of the 8th inst which informs me, you have not rec'd a letter from me this month past; I wrote a letter to you last week by mail with hope you have rec'd by this time; my time is so taken up in my studies that I scarcely find time to do any thing else; I hope therefore you will excuse me from writing so often as I should if I had not my studies to attend to; I am reviewing Geography & Greek Minora & wish to go perfect in them, therefore I employ all my time to hinder me from doing other things that I wish to do;
I am glad to hear that Edward & Richard are about to enter this college I hope Wm Walker will come on with Edward, for I have got an excellent room in college, for him & myself, the best room in our class, & yet I had the last choice, but those who have the last choice, have the privilege of taking the first vacated room, which is my case, & an excellent room has fallen to my lot.
You mention that Mama had written me a long letter; I have not yet rec'd it I hope I shall soon.
I am in good health, & spirits & am delighted with college; I long to be a Sophomore.
The influence begins to spread in town & among the students but I believe it is not dangerous; it prevails in New York very badly & some fear it will end in the Yellow Fever.
N.B. (Excuse my bad writing, mistake, Volck) In haste Yours S.F.B. Morse.
Sam L. H. B. Rowe

My Dear Mother,
We arrived here safely last Wednesday, even
we are well and contented, and do not feel homesick in
the least; Our things have not yet arrived from Boston,
we expect them soon. Papa went on board the packet
for N. York. last Friday even. - & as he had a fair
wind I expect he has arrived there in this; he bought
for us before he went- 2 leafblairs, 3 common dittos
1 pair andirons, 1 lookingglass, 1 Washboard, an ax, ham-
mer, skillet, wood, &c. - I will write you more particu-
larly concerning things in my next, as I have
but very little time. Edward has got a room
very handy for him to come to mine when necessar-
ly he and his roommate (Mitchell) will sleep in my
room so there will be 4 in a room at night. Edward & I make out to sleep upon the floor till
our things come from the vessel. I took a letter
out of the office for Papa from Richard, & as he
(Papa) was gone to N. York I opened the letter and will give
it to Papa when he comes here again
My next shall be longer.
Your affectionate Son
S.F.B. Morse

Dear Parents
We have just received a letter from Mama dated Nov. 23d
in which I am informed that you have not yet received a letter from me since Papa left
here I have written no less than three previously as you directed me once
a fortnight, I think it is very strange that you never get any letters from
me. Edid? is now a witness that it is not because I don't write them,
I sent a letter & a small package of catalogues to you by Col. Humphreys
more than a month ago I don't know what has become of them.
Concerning my French studies, I have been to Mr. Bache 1 month
which makes up one full quarter, but have not time to attend to them
any longer for instead of having more leisure time this term, I have much less, who
ever entertained hopes of I shall have sufficient time to attend to such things
& if opportunity offers can render my studies with greater convenience,
for their growing leisure time is employed in writing compositions &
earning pieces to speak & many other things which make it very inconvenient
to attend to French. We have neither of us had our hair
cut since we left Yale here, but think we shall soon, ally hat has
not yet been new found I will carry it to the hatters shortly.
In future I shall keep an account of the letters I send to
you & note their dates in a book, for I cannot conceive when
letters can have gone, especially the one sent by Col. Humphreys
I have been very particular in writing to you in my turn & now
write you at the it is Edidts turn.
Mr. Murray of Boston the Universalist is in town &
preached on Monday & Tuesday evening I meant to have heard him
but had not time, Some of the students heard him & I talked with
them afterwards & asked them what arguments he brought in favor
of his doctrine, they said, that this was one, that Christ came into
the world to save sinners, & if these were not saved Christ's coming
into the world was not answered; I asked them how he got over this
happage in the Bible & how shall go away into everlasting punishment
but the righteous into life eternal; they answered that they would go
away into "everlasting punishment prepared for the devil & his angels"
but not for them, that they would remain there till their sin were purged
away & then would be rel. into the kingdom of heaven. I wish some
information on this subject & would be obliged to you to write me a
long disputation on "Universal Salvation" for I wish to reason some
of the students on this head.
I would thank Popk very much to send me one of the
Boston Newspapers. I wish to know the news, & what is doing at
Boston.
Please to give our particular love to Richard
Grandmama & Aunt Abby & cousins W. & M. Rockwood
& Remember likewise to Betrey and all who inquire after us.
Mr. Billiman desires to be particularly remembered
to you & likewise Dr. & Mrs Dwight with Tutor Bright.
We are all well & please more & more with
college, we don't blow up our bell here, as they do at Cambridge,
please to give me the particulars of that adventure & wish
to know how things go on there.
I hope this letter will arrive safe
I am in haste therefore please to excuse all mistakes &
the handwriting.
Your affectionate Son
S. P. B. Morse
