Yale College. N. Haven. Jan 29th 1811
Dear Parents.
The vacation is about to close - a vacation
which has been of little use to me in the way of improvement. For the first few days I was occupied in arranging
the books belonging to the Brother's Library and preparing a Catalogue for the Prep - After that business was accomplished
I attended the Superior Court for a week, and heard several lawyers upon interesting cases - Since that time I have
kept my room, and spent my time in idleness. Richard has been confined there with a sore swelling upon his
seat - The Doctor has seen it and says that it is a swelling which goes by no particular name - that it will break
in the course of a day or two, and discharge - As soon as Richard recovers from this sore he proposes to start
for Charlestown - thinking I suppose that home will be a cure for every disorder. I have so little confidence however
in this sovereign remedy, that the next blood is not in the best state, and tho' I suspect I am possessed of the State, I
shall nevertheless remain at N. Haven. If my suspicions respecting this doctor should prove true, what would
you advise me to use for a cure - No mercenary interest of course. I wait your orders. Safford arrived on
Saturday evening, and brought us your very desirable present. Richard was then confined with his son and the
reception of such articles at such a time was to him peculiarly pleasing. The pie we ate was a rich pie - I
think I shall not go to the office again until the end of the month. I am your affectionate son
John H. Safford
I thought so. As Richard expects to return
home soon he will supply the deficiencies of this letter in
point of information. I leave Safford to finish. Adieu!
I am your affectionate son
Edwards Masse
P.S. Have no fears about me. I shall take the most effectual way of
getting thoroughly rid of it - I shall do nothing without
the advice of friends.
2. P.S. What was the reason of Finley's leaving M'Allattion?
If what I hear is correct, I stand in a fair way to lose my bottle cider. May how does cider sell by the
bottle, and how much will T. want upon his passage - If you can accurately calculate the expenditure you may
draw upon my banker for as much as is required to pay it. Tell Finley if you please, that I wish him a happy passage.
Tuesday evening June 29th
A few words will be all the finishing time will allow
me to give to this letter. After a comfortable ride arrived on Saturday about 8 P.M. I left the looks agreeably to direction - I found Richards in pretty low spirits. He
well he might be, for he had been afflicted far more than a week with what I others suppose to be
a bilious. Dr. Ives had given him a small plaster which he kept on for several days - But as it appeared to do no good
he took it off and put on a poultice of molasses & flowers
advice of one of the students - This however was without effect -
I immediately turned quarter & applied a portion of wheat
bran and milk, which eased him considerably - His head
kept on frequently changing it - This morning morning when
I went to Dr. Munson, who is found, as not able to put
it off - The division of grain him he supposed it was not a bill
and divided a portion of wheatbran and bye - Today he
came & examined it - He said it was a swelling but gave it no
name - After this portion has been kept on two or three
days, he says it will break & discharge, and then get well -
He observed that it was a great pity that one of Dr. Munson's men
should be fundamentally erroneous - His inconvenience is
such arising from its situation that he hopes his bill a consideration
part of the time - The pain of the swelling I believe
is principally nerve. He is in better spirits - I have got him
some wine - He has boarded at Mrs. Haroligs - His wife
are now sent to him - His appetite is totally gone - I have
been thus particular because some parents love to know
justifications respecting their children, especially when so dear
ag. R. - I think he will get about in a few days. Perhaps, as
this will reduce him somewhat in the Divisibles for him to
take a journey to C. H. is fully of the opinion I am respecting
this the Divisibles will be contented - Perhaps you will have
time to write before he will be able to put out - I hope you
will not be concerned about him, as he will have attention
brothers & friends can quite - I fear they are not cured of the it -
Be does not complain - Your instructions last 31st February 1845

Dear Kinley
Yours of the 6th ult. I received together with
the books enclosed, which I delivered personally, according to your request.
Did I not know the nature of your desire & the state of your
govern'd I should really be surprised at the commencement & indeed
the whole tenor of your letter but as it is, I can excuse & feel for
you. Have I commended a letter with the French Helas! it
would have been no more than might reasonably have been expected
considering the desolate situation of NewHaven & the gloomy prospects
before me but for you, who are in the very center of fashionable life
I surrounded by the amusements & bustle of the metropolis of New
England, for you to proclaim "how lonely I am" is uncomparable or at
most admits of but one excuse (to wit) that you can plead the fulness
of the youth who exclaimed "Gods annihilate both time & space & make
two lovers happy". You suppose I am so much taken up with the
ladies & other good things in N.H. that I have not time to think
of one of my old friends, - shall I Morse, there are no ladies or any
thing else to occupy my attention they are all gone & we have no
amusements - even old Value has deserted us, whose music though
an assembly of unharmonious sounds is infinitely preferable to the harsh
grating thunder of his Brother - NewHaven is indeed the worst place
I wrote you about a month since & did then, what you wish me now
to do - I mentioned all that is worth mentioning, which by the way is
very little about New Haven's inhabitants - Since then I have been to
New York & saw the Misses Keadleiffs & in passing through Stamford the
Mrs. Ravensfells -- The mention of the name of Bavenport would at one
time have excited in your breast emotions unutterable, but now though
there is as lively as ever, your heart requires the influence of another heart
to quieten it perturbations -- The sight of these girls brought to my mind
senses to agreeable even to return -- they were well & I suppose happy till
S. Hilthase that time is as lively & as blooming as ever -- as to the girls
that are left in New Haven I know little about them -- The Miss Suffle I never
visit & seldom meet Mary S. U. I have not even seen her in two
months Mrs. C. Mills is at present in New York when she has been all
winter as I suppose nothing & about forty being constantly -- her train -- The Miss West of
an as usual at home & when seen as lively & agreeable as ever -- last
but not least -- (you see I take the Ladies in the same order that you mention
ed them) comes the allconquering, the angelic queen of Harls I have not seen
her since she left New Haven but have heard from her Sister Elvira that
she is in good health & is going in April to New York with Mr. Harless to
spend the summer & perhaps a longer time, when she will probably break
many a stubborn heart I had many a stubborn knee - I fear more
unhappiness you have her family in your tail - I fear she may not be able to
withstand every attack for new york stands with elegant & accomplished young
men -- you mention that you have again changed your mind as to the
bursary which you intend to pursue -- I really thought that the plan of becoming
a bursarite would be permanent because sanctioned by practical authority
but I am now convinced that your mind is so much bent upon
painting that you will do nothing else effectually -- it is indeed a noble
art & if pursued effectually leads to the highest eminence for painters rank

My Dear Brothers,
We are, & have been for some time
anxiously waiting for a letter from you; Richards
letter informing us that he was better was the last
we rec'd. I can write you but a few words,
as I don't feel much in of writing mode, we are

New Haven March 31st 1811.
It is several weeks since I received your letter, my friend, accom-
panying the last volume of Scott, and though I have suffered them
to pass without bearing you my thanks, the only acknowledgements
I have it in my power to make, I cannot let you think I am
either ungrateful for these proofs of your friendship, or the flattering
regard you express for me. You did me justice when you said
"you are my friend, Mrs J." I am indeed, and no one who knows your
would be happier to prove himself such than she who has known and ad-
mired the delicacy of your conduct, and who has no need to take as painful
the friend in whom she has seen nothing to blame.
My sisters thank you for your remembrance of them, and
unite with mine their best wishes for your happiness.
We are just leaving this place for New York, but I could not depart
without expressing, my pleasure at a confidence, and my gratitude for a
kindness which I know not what I have done to deserve, except it be from an
appearance, which I am happy to repeal, that I am
your friend.
S. H. Jarvis.
I take this opportunity, my dear Sir, to acknowledge the receipt of the "Signs of the
Times" which you were so obliging as to send me; and at the same time to return
you my thanks, not only for that instance of politeness, but also for the many decla-
rations of friendship which you have conveyed to me through the medium of

My Dear Parents,
I arrived here this morning about 5
o'clock safe & in good spirits, though not a little
fatigued with my very unpleasant journey.
After bringing you Farewell in Hartford
at nine o'clock, rested there that night, &
started the next morning for Utica, & I am
about 6 o'clock about half an hour after
the mail stage had gone for New-York. I find
my brothers well; got no letters of introduc-
tion from either Dr Dwight or Mr Silbene
found the latter had received a very bad res-
ident from the explosion of fulminating
silver, and is in great danger of losing his eye-
ight altogether; in the evening of Wednesday
went on board the packet for New-York, was
becalmed for two days, and arrived in this port
after being in great anxiety all day on Fri-
day last the Lydia, sh sail; but find she
does not sail till Tuesday the 9th.
Mr Alston arrived last evening well
and I am on board our ship to see what ac-
tions he has taken in the matter of the
protection of the Union.
I am your affectionate son
Samuel

On board the Lydia

My dear Parents
After waiting a great length of time
I have got under way, we left New York
harbor on Saturday 13th. about 12 o'clock
and went as far as the quarantine house
on Staten Island, where on account of
the wind we waited over Sunday.
We are now under sail, with the
pilot on board, we have a fair wind
from S.S.W. & shall soon be out of
sight of land. We have 14 very agreeable
passengers, an experienced & remarkably
pleasant captain; and a strong,
large, fast sailing ship: we expect from
25 to 30 days passage. There are two
ships in company, one to Liverpool the
other to Limerick, Ireland. Mrs. Allston
& lady are well & in good spirits
she is writing home by the pilot likewise.
We have a piano forte on board for
two gentlemen, who play elegantly, so we
shall have fine times; I am in good
spirits, tho' I feel rather singularly to
see my native shores disappearing so
fast, I for so long a time. I am not
yet sea-sick, but expect to be a little
so, in a few days. We shall probably be
boarded by a British vessel of war soon,
there are a No. off the coast, but they
treat American vessels very civilly.
I must bid you good bye, you
shall hear from me again very
soon.
Your affectionate Son
Sam'l J. B. Motser

Liverpool August 7th 1811
My Dear Parents.
You see from the date, that I have
at length arrived in England; I have had
a most delightful passage, of 20 days from
land to land & 2 in coming up the channel.
As this is a letter merely to inform you of my
safe arrival, I shall not enter into the particulars of our voyage until I get to London
to which place I shall proceed as soon as
possible Suffice it to say that I have not
been sick a moment of the passage, but on
the contrary have never enjoyed my health
better. I have not as yet got my trunk
from the customhouse but presume I shall
meet with no difficulty. I am now at
the Liverpool Arms Inn, it is the same inn that
Mr. Saliman put up at; it is, however a very
expensive; they charge the enormous sum I believe of
a guinea, or a guinea & a half a day. If I should
be detained a day or two in this place I shall en
deavor to find out other lodgings; at present
however it is unavoidable, as all the other
passengers are at the same place with me: You
may rest assured I shall do every thing in my
power to be economical; but to avoid imposition
of some kind or other, cannot be expected, since
every one who has been in England & spoken of the
subject to me, have been imposed upon in some
way or other.
You cannot think how many times I have
expressed a wish that you knew exactly how I
was situated; my passage has been so perfectly agreeable,
I know not of a single circumstance that
has interfered to render it otherwise thro' the
whole passage; there has been but one day in
which we have not had fair winds. Mrs Allston
is perfectly well, she has been seasick
but has been greatly benefited by it, she is
growing quite healthy. I have grown about
3 shades darker in consequence of my voyage.
I have a great deal to tell you, which I must

My Dear Parents,
You see from the date that I have at
length arrived at the place of my destination; I
have been in the city about 3 hours, so you see
what is my first object.— At Liverpool Irot
you two letters by two different vessels the Alpha
for Phila & the Aristomenes for New York, all
vessels were the first that would sail for America;
I informed you in them that I should
write immediately on my arrival in London
& I am now fulfilling my promise with
pleasure of giving you some particulars
respecting my voyage & journey hither.— Our
voyage was attended with nothing of consequence
excepting remarkable fine winds & fair
weather from the time we left New York till
we reached Liverpool; we arrived after a passage of 22 days, which is remarkably short and
especially for this season of the year, when the
wind is generally so light, you can perhaps
conceive my emotions on the 20th day of our passage
when we heard the Capt cry out from the mast
head, land! you may be assured I was joyful
enough, although I was by no means tired of the
voyage, for I cannot recollect a single circumstance
that was disagreeable thro' the whole voyage.
there were no quarrelsome persons on board, all
things went on smoothly and gaily; there was
no seasick one (excepting the Captains
lady) of consequence; Mr. Waitt who has crossed
the Atlantic 6 times, was sick almost every day
but excepting her, there were none who were
seasick after the 2d or 3d day for my own part
I felt a little disagreeable the 2d day on
account of sleeping very cold, & catching cold;
yet I did not feel one moments seasickry
thro' the whole voyage; I think mama may
safety venture across the ocean for I have not found
it half so tedious or disagreeable as the 3 days passage from NewHaven to NewYork, & not by any means
so dangerous: if we were in any danger of accidents, it was in coming in to the wharf at Liverpool; there, indeed, we came very near being
tashed to pieces, against the head of the wharf, tho' the carelessness of the pilot; we were going
at the rate of 6 or 7 knots, with the wind & tide in our favor, & just as the head of the
wharf was within only 4 inches of the wharf, she was fast in the mud; the Capt'n who was on
deck was as pale as ashes and we were all very much frightened, & now when I think of
it, it seems almost a miracle that we were saved. After we had brushed ourselves up a little
we went ashore, & as all the passengers went to the Liverpool Arms Hotel, tho' I would gladly
have gone some where else, as I was a perfect

monious man; they requested me to come at any

five dollars

American measures affect this country more
than you can have any idea of; the embargo
if it had continued 6 weeks, it is said would

paper of the banks of England which, never has

lish dollar which used to pass for 5s is now raised to

affairs. -- property here is very high -- & would
at other times would cost 1 guinea, & I have been that to be very
fortunate in obtaining them for that price. -- But
what I lose in one way I hope I shall make up
in another.
I did not call on Mr. West today as Mr. All-

My Dear Friend,
I have at length found a little leisure from
the hurry and bustle which naturally attends a stranger in such a place as this, to write to one of my best
friends and to give a slight account of my voyage. I depart from NewYork informing you of the
time I expected to sail etc. On Saturday July 13th we left the harbor of NewYork & lay at Staten Island until
Monday morning for a wind, and in the course of a few hours we lost sight of land; the passengers on the second day
and some indeed on the first began to be sick, for my own part I was not in the slightest degree seasick tho the whole voyage, tho' I must confess, seeing
some of them so deadly sick made me feel disagreeably after the 3 day however the passengers began to recover &
continued well thro' the remainder of the voyage; Our passengers 14 in no were perhaps the most agreeable sett ever
collected together, we had one odd character among them who made us an excellent butt, a Mr Minshull, the
same which Palmagundi mentions in his satire upon Ferdinand, he is an Englishman by birth, but a citizen
of NewYork, he pretends to be a poet, and is the author of a number of comedies, which were it not for the title
2. pages would read as well by beginning at the end of
them: he created us a great deal of diversion by some
of his poetical effusions, I will transcribe a specimen
of it which will give you a better idea of the man
than all I can say of him: the following he wrote on
our leaving NewYork;
Farewell to NewYork Manhattan's fair isle
May plenty and trade make the citizen smile
On board the Lydia each man takes his glass,
The next, sweethearts, and wives, is the theme of our toast
The cocks proclaim the morn, and the ducks quack the worst
With fortepiano & flute, we charm the gods where Neptune
reigns
Whilst gliding over the watery main
This is a true copy & word for word as he wrote
it; the two first lines are uncommon for him they really
do him great credit -- the sixth line was our phrase
which we were constantly repeating afterwards through
the whole voyage -- As to the rest of the passengers none
were so eccentric as to need particular description
they were gay, civil, & accomodating, each seemed desirous
to contribute his share to the diversion of the whole;
some parts of the day we were entertained by music; one
of our company playing admirably on the piano forte,
after dinner, a song from the captain, who was a
man with one of the best dispositions in the world
and one who took the greatest pains to make
his passengers cheerful & happy, some of an even-
ing amused themselves with cards, & some with
backgammon, & we were never at a loss for some-
thing to amuse ourselves. I often look back with
some surprise to think how thro' the whole voy-
age every thing that happened was of the agreeable
kind, and wondered in what consisted the tedious
& hazard of a voyage across the Atlantic: perhaps
our voyage was rendered uncomonly pleasant on
account of the winds, which excepting a little,
more than one day, were favorable thro' the
whole voyage, & our cheerfulness perhaps arose
from the anticipation of seeing land in a short
time. On the 19th day we were out we had calcu-
lated we were within 180 miles of land, & of
course the next morning we were early on the
look out, the captain came to us as we were sitting
on deck, & told us he intended going to mast-
head to see land, he went up and in a few mo-
ments cry'd out, land! land! we all ran as
many as could up the stairs, and sure as
nough we could very faintly see almost direct
ly ahead, a light misty appearance in the
horizon, like a mountain; none but those who
have been out of sight of land for 20 days can
justly conceive our sensations at the sight, all was
joy on board, & even the dogs & pigs discovered
evident tokens of pleasure, by putting their noses
over the bow of the ship, & whining most mus-
ically. In the course of a few hours, more land
appeared rising up & we sailed fast into St.
Georges channel, as we passed Cork harbor we
were visited by a small fishing vessel with 4
or 5 raw Fishermen in it, who broke us fish and
potatoes, it was laughable to hear them talk
in the true Irish Rogue; we passed the Tuscar
rock a dangerous celebrated rock on the Irish
coast, there were thousands of seafood upon it
and over it, after passing this rock we steered
across the channel towards the Welsh shore, &
came in sight of Holyhead on the island of An-
glesea, the mountains in Wales are very grand
it is very common to see the clouds envelop-
ing the middle of the mountain, while the top
is seen above them; on the evening of the 6th Aug.
we lay to, for the tide, opposite, a very high bluff
called Great Ormes Head, about 30 miles from
Liverpool, & early on the morning of the 7th we
got under weigh, and dropped down the river Mer-
sey towards the city, which was distinguishable from
its smoky atmosphere at some distance, and about
12 o’clock I once more placed my foot on land;
Thus ended a voyage thro’ the whole of which I
cannot recollect a single disagreeable circumstance
and which was performed in the remarkable short
time of 22 days. I then went with the rest of
my fellow passengers into the city to look out for
lodgings, we at length fixed upon the Liverpool
Arms, the same hotel at which Professor Silliman
staid while in Liverpool. I saw the same French-
man whom he describes in his journal, he did not
seem to show the same attention to his guests as for-
merly. What little leisure I could get I employed in
looking round the city, it is situated on the river
Mersey, the streets are very irregular and dirty,
it is about the size, and has the same no. of inhab-
itants as NewYork, but I think NewYork far surpasses
it in beauty; the public buildings are in a
magnificent taste, but have a black, smoky ap-
pearance which arises from the custom of burning
sea coal almost altogether, the private dwelling
houses likewise are very plain, there is scarcely
to be seen throughout Liverpool a 4 story house they
rarely ever exceed three.— I met with no difficulty
at the customhouse with my baggage which
I had very great reason to fear from what I had

Last Sabbath I went to Saint Paul's & heard
every good a good sermon, but what struck me as very
singular, was the constant change in the congregation
some coming in & others going out, thro' the whole service
the sermon was at least well distributed; it reminds
me of Professor Sittman's explanation of the proverb of
boiling, when he says that on a particle of water at the
bottom of the vessel, in his lectures a particle of heat, & then
another particle of water comes, it does not till every
particle has taken its place -- Over the left entrance
into the church is the epitaph of Sir Chris. When
the celebrated architect, & builder of St. Paulo
you have probably heard of it, it is short & fulthy.
It runs thus, Subitus conditor hujus ecclesia et
annos supra nonaginta, non sibi, sed bono publico.
Lector si monumentum requisit, circumspice.
The latter sentence struck me as remarkably fine -- I have not yet visited
Westminster Abbey but intend it shortly. --
Mr. & Mrs. Allston have taken a house very
near me, I am in & out these evening day; Mr.
Allston visits me every evening to smoke a social
sesar & talk of painting, & home Vabein so that
upon the whole I pass my time very pleasantly, my
principal amusement is music, I have a piano
forte of which I was always very fond, & in my leisure
moments (which indeed are few) I am endeavour to learn
upon it. -- I live quite in the old bachelor
style entirely by myself, I have 3 rooms, a
bedroom, & dressing room, which fire is made for me
in the morning before I get up, & my breakfast
ready at a minutes warning; but as I appeared at first
very odd to me who have always been accustomed
to have my meals with at least 8 or 9 & in College
with nearly 100, the first time I could not eat
with any pleasure, & after I had finished I felt
as if I had eat nothing; but I have got accustomed
to it now, & do not complain. of The customs here, for those gentlemen who
take lodgings to dine at an eating house
it is not expected, that you, The custom with
respect to boarding out is entirely different from what
it is with us, if a person in America wishes to board
at a place he agrees for a certain sum per week
to have his food & rooms, & this sum is regular thro'
every week, but here, there is no provision made
for food, for the room is paid a certain sum
per week, but for breakfast & supper it depends
upon what is made; If I wish for any particular
thing I can send for it, & it is charged in the weekly
bill, so that in this way persons who live as economically
as they please it is not expected that you will dine at home, gentlemen
who are in lodgings
generally dine at an eating house, an establishment
which we have not in America, they are here
in almost every street, the advantage of them is very
great for gentlemen can dine on what they please
& at any time at a minutes warning; They cries of London of which you have
doubtless heard, are very annoying to me, as indeed
they are to all strangers, the noise of them is constantly in our ears from morning till midnight, &
with the exception of one or two they all appear to be
the cries of distress, I don't know how many times
I have run to the window expecting to see some
poor creature in the agonies of death, but sounds to my Surprise that it was
only an old woman crying "lardin apples," or some
thing of the kind; Hogarth's picture of the enraged
musician will give you an excellent idea of the
noise I hear every day under my windows
I dined a few days since at an American
gentleman's house, with a party of 18 Americans it
made me feel quite at home. I assure you
The English winter is now beginning to
set in, it is strange weather, at one moment the
sun is shining in a cloudless sky and the very next
a cloud passes over, so dark, that candles are almost
neccessary, it then rains, and the sun shines again &
this happen five or six times in the course of a day
there is a singular custom with respect to
knocking at the doors of houses here, which is strictly
adhered to, a servant belonging to the house brings the
bell only, at strange sent. knocks once, a market man
or woman knocks once & rings, the penny post knocks
twice and a gentleman or lady half a dozen quick
knocks or any number over twenty a nobleman gen-
erally knocks 8 or 10 times very loud.
The accounts lately received from America
look rather gloomy, though thought here to be
more threatening, from my own observation and oppor-
tunity of hearing the opinion of the people generally
they are extremely desirous of an amicable adjust-
ment of differences, and seem as much opposed to
the idea of war as the better part of the American
people. In case of war I am doubtful whether
I should return home, or go to Paris (as Americans
would be ordered out of the country) but that probably
should choose the latter.
In this letter you will percieve all the variety
of feeling which I have had for a fortnight past, sometimes
in the balance of equality of each, which, latter tho' most desirable
I seldom have, but generally am at one extreme or the other. I wrote this in the evenings of
the last two weeks, and this will account, & I hope, for a fortnight past, sometimes
apology for its great want of connection; I know I am writing to my friends, & such friends, as will
overlook its faults, & I must now conclude my dear friends, by requesting you to remember me to all
my friends; to your parents, respectively, to Miss Ann Hart, Mary Ann, Jennette, Augusta, & the others, to
the Miss Stuarts, Miss Isaaces, to my cousin Capt. & Mrs. Stout and in short to all who inquire after me; & receive the further assurance of the lasting
friendship, & esteem of your sincere
Miss F. with your affectionate regards
Friend Bancroft J.B. Morse

My Dear Parents.
As I understand the Calen is to sail
again in a few days for Boston I improve the
opportunity of again writing you, altho I feel very
little in a writing mood today, having caught a
slight cold which has made me feel dull a little for
a few days past, but I am regaining my spirits
very fast so you must not think any thing of it, for it
would be strange if I did not feel dull sometimes
since it is constitutional; I do all I can to resist it
by applying myself to my studies, strictly; I shall
offer my drawing to the Royal Academy next
Monday week, as it then opens for the admission of
students, I will then write you whether I am successful or not. I have not delivered many of my
letters of introduction; Mr Bromfields, Dr. Luttmans
& Mr. Wests are the only ones as yet. Mr. Burder
lives 4 miles out of town at Camberwell Sir
Joseph Banks is not in town, Mr. Wilberforce lives
about 3 miles from me &c. I have not as yet found
time to call on them but certainly shall as soon as it
is in my power. I was invited a few days since
to dine at Mr. Higginsons with Mr. & Mrs Allston, whom
invitation I accepted; they are very polite & attentive to
me -- it was a party consisting of 18 Americans; it made
me feel quite at home; we sat down to dinner at 2 p.m.
six o’Clock by candlelight, & rose from dinner about 9 o’clock
they you see are fashionable hours.
In my last long letter I told you I believe every
thing that was of importance; I have but little opportu-
nity of seeing any thing being shut up from morning till
night. One thing which annoys me very much is the
various cries of London; you may perhaps recollect I
was describing to you one of Hogarth’s pieces called the
enraged musician, in which every noise was collected under
his window; but I have experienced every day the same
noises, for at a certain part of the day the whole variety
of chimney sweeps, ballad singers, dust cart men with bells, beggars
by hundreds; and old women with wheelbarrows, some with
potatoes, some with apples, some with fish, rabbits, fleurs, &c
in fact every different article you can think of, & all
these crying at once their different cries; when I first came
here, I that some of the cries were made by boys who were
mocking these old women, they were such terrible noises, but
upon looking out of the window I found it was made by
half a dozen old women collected together at the corner of
the street to try to see what could scream the loudest.
I find I cannot send any thing home, not even
Mr. Collier’s books which he wished me to forward as soon
as I could, when the nonintercourse is taken off I will
send them; I endeavor also to send you a Bilton cheese
which are the finest that are made in this country, I would
suit Papa’s taste exactly, as they keep sound but a short time,
My expences have exceeded but a little what I had cal-
culated for Week, the sum total to the present time is
£ 3418.8.2.— this includes my expences from Liverpool, and all down
to the present.— what little I have exceeded I shall make up
by future economy— I suppose you do not wish to know
the items of every of I spend, if I give you the total anno
from time to time I suppose it will answer— I endeavor
to be as economical as possible & am getting into the habit
very fast, it must be learnt by degrees, I shall not say, as Sal-
maggiendi says, "I shall spare no expence in discovring the
most economical way of spending money," but shall endeavor
to practise it immediately.— I want to hear from you
very much and good long letters like your last, you cannot
conceive how much joy it would me to hear from you, it seems
so long before a letter can get from one to the other I often
think of Mama & imagine her thinking of me; I hope she
will keep up her spirits, and think, as I do that 3 years will
soon pass away, & then I hope we shall see each other again;
till then I shall employ all my time in improving myself in
every thing that is useful— Sidney. E. & Richard. E. I suppose
are now at home; I that of Edwin on his commencement
day thro' the whole day, give him joy on his Bachelorship
for me, I wish Edwin & Rich? would both set down & write
me long letters, and give me any minute circumstances
which will interest me, in fact every thing will coming from home; I
feel myself an American more than I ever did before.
I should like a triennial catalogue, as I think they come
out this year— If any vessel should arrive from this
96516
place to Boston or NewYork and not have letters from
you must not feel anxious, for I am not in a part of
the town to hear of myself, and it is almost by chance that
I hear of any; if you should hear from me thru Mr. Cheney
of Boston from Mr. Allston, you may always know that
I am well; sometimes she writes by vesper, which I had
heard of till yesterday; in short you must always
think the best. I am in and out at Mr. Allston's every
day he lives close by me. He & Mr. Allston are very
friendly & sociable with me, he comes to my room at
most every day Mr. & Mr. Allston are in excellent
health Mr. Allston says she never enjoyed better, the other
day did her a great deal of good. There is Capt. Van
Rensselaer, who came passengers with us, who lives
a short walk from me, they are likewise very kind
to me she was a Van Rensselaer of New York state
cousin to young Van Rensselaer with whom I am acquainted
& who is in this country in Edinburgh
shall probably see him soon. I do not hear any
of Mr. Isaac Hurd, only that he is in Edinburgh, if
you want to address a letter to him I should do
it to him know I am here. I wrote you a very long
line by the return of the Lydia a few days since, as I had
no moment to write it in. I shall certainly write by every
vesper that I hear of. I went the other day to see
very singular sight, it was St. Bartholomew's fair, it
held in this city once a year & continues for 3 days
the Lord Mayor opens the fair with some ceremony
which I did not see, the lower orders of society are let
loose on those days and are allowed to amuse themselves
in any lawful way they please; their principal amusement
was swinging, the swings were large frames in which
a box capable of holding 4 or 5 is suspended, there were
upwards of 300 of these to speak within bounds, placed
round Smithfield market, in which place the fair is always held;
it almost made me dizzy to see them all
in such a variety of motion; as there was no room
to spare they were huddled up as close together as
they could get them without striking each other, another
machine was the wheel such as is sometimes seen on our
election days, & another was a wheel revolving parallel to
the ground on the circumference of which were the figures
of the heads of horses, & saddles; & in fact every
variety of motion which you can conceive of, in the centre
of the square was every thing, in the world, theatres,
luscious nature, wild beasts, & tame four footed & two, mountebanks,
buffoons, ventriloquists, dancers on the slack wire,
tumblers, fighting & swearing, pocket picking & stealing,
music & dancing & hubbub & confusion such as I never
witnessed before; the theatres were temporary buildings
all hung round with tapestry, & adorned & illuminated
on the outside with various colored lamps; strolling
players generally occupy them, & between the plays
wh take up but 15 minutes each time, the actors &
actresses exhibit themselves on a platform before the
theatre & flourish about with drawn swords in all
their spangled robes & false jewels, till the house is
filled again, & then they act the same thing over again
& so they go on thro' the 3 days & nights; there
are 5 or six of these theatres, & they appeared to be
in opposition to each other for as soon as the band
of music which belonged to one theatre had ceased
they would strike up & make such a noise as to drown
every word that is said, tho' the other noise would I
think be sufficient for that, I said music because
we generally call the sound of a musical instrument
music, but if you can conceive of between 20 & 30
different bands, all within hearing of each other,
all playing at once, & all different tunes, in different
time, you can have some idea of the music I mean.
Contiguous to the theatres were the exhibition rooms of the
Mountebanks & buffoons, who between their exhibitions
also, showed their antickicks before the public, but if I was
to attempt to describe every thing whil I saw at the fair, I
should fill a quite of paper. I soon expect to witness
a much more interesting scene, I mean a Coronation
the King is declining every fast & his death is daily ex-
pected, & I understand that the ceremony of the coro-
nation instantly takes place, I will send you the
papers at that time which will give you perhaps more
information concerning it than I shall be able to do.
Had I not better take one of the newspapers regularly
and after having read them, send them to you by the
wh ich carry my letters? I wish I felt more in a commu-
nicative mood than at present; I seem to have forgotten
all I wanted to tell you; but I hope you won't think
this a short letter, because the others were longer.
I go to a ch urch in Swallow Street of our denomina-
tion; it is the same I believe in which Mr. Bodman used
to preach. I must close this as it is growing late & I
must send it on board tomorrow morning by requesting you
to give my particular love to Grandma ma Breese, Uncle
Aunt Salisbury, to Miss Russell, Mr. Brown, Mr. & Mrs. Rock
wood, Mr. Evarts, Catherine Dexter, Sam uel Ward & his father's
family, to the Hurd family, to D r Bartlett family, Capt.
Pratts, Mr. Bridges, Mr. & Mrs Cleveland, Mr. & Mrs Knowles
Capt le Walker's family, Aunt Dowse, Mr. & Mrs Rogers, Miss
Bradstreet's; to my dear Brothers, Nancy, Betty, Caroline, &
Joe; To every one who enquires after me; to Mr. Codman
especially. & take as much love as I bear to all these
together for yourselves, & believe me your ever affectionate
Son
Sam uel B. Morse. Esq r . A.B.

My Dear Parents,
I have just received papa's letter
of Augt 16th by the Reaper via Bristol; as the
Galen goes to morrow morning it will be out
of my power to send any thing wt you have
requested but by the next opportunity will have
all things ready & will call on Mr. Taylor
& transact the business as you direct.— I hope
you have long ere this received some of my letters
whk I suppose are at this moment in all parts
of the world; I drop't you a line at sea, by
a vessel bound to Quebec but I don't know
that you have rec'd it.— You will see by the
papers which accompany this what a report re-
specting the capture of the U.S. frigate President,
by Melampus frigate, prevails here; it is suffi-
cient to say it is not in the least credited.— In
case of war, I shall be ordered out of the coun-
try, if so, instead of returning home had I not better
go to Paris, as it is cheaper living there even than
in London, and there are great advantages there; I
only ask the question in case of war.— Mr. & Mrs.
Allston are very well; I wish in your better you
would inform me of Mr. Allston's friends health
as it would be gratifying to her just to have you
mention it. I am going on successfully
next week on Monday the Royal Academy opens
& I shall present my drawings. I want to hear
that some of my letters have reached you, that
I may know you are relieved from anxiety.
The King remains the same in health.
Do write me every opportunity, as I shall
love to all. Your affectionate Son
Sam'l P. B. Morse.

My Dear Parents,
As I write this in haste I cannot
be particular; I only will inform you that
I remain in perfect health, and in high spirits;
it is some time since I heard from you
the last way via Bristol; I long to hear again
the papers mention that there will probably
be an embargo in the U. States, if so our correspondence
will be at least embarrassed
the only communication, will be via New-
York & Falmouth (Eng.) by the British Jack-
ets; I wrote you by the Galen about 3
weeks ago; and have this moment heard
she was still in the Downs; I was really
provoked; there is great deception about
vessels, they advertise for a certain day to
perhaps do not sail under a month after;
the Galen has been going and going, till I
am sick of hearing she has not gone; if I
had had any idea of her being thus delay'd
I should certainly have contrived to put
Papa's things on board; I shall go to-morrow
into the city (which I suppose you know is a
distinct part of London,) I live in Westminster,
which is three miles from the business part
I will immediately have them put up per-
haps it may not be too late to send them by
her yet; tho' there would be the difficulty of
getting them to her -- if I send them to New York
I will direct them to Messrs. Williams & Whiting
I was a few days ago violently attacked
by the rheumatism in my arms, and was told
to wear flannel which you know I have never
done as yet; I have accordingly had made for me
4 flannel waistcoats; the English climate being
very damp, subjects stranger, that train of disord-
ers attending damp climates; -- I did not
mention that I had an attack of the same
kind at sea owing to my lying upon two chairs
on deck which had accidentally got wet --
I have not had another attack since wearing
flannel, and do not think I shall if I take
care to keep myself warm.
I dined at Mr. Bromfield's a few days
since with a number of Americans, among
whom were Mr. & Mrs. Sears, and Mr. Phd.
Perkins, of Boston, Mr. Sears & family were
to go to France yesterday in the car--
perhaps it may gratify their relations, to be in-
formed of it, if you should see them -- Mr. &
Mrs. Allston are very well; he is very intimate and
sociable with me so as to make me
his confidant in some important things --
Wednesday Nov. 6. 1811
After leaving this letter so long, as you see by the
different dates, I again resume it; perhaps you
will be surprised when I tell you, that but
yesterday I heard that the Garden is still wind-
bound, it makes my letters which are on board
of her about 5 or 6 weeks old, beside the pros-
pect of along voyage; however, it is not her
fault; there are 3 or 4 hundred vessels in the
same predicament the wind has been such
that it has been impossible for any of them
to get under weigh; but I must confess I feel
considerably anxious on your account; I would
only request that you would always think the best,
when there is a long interval between hearing from
me, a thousand accidents may have prevented the
letters from reaching you; at such a distance too as
I am; you can't expect to hear from me so often as
if I was at New-haven; and if vessels arrive at
Boston, from England, and you have not letters by
them, I hope it will not make you anxious, even
if they came direct from London, for at such a dis-
tance -- I am from, hearing of vessels, that it is
almost by accident that I never hear of any, and it
would employ almost all my time to go into the
city every time I wished to know of vessels; if I have
business in the city, I generally wait till it accumu-
lates a little, and then take a day, to transact the whole
for the day is completely broken, as it takes almost the
whole of it only to go and return: so you must take all
these things into consideration, and make due allowance
for them. Now I have not heard from you this long
time, and there has been five or six vessels from New-
York direct here, 3 or 4 to Liverpool from N-York, &c
one to this port from Massachusetts whose letter bag
was up in Boston, by none of which vessels have I had
letters; it does not however, depress me, as I can con-
cieve that there are many things which may have pre-
vailed, but still I do not feel the less desirous to hear
from you -- you may always be certain of this, that I
shall never forget you, it is as impossible, as for you
to forget me -- Mr. Allston mentioned to me that he
was once eighteen months without hearing a syllable
from home.
I mentioned in one of my other letters that
I had drawn a figure (the Gladiator,) to admit me
into the academy; -- after I had finished it, I was
displeased with it, and concluded not to offer it, but
attempt another; I have accordingly drawn another
from the Laocoon statue, the most difficult of all
the statues, have shown it to the keeper of the acad-
emy, and am admitted for a year, without the
least difficulty; Mr. Allston was pleased to compli-
ment me upon it by saying that it was better than
two thirds of the drawings of those who had been
drawing at the academy for two years; -- I feel en-
couraged likewise when I think that those who have
gained admittance at last, have drawn three or four
years before they have ventured to offer a figure
for admittance, and then have some of them been
refused the first, and sometimes the second & even
a third time, whereas the second figure I ever
drew from plaster is accepted the first time; or
I shall on the strength of this go to work and con-
tend for the prizes which will not only gain me
credit but money; the prize for the best historical
piece on a given subject is upwards of 200 guineas
beside the piece which remains with the artist; this
prize however is at present beyond me, I must
creep along gradually towards it -- I have
completed a landscape, which I shall show to Mr.
West in a day or two; I am at present copying a
portrait of Van Dyke's from a copy by Mr. West, a
fine picture; I shall probably have finished
that landscape by the next exhibition at the
Royal Academy, and may offer it for exhibition, but
it would indeed be a wonder if it should be accepted.
I can however but try -- I am getting along com-
fortably, I once in a while am troubled with the
return of my colick -- This is but a stupid letter
for to tell the truth, I feel very stupid, owing to a
cold I have had for some time; my next letter
shall be more particular and longer -- This will
probably go by the Orion via New York, and as she sails
to-morrow, I must close. I send a file of Sunday
newspapers, which contain a summary of the week's news:
I shall write you again soon; so good bye; give my love
to all those whom I have mentioned in my other letters,
In haste Your affectionate Son Sam'l F. B. Morse
this third. Nov 6th 1811

My Dear Friend, I have heard of your safe
arrival in London, and that you had a
short and pleasant passage, on which event
give me leave to congratulate you. — Also
I have received nothing from you, the which
I attribute to your having been occupied in
writing to your family, and those who perhaps
have a greater claim on your favour than
myself, yet I do hope you will have written
me before you receive the present, it will at
least manifest a disposition on your part
to cultivate a correspondence from which I
assure you I should promise myself much pleasure.
I saw your father a few days
since, he desired me if I wrote you to say the
family were well, your friends here generally
I believe are also all well; I wish I had any
thing else of interest to communicate, picture
to yourself Charleston and every thing that appears therein following its old routine without
interruption and you will see its present state,
it is as pleasant this year as it was the last, tho'
the society has rather thereand, that is the society
of young ladies, which I suppose is all young men
mean
mean when they say Society, those who remain
however are quite agreeable: they I think you
found out before you left, it is well for us
here they are, for you know we are not overrun
with amusements, particularly of a public nature.
The theatre has been open a for the season and it has
been newly painted, but there is a sett of miserable
plays, I think you must have discovered some
difference between London and this place or
that season. -- I am now confined to the packe
how joy of plodding on from house to house and
star to house, but I have it in expectation
and really anticipate the pleasure of seeing
you in England before you return, -- (Greene
my partner, I think you knew him) said from
here the 1st of Augt. in book, from there he was
going to Liverpool and would probably visit
London, so alas it be the case and be fine as
you will I think you must have
been highly gratified with the different
scenes that London has presented you and
I suppose you are now engaged in the study
of your favorite profession in which be
aspired I most heartily wish you all the
success that you can write yourself. I am your obedient servant

My Dear Parents,
As I understand there is a vesel up
for New York, and as I omit no good oppor-
tunity of writing you, I take advantage of a few
leisure moments to add another letter to the many
I have written you since my arrival; I have
written 10 letters to you since I have been in England;
this makes the eleventh: 1 from Liverpool
by the ship Aristomenes and another postal for the
District of Maine whose name I have forgotten; 2
from Liverpool by the ship Prince of Boston; 1
by the Lydia via Liverpool for New York; 2 by the Galena
dated Oct. 3rd 1 dated Nov. 3 sent by private opportu-
nity to Liverpool to go on board a ship for New York, and
1 I sent a few days since to young Mr David West
of Boston who was to sail in a day or two; I hope
at least some of them have reached you before
this, and that you have received information of
our safety; I have been anxiously expecting
letters from you for a long time, but have
not received any information from you since
the letter via Bristol; but I know how to make
allowances for accidents and delays, and only hope
in case of a long interval in hearing from me, you
will make the same allowance, and find a sign the
true cause of some accident or delay befailing the
letter, for I shall always write, in the space of 3
months, averaging 2 letters in three weeks; I assure
you I am extremely desirous of hearing that you
know of our safe arrival, and expect before you
get this, I have received letters from you, and more
so, as I understand there are two vessels expected
at Liverpool every day from Boston.
My health is very good and has been so since
I have been in London excepting a few dull turns
which are natural to me, you know, they seldom
however, last more than half a day; it would
indeed be singular if I should not have them
in November, as you probably know it is called
the Englishman's month, in which more
suicides are committed than in all the other
months together; this November however, has I
understand, been unusually fine, and if it
has, the month of November in its true state must
be dismal indeed, for almost every morning as
yet, till 12 o'clock it has been so dark, that one could
not see to read without sitting by the window
and the appearance of objects, in and out of doors,
was the same as appears on looking thro' a piece of
a green glass bottle; but I must give November its
credit, for some days have been remarkably clear &
beautiful.
I mentioned in my last letter that I had entered
the Royal Academy, which information I
hope will give you pleasure; I now employ my
days in painting at home, and the evenings in
drawing at the academy, as is customary; I have
finished a landscape, and almost finished a copy
of a portrait which Mr. West lent me, Mr. Allston
has seen it and complimented me by saying it was
just 100 times better than he had had any idea of
being able to do, and that I should astonish
Mr. West very much; I have also begun a land-
scape a morning scene at sunrise, which Mr Alston is very much pleased with. all these things encourage me and, as every day passes away I feel increased enthusiasm
Mr Isaac Hurds is in London and also Mr Parkman the Clergyman, they will spend the winter here and return home in the spring, they are very friendly and sociable, we shall probably meet every day at our chef-house to dinner, as it is situated between us, we live about 3 miles apart, they have taken lodgings at No 36 Norfolk street, Strand, a few moments walk from Somerlot house, where I go every evening to draw, so now I have company and it keeps me in excellent spirits, Mr Parkman has just returned from Paris. The Higginsons here are bankrupt which will undoubtedly cause the same in tune to the partners in Boston, his B2
Stephen &c. The circumstance reminds me of an observation of Mama's, that those who endeavored to injure Papa, were sure to meet with some punishment, and I consider this in that light, tho' I feel very much for the Higginsons here as they are very benevolent and are considered excellent people.
I have delivered my letter to Sir Joseph Bankes he received me very kindly. I must close this letter as it goes via New York. if you have any more orders for books or the like, I will get them ready to send by Mr Parkman or Mr. Keene in the spring as now it is impossible to send anything on account of American measures. Distresses are increasing in this country and disturbances, riots &c. have commenceded, as you will see by the papers which accompany this, they are considered very alarming.
I can only add give my love to all whom I mention in the other letters, especially relations, and Mrs Russell, and Mrs O. Brown, Nancy &c. &c.... good bye. Your affectionate son
Sam'l F. B. Moslem

My Dear Parents,
I have but a few moments, just to
say that I am well, and that I wrote a few
days since by the ship Paragon (I think) via N.York
this makes the 12th letter I have written to you since
my arrival and I have been for some time in anxious expectation of a letter from you, acquainting me that you have heard of our safety, no account has reached us to that effect, excepting that the news of the safe arrival of the ship had been received at NewYork, saying nothing of the passengers.
I hope some of my letters have reached you before this: -- This is the first letter that I have received but in future shall do it, as I think it a good plan for you well to know the order in which you receive them, and whether any are missing.
Decr. 6th
I have just recieved a line from Mrs Vose of Charlestown, and by him learn that you have heard of our arrival and that you receive well, but did not learn whether you had heard by letters from me, or some other way; Mrs Allston has also just received a letter from Mr Channing in which he mentions he has only received 1 letter, and she has written, 13, -- there seems to be a strange fatalilty attending our correspondence, you must have written to me certainly, but there has no letter reached me since the one via Bristol; in one of my letters I recommend
ted against sending letters by passengers, for they
have other things to do, and think of, on their first
arrival; and it is generally a week or 10 days after
every one else has recieved their letters that you get
those sent by passengers, or otherwise sent by post from
the place where they arrive; so that on the score
of expence it is the same if not more, and the
delay is certainly vexatious; the expence of a letter
would be at most 1/2 sterling, now the beer which
I drink at dinner amounts to 4. dins. per day, so
that if you will only send the letters by the letter-box
I will, after the receipt of one, instead of drinking
beer, drink water for dinner for 3 days; for a letter
loses half its interest, when you know that all
your friends have received theirs by the same vessel
a week or ten days before you. I only mention
this subject, and you can do what you think will
be best?— Mr. Bromfield wrote me yesterday
that he had just recieved a line from you, enclosing
a bill for 105,, 13,, 6,, in this I have no doubt
will get me thro' the year very well; living here
is very expensive however; I am pursuing my studies
with increased enthusiasm, and hope before the
three years are out to relieve you from further expences.
Mr. Allston encourages me to think thus from
the rapid improvement he says I have made; you
may rest assured I shall use all my endeavors to
do it as soon as may be. I have kept a regular
account of my expences, and at the end of the year
will send them to you at large, it has been of great
use in restraining me in my expences and would not
leave it off on any account; for having ascertained
my allowance for a week, I put the sum in large
characters on every leaf of my account book, and at the end
of the week I sum up the expense and compare them,
if I find I have exceeded my allowance, I set down
the excess and bear it in mind the next week, so that
if I find myself inclined to purchase anything which
is not immediately necessary, I restrain myself, untill
my weeks expense falls short of my allowance, &c.
I am at present a little in debt to my account
owing to the expense of setting myself out at the begin-
ning, but hope to square my accounts at the end of the
year.

This country appears to me to be in a very

Charleston Jan 6th 1812.
Dear Brothers.
I write by Capt. Holmes who sails tomorrow morning for Liverpool. I am at present
employed in preparing Geography for Papa -- His next edition will be out in a few months
and it is as much as both of us can do, to supply the press with copy. Richard is at
New Haven & when I left there, was as well as usual, excepting, that he was at times a
little nervous. We were very much pleased with the long letters which you sent us; but were
sorry to hear by your last of the attacks of rheumatism and cholic. Mama has written
you a long letter on that subject, and given you cautions and prescriptions and antidotes
&c. It rejoiced us much that thou wert admitted into the Royal Academy & I congratulat
thee upon it, inasmuch as thou didst me
upon the title of A.B. Many persons frequently
enquire about thee, and take a great interest in
the letters which we receive, Ergo, continue to
write often. Your friends too at New-Haven make
frequent inquiries, and when you write to this
country I wish you would be more particular in
your mention of them. Your classmate Hillhouse
resides in College as a Graduate. Goodrich is stud-
ying Divinity. I see both of them frequently. Mr
Woolsey is frequently at Dr Dwight's, it might be well
to mention them all particularly. I know of little
that I think would be interesting to you - Every thing goes on in its usual channel, or rather I get so
soon familiarized to change, that every thing seems new. Commodore Nicholson died a few days since
of a paralytic stroke, and was buried with naval &
masonic honors. Minute guns from the castle
kept up a constant fire during the march of the
procession. I saw Sam Ellwood a few days ago. He
seemed well. Poor Millbury whom you so much
respected is within the debtors limits in Boston. We
have just received news of a very fatal fire at Rich-
mond (Vir.). We send you the printed account. None
of your friends, or friends relations are injured as you
will see, right Miss Mayo, the was sister to my classmate May.
A new periodical publication has lately appeared in
Boston in which the advocates for liberal Christianity
will put forth all their strength. The P.T.F. affair
is put off till the spring session. I have not seen
Rosseter since you left this country. Henry Hagg of
my class was married last March, notice of
his marriage was published immediately after Commencement. He is at present in New-Haven stud-
ying law. He set out with his mother a few weeks
ago to go to Charleston, but his mother was
taken sick before they had proceeded far and
they returned. She is not I believe very seriously
sick. Mrs S.E. Dwight has been married
to Miss Daggett since you left us. I write, as you used
to say, any thing that comes uppermost you must not
direct much connexion. I am very busily employed
for Papa or I would have taken more pains.
C. Hard is at Portsmouth. J&G Adieu!
Bartlett in Boston. Grandma and Your brother
U Va. Salisbury all well. not Sidney Edwards Mor
but simple.
Edwards Morse.
Samuel F. B. Morse
London.

Bloomingdale January 6th. 1812.
My dear Sir,
I have to acknowledge the receipt of five letters from you; one
was off Sandy Hook one from Liverpool, & three from London, on Sept. 30th, & the third of Nov. 9th 1811, the last of which I received the day before yesterday. As I am so far distant from town, I never hear what ships are about to sail for England, and this I trust will accoust to you sufficiently for my not having written sooner. But waving apologies I return you my hearty thanks for the entertainment which I have received from the formal of your packet of Sept 30th. The subject of painting is always interesting to me, and it becomes still more so, under your sun. I hope you will take a copy of the Egyptian Hieroglyphics in the possession of Lord Elgin. What you say of Mr. West delights me. I have something or other, felt for a long time, a strong attachment to that man I have often hoped he would visit America, that I might have an opportunity of seeing him. I saw one of his first pieces in Philadelphia, painted with as much care as Lord Elgin can take of his Athenian & Egyptian antiquities. Pray have there not been engravings made from some of his best Scripture pictures? If so, during your stay in England you will confer upon me a great obligation by making a selection of the best prints from Sacred History, whether copied from him, or the works of other great masters.— As for paintings, they are too far above the reach of my purse for me to think of them; but a collection of such pictures as shall pass the ordeal of Mr. West's judgment would be to me invaluable.— Your observations on the English customs amuse & gratify me. I say gratify because they are so minute. A traveller who writes for the public usually puts his mind on the rack to discover something which will surprise or astonish. But it is not prodigious or uncommon events which I seek. Your letter, are just what they should be.— You tell me of incidents in that easy natural way, which the incidents themselves occur to your mind. In case you leave England what
route shall you take? Will you go directly to Calais or pass this Holland?
I know not what to think with respect to the differences between our government
& the English. I find the opinions of people in general seem now to lean to
wards the probability of war. I cannot but hope, however, that we shall continue
at peace. We have so long enjoyed peace that we know not all its
blessings. On the subjects of politics however, I cannot find anything new or interesting.
You doubtless see the American papers of a much more recent date than
that of this letter. Does it not amuse you to hear the observation which are
made on the state of parties in this country -- or rather does it not make
you ashamed that all the abuse & ribaldry vented in our papers should ever
meet the eye of a foreigner? Pray is there as much violence in the disputes
between the ministerial & opposition prints? -- It would I think be an interesting
subject of speculation, to trace the features in which the English & American
represent each other & those in which they differ? So far as the latter are derived from the former it would enable us to perceive the effects
produced by separation, and local circumstances. -- And when there
is a measure of other nations we should be better able to trace the progress
and influence of their respective peculiarities. --
But no more of England, let us now talk of America. I am afraid my
dear sir, you will not find my letters a source of great satisfaction in this
head, because I cannot give you those details with a correspondent in the
city courts. We live a very secluded life -- cut off from almost society but
our own. Mary Shaw spends the winter with us. We have at present
but one or two near neighbours, and my whole parish (excluding about
60 young masters & pupils in the neighbouring boarding schools) consists
of but six families. I have not (indeed not one of us has) been into the city
for three weeks. Every morning I spend in my study, & the afternoon when
the cloth is removed in reading to Mrs. J. & her sister. This is almost
my constant routine, & therefore since I have no company, nothing new
or strange or surprising, to defecate my standing pool you must expect
to find me rather dull. It is now some days since we have received letters
from Connt. When we last heard all was well. I forwarded your letter
to Saybrook agreeably to your request, a day or two after it came to hand.
Your friend Miss Jacobs spent the Christmas holidays with us. She is
very well, and desired me when I should write, to include her compliments
& kind wishes, with those of my family. Capt. P. M. Hunt I have
never seen since your departure. I intend, if possible, to call upon them
the next time I go to the City. Mr. Hogan the younger was
time since, I said they were both very well.
It gives us all great pleasure my dear Mr. Moser, to learn
been received into the Royal Academy. Your having thus
a subject as the Lacocinin renders your reception so much
honourable and of course the more satisfactory. I
will shortly attend you, and may your name be enrolled
in the list of those worthy who have, by their talents
added the American name.
You mention Mr. Palmer. I have received a letter from him, as
to him immediately, to send however by another ship, which will
enable of sending a duplicate. When he arrives in London, you
goodnly to say to him that I have answered his few of the questions
of my letter was to request him to purchase for me -- For the
Outham de Sacrificiis. Raphetic Annotations. Hammond's works. Campbell's translation
of the Gospels. Marsh's Michaelis. Pearson on the Creed. Watson on Infant
Baptism. Burn's Eccles. Law Leslie & Thiberg. Works, & Ready edition of
the Ecclesiastical Historians. -- Cloth for two Bails of clothes, bedding -- in case
Mr. Palmer delay his return I am more speedily directly opportunity presents
itself. I will be much obliged to you my dear Sir to send me the letter together
with information thro' whose hands I may remit to you the money with you
Samuel F. B. Morse Esquire

My Dear Son
Your Papa and both your Brothers are at
this moment engaged in writing you by the Ship
Plato which sails to-morrow for London
I have written you a long letter which was to have
gone in the Sally Ann Captain Holmes for Liver-
pool sometime ago but we find by the papers
that she sailed this morning Your Papa has writ-
ten you a few lines by her but we kept the largest
packet to go in this vessel direct for London we
hope she will have a quick passage.-- Mr Codman
lodged here a few nights ago We read him your
letters he was much pleased with them and that
you went to church in Swallow Street he says
the minister is an excellent man and that he will
write him and introduce you to him you must be
sure and be acquainted with him and attend constantly
on his ministry Mr C says he wishes he was with
you. they plague his life out where he is but he will give
superior to them he is a good man sends his love to you
as do all your Friends whom you have mentioned in
your letters we read your letters so often to our Friends that
I expect we shall get them by heart. You will draw the con-
clusion from this that we do not forget you as yet. - Mr
Godman asked me whether you do not make your own
Tea af a morning, I could not tell him, he said he always
did as it was not safe to let it be made for you as you would
probably be cheated out of a great deal of Tea & Sugar by the
Servants how ever honest the people themselves might be
he said he always kept his Tea & sugar Under lock & key
the people Boiled his tea in a kettle for him and bought his
rolls, or crumpets & butter, for him and he made his own
Breakfast in the morning and Tea at Night. I told
him I would write you how he managed his money
and I must now bid you Adieu Nancy Betty & Joe &
Cardines all beg to be kindly remember to you a remain
as ever
Your affectionate
brother E A More

Charlestown Jan 18th 1812.
Dear Brother,
Capt Holmes was detained a
week longer than he at first expected, and as he
went by the way of Liverpool, we troubled him only
with a single letter; the rest we send by the Plato
Richard says we shall garden you with reading
letters, but notwithstanding his remonstrance Papa
insists upon my writing you this second, although I
am obliged to do it in the parlour surrounded by
prates, and harassed by messages flying in all
directions.= Under these circumstances you can expect
nothing but apologies -- and the the have I am
sitting in the parlour in the arm chair, on
the right of the fireplace and as I hold my paper in
my hand, with my feet stretched out before the fire,
and with my body reclining in an oblique position
against the back of the chair, I am penning you a
letter, such as it is, and for the inverted portion of the
letter I beg to apologize.
As I turn my eyes upward, I perceive
I behold the family picture painted by an ingenious artist
who I understand is at present residing in London. If you
are acquainted with him, give my love to him, and my
best wishes for his prosperity, and success in the art to
which if report says true he has devoted himself with much
diligence.
Richard sits before me, writing to you, and Mama
says (for I have just asked her the question) that she is engaged
in the same business- Papa is up stairs, very nicely
engaged in the self same employment. Your hands
are now at this instant uniting to produce give
you at some future moment the pleasure of perusing the
present products of their present labor. Your imaginations
are now employed in conceiving of a son or a brother in
a distant land - Therefore we may draw the conclusion
that you are not universally forgotten, and consequently
all do not forget you.
I have written you this long letter because
I knew that you would be anxious for the infor-
mation it contains, because Papa told me I must
write, because Mama said I had better write,
because I had nothing else to do, and because
I hadn't time to write a shorter. I trust for these
special reasons you will excuse me for this one,

out I expect in April. The Vol. which treats of America, I shall revise after it is out, I send it to
you to have reprinted in Eng. for your benefit. Probably you may secure the copy right
in your name. More on this subject by the Galen. In the mean time you can enquire of
the proper persons what can be legally done in such a case. You can make a conditional contract
with some honest & responsible individual. This new arrangement will be certain enough to interest the British public.
Much is said about dear old Great Britain but I have no belief that the Govt. is
in earnest in the business, notwithstanding all that is said in Congress that looks that
way. Our legislature, as you will see by the Govt. speech, & the doings of the legislature
are prepared to go great lengths. They have inserted an entering wedge in regard to the
College (by calling on the Corporation for a statement of the College funds) what will be their
future course, cannot be foreseen. They keep their plans to themselves.
The Bodman has put to press a collection of papers which contain the whole history of
his difficulties. I will send you a copy of the Galen. It will be an interesting pamphlet of
about 100 pages &c. The features of the opposition
are marked with a malignancy, & wickedness
altogether unparalleled in this country. To
find balance are the attacks on the characters of those
at the seat by their opposers, that I know not but
it will be necessary for us all to vindicate
ourselves by publishing the truth.
Things remain in this town pretty much
after the old sort. The talk made for a time
some noise in consequence of the violent opposition
made to it by some individuals. And
within a few days I learn that a petition is
in circulation, to be presented to the Legislature,
to let aside the act incorporating this Parish.
I have very little anxiety about the issue,
it will be what it may. Every thing appears to
be in an unsettled & in calculable state.
Our children are our greatest earthly comfort.
Your affectionate concern for our happiness has returned
for ours in regard to you, yielded us much
consolation under all our disappointments. Truly
what are not a few -- Your letters have afforded
us much satisfaction -- continue to write us -- We
cease not daily to remember you in our prayers. For
if not my son, to remember your parents, brothers in
spirit, be virtuous & be happy.

enquire after you affectionately. I wish to be remembered

My Dear Parents,
It is an opportunity to write to you a few moments for the purpose; I wish I had been able to write you a longer and more particular letter, which I intend doing soon, for I can scarcely find leisure at present to eat my meals; I feel every day an increased enthusiasm, and encourage you that I had received your leave by the Baltimore and Liverpool packet, and have also sent you letter No. 12, by the Miss Lynders, Gen. Lemans daughters who embarked for Philadelphia in a few days in the ship Aurora Maria.
I delivered your parcels to Mr. Burder, he is a very friendly good man, who receives me very kindly; -- Mr. Duncan Smith likewise, Mr. Evarts's clasmate, is very attentive to me, and desires remembrance to Mr. Evarts. On Tuesday last I dined at Mr. Wests, who requested to be particularly remembered to you he is extremely attentive and polite to me; I have just purchased a sketch of his face from it and send it to you; when I return home I shall bring it with me as I consider it very valuable -- Mr. Hurd and Mr. Parkman are still here, they are often in and out at my lodgings and are well. -- I have changed my lodging to No. 82 in the same street, and have room with Mr. Leslie of Philadelphia who has just arrived, he is very promising, and a very agreeable gentleman, we are in the same stage of advancement in the art. I have painted 5 pieces since I have been here, 2 landscapes and 3 portraits, one of myself, one a copy from Mr. Wests copy from Van Dyke, and the other a portrait of Mr. Leslie, who is also taking mines. I find a short time since at Dr. Lettsom's who requests his remembrance to you. I delivered my letter to Mr. Vaughan who is a very hospitable
I shall write my brother shortly.

so that by comparing with the other I can give you a better idea of the art by

since William the conqueror, also the crown which the

also the golden sceptres, of king, and queen, the gold eagle
which holds the consecrated oil and the spoon of gold into

ourry, the kings of England with each his suit of armour

I gave you a hint in letter No. 12 and a particular

this city, it has been pretty well ascertained from a variety

have been very frequent of late in all parts of the city;
and even so near me as within two doors of me in the
same street; but do not be alarmed; you have nothing

same room, and sleep armed with a pair of pistols and

these alarms are less frequent, and the police is strength=
ened and more vigilant, so that you must consider
the danger as over.— The Prince Regent will have
his restrictions removed before this reaches you, on the
18 of this month, when we expect there will be an alter=
ation in favor of America.— In my next I shall give
you some account of politics here and as it respects America
the federalists are certainly wrong in very many things.— Be assured
again that I am in good health and spirits and more than ever enthusiastic
about France's book's &c.
I have yours affectionately Samt. H. T. Mosel.

My dear Son, I am informed that a rebel U.S. sail for Ireland on Tuesday
offered to take charge of a letter to put on board for you. (Hope the boys Mr K. has a fine for a few days old. Your
remembrance of them by name was grateful as it was to them named) Your Mama wrote you a long letter two days ago, to go by the Missouri for Liverpool, to sail also on Saturday. We improve both opportunities, as we know it will gratify you to hear often from us and we once you thin attention, in return for yours to us we have received all your letters, mentioned by you except the one by the West-ship written at sea we did not notice in any of the papers, that you were spoken with at sea. Mrs in her last letters to her friends speaks of you in favorable terms, which gave us great pleasure. We are, as you know deeply concerned in every thing that concerns you - I am made very happy when we hear well of you - All our sons are giving us much comfort & pleasure by their good behaviour. We regret the failure of Mr H in London, his efforts here on the other branches of the house, while I desire to give them with suitable feelings, the hand of Providence in this event. Persecutions still continue of the old kind as bitter as ever - The Lord however greatly prosper the benevolent plans of the present, for bevailing
pursuing which, with success, the preceding spirit has
been exerted. — The late Act (1810) changing the
Board of Assessors has been repealed within a
few days. That Board is now as it has been since
the Adoption of our Constitution. — The Common-
wealth has been strangely Districted for the choice
of Senators & Members of Congress, to answer po-
litical purposes. — The burghers has probably been
overdone — The candidates for Gov. & Lt. Gov.
are Gov. Strong, & Dr. Phillips (very popular nomination,
likely succeed) — Gov. Gerry (from Wm. King, an
other side) & Gen. Tracy having declined.
Congress are doing strange things also, what they
will open the eyes of the people, to effect a change in
the Administration I have never for a moment
believed we should declare war agt. Great Britain
The people, I believe, are generally agt. all po-
litical parties. The restrictive system, I hope
is nearly at an end but we are in an incalcula-
ble state — Earthquakes have been felt
in many places very severe & alarming in various
parts of our country viz. Connecticut river, particu-
larly on the Mississipp river in some of the
Southern States — a volcano, it was lately S.C. had
burst out in one the western counties of S.C. Carolina
& changed the course of Broad river — This is doubtless
however — It is, on many parts, a wonderful period in
all we live in & I have often thought of late that
you had chosen a profession remarkably suited to the
present times, to preserve you from party feeling,
I am engaging in the contest, that are deluding
the world in misery & blood -- If my dear son, you
will unite with your profession, the choice of the
one thing helpful the poor part, which shall never
be taken away from you, you will fulfill the most
desires of your parents. That your fortune
may prosper this good by portion, is their daily prayer.
