My Dear Parents,
I have the pleasure to inform you that I
have just received your good letters by the ship Pluto
for which I thank you; I must relate a circumstance
however, with respect to my getting them; Mr Brownfield wrote
to me and said there was a parcel for me, in the Post Office
which he supposed contained newspapers only from home, and
that the charge of Postage was 2s 5d or 10 dollars, wishing
to know if I would take them at that enormous charge
or let them remain in the post office; I immediately
waited on him to see about it, and told him there were
several letters in it, wishing to know what I could do; he
told me he would go with me to the post office and see
what could be done; I then went with him, and stated the
case to them, telling them, I was willing to pay the postage
of all letters contained in it, and told them they might open
it, which they did, but, as good luck would have it, they
found a corner of the letters which were in the newspapers, they
told me as there were no letters I might have it by paying
15 shillings, I was going to decline, when by accident I discovered
a corner of the letters, and wrapping it up, lest they
should make another search, I paid them the 15 shillings and
took it, although that was a great sum for postage being about
a dollar a piece for each letter; I hope you will not blame
me for paying this neither than let them stay in the office, when
you consider the case, that I do not very often hear from home
and how great the temptation was, knowing that there were
several letters directly from home, and that if I paid 15 shillings
I could take them and not without, but I will not palliate,
I know you won't blame me, they were letters from home.
But to remedy this in future, you will find it the
least expensive to put the letters separate into the letter box,
the postage then is only 1 penny each letter, and perhaps you
will not expect me to pay postage on letters which are
not intended for me.
With all my love to your family
Ever affy

bull, but I should wish not to have any more letters of introduction to any body else, I have not yet delivered those which
I have received. I find they only retard my progress, for were I
to pay the due attention to every one I have had letters to,
all my time from morning till night would be taken up in preserving the acquaintance, I begin to wish I had
brought but one or two; I think letters of introduction are less necessary to a young artist than
to any other class of people, for his attention to his art ought never
to be diverted; now a young man studying divinity or physics
or any thing else can bear to have his mind diverted, and it
would seem necessary, but it appears to me it is not necessary for an artist, he can find amusement enough and dancing
too, in his art, for my own part I feel sometimes, that I should like to live entirely abstracted from society, and devote myself solely to painting, but that I know it is impracticable. If I should wish for letters of introduction to any
particular person, or to any particular place, I will write you
for them.
I am glad to hear the Geography is going on so well, I
am afraid, I shall make but a poor bargainer, but I will

By this time, you have probably received notice of

I am afraid my expenses will exceed my allowance for
the first year, but the next will make them even again, if
I exceed it, it will be but by a few pounds; Mr Bromfield
said he expected it would be so, on account of my necessary
expenses in establishing myself; I shall use all my inducement
to economize as much as possible, and reduce my expenses
to as narrow a compass as possible.
We make our own tea and coffee just as Mr Codman
used to do. I mentioned to you in a former letter that I have
removed my lodgings to No 82. in the same street where I am
much better situated with a young american artist from
Philadelphia by the name of Leslie, you heard me mention him
when I was at home, he is the young man who gained so much
reputation in Philadelphia by taking the likeness of Cook in his
celebrated characters, he is a very agreeable industrious, steady,
young fellow, and our best together makes my absence from home
very agreeable; Mr Parkman returns in a few days to America and
will tell you all about us, he was quite socialable, and intimate intimate
with us, I like him very much.
I have delayed this letter until I should have seen Mr Taylor on Papa's business, I drank tea with him last evening; Mr Bruder was there; after tea we looked into your account which I give you at full length, you can perhaps understand it, though I confess that my mind has been so habitually employed in works of fancy and imagination, that I found myself perfectly stupid, the moment I thought of the plain, dry matter of fact, book accounts, and I was perfectly lost in the business, and
understood it about as well as I did Chinese, this is the account however, which I copied from his books;

My Dear Friends,
I have long been waiting in anxious expectation
for an answer to some of my letters, this is the fourth I
have written to Miss Dannette and an one to Miss Mary Isaac, the two last with one other to
you went by the ship Louisa for NewYork in Octr. last, we
have heard of her arrival at this port, I hope you have received
some of them, I wrote one by the Lydia the ship in which
she has been to NewYork, and has arrived again at Liverpool
but I have received no intelligence since I have been here from
NewYork altho' I have no less than 6 correspondents and some
too my clafmatip and have written them all once and
some twice -- but I will not complain, I never can suppose I am forgotten; the distance is great and there are thousands of accidents to which a letter is liable in passing such a
distance; my letters have probably miscarried or are delayed on the way, I am still on the expectation I am
not so particular as some who never write a second letter till their first is answered; so I will improve an opportunity that offers for the purpose, and write my fourth
letter.
I have been employed for my own part in pursuing my
studies, in my art, for which I feel greater enthusiasm than
ever; the fine collections of the nobility open always to artists,
the conversation of men of the highest rank in the art, and
especially the advice and hints of Mr. West, all conspire to keep that enthusiasm alive, and, I am as happy as
any one can be who is absent from his native country and
friendship. I dined with Mr. West last Tuesday with a
number of artists, Mr. West is now in his 6th year, from his appearance you would not suppose him to be
less than 50 years of age, his white locks give a venerable appearance, he has a countenance full of dignity and
his manners are polished, and the moment I am in his
company, he is a very mild affectionate domestic in his attentions and affection for Mrs West who is in her dotage
still remains as ardent as ever, he has declined many invitations I foregone many pleasant engagements for the purpose of affording comfort, by his company, to his wife
I called on Sir William Beechey yesterday, he is considered the best
Colorist now living, he is also remarkable for his liberality to
artists; a circumstance in his life is peculiarly encouraging to
the young painter, he labored no less than seventeen years before he produced any thing of merit

As to your brothers, I trust, with your edu-

My dear Son
Three days ago we received your acceptable
letter of the 30th June 7, your 14th. The two preceding ones by
Miss Lyman's, 2 Novr 13, we have not yet received. You do well
to number your letters, I to write often as we feel a
deep interest in every thing which concerns you, as well
as our other children. We have not numbered our
letters to you but shall in future -- we suppose we have
written you about as many as you have written
us -- We are pleased to find that your ardor for your
profession continues. A line from Mr Alston's brother
as to your proficiency would be very grateful to us.
We hope the change in your lodgment, & your connection
your self with Mr Leslie, will be for your advantage
but at this distance we cannot judge for you -- I trust you
confer with Mr & Mrs Alston, Mr Bromfield, & Mr Smith, in all your important
movements, & especially in the choice of your companions,
which is of infinite moment to you -- We are unacquainted with Mr Leslie, but presume
he will be helpful to you, not only in your professional pursuits, but in all virtuous counsels.
I in every thing which will tend to promote your best interests, your eternal welfare. We feel, my dear son,
be assured a very deep & tender concern for you
continually in regard to these things -- By regarding
our wishes in these things you will give us the most
comfort in neglecting them your will help to bring down
our body hardy in the honor of the brave.
We observe that you do not mention Mrs. Astor in your last letter. You will take care always to
mention them particularly in future that I may inform their friends, who ask after them. Request him to write
me, I remember us particularly to them and to all others who ask after us, especially to Mrs. West. Dr. Lettsome. I hope
before this you will have delivered all your letters. You do not have delayed them so long as the gentlemen
think themselves neglected. You do not mention having received Mr. Van Hope's last fall
draft on him. It is mentioned in your letter by Miss Hyman's. I know not when I shall be able to send you more,
as we every day expect an embargo, I expect, war with Great Britain but I hope the elections of this day, will
convince our distracted government, of the inexpediency of folly of such a measure. The state of this
country was never more critical. The result of today's elections will produce almost important effect but

My dear Parents,
I have this moment received your letters of 25th
and 28th of September, have afforded me very great pleasure
I have heard nothing from you for a month, or part of it
I am afraid my letters in future will not be so interesting in
any particular, as my former ones, my studies occupy so much
of my time now that I shall not be able to give you in
them descriptions of what I have seen in this strange country,
as I could wish, I don't know but I must defer them till
I shall see you again; whenever I can however I will narrate
some things which occur that are novel, and that I
think will amuse you, but in general they will look in form
to the state of my health and the advancement of
my studies, the I know will interest you; I am at present
in perfect health and spirits, and Milpster says I am
making great improvements, my whole attention is fixed
to my studies, and my friends and acquaintances
think I am industrious and some too industrious, but
as long as I find my health improving I shall not think
the latter the climate agree with me extremely well
I am more fleshy than I ever was, I have gained twenty
seven pounds of flesh, which is something I mentioned
in my last letter that I should probably exceed my allowance
this year by a few pounds, but I now begin to think
that I shall not I am trying every method to be economical
and hope it will not be too long before I shall relieve
you from further expense on my account, be assured
as soon as I am able I shall endeavour to do it if I
can at all calculate, I think I shall be able to do with
another year's support at first I sent you in letter no. 15 or 16.
96683 I hope you will receive before this I should like a little of that kind of business
as possible, but am willing if required to do away things for
papa that is in my power, as I am under obligations to you
wh I shall never be able to repay; as for transacting business
for other reasons I hope they will excuse me as it is so perfectly
inconsistent with my profession; I hope you will not impede
from this an unwillingness to do any thing which you request,
I will even do it cheerfully but my art requires such constant
and undivided attention that it would be a great drawback
on my progress were I to do the same for others; excuse
me mentioning this I am sorry to find by your letters
that there has been such serious disturbances at Yale, and
that young Cooper was concerned in them, I was acquainted
with him slightly, and was pleased with him on account of
his gentlemanly manners, and hope he will retain his character
With respect to politics they appear gloomy on both sides;
since I have been here I have a more favorable opinion of the
measures of our government than I had in America, this country
has injured us more than the federal papers wish to believe, the orders in
council are in full operation, and the commerce of departments
of the papers are filled with names of American vessels
detained or captured under those orders, while licenses
are granted every day to carry on that trade direct from
this country to France, for which our vessels are seized
and occasions a great outcry against the ministry, you
may depend on it England has injured us sorely, and our
relations with you will believe what is said in some of the Federal
papers that that measure has no effect on this country,
you may be assured the effects are great and severe, I am myself an eye
witness of the effects, the country is in a state of rebellion, from literal starvation, accounts are
daily received which grow more and more alarming from
the great manufacturing towns, troops are in motion all
over the country, and but last week measures were adopt-
ed by parliament to prevent this metropolis from rising
to rebellion by ordering troops to be stationed round the
city to be ready at a moments warning; this I call
an alarming period, every body thinks so and Mr. Perceval
himself is frightened and a committee is appointed to take
into consideration the orders in council; now when you consider
that I came to this country prejudiced against our
government and its measures, and that I can have no
motive in telling you these facts, you will not think hard
of me, when I say that I hope our non intercourse law
will be enforced with all its rigour, as I firmly believe it
is the only way to bring this country to terms, and that if
persisted in will certainly bring them to terms; I know it
must make some misery at home, but it will be followed by
a corresponding happiness after it. Some of you at home
I suppose will call me a democrat, but facts are stubborn
things and I cannot deny the truth of what I see every day before
my eyes; a man to judge properly of his country must,
like judging of a picture, view it at a distance.
In the papers you will probably see before this reaches you
the declaration of the Prince Regent, in all he promises
the repeal of the Orders in Council as soon as Brian ofte shall
repeal the Berlin and Milan decrees expressly and unconditionally
recollect the word unconditionally, those decrees in this way will
never be repealed, so that it is but an artifice with the prince to
gain popularity, with he very much wants. — But these things
you will see discussed at full in America, so I will not
waste any more time or paper in writing what is not very
interesting to me, the subject of politics. — This letter I think
will go by the ship Sally Ann which is advertised to sail tomorrow.
So I must close. Love to all friends and relations, always particularly
to those who are particularly interested in former letters. Adieu.
and Mr Allison are well and send respects.

My Dear Son
We received your good letter, dated March 11
last Tuesday, on our return from Andover where we had
been to Attend the funeral of good old Egbert Samuel
Abbot. - the good man is gone we trust to inherit the
promises in the kingdom of his Heavenly Father he has
left a very handsome property (after a Number of
legacies) to the Theological Institution in a very
indicious manner and with a determination to have it
do a great deal of good. - Next week we expect
Edward's home from M'Havan as the vacation will commence
next Wednesday Richard chooses to stay till the
Senior Class is finished in July and then come home Ed.
has been making out an Index to the first volume
of the Geography it has cost him a great deal of labour
& patient Industry which you know he is capable
of but I fear it will injure his health & Spirits to apply
himself so closely he writes for Dr Dwight five hours
every day which is enough with reviewing his Studies
Richard will probably take his place next fall as the
Amannenship. they are well as we learn from them by
letter last week. - We are much pleased to find by your
letter that your enthusiasm for Painting continues and
Charles town May 3, 1812
increased as this is your own choice I hope you will have
no pains (consistent with your health and eyesight) to exert
in it, we are much pleased to find that this is your resolution
- Mr Shankaran has not yet arrived but is expected
hourly this letter Mr Williams (Whom we mentioned to
you before and who has a Brother in London a Merchant
has kindly offered to send to you by the London packet from
Philadelphia & Norfolk.
and your Papa intends to get a Bill for you if he
possibly can he is much put to it to get money to purchase
one at this time as he has not received any from Quarters
where he had confidently expected it and the P&P case
remains undecided yet which is a source of a great
deal of trouble & embarrassment to us, and when it will
be settled is impossible for us to say - I hope you will be
able after this year to paint so well as to be able to continue
for some handsome prize so as to be some relief to us but
all in good time. - I wish you would give us some account
of the manner you spend your Sabbaths, who you hear preach
and how you are pleased & improved by the Discourses of
Morgan, you hear believe me my dear Son religion is of the
first importance to creatures born for Immortality learn
my Child to be wise for eternity and claim the God of
your Fathers for your everlasting Inheritance -
I have just returned from our Even'd Sat'd Lecture with a bad
head ail, & have a few minutes only to add to your to your Memphis letter. We & your friends have great pleasure from your letters,
& hope you will persevere in the course on which you have
entered with apparent good success.
I am happy to hear that my last visit to Mr Taylor has at
length been brought to a settlement. I have not had time yet to
examine & compare it with my own, but think it is probably
correct. There is property sent me by Mr Taylor to a considerable
amount which remains uncollected in the greater part of which
the principal works have been forwarded regularly. Give my regards to Mr Taylor, inform him that I will
write him soon in answer to his letter, that I shall be glad to
receive the Panorama beginning with April 1808 (to which
time I have red them) on the terms he mentions, I will send
him the Panoptist regularly, & other publications to the time
of the Panorama. Would not Mr Taylor republish the
Georgian Epic? If you may confer with him on the subject.
Mr Smith is apt to make it inconveniently frequent to call in at
Mr Taylor's as he appears quite disposed to be friendly
to him. I request him to send me the continuation of Milton's
immediately after its publication. Many other valuable works
that it is to reprint here. A little attention to these things
will not too much divert your attention from your proposed
journeys, without greatly oblige me, I contribute to enable me
to transport you with in the present state of our affairs in
subject to as little inconvenience as I submit to
knowing your advantages are disposed to be found in your
expensurables.
You did right to take the package from the
post office. It was given to Capt Holmes in this town in the full
expectation that he would deliver it himself, or send it to the post office. I shall take a notice of the face of the
letter and send it here. He is a favorite writer with her and she has a great
desire to see the title of his countenance. I am confident I shall find it in a gentleman
with a tract about my business, his age & character.
You will be able always to find the latest Boston papers
at the American Coffee House, where it will be well for
you occasionally to call for the purpose of learning the
political state of your native country. There is a part
part of a change of our federal administration, at the
next General election New York has elected a federal
legislature. The house of Representatives in this state will
probably be federal, with the Senate in the democratic.
The season is very backward indeed. On Monday
last snow fell 12 or 15 inches deep with made good sleighs
in N. Hampshire. The Govt is completed, all but
the ministers, & Appendix. It is a great burden off my
mind. Matters move precipitously in regard to the
Parish. Theological Seminary, Mr. McCombman has

London. May 12th 1812.
My Dear Friends
I write in great haste, just to inform you of a dreadful event which happened last evening, and
rumours of which will probably reach you before this; not to keep you in suspense, it is no less than
the assassination of Mr. Perceval, the prime minister of Great Britain; as he was entering the House of Commons last evening a little past 5 o'clock, he was shot
directly through the heart, by a man from behind the door, he staggered forward and fell, and expired in about
10 minutes; this mention of this shocking affair is but to remove any doubts you might have of the fact; I heard
of it last evening, about 3 hours after it was perpetrated in the morning papers, and my own eyes, confirmed it; I have just returned from the house of Commons, there
was an immense crowd assembled, and very violent; in the hall was written in large letters, "Peace, or the head
of the Regent," this country is in a very alarming state, and there is no doubt but great quantities of blood will be spilled
before it is restored to order; even while I am writing a party of Life Guards are patrolling the streets, London must
soon be the scene of dreadful events; last night I had an opportunity of studying the public mind; it was at the
theatre, the play was Venice preserved or the plot discovered; if you will take the trouble just to read the 1st Act, you will see
what relation it has to the present state of affairs, when Pierre says to Jaffier, "Can'tst thou kill a Senator; there were three cheers
and so thro' the whole, whenever any thing was said concerning
conspiracy and in favor of it, the audience applauded, and
when anything was said against it they hissed; when Pierre asked
the conspirators if Brutus was not a good man, the audience
were in a great uproar, applauding, so as to prevent for some
minutes the progress of the performance; this I think shows
the public mind to be in great agitation; the Play of Venice
preserved is not a moral play, and I should not ask you to
read any part of it, if I could better explain to you the feeling
of the public: you must not feel anxious respecting me, I
can take care of myself, for tho' London will probably be
the scene of much bloodshed, I hope I shall have prudence
enough to keep clear from danger, if I follow my pursuits with
out meddling with the affairs of others, I shall remain un-
molested, so don't feel anxious.
This is written in haste, the papers will give you
more particulars.
Yours Ever
Perry

My dear Brothers
I have just a moment's leisure to write you
a few words in answer to your letter some time since,
I should have written you before, but my time would
not permit me, and now can write but short if
I had time I would willingly devote a great deal of
it in writing you and the rest of the family, and relate
all that would be interesting to you. It is
not for want of matter, or inclination, that I
have not written you before, but really for want
of time, I am going to write Papa to-morrow and
shall tell him minutely how I employ my time
so you will easily see the reasons of my little life.
I shall have the more to tell you when I come
home, and indeed what I have already observed
in this strange country would employ me many
months to narrate, whenever I have leisure I shall
tell you something or other.
At present I shall give you the particulars of
an affair which employs the months and ears of every
one in this country, it is the assassination of Mr. Per
ceval the prime minister of Great Britain on Monday
last, the 11th as he was entering the house of Commons he
was shot directly thro' the heart by a man of the name of
Bellingham, he was removed into a room adjoining &
died in a few minutes, his death, has caused great
perturbation, and in the towns where they are the most
victious such as Nottingham and Manchester there were
rejoicings on the occasion; the assassin Bellingham
was immediately taken into custody, he was tried, on
Friday, and condemned to be executed to-morrow morning
(Monday 18th) I shall go to the place to see the concourse of
people, for to see him executed, I know I could not bear;
but the crowd will be immense and you must expect
to hear of many lives lost, I should not be surprised
if an attempt was made to rescue him, the people are
very violent, and this country is in a very troubled state,
I will leave a place at the end of this to finish tomorrow
after his execution, and will then tell you what happens
at it; At the time Mr. Percival was shot I was at
concert in Hanover Square having had a ticket presented to
me, by a friend; I did not hear of it till after the concert
and could scarcely believe it, till the next morning I went
to the House of Commons and saw for myself there was
an immense concourse of people, who were very noisy, some
rejoicing and some crying out, Burdette forever!.
But enough of this; you will probably hear the
whole account before this reaches you; I am wholly absorbed
in the studies of my profession, it is a slow, and arduous
undertaking, I never knew till now the difficulties of the
art, and no one can duly appreciate it, unless he has
tried it, difficulties however, only increase my ardor, to
make me more determined than ever to conquer them.
Mr. West is very kind to me I visit him occasionally
of a morning to hear him converse on the art, he appears quite
attached to me, as he is indeed to all young American artists, it
seems to give him the greatest pleasure to think, that one day the arts will
flourish in America, he says that Philadelphia will
be the Athens of the world, that city certainly gives the
greatest encouragement of any place in the United States,
Boston is most backward, so if ever I should return
to America, Phila or New York would probably be my
place of abode.
I have just seen Mr Stephen Van Rensselaer, who
you know was at College with us, and with whom I was
intimate, he has been at Edinburgh, he was very glad
to see me, he calls on me every day while I am painting,
he keeps his carriage and horses and is in the first cir-
cles here. I ride out occasionally with him, I shall begin
his portrait next week, if you could contrive to let Mr
Ralph Ingersoll know the circumstance of his being here in
London it would gratify him; Van Rensselaer speaks highly
of Ingersoll, and desired if I wrote to any one near him to re-
quest his remembrance and love to him, and other friends he
to France he told me in a few weeks.
When you write you must tell me every thing
acting college and every thing which you think I
hope I may see you here before I return home.
Little Zerah Colburn has just arrived here I have
not seen him yet, but shall call at the New England
Coffee house to see him, soon.
Remember me to all my old acquaintances in
New Haven, and all who inquire after me; especially
to the young ladies if you are a gallant among them,
Mrs. Leffingwells, Ingersoll, Woolsey and the rest
I received a letter from my classmate Robeler a few
days ago, and am now answering it; if he is in New Haven
remember me to him. My respects to Dr. & Mrs. Dwight
to Professor Silliman and the rest of the faculty.

(with you know is to prepare all my colors, and about nine
o'clock I am prepared to begin I am painting portraits alone
at present, our sitters are among our acquaintance, we
paint them if they depray the experience of canvas and colors,
the improvement is the only profit we can expect
for some time) our sitters come at nine and stay an hour
or two each; since the days have become so long, we dine at 2.
o'clock; after dinner, paint till dark what is not till 9 o'clock,
in the evening draw from plaster casts of hands and feet, or call
on some friends, Mr. Allston, &c. or else see company at home.
This is the general method of employing our time, on Tuesdays,
and Thursdays we draw at the British Museum from 10 to all 5
o'clock: we got admission there thro' the influence of Mr. West.
The Museum contains a superb collection of antiques, and
other things very useful and necessary to be studied by artists.
Mama wished me to send some specimens of my painting, hoping
that you might see my improvement; the pictures that I now
paint would be uninteresting to you, they consist merely of
studies, drawings from plaster figures, hands and feet &c. Such
things; the portraits, are taken by those for whom they are
painted, I shall soon begin a portrait of myself, and will
try and send that to you, it will be an experiment, I wish
to try the effect of candlelight upon flesh, and shall take
no own head for the purpose, so if it should not be such
a thing as you wish, you must excuse it as it will be an
experiment. I feel that I am improving every day, for every day
gives me a greater insight into my art, and shows me how much
study and perseverance it requires to be a painter.
You sometimes mention the American hotel; there is

the allowance for this year will carry me through

should break out, I should try and get to France, for

June 16. Tuesday
Mr. Hurd call'd on me today and said that he
should leave London on Thursday, by him I shall send
this letter and with it a parcel for you, he will inform you
all about me, I have charmed him to go and give me
a full account of me, how I look &c. &c. with I hope
he will do, he goes in the Galin, there will be a number
of Boston people who go out in her, Mr. and Mrs. Higginson
(the old folks), Mr. & Mrs. Emery, Miss Tudor, and some others;
the Americans seem to be moving off, Col. Trumbull and
his lady visit New York this week.
The administration is at length formed, and to the
great sorrow of everybody the old ministers are recalled.
The orders in Council are the subject of debate at the
House of Commons this evening, it is an important crisis,
though there is scarcely any hope of their repeal; if they are
not I sincerely hope that America will declare war.
What Lord Castlereagh said at a public meeting a few days
ago ought to be known in America, respecting the orders in Council
when some one said unless they were repealed, War with America
must be the consequence, he replied that if the people would
but support the ministry in those measures for a short time, America
would be compelled to submit for that she was
not able to go to war -- but I say, and so does every American
here, who sees how things are going with this country, that
should America but declare war before hostilities commence
Great Britain would sue for peace on any terms, Great Britain
is jealous of us, and would trample on us if she could, and
I feel ashamed, when I see her supported thro' every thing by
some of the Federal editors I wish they could be here a few
months, and they would be ashamed of themselves, they are
injuring their country, for it is their violence, that induces this
government to persist in their measures, by holding out hope that
the party will change, and that then they can compel America
to do anything, if America loses in this contest, and softens her
head again, you must not blame me for being free on this
subject, or think I have turned democrat, I came not of the sentiments
I was in America, for I have come to the knowledge of too
many truths, since I have been here, to be any longer of those
partial feelings towards this country, I am of no party, but am
an American, and feel for my country, and am mortified
fied to find so much paper, ink, & breath, thrown away
for nothing, or rather worse than nothing, in supporting the
pride of party, if you could be at this distance and see
how they appear here, you would throw off all
party feelings and be neither democrat nor federalist but
an American -- You can know more of this subject by con-
versing on it with Mr. Hurd, Mr. Emery, or any other American
who has been here and they will confirm what I have stated,
I could write more on this but I fear you will not be
pleased with it, unless you have the opportunity of knowing
so much on it as I have, who am in the centre of political
discussion. -- I write these sentiments the more freely as this letter
goes by Mr. Hurd, and of course cannot be in any danger of
being intercepted. I should not dare to write this thro' the post-
office --
I am in excellent health and spirits, and more
pleased with the profession I have chosen --
I wish I had time to write you something interesting &
new -- I could write volumes on what I have seen
in this strange country but it would employ so much of my
time, that I should neglect my studies, I shall write Edwin's
an account of some things; which as you will all see letters
that are in the family, I need not put in this letter.
I must now bid you adieu!
Remember me suitably to all friends, always, particularly
Grandma, Aunt & Uncle Salisbury, brothers Russell, Mr
Brown, Evarts, J. Bartlett's family, Nancy & in short to all to
whom you had this letter you are at liberty to make particular
mention. -- Hoping that my country will maintain her honor
in spite of party spirit; I remain yours very affectionately
Saints J. D. Moser
(Wednesday) London, June 15th 1812.
My Dear Mother
I have only a few moments to write you
up to day the galleries of the Marquis of Stafford is open
to artists, and as it is but one day in the week for two months
in the year I cannot well miss it, and Mr Hard goes on
Thursday, so I shall only tell you something that may amuse you.
The Queen held a drawing room a short time since
and I went to St. James palace to see those who attended,
it was a singular sight to see the ladies & gentlemen
in their court dresses, the gentlemen were dressed in buckram
skirted coats, without capes, long waistcoats, cocked hats
& bag wigs, swords and large buckles in their shoes, the ladies
in monstrous hoops, so that in getting into their carriages
they were obliged to go edgewise; their dresses were very
rich, some ladies I suppose had about them to adorn
them 20 or 30,000 L. worth of diamonds, I had a sight
of the prince Regent as he passed in his splendid state
carriage, drawn by six horses; he is very corpulent, his
features are good but he is very red & considerably bladed
I likewise saw the Prince, Charlotte of Wales, she is handsome,
the Dukes of Kent, Cambridge, Clarence & Cumberland,
Admiral Duckworth and many others — The Prince
held a levee a few days since at which Mr Van Rensselaer
was presented.
I went out to Epsom Races with Sam Rensselaer
in his carriage, a short time ago, rather for the ride
than to see the running, Epsom is about 9 or 10 miles from
London, I saw a great many splendid equipages
and a great deal of company, most of the neighboring no-
bility were there, there was very good racing, I was on
a hill in the centre of the course, so that I could see
nearly the whole course which was a mile and an half in length.
I occasionally attend the theatres at Covent Garden
there is the best acting in the world, Mr Kemble is
the first actor now in England, Cook was a rival, and even
calls him in some characters; Mrs Siddons is the first tragic
actress perhaps that ever lived, she is now advanced
in life and is about to retire from the stage, on the 29th
of this month she makes her last appearance, I must
say I admire her acting very much, she is rather corpulent
but has a remarkable line face, the Grecian character is fine
by Portrayed in it, she excels to admiration in deep tragedy,
in Mrs Beverly in the play of the gamblers a few nights ago, she
so arrested the attention of the house, that you might hear
your watch tick in your job, and at the close of the play
when she utters an hysterie laugh for joy that her husband
was not a murderer, there were 3 different ladies in the
boxes who actually went into hysterics, and were obliged
to be carried out of the theatre, this I think is proof of
good acting. Mrs Siddons is a woman of reproachable character
and moves in the first circles, the stage will never
again see her equal. You mustn't think because I praise
the acting, that I am partial to theatres, I think in a certain
degree they are harmful, but too much attended they
disipate the mind, there is no danger of my loving them
too much, I like to go once in a while after studying hard
all day.
Last night as I was passing thro' Tottenham Court Road, I
saw a large collection of people of the lower class making
a most terrible noise by beating on something of the sound-
ing genus, upon going nearer and inquiring the cause I
found that a butcher had just been married, and that
it is always the custom on such occasions for his the couple trade, to sevenade
with marrowbones & cleavers, perhaps you have heard of the phrase "musical as marrow-
bones and cleavers," this is the origin of it; if you wish to experience the sound, let each one in the family take a pair of
longs and a shoeel, and then standing all together, let each one try to outdo the other in noise, and this will give you some
idea of it how this custom originated I don't know; I hope it is not symbolical of the harmony which is to
exist between the parties married --
Mr. Van Rensselaer has gone to France he was the bearer of dispatches from Mr. Russell to Mr. Barclay, he went
on Friday last. I am very well acquainted with Mr. Russell our ambassador, he is a very pleasant man &
is attentive to men --
The days are very long here now, it is twilight all night long you can see to read at half past 10. and at half past 2 in the morning.
I walked to Greenwich a few days since I was at the observatory, on the spot where longitude commences, I went
thro' the hospital it is a noble building, one of Mr. West's finest pictures is there -- Excuse the incoherence of this letter
it is made up of a little of everything, write me soon a good long letter. -- Love to all. -- Good bye --
Mr. Edwards Mosse --
Sam'l J.B.Mosse --

My Dear Father,
Permit me to introduce to you Mr. Cha.
King, an American artist, who has been in this country
four or five years to improve himself in painting
with Mr. West, he has been one of my most inti-
mate friends, and has been very useful to me, when
I first came he was very attentive to me, in find-
ing me lodgings, and in seeing me comfortably
settled; he arrived in London on Saturday on
his return to America, if you can render him
any service, or show him any attention, I shall
feel very particularly obliged to you; I esteem
him very much, and it is like parting with a brother
to part with him; Mr. Allston, Mr. King, & Mr. Leslie,
were my most intimate intimate and confidential associates,
we used to see each other every day, and we became
all of the same family: Mr. King is from Newport
(R. I.) he is not in very good circumstances as to prop-
erty, and returns to America to settle with Mr. West

My Dear Son
We have received your letter by the Sally Ann and rejoice to find
that you are in so good health & spirits and growing fleshy and
that you are making such Landable progress in your profession
as that in addition to your gaining so high reputation as an Artist
you will so soon be able to relieve your parents from much
more expense on your account. not that we have the least
degree been unwilling to hear this excuse but are really unable
the proficiency you have made my dear son has confirmed us in
the wisdom of having sent you to your present place of destination
and although we long to see you yet we rejoice that you are so
happily situated at so great a distance from our at present
wretched miserably distracted country whose mad orders
are plunging us into an unnecessary War with a country that
I shall always remain as doing more to spread the glorious gospel
of Jesus Christ to the benighted Heathen and those that are
preaching for lack of knowledge, than any other nation on
the Globe – our hearts bleed at every move to think of again
being at War we have not yet forgotten the wormwood & gall
of the last revolution – We hope you will steer clear of any
of the difficulties of the contest that is about to take place –
We wish you to be very prudent and guarded in all your conversations
& actions and not to make yourself a party man on either side
have your opinions but have them to yourself and be sure you do
not commit them to paper it may do you great injury either on one side or the other and you are
not in your present situation as a politician but as an Artist
June 30th thus far my dear Son I had written three days ago expecting to
find it by the Ship that Mr. Justin the British Minister was to embark
for London in but a more direct way presenting by the way of Eastport
and Halifax I shall finish and send it in this way our Country is in
a trying situation but the Lord wissen and this is our greatest comfort
our Children are all in very great comfort to us We rejoice to think
that none of them is in a situation to be drafted as Soldiers in these
times Edwards has determined to begin the study of law as soon as he
has got through with being Amannensis for Dr. Dwight Richard
is to take Edwards place next year at Dr. Dwight's what he will
succeed as his Professor I know not they were both well when we
last heard about a week ago I have just returned from a visit to
Andover all your Friends enquired after you I read them some extracts
from your Letters which gave them much pleasure as the reading of
them has many others I must leave room in this letter for your
papa to add what he wishes I long my dear son to learn from you
that you have chosen that good part that I shall never be taken from
you this would rejoice our hearts more than anything that you can
conceive of Oh my dear very dear Son I have, early chosen the God of
your Fathers to be your God forever Use the means appointed for you
to pray, ponder, read daily the holy Scriptures attend constantly and devoutly
the preaching of good Ministers such as will teach you the purest
of your Church, give yourself to the Lord in a covenant union
to be forgotten this is your reasonable Service you are now at age
21 the 24 of last April let the life that the Lord has made in
you be devoted to his Service and to the promotion of his glory
in the world thus far from your affectionate Mother
C B M
My dear Son
The dire is cast our country plunged in War on
this subject, irritated in both of us me, I can say nothing. I doubt
will be a short war. The next election of ministers, of Resident at
representatives & Congress, will determine what are the Sentiments of the people concerning this war. There is great opposition to it in the country. The papers, with you will have opportunity to inform you of the state of parties. Your Mother has given you sound advice and respects the course you should pursue. Be the subject wholly of politics altogether. I enjoy it that you are where you are at the present time. You will do what you can without delay to support yourself, as I know not how we shall be able to procure funds to transmit to you, if we had them, how we could transmit them. The war will greatly depreciate our property. I enclose you the second exchange for $100 on Sam. Williams Esq. I sent the first about 40 days since I hope it will reach you safely. You will consequently improve every opportunity to write us as we shall give you.
It is rumored in Boston to day, that the President of the U.S. has directed Genl Dearborn to provide a vessel to carry the Yorkee to London in a few weeks if so luck would give you that vessel more particularly.
Fortune will offer frequently, I expect, from it. I go to the place, to write you I cannot now add the Parkman arrived in the Sally Ann, I gives us every good news of you -- We hear also from other quarters that you are doing well.
Resent my regards to Mrs. West, Alston, Bannister, Taylor, Bromfield, Dr. LeRome &c Your friends here are generally well, I send them love to you, Miss Rapillet

without becoming acquainted with one of my best friends,
any attentions shown him, will be considered by me as
shown to myself, & I shall be proud to show every atten-

to introduce to me while in this, or any other country.

answer them immediately. Your letter of Jan. I received

apologize for my not writing you often. You must
not be ceremonial but write whenever you feel an inclina-

very grateful to me.

Mrs. Lannette, and the rest of her amiable sisters;

My Dear Parents,
I am improving perhaps the last of opportunity
I shall have for some time to write you, Mr Wheeler an
American, who has been here some time studying portrait-painting
has kindly offered to deliver this to you. Our political affairs
it seems have come to a crisis, which I sincerely hope will
turn to the advantage of America, it certainly will not to
this country. -- War is an evil which no man ought to
think lightly of, but if it ever was just, it now is, the English acknowledge it, and what can be more convincing proof, than the
confession of an enemy. I was sorry to hear of the riotous proceedings in Boston, if they knew what an injury they were doing
their country in the opinion of foreign nations, they certainly would refrain from them; I assert (because I have proof) that
the federalists, (as they call themselves,) in the Northern States have done more injury to their country, by their violent opposition
measures, than even a French alliance could, their proceedings are copied into the English papers, read before Parliament, and
circulated thro' the country, and what do they say of them? Do they say the federalists are patriots, and are firm in asserting the rights
of their country? No, they call them traitors troubles towards, a base sett, say they are traitors and ought to be hanged like traitors, these things
I have heard and read, and therefore must believe them. I wish I could have a talk with you, Papa, I am sure I could
convince you that federalists, nor democrats were Americans,
that War with this country is just, and that the present administrations of our country have acted with perfect justice in all
their proceedings against this country; You will perhaps wonder
at my writing in this strain, and may think some persons have put
these sentiments into my head, but I assure you they have not, for it
would have been as easy for a democrat to convince a federalist
in America as for me to be charged, when I first came, I only wish
you, and all those who are federalists, would come and stay on
London a month or two, if their party enthusiasm was not at
that time a little cool'd. I would engage to forfeit my right
hand, to observe the contempt, with which America is spoken of,
the epithets, of a nation of cheats, scroungers, pusills,
imboys, cowardly, and such like, these I think are sufficient to
make any true American's blood boil, these are not used by
individuals only, but on the floor of the House of Commons.
The good effects of our declaration of war, begun to be seen
already, the tone of their public prints is a little softer and more
submissive; not one has called in question the justice of the declaration
of war, all say "we are in the wrong, and we shall do to get out of it as soon as possible;" I have had conversations with
strangers who have not known I was an American, they put on
long faces and say "we are a ruin'd nation, america has been
too lightly treated by our government, unless america will retire
after the receipt of our revocation of those foolish Orders in Court
I do not see a single hole for us." I always acquiesce. I could
tell you volumes, but I have not time and it would perhaps be in
politic in the present state of affairs. But I only wish that among the
infatuated party men I may not find my father, and I hope that I
will be neutral, rather than oppose the war measure, for, (if he will
believe a son who loves him and his country the longer & farther
(from them) this war will reestablish, that character for honour,
spirit, which our country had lost thro' the proceedings of federalists
But I will turn from this subject— My health and spirits are excellent,
and my love for my profession in every way, I am painting a small historical
piece, the subject is Marius in Prison, and the soldier sent to kill him
who drops his sword, as Marius says, "Dost thou kill Caius Marius?" the
historical fact you must be familiar with, — I am taking great pains
with it, and may possibly exhibit it, in July at the British Gallery.
Mr. Allston is painting on a large picture 10 feet by 14 with 15 or 16
figures larger than life, he will probably exhibit it in July. Mr. West
call'd to see it for the first time a few days ago; he was in rapture
before it, and upon observing a large clay head which Mr. A. had
modelled for one of his figures, he observed "there was not a sculptor
in England could do like it," and wish'd a cast of it, this, from Mr.
West who never will compliment at the expence of truth, I think
must be encouraging to Mr. Allston. I never think of my situation
in the profession of my choice, and for making so many sacrifices to
gratify me, I hope I shall always feel grateful to the best of parents
and be able soon to show them I am, in the mean time, if industry
and application on my part, can make them happy, be assured I shall
use my best endeavors to be make them comfortable. One of
my greatest blessings here is Mr. Allston, he is like a brother to me,
and not only is a most agreeable and entertaining companion, but
he has been the means of giving me more knowledge (practical,
as well as theoretical) in my art, than I could have acquired by
myself in 3 years. In whatever circumstances I am, Mr. Allston, I
shall esteem as one of my best and most intimateate friends, and in whatever I
can assist him or his, I shall feel proud in being able to do it.
Mr. Allston are well, I dine with them yesterday at Lady Fitzhugh's, whom I
have mentioned to you before as one of our passengers, he is very attentive to us, visits us
constantly and is making us presents of various things such as half a dg. best medicine etc. he
came out here with his Lady to take possession of a fortune of $20,000, and was immensely rich
before having married Miss Van Renselaer of Albany. Our friends are confined to a few

field land, can you conveniently pay them

Mama has communicated to me
the information in her letters, respecting
your new college. For your friendly
feelings & assertions, I thank you as much
as if you had been successful. Your
disappointment, I appreciate affects you
more unpleasantly than me. Am sorry
to announce Dr. Miller as your President. Elect.
As Dr. Smith, I understand, chooses not
to relinquish his station, probably he (Dr. M.)
may assist his appointment. He will be
the man for you, I think -- or Mr. President Davis, w? do well -- I know him -- I think
highly of him -- I wish all success to your
new Institutions -- Will you engage of
Genl. Platt, whether he has received his com-
mission to settle the dispute between Mr.
Sergeant & the Indians, which I sent him
some months since, & whether he accepts
his appointment? Has attended to the business?
We are all pretty well -- have heard from Finley as late as May 12th
when he was well -- Your son, from fellow --
I think, has probably gone to France with
our little navy, for no good purpose --
I wish your son were at home & fancy he wishes to too -- but so? he be spared
& return -- as I pray God, he may be, it may be what he has suffered, will
be the means of lasting good to him, & I hope & trust, he will yet be a great
comfort to you, & a blessing to his country. We can see but a little way into the
designs of Providence --
Mama is with us, & a great comfort to us -- she enjoys every good health
for her, & is in good spirits & is company for your sister in her situation deprived of the Society of her children.
The aspect of our national affairs is some-
what brightened by the news of the revoca-
tion of the Orders in Council. The voice
of the hatred of the war, weaker, louder,
louder, that in its favor, weaker, weaker.
Persistence in the war I think, will
certainly change the Administration.
At any rate, I trust it will be changed.
De Witt Clinton appears to be the most
prominent candidate for President, in
opposition to Van Madison.
We rejoice with you & sister, in their
addition to your family. May your chil-
dren be blessed of God, & constitute for
a goodly testimony.
Mama, & your sister, join me
in love to you sister, all the
branches of the family around you
Your affectionate brother
Snodgrass

My Dear Parents,
I have a few moments to write you a
line by Mr West of Salem, (Mass.) who goes to
mortgage to Liverpool to embark for NewYork; he will
tell you that I am well, — My last letter was by
a Mr Wheeler, and I expected it would be the last for
some time on account of the state of affairs; but I
am glad to have an opportunity again to write you.—
I have had no letters from you for a great while, I wish
to receive a good family letter that I may know how
you are situated.— I am pursuing my studies, and
am convinced you would find no fault with my application
I employ all my time in acquiring something that is necessary
to my improvement in my art.— I have just returned
from a little excursion on the sea coast, whether I went for
a little relaxation, and to see the country, will a view
to my profession; I first sailed down the Thames to Margate
which is on the coast and upwards of 70 miles
from London, Margate is a celebrated watering place, and
in the summer season is the resort of many hundreds
from the city of London; the common conveyance is by
a hoy or packet vessel which carries from 50 to 80 passengers
at the first scent of the sea air, many of them are seasick
and if the water is at all rough nearly all of them: on
board the hoy in which I went, there were about 50
Georgians, the air was very clear, and a strong head wind
2: prevailing they were all sick but three, I was one of the
three, and being accustomed a little to the sea, I soon found
my sea-legs, while the rest of the passengers were tumbling
about at a pitiful rate, we got into Margate after being out
26 hours which is considered a long passage.— Margate is a
gay place and it was crowded with visitors while I was there;
My companion was a Mr Earl an artist whose father was an
American, we staid in Margate two days and then proposed
an excursion to Ramsgate about 4 miles from Margate, this we
accomplished in an hour; we staid but a short time in Ramsgate,
it is another watering place, and I think a much more beauti-
ful place than Margate; its pier is one of its greatest artifi-
cial curiosities it is a quarter of a mile in length, is circular in
its form, and encloses a large basin for the reception of vessels,
from this place is seen the Downs so celebrated for its ships
anchorage; (our excursion recollect is pedestrian) we went from
Ramsgate to Sandwich along the cliffs which bound all this
shore composed of chalk, we dined at Sandwich, it is remark-
able only for its age, having been built in the time of the Ro-
mans; just before we entered Sandwich, we saw a pile of
ruins about a mile on the side of the road; and we crossed
over the fields to see it, but just as we came within a stone's
throw of it, we were stopped by a wide river which runs
by the foot of it, so, finding no possible means to come at it
we were obliged to return without gratifying our curiosity,
I have since heard that it was a famous Roman & Celtic ruin
called now Richborough castle; after dinner we pursued our
journey to Deal across a moor or heath which seemed to be
without end, we loitered along till dusk, when we came to
a most wretched sandy road, here a large stone like a grave-
stone stopped us, by which we learnt that on that spot was
committed a murder, this was not very pleasant informa-
tion to us, especially as it was growing dark, the road lay
tho' a most gloomy assembly of little sandhills, and we
were two miles from Deal; to increase our difficulty, we
lost the road, the sand became deeper, and more uneven, and
the only prospect was sand hill over sandhill, seemingly without
end, at a little distance, however, the towers & battlements of
a castle were just seen, with armed men walking to & fro on
the morning's pursuit our walk towards Dover which we reached
about 10 o'clock: the first thing that struck us after leaving Deal
was the sight of the towers of Dover Castle at a distance, we
slowly approached it, and from the mountain on which it
stands had a most delightful view of the town of Dover, &
the surrounding country, the sea, & the French coast. Dover
is situated in a deep valley between two high mountains
or cliffs of chalk, these are strongly fortified, so as to render them
impregnable, on one the castle stands, it is a
very ancient pile of the Gothic order, and is perhaps in the best
preservation of any Gothic building in the country, it occupies
a great quantity of ground, and is a little city in itself, we

4 were not permitted to go through it; I send with this a very unfin=
ished outline of it which I took upon the spot, I had but half an

I confined myself merely to the top outline which you may rely

ed Shakespeare Cliff, so called from the circumstance of

sing that sublime & poetical description of a view from a

given a very just description of it, a little embellished

distant, casting your eye round nothing catches the observation

and the cliffs seemed to correspond with those on the English
side, the only thing to be seen in Boulogne is the pillar ex=
tid
ted I believe to one of their celebrated admirals; there were on
the cliff with my two or three men who are constantly on
the look out with glasses and give notice of every thing that
passes in the channel, they lent us their glasses a few minutes,
through them we saw the houses on the shore, windmills in
motion, and men on board a French lugger, who were close
under the shore and towing an English sloop from Boulogne
to Calais, the cathedral of which latter place, we could just
discern with the glass: towards the north were seen the castle,
and the fortifications of Dover, which completed the view;
after having spent the day in looking at the different objects
worthy notice in and about Dover we retired to rest, determining
in the morning to return home to Margate, in the morning
however, I thought I could not leave Dover without paying a
mother visit to Shakespeare Cliff, this detained us till 10 o’clock
when we commenced our return, dined at Deal & spent 2
hours there, and arrived at Margate, a distance of 30 miles
a little after dark, this for experienced pedestrians, I
think is something of a fete; when we arrived at Margate
we found the hoy had just sailed so that we were under the
necessity of waiting another day, this day we employed, on a
fishing party which was very pleasant; the next day we took
our passage for London, where we arrived safe after a passage
of 30 hours, if I had picked the most pleasant days out of
the season I could not have pitched upon any more delightful,
the days were all clear, and not a drop of rain during
the whole time, a thing very remarkable and uncommon
in this country; our absence occupied the space of 8 days
6 Thus I have given you a slight account of my excursion, hoping there may be something in it which may give you pleasure. I have just finished a model in clay of a figure (the dying Hercules) my first attempt at sculpture; Mr. Alison is extremely pleased with it, he says it is better than all the things I have done since I have been in England, put together, and says I must send a cast of it home to you, & that it will convince you that I should make a painter; he says also he shall write to his friends in Boston, to call on you & see it when I send it. Mr. West also was extremely delighted with it, he said it was not merely an academic figure, but displayed mind, and thought; he could not have made me a higher compliment. Mr. West would write you, but he has been disabled from painting, or writing for a long time, with the gout in his right hand, this is a great trial to him. I am anxious to send you something to show you that I have not been idle since I have been here. My passion for my art is so firmly rooted that I am confident no human power could destroy it, the more I study it, the greater I think is its claim to the appellation of divine; and I never shall be able sufficiently to show my gratitude to my parents for their indulgence in so greatly enabling me to pursue that profession without which I am sure I should be miserable; and if ever it is my destiny to become great, & worthy of a biographical memoir, my biographer will never be able to charge upon my parents that bigoted
attachment to any individual profession, the exercise of which
spirit by parents towards their children has been the
ruin of some of the greatest geniuses, and the biography of
men of genius has too often contained that reflection on
their parents— if every the contrary spirit was evi-
dent, it has certainly been shown by my parents towards one,
indeed, they have been almost too indulgent, they have watched
every change of my capricious inclinations, and seem to have
made it an object to study with the greatest fondness; but I
think they will say that when my desire for change
did cease, it always settled on painting; I hope that one
day my success in my profession will reward you in some
measure for the trouble & inconvenience I have so long put
you to.—
I am now going to begin a picture of the death
of Hercules from this figure, as large as life; the figure
I shall send to you as soon as it is practicable; and also
one of the same to the Phila Exhibition, if possible in season
for the next in May.— I have enjoyed excellent health
and spirits and am perfectly contented; The War between
the two countries has not been productive of any measures
against resident American citizens; My love to my brothers
& grandmama, Aunt & Uncle Salisbury, Nancy, and family—
to Miss Russell, Mr. Brown, Evarts, Dr. Bartlett, & all
to whom in former letters I have desired remembrance in
regular remembrance you.— Mr. Brown's field has rec'd 25L. on Soc. in Scot. from you.
I remain your very affectionate Son
P.B.Morrison
