My Dear Parents
Mr. Plummer of Boston has just called on me
and informs me he is going home in a day or two, by land I
send this in answer to U. wh I have bee from you lately
the last was of Oct. 2d via Halifax accompanying your sermon
on fast day, the letter gave me great pleasure, but I must confess
that the sentiments in the sermon appeared very strange
to me, knowing what I as well as every American here does,
respecting the causes of the present war; I am sorry that federalists
make so much opposition to it, when every one here, Englishmen
as well as Americans not only know that the war is just
on their part, but confess it, the only persons in the world who
assert the contrary, are the federal party in America; a proof
of this is that no English publication, to my knowledge, has dared
to justify the government, or accuse ours of injustice in
declaring war, on the contrary, they throw all the blame on
the administration here, and say the Americans could not
in justice, or honor have done otherwise; what can be a
clearer proof than the acknowledgement of an enemy as to
this fact? I do not merely assert this, every American here
knows it. The Federalists universally as a party I believe mean
well towards their country, and if they knew facts, would certainly
join heart and hand in this war; they are too much
blinded by the real of party spirit, and too much led away by
wiful misstatements, in violent part papers to act cool
and weigh matters before they decide, I say this
government has not injured us, when the Orders in Council
were such a flagrant proof of it, by virtue of which they
2. barred us from trade with France and her dependencies, under
pretence that we supplied them with articles of war, while they
granted by means of licences, that same trade with France
to their own merchantmen, and only that but cloth was made
here for the express purpose of exporting to France, for the clothing
of French soldiers; this is a fact brought before Parliament, so it
cannot be denied in this circumstance alone is a sufficient
cause for war, or we cease to be an independent nation
A great noise appears to be made in America
respecting an apprehended alliance with France; it is
a bug bear conjured up by the federalists, and the inflammatory
pieces in the federal papers have been copied into
the English, till they almost begin to think there is a foundation
for it; I have often blushed for my countrymen on reading
some of those violent party essays & to see how men for the
sake of party will justify, or rather attempt to justify
this government this all their base and unwarrantable
proceedings; I would ask, because England is at war
with France, is it not possible to chastise England for injustice
towards us without uniting with France, must England
treat us worse than her own subjects, shall she dictate laws
to us & shall we obey, for fear of having it said by a few
selfish, interested men, that we are uniting with the great
tyrant of Europe to destroy the only remaining spot of liberty
in the old world; the object of France is to annihilate
this country, that of America to obtain redress from her, can
we not obtain redress without annihilating this country;
Great Britain would be very glad to come to our terms long before
she was in danger of annihilation
you ask in your sermon "how can a Christian pray for success
against the only Christian nation beside ourselves?" I answer,
when the administrators of this government, act as becoming
Christians towards us, and "do to others as they would be done
unto," then it will be time for a Christian to ask that ques-
tion, but while they act in direct contradiction to this
divine precept, while they do to others what they would
on no consideration suffer to be done to them; they deserve
no indulgence as a Christian nation; the few Christians
among them should not shelter them from punishment, nor
justify them in that overbearing spirit which they uniformly
manifest towards every nation with whom they deal.
The question I think might be asked with great
propriety if it was the object of our war to pull down
the Christian religion, no one will dare to say this is the
case if the majority of this country are unprincipled, and are
uninfluenced by the laws of justice in their dealings to the
nations, and by their unjust measures they provoke a country
to war, is that war levelled at the Christian religion? The
case I believe is plain -- I could write a volume in favor of this
war to show the good effects which will result from it, but I shall only relate the visible effects of which I am
an eye & ear witness. 1st It has raised our country from
the degradation which it has long laid under in the opinion of
Englishmen -- before the declaration of war, America was
spoken of with the utmost contempt, the papers teemed with
calumies & insinuations against her courage; we were call'd
cowards, sprung from a race of convicts, we were proved-
rial for a weak, inefficient, race of beings, our navy they
4 would sneer at, as (to use their own expressions) below the
Chinese, we were called savages, dishonest in our dealings,
and in short every epithet of opprobrium was exhausted
upon us; -- the moment war was declared by us, it seemed
to come like an electric shock, all was silent in the papers
for some weeks with respect to us; what! thought they, is
this the cowardly, weak, inefficient race of men, we have
so often sneered at; they began a little to recover from the
shock, some began to say, we never thought they would
have declared war. it is a sad business, we have provoked
them too far; when they hear to the proclamation, every man
read it & was dumb, or else with eyes turned up and
a deep sigh, exclaimed in a woful accent, "it is too true."
no comments have been made on it in any English paper
that I have met with or an attempt made to refute a
single charge, after a short time spent in this manner
they began to resume their taunts and most particularly
against our navy, "oh! said they we shall soon see their
frigates in our ports," well show them a little English thunder & lightening;" in the midst of these exultations came
the news of the capture of the Guerriere, if ever a shock
on the community was distinctly visible, it was in this
instance, it would have made a subject for a Hogarth
to have seen the woful faces, the day the news reach London;
Can it be true? What! Americans fight? This Chinese
navy take an English frigate? No! it cannot be true!
It was then announced officially, and since that time
what has been the tone of the English journals; why the
Americans are like ourselves, they inherit the same spirit
with Englishmen; they have acted like brave fellows," Capt.5
Hull is a brave man," has behaved like a brave enemy," nev-
er was it known in the naval annals of England that a Brit-
ish frigate ever before struck to an American," and many
such expressions as these; are not these, extorted words of
respect? Is the character of Englishmen to be haughty,
proud & one hearing, if this conduct meets with no resis-
tance, their treatment becomes more impertinent, and
the more submissive and conciliating is the object of
their impertinence, the more tyrannical are they toward
it; this has been their uniform treatment towards us,
and this character pervades all ranks of society whether
in public or private life; The only way to please John
Bull is to give him a good beating, and such is the singu-
larity of his character, that the more you beat him
the greater is his respect for you and the more he will
obey you.-- 2. Another good effect of the war I think
will be to convince ourselves that we ought to have a navy
and from every consideration I think this will now be
the case.-- we have seen that we have the courage
skill & power to combat with the boasted King of the
Ocean, and what power may we not infer we shall
have from this superiority, we can then (and not till then)
Chastise France for her insolence towards us, The Danes
The Tripolitans & Algerines, & in fact every nation, who
can know, from our want of a navy, insult us, and com-
mit depredations on our commerce, with impunity; England will
feel it her interest to be at peace with us, and will no
6. doubt be glad to conciliate us, and what may not be expected from the coalition of two Christian powers, united by the all-pities of blood, congeniality of disposition, and equal courage and skill. 3. May it not be a means of uniting the two great contending parties in America?
This is certainly a great desideratum, for until we have peace at home, we can never expect to be powerful abroad as it is in the human system, when the heart is diseased, the extremities lose their capacity to perform their offices, & become weak; so it is with the lady holistic constitution of a country, if at home they are torn & disturbed by intestine quarrels & dissensions they are incapacitated to do anything efficient abroad, and here let me observe on the newspapers of our country, the corrupt fountains of more corrupt information, to these which keep alive the coals of dissension among us, until these are reformed, until the editors of each party cease to irritate and inflame each other, by continually overreaching each other in extravagant misrepresentation, and endeavors in fact to outlie their opponents, until the sources of political information become pure, in short until there is a third party formed on the real principles of patriotism, I fear our country will long want a government of sufficient force either to demand obedience at home, or command respect abroad.
After all that I have now said you may perhaps call me a democrat and say that coming to England has changed my sentiments, if you think from what has
gone before and what is to come after that I deserve
that name, then I must be content to bear it; my ear
shall always be open to truth, and my heart to conviction;
if I see England abusing us, and the Federalists
bearing her out in it, when she dare not do it self, so far
I am not a Federalist, & when I see France injuring
us and the democrats, endeavoring to hush it up or to
justify her, or deny the charge, so far I am not a Democrat;
The fact is I am of neither party I have been in England
long enough to see that the Federalists are not in the
right, and I see democratic papers from America, which,
by their gross libels on this country and their violent
French spirit, show me they are wrong.— as for the
present war, for reasons which I have given you, I think
it a just one, and will be productive of good effects; as
for its tending to destroy this country, I do not believe it, &
I am far from wishing it, on the contrary, England may
to America, is the country for which I would pray, day
and night, might be proscribed over all other nations, she
is a country which I love with all her faults, and no
Englishman would be more sorry to see her sink before
any power on earth, for I well know that were she
to fall, not only Christianity, but liberty itself would
fall with her; but that she may be made to feel the
injustice of her measures towards us I do sincerely
hope, and that even she may be bro't to the very verge
of destruction, unless she gives up the principles on which
she laid her orders in councils; England is a proud nation
3. and much of that pride must be sacrificed, if she intends
to hold up her head among the nations of the earth.
Your letters tell me not to meddle at all with politics
but attend wholly to my art; How is it possible for me
to remain an unconcerned spectator of events which are
happening every day so important to the interests of my country?
my nature must be changed before I can see my country-
men led away by error, which are ruining their country, when
I sit by and calmly see them go on, & not even make an
attempt to set them right; my motive in thus freely writing
to you is to let you into the truth, and prevent myself the
mortification of seeing my relations involved in error, which are
doing so much injury to our country; What I write comes
from the heart, I feel the importance of this subject, and I
have long been waiting for an opportunity to write my
opinions fully upon it; I have too much prudence to write
such sentiments by post, and unless I had so excellent an
opportunity, I should have waited till I could see you, I give
this letter into Mr. Plumme's hands and he is to give it
into yours. You are at liberty to show this to any one, I never
shall be ashamed of owning myself an American, but till the
two parties become more moderate, I shall be ashamed to call
myself a democrat or a federalist. I am for truth, & truth
is of no party; for as Swift says "Party is the madness of many
for the gain of a few." if after all that I have now written
you still think that this war is unjust and think it worth
the trouble, in order to ascertain the truth, I wish Papa would take
a trip across the Atlantic, and if he is not convinced of the
truth of what I have written a bit than two months, I will
agree to support myself all the time I am in England after this
date, and never be a farthing's more expense to you; or if
Papa can't come let Edw's or Rich. come, and they will write
you the same sentiments, before they have been here 3
months, this I am confident of.— But as I have now
written so much on politics I will now leave them, only
adding that with this I send you some of the principle
public prints in with you may see a little for yourself,
what are the sentiments of the people, I would observe also
that the Morning Post, is considered the most scurrilous
paper in England, and has been notorious for its abuse of
America. There is a report current now in London that the Essex Amer. frigate has taken the Maid-
ston British frigate, I am all anxiety to know if it is
true, I hope with all my heart it is; nothing would raise
the American character so much in England, as doubling
that better dose: Oh! if we had but a navy, how much
contention among ourselves would it prevent.—
I was glad to hear that cousin Saml. Breese is
in the navy, I really envy him very much, I hope one
day as a painter I may be able to hand him down to
posterity as an American Nelson; I give Richard
joy on his bachelorship, and am glad to hear he acquired
himself handsomely— I understand a few days since
that Siml. Dexter Esq. was in favor of this war, I hope it is true
and that Rufus King Esq. of N.York was of the same opinion
10 with respect to it. All the bills of exchange which you
have sent have been received as yet I have not been able
to make any thing from my productions, and am not able
to say when I shall; allowing me 200 pounds each year for
the last and this, I think will carry me through them very
well, I will let you know in time, when I shall be able
to realize any thing from my profession; the third year I
shall do all I can to support myself, if not I shall come
home and by painting portraits in America, collect enough
to bring me here again, for it is important that I should
lose no time while I am here, and I am in such a stage of advancement,
that were I now to leave this country, it would injure me
materially ever after; I could not help smiling at an observation
in your letter, that when I acquired sufficient knowledge in
my art I must return home; Michael Angelo studied 70 years and did not get sufficient knowledge; Mr. West has
studied 60 and is still learning; there is no such thing as
being taught the art of painting; to learn it a man must devote
his whole life to it, and he learns by constant practice, and
observation, and that too, by steps, imperceptibly; the as it is with the hand of a clock which moves slow, and imperceptibly towards its
point of destination, and it is with still by steady perseverance he
gains the object of his study. at length and here let me observe
on my letters of introduction; I find that a painter and
a visitor cannot be united; were I to deliver my letters, their
acquaintance could not be kept up, and the bare thots of
encountering the English reserve, is enough to deter any
one; 'tis not like making an acquaintance in America,
before you can feel at ease in an English family, you must
visit them constantly, almost beg for a shake of the hand,
and be met with such cool, suspicious, looks as is enough
to freeze the warmest heart; I do not blame the English for
it; they have so often been deceived by impostors that they
must be on their guard; but for all this I cannot relish it;
I can't go into a family, where at the first, they look upon
me as an impostor, or are prepared to think so; I, who have
been accustomed in my own country to be received in so warm
a manner; this objection, however, might be got over, did
it not take up so much time, every moment is precious
to me now, I don't know how soon I may be obliged to return home,
for want of means to support me, for the difficulties which are increasing in this country, take off the attention of people from the fine arts, and they with hold that
patronage from young artists, who they would, from their liberality, in other circumstances, freely bestowed. -- You may
say that I need recreation, I find recreation enough in the various parts of my art; if I want exercise, I walk
to the different galleries of the artists, & replenish my mind with images &c, and at home I always find employment,
in studying out my pictures, and in writing to you. -- With regard to the Geoq. I shall not be able to realise any thing from it;
my friends here think it would be risking a good deal to have it published here, and that no
12 book-sellers would allow me anything for the first copy, when
by waiting a few months they could obtain a copy from America; to make anything by it I should have to advance money
and employ so much of my time, that it would both injure
me in pocket, and proficiency in my art, to undertake it.
You shall I thank Miss Russell for all her attention
and kindness to me, present her with my best respects for
the present, and assure her I feel grateful for her gifts, and will
ever long show her some testimony of my gratitude.
My good friends Mr. Brown & Mr. Evarts will excuse me for not writing them when they know how I am pressed for time, they cannot think it neglect when they
bare that my parents are the only persons with whom
I correspond.— If I had time I would willingly hold a
correspondence with them, and with many other dear friends
whom I shall never forget.
You mention that some of the Ralston family are
in Boston on a visit, and that Mr. Codman, is attached
to Eliza; once in my life, you know if you had told me
this, and I had been a very blood-sinned young man, who knows
but Mr. Codman might have been challenged, but I suppose he takes the advantage of my being in England; if it is
as you say I am very happy to hear it, for Elizabeth is a girl
whom I very much esteem, and there is no doubt but she will
make an excellent wife, if she is still in Boston remember
to hear of Mr. W. Ralston's death, it must have been a great
shock to the family, as I know he was a favorite; I sincerely con-
dele with them.
I was sorry to hear of the indisposition of J. Ward. & S. Barnell
remember me to them and families

Mr. Allston is getting on finely with his large picture, it
will be exhibited in Feb'y. it will make them open their
eyes, Mr. West says there is not another like him in
this country. He and Mrs A are well & desire to be remembered
to you I am at present upon a large picture 8 feet in
height by 6 1/2 the subject is the Death of Hercules, the figure
is from my little figure which I have before told you
of in a former letter, the model I shall exhibit at
the British Institution this Feb'y. Mr. West and Mr.

My affectionate love to my brothers, to Grandmam
Aunt & Uncle Salisbury, Nancy & family, and remember

Write me good long letters, and often; and may

Your very affectionate son

I have just read the political parts of this letter, to my good
friend Mr. Axxxxn, and he not only approves of these sentiments
in it, but pays me a compliment, by saying, I have
expressed the truth, and nothing but the truth, in a very clear
and proper manner, and hopes it may do good by his advice.
I proceed to state a few facts, which I give you on his authority:
he has had an opportunity of knowing them as he has for so long
been conversant with the different classes in this country:
he says, that every Englishman has a natural & inveterate
hatred to Americans, that even those who appear to be most
partial to America, look down with contempt on them, they think
14 them an inferior race of men, and such is their want of delicacy
or even of common politeness, that wherever an american
chances to be in their company, the abuse of america is the
common topic of their conversation; This I am also a witness
of, for when I dined at Mr Macauly's a gentleman who
dined there, with me, while at table addressed some most
impertinent remarks to me, on the literary characters of
my country, saying that it would be long before we could boast
of any literary characters worth the notice of Englishmen, and
appealed to me for the truth of the observation; another young
gentleman at the same place, the moment he was introduced
to me as an american, addressed this as his first question
to me, "Pray how many ships have you in your navy?"
I answered him very candidly, repeating their names, "is
that all?" said he, and laughing in my face turned on his
heel and walked to another part of the room; Is this not
enough to stir up all the American blood in me? Judge then,
how can an American enjoy himself in the company of En-
glishmen! These are not exaggerations, I could relate instances
of the same kind without number which have happened to
Mr. A --- in to my roommate Mr. L ---, and to almost every
american with whom I am acquainted; Now is it possible
for a man born in a free & independent country, of
connections as good as any in England, to sit calmly
and hear his country abused, in so indecent a manner
as is so generally the case in the company of Englishmen; if so
he must be made of a more gentle spirit than mine; --
often have I heard Englishmen, at the place where I dine, run
out into the most extravagant abuse of America, and if
our navy was mentioned, it was the subject of laughter for
half an hour; 6 frigates they said could blockade our whole
coast, that any sloop of war in the English navy, was a match
for any American frigate, whenever any of our Enslaves
came with dispatches, to bring a minister, or the like, a
paragraph in the papers, (generally mis spelling their names)
saying how badly she was managed, what little discipline there
was on board, and such kind of remarks as evidently should
with all their success there was mixed a portion of envy;
It has been a standing toast for many years among the
officers of their navy, "An American war." Now under
these circumstances, has not our war been of service? if it
was only for the simple capture of the Guerriere; it has silenced
all those sneers, nothing has been said of blockading America with
6 frigates, when they recollect the Alert sloop of war, they cease
to persist in affirming that a sloop of war is a match for our
frigates, and find no fault with the management, or the
discipline of the Constitution, except that she had too much
to suit the taste of an Englishman.— the officers of the navy
too have had their wish, but would rather an American
should not choose for them again, the manner in which it
is to be conducted.
If the federalists would but candidly consider the
case, lay aside their prejudices in favor of this country, who
she does not deserve, and unite with the war party in
prosecuting this war, it would not only be of ultimate
advantage to the country, but would make the war shorter,
for all that the English only upon is the party against the
16. war, and it makes them resolute in holding out a show of resistance
alone, they'll fight it out among themselves, we need not interest ourselves in it. As for
justice in this government, any farther than it suits their own interest, there is not a particle of it, if it suited
their interest to burn all our towns; justice would never stand in the way of it; their naval superiority has begot
in them such insolence, that it has entirely taken the place of justice, and they assert that power gives right,
that is, because they can insult every nation, on the ocean with impunity, therefore they have a right to do it, this
principle they maintain: and when I attempt to reason with them on the injustice of such a principle, they come
off by saying, "who can hinder us from doing as we please." I may answer, Americans! the despised American!
and that America may shew Great Britain, that at least she shall not tyrannize over her, is the sincere wish of my heart, as it ought to be, of every true American,
of those who can sacrifice the pride of party for the good of their country. -- when I hear men in Boston,
Newburyport & other seaports, making such an outcry against the war, & engaging up the spirit of '76 to support
them in it, I cannot but suspect, that interest has taken the place of patriotism in their breasts, and that they had
rather see their country disgraced, than their private persons suffer; Do this the spirit of '76? the spirit of '76 was the
sacrifice of individual interest for the good of the public,
their spirit seems to be, the sacrifice of the public interest
for that of the individual; who are these men that
make the greatest outcry, are they not men on whom
the war bears some what hard, in account of their
great commercial concerns; is it not therefore natural
they should be displeased with the war, they look
no farther than the present moment, because the war puts
a stop to their business for a time, they consider
all as a gone case with them, and raise up the phantoms
of French alliance, sack'd towns, and total destructions
to frighten themselves and their neighbors, into resistance
to the war; if, when a nation treats us with the
greatest indignities, when the private, as well as public
voice breathes forth nothing but contempt towards us,
when we are prohibited from trading to countries
under false pretences of assisting an enemy, while they
trade themselves direct to enemies ports, when the savages
on our frontiers, are excited against us (of which there
can now be no doubt) when our seamen are taken, and
presed into the English navy, (a part of which are American
seamen; I say, when this is happening every day
before our eyes, too plain to admit of contradiction,
if it is not time to declare war against a country,
when is it? I well know what answer I should receive
from some federalists, or rather question by way of answer,
Has not France injured us? why not declare
18. war against her? I answer with another question
what good it would do; in what manner can we injure
her; will the mere act of declaring war, hurt her; can
we send armies to France; can we send a navy;
has France any settlements on our continent which
we can invade; what then can we do to her; by the
act of declaring war we shall show our spirit, and
our justice, but with it, our folly; for turn the tables,
Can France injure us; yes, she can confiscate the
millions of american property in her power; now
has not our government at least in this instance shown
some wisdom; Why is it said, so much blood must
be spilled, so much property must be expended, taxes
must be levied; &c. What else can be expected from
war; England is an example herself of what deprivation
individuals will suffer for the good of the public, every
individual in the single tax upon income pays 7/10 of it to
government this is but a single tax; and cannot the
patriotic Americans bear a slight tax for the good of
their country, or will they make good the opinion the
English have of them, that the moment their purses are
touched they are ripe for rebellion. Do consider these,
things, my father, before you decide on such an important subject as this, do not let the sneers and taunts
of men who would sacrifice their country, to
promote the interests of their party, deter you from doing
that which you think just; pardon, me for daring to
advise one whom I know would never do anything
wrong, to please the whole world; I know you will forgive
me for this warmth; if I did not feel the truth of the
sentiments which I have been writing, you know I would
not dare to utter them. Believe me as ever your
Affectionate Son.
Charleston Nov 7th 1861.
Dear Brother,
I write hastily by M Langdon who
fails tomorrow in a cartel for Europe, I wrote
you a few days since by the cartel from
Boston to London direct.
Many things of much importance
are occurring daily. But we have become so habit
accustomed to change, that when we write
every thing appears to be the same old story.
Representatives to Congress were elected
throughout this State a few days since. In
Charleston the Federal Candidate had the
majority. The probability, may be certainly
is that 19 out of the 26 to which this State is
entitled will be other Federalists or Clintonians.
This State is strongly decided in its
favour of Peace measures and Peace men.
News from the north, have been
hitherto without exception nothing but tales
of disaster, defeat, disgrace to the Americans. Our soldiers have their share of bravery
acknowledged even by the enemy, but not
without clothing, provisions, ammunition,
or any of those necessities which a wise
administration should have provided.
Popular opinion is becoming every
day more and more decided against Mr.
Madison will probably lose his election.
Already do his Weathercock partisans begin
to turn as they feel the wind shifting. The
Madisonian and Clintonian party at this
moment nearly equally divide the coun-
try, but every day brings good news to Clinton.
Our little Navy has done well bravely.
Besides the brilliant affair of the Constitution,
the Wash 18 guns, fought & captured
the Frolic 26 guns & superior force, I mem-
bers, but was obliged to relinquish her
prey, and surrender herself to a fleet
of the Line 74 guns.
The Americans have met with
no success in any quarter except on the
Ocean, and that is to be ascribed entirely
to our Navy, the increase of which has
always been a favorite measure with Fed-
eralists, and opposed by bitterly by present
Administration. No thanks to them therefore
for the honor we get on this way.
We are surrounded by enemies. The
English on the North in Canada, & on the
East, on the Ocean, on the South by the
Spaniards in Florida, where we are usur-
ping most wickedly and most meanly the
territory. & on the West by the Indians.
When the Jeffersonian dynasty com-
menced its operation, we were at peace
with the World. Our canvass whitened every
sea, the voice of prosperity was heard in all
our dwellings, -- This is exchanged for the
terror of War -- the scalping knife & tomahawk
misery at home and abroad -- Americans
are beginning to be ashamed of themselves.
Papa's affairs begin to look a little
brighter. At best but gloomy.
All desire to be remembered.
P.S. General Van Rensselaer has resigned his office
in the army. Write us by every opportunity and
I will you should have written longer but
prest it for time.
It convenient wish you to inquire if
Taylors Edition of the Poets is completed. How
many and what Poets it includes. What
the size, price, and manner of execution
of the work, and write me in your next.
Don't forget this, if you ever have opportunity,
to inquire.

My Dear Friend
I wished must to have seen
you ere this but a violent cold & diarrhea almost
amounting to dysentery must plead my excuse
I dined on Monday foot with Mr. Thornton
he thanked me very heartily for the sermon of
your father's which I sent him, he told you
address and desired me to tell you that he
would be pleased to have us together at his house
and would let us know when the Parliment
were engaged on an interesting subject when
he should be happy in our company to dinner, I
afterwards let us in to the Houses of Parle the debate
Mr. Wilberforce took my address and will if
he chooses ask me to dinner or show me
any politeness he sees fit. He expressed some concern
that your father had not informed
him of your residence in London. From confine
to the Borough for a week which I hope will
be Wednesday next, after which I shall have
the pleasure of seeing you at your house, if I
can come over London bridge before that time
I shall be happy to see you. My best regards to
Mr. Astor and my friend Leslie
With much affection

My dear Parents,
I have just received your letters of Oct.
7th by Mr Lyman, with a found of Chinese Vermillion. Capt. Langdon has not yet called on me,
nor Mr Parkman, by whom I suppose I have also some things from you; they have not yet
I believe arrived in town. The Vermillion is of the quality I wished, and I cannot sufficiently express my thanks to Mr Russell, whose kindness & attention to me I hope one day to
deavor to repay, though I fear it will give more & more impracticable, while she lays me under
such repeated weights of obligation; in the mean time express to her my warmest thanks.
Janr 1st 1813.
I was obliged to leave my letter unfinished till now, since writing the above, Mr Parkman
has called on me, he has not, the edition of George & Atlass, for which I thank you Capt. Langdon
has not yet arrived. Just Thursday week I received a very polite invitation from Henry
Thornton Esq to dine with him, which I accepted, I had no introduction to him, but hearing that your
son was in the country he found me out, and has shown me every attention, he is a very pleasant
sensible man, but his character is too well known to you
to need any eulogium from me; at his table was a son
of Mr. Stephen, the author of the odious Orders in Council,
Mr. Thornton asked me at table, if I thought that if the
Orders in Council had been revealed a month or two sooner
whether it would not have prevented the war, I told him
I thought it would, at which he was much pleased, and
turning to Mr. Stephen, he said "do you hear that Mr. Stephen,
I always told you so" -- Last Wednesday I dined at Mr.
Witberforce's I was extremely pleased with him, at his
house I met Mr. Thornton & Mr. Grant members of parlia-
ment, in the course of conversation, they introduced America
Mr. W. regretted the war extremely, he said it was like
two of the same family quarrelling, "that he thought it
a judgment on this country for their wickedness, & that
they had been justly punished, for their arrogance & insolence
at sea," as well as the Americans for their vaunting
on land -- As Mr. Thornton was going, he invited
me to spend a day or two at his seat at Elpham, a
few miles out of town, I accordingly went and was very
civilly treated; the reserve which I mentioned in a former
letter, was evident, however, here, and I felt a degree of
embarrassment arising from it, which I never felt in America;
the second day, I was a little more at my ease: at
dinner were two sons of the Mr. Grant I mentioned above
they are perhaps the most promising young men in the country,
and you may possibly one day hear of them as at the head of
this nation; after dinner I got into conversation with them,
and Mr. Thornton, when America again became the topic
of conversation. -- they asked me a great many questions
respecting America, which I answered to the best of my a-
bility; — They at length asked me if I did not think that
the ruling party in America, were very much under French
influence; I replied No, that I believed, on the contrary
that nine tenths of the American people were more disposed
strongly in favor of this Country, as a proof I urgeded, the
universal prevalence of English fashions in preference to
French, English manners & customs; the resounding on the
succès of the English over the French, the marked attention
shown to English travellers & visitors, the neglect with
which they treated their own literary productions, for an account
of the strong prejudice in favor of English works;
that every thing in short was enhanced in its value by
having attached to it the name English. — On the other hand
I told them that the French were a people almost universally
despised in America, and by at least one half hated; as in
England they were esteemed the common enemies of mankind,
that French fashions were discontenanceed & loathed, that
a Frenchman was considered as a man always to be suspected,
that young men were forbidden, in many instances
to associate with them, considering their company & habits
as tending to subvert their morals & to render them frivolous
& insincere. I added, that in America as well as every
where else there were bad men, men of no principles,
whose consciences never stand in the way of their ambition or
avarice, but that I firmly believed that as a body the American
Congress was as free from corruption & foreign influence
as any body of men in the world. They were very much

going on to observe something respecting the French decrees when
we were interrupted, & I have not been able again to resume the
conversation as I returned to town with him shortly after
in his carriage, where as there were strangers I could not intro-
duce it again -- I shall take the opportunity some time to
pursue the subject with him. -- The Prince declar-
ation, vindicating the English Govt. from blame in the war
with America, has been published some time, it is a flimsy
thing and by the friends of administration thought to be but a
very weak defence. 58641 A accompanying this letter is one
which I have had written some time but wanted a fair
opportunity to send it; I have had no reason to alter my sentiments from those contained in that letter;
you say in your last letters, "were you here, you would be as warm
a federalist as you ever was," had I never visited England, I
probably should for then I should never have known, perhaps
the truth with I now know, 58641 you requested in your
letter, to ask the opinion of Mr. W. & Mr. J. by what I have
written above you will see that I have done as you requested
and you will see also that I have some reason for my change of
sentiments, (not from federalism to democracy, but from neutrality to
federalism but from neutrality to neutrality) When
I hear such principles avowed by this government as I have mentioned,
when such a contemptuous disregard of American rights
is manifested in their measures, when, after our declaration of
war, they neglect to answer it for six or seven months, and then
in so unsatisfactory a manner as to give general dissent, and
when I find no one, in short, attempting a justification of them-
selves, what must I think, what must any man think in
such a case; would you have me in the face of all this to retain
my federal feelings, and justify them through every thing, when they cannot
and dare not do it themselves. To sum up my sentiments thus in
a few words, I believe that in declaring war America has
acted justly, that had she done otherwise she would have, been
justly entitled to the epithets so liberally, (before the war) bestowed upon
her of cowardly, imbecile, & the like, that the American
administration were impudent to say the least in not having prepared
before for such an event; I think that the American character
has risen beyond the bounds of the most exaggerated expectation,
since the declaration of war, we are raised from "mere descendants
of convicts," to a level with a nation who pride themselves
as the first in the world, and by whom, not only by all the powers
on the continent, but by England herself as proof of this I could quote
passages from every paper in the country, I would certainly amuse you
to see the difference in the tones of the public prints from what
the war, they were filled with abuse of America, and I have quoted in
my other letter instances, how do they speak of her now? with sneers
& contemptuous insinuations? No; with the greatest respect, they
now for the first time claim relationship with us, and speak of
us as deserving an equal standing with themselves. But I
must abruptly close as I am to send this directly. You will
have heard before this arrives, of the glorious news from Russia,
Buonaparte is for once defeated, and will probably never again
recover from it. With respect to the Geography I shall see Mr.
Thornton, (who is now reading it) about the practicability of publishing
it here. Richard asks if it is the custom in England to walk
fast, or is it peculiar to M. King. It is the custom, for they
rather fly than walk. Mr. Stewart, I feel quite flattered at his remembrance of me, tell him that by coming to England, I know how more justly to appreciate his great
merits, there is really none in England, who equal him. I omit much for want of time. I shall write again soon.
Love to all friends. A lieux! Yours Vc. H.

London Jan 7. 5th 1813
Dear Monk,
It is so long since we have
heard from you that, unwilling to
believe ill wishes the cause of your silence,
we conclude you have become very
industrious, and employ your time
to more advantage in writing
to your friends.
I have been unwell part busy,
but I am now much fully recovered
from my indisposition, also
more of himself, though perhaps the
last belief is not to be rejoiced at.
Mr Allison & I have sent our pictures
to the Gallery. He has made good
interest to get his large one placed
at the end of one of the rooms. As
to mine it is of small consequence
where they put it. Mr Hafter
finsihing his Diana showed it to
Mr West who was (it speaks even
moderately) in raptures with it. He
unmistakably called his sort Raffaello,
"there says the old gentleman "there, why
there is nobody who does any thing
like this." Raffaello exclaimed "it
looks like a bit of Titian". "Is yes
answered his father "that Titian's
flesh, that Titian's flesh." After this
show of compliments Mr Allston sa
"I am very highly gratified to find
it meets your Probation." He said
Mr W. "I can find words to
express what I think of it". He then
proceeded to praise the beauties of
the parts & the composition
drawing &c &c as he had done the
colour. He seemed particularly pleased
with the landscape. He told Mr
Allston to follow this up, adding "Sir
you will find thousands of people
who will give you two hundred guineas
for a picture of this size, who have
not room in their houses for long
ones." He said he could have sold
all the small sketches in his galleries
many times over, but he chose to
keep them himself. Several pictures he
has sold and painted duplicate of
them. Mr A mentioned his subject
of Venus & Adamis, & Mr W. advised him
by all means to paint it but not
to have the figures the size of life.
Mr Allston is going to begin the old
Gentlemans portrait very soon, he
promises himself much pleasure in
the execution of it. I am to
dine to day with Mr Brown &
spend tomorrow at (Twelfth Day) at
Mr Leckie's a neighbour of his.
I would be much obliged to you to
deduct the sum I had given you
visitot from £2911.0 and send
an order on Mr Bromfield for the
remainder as I am in want
of it, it being the awful time when
tradesmen's bills make their appearance
& I not having the wherewithal.
We are all very anxious to hear
how Mrs Vigors family are. Please
to remember all the good people of
London to them, that is Mr & Mrs
Allston & myself. Wishing you
a very happy New Year & hoping
you have had a very merry Christmas
I remain your friend
C Leslie

My Dear Son
With you a happy New Year. I have been
intending to write you by the two or three last opportunities
but have been prevented from cause to communicate to be met
with at present. Your last letter that we have received
is dated the 20th of September in that you informed us
of your point to Mangate & your arrival at the little port
of Dover Castle which is the first occasion that you have
written since you left home at your departure. We are all very
anxious to see some of your performances in the way of
music & mathematics and have been expecting something one
thing I have told Mr. Russell your Aunt Salisbury & Mr.
Barlett that you intend sending each of them a picture
the two latter are hoping to have but for your mantle
piece for the future they expect from you. I think
thereupon you have anything of that kind or any thing
desired in the way of your profession to send us and will
not put up with great care that Mr. Brownfield or Mr.
Samuel Williams will be able to furnish you with a safe
conveyance or Captain Langdon of this town would be
a fine opportunity for you to send us any of your perfor-
mances as he is your Friend and would put himself
to his convenience to oblige us. I want to see your Heroism
that has pleased Mr. Redding Alston so much because
he is a fine man.
We sent you two pounds of Chinese Commissions purchased at the
harbor in Court Street agreeable to your direction, by Henry
Mr Parkinson who sailed last Nov in the cartel for Liverpool
from Philadelphia the name of the ship was the Penn
Sylyvania I hope you have received the packets sent by him
before this the painter on a permit from Miss Harpett. You
will of course thank me for her kindness to you. She hopes
to be particularly remembered to you as does your grand
mother. Your Uncle & Aunt Satisfaction indeed will our
regnanccce Your letters are read with great pleasure
by your acquaintance I do not think them in which you
say any thing on politics, as I do not suppose your camp
and think it would only prejudice others for that reason
I do not wish you to write me that subject as I love
to read all your observations to your Friends as they appear
to please you. Edward in writing you your Papa
also I shall therefore add but little more to expect
Richard home this week to spend the vacation with
us in the quiet. I think tea with one not long ago
they all send their kind regards to you. We cannot get
Edward to be a ladies man at all he will not visit
among the young Ladies he is as old as 50 at least
Richard says that Edward Taylor have been to Journey
and that Miss Caroline Lefing well & Sappond her though
Richard Board at Mr Taylor he says they had fine
times from enough I presume as is a pleasant girl
improve every opportunity to write us and send us
all that you can Spare of your own productions to
leave us and all your Friends that Whatever been
expended on you has not been in vain –
I have all other things but first the kingdom
of God and the righteousness there of and let
us know that this is your Choice Adieu my
Dear Son I cannot see to write any more
as it is very dark and the letters must go to
night. This is terribly difficult to go to England
Your affectionate
mother E A Morse
Jan. 11. 1813
Mott.
Charlestown Jan 9th 1812
Dear Brother,
I write in great haste by a gentle-
man who will carry this letter direct to
London. We are all well and in good spirits.
Received letter from Richard to day. He is
well also.
Sam Breeze is now in this port. He has
just arrived from a long voyage in company
with Commodore Rogers - The squadron was
visited the common cruising places of the
British Frigates in the Atlantic, but could
find nothing - They have sent in two
prizes - worth 300 thousand dollars -
Captain Hule of the Constitution was
married a few days since to Ann Hart of
Saybrook (Conn.) - He is coming with his lady
to reside in Charleston immediately as Super-
intendent of the Navy Yard.
I have been engaged for several weeks
past in writing for the News Paper - and am forever
your
affectionate brother
Geo. Washington
Our Congress are engaged in making
provision for a prosecution of the war as soon as the
Spring opens -- Once in a while they hold out a pre-
sence that they shall speedily make peace. But the
knowing ones tell us they are merely peace battles to
calm gudgeons. -- The States north and East of
the Delaware are violently opposed to the war --
Vermont has returned democratic Electors & Repre-
sentatives -- But they had only 200 majority, and
it is supported that the State is the only demo-

it has been Gerrymandered will return 22 Repre-

Bloomingdale, New York March 4th 1843.
My dear friend:
I am fearful you will hardly remember, now as one when you
invited to enter the list of your correspondents, and I am well aware that almost
two years inattention to your request does not entitle me to such remembrance.
I intended however that you should receive the letters of my husband
as from me, inasmuch as he is now by proxy, and I confess I am quite offended at you for not
having addressed me line to one in return. -- We were much gratified by
your letter which gives us so pleasant an acquaintance as your friend Mr King; but
we should have been better pleased if he had delivered it earlier that we might have
had more of his company. -- I believe he has established himself at Philadelphia
which is indeed a more eligible situation for an artist than this city affords, and
where, I doubt not, he will receive very flattering encouragement. -- I am in general
ab proved of the spirit of my country men; but there is too little attention paid to the
fine arts, to merit taste and science. Man here is weighed by his purse not by
his mind, and according to the preponderance of that, he rises or sinks in the
scale of individual opinion. A fine pointing or marble statue is very rare in the
houses of the rich of this city, and those individuals who would not pay fifty pounds
for either, expect no doubt that sum to go with a napkin in a piece of furniture.
But do not tell tales. I would not say this to an Englishman, and I trust
you have not yet become one. This however is poor encouragement for you to return
to your native country -- I hope better things of that country before you may return;
and I sincerely believe that the time is not far distant when a West (of such another
star should use no other horizon) and a Vanderbilt may be restored amongst us --
He is left
Before this can reach you, will doubtless have seen American papers announcing the
marriage of my sister to Capt. Houlf of the navy. They are at present at Boston, but it is not
improbable that they may reside in the navy house at Charleston. My daughter too
is married to a Mr. Watson of New Haven. But Jannette is writing to you at this moment,
and I have to hear all domestic news. We hear much of the war and an intention of
both countries to prosecute it now vigorously. God grant some happy event
any turn so bloody and unnatural a purpose.
Mr. Jarvis will fill up the paper, and nothing remains for me but to assure you that the friendship which you awakened
in my bosom on our first acquaintance, is not weakened by the lapse of years, neither by your silence. I am, my dear friend, deeply interested in your welfare, and what ever your situation in life may be, do not forget that in this little corner of the world, there
is one who loves you, and who will ever rejoice in your happiness.
Heaven bless you
Sarah W. Jarvis

If on my part it has languished I beg you will attribute my silence to any
other cause than a diminution of esteem. — At this distance from the City, in the present
unhappy obstruction of intercourse, I seldom hear of an opportunity till it is too late. If this circumstance is the only cause why I do not write sooner, — the principal subject of conversation in the political world is at present the gallant exploit of
Comm. Bainbridge in capturing the Java of which you will doubtless have received the details before this letter arrives. — Do you receive the American papers regularly? If not I will endeavour to send them to you, though at this distance from the City it will be impossible to send them regularly. Our success upon the ocean must
excite a glow of triumph in the heart of every American, & the more so because we have been mortified at the degradation of our national character which our repeated Naval victories will doubtless render. — But I confess to you, my dear friend, that this triumph is in my breast not unmixed with pain. I fear these events will produce this unnatural, & I think I may say, unnecessary war.— If so the wishes of individuals for peace will be destroyed. But I will not anticipate evils which I pray God to avert. — You who are now in a land of enemies doubtless feel differently from what I do, with respect to the causes & consequences of the war. We
however unite in the wish that a speedy & honourable peace may restore the amicable relations which ought to exist between the friends the happiest, the most intimatemately related nations in the world. — Mr Palmer on his return, mentioned to me that he left a letter of mine to him in your hands, containing a list of books which I had requested him to purchase. — If it will not be inconvenient, will you have the goodness to purchase for me the following books, & any other in that list which from time to time you may find cheap? — Then you can probably from time to time transmit to me by some safe conveyance, as private property, if you cannot they can remain on your shelves till there be peace, — the money shall be paid to your order at sight. — I am, my dear Sir your very sincere friend

My dear Genl
Capt Pratt has just informed me
that a Cartel is about to sail for Halifax. I am
impressed with opportunity to drop you a line. We
wrote you largely by Mr Wilder a few weeks
since, who expected to sail from New-York in the
Pacific but I have just heard that she is not
permitted to sail. I know not why, or that it is
time. Possibly Mr W. may not go so on
parcel by him will be returned if so we
shall be sorry. As was written very fully by him
I sent you some of the newspapers of the day.
I enclose also by him a first exchange of
£25 on the Society in Scotland drawn by
Mr Foxeant. If it shall on further enquiry
be thought safe I shall enclose the second
in this letter.
We are very anxious to hear from you. Your
last letter, which we have received, was dated the 20th Sept.
almost 6 months ago at much longer interval, than has
passed without hearing from you, since you left us. We
presume you have written but your letter must have
been carried. Mr Ingram has arrived, who he says dined with you on the
5th of Decr. I should be bring letters from you.
but you informed him you had lately written (we
suppose by Mr. Chamberlain who has not arrived, but is supposed to be at
the post having, as is supposed been out now 100 days)
It would be well to write by every possible means if it is within
few lines I am anxious to know the state
of your finances, especially as particularly
as you gave them in your first letters. You
last have all been silent on this subject.
Mr. Douglas informed us that he saw your day
signs, & your printing from it which in ten did for
the approaching exhibition. I spoke flatteringly of
both -- We shall be glad to hear of your success.
You say nothing respecting the Geo. -- Whether
it is republished in Eng.-- or in what way it is
for your benefit These matters should be omitted,
amongst your other & more appropriate
attentions -- While pursuing your philosophical
studies, you should not neglect to provide for
means which are placed in your power, of your
own support -- It will be profitable for you to
diversify your attentions in degree yet so as
to further your prime object to the greatest ad-
vantage. Your friends here all express after you
with interest -- The Mug. wards were overtaken by your
Mama read them a part of your last letter giving
an aut of your commission to Dover Castle. They
were gratified to be remembered to you --
The last heard, all were well at Mrs. Chinnings.
Hope you have long er this called on Mr. Wilkerson
to Mr. Macaulay -- if not fail not to do it without
delay, I make to them your humble apology for your
neglect -- Present my respects to them both -- I will
write them when we have peace. With I hope will
be effected in the course of the Spring -- I presume
on your prudence, my son, in the then critical and
unhappy state of affairs between the two countries. Mind
your own business -- I leave political concerns, with
whose proper business it is to manage them. The New-
papers, with you will have only to read well in form
you of the train of events of every kind, in this
Country to them I refer you -- Young Lt. M.
Walker is to sail for France in a day or soon --
he goes out to spend a year in order to complete
his medical studies -- He may visit you in
before his return -- or Mr. Sp. the time, admit, you may
see him in Paris -- but you will not so think but
under the most favorable circumstances -- till
affairs shall become settled in that country -- I doubt
you by Mr. Walker but know not that it will ever
find you through that channel.
We are all pretty well -- Your Grandson Breese is
with us -- Your brother Edward is at home commencing his
law studies -- I am going to Lititz Field in a few months -- Ruth
was well at W. Haven a fine day ago -- Nancy & Bethey Cannon
are still with us -- All join in love to you, with your love
to me. Remember us to Mrs. H. Wilkerson, Mrs. Thomas Brownfield
(whose friends are in unusual health) & Mr. West -- Dr. Leake -- Your ever
affectionate father E. Morse

My Dear Sir
Your favour I received
from the hands of the King and have been
very much gratified with the introduction it
afforded me to this worthy gentleman. You have
not only heard of his safe arrival in safety
of his having commenced his career in America
where I am sorry to say the arts are not as yet
so much patronized, as I hope to see them.
Those of us who love them are too poor, and those
who are wealthy regard them but little. I
think however I have already witnessed an
improvement in this respect and the rich mer-
chants & professional men are becoming more
& more liberal in their patronage of genius
when they find it among native Americans.
Our country is making a second struggle for
independence, and I hope the time is not far
distant when we shall cease to depend upon
Great Britain for any thing; and when we
shall owe to her nothing but gratitude for
right examples of every variety of individual
excellence! This debt we shall never discharge
discharge. She has afforded to the world in her
Religious, Charitable, & liberal institutions, a
specimen of neatness, & of goodness which other
nations have aspired in vain; but as a nation
her conduct to our natural fellow country has been
such as to rouse the indignation even of moderate
politicians. From the favourable circumstances,
under which your studies are progressing; from
the unrivalled talent of the gentleman who con-
ducts them, & without flattering myself to add
from the early proofs of your own genius, I
anticipate in common with many of our
fellow citizens, the addition of one artist to
our present roll, whose name shall stand high
among American painters. In your companion
Leslie we also calculate on a very distinguished
character, his pivenile efforts have already ac-
quired for him high & deserved reputation, and
it delights me to hear that he has been much
extolled by the friends he has acquired in England.
On the subject of the arts, there is little in
America worth communicating, tho' much
to receive from your side of the Atlantic --
our Acad y of fine arts have begun the all im-
portant study of the live figure. Moskelly
Mr. Peale Mr Fairman the King & several
others have devoted much attention to this branch
of the School & I hope to see it in their hands
highly useful & improving. The drawings are of
first rate excellence which have already been pro-
duced & are studied for future composition, the
result must be invaluable. The Society of Artists
are about establishing a similar school, and
have done me the honour to elect me their
Prof s of Anatomy. Dr Chapman is Prof s to
the head s of arts. No lecture have yet been
delivered, but I shall commence in a few weeks
a professor, could you do me the favour to give me
a short account of the manner in which anatomy
is taught to the artists in London? What is
the number of Lectures delivered annually & upon
what particular subjects do the professors dwell
most minutely? If there are any publications
on this subject (except those of Charles Bell & Dr. Jones
hun) I shall be much your debtor if you can
inform me in your next how Mr West enjoys his
health & what he is doing. I am all anxiety
expectation about the hospital picture, as one
of its surgeons I have a lively interest in
the affair & sincerely hope we shall ere
long
have the pleasure of seeing it - may tell me
what state it is in.
The last annual exhibition was very
splendid for us. Some very capital landscape
were produced - Many admirable portraits, and
one or two historical pictures. The most con-
spicuous paintings were Mr Peale's large picture
of the Roman Charity (on if you please the Greek
daughter for Murphy has it so) & Mr Sully's
lady of the lake; the former was in general
most admired, the reasons of this admiration
(as I think I will not dispute the size of the pic-
ture, the figures being a large a life; the great
force of shadows which brought out very finely
the female figure, & the contrast of a fine
reverend head with a beautiful young
female countenance. In addition to these
attractions the picture was well drawn &
very tolerably painted. The defects I shall not
notice, as you will probably see the picture when
you return home. Sully's picture had in my
view, more beauties & more faults (which
you will say indeed more serious) it is now
in my parlour where I hope you will enter
it. Peale & Sully are certainly excellent painters

Sunday evening or rather Monday morning 1. o’Clock
London May 30th 1813.
My Dear Parents,
I just have time to drop you a line by an
opportunity which I learnt, but a few hours since;
and am sorry I have not a longer time to write you
a longer letter; this is just to say that I never was
in better health and spirits, that as far as I am
able to judge I am going on prosperously, and that
I have commenced writing you a long letter giving
an account of my journey to Oxford etc: the ceremony of delivering the Gold medal to me a few
days ago, and various Yes. I get so little time
to write that I am a great while in finishing
a letter, for I think a letter ought to be long
that is to go so long a voyage.— I will now
tell you the reason of my not writing so of
late, Mr Allston has been extremely— and
Mr Allston feared if I wrote and did not mention
they were well, that it would create anxiety in
his family at home & wish’d me to wait till he
was better, he was ill for 2 or 3 months; but I
am now happy to say he has not only completely
recovered, but is in much better condition than
he has been for many years, he has abandoned
smoking altogether, and is now working upon his
great picture, which will be completed in a few
days, and open to the public. Owing to his illness
he was unable to finish it for Somerset house.—
I never felt so low spirited as when he was ill, I often
thought if he should be taken away at this time, what an
uncomparable loss he would be not only to me, but to America, to
the world.— Oh! he is an angel on earth, I cannot love him
too much.— Excuse my warmth, I never can speak
of Mr A. but in rapture.— More anon,
Remembrance to Miss Roswell etc.
Love to all. Adieu
Sam! H.B. Morne.
Rev. Jedidiah Morse. D.D.
Charlestown near
Boston. Mass.
North America.

My Dear Parents,
I wrote you a hasty line a few days ago, and
see? since, your letter via Halifax of March 9th
enclosed the 2d bill for 25 pounds on the Joe, in Scot
land; I write now in great haste, for indeed I find
but little time to write at all, and I feel sometimes
as though I neglected writing too long, for the days run
away so fast, that on looking at my letter list I find
I am often a week in arrears, and I scarcely finish
one, before it is time to begin another; as to my
health, it never was better, and I am in excellent
sprits; the only thing that causes me to be low spirits
at times, is my expences, I must confess though reluctantly,
that 200 pounds are not sufficient to support
me for a year; my first year exceeded it 10, or 12
pounds which I borrowed of the 2 years allowance
and this second year, I fear will run over perhaps 20;
what distresses me is, that it is unavoidable, no
one can accuse me of extravagance; on the contrary
I have pinch'd myself in my expences so much, that
I have certainly for some short time past impeded
my progress in my studies, not being able to obtain
many things on account of the expences, unless you
were here, you can have no idea of the constantly
increasing price of everything; I will give you an
account of what I must expend in order absolutely

In this statement you will perceive by calculating over after me
that I have underrated rather than overrated that to prints, books
and many other necessaries such as subscriptions to Circulating libraries
(which by the way is 3 guineas a week) I have set down nothing against

I have candidly given you an accurate account
of my expenses which I have heretofore found to do, for many reasons
I knew you were embarrassed with the P. estate, and I did not wish
you to know the true state of the case, supposing that by my industry
I might make up the deficiency without your knowledge, in fancy
proprietors; but people here will not sit to persons who have no name
and take no interest in foreigners, especially Americans at this time when
they hate with a mortal hatred. Another reason for not telling you
before was this; that I had given you no proof that I had done anything
since I had been here in London, and if I told you that I had not
sufficient to live, you might suppose that you were only mispending
money on me, and this I knew would distress you. I tell you
the true state of my finances now, because you say in your last
letter that the suit is settled and has turned in your favour,
therefore, you would not feel so distressed as before; another reason is, I have done something since which, will convince you
I have not misspent my time, or my father his money; for I sent by this opportunity (Mr. Elisha Goddard) the little cast
of the Hercules, which obtained the prize this year at the Adelphi, and also the medal which was the premium,
presented to me before a large assembly of the nobility & gentry of the country, by the Duke of Norfolk, who also
paid me a handsome compliment at the same time:—there were present, Lord Percy, the Margravine of Anspach, the
Turkish, Russian & Russian Ambassadors, who were joined out to me and many other noblemen whom I do not now
recollect.— My great picture also has not only been received at the Royal Academy but has one of the finest
places in the rooms, it has been spoken of in the papers, which you must know is considered a great compliment, and a
young artist unless extraordinary is seldom or never mentioned till he has exhibited several times; they not only praise
me, but place my picture among the most attractive in the exhibition: this I know will give you pleasure and
I write it with great pleasure, I also send a catalogue of the exhibition, with one of the papers which criticise
my picture that you may see for yourselves.—
In my last I mentioned that I had begun an account of my jaunt to Oxford, it was to be in this letter but I am obliged to
write this in haste as Mr. Goddard goes to the new-moon's care by.— I should have mentioned among my expenses the postage
of letters, which is enormous, the last letter by the Pacific Mail Station 5 in number amounted to £3.000 this was unavoidable
every American complained of enormous postage by that reason
rival, one gentleman's was $50.00. I see no other remedy
than to write very small and close on large thin paper, and to put
little or no sealing wax on it; if you recollect the last sent
to me were exactly the reverse of this, they were written wide
apart, large, on thick paper, a great deal of sealing wax, one
or two strings, and only one side half down in two of them;
this is paying dear.
By the way I feel very much obliged to Mr Brown
and Mr Evarts for their kind remembrance of me, and wish
my best wishes to be tendered to them, if I had time would
write to them; My love to my brothers whom I wish would
write long, long, very long, & very particular letters, let me
know every thing, for I am from home, and cannot
learn what is going on there unless from them. Love also
to Grandma Ma Breese, Uncle & Aunt Salisbury, Miss
Russell, Dr Bartlett, and in short every body; to Nancy
Betsy, Caroline, & Joe. Adieu!
Will write again soon.
Mr Allston & Lady one in perfect health, and his large piece
will soon be the wonder of the world.
Young Payne the actor, is here, and has performed at Drury
Lane with the greatest applause, he is certainly in his morals
an exception to actors generally, I am acquainted with him
and am much pleased with him.
Could say much more but no time. Yours very affectionately

Dear Son
The last letter we received from you was dated
January 27th 1813, that is since nearly six months ago others have
received letters from their friends in London long since, then even
down to April 8th many of the letters dated in March
mention you as well. We have not heard within you have
exhibited your pictures and what has been its reception we hope
favourable We are quite anxious to hear from you direct &
wish you to have letters constantly in such a state as that
you can give and send them when ever an opportunity offers
Mr Broomfield & Bremer would have the goodness to send them
at any time as he undoubtedly knows of frequent opportunities
one way is to fly from and from hence here in limited supply
you have now been gone two years have one more to stay I
hope you will improve this last year in such a manner
as to render it unnecessary to return again - Young
Worthingham is doing very well in taking portraits he has
for some fifty & for others seventy five doll which I suppose
will afford him a good living he has taken Doct Bartlett
& Mr I have so like him they are excellently well done &
give great satisfaction - Mr Stuart has a nephew whose
Name is Newton who I am told bid fare to be a proficient
in the Art there is Mr Sargent who has lately finished
a fine painting of the landing of the fore Fathers at Plymouth
which I understand he intends to exhibit in expectation of gaining
some thing by it I feel in hopes by the time you return
next year that prospect will Brighten as to your profession to
enable you to remain in your native Country and permit it
to advantage but Providence will I trust direct to the most
suitable and best means to be used by you & by us all I must
daily acknowledge him in all our ways for our comfortable
substance While traveling through this Pilgrimage.
We wish most of all your spiritual Improvement I wish to hear
what your thoughts are on the subject of Religion if you will
write us as fully on this important subject as you did on
politics. We should be better pleased with the contents of your
letter as we should agree in sentiment on Religion much better than on politics next to changing
your Religious opinions which I trust are than in which
you have been Educated most carefully I should depreciate
your changing your political party to that of returning to politics
but I feel persuaded your present apparent change arises from
your information entirely I therefore beseech of you to suspend your
opinions till you return home and then you will have an
opportunity of judging for yourself and I will venture anything
you will think better to say your good Friend Miss Buel
also who request to be kindly remembered to you this well
thinks that you have been treated with great politeness
and attention since you have been in England and by
far above you in rank & station you ought therefore to feel a
high sense of gratitude for the politeness of the well bred and not
regard the sneers & reflections of others & take no notice of them
you need not appear to hear them I presume you would not like
as it appears you do not to have your countrymen represented
by some of the rude ill bred creatures whom a Foreigner may
meet with in our gentul circles who would probably abuse
an English man as badly as they do Americans it is not from
that class or even from the observations of members of parliament
when debating on questions in which the interest of their constitu-
ents are involved that we are to judge of the sentiments of the
nation with respect to our nation or things that they may have
occasion to introduce. This much I had written yesterday when I
had to break off and take a ride to Rochester to call on Commodore
Hillhouse with your father & Edwards. Mr. Hillhouse is a pleasant
ride with Mr. Commodore Drank Tea there Mr. Codman is married to Miss Wheler
of Newburyport so you need not have any need of challenging him
on account of Edwin Edwards has began a letter to you but his
so taken up at the reading room that he can be prevailed on to do
little else than what relates to the society there. Mr. Knickerbocker
is a prisoner of war & many of the other gentlemen of this city
are in the army & I am sure that if our lives are preserved
& I sincerely hope our British Car will beat an end by that

Dear Brother Charleston July 8th 1813
We received a long letter from you this
morning, dated April 25th. The information it contained
was very gratifying to us all. -- I have received your
letter a few days since on the subject of the War,
but have understood since that no letters on political
subject would be received. In that letter also I gave
several particulars respecting the capture of the Ches
apeake which you will probably meet with either
in the English or American papers. An abstract of
these remarks I here insert: -- The Chesapeake sailed
from Boston harbour, the Shannon in full view about
9 miles off -- We saw the two vessels till 1/2 a few
from the top of the Exchange, till about an half
hour before they engaged. -- The circumstances of
the Chesapeake were these: -- In the first place,
she was notoriously the poorest vessel in our Navy,
very unpopular with the sailors -- She lay in this
harbour for months last fall after she was ready for
sea for want of a crew. The sailors would not enter her,
and the rendezvous was finally opened in New-York
where the vessel was unknown; and there they obtained
their crew. -- In the second place, Capt. Lawrence,
her commander, had been on board the frigate
he was, therefore, of course wholly unacquainted with her peculiarities in sailing &c. which
with such a misshapen vessel you know is a very important
particular. In the third place, the first & second Lieutenants were in the same predicament with Capt.
Lawrence, they had never before sailed in the vessel. In the fourth place, the third & fourth
Lieutenants were merely Senior Midshipmen acting
as Lieutenants. In the fifth place, the engagement engagement
took place immediately after the Chesapeake left port.
Her crew had been on shore 3 months, doubt half their
time; and and and in any good fighting time place to have been in a proper fighting mood experienced sea captains say, they ought to have been at least ten
days in the time place These are the disadvantages under

Charleston July 10th 1813
My dear Son, yesterday we had the highest satisfaction
receiving your good long letter which was concluded
the 27th of April. We all thank you for it. The serious
matter it contained gave us much pleasure, except
your disappointment relative to the Jacket sent by
Mr Woodson. Possibly he may have left it with
some friend at Liverpool who sent it into the office.
Whoever did it was to say the least, very inconsiderate
& disabling. I do not particularly mention its
contents as I have sent you so many letters since
July of which I keep no record or use.
Your dialogue with conscience in a good one
I am glad you have so faithful & good a friend
always near & that you are disposed to listen to his
reproof & yield to his arguments & monotonous.
I hope my dear son you will always be enabled to conduct
in such a manner as to have a friend in your
own bosom in an enlightened tender conscience. If
you have spared with your God, your condition on
Spirits grounds the highest happiness will be your
portion let what will happen to you in this changeful
& mixed state.
Your becoming industry & success in performing
your professional studies give your affectionate parents
the highest gratification & reward. We wish you to avoid
carrying your economy to an extreme. Let your appearance
be suited to a respectable company, you keep, & your
living suit, as will conduce most effectually to presence
health of body & vigor of mind. We shall all be
willing to make sacrifices at home, so far as may be
necessary to the above purposes. You did right to make
the excursion you did after so long confinement & must
be successful & free of your winter's labor. I hope to be
glad to have you visit Edinburgh if you can before

Donson Mr Jones falls in half an
hour -- I add a short letter to the Packages
delivered on Saturday -- Mr Hillhouse
has also added a letter -- I hope all will
reach you safely -- Your friends here
take a deep interest in your success -- Dr
Goddard yesterday sent me a note con-
tain'd in an Envelope from a letter from
Eliska dated 10 or 12 days after yours
that we received with some joy another
revel -- Goddard writes thus -- "I have
gained much honor & credit, and aspire
from the Royal Academy -- by an elegant
painting of a Lying Female, opened in the
Academy" -- We don't understand this --
Does he not mean the prize you mention
from the Philadelphia Society of Arts for your
Plaster cast? or have you also received
a prize for your painting from the
R. Academy? We wish you had described
a line on the subject -- send us with your
reply in Mr West's note to a line or two
from Mr Alston --
The season continued remarkably fine --
It is generally healthy in this region -- nothing
new since mine of Saturday -- I forgot to mention
that a 74,1 a troop of war, are building
in this town -- will make it at present a pretty
busy place -- Mr Jones, whom I hope you
will see, will be able to communicate
verbally many things which I cannot
write -- Will you see Mr Wilberforce,
Mr Mannering -- Mr Thornton -- Dr Letham --
Mr Bender present my regards? & those --
I say to them, that my sentiments towards
the War remain the same as contained
in the extract from my sermon published
in the Daily No. of the Christian Observer -- I trust
I hope their influence will be used to
effect a speedy peace, in equitable terms.
I shall send Mr Bromfield a bill soon --
write as often as you please, if but short
but don't omit long letters -- Let us have
an ant of your excursion to Windsor Castle.
We wish you to send us a miniature sketch
of your Meninles with the cast of your
figure with you long ago promised - Capt
Lungdon will bring them - I am tired of
books pamphlets &c. but you may wish to
see? - Get your parcels ready - before hand
opportunities will offer - write us via
Lisbon & Liverpool to the care of Mr Hoodry
or Mr Breed - If letters were deported
with either of them they would find their
way to us - you C.O. send them by
some private officer to them.
I have no time to add.
We are all well & in good spirits -
I send you a great deal of love
Your affectionate father
Emose
