LONDON
very Dear Son
Soon after I had written my last letter to you we received
your agreeable favour of the 27th of April there have several Vessels
arrived since from different parts of Old England but no letters
from you since have come from London Direct letters have arrived
to others from their friends in London which mention you
and confirm the impression that your own accounts give us
that you are doing well, we long to hear the progress of the medical
picture, and are anxiously looking out for letters every
time we hear of an arrival that shall convey to us this information,
We learnt from Mr Channing that they had
long particular letters from Mrs Alston this week and
that Mrs Alston's health is not good which we are very
sorry to learn we hope however that his indisposition is
temporary and that one this reaches you he will be quite
recovered give our kind remembrance to them – I hope any
dear son your success in your profession will not have a tendency
to make you vain or embolden you to look down
on any in your profession that Providence may have been
less favorable too in point of talent, for that particular
business and observe a modesty in the reception of premiums
and praises, on account of your talent, that shall shine to those who
besides them that you are worthy of them in more senses than
merely as an Artist it will likewise convince those who are
less favoured, that you are far from exerting in their disapprobation
- as I hope is truly the case - and prevent that jealousy,
and envy, that too often disfigures itself in those of the same
profession. - I think Mr Alston has ban a pattern to you in
this respect, I hope you will be enabled to follow all that is good
in him, by Mr Best, and other worthy characters, that you may
meet with, and that you will have afforded you that good sense
and sound discriminating views, of what is truly good as they
enable you to judge correctly, what is, in what is not, to be imitated
by you, in any or all the good people you may meet
with in this very wicked world, we are to hope constantly in
mind that perfection, is not to be found in any of our fellow
Doormen but that we are called on by our bibles to follow as our
Perfect pattern, our Lord Jesus Christ who did no sin, in following
him we cannot excuse excuse and to be like him must be our daily aim
if we hope to be with him through an endless eternity. I hope
you constantly attend church, under some evangelical preacher
you have not said anything about your Church, or your Sunday
lately, I hope my dear son that you will constantly keep
in mind this important part of your Education, to keep holy
the Sabbath day on no account but let each day you will spend
the house of God, and sh't let the goodness of God to you lead you
to repentance, and to a conscientious discharge of all your
duties, to your Maker, & preservers, your parents, & benefactors,
your Brothers connections & fellow men of every description
and to your own Soul and then through the mercies & Atonement
of a precious Redeemer, you shall be blessed & happy through
life, prepared, & ready for Death, and at last admitted to
a seat at God's right hand. We are pleased to receive
your observation in your last letter that the good instruction & advice
given you by your affectionate parents has been of great advantage
to you in restraining you from a participation in the vice & folly
of the present day. In your present situation in particular I have
induced you to continue my advice to you as formerly. I pray
that it may be accompanied with a divine blessing than shall
I rejoice indeed in having enjoined it so frequently. Be exceeding
joyed in all your success and hope you will however, remember
how very soon it is easier to get a reputation than to keep it
unspotted in the midst of so much pollution, and are surrounded
with, strong, active, industrious, economical
men. Your Papa intends to strain a point to allow you the sum he
gave you reason to expect he would for three years viz. two hundred
& six thousand pounds a year, he has just purchased
a bill of between two & three hundred L. & I have enclosed to Mr. Beecham

child for you, & hope you will receive it safely Your Brother Richard
Write on this week that he might you could send us some maps or
drawings of Virginia if that are accurate if they do not cost too much
we will be gratified by their attention. - I Dexter thanking you for
your attention to her request as it respects South Philadelphia she does
not wish you to take too much pains & trouble to get it but she

If you should get acquainted with him inform him that a very

Dear Parents,
I improve a few moments to write
you by Mr. Parkman who goes in a day or two;
My two last letters were sent by Mr. Goldard N.
Bay & Ba in one, I give a statement of my ex-
penses in order to show that 200 L is not suffi-
cient for a year to support me, I forgot to add, that I
do not expect you to advance me more than the
200 unless completely convenient, what expenses?
May in our over 2 above, I will try all in my power
to discharge from what I may make if I should be
able to make any thing. Daily thought it was but
a duty I owed to you as well as myself to tell you
the truth for though when I first arrived 200
would be sufficient, now, the expense of living here,
and the enormous taxes which are still increasing
has grown so great, that what cost 200 then would
now amount to 200; I am in perfect health, and
in excellent spirits as can be expected considering
I am absent from home, and in a country where
there now exists the most mortal hatred to America;
there is here no disposition to speak, and from what
I can learn they intend making us feel how their
words what it is to be so insolent to a nation who have
been so forbearing to them; I hope we shall make
them feel their rudeness towards us, for indeed they
are excessively proud, & overbearing; It began to be
shame of my native state, and of the Federal party,
which is the cause of the abhorrence which has cited the abhorrence
from every American here, one
sentiment pervades the whole, that the American schoo
longs the enemy, that the navy should be kept in readiness, that an independent
navy is necessary to the safety of this Nation, and that it is a
very impossible thing, especially at this time, to me ask, is it
the fault of our gallant naval heroes that this war is declared; if it were, it would alter the case, but after they
have done so much, & have raised the American name
to a higher standing than ever it was, when they have
done their duty (no matter whether in a just or unjust cause,
they are not the persons to decide,) does it become the
Mass. legislature to pass such resolutions, it is not the
way to make naval officers; Mass. boasts how much
she has always been in favor of a navy, and the first
time that navy distinguished itself, they not only do
not praise the officers of that navy for making it the
wonder of the world, but actually disapprove of their
conduct by vilifying them, and and the Democrats
have always opposed a navy, and the Federalists of Mass.
have now given the finishing blow to it. This is not the
way they make naval officers in England. Nelson when
he took the Danish fleet at Copenhagen, was applauded
by every man throughout England, for the great gal-
lantry displayed in the capture of it, yet there is
not one man out of ten, but will execrate the measures
the blame lies at the doors of the government,
not on the officers, who have no right to question the
policy or justice of the measures which they are com-
manded to execute; their business is to execute without
a word; and if they succeed they are as much to be ap-
plauded for their faithful discharge of their duty,
in a bad cause as in the best of causes.
What kind of government must that be where it
servants, or executors of its measures, may stop and say
I shall not do this, or that, because I think it unjust.
I think you cannot approve of such a government, I
should like to know your opinion on the subject, however
for I do not accuse you of thinking with Mr. Quincy

Since writing the above Mr. Parkinson has some

I have just received four very acceptable letters
by Mr. Jones they came to me free from postage.
They all gave me great pleasure; Goddard must have
made a mistake in his information to his father, there
are no prizes to contend for at the Royal Academy
at the season of the Exhibition, of course I could not
attend to the Students for the prize; I could not
attend to the Students only, the subject is given out for next Decr. I am
referring to painting Achilles for the body of Hector. I did
not intend to paint for the prize this year but the
subject is one which does not take hold of my enthusiasms
and I have abandoned it as I think I can
employ my time better. I gave Goddard the gold
prize medal to give to you, as it was of no use
to me here, it was from the Adelphi Soc. of Arts,
I was not the Roy. Acad. Mr. West promised
me a note to you, but he is an old man and very forgetful,
and I suppose he has forgotten it, I don't
wish to remind him of it directly, but if in the course
of conversation I can convince to mention it, I will.
Mr. Allston has not rec'd your 2d letter which you mention,
he will write you, however soon he is well
as is Mr. Allston; and desire their respectful remembrance
to you; I shall not write on Mr. Allston's success
or goodness, for I should never stop, if I once began,
so I will leave off before I begin. You give me leave
in your letter to go to Edinburgh, and to see as
much of England as I conveniently can, you have
anticipated a request I was going to ask, and I
cannot feel too thankful for your kindness. Edinburgh
and the Highlands of Scotland, have always
I have always wished to see; I have thought
what time would be most convenient for me and
I have fixed upon next April, if I should live;
that is generally a leisure time with Artists, they have
painted their exhibition pictures, and sent them, and
during the exhibition they have time for a little amusement.
With respect to returning home next summer Mr. Allston & Mr. West think it would be
an injury to me; Mr. A. says I ought not to return till I am a painter; I long to return as much
as you can wish to have me, but if you can spare me a little longer I should wish it; I abide your
decision however completely; Mr. Allston will write you fully on this subject, and I will endeavor to
persuade Mr. West also to do it. France I could not at present visit with advantage, that is to
say, for perhaps a year, Mr. Allston thinks I ought to be well grounded in the principles of the English
school, in order to resist the corruptions of the French school, for they are corrupt in their principles of painting
as in religion and every thing else; but when well grounded in the good principles of this school, I could
study and select the fine beauties of the French, without being in danger of following their errors, the Louvre alone,
which is about a year's stay, would be of the greatest advantage to me, and also the fine works in Italy.
I was sorry Rich was depressed and a little ill, he must come to Eng., he and Edw. is too, to be reformed
in their politics. The pamphlet you sent me by Massachusetts, I can guess E.H.B. was the author, if so it
Charleston August 15th 1813.
Dear Brother.
I write you in great haste by Dr
Romeyn who leaves New-York in a cartel
for London for the recovery of his health.
We have had a good many loose reports
about you & your paintings lately. We were
told that the English papers claimed you
as an Englishman, and denied you that
you was born in America. We heard like
wise that your painting had obtained
the prize. We don't believe any thing till
we find it confirmed by your letters. So
write us often, especially good news. We had
a letter from Richard a few days since
he was not very well, his writing had
affected his health & spirit, but a jour-
ney in the fall will set him up again
as it did me. He wrote us that Thay
Sanford of his class was dead. In his
returning from Virginia (where he had
been keeping school) to Connecticut,
he was taken sick with a fever, from
which he recovered, but continuing his
journey too suddenly, he relapsed I did
Simmonds also of the Class before you, died
in a most shocking manner. He was pri-
soned by a mistress of his keeping, in revenge
for his having married another woman. —
Your classmates are all well as far as my
knowledge extends. Northrop & Bill Huntington
& my class are Officers in our Army. —
Isaac Larkin, & John Larkin (who used to live
at the bottom of our garden) are Midshipmen
in the navy. — Boston looks quite dreary & desolate.
No American shipping in the harbour, except
ships stripped of their rigging and by nothing at
the wharves. It is no uncommon thing
to look round the harbour and not see a single
American flag. The town is depopulating
rapidly. Charleston is a little more busy.
The 7th A 7th, & a shop of war are building
here? — The season here is uncommonly fine.
The crops of grain & grass are immense. A good
season was never more needed. Our coasting
trade is entirely destroyed. All the flour from
Pennsylvania & Maryland is carried to Boston
over land, a thing unprecedented in this
country till since the Declaration of War.
Papa & Mama have gone to Andover to spend a
few days. They are both remarkably well. This
summer. Papa hasn't been so well this many
a year. I go to Roulstone's Riding School.
You have tried to find a different
from them in me. I have taken three or four
lessons and can trot rapidly though not Canter
yet. I have read a description of Wests famous
painting in the Cambridge Report
extracted from an English Magazine. It is
a very interesting piece from the description It
must be worth as you say a voyage across the
Atlantic.
I would write you longer but the gentleman
is to carry this to N.York cannot.
I am your affectionate brother.
Sidney Edwards Mosse

My dear Brother I am commissioned by Papa to write
you by a cartel, I only have half an hour to write. I am
told to write all I can think of.
At present our house is full of company. Dr. Dwight &
his son William Skinner of N. Haven are here with other
company. Madox is sick up stairs with a painful swell-
ing which prevents her sitting up. She hopes to get rel-
ief from it in a few hours. Edw. S. & myself accompany
Dr Dwight on his journey to Portsmouth & Munificence
Lake. We go on horseback.
Saint Salisbury & are well. Betray Brazier Uncle Ar-
thur's second daughter spends the next winter in Boston.
Edw. S. & myself spend the next twelve months at home
& in Mr. Rockwood's Office & I, to recruit & confirm
my health, in a most anxious manner.
It was quite sickly with the dysentery at N. Haven
when we left there I continue so. Three Students died
so fast has been dangerous ill. We are anxious to
hear from him. Rosseter devotes himself quite as
much to painting as to Law.
Simonds the Mulatto in Mr. Hitchcock's class died
a shocking death in his own country. He was poisoned
by a kept mistress of his, because he married another wo-
man. Poor Sanford too died of a fever a few weeks since
who was so ambitious to be distinguished.
We had a very good Commencement at Yale. A small
class entered, but we shall have near 300. next year.
A medical Establishment is now connected with the
College in the large plaster house belonging to Mr. Kil-
house. The celebrated Dr. Smith of Hanover is one of the
professors & Dr. Ives too. Hamilton College near Utica,
(New York) takes many of our College Students. It is un-
der Dr. Backus, is magnificently endowed & its situation
is favourable to its being one of the first Seminaries.
Miss Welsey (the eldest) is married. Young Edwin Porter
will be soon & Rev. Welsey. Robert Kane who was here
with the Ralstons is dead. There is a Benevolent Society
in College to aid indigent Students. It is hoped this will
be an era in the History of our Literature.
You may consider Charleston as permanent-
ly Washington & Federal. We have an Establishment called Washington Hall, and a Washington
Reveolent Society which will strengthen each other
hands.
Here I'm call'd to give my letter. I'm sorry
I can't write you more I will finish another time
All send love. I am your affectionate brother
Rb. Morge.
Note We have too a Society for suppressing Intemperance & other Vice. Its good effects are felt. None of our fruit has been stolen this year.
Mr. S. F. B. Morse.
London.
My dear Son, I have time to write you but
a very few lines. Your last letter rec'd was dated
the 30th of May in which you mention that you
had begun a long & partular one, which we
are anxiously expecting. Capt. Langsdorff in a
letter to Mrs L. of the 20th June informed that you
were then well & doing well. All are safe and if
you have given us pleasure & comfort I trust
you will be enabled to persevere in a good
course & continue to be successful. We shall
calculate to see you by leave of Providence
before the War Commences at N. Haven.
You had better make your arrangements to leave
Long Island in July next, & do me all you can
to suit you. From reports which have reached
us we shall expect a good deal of you &
hope you will do what you can to deserve
the reputation you have among us.
We are all well except your Mother who
has been previously afflicted with a boil for a
week past but we trust her extreme pain
is nearly over. I attend to W.H. Conklin
your brother in every way. He is a prosperous
man. I am
Ever affy

Dear Brother
Charleston Novt 17th 1813.
We received your letter and medal a few
days since, and were highly gratified with the tokens
of your improvement in painting. The engraver of the medal was the handsome Mr. Stanhope, and
Goddard had not arrived. He transmitted the letters of from
Washington, and stated that he should sail to bring with him
the statue by the next ship. Allston's Poems have been re-
published in this country, and are very well spoken of. They
have been out of print but a few days, and have therefore
not yet seen recrud. I have read them & was much
pleased. Great expectations are entertained of his future
eminence.— About a month since I entered my name
in Mr. Rockwood's Office, where I shall stand six or eight
months.— Rich spent the winter with us engaged in miscellaneous
Mama, Richard & Nancy went to Woodstock last week to see
Grandfather. He is now 88 years old. He had received
from the train which he received by his fall, so far as to
go from one room to another. Mama showed him the golden
medals. I read your letter. He was much delighted with every
thing but the politics. Charles & Jedidiah to have gone with
their families settled in the Genesee country in the
west of N York. Lyman stays at Woodstock. I will visit
the homestead of the Moore family. Lyman had been in the
service of the State of Conn. to defend Delawors. Lyman
you have doubtless long since heard of the gallant exploit of
SPERRY in his crossing on Lake Erie. Our regrettings on this
occasion are mingled with sorrow. By the last mail from
the North Wilkeson with from 6 to 10,000 men was sailing
down the St Lawrence for Montreal. It was 100 miles distant.
Hampshire will join him with 4000 in the neighborhood of that
city. He ought to succeed. Our weather on this subject I
know differ from mine, but I shall not cease to desire it.
96724—The Constitution now lies in our harbour ready for sea. The Indigo, a new 20
gun sloth of 1100 will be ready in a few weeks. The 74 which
with carry when finished 90 guns and be a match for
any ship that swims, is for the stocks. It will be finished
by next July. There is another building at Portsmouth, &
another in Philadelphia. Boston is debouching. Emigrations
from every part of our England to the Western States increase
daily. The War has deprived large classes of our citizens of
employment and they go neither for subsistence nor confidence
England is interested in Japan as she is in her commerce.
She is now reduced to the rank to which
her population & financial resources entitle her -- The English
suffis have announced that a division of the States!! this is rather
premature -- Neither has the Macedonian been captured by the
Syndesos -- We are all on tefelor for news from Europe. The last
accounts left Bonaparte in Dresden Report have stated that he
executed it on the 13th September -- Now that one thing must have been
decided, and with it the fate of our hopes in Europe -- The
Report says that Bonaparte has threatened us with that of our
ambassadors make Peace with England. Then our Naval War
for us -- I must defer giving my reasons for now not thinking
Poetry superior to Paintings. I will mention only, the use of
the principles upon which I ground my Judgment. Genius
is defined here in both their arts, genius is the power of
making impressions. The question then is, which artist
is capable of making the strongest impressions, which
can impress upon the mind most strongly, a sublime or
a beautiful idea? Does the sublime passage in Milton
or the sublime painting of Michael Angelo create a stronger
sensation in the mind of a man of taste than the sublime
painting of Michael Angelo? Or to put the two cases more
completely make the parallel more complete. Can
Michael Angelo convey to you a stronger impression of the Last Judgment
by his painting, than Milton could by his Poetry? Could
Michael Angelo convey a more sublime idea of Death by his
painting than Milton has in his Paradise Lost? -- These are the
principles upon which "divine art" is to be degraded below
Poetry. Addressed to my affectionate brother S.S. Morse.

SIR,
THE Artists of the United Kingdom are respectfully invited to join a
select Number of Painters in an Exhibition of native Talent, at the commencement of the
ensuing Year, being a Period when only one Exhibition of Art is open, although the
Attendances required upon Parliament, the Courts of Justice, the Vacations of the
Universities, and all the Seats of Learning, cause the Metropolis to have a great influx of
its Residents and Visitors; they therefore purpose sending their Works here on the 5th
and 6th—open the 15th, of January; and close precisely on the last Day of March.
They feel anxious to receive Pictures which have not been exhibited;
but that Circumstance will not, in the present instance, be considered, as an Assemblage
of Talent is their chief object.
The Names of the associated Artists may be seen at the Room; no
Expense will attach, except a Commission of 5 per Cent. upon Works sold. Should this
Exhibition meet the expectations of the Public and Exhibitors, it is intended to be
continued Annually.
I am,
SIR,
Your respectful and obedient Servant,
WILLIAM LAXTON,
SECRETARY.

My Dear Son
our State Thanksgivings in this day by the appointment of our excellent Governor Strong & your brothers are both at home & only await the pleasure of your Company to complete our little group which would make us very happy but we cannot expect uninterrupted happiness in this Vale of tears & must regret not to devote our self to it. I shall wish your good health and success in your profession in a glass of wine at dinner which I doubt not you will re
appricate by wishing ours when you receive this. I am all well and in pretty good spirits. Your paper of Edwards wrote you a few days ago by the way of Lisbon this will be handed you by Capt. Pratt who will tell you all about us he expects to leave his son Edward in England & will probably return himself in the course of a twelve months (when he comes if you don't return this year) I hope you will get him to take Charge of the three pictures I have so often mentioned that I wish you to prepare for Ship Russell Dr Bartlett & Aunt Salisbury I give you the dimensions of the pictures for Dr Bartlett in a former letter I hope my son you will attend to this request it is not necessary to tell Capt. Pratt that you are preparing these pictures for the persons I have named till they are completed and put under his care.— We are anxious to see the painter's cost but fear it will be injured before it arrives as E. Goddard has sold his ship which was to have brought it I want your Friends should be gratified by seeing your improvements in your art as soon as is convenient, Edwards & Buchard are enjoying themselves with us at home they and we cannot help troubling at your political observations we all wish you would leave politics to them who have to act in them and not trouble yourself about them
with all your feeling you from we cannot alter let us leave these
things to those who with ourselves will have to answer at a higher
tribunal than any their fellow creatures can erect for all
their conduct while in this state of existence. I must remind you
of some observations you made to me before you left home with
regard to politics. You said you was glad that you was going to
a country where the people minded their own particular
business and every man was not as in this country Apposition
especially you observed that those who engaged in the fine Arts
never nor cared about the politics of the day, now I can
truly say I never was more surprised than to find you so
deeply engaged in the state of public affairs on both sides the
ocean as your letters indicate. you think you have the best means of
being well informed on the subject of Politics we think the reverse
of what consequence is it to either as we have not the power of
attaining any measures of either government if we wish it it
had better not fill our letters with disputes on the subject.
With regard to the Americans being disfined & hated in England
you were apprized by your Uncle Salisbury & others
before you left this country that that was the case and you
ought not to be surprised when you realized it the reason
given was that a large portion of those who visit Europe are
disputed Infidels which has justly given the English a bad
opinion of us as a nation, but we are happy to find that there
are many exceptions to those who do honour to the country
which gave them birth such as a West an Ulster & many
others among whom I am happy to say that we hope
you may soon will be enrolled at no very distant day
your fond parents, & affectionate Brothers to gether with Mrs
Rufsell & many kind friends are much gratified at your suc-
cess & the honour confided on you in consequence & we are
extreamly anxious that you should conduct in all respects
with great prudence & circumspection & recommend your-
self as much by these & other good Qualities as by your
Art, we are much entertained with any descriptions that you have
given us of your journeys to different Places we are still anxious
to see your account of your Oxford visit and shall wish also to
hear how you are pleased with Bristol and how you found
Mr Rufsell family & we are likewise very desirous of knowing
here you attend Church and how you like the preaching & speaking
in which you have been instructed from your infancy & with
whence you have been instructed from your infancy & with
whence you have been instructed from your infancy & with what
is going on in the Religious World by keeping up your acquaintance
with Mr Burder Mr McCarley Mr Taylor & others of that
description you might afford us great pleasure by letting us
know what was being done to spread the Blessed Gospel through the
medium of Bible & Missionary Societies as you mention you
had begun to reform by attending to some of your papers (which
we have not yet received) we hope you will extend your good
dispositions still farther and attend to what is mentioned in
this letter. you mention being acquainted with young Payne
the play actor it would scarce you acquaint any acquaintance with
96728
that description of people as it will sooner or later have a most
corrupting effect on the morals, and as a man is known by
the company he keeps I should be very sorry to have you enrolled
with such society however pure your morals may be Your father & myself was elven days in company with him
in coming from Charleston SC his behaviour was quite unexceptionable then but he is in a situation to ruin the best morals I hope
you do not attend the theatre as I have ever considered it a most

Daughter Betty is spending the Winter with your Aunt Salisbury, she is quite a pretty girl, they are all much pleased
with your letters (all but the politicals) With your success, generally I

Your acquaintance also beg to be kindly remembered to you

you very much Your papa is writing you & your Brother Richard
has begun a letter to you my paper is full so I must bid you adieu
many, many best blessings and I am in the constant prayers of your
most affectionate mother Edith

My dear Brother, Your letters by the September & also the
medal gave us great pleasure. The politics however were
very disagreeable & occupied no inconsiderable part of your
letters. Your kind wishes for our reformation we must beg
leave to retard by hoping for your speedy amendment.
A friend who was here & heard the letter in which you
long'd to be in the navy, suggested it as a good subject
for you, to represent yourself "hastising the insolent
Englishmen." We do not however read the political
tracts to your friends. They are marked off & always passed
over. Your accounts of your excursions of your em-
ployments are what we like to hear. Indeed every step
you take gives us pleasure to know.
I am spending the year at home recruiting my health
which suffered from too close confinement last year. I gave
you an account of the journey we took with Dr. Dwight
since that I have taken another with Mann & Nancy
to Woodstock. We went in a hack, were gone 5 days. Mann
raps was comfortable. He has Aunt More to take care of
him. He moves from his room to the other to meals
by taking hold of the arms of his rocking chair & having
it between him. He has a stick suspended from the
wall over his bed & by taking hold of this with both
hands raises himself up from the bed. Walter is a
curiosity for his height six feet four inches & very slender.
He is quite a mechanical genius & is at the shoemaker's
trade. Charles & Peddicial had lately moved old
to the western parts of New-York State. to Painted Post.
They had just heard of them. Jeds was settled & Charles
was within 2 days journey of the place. He set off, his
96731
family & goods in an ox-waggon their wardrobe perhaps
in a pack'd up in a firkin &c he trudging a foot.
We read your letters to Grandpapa. While, Lyman, &c
They were highly amused with your accounts.
There is much to interest you. Papa will send you the pa-
pers & pamphlets which will give you information of the
situation of our armies. The Massachusetts legislature
meets in January. There are many grounds they may
take bold & spirited. The retaliatory system our gov. have
adopted on account of the 23 British taken fighting
against their country threatens to make the war a war
of extermination & to bring destruction to our seaports.
If so Mass. will adopt measures for self Preservation.
But probably the gov. will back out "tho' to act con-
sistently with their own principles, they are bound to
protect those 23 British subjects.
Again, The Russian Mediation has failed. The Govern-
ments papers have avowed that they have not any with
expectation or any wish that peace should it should
bring a peace. Since then the only door by which the
New England states, hoped for peace is shut & there is
now no prospect before us but a long war, it is not im-
probable she will extricate herself from it, since her
petitions & remonstrances are disregarded by her author-
ity as an Independent State. She is no longer bound
to the Union, as the constitution has been broken
& the admission of other new territory to the rights of
States has taken away the power & influence which
she originally had. At any rate you may expect measures
worthy of her high character.
We hear little of New Haven. Safford has been twice
severely sick once his life was despaired of. He is slowly
recovering, but is so feeble as to render his situation
pneumaticous. Nothing from any of your class. Edw. is in
Mr. Rockwood's office, mayt spring he goes to Litchfield &
probably will after that study in Connecticut or New-
York. What serious business I shall pursue at the end of
a twelve month is quite uncertain.
Papa keeps a horse so that we are able to ride. Edw.
spends much of our time at the Reading Room. a sort
of office where the respectable gentlemen meet.
Cousin Betsey Broce is spending the day with us &
sends her love to you.
The 74 will be launched by next June. The Constitution
is ready for sea. & the Trolic Hoop is in our harbor.
There is a great deal of smuggling. Many merchants
are engaged in manufactures & some loan their
money to Gov. By these means the war is opposed becoming less opposed
by the wealthy but the poor & the common people
will be the next to complain. There has been a surpris-
ing number of tragical events a consequence of the
war. An Indian & his squaw were wantonly shot at
Malden a day or two ago. Many soldiers shot for deser-
tion & many murders are committed.
I saw Edw. Cotton your former master in the avenue of
the Exchange Building. He is quite a sputtering politi-
cian & has changed his principles for he was labouring
to prove that the Canadians would not fight for their
Government but were quite willing to submit to the
U.S. I have nothing more at present.
Your affectionate Brother
R.C. Morse

Dear Brother,
I wrote you a long letter a few days since
by Mr. Abbott. Papa, Mama, Richard Ve have written repeatedly
within a few weeks, so that I very much fear you
will be inundated with congratulatory messages. I have
during the past year heard my long epithets to your
name and written frequently for the New Yorker, and
exited much democratic wrath. I have been loaded
with the epithets, Tory, Traitor, British partisan, &c
&c, but have happily survived. The democratic paper of this morning speaking of one
of my pieces in the Centinel, says "The fault in the Centinel deserves the severest castications. The writer
has given the strongest possible proof of his attachment to Britain, and as a punishment for his
crime he ought to be made to run the gauntlet from Maine to the Mississippi." The piece they
refer to is in the Centinel of the 24th Novr headed
"Harrison & Perry." You may have an idea of pursuing it.
Our Canada Expedition has terminated most disgracefully by the acknowledgement to all parties the jubilee
which had been excited to the highest pitch by the promises of the War Hawks. The 15th of Novr was the
day lived upon for the capture of Montreal. Wilkinson & Hamilton were to form their junction on the 14th but for the
city, I were to dash like a thunderbolt upon the
purified Canadians." Bets were laid to a large amount
that Montreal was ours on the 15th. In this state of
things the news came that a large detachment of Wil-
kinson's army had been betrayed into drawers between
into an ambuscade where they were placed between
two lines of cannon. I were moved down most terribly
The next news, Wilkinson was building huts to winter
in, Hampton had gone into winter quarters, and
all thought of Montreal was postponed to another
& more convenient season. I have no time to add
further.
Your affectionate brother
I E Lee

Wednesday 12th June, 1814
My dear Sir
Having a great deal of business
to attend to this morning, I can
spare but a moment for writing.
I must however wait myself of that
to thank you for the agreeable intelligence contained in your letter to Leslie: but in a particular manner
to request (for rather to advise) you not
to take a share in the intended raffle.
For this I can offer two reasons:
first, that the price of a share is so
much for you to risk upon another
uncertainty; second, that I much
fear, should you win, that the world
will may suspect (on account of
our connexion) that I was in some
way interested in it. I think
upon the whole you had better not
take one; but wait until you can
paint an a landscape equal to it yourself,
which I make no doubt, you will ere
long be able to do if you are industrious.
I shall follow your advice in not
being too sanguine respecting its success.
But hope is pleasant, and I shall therefore
indulge it until I hear from you again.
I am quite satisfied that it should go
at five hundred; and as soon as it is
sold I shall, according to my promise, be
at work on an elegant frame for it.
I have at last the satisfaction
to inform you that my large Picture
is in the British Gallery, and, more
happily in the place where Mr West's was.
You have added much to the above
agreeable intelligence by your favourable
account of the invalids at Mr Dungers.
Give our love to them all.
Yours with as much sincerity
as possible, H Hinton.
P. I. On your letter to me (received a week since)
you omitted the Fitzroy Square in the superscription.
You must recollect it in future; as some of
my letters have been lost in consequence of that
misfortune; there being several London Streets in London.
I wrote to my good Mr King the other day.

Washington, January 12th 1840.
Esteemed friend,
I was fearful you might think me negligent in
not writing agreeable to promise, and obtaining the registered
certificates from the Office at this Depot. I would
have the goodness to excuse me for that neglect when I inform
you, that as I forgot my valuable friend in the Office, I returned
to me his intention of writing upon immediately, and I consider
it unnecessary for me to write until I heard from you upon
the subject. I expect you have received his letter, with
its valuable advice, in which much confidence of success may
be placed. I hope not to be found wanting in any thing
that may contribute to your benefit. I am human in demanding
for my removal from the unhappy place. The business of
the Office might have prevented Mr Sergant from writing,
so soon as you wished, which was the next morning.
As some time has elapsed, my anxiety compels me to
write, hoping it will not be considered premature.
As soon as convenient undoubtedly you will let me know the
prospect of success. – The money which I received was a
step to make me comfortable in the prison, during this
inconvenient season. – In case you should not succeed in
obtaining my liberty of parole, I have a prospect of going
into some little bump of malnage which will support
me during the winter if you can let me have about
five pounds, and I shall not be necessary to trouble you
again on that subject. – It will be necessary for me
to give you a receipt when ever a convenient time may
offer. — I still place confidence on your endeavors for
my freedom, but we not without my fear. — I hope you
will have the goodness to let me know soon. —
A kind providence preserves my health, may the time
elapsing attend you, with a prosperous new year & many
succeeding years of happiness & prosperity. I am dear friend
& most affectionate your faithful friend & servant.
Wm. Bennitt.

Chapleton Prison February 22d 1844
Respected Friend
I received your letter of the 19th. Your kind efforts for
my release, having failed, yet I shall hold in grateful remembrance
the exertions which you have made, and your solicitude for my
welfare. It is indeed a consolation to think that negociation
is going on for the purpose of putting an end to the miserable war.
I feel interested for my country's welfare as well as desire for
liberty from Prison. As to the probable result it is not for me
in the situation to form an opinion as means of information are cut
off. — No letters have as yet been received from America
by any of the prisoners from their friends arriving here expect
by the arrival of the Fair America at Liverpool. — A letter
has however been received from Mr Brown, harbour Master of
this port stating that he expected we would be on our passage home
before his letter reached England from this we expect something. —
I am in daily expectation of letters. — You mention that it
will be as late as May before you shall see me again.
I hope you will not think I trespass on your goodness in
aspiring the further assistance of two pounds, as I had made
some calculation, and if I can have it soon I will put me
in the way of some little business, by which I shall be able to
support myself comfortable, and will trouble you no further
until assistance from home. By enclosing it to the care of
Mr Sergeant it will come safe as many prisoners receive money
the way from different parts. — any way you may find out by a
receipt or an order shall be punctually attended to & as soon as I receive
letters from home by your grateful concern find a seat.
Mr S J B Morel.

My Dear Twenty,
I have had for writing a long letter, the twelve months, Mr.
Barney Smith of Boston, and family, are going in the fair
American capital and have kindly offered to take a letter
to you, for me, as the vessel I understand is not allowed
by government to take a letter bag. Mr Smith and family
have been extremely attentive to me since I have been
here, notwithstanding the great difference in our political
sentiments; Party distinction among Americans
in this country is soon lost, and their only ambition
is to see which can be the most hospitable to Americans;
I wish it was so at home. Mr Smith will call on you and tell you all about me. Mrs
Lydia Smith, (the daughter) is a very accomplished
girl, among other acquisitions, she has a good knowledge
of painting, and her talents are such for the art,
that she bids fair, not only to excel, but to be
another ornament to American genius in the
arts, and to have her name on the list as the first
and female artist of any age.
I have been to the Plantation office for
Papa, and the clerk is copying the record for me,
which if done in time I shall send with this
it is of some import.
I have just received your letter by Capt. Patt which
he sent me from Liverpool; the parents I suppose he will
be here in a few days.
London March 1st 1814.
I improve the first goods of opportunity
to you, as the vessel I understand is not allowed
by government to take a letter bag. Mr Smith and family
2 reserve till he comes to London himself. There is a great
drawback on my writing long letters to you, I mean the
uncertainty of their reaching you, I wrote a letter the
other day by a Russian Cepel, which has since put
back and is not going what will become of her letter
I do not know, there is now seldom an opportunity.
Mama's long letter gave me particular pleasure, some
of her observations however made me smile, especially
to reason she assigns for the contempt and hatred of Eng-
land to America; first I am inclined to doubt the fact of
there being so many infidel Americans in the country, second
if there were, there are not so many religious people
here who would take the pains to inquire, whether they
had religion or not, and third, it is not by seeing the
individual Americans that an opinion unfavorable to
us is prevalent in England; I could give a much more
plausible reason I think, and one which will not be
found to be far from the truth; It is founded in a regular
system of the British Government to belittle America, to
make it appear the most miserable country in the world, as
pickly, under a complete anarchy, a country which is
productive in none of the necessities of life; &c. &c. and all
this, for what? to prevent Emigrations, this is a fact,
too well known to be denied; have they not here travellers to
write about the country & misrepresent it? I have such
proof of this by an accident which occurred to a friend
and countryman of ours, that the truth is too well established
to admit of a doubt. I will relate it to you when I re-
turn home. I find you have completely mistaken my
opinions of politics, because I have completely diverted
myself of party, therefore I must be a democrat, this I
think is very unfair that I cannot differ at all from
Yoderahits but with one jump you set me down on the
other side. With out entering into the subject of politics
or giving you a detailed account of my reasons for think-
ing as I do, I declare once for all, and solemnly, that
I am as far from one party as the other, I despise them
both, I consider them both mistaken, each endeavoring
to establish a superiority over the other, without regard-
ing the the interest of the country at large, each would
rejoice, at the downfall of its opponent, events were
the disgrace of the United States the consequence, each
calling the other hard names, tell the whole Billingsgate
vocabulary, exhausted of its most vulgar epithets.
This may appear as were opinion, but it nevertheless ex-
actly my sentiments, I consider myself as old except
to have an opinion of my own, I can see and judge
for myself, but as I said in a former letter, my heart
is often to conviction, and whenever I find reason to
alter my opinion, and my conscience shall tell me I
am in the right I shall do it & not till then. At present
I see no reason to change my opinion, I am not Federal-
ist enough to wish for the disgrace of my country, nor
Democrat enough to wish for the destruction of England, but
I am just American enough to wish for a speedy and
honorable restoration of peace between us & Great Britain.
Thus endeth Politics.
With respect to my religious sentiments they are unshaken,
their influence I hope will always guide me through life;
I have various preaching on Sundays, sometimes Mr. Burdett,
but most commonly the church of England clergy, as a
church is in my neighbourhood and Mr. B's 3 miles distant;
when in Bristol I most commonly heard Dr. Biddulph of
St. James's Ch., a most excellent orthodox evangelical man.
I was on the point many times of going to hear Mr. Lowell
who is one of the dissenting clergymen of Bristol, but as
the weather proved very unfavorable, uncommonly so
every Sunday I was there, and I was at a great distance
from his Ch., I was disappointed I shall endeavor to
hear him preach when I go back to Bristol again.
I have returned from Bristol to attend the
Exhibition, and to endeavour to get a picture into
Somerset House; my stay in Bristol was very
pleasant indeed, as well as profitable, I was then
5 months, and in May shall probably go again &
stay all summer, I was getting into good business
in the portrait way there, and if I return shall be
enabled probably to support myself as long as I
stay in England. The attentions shown me by
Mr. Harman Visser & family whom I have mentioned
in a former letter, I shall never forget, he is a rich
merchant, an American, ( cousin to Capt. Vischer my fel-
low passenger, by whom I was introduced to him,) he has a fam-
ily of seven children, I lived within a few doors of him
in Bristol, and was in and out at his house every
day
vented by illness from writing before. I shall ende-
avor to support myself, if not, necessity will compel
me to return home an unfinished painter; it
depends altogether on circumstance, I may get
a good run of portraits or I may not; it de-
pends so much on the whim of the public; if
they should happen to fancy my pictures I shall
succeed; if not, why, I shall not succeed; I am,
however, encouraged to hope.
I have given up the thought of visiting
Stirnburgh, it will cost too much.
I was extremely happy to hear that you
had given my brothers your Georgian Gazetteer , I
will certainly aid them all in my power, by pur-
chasing books, maps, &c. which they shall wish, or
I chance on any new work of use to them I will
purchase it and forward it. If I am prohibited from
writing or thinking of politics, I hope my brothers
will not be so ungenerous as to give me any. Every
thing is interesting from home which is of a pleasant
nature; now they certainly cannot suppose
that a black catalogue of all the disgraces
which we have suffered since the commencement
of the war, with numerous alterations, and additions,
being a 3d or 4th edition of the continual
changes which are rung in my ears from morning
to night by the English newspapers, can be
very pleasant to me; it is hard enough that
10 they are true, harder to hear them from English mouths,
and what must it be, when, after the cry has a little
subsided here, to receive a budget of letters, blaying
forth the same disgrace in the most glowing colors, and telling
me for my consolation that my country is fast going
to ruin: no accounts of some gallant exploit of
a Perry or a Barroughs, a mere general out-
line of which is given here, leaving the particular
to come as they may. — I am not so much of a
partisan yet as to feel rejoiced at any misfor-
tune of the Americans' arms merely because it was
a scheme of a man of an opposite opinion in
politics to myself; I look to the general conse-
quence on the world at large, I find the A-
mericans disgraced, I don't ask did Mr. Madison
plan the scheme; will it not help our election;
will the Federal or democratic cause suffer
or gain in consequence? These are questions
which may be asked and answered by selfish politicians;
I ask what will Europe think of us,
will they say the democrats are beaten, the
Federalists have gained their point; No, they say
the Americans are beaten, the English have
gained their point. — I am well aware that
my sentiments must appear strange to you all,
but if it is any satisfaction to you (and I have
no doubt it will be) I know that I act I speak
completely from the heart, I have not disguised in
the slightest degree, my conscience bear me out
in every thing. I find I am three and twenty
years old, that I am neither blind nor deaf, can
hear, and I hope understand, that I have some
judgment in many things, that I can trace the cause
of that judgment to their sources; and I also have
found that I am in England, wide awake & that it
is no dream; now having found all this I begin
to exercise my judgment (which at 23 years of age
ought to have acquired a little strength,) and I do
and hear things every day & decide accordingly
and yet my brother tells me they have all the means
of knowing & I none, they are right and I am wrong,
when I see a thing I must believe it, when I hear
a sentiment I must believe I heard it.
Good night.
Marl. 14th. J. C. Dick.

Mr. Allston's large picture is now ex-
hibiting in the British Gallery, it has excited a
great deal of curiosity, and he has obtained, a
wonderful share of praise for it with this, I
14. send you the Examiner newspaper containing a
critique upon it, the picture very deservedly ranked among
the highest productions of art, either in ancient or modern times, it is really a pleasant consideration, that
the palm of painting still rests with America, and
is, in all probability destined to remain with us; all
we wish is a taste in the country, and a little more
wealth; taste is altogether acquired, any man of good common sense, who will interest himself in
the thing and study, closely apply himself to acquire it,
may in a short time become, a man of taste, be able
to discover the different kinds of excellence in art,
separate the real from the fictitious, and justly to appreciate
merits. In order to create a taste, however, pictures, first-rate pictures, must be introduced into the country, for
taste is only acquired by a close study of the merits of the old masters; In Phila. I am happy to find they
have successfully begun; I wish Americans would
waste in the thing, throw aside local prejudices, and
give their support to one institution, let it be
in Phila. since it is so happily begun there, and
let every American feel a pride in supporting that
Institution, let it be a national not a city business,
then might the arts be so encouraged, that American
artists might remain at home, and not, as at present
be under the painful necessity of exciting themselves
from their country and their friends. This will
come to pass in the course of time, but not in my day,
I fear, unless there is more exertion made to forward
the art than at present. I wish Edwards would
extract the critique on Mr. Allston's pictures, and with
some few prefatory & complimentary remarks, have
it inserted in one of the papers, it would be grati-
fying to Mr Allston's friends I think, and it would also
be to me. I could write you longer, for I have many
more things to say to you, I wish to see you very much,
but I must forego that happiness, for my future
advancement in the art, which I have chosen, my love
for it is unabated, or rather I may say increased,
for the more I study it, the greater reason I have
to admire it, & to bless heaven for giving me
parents who have thrown no obstacle in the way
of my unlimited pursuit of it.
I wish you to remember particularly, that
although (through want of time to re-write this) I
have confounded the political part of this letter
with the rest, I intend the political for my brother,
and do they shall be the last opinions I will write to
any of you; for upon re-reading them, I see the
inutility of telling you them, for it is impossible, you
should see what I do, there, nor you cannot straight
the matter properly: I may be wrong & you may be
wrong, but as different circumstances operate to
form different opinions in each of us, we had bet-
ter not waste our time, and destroy our mutual
pleasure in receiving letters by discussing, so endles
a topic as politics, and I agree to drop them altogether.
16. I am in very good health, and I hope I feel grate-
ful for it, I have not been ill for two days together
since I have been in England; I am however of
the walking-stick order, and think I am thinner
than I was at home, they all tell me so; I ain't
so good-looking either, I am told, I have lost
my color, grown more sallow, and a face ap-
proaching to the hatchet class; but none of these
things concern me, if I can paint good looking
plump ladies and gentlemen, I shall feel satisfied.
Mr. Allston has had severe illness, but
he has happily recovered, not only his former health
but I think has got a complete new constitution
he is stouter, and more healthy than I ever saw
him before; Mr. Allston is also in good health.
They both devise particular remembrance to you.
We have had a dreadfully severe winter here
in England, such as has not been known for 22
years; when I came from Bristol the snow was up
on each side of the road as high as the top of the coach,
in many places, especially on Marlborough down,
and Hounslow heath.
The copying of your second from the Trade
office, cost three guineas, which I shall charge
to you. I have not time to copy it as you desire
for I have to lose so good an opportunity.

since from Mr. Wm. Walker in Paris, wishing

London, 15 March, 1814.
My dear Sir, Though your son has informed
me that you mention having written me
twice, I have not had the pleasure of receiving
more than one letter from you. In reply to
your inquiries respecting the necessity of
his continuing longer abroad, I have no
hesitation in saying that his return
home at present would be of the
greatest disadvantage to him; having
arrived just at that stage of his art
when, as he is most capable of appreciating
their excellence, his studying
the works of the Old Masters in the most
neccessary, and here perhaps, it may
be well to observe that of the time
required to complete the education of
an artist no calculation can be made
from what is usually allotted to the
study of the learned professions. Three
years is, I think generally considered
sufficient for the Law and Physick; if
not sufficient to make able professors,
at least, enough to qualify, and entitle
students in the privilege of practice. This,
however, is very far from being the case
with respect to the higher departments
of the Art. In the first place, the rudiments
must be collected; then materials
must be collected; and, lastly, a taste is to
be acquired, which is to regulate the knowledge
thus acquired, or in other words, to
animate the mechanic with the intellectual
as the term required for the attainment
of which must in a great measure depend on
the degree of ability in the student, it
is impossible to fix any precise limits.
If we would learn
something, however, how little of the art a
student is allowed by Nature to carry to
his first lessons, might perhaps, be estimated
when we know that there are few artists,
who are capable, after three years
study, even of perceiving the higher excellences
of the Great Masters.
With regard to the progress which
your son has made, I have the pleasure to
say that it is unusually great for the time
he has been studying: and indeed such as to
make me proud of him as a pupil, and to give
every promise of future eminence. He has arrived, as I before observed, at a stage in
his art that enables him to converse with
the old Masters, at the time to profit by
the experience of ages; in short, to become
acquainted with his own powers, or rather
to learn how to use them. Should he
be obliged to return now to America, I
much fear that all which he has acquired
would be rendered albatross. It is true,
he could there paint very good portraits;
but I should grieve to hear at any future
period that on the foundation
now laid, he shall have been able
to raise no higher superstructure
than the fame of a portrait painter. I do
not intend here any disrespect to portrait painting; I know it requires no common talent to
excel in it. His model of the dying Hercules, which I suppose you have already received, will make any thing more that I can
say in favour of your son's genius appear unprofitable.
In addition to this professional merit,
I have the sincere satisfaction to give my testimony to his conduct as a man; which is such as to render him still worthy of being affectionately remembered by his moral and religious friends in America. This is saying a great deal for a young man of two
years in London; but it is not more than justice requires me to say of him. Wm Allston writes with me, last
respect to yourself & Mrs Allston. I am, dear in truth, affectionately
your obedient servant Wm Allston

Charleston March 17, 1814,
My very Dear Son
It is very long since we have had any accounts from
you, which occasions much solicitude. We are anxious to know how
your healthy spirits are, and hope you succeed in your profession your
last letter was dated the 14 Sep. 1813 your success as to the reception
of your statue of Neptune was flattering & I hope your success
since we have announced your expectations. The little cast
you mention sending has not yet come to hand we wish much
to suit it but fear we shall not very soon for we are very desirous
of giving you this summer but do not wish it in such a way as
to have you injure yourself greatly in your profession to gratify
us, especially if by continuing a year longer you can get into
such business as will enable you to support your self afterwards
which I hope is an object with you, we wish much to see
our three sons in the situations to support them in comfortably
& as fast as should we need their help in our old age, and to
be able & willing to do good to their fellow creatures as opportunities
occur, you know perfectly our feeling on this subject and
that we would much rather see you all good & useful in every
situation into which your lot may be cast, than rich & great,
without a heart to do good & be useful to all your brother Common
has begun a letter to you but is prevented from finishing it just now
by a painter that you know he is a little subject to. I hope he will
be able to renew the letter before this goes. Richard is at Utica at
your Uncle's at Arthurs. We had a letter from him yesterday he was
well and in good spirits, he talks of going with Cousin Sam Brown
to Sackets Harbour, merely to see the place. We are pleased to find that
he appears to enjoy himself so well as he was rather despondent when
he left home he intends going to Andover in the fall & study. During
Edwards will go to Litchfield some time this summer & study. Last
if we live till next winter we shall be quite happy not having any
of you with us unless you should come & keep us Company. The
letters we write to each other are liable to be read by the officers of
the Government, we shall therefore say nothing on public affairs, in
the news papers which you doubtless see every Sunday in American
newspapers to go into particulars. – Then did I page on Aunt M r
Wilberforce? M r Thornton? Dr Lettsom? M r West? M r Alston
& other good Friends! Remember us very respectfully to them
when you see them & particularly to M r West & M r Alston
who we hope are quite well, M r & Mrs Botterill William, I have heard
is going to marry his Cousin Miss Gibbs, probably next month I
believe the family are well. – I hope you have painted the three
handsome pictures that I requested you too, one for Mrs Dr Bentlett,
one for Miss Huskill, & one for your Aunt Salisbury, I know not
when you will be able to send them such is the state of things
at present, but be sure you do not venture them till there is a
prospect of there getting safely to us, your Papa is publishing a pamphlet
which occupies much of his time at present to liberty to the Public
how he has been treated by Miss H. Adams & her Abbotson S. Higginson
& Shaw & others. When he has an opportunity he will send one or
two Bills, that your Papa has sent you lately & one small one
some little time ago, we wish to have M r Broomfield's statement,
of the manner in which our accounts stand. I hope my son you
are extremely careful that Company you keep. I hope you will keep
yourself from the Gay, the Disputation of the Prophane Reminiscences dear
to your early Education, & how very much depends on the manner
in which you spend & improve the present moment, that an eternity of
happiness or misery will be the consequence. I intrust you to think much
of the all important truths contained in your Bible & pray to meet
your God in peace. that if we are not permitted to see each other in
this world we may meet in that better World above & spend an
eternity in celebrating the praises of redeeming Love. This is the daily
prayer of your affectionate parents for your own other love make it
your own or it will be in vain for us to make it. I have been confined
the greater part of the Winter with the Ague in my face hair had
two teeth extracted but still wear a bandage of any face your paper
wishes me to tell you that he wrote you a fortnight ago by the
way of Halifax, by a Cartel, and sent the Bills mentioned to
Mr Broomfield, to whom he wrote also. We wish you to have
a letter from Mr Alston & Mr West with respect to your con
tinuance another year.— we wish a description of your house, to Ex
ford & Bristol &c &c and what pieces of Painting you are engaged in
at present.— Your Friends are continually asking about you and
are pleased to hear of your success Mr James Frothingham has taken
the likeness of your Father it is thought to be very good wish
we could have the likeness of Miss Hannah Moore & Mrs Wilberforce
& Dr Buchanan. Your Father Nancy Betsey &c join with me in
love to you Miss Russell Mr Evans Mr O Brown &c a great many
others beg to be remembered to you. We all want much to
hear from you much often than we do it is longer than it
ever has been. I must now bid you good bye my dear Son &c remain
your affectionate E. A. Betsey
Mr. Winter.
Sam'l G B Morse

to the care of Mr. Brownfield
of St. Barnabas Street
London
Mr Vinton.
Letter of Introduction.
Dear Brother
We have received no letters from you since
November. Your last was dated in September We have improved every opportunity. We are all well in good spirits.
Mama has been troubled with a pain in her gums & face in consequence of the extraction of two teeth. Richard has spent the winter at home. He has been very dull & low-spirited. A few weeks since he went to Utica in company with cousin Sam Breeze, We have received two letters from him since. He writes in remarkably good spirits, & appears as happy as a King. - Cousin Sam has just returned from a cruise in the Congress; the third since the war, but he has met with no frigates or armed vessels of any description.
Papa has published an Appeal to the Public, on the subject of Miss H. Adams's charges. He is now publishing a pamphlet which will contain all the particulars & details of the controversy as connected with the True Reasons, and Harvard College.
Richard has not yet fixed upon his professor. I am still studying on Mr Rockwood's Office but shall go to Litchfield soon.
Mr Abner Rogers whom you well know & where brother is in London, died a few weeks since. He had been very inattentive to his health, and suffered his disorder to increase till it was beyond his control. The immediate occasion of his death was a copious bleeding at
lengy. - Judge Parsons died a few months since of a
pulmonary Shock.-
You will be astonished to hear that Mr Dexter
is the democratic candidate for Governor in opposition
to Caleb Strong. He has expressed himself in a letter to
the Electors as decidedly opposed to the whole course &
conduct of the General Government. He styles their
measures "unconstitutional, unjust, oppressive, demon-
atizing." He says, "They cannot be executed, & if they
could they would be ineffectual; that they make
perjury familiar; that they aim a fatal blow at
our prosperity; that they sacrifice our dearest rights
& interests." Yet the democrats will support him. The
great point in which he differs from the Federalists
is this. He says "it is our duty to submit implicitly to
every violation of the Constitution, and every species
of oppression." Federalism I need not tell you will
never go to advocate such Toryism.
The New Hampshire election has issued in favour of
Federalism. Our Charlestown Meeting for the Election
of Town Officers took place about a fortnight since. The
Federalists carried their ticket by a majority of 50.
The democratic majority last year was 37. Charle-
town has been democratic till now for 13 years.
Massachusetts has an overwhelming majority of Federalists
Last year 14,000.—
Nanny Rayner is dead. She left her property,
between 5 & 10,000 Dollars, to George Bartlett.—
Elizabeth Hooker, the daughter of Mr & Mrs Hooker
who were with Papa & Mama in Carolina, is now
living with us. She is about 10 years old, and is a very
lively, figgetty, horty-torty kind of a baby.—
Cousin Betsey Breeze has spent the winter in Boston
with Aunt Salisbury. She is well, and all our Utica relations
Grandmama is at Utica.— Grandpapa Morse has been
confined to the house by a blouse which he received in a
fall. He will never perfectly recover.— Uncle Jonathan talks
of selling his farm and removing into the Western country
under Wilkinson. One of Uncle Calvin's sons is in the army
Elisha Goddard has not arrived in America. We
have been waiting with great impatience to see your statue.
Write us more frequently.— Your friends here constantly inquire
after you.—
I am your affectionate brother
Sidney E. Morse.
Mr Samuel J. B. Mosse
to the care of
Henry Bromfield Esq

is the spirit of religion, & consequence of humanity which has constantly marked

My Dear Sirs
Your last under date of the 4th March, I have just
received, as has also Mr. Bromfield the letter enclosing the
bills of exchange &c. of Mr. Harpurt for 25. of D. Wheelocks
for £6316.9. and 300 lb. for £8500 to the State of my
fancy, you will see by Mr. Bromfield's account separately made
out, sent by the first american packet which you will by this
time have received, you ask if you are to expect me this
next summer? This leads me to a little enlargement on the
peculiar circumstances in which I am now placed, Mr. Allison's
letter by the same postal (as mentioned) will convince you that an
admission and application has not been wanting on my part, that I
have been made greater progress than young men generally, &c. &c. End
of how great importance it is to me to remain in Europe for some
time yet to come, indeed I feel it so much myself, that I shall be
delivered of all risks, if I find I cannot support myself, that I
am contracting debts, which I have no prospect of paying, I shall then return
home, and settle down into a more practical painter for some time, but from
certain difficulties to return to Europe again, for I cannot be happy even
if I am pursuing the intellectual branch of the art, portrait painting
is, landscape has some of, but History has it wholly, I am
certain you would not be satisfied to see me sit down quietly spending my
time in painting portraits, throwing away the talents which Heaven has
given me for the higher branches of art, and devoting my time only to
the interior; I need not tell you what a difficult profession it is an
undertaker, it has difficulty in itself, which was sufficient to deter any
man who has not courage enough to go through without all hazards with
out meeting with any obstacles aside from it; the more I study it, the
more I understand well it, and the greater my progress, the more am I
struck with its beauties, and the perseverance of those who have dared
to pursue it, through the thousands of natural hindrances with which
the art abounds, I never can feel too grateful to my parents for having
assisted me thus far in my profession, they have done
more than I had any right to expect, they have conducted with a liberality
towards me, both in respect to money, and to countenance, me in the
pursuit of one of the noblest professions, which has not many equals
in this country; I cannot ask of them more, it would be ingratitude.
I am now in the midst of my studies, when the great works of art
and use of the utmost service to me, political events have
just thrown open the whole continent. The whole world, will
now leave war and bend their attention to the cultivation of the
arts of peace, a golden age is in prospect, and art is probably
destined again to revive, as in the 16th century; the American artists
at present stand unrivalled, it is my great ambition (and
it is certainly a commendable one) to stand among the first, my
country has the most prominent place in my thoughts; how shall
I raise her name? how can I be of service, in refuting the
calmings industriously spread against her, that she has produced
no men of genius? it is this more than anything (aside from thanking)
that inspires me with a desire to excel in my art, it arouses
my indignation, and gives me tenfold energy in the pursuit of my
studies, I should like to be the greatest painter, surely out of society,
but what a damper is thrown upon my enthusiasm, when I find
that the moment when all the treasures of art, are before
me, just within my reach, that advantages to the artist, were
never greater than now. Paris with all its splendid depository,
of the greatest works, but a day or two's journey from me,
and open to my free inspection, what a damper, I say, is it
to find that my three years allowance is just expired, that,
while all my contemporary students and companions, are reveling
in these enjoyments, and rapidly advancing in their noble
studies, they are leaving me behind, either to return to my
country, or by painting portraits, just to be able to live through the
year. The thought makes me melancholy, and for the first
time since I left home have I had one of my desponding fits.
I have got over it now for I would not write to you in that
mood for the world. My object in stating this is to request patronage
from some rich individual or individuals, for a year or
two longer at the rate of £250 per year, this to be advanced
to me; and if required, to return it in money, as soon as I
shall be able; or by pictures, to the amount, when I have
completed my studies. I ask for 250, because two hundred
has but barely been sufficient; and has left me nothing to
purchase prints, casts, &c. so indispensable at the present
time; if Uncle Salisbury, or Mrs. Russell, could do it, it
would be much more profitable to me than from any others.
This may seem to you an odd request, but I really do not
see any other alternative, if you wish me to be a great painter;
if you wish me to be merely a portrait painter, I can
return and obey you, but I should be miserable. Perhaps,
there would be some delicacy of feeling, in requesting such assistance,
but it might be done in the form of Commission, as
McLellan, has in some instances; for instance let some one
commission me to paint a picture for any sum, when I can
conveniently do it, and advance the sum; this is not perhaps,
strictly mercantile, but I rely on their confidence in my
integrity, I hope I have honorable feelings, and it could
be only consistent with the basest ingratitude, and total
want of honor, to deceive in such a case. But I leave
the management of this to you, whatever can be done to enable
me to prosecute to the end, my favorite studies, I shall
require see in, but do write soon and relieve me from a state
of great uneasiness. The box containing my plaster cast
I found in enquiry, is still at Liverpool, where it has been, to
my great disappointment now nearly a year. I have given
4 orders to have it sent by the first of opportunity. Mr Wilder will
tell you that he came near taking out my great picture of Hercules to you, it seems as though it is destined nothing of mine
shall reach you; I packed it up at a moment's warning and
sent it to Liverpool to go by the cartel, and I found it arrive
the day after she had sailed, I hope it will not be long, for
before both the boxes will have an opportunity of reaching
you. I am exceedingly sorry you have forgotten a passage
in my former letters where I wished you not to feel anxious if
you did not hear from me as often as you had done, I take
the reason, that opportunities were less frequent, more circuitous, and attended with greater interruptions, I tell you that
I should write at least once in three weeks, and that you
must attribute it to any thing but neglect on my part; Your
last letter has hurt me considerably, for owing to some accident
or other my letters have miscarried, and you will aid me
with neglect, and fear that I am not as industrious or correct
as formerly; I know you don't wish to hurt me but I can't help feeling hurt when I think that my friends
have not the confidence which I thought they had in me, that
some interruptions, (which all complain of, and are natural to
a state of warfare,) having prevented letters which I have
written from being received, instead of making allowances for
these things to have them attributed to a falling off in
industry & attention, wounds me a great deal. -- Mrs Allston to
her great surprise received just such a letter from her friends, &
it hurt her so that she was ill in consequence -- I have written
long letters and as frequent as formerly, but you must allow
that having long letters miscarry, which have taken so much time
to write, is but slender encouragement to continue them. --
My Oxford excursion contained I think 5 sheets & an 1/2
which by this time I hope you have received. I wrote 3 I think
from Bristol, 1 just before, which is the last you say you
received, one since my return, via Lisbon, or Halifax 2 for
which, a good long one by the Fair American cartel, and one
which arrived too late at Liverpool to go by the cartel and which
will go by another opportunity. For one of those from Bris-
tol, or the one since, I gave you a slight account of my ex-
cursion to Bristol, Please write me if you have received
it, if not I will write it over again. This will probably go by a cartel from Gotterburg to Boston, to touch here.
The Exhibition at Somerset house opens to day at 12, I shall
go then and give you a little account of it, where my pictures
are placed No. 40, send you a catalogue, and any critiques,
which may be made on any of our pictures Mr. Allston's
Mr. Leslie's or myself. I dine at Mr. Macaulay's at
5 o'clock to day, and shall attend the House of Commons
to-morrow even, when I expect to hear Mr. Wilberforce
speak, on the Slave Trade with reference to the property of making there an article in the pending negotiation
if I have time in this letter I will give you some account
of it. In the main time I will give you a slight account of some scenes of which I have been a happy witness
on the great drama now acting in the Theatre of Europe.
You will probably before this reaches you, hear of the
splendid entry of Louis 18th into London; I was
a spectator of this scene; On the morning of the day
about 10 o'clock, I went into Piccadilly, through which
the procession was to pass, I did not find any great con-
course of people at that hour except before the Pallmey
Hotel, where the sister of the Emperor Alexander resides
6. on a visit to this country, the Grand Duchess of Old-
enburg. I thought it probable that, as the procession would
pass this place, there would be some uncommon occasion
to take place before it so I took my situation directly opposite
determined at any rate to secure a good view of
what happened; I waited 4 or 5 hours during which
time the people began to collect, from all quarters, the
carriages began to thicker, the windows & fronts of the
houses began to be decorated with the white flag, white
ribbons, and laurel, temporary seats were fitted up on
all sides which began to be filled, and all seemed to be
in preparation; about this time the King's splendid band
of music made its appearance, consisting I suppose of more
than 50 musicians, and to my great gratification placed
themselves directly before the Hotel, they began to play &
soon after, the Grand Duchess, attended by several Rus-
sian gentlemen, made her appearance on the balcony, fol-
lowed by, the Queen Infant, the Princeess Mary,
Prince Elizabeth, and all the female part of the Royal
family, from this fortunate circumstance you will see that
I had an excellent opportunity of observing their countenance.
The Duchess of Oldenburg is a common sized woman, of
about 4 or 5 twenty, she has rather a pleasant countenance
blue eyes, pale complexion, regular features, her cheek bones
high but not disagreeably so, she resembles very much

My dear Sir,
I wrote to you by the pacific last year, but not having
since heard from you, fear that you did not receive my letter.
Mr. Jarvis two months ago presented me a son, and to day
we set out for Saybrook to show the little stranger to
his grandparents & Aunts. I have only time therefore
to say that your friends remember you with affection
and that there is one in Saybrook who thinks of you more
than you imagine, & more than she knows herself.
I give you this hint, my dear Sir, because I feel a strong
friendship for you as well as for and wish that all those
little impediments which hinder persons of real worth from
forming a union may be removed. I would certainly aim
giving you hopes which might end in disappointment
I on the other hand if you have altered your inclina
tions would wish to spare her feelings. In such case
you will I trust keep what I have said to you a pri
found secret. I shall always be happy to hear from
you & to serve you, my dear Mr. Morse, for I am indeed
and you will & trust find me to be
Your friend
