Mr. John E. G. Colville
to the Genl. Staff, Washington
10th Oct.
New York City
Genl. Colville
My Dear Parents
Three of your letters are now before me which
I have this moment received, of the following dates, Nov.
23d, 1814, Dec. 19th 1814, & Jan. 25th 1815, so that one,
you will perceive, has been 5 months on the way.
Your letters surprise me in Paris, but I am
not there; you hope that I went in Oct. last. I intended
to go and wished it at that time exceedingly, but
I had not leave from you to go, and Mr. Bromfield advised
me by no means to go until I heard from you, you
must perceive from this case how impossible it is for
me to form plans and transmit them across the Atlantic
for approbation, thus letting an opportunity slip
which is irrecoverable; I wish I could persuade my
Parents that they might place some little confidence
in my judgment at the age I now am (nearly 24)
an age when in ordinary people the judgment has
reached a certain degree of maturity; it is a singular
and I think an unfortunate fact that I have not that
I recollect since I have been in England, had a turn
of low spirits, except when I have received letters from
home, it is true, I find a great deal of affectionate
solicitude in them, but with it I also find so much
complaint and distrust, so much fear that I am
doing wrong, so much doubt as to my morals and principles,
and fear lest I should be led away by bad
company, and the like, that after I have read them
I am miserable for a week, I feel as though I had
been guilty of every crime, and I have passed many
sleepless nights after receiving letters from you, I shall not
not sleep to night in consequence of passages in your letters
just received. I will quote some passages from them; Mama says
"I am sorry you do not feel the importance of fulfilling your
"engagements with more punctuality, you must be more attentive to your friends or you will grieve and loose them." In another
letter after giving an instance of a young man living for 600 dollars
per year in London out of consideration to his Parents and gratitude
to them, who were worth 150,000 dollars you say, "now think my
"son how much more your poor parents are doing for you
"how good your dear Brothers are, to be satisfied with so little
"done for them in comparison with what we are doing for you"
"and let the thought stimulate you to more economy and industry
"as I greatly fear you have been falling off in both these"
"since the relief you received for your first performances, it
"has always been a failing of yours that as soon as you found
"you could excel in what you undertook to be tired of it and
"not trouble yourself any further about it, I was in hopes that
"you had got over this fickleness ever this." Now as to the
young man's living for 600 dollars, I know who it is of whom
you speak, it is Dr Parkman, who made it his boast that
he would live for that sum, but you did not inquire how
he lived. I can tell you, he never refused an invitation
to dine, which he used to obtain often by pushing himself
into every body's company, when he did not succeed in
getting invitations, he invited himself to breakfast, dinner
or sup with some of his friends he has often walked
up to breakfast with us a distance of 3 or 4 miles,
if he failed in getting a dinner or meal at any of these
places, he either used to go without or a bit of bread
answered the purpose till next meal. In his dress
he was so shabby and uncouth that any decent person would
be ashamed to walk with him in the street, and above all
his notorious meanness in his money dealings, his sticking
with his poor washerwoman for a half penny, and with others
for a farthing, and his uniform stinginess on all occasions,
rendered him notoriously disgusting to all his acquaintance, &
affords, I should imagine, but a poor example for imitation.
But all this is not to the point; you must perceive, that
the object of your sending me to London, was improvement
in my art, to the extent of 200 pounds per Ann. now I should
conceive I was abusing your goodness if I did not employ
it all for that object; suppose, instead of purchasing frames,
carts, &c. paying models, &c. I should at the close of
year write you word that I had the happiness, to say that I
had expended but 100 pounds, that I had found very cheap
lodgings, but my room would not answer for painting because
it was small, had a low ceiling, and I had my bed in it, that
I lived on little and to save expence of cooking, I was my
own cook, but that most of my day was employed for that
purpose, in purchasing my food, dressing it, and clearing away
my cooking utensils; that I made out to paint with few
colors and cheap ones, and cheap tools, but that the
colors and tools were of inferior quality; suppose I should
say this in a letter, would you be satisfied with my years
work, would you not say, why did you not get a more
convenient room, when you were allowed ample means
for the purpose; and also better colors & tools; and why
did you expend your time in cooking, when you had
sufficient to pay others to do it for you? The fact is I
could live for 50 pounds a year if my only object was to live
cheap, and on the other hand if I was allowed 1000 pounds
a year I could spend it all without the least extravagance
in obtaining greater advantages in my art; but as
your

4. goodness has allowed me but 200 pounds, (and I wish you again
to receive my sincere thanks for this allowance, for my
sole endeavor be to spend all this, to the utmost advantage,
to keep as closely within the bounds of that allowance
as possible, and would not economy in this instance consist
in rigidly keeping up to this rule; if this is a true statement
of the case, then have I been perfectly economical,
for I have not yet overspun my allowance, and I think
I shall be able to return home without having exceeded it, a
single shilling, if I have done this, and still continue
to do it, why, in every letter I receive from home, is the
injunction repeated of being economical; it makes me exceedingly
unhappy, especially when I am conscious of having
used my utmost endeavors, ever since I have been in England
to be rigidly so. — As to Industry, which means
I am falling off, I gave you an account in my last
letter (by Mr. Kalston) of the method which I use in parcelling
out my time, since writing that letter, the spring and summer
is approaching fast and the days increasing, of course
I can employ more of the time than in the winter, Mr. Leslie
and myself, rise at 5 o'clock in the morning, and walk about
a mile and a half to Burlington House, where are the
famous Elgin marbles, the works of Phidias and Praxiteles
brought by Lord Elgin from Athens, from these we draw
3 hours every morning, wet or dry, before breakfast,
and return home just as the bustle begins in London
for they are late visitors in London, when we go out of a
morning we meet no one but the watchman, who goes
his rounds for an hour and a half after we are up.
Last summer Mr. Leslie and I used to paint in the open air
air in the fields, 3 hours before breakfast, and often
before sunrise, to study the morning effect on the landscape
now, being conscious of employing my time in the most industrious
manner possible, you can but faintly conceive the mortification,
and sorrow with which I read that part of
Mama's letter, I was so much hurt at it, that I read it to
Mr. Allston, and requested he would write to you, and
give you an account of my spending my time, he seemed
very much astonished when I read it him, and authorized
me to tell you from him that it was impossible for
any one to be more indefatigable in my studies than
I am! —
Mama mentions in her letter, that she hears
that Mr. Leslie supports his mother & sisters by his labors,
this is not the case; Leslie was supported by 3 or 4 individuals
in Phil: till within a few months past, about
a year ago he sold a large picture which he painted
(whilst I was on my fruitless trip to Bristol for money)
for a hundred guineas, since that he has had a number
of commissions in portraits and is barely able to
support himself, indeed he tells me this evening that
he has but 20 pounds left, he is very economical
and a most excellent young man, his expenses in
a year are on an average from 230 to 250 pounds,
Mr. Allston's (single) expenses not less than 300 Pounds,
and I know of no artist among all my acquaintance
whose expenses in a year are less than 200 pounds.
Mama accuses me of neglect in not mentioning Mr.
Russell and family in my letters from Bristol, this was
certainly an oversight in me in not explaining the cause
the fact is I saw Mr Russell but seldom, or the family
they were exceedingly kind and hospitable to me, but I
lived between 5 or 6 miles from them, they in Clifton and
I at the other end of Bristol, the way to them was very
dreadful and considered not altogether safe for a single person
at night; night was the only time when, from the nature
of my studies I could visit them, it being winter and on
little daylight, beside the dreadful state of the weather
in the winter season, if I had visited Bristol in the
summer I should have availed myself of every oppor-
tunity to call on them for they were a charming
family, and I feel very grateful for their kind atten-
tions to me; as to the portrait which I painted of Mr
Russell, I am sorry you mentioned it to Miss Russell, as
I particularly requested you would not, because in case
of failure it would be a disappointment to her, but
as you have told her, I must now explain, in the first
place then it is not a picture which will do me any
credit, I was unfortunate in the light which I chose to
paint him in, I wished to make it my best picture
and so made it my worst, for I worked too timidly
on it, it is a likeness; indeed, a very strong likeness,
but the family were not pleased with it, I had not flat-
tered him, and made him too old, so I determined I
would not send it, indeed, I promised them I would not
send it, but notwithstanding, as I know Miss Russell
will be good enough to comply with my conditions, I
will send it directly, for as it is a likeness, every one
except the family knowing it instantly, and Mrs Allison
saying that it is a very strong likeness, it will on that
account be a gratification to her, but I particularly
and expressly request that it be kept in a private
room to be shown only to friends and relations,
and that it may never be mentioned as the painter
and moreover that no artist or miniature painter
be allowed to see it; on these conditions I send it,
taking for granted they will be complied with
and without waiting for an answer. I did not
know you had even hinted it to Miss Russell,
and I intended to let the thing die away.
May 3. 1815.
With respect to returning home, I shall
make my arrangements to be with you, (which
my life be spared) by the end of September next
or the beginning of Oct. but it will be necessary
that I should be in Eng. again (provided, always,
Providence permit) by the Sept. following, as arrangements
which I have made will require my presence, this I will
fully explain when I meet you, the moment I get home
I wish to begin to work, so that I should like to have some
portraits bespoken in season, I shall charge 40 dollars
less than Stuart for my portraits, so that if any of
my good Friends are ready, I will begin the moment
I have said "how do ye do," to them, I wish to do as
much as possible in the year I am with you; if I
could get a commission or two for some large pictures
for a church, or public hall, to the amount of 2 or 3
thousand dollars, I should feel much gratified, I do
not despair of such an event, for through your influence
with the clergy, and their influence with their people, I
think some commission for a scripture subject, for a
church might be obtained, it may perhaps be said
that the country is not rich enough to purchase large pictures;
yes, but 2 or 3000 dollars can be paid for an entertainment,
which is gone in a day, and whose effects are to
demeoralize and debilitate, whilst the same sum expended
on a fine picture, would be an ornament to the country,
which would be lasting, it would tend to elevate and refine
the public feeling, by turning their thoughts from sensuality
and luxury to intellectual pleasures, and it would encourage
and support a class of citizens, who have been
reckoned among the brightest stars in the constellation of
American worthies, and who are to this day compelled
to exile themselves from their country, and all that is
dear to them in order to obtain a bare subsistence;
I do not speak of portrait painting, had I no higher
thoughts than being a first-rate portrait painter, I would
have chosen a far different profession; my ambition is
to be among those who shall revive the splendour of the
15th century, to rival the genius of a Raphael, a Michelangelo,
or a Titian; my ambition is to be enlisted
in the constellation of genius which is now rising in this
country, I wish to shine, not by a light borrowed from
them,
but to shine the brightest; if I could return home and stay a year visitors my friends in various parts of the union, and by painting portraits make sufficient to bring me to Eng. again, at the end of the year, whilst I obtain commissions enough to employ me and support me while in Eng., I think in the course of a year or two I shall have obtained sufficient credit to enable me to return home if not for the remainder of my life, at least to pay a good long visit; all these plans I wish you to understand me as always taking into consideration the will of Providence, and in every plan for future operation, I hope I am not forgetful of the uncertainty of human life, and I wish always to say should I live, I will do this or that.
Will you be so good in your next letters as to repeat all former orders for books, &c. (as many I am confident from your late letter must have miscarried) that I may in season get every thing together for home; you had better not write me after the end of June or beginning of July as letters may be detained, and I shall endeavor to get away as near the beginning of Sept. as I conveniently can.
About my finances I don't know how they will hold out in the various great and small expenses of returning home, I calculate they will exceed considerably what I have got left; should this be the case I will refund to you what I expend on my own account the rest of course will be yours. I perceive by
96915
10 your late letters that you suppose I am painting a
large picture; I did think of it some time ago
and was only deterred on account of the expenses
attending it, all this I will explain to your entire
satisfaction when I see you, and why I do not
think it expedient to make an exhibition
when I return: I percieve also that you are a
little too sanguine with respect to me, and expect
a little too much from me; you must recollect I
am yet but a student, and that a picture of any
merit is not painted in a day; Experienced as
Mr West is, (and he also paints quicker than any
other artist,) yet his last large picture cost him
between 3 and 4 years constant attention; Mr
Allston was nearly 2 years in painting his large
picture; Young Haydon was 3 years painting
his large picture, is now painting another on
which he has been at work 1 year and expects
to be 2 years more on it; Leslie was 10 months
painting his picture, and my Hercules cost me
nearly a year's study; so you see that large
pictures are not the work of a moment; all these
matters we will talk over one of these days, and
all will be set right; I had better paint Miss
Rufelli's Aunt Salisbury's and Dr Bartlett's pictures
at home for a very good reason I will give you.
Love to all. I must close abruptly. With affectionate
Yr Affectionate Son
D. H.B. More.

pleasure in rendering any service in my power
I am
Very sincerely

Mar 5. 1865.
My dear Son,
Capt Rogers of this town is to sail to-morrow
for Corwin, & thence be expectd to go by land to London
& kindly offers to take a panel for you. I prepared
in great haste. We have rec'd a few days ago your
letter of Decr. 22, just after your return from Boston.
Also yours of the 314th of Feb. announcing the
melancholy tidings of Mrs Alston's death. The
enclosed letter to Mrs McChanning was immediately
handed to the family whom I have since seen.
Everything proper has been done to soothe their
gloomy sorrow. They are most obliged to you for your
sympathies & kind attentions to Mr Alston & feel
toward you very affectionately. You will express
& Mr Alston our tender sympathies under his
afflictions. Your letter arrived was received
as I was going to the funeral of our friend
Mr Rockwood, who died of a rapid consumption
after about a month's confinement. His loss is
deeply felt & lamented. Mrs R. will go back
to her father's at Phila in a month or 6 weeks with
two of her 4 children the other two remain with
his father at Wilton. I do not now recollect any
other deaths among your acquaintance except of Mrs
Whitmore, who married you & your brother. The was buried
this week a good woman. We have just heard of the
death of Dr Ramsay who was shot by an insane man
a great loss to his family & to the public.
Many things real & changes are taking place among
us of a local nature, religious, civil, literary & po-
litical, What we? interest you, could you know them
fully but as I have not time to go into detail
of all them I must refer you to the papers pamphlets
& verbal communications of those who call on you
from this country for information of this kind - All
is well in the parish & town -- in general through the
State since the peace commerce is gradually increasing
We know not how we shall ultimately be affected by the
late wonderful revolution in France -- Your views on
that event entirely coincide with my own -- I have
expected that Bonaparte will be established on the throne of
France, I remain the source of the world for their
iniquities -- But we can see but a little way into
futurity -- We can safely leave all in the hands
of Him who manages all things wisely -- All we have
to do is to secure his friendship & protection by
a diligent discharge of all our duties.
To-day we have received your letters & March 23d.
by Mr. Ralston via Phila (Postage $1.22) You had
better send by direct to Boston as often as possible you
did right by all means to send by direct an Express as Mr.
R. have gladly pay postage for all your letters -- You
evidently misconceived our views in the letter to which
you alludes; I felt much too strongly our advice &
remarks in respect to your writing us so much on
politics -- What we? was the affectionate advice
of your parents who loved you very tenderly & who
were not unwilling you had judge for yourself, though
you might differ from them -- We have ever made
a new candid allowance for you to have all
your friends. You have never for a moment been
liened, we think. Differs, a fortnight after you did come
home, I converse with us. You have done the honor
of feeling, constrained from observing in our letters
as censoring you, I would not design to your feelings, that were not
intended in the remotest degree by us, for any such profession
of regret in your letter will satisfy you of this
I am sure, have been that your entering so warmly into Politics,
has seriously impeded your professional pursuits. Your
last letter on this subject, has greatly relieved our minds.
We regret your disappointments at Bristol. You will
from these learn a useful lesson. Then finally if your
wife may turned to good account.
We anticipate the pleasure of soon receiving
by the mail, who is hourly expected from Liverpool, your
plaster cast, I painting it from Philadelphia, those which
Mr. Kelston may have brought. We have hoped
that you would have yourself accompanied these yourself,
as we are very anxious to see you. You have
not probably read my letters proposing your
return this summer or autumn & plan for you
to pursue it if you & Mr Kelston approve it, it
will be very pleasing to us & we think would do
well. My letters on this subject, I expect you will
have received this. I think you will find such
fortune in this country for a year or two, as will enable you to return to Europe, & travel to advantage.
But on this subject I must leave you to judge,
with the advice you can have on the subject. If
you can paint a large picture, bring it over for
exhibition in this country, with your other, there
paint the battle of Lake Champlain, after having
visited the spot. I take M'Donough's likeness,
that of other officers you might succeed very
well better probably than where you are
such a picture engraved & well here in
Europe. The battle of Lie, of Orleans, will
give you full employment -- I doubt as to
your feelings -- In the mean time things might become
more settled in Europe, & you might visit the continent
to greater advantage -- Think on this subject
seriously, & determine wisely for yourself.
I admit your apologies for not sending me books --
tho' you return in Augt. or September, as we hope, you
may thus bring out the books I have ordered -- otherwise
you need not give yourself any trouble about them -- You
will let me know how you stand with Mr Bromfield -- what are
your prospects of maintaining yourself -- Tho' you
remain, it will not be in my power at present to
send you further aid -- as the Putnam estate is still
unsold, & now without attendant I am extremely
pressed for money to pay my debts. I will do what you require
in regard to your pictures, & the public notice of them -- Tho' you
will after all, require in England, though it will be a
point of importance to you, I will support you in
point of fact, & give you encouragement & support. We
can to give you encouragement & support. We shall hear from you often -- & you from us, notwithstanding
the public notice of them -- I am very anxious that you should keep up your acquaintance
with Mr Wilberforce & Dr. Letham -- Call on them as friends, thankfully
tell them how you are situated, let your visit suit your time
convenience. I sent you out by the Liverpool packet two interesting pamphlets, which I hope you have, & in this regard
I am very anxious that you should keep up your acquaintance
with Mr Wilberforce & Dr. Letham -- call on them as friends, thankfully
tell them how you are situated, let your visit suit your time
convenience. I sent you out by the Liverpool packet two interesting pamphlets, which I hope you have, & in this regard
I am very anxious that you should keep up your acquaintance
with Mr Wilberforce & Doctor Letham -- Call on them as friends, thankfully
tell them how you are situated, let your visit suit your time & convenience. I sent you out by the Liverpool packet two interesting pamphlets, which I hope you have, & in this regard
I am very anxious that you should keep up your acquaintance
with Mr Wilberforce & Doctor Letham -- Call on them as friends, thankfully
tell them how you are situated, let your visit suit your time & convenience. I sent you out by the Liverpool packet two interesting
pamphlets, which I hope you have, & in this regard
lest they Sh p . have failed I send you others by Capt 5
R. If both the reach you, you may give the topic of
American Unitarianism to Mr Burden & the Remarks
in the Quarterly Rev. of Inching in letters to Dr. Let some
or any other gentleman you please Mr Wil-
berforce has one -- I am sorry to hear of
the death of Mr Thornton He was a good
man -- If one of your letters you mentioned a likeness
of Mrs Russell of Bristol for Mrs Russell his sister,
where is it? Your late letters are silent about it.
We wish it sent out, if you have it, as soon as you
can have opportunity -- Put it in to the hands of Mr Wilder who
will call on you, & he will take the trouble to
send it with any other pictures for your Uncle
Taliburny, Dr. Bartlett or your parents, which you
may wish to send --
Mrs Russell has been feeble in consequence
of a colt but is now recovered Mrs Donne is well
Your Mother & I Mary & Caroline constituting
our present family Betsey is with your aunt & they
are all well -- Your brother at Litchfield was well
a fortnight ago -- Rich d is on a visit to Woodstock
& well -- Your Grandfather Morse is still alive I will shortly
enter his 90th year -- Your Aunt May died before
written to you, died last November -- Your Uncle &
their families are well -- Your Grandma Breeze,
is nearly blind with a Cataract. She talks of
coming depending the rest of her days with us,
but nothing is yet determined on the subject.
The minds of both your brothers have been very
serious for some time past. I hope they will both
have secured for themselves the good part which
shall not be taken away from them -- We
earnestly wish you would join them in this
choice -- We are glad to notice that you
have in viene in pursuing your favorite
art "the glory of God, the glory of man" --
Thee undoubtedly will be your object. --
Our first wish is that our children
may be good; then great eminent in
their professions -- If they cannot attain
both, we far prefer the former --
We notice have preserved your seat as a
curiosity. You have mentioned in former letters that
you were studying for some great picture -- what was
your subject? Have you begun it? -- Moses sitting
on the Rock, we thought a good subject -- one you thought
of here -- On Thursday I saw Mr Sergenth picture
the Landing of the Fathers -- I think it a fine painting --
It does honor to the Painter & to our Country --
This exhibition is a good beginning -- 25th admission --
many visitors.
Your Mama & family with Miss Russell, I your
other friends, join in love to you -- Your brave
& I wish to be kindly remembered to Mrs Alston
& to Mrs Leslie -- we had hoped you would come home
together this fall -- summer & heat fall --
Your affectionate father
Emmott

Dear Sir
Your Letter of 15th Mr. having come
to hand at a time of many engagements, having required
some attention in order to answer the Enquiry made in it,
a delay has occurred beyond what was intended.
Below is a statement of the D. P. side of your Actio from your
2 years, whereby it appears that in the year 1812 (the year in
which the Brooks were paid for) the Amo did not much exceed
that of one thous. dollars, but the following year did
considerably exceed, so that in except of the two years more
than balanced the Bill received in pay for the Brooks,
consequently, the Amo did must be considered as already
absorbed in your expenditure –
The Expenditure of the present year already amonts to £131.9.1
to which is added the sum now called for 20.—
the sum you mention as being for 60.—
and you will perceive that their united Amo 211.9.1
added to that of the preceding years 704.0.9
will exceed the four thousand dollars 915.9.10
attested by your Father – This will undoubtedly
prove a satisfaction to you, but still what you may
want for your Experiences shall be furnished, it also
the sum necessary to procure the Articles requested by
your Father, who in his Letter to me supposed that the
Commissioners
Remittances he had made would be sufficient to pay
all your Bills & your Passage home, & also to purchase
some Books & Articles of Clothing, but during, if there
should be any Deficiency, thus I will advance it.
These are all the Particulars he has given me & I trust
your Wish that what is advanced for articles to be procured
for him be kept separate from your Own & you
will at the time of receiving it let me know to which
& how to place it.
The Revolution you have formed of returning to America
is in my opinion tedious, for the Multitude of Competitors here in the Line of your Profession is so great as to render the Chance of Success in it much greater than
altho the Field of Improvement may not be so extended.
There also you will be in the Midst of your Friends, an
Intercourse with whom will enhance the Enjoyment of
Life, while it will tend to mitigate the adverse Occasions
that must be calculated upon. The difference between
the two Countries in the Expenditure of living is not an immaterial object.
The Letter for your Father shall be forwarded when
any opportunity offers. The Galen I hope will get away
in about three weeks whether any will be going to
Boston sooner from Liverpool I am not informed.
I enclose the Twenty Pounds you have requested
Sincerely wish you success in the object of your present
Engagement remain as truly
Yours Your Friend & etc etc
C Bromfield

Dear Son
Received your Letter of the 21st of March was happy to find
by it that you were in health and industriously pursuing your Profession
we were pleased to find that you were receiving some money to support
yourself we hope your means will increase and that you will be able to
do as Mr Leslie does, and be independent, in time we were relieved from
any further responsibility as to your support if Providence should enable
us to do as much for each of your Brothers as we have done for you
we shall be thankful that , but we know, not what is before us, in the
Cities we received from you during the two first years of your bringing
London you appeared pretty confident that by the end of the two years
you should be able to support yourself, this you find has not been the case, we
give you reason to expect that we would allow you $300 a year for three
years we have since added 200 a year to the thre fourth year also a 1000
for a fourth year, all of which except 100 or 150 have been transmitted to
you making as you will see $4000 which we have hired and are now
paying interest for, to gratify you in the permit of your favourite
Profession – I don't mention this by way of complaint, in the proportion
you have made in your Profession, from the reports we have had, and
with the accounts of your correct conduct otherwise we are well pleased
and also with your expressions of gratitude in your former letters to
us for making the many sacrifices which under our many circumstances
we have carefully made to aid your views, you requested in
some of your first letters that your affectionate parents would continue as
they ever had done to counsel, reprove and advise you from time to time
as they should in their wisdom deem necessary and give us reasons
believe that what we should be improper to do in this way would be received by you as
a wise & dutiful son ought ever to receive advice & reproof from affectionate fa-
thers, whose constant language to their children has ever been to yourselves
no harm. With the strongest feelings of the importance of the utmost prudence
in a young man who had his living to obtain from his profession we have felt the necessity of advising you not to meddle with politics, which
your sentiments coincided exactly with our own we should have advised you
to keep them to yourself your busying yourself with such things, could do no good
to anyone, and was calculated to do yourself, more harm, than any other person
could do you, by making enemies of those who might have it in their power, to serve you
spiritually, in the way of your profession, did you not offend their prejudices: I do not charge you with being so imprudent as to have
caused any alterations of the kind which have suggested, by expressing
such sentiments to those around you, as you have, from time, to time, expressed in your letters to us, but fearing you might in your zeal to defend
the character of your country, drop an unguarded expression, which would
injure you as to your prospects, we have thought it our duty to advise you, to
be prudent, in this respect, and not give your tongue, as much latitude, as
you did your pen, we should love you much less than we do, if we thought
you capable of not loving your country, with all the ardour which you
express for it, we consider this as a very amiable trait of character,
which we have not the least desire to eradicate, but would cherish,
still a person may be placed in a situation in which it is best to keep
this to himself. We have never in any letter we have written you given you the
least reason to believe we thought you criminal in regard to your politics, or
company, as your last letter intimates we have cautioned you with regard to
what company you kept, and what amusements, you attended, but have
never impeached the moral character of Mr. Bayne, in the slightest
degree, as you intimate to look at our letters when you undertake
to answer them, & then your letters would be more correct recollect saying
of Mr. Haynes, in one of my letters to you that I understood that he maintained
a very good Character, but hoped being acquainted with him would not lead
you into the company of men of that profession, as they were not generally
the best sort of Characters -- in short all the advice we have given you
has been such as you ought to thank us for with as much filial affection
as you ever did for any remittances of money we ever made you as
you can have no doubt that our object in both is the same to do you
the greatest possible good -- and here let me give you a word of kind advice
and receive it kindly let your letters be in future fraught with the
same tender affectionate expressions of duty and love and all that is good
that they Used to be, before you had your mind so soured by the state of
publick affairs, let your letters, and your actions, both show that you are
of a truly gratefull disposition, and be ready to fulfill any Commission
that your parents may request of you, even if you should have to stand
still in your Art till you had accomplished it, to me, were it in your
place the heart felt pleasure I should feel from having done a kind
act, to oblige my parents would more than make amends for
all the time spent in executing it. we do not intend to be troublesome
to any of our Children or Friends. You wish to be known in this country
as a painter in order to this you must send pictures of your own painting
as yet not the slightest thing has ever been seen of yours since you left this Country
except the little portrait of yourself in India Ink. -- You will recollect I do not blame you for
this but ascribe it to the times but now it is peace times will show be
96927
different we have not got your picture from Mr. Bolstone yet but hope
we shall soon, the little picture you mention that was exhibiting at
the British Gallery we shall be glad to receive I wish you not to ask
us to remit the expence of a frame of picture that you may see proper
to send us at any time but only let us know what the actual cost of any
picture or frame has been to you, leaving it to us, to do what we think proper.
I believe you will be safe in doing thus. I excuse this on the ground of your having
been mortified by the ungentlemanly treatment that you met with by some
of the Bristol men had it not been for this I am sure you would not have
thought of saying anything about the expence of frame of that magnitude to
your parents. I am very sorry for the disappointment which befel you
at Bristol in respect to your business, but any sort of it will be a lesson to you,
which may do you good in the end, it will show you how little dependance
is to be placed in promising professions of worldly men, and keep you
from placing too much confidence in them, if we are faithful to ourselves
We may extract good from every thing, troubles & miseries -- I feel very
tenderly for Mr Alston, in the loss he has sustained, of his beloved wife I
hope he is all concerned, will improve this affliction as to be made
wise, and better, more weaned from this world, and your heart more
placed on things above, and be daily placing your Affections where Christ
sitteth at the right hand of God. -- Your Brother Richard is we trust choosing
that good part that shall never be taken away from him and
which we (and all our Friends of the Clergy that visit us and which are
numerous at this time) pray daily may be the happy portion of your
other Brother. Indeed my Child you have many prayers daily offered
to God for you which we hope will get bear wind in your Salvation. --
of greatly disappointed in not seeing you this Summer, as does your Friend,
and acquaintance, here, but we submit, we think you are right, in endeavoursing to establishing a reputation, that may insure you success with
the Blessing of the Almighty. Without this you cannot, and ought not,
to expect to be prospered, I was glad to find you observing in your letter that your object in wishing to excel as a painter was to promote the
Glory of God if this is sincerely your aim, it is known to him who reaches all hearts,
and if he finds that your success in your Art will have a tendency to promote his
Glory, he will grant you all that prosperity, which is consistent with this
end, and with the same kind designs, will deny you that success which
you may be desirous of enjoying, as knowing far better than we poor short sighted
women can possibly pretend to, what will have this effect and what not
It is therefore our Indispensable duty to beg daily, that God will may be done
both in us and by us and that all we say and do may end in his Glory &
the best good of our own souls & the souls of our fellow mortals. – Indeed my
dear son your affectionate parents are vastly more interested in having
you profess of that honour that cometh from God, than all the facing
praising honours, that are derived from fallible man, these last,
are not to be desired as but they may have a tendency to place
us in situations to be more abundantly useful to our fellow men
but they are by no means to be sought for merely to gratify our ambition
of distinction, and the pride & vanity of our own foolish hearts, we
ought daily to be searching into our motives and making the public
of thealmest. Hearch me Oh God and know my heart try me
and know my thoughts and see if there is any wicked way in me and
lead me in the way everlasting, – Hope my son that you remember
the Sabbath day to keep it holy and that you constantly attend the publick
Worship of God both parts of the day let no such early and highly important
habit, even if it were nothing more than a habit, be ever laid aside, but
with you I hope the attention to the ordinances of religion, will be attended
with far higher motives than can exist from mere habit and early education
I wish to hear from you on the subject of religion, or your own views
on this all important subject, believe you attend church, and that is going
on in the Religious World write us on these subjects, as much as you
can spare time for, We were much pleased with your letter giving an
account of the Death of Mrs Aston as discouraging a tender of prosperity
in the affliction of that family which was great. We need not tell you that
we take no comparison more satisfaction in commending and approving
and having others that are good people like him commended & approve
the conduct of our sons than in having the slightest reason to curse
or condemn them, and we acknowledge them with gratitude to our Heavenly
Father for his protecting & restraining grace granted you all that you
have afforded us the highest satisfaction that we are capable of enjoying
next to having the assurance of your all having been the subjects of
the renewing and sanctifying grace of God, which we hope if it be the will
of God we may yet live to see or hear of it. – In perfect consistency with
the feelings towards you all above described we may and ought to
tell you and that with the greatest plainness of any thing that we
seem improper in any part of your conduct either in a civil social
or religious view and this we feel it our duty to do and what we shall continue
to do as long as we live, and it will ever be your duty to receive from
us the Advice counsels and support which we may from time to
time favour you with, with the most perfect respect and dutiful obser-
vance and when you differ from us on any point whatever let that differ-
ence be conveyed to us in the most gentlemanly manner
and let this be done not only while you are under age and dependent
on your parents for your support, but when you are independent and
then you are head of a Family and even of a profession if you even should be

Remember more such as your picture of Mrs Payne & Barathia and any

London, June 26th 1815.
My Dear Parents,
I just drop you a line by the Gales
to inform you that I am well; I am making
my arrangements to leave about the end of
August; my time is now very precious to me
and this must therefore be short; you must
be aware that I shall be under the necessity
of drawing in advance for many of next year
expenses such as clothing and printing materials,
all which I shall expect to refund you, as well
as what I may exceed in my proper allowance
for the 4 years, I trust it will not
be much though I fear it will be a few
pounds. There is one thing I wish to notify to
you; my friend Lieut. Newcomb of our Navy
went to Paris a short time since, I gave
him a commission to get me a large lay figure,
which will cost 30 to 100 guineas; the prices
are from 30 to 100 guineas; my reason for
deciding on such a step without previously
notifying you of it, was that they are to be obtained
no wheres but in Paris so cheap & so
good, that a dreadful campaign was about
to open in France & that the Allies threatened
to destroy every thing before them and to burn
Paris; that this state of things, would render it
next to impossible to obtain anything from France;
a lay-figure is absolutely indispensable to an artist.
I have got along since I have been in England by
borrowing one, of my different Friends, but I shall
be deprived of that indulgence on returning home.
Lieut. Vinromt promised to execute the order, &
to pay for it himself, and he would receive the
money in America whenever I could make it
convenient. it will be shipped for Boston
from France; so do not be alarmed if you
should open a long box and see a figure in it.
I thought I never should have a better opportu-
nity, and was unwilling to let it pass. The price
is not to exceed 30 louisines. This sum I con-
sider as borrowed from you and will refund it
you from my first profit should it be necessary.
You will have heard of the dreadful
battle in Flanders before this reaches you, the
loss of the English is immense indeed, almost
all their finest officers and the flower of their
army, not less than 800 officers, and upwards
of 15,000 men, (some say 20,000) but it has been decisive, if the
news of to day be true that Napoleon has
abdicated. what the event of these unpar-
allelled times will be, no mortal can pretend
to foresee. I have much to tell you
when I see you. Perhaps you had better
not write after the receipt of this, as it
may be more than two months before an
answer could be received.
Love to all
Good Bye.
Your affectionate Son
Sam. J. Moser.
P.S. The Paper of to-night confirms the news
of this morning; Bonaparte is no longer a
man, he has abdicated; and in
prorbility a Republican form of government will be the future government of France, if they are capable of enjoying such
a government. but no one can foresee events
there may be a long peace, or the world may
be torn worse than it yet has been. --
Revolution seems to succeed revolution so rapidly
that in looking back on our lives we seem to have
lived a thousand years; and wonders of late seem
to scorn to come alone, they come in clusters. a
P.S. 2. I have just received your letter of 20th May which
gave me much pleasure, I still intend returning by the
end of Augt though I cannot be sufficiently grateful
to you for your kind offers of encouragement & support for
another year. I shall tell you my plans when I get home.
Excuse me for not enclosing as I am in a great hurry.
Yr most affectionately
Sam Moser

Bloomingdale November 2. 1815
My dear Sir
It is but a few hours since I received your letter
announcing your arrival in your Native land, and I hasten
to express my heartfelt pleasure at an event to me so unexpected
and so desired.— The intelligence gladdened our evening circle and
Mr. Jarvis and myself made it the occasion of recalling many
grateful recollections of the past, as well as that of anticipa-
ting pleasures which are still in store for us when you
shall become once more an inmate under our roof.—
We have lately removed to Bloomingdale, and are within
sight of the house in which you visited us just before your
departure for England. This of course brought to mind all the
associations connected with that visit and we could hardly
believe, so rapidly has time flown, that more than four
years had elapsed since you walked with us over the
lawn.— Your time must be so much engrossed by those
friends who have a stronger claim upon you than
we can possibly have, that I am afraid it will be
some time before we shall see you in New York. I
can only say therefore that there is a room for you
whenever you shall choose to occupy it and I am sure
I need not add, what I trust you know full well already,
that the sooner you take possession of it the more will
you enhance our pleasure. - It is not impossible indeed
that I may see you in Boston in the course of a
couple of weeks, as I promised my sister Mrs Hull to
pay her a visit this autumn; and though I have hitherto
been prevented from fulfilling it I have not laid
aside my intention. - A clergyman however is so con-
fined, that he cannot wander at will, and should it
so happen that I shall be disappointed, I hope you will
not let the winter pass by without paying us a visit.
Upon casting my eyes upon the date of your letter when
I had before overlooked, I find to my great surprise
that it bears date Octob. 19th. - Where it has been all
this time I cannot positively divine, but it fills me
with regret to think that you have been a fortnight
arrived without receiving my congratulations, and
what is still worse that I had seemed so negligent
and cold hearted. - Do my dear Sir, let me hear from
you by the next mail. - I have a thousand questions
to ask you.
As to the Books you have had the goodness to bring me,
I cannot at present say anything, as I am ignorant con-
the safest mode of conveyance. I will make the necessary inquiries and inform you in my next.
Mr. J. intends to add a postscript herself, and would have done so to night had it not been for the lateness of the hour.
She says, for fear I should not have an opportunity in the morning, you will say that I send my kindest good wishes and congratulations.
Have the goodness to present my respectful compliments to your father, for whose happiness on account of your return I most sincerely rejoice, and believe that Mrs. J. & myself are as well. Your warmly attached, & affectionate friend.
Sam F. Jarvis

My dear Sir,
Having just heard of a private conveyance for this letter,
I embrace it merely to tell you that your favour of October 19th was
read and answered by me the 2d of November, I put into the of
office the 3d. I presume therefore you see it the beginning of the
last week. At the time of writing it I indulged a hope which
I have now in great measure abandoned of seeing you in
Boston this season. In that case I should have taken
charge of the books myself. As it is, I am at a loss what
to say. The Navigation from Boston is not I suppose
very safe at this inclement period of the year. On the
whole therefore, I must beg you to direct them to the care
of Henry Fisher Esq. and give them to Capt Hull. He
may probably know of some safe conveyance. There
may possibly be some officer coming to New York by
water to whose care they may be entrusted.
In hopes of soon hearing from you, and begging you
to excuse this hasty Scrawl I remain as ever
Yours truly
Saw F. Jarvis

since you I have cause, my acquaintance is not stopped with Mr. West, I see him

leave to go to Paris, you did not take into consideration the difference
between the profession of an artist and every other, that an artist is obliged
to order to complete his studies to visit and study in several different
places, as Eng., France and Italy; whereas in other professions it is usual
to remain in one place, you did not consider this, or that it was by the

me act according to my own judgment, opportunity offers, I have now
completely been deprived the advantage of your kind leave, it has nearly
by a year since I first wrote for permission, it has just been received,
and now the opportunity has gone, for France and Italy are again
deluged in blood through the near-sightedness and misconduct of the
conquerors of Europe; In your request to send books, pictures, &c.
you make no allowance for accidents, impossibilities, delays, or
difficulties, but charge me directly with "negligence," and "ignotitude."
The fact is I have attended to every order of the kind; was it
my fault that the box with my pictures cast and books from Mr. Taylor
were stopped at Liverpool, and that one great picture of Hercules
whilst I dispatched as soon as was possible to Mr. Wilder at Liverpool
did not arrive in time to go by him, were the hindrances of the way,
nothing, or the expence of indirect communication? The fact is I came
not without great loss of time and completely unsuiting myself for
study attend to orders respecting books and bills, London is not like
Boston or New-York where a man has a few moments to spare and he
can set out and is this or that, I am quite removed from the city 4
or 5 miles and any business that I have there always takes me a day;
all your orders the moment I have received them I have sent in letter
to Mr. Taylor, I could do no more if I could call on him; any parcels or
letters I wish to send to America, I transmit to Mr. Bromfield by post,
I thus save a great deal of time; Mr. Jarvis' books I obtained for him in the
way, I wrote a list of books to be got at Messrs. Rivingtons, who I required
me to keep till Peace, I wrote to Messrs. Rivingtons requesting them to send me
the books lowest prices & bill, they came the next day and the man that bought
them received my order on Mr. Bromfield, the whole transaction did not take me
20 minutes; now what difference would it be to you if instead of writing

to Mr. Taylor through me, you should write directly to Mr. Taylor and request
him to send anything he has for you to Mr. Bromfield; however, on this
point I think it would be better to write to me on account of postage, and
I will transmit your request to him by letter. I forgot postage; but you can
not expect that I see packages on board ship when the place where
American ships lie is nine miles or more from me, which by
just putting in to the case of Mr. Bromfield or any merchant, who
understands business they could be transmitted without loss of time; I am satisfied
you must have misconceived the matter or you would not make many requests
you have. — Do not attribute their observations to a wish on my
part of saving myself trouble, it is not the trouble, but the time which I wish
to spare, and I am convinced my parents would not wish me to lose any
time when every moment is so precious to me. I am sorry when they
learn that their wishes can be complied with without any sacrifice of that
kind. A glorious and honourable Peace being obtained, you can now have
an opportunity of receiving many things which it was utterly impossible
you could before; the moment peace was announced the 27th of Decr. 1814
I wrote to Messrs. Carter and Storr of Liverpool, in whose possession are my
two boxes containing Master cast books and pictures of Hercules, and
requested them to send by the very first direct opportunity to Boston;
some of your letters may have miscarried, if so and they contained orders
for books, had you not better send duplicate orders, and I will transmit
them to Mr. Taylor; I have finished a portrait of myself expressly for
you since the peace, and also a little cabinet picture the interior of an
apartment exhibiting now at the British Gallery, both which I shall
send you by first opportunity, in the latter is also a full length of myself
though no likeness, I wanted a figure there, so I put myself without
attending at all to the likeness, there is a story attached to that picture
which I shall allude to in another part of the letter.
Painting is like poetry in this respect, a painter has his happy moments
like the poet, and nothing is so vexing, and so destructive of his spirit
as to be disturbed in these moments; moreover, a painter is obliged
to abstract himself entirely from the world, nothing closters so much with
his feelings as the bustle of commerce, he is obliged to work himself into
an artificial state of mind and as long as he keeps that state he
can paint with spirit, but let it be broken by any thing foreign, and his
talent becomes useless; there is no profession in which a man is so perfectly

My dear Sir Copied
There seems to be a fatalilty attending our correspondence.
At least your letters to me constantly miscarry; mine to you I
hope are more fortunate. Your favour of November 29th 1815
I did not receive till the 12th inst and while I was making
arrangements to send you a draft for the amount, I received
a letter from Capt Hull mentioning that he had paid you
and drawn on me. As he observed it was at your request
I am afraid you thought me remiss, but this letter will
explain to you the cause of my not having written you
sooner. I feel under many obligations for your kindness
in putting yourself to so much trouble on my account,
and I would not be so ungrateful as to neglect for a mo-
ment any account you should present. Be so good in
future as to direct to me, merely at New York, as I am
persuaded your letters have failed of immediately being re-
ceived on account of the name "Bloomington" which is probably
not known beyond the bounds of this City.
You are now I suppose unmittingly engaged in the pursuit of
your profession. It will gratify me much to hear what you are
doing. Portrait painting alone is profitable in this country;
out rich men not having yet obtained that relish for the fine
arts which would lead them to admire a painting for its own
sake or to patronize Genius from the noble principles of love
for excellence, & love for country. The Bostonians probably will
patronize you however because you are their fellow citizen,
and though the thought of being indebted to that motive cannot
be a very pleasing one to you, yet it may in time lead to just
views. You know I presume that Col Trumbull has seated
himself down in this city, and his collection you are prob-
ably well acquainted with. Our Academy of Arts is at present
in rather a languishing state: but I trust we shall soon be
able to make it worth attention. The Corporation of this city
have given or are about giving a large lot near the new
City Hall in Broad Way, where it is proposed to erect a
building to correspond with that noble edifice (not to vie
with it of course, but as a sort of appendage) which is to be
devoted to our literary, scientific, elegant institutions. We
are to have in it, the City Library, Scudder's museum. The Academy
of fine Arts, a Chemical Laboratory, and apartments for the learned
Societies. The NY. Histor. Soc. The NY. Lit. & Philos. Society
&c &c. I hope they will institute an Academy of Painting
and it would give me great pleasure to see you one of the
professors of it. -- Why will you not let us have the pleasure
of seeing you, when we can talk over these matters at our leisure?
I am reserving the printing of my thing for your present, and as they
tell me I look best in the winter, because tallest, you see it is of great
importance that I see you at this season. -- Have you attended as often
to architecture? That is with me a favourite science, tho'
I know but little about it. I hope some time or other to be
a Gothic church erated here, and I must consider your taste
concerning the plans. That has been a Gothic Church erected at New
Haven since you were there; and it is my intention to put up a
monument in it to the memory of my father, which I wish to have
correspondent with the style of the building. As you have probably
noticed the principal monuments in England, it may be on your power
to furnish me with a design. I wish it to be attached to the wall
in the Chancel, near the Altar, and I think of some such inscription

you have been pleased to show me. – It has always been my

Dear Sir,
Your letter of the 29th instant was duly received & I write to you
in such a state of mind & heart that I can with reason beg that no part
of this letter may be made known to any one — I shall as much as I am
able endeavour to repress the feelings under which I am labouring & commu-
nicate my ideas with betraying as little of my weakness as
the nature of the case will permit me — The Portrait, intended to be
my last letter, is a full length one as large as life of my beloved
daughter whose existence in this world will very soon terminate.
She is in a deep consumption her frame is wasting very fast & the destroying hand of this incurable
disease has at length reached her face which is generally the last part it touches — In two days after you receive
this you will either find her at Mrs Coleocks or learn where she may be found — I will give you the price you require for the picture say
six hundred dollars and pay you two hundred dollars of it as soon as you finish the head; the arms & hands you must not attempt to finish but
only take a sketch of, as it will be impossible for you to determine the
attitude (on which my very soul is fixed) without the most mature deliberation & the finishing of them at this moment would be injurious.
You perceive the necessity of finishing the head with as little delay as the
difficulty of it will admit, in accomplishing it I trust it is unnecessary for
me to say that no consideration whatever ought to hurry you in the
least bit that you ought to take as much time literally as if you
had nothing else to do. I trust I have no appeal — I wish I could write as I feel — I trust that on such an occasion you
will put forth all your powers — that you will make the canvas
speak — I have seen several of your portraits before one of which I
often sit & admire, but I will not have you believe it as which tells me
it is, far from it, I admire only in it the genius which it could inspire
form were it pressed — In the countenance of my daughter you
must give all the animation in your power, you must let from
her expressive eye her soul distinctly speak — Every muscle of her
face must be full of motion and expression instead of the flat & com-
municative expressive likenesses that are & which are usually denominated
(though falsely) striking ones, you must exhibit a picture
truly animated — It is not possible for you to have such another opportunity of placing me under such obligations to you as the present,
Is there a spectacle more interesting to humanity than that of
a father imploring from your genius an image of his departing
only daughter, that daughter too the representative of his
deceased wife? As soon as you will inform me that the head is
perfectly finished & that you have no further occasion for her attendance
I will then call to see it — The extent of the landscape I have already described — It must be divine — May you exhibit in this picture the learning of Michael Angelo, the grace of Corregio, the coloring of Titian, but
above all I will invoke the spirit of "the divine Raphael" to inspire you
with the attitude — How often shall I leave the grave of my child

Dear Sir,
Your favor of the 4th ulto was duly received
& I cannot find words sufficient to express my gratitude for
it - To have such an appearance from you, on a subject of such
importance to my feelings, is more gratifying & acceptable to me
than anything else in the world that could be offered to me,
upon the reception of this picture (the full length likeness of my
daughter as large as life, of such a description as to the size of the
Cannons & Landscape) it will only remain for me to testify
my gratitude in a manner worthy your pencil & my
honor - I have already said to you, that in order to give you full
time to accomplish my object, this picture is not to be delivered
until twelve Months from the time I made application for it,
or longer if you choose. - My Daughter is at the boarding
school of Miss Fraser & will attend you at any time, & should you
experience any difficulty in her attendance I request you will
acquaint me & I will have it removed. - You have been
good enough to promise to execute a full size half Portrait
of each of my Sons with hands & landscape, & Sam to pay you
for each of them 150 dollars; It is proper for me to apprize you
that my Sons will return to the country on the first of April
& will remain during that month & very probably may not
return to Charleston until the end of May, your time may then
be too limited to their pictures - The object of this letter is
to beg the favor of you to finish the heads of each during the
present month, so perfectly as never again to require their atten-
dance for them - I shall send them to the North this spring
to remain for some years & I do not think you will have another
opportunity of seeing them — As they may never return to me
I feel extremely unhappy about these pictures & I beg the favor
of a line from you about them as soon as convenient; will
you finish them before you leave Charleston or take them to
the North to complete? Should you intend to take them with
you, I beseech you to finish the heads perfectly as you perceive
you cannot again see them — I wish the heads finished at
any rate as soon as possible for should you conclude to take
them with you & they are executed late, upon being packed
up soon after & excluded from the air so long, they will cer-
tainty turn yellow & get otherwise injured — excuse, my
Dear Sir, this freedom, & impede it only to the affection
of a father — You had hardly reached Charleston bar last
year before my youngest son was given over by the Physi-
cians, he was near expiring in convulsions to which he is
subject, & should this again occur I may lose this picture,
the first thing I thought of when he was in peril was
the likeness you had taken of him, and this, on account
of your desire to gratify me you have condemned, so that
had he died I should not have had a fine likeness of him.
I wish to be assured against this misfortune — I wish
you to let me know what will be your price for each of the
small portraits of my sons which I hope you will finish
before you leave here, I make the request merely because
it will be necessary for me to give my factors directions as
to their payment, I have forgotten to request the price of
the small Portrait of eld2 Dunkin which I beg you will
not fail to execute — My Sister will attend you on a
few weeks — I thank you for the impression of the seal you
sent me, it will probably be the subject of a communication soon
time hence — Accept, Dear Sir, the appearance of my respect & regard
Y. T. B. More humble

Charleston S.C. Mar. 26. 1819.
My Dear Parents,
Two of your letters have been lately
reached, detailing the state of the parish & church; I
cannot say I was surprised for it might be expected from our people.— Before saying anything on this
subject, however, I will just say that Lucretia is just
recovering from a severe bilious fever, which has confined her to her bed for several days, she has, however, by the blessing of God on the means used for her recovery, safely passed through it, not however without considerable alarm on my part and indeed on the part of Uncle Finley and our friends generally, in consequence of her delicate situation, she is now comfortable and recovering fast, she exhibited a pattern of patience through all her sickness, making no complaint, and expressing no unreasoning; as to returning home in the way I mentioned Mama need not be at all uneasy on that score; it is necessary I should visit Washington, as the Pres' will stay so short a time here that I cannot complete the head unless I due him in Wash. (by the bye the City council have passed a unanimous vote to request me to paint it for the City Hall and have agreed to give me more than Dashed, 750 dollars,) I therefore, propose leaving here for Baltimore by water, leave Lucretia in the case of Nancy at B. and go on to Wash. to complete my business there, then proceed to B. and soon to Phil.
by steam boat and stage, stay a few days there, or a day as may be, then to New York by steam boat and stage, a day or two there, then
by packet to Providence, from there home by easy stage; there can
be no danger but rather benefit I think by such a plan there
will be very little land carriage, and plenty of time to rest, after
every short journey. Aunt Finley thinks there will be no danger
but rather benefit, and she, you know, is a good judge in these
matters.
Now as to the Parish and Church business, I hope all things
will turn out right yet, and I can't help wishing that nothing may
occur to keep you any longer in that nest of vipers and conspirators;
I think with Edio's decidedly that on Mama's account
you should leave a place which is full of the most unpleasant
associations to all the family and retire to some place of quiet
to enjoy your old age; why not come to Charleston? here is
a fine field for usefulness, a pleasant climate especially for
persons advanced in life, and your children, here I
seriously think of settling in Charleston, Lucretia is willing
and I think it will be much more for my advantage to remain
through the year? Ricl. can find a place here if he
will, and Edio's can come on, and be Bishop or Presb, or Professor
in some of the Colleges, (for I can't think of him in a less character)
after he has graduated: If I wish seriously, you would
think of this, your friends here would greatly rejoice if an
opening could be found I have no doubt Christians want
their hands strengthened, and a veteran soldier like Papa
might be of great service here in the infancy of the United
States, who finds its easy and fascinating tenets.
to receive any character well disposed to receive any character
with its easy and fascinating tenets.
I have not received any money lately of sufficient importance
to send you, but hope to send a remittance soon; I shall not
make so much this season as last, from a variety of causes all
of which I cannot explain in a letter, one is that Lucretia's
illness has caused a considerable expenditure of time to me
and there have been several pictures which I painted last
year that I have redeemed by painting them over again.
Will you be so kind as to inquire of Mr. Arthur Benjamin in
Broad st. Boston whether he has obtained for me the Kremlitz
White which he was to get from Germany for me; I hope he
has; I found a small quantity in Charleston and have sent for
more from Germany through a German who informed me there it was
manufactured, it is at a place called Kremlitz in Silesia,
which is famous for its manufactories of this pigment; I
tell Mr. Benjamin of this fact, as he was ignorant of
place where it was to be obtained. -- Has not my last
figure been heard of yet? I sensibly feel the want of it.
Please give my love to all; will write again soon; this is
written in great haste. -- The Surf-Times arrived safe some
time since 344 days passage, we got the bundle of kinns, but no
books; I shall go and inquire again particularly for them. --
Good bye. Lucretia sends a great deal of love.
Remember me particularly to Mr Alston, shall write him very
soon; have not got his picture.

Had we known of it at the time she suffered
I had prayed for her, particularly in reference to

design, with they were even cunning, almost as

Dear Sir,
Your favor of the 31st ult. was duly received, & I would
have answered it immediately, but was desirous of seeing your Por-
trait of my Daughter before I did so; four days ago I had the pleasure to
view it I have been since then too ill to write to you, I hope you will
deem this apology sufficient. — I wrote immediately upon the receipt
of your favor, to Messrs. Kirshaw & Lewis, and requested them to pay you two
hundred dollars, according to my promise, as part payment for the full
length Portrait you are to execute of my Daughter as large as life,
& I also requested them to pay you sixty six dollars for the frame of
the small Portrait you have just sent me, both of which payments
I suppose they have by this time made you. — The account you
have been pleased to give me of your painting of the head of my Daughter
together with the numerous reports of others on the same subject, has
so completely overwhelmed me that I shall not express to you my
feelings or my gratitude. — My obligations are eternal, they shall
long, very long, be substantially expressed to you — There is nothing
I have, or can have, so near to my heart as this Picture — My soul
hovers over it even in imagination, & should it meet my expecta-
tions, it will cling to it as to the Angel of mercy — Your first
letter consenting to undertake this Picture shall always be preser-
=ved by me, it reflects as much credit to your head & heart, as any
of your productions will to your pencil — Let the suitableness of the
drapery, the variety, the contrast, be beautiful
in perfection — but above all, so peaceful, that it may never
be equalled by any one — Whenever you will inform me of any
of the rest of the Pictures being ready for delivery, I will direct Messrs.
Kirshaw & Lewis to receive such pay for them — Is it your
intention to take any of them to the North to finish, & if so which
of them? I ask this because I shall in such case insist upon
paying half of the price, as there is to be a beautiful landscape to the full sized half Portraits of my Sons, & also to the
full sized half Portrait of my Daughter, I fear it's being done
here — but this I leave to yourself — Though my letters are
dated at Georgetown I reside eight Miles from that place — Your
Portrait of my Daughter was left in Georgetown at the house of a
friend — Nearly all of the citizens have seen it & I really think
it will occasion you some applications — I found several looking at it & even his honor the judge who happened at that time
to be holding the Circuit Court — everyone thought himself at
liberty to make remarks — some declared it to be a good likeness,
while others insisted it was not so, & several who made such remarks
I knew had never seen my Daughter — At last a rich Gent
leman observed "it was the richest piece of painting he
ever seen" this being so much in character, that I assure you
Sir, I could contain myself no longer, which speaking among the
audience occasioned not an unpleasant moment —
I am extremely pleased with it — There is certainly very consi-
erable likeness, & the more I examine it the better pleased I am
but I do not think the likeness quite as striking as I could have
wished — with regard to the painting, you know, nothing can
exceed it — as a painting alone I would have given much
more than it cost me, & considered myself fortunate in me-
eting with it — Some of my friends think the likeness extrem
strong — I am satisfied it is the best ever taken of my Daughter —
I should be much gratified to see the fine Picture
of Mr Washington Allston, but must decline the purchase
of it — It has always been my intention to procure a piece
of Mr Allston's painting & I am sure I shall do so even though
it cost more than the present one — but I would greatly
prefer some of his figures to a Landscape, & would wish
more over to have one of his last productions as
every one will constantly improve — I certainly shall
at some future day apply to him — I assure you Sir, I feel
much flattered & gratified at your kind letter in assisting
me to procure these fine paintings — it will induce me
to take the liberty of getting your assistance at some time
hence, which otherwise I should not have ventured upon
With regard to Mr Fisher's painting of the fall
of Niagara, I wish you when you next write, to have
the goodness to state to me his price & the length & breadth
of the picture & will then determine upon it — In the
mean time receive my very best thanks for the prefer
you have been pleased to give me — His fame has reached
me — it is as loud as that Cataract — Believe me
Dear Sir, with much respect & consideration —
Your obliged subser
John H. Allston

My dear Friend
I received your letter this evening, and have had a long and full
conversation with my father on the subject of it; and I think I shall be
able now to give you precisely the state of their feelings.
The course which my father would prefer before all others would
be this: that you should come and be the minister of Charleston, and
connexion with his people for sometime to come as colleague pastor
for some time to come. – Discouraging his wish would be that his connexion
might be as nearly nominal as possible – the responsibility and direction
of affairs to belong to you. – The advantages of this course he thinks are
the following.
1. He believes it is the only course which will secure the union
of the church and society. His reasons for this belief are as follows:
2. You would wish to revise the discipline of the church, and to
introduce a change in this practice which would be in the interest of Baptists.
My father thinks that he could not sustain the change without remaining
connected with the people he could assist you in their plans, and render the
revolution less hazardous.
3. With respect to himself personally, it would be desirable that the law relating to Overseers of Harvard College will
be repealed – and then the proposed plan will give two orthodox overseers
from Charleston.
4. – On the proposed plan my father retains his connexion with
the Anderson Institution, the Prudential Committee, and the various
donations to which he belongs.
5. With respect to himself personally it would be grateful to
his feelings – because it would give him an opportunity to wind up his
affairs, and gradually to deliver the church and remove this region.
It would give the occasion for the admission of an enemy to triumph. He
now feels that the public impression will be that he is driven away.
It would be much more pleasant to leave the impression
under which he will learn in that case he will be much more likely to his feelings.
He thinks it would effectually destroy all the
animosities in the happiest manner possible between
him and this people.
On every account, therefore, with as regards the property, & good
of the society, & your usefulness, & his own reputation, he
believes that the plan is desirable
With respect to the practicability of the plan, my
father believes that if you are willing it might easily be effected
through the instrumentality of the Professors to whom he wishes,
you would communicate this view of his feelings, & take their
opinion as it is wisdom upon it. -- This is the course with

man -- If the plan of colleagueship is impracticable
whether you come as colleague or sole pastor or either as

if in fact he is so heard of that it is understood
between the Bishop & Committee The person employed

to the Vestry & who are not allowed to speak as Candidates, the Pastor

him. This will give the desired opportunity to the Congregation
to judge of their talents & qualifications for settlement.

Dear Sir.
Received your letter on my arrival
at this place, which has deferred far beyond the period
that I had anticipated, when I had the pleasure of
meeting you at Charleston.
The President will leave Washington
in a day or two for his farm in Virginia. He is much
engaged at the present moment, and it is impossible
to say with certainty when he may return to the city.
In these reasons, his family have requested me to
inform you, that in their opinion, it would be better
to defer the execution of the portrait, until a more
convenient opportunity may occur. During the winter
he will be constantly at this place, and as the seat
of government offers much more inducement for
a visit at that season, than at the present, it
has occurred to me, that it might be equally
agreeable to you to postpone it for the present.
With great respect
I am

My Dear Senator
I received your long kind and affectionate letter on yesterday, and I would have answered before now but my nerves were on full
loom, loss of sleep, that I was unable to do. I do return him many thanks for it, and for his kind offer of doing
any thing that lies in his power for himself and my father's children. In time it is as he has said, that
he has lost the best of husbands and they the best of fathers. How mysterious are the ways of Providence
Had Uncle a father should be taken from children just entering into life one so well qualified to understand them in things both spiritual and
temporal. I feel he lost a great deal more with regard to my children than myself do. He is all human probability I shall soon follow him.
Great indeed must have been the shock to you and my dear Lucietta after leaving him to well on Saturday. The Monday
before you left as he was bent for to go to James Island to Mr Wilson after ten o'clock at night
and bid to go part of the way by water and to ride three miles by land. It is generally supposed that in riding through the dew he took
the country fever. The Monday night you left us upon his coming to bed I observed that he had the fever but did nothing as
he did not complain, until the next morning when I told him I had observed that he had the fever, he got up and went down stairs, but
did not remain there five minutes before he returned, and layed down and the fever never left him. I heard him call Rhayne
to finish one thousand and two hundred thousand
thousand and two hundred thousand to maintain
the fortifications of the city of Boston, to prevent
the enemy from making an attack upon it, and to prevent
the enemy from making an attack upon it, and to prevent
the enemy from destroying the harbor of Boston, and to prevent
the enemy from destroying the harbor of Boston,
And he has indeed acted the part of a
son to me and a brother to the children
he has requested me to look upon my
purse as my own
I will hereby thank you my Dear
Finley for your kind offer and
if ever I stand in need of it I shall
certainly accept of it. But I must
insist upon you bringing Lucretia
with you, we are going to move in
a new house of my Brother's near
South Bay. I have a room that I
can spare to Lucretia and
yourself, and as I am going to
thin out some of my servants
I can let you have a nurse
all the Children join in this request
even Rush who although he has not
yet seen you, says that he is sure to
fall in love with both of you
The Girls have given such favourable accounts
Do let me hear from you
as soon as possible after Lucretia's
confinement and say that you will bring
her with you - Rush is with us and is preparing
to study surveying and Engineering with Maj Wilson
who has advised him to study drawing so that he
will stand in need of your assistance
Peronneau will continue at Princeton
We all unite in sincere love to your father
mother, Lucretia & your self
I Remain
your affecte Aunt
Mary Finley
