My Dear Father,
I improve a moment to write you in answer to
your letter we have received from you, we are all well and send
you many love, Lucretia is fast recovering, and dear little Susan
is healthy and thriving. As to the concerns of the old Parish I
shall devote the greater part of this letter to that subject; and I
have proceeded to the statement of circumstances without preamble,
the project of friends which you were so much interested in,
will not, (in all probability) succeed, the project was intended to
appear immediately, (how we know not,) and we have reason
to believe that we have taken efficient measures to counteract it. I never
could feel satisfied myself as to the propriety of this measure,
it looks, under hand, I hope, you will excuse me if I say, I wish
you had not continued it, the motive was unquestionably
good, but the end does not justify the means, your friends
and family all know how to account for these things in you, but
does it not, my dear father, give occasion for your enemies, and
those that have been warning, to ventilate the cry of "a plotting
deserving man," and will not the constant failure of schemes in
this business at length induce the few remaining friends, to say
that you are desperate, and will cater at any thing to support
you and will tread so near to the line of honorable, of course necessary
that enemies will easily mistake, and friends can scarcely dis-
luciate you: Excuse the freedom I take in being so plain, my dear
Father I do not intend to express any thing which will wound you
in the least degree, or lead you to think I am wanting in that respect
which is gratefully due from me to you, but as this is entirely between
ourselves, and I know of no friend who would feel authorised
to tell you all their hearts in this subject, I have ventured to do
it but I hope in a manner that is proper for you to refer to your
a beloved and respected parent. I have conversed with Mr
K. U. with Mr Q. D. K. & Mr B. -- the two
former told me plainly they did not think it would do for you
to think of staying, or that any measures that looked like it should
be adopted, it keeps alive the opposition, by giving them an object to
aim at, keeps those men in power, who have all along been so ob-
vious. -- Mr Hay preached last Sabbath 3 times to great accept-
ance, the audience were solemn and seemed much affected, I
was myself exceedingly pleased with his manner, style, and doc-
trine and think him well calculated to unite the good friends
of this Society, and I find that the friends of both sides
as far as I have heard, speak in high terms of him; now my dear Father, is not here an indication in pro-
vidence of union in this Society, and union too complete that
very influence, which we now feel it our duty to oppose, will
those men be likely to retain influence, under such doctrine
and with a phalanx against them composed of all the friends
and well disposed in the Society; let the Lord send by this hand
of him whom he will send, it does appear to me as plain as
the sun that it is your duty, as well as your interest to leave
this spot and that too immediately, or at any rate sooner than
May next, you say, wait and see the result of the number of friends,
what has been heretofore the result, and what is now the result; nothing
has occurred in the least encouraging to the success of the method you
propos of destroying this influence: "Vengeance is mine I will repay
with the Lord," is it therefore duty for us to devise any measures
against adversaries, who shall put them into disgrace, except by preaching
the truth, especially too when it calls into exercise such passion
from the opposition: what if the child "behave himself proudly
against the ancient, and the base against the honorable," is it not
by permission of God, and is it not for wise purposes to humble
us: and by resisting in the way we do, are we not whipping the
rod instead of humbling ourselves under it, should we not let
Providence punish our enemies in his own time and way.—
In view of things at present I should suggest this course, to acquire
excuses, and encourage in your friends the disposition to settle Mr.
F. to rejoice that your end was at length accomplished, that you
left the Chk. entitled under a good man, one whom
would build them up in the faith; and as for
them, would you were willing to think that most of
them were guided by good motives, that as for those
whom you believed to be your enemies, you forgive them
and pray God to forgive them by taking this noble
father, it does seem to me you come off with honor &
as W. — I. P. L. you get nothing but disgrace, whether
successful or unsuccessful.— No one can say you deserted your
post, you must stand acquitted from any evil that results from your
removal, your opposers have to bear all the weight of responsibility.
Do not raise objections to Mr. F. among your friends on Hopkinsian
ground, what are those differences worth, if you begin a contro-
versy on their points, it seems to me your troubles will cease
only with your life, let those that settle him bear all the re-

My Dear Mother
I arrived safely last evening in this city,
much fatigued and with a severe cold upon me,
but this morning feel entirely well and in good
sprits. I found Papa at Mr. Coils looking I
feeling remarkably well, he will probably leave
N.York for N.Haven on Tuesday. I was disappoint
ed in not meeting him at N.Haven but think upon
the whole that the business of the house can be ar
ranged by us here as well as at N.Haven, I went
up into town at N.Haven while waiting for the other
boat, and in walking about, I asked what houses
were for sale. I found among others that Mr.
Woolley's house was to be disposed of and Papa
thinks that is just the thing. it would be a
fine situation for us and would make a double
house. I shall leave N.York for Washington on Thursday
in company with Mr. Caldwell of Washington. I miss
Lucetia if little Susan more than you can think, and
shall long to have us all together at N' Haven in
the Spring. We are all going to chch so good bye
for the present
Yr Affectionate Son

Washington Dec. 17th 1819.
My Dear Parents.
It did not occur to me till just now that
I had not written you since my arrival in this city;
I have written 5 or 6 letters, but they have been to Charleston S.C. & to Lucenia; I have been here nearly a fortnight; I commenced the Presidents Portrait on Monday, and shall finish it to morrow. I have succeeded to my satisfaction, and what is better to the satisfaction of himself & family, so much so that one of his daughter's wishes me to copy the head for her; they all say that mine is the best that has been taken of him, the daughter told me, (she said as a secret) that her father was delighted with it and said it was the only one that in his opinion looked like him, and this too with Stuart's in the room, the Presd. has been very kind and hospitable to me I have dined with him 3 times and taken tea as often, he, and his family have been very sociable and unreserved. I have painted him at his house, next room to his cabinet, so that when he had a moment to spare he would come in to me.— Wednesday evening Mrs. Moonroe held a drawing room, she was splendidly and tastily
made my bow, she was splendidly and tastily
desped, the drawing room, and suit of rooms at the
Presidents are furnished and decorated in the most
splendid manner, some think too much so, but I do
not, something of splendour is certainly proper about
the chief magistrate, for the credit of the nation, plain-
ness can be carried to extreme, and in national build-
ings and establishments, it will with good reason be styled
meanness. I understood after I returned from the
drawing-room that John Lowell was there, as I never saw
him, I should have been curious to have seen him.
I am painting, Dr. Sewall, he will pay by note
for a year, in consequence of his friends not being at
command at present, as he is removing to settle in
this city with his family; he is a man with whom I
have become intimate, a pious man, eminent in his pro-
fession, and moving in the first rank in society; I have
no other portrait as yet engaged but presume when
the Poets and Dr. Sewalls become known I shall have
as many as I want, to employ me till the middle or
perhaps end of next week. I am doubtful how
I shall go on to Charleston, I am just going to write
to Baltimore to know if there are any packets ready
for Charleston if there is one I shall probably go to
Baltimore and sail for Charleston, as the best &
pensive, and least tedious, and perhaps best dan-
gerous rout. -- if however, I should not find a vessel

first contemplated, by land. -- I will inform you

Washington Dec. 23. 1819.
My Dear Parents,
I received Pat's letter of 17th inst. this
morning, and snatch a few moments to answer it; I
have thought a good deal on the subject of staying
until the 10th Jan'y but conclude on the whole that it will
not be well; board is very high where I am, 2d class for
day, and I have no applications for Portraits except
Dr Sewall's & the copy of the Pres' for the family, the
former of which is completed, and the other commenced
and will be done this week, I have but one piece of
canvas left, and my materials, colors &c. running short,
so that I should be more than a fortnight without
any thing to do paying a great price for board, besides
this I find Henry has arrived at Charleston, and will
feel long pained until I join him; he writes me that
all my things arrived in good order, it is thus obviously
for my interest to hasten to Charleston, as I shall there
be immediately at work, and this is the more necessa-
ry as there are a fresh gang of adventurers in the
brush line, gone to Charleston before me.
You mention having written me from N.Haven
I have not received the letter, and therefore cannot
say anything on affairs in N.Haven. — Perhaps any
purchase or lease had better be deferred until my
return in the spring, if arrangements could be
made to board Lucretia & myself & little Susan
with you for a short time previous to my returning
and so let me find Lucretia & Susan at N.Haven
when I return northward, it would perhaps be
best under existing circumstances. — I am sorry
your letter from N.Haven is missing as I have been
anxiously expecting it ever since I have been in Wash-
ington, it may be delayed and I may yet get it —
All monies, as you request, that I shall not im-
mediately want, shall be remitted, I fear I shall not
be able to send any from here; my stoppages on this
journey have consumed my funds pretty fast — as soon
as I get to Charleston I will endeavor to send you some of
what is due promptly paid to me. —
I miss my dear Lucretia & little Susan more than
you can imagine, I did not think I should find it
so hard to part from them, it is a new experiment,
and I don't care to try it again. —
I wrote you but a day or two since, telling you
all about my success with the Portrait of the Presd.
it is acknowledged by all that have seen it to be
the best ever taken of him.— my taking a copy for
the family proves how they estimate it.—
In taste but with sincere affection
Yr Son & F. H. Mott
Love to all the family, Edwards,
Nancy, Betsy O'Sally — I shall probably leave this
city next Monday.
Rev. Judt. Morse. D.D.

Fredericksburg Virginia Dec. 31st 1861.
My Dear Father,
I left Washington Wednesday last at 4 o'clock
on my way to Charleston, arrived here yesterday much fatigued and cold with a severe cold on my lungs, but
am better to day; I am in Company with Mr. Silliman of
New York brother to Prof. S. P. we stop here to day, and
shall proceed to tomorrow to Richmond stay the Sabbath, and
then to Petersburg and so on I shall be with Mr. S. till I
arrive at Fayetteville N.C. where we separate, he for Augusta
Geo. and I for Charleston -- we had a dreadful time yesterday
in the severest Snow storm I have experienced for a long
time. It is pleasant here to-day -- I direct this to Math.
supposing you will be there in a week or two -- I left the box
containing the large canvas with the Pres. had upon it at Davis'
hotel in charge of Mr. King the painter to forward to Boston,
I will thank you to see me King on the subject, and if not forwarded to Boston let it be sent to me in Charleston -- I have
as I think it will be easier transported from Charleston than from
Boston to N.Haven, -- my funds will but barely hold to Charleston,
and if I had not painted the portrait of the Pres. and
sec. 80 doll. from him for it I should have been compelled to
have borrowed to carry me through; I have however the note of Dr. Swall
for 80 doll. to be paid in a year. -- By the way, Dr. Swall with
me to leave him a line of introduction to you, which I promised
but forgot. You will find him a very worthy, pious man
and I hope you will see him, he is at Mr. Queen's boarding
house, nearly opposite Davis' hotel, Pennsylvania Avenue.
I will remit you all I possibly can as soon as I get to
Charleston.
Good bye my dear Father and
believe me your affectionate Son
Sam'l F B. Mosby
I spoke to Mr. Caldwell on the
subject of a boarding place for
you, he told me he knew of none but
thought you might get such a place as you mention. I
am sorry we could not have arranged to meet in Washington
but I think all circumstances considered it was best for me to
come on as I have. I am glad I was on land rather
than the water yesterday.

Richmond, Virginia Jan 2. 1820.
My Dearest Wife
I wrote you a letter from Fredericksburg a
day or two since, and according to my promise I sit down
to inform you of my safe arrival in this city, we left Fredericksburg
yesterday morning at 3 o'clock, a most bitter cold
morning, but clear, with a bright moon. With all my precautions of
leggings, gloves, & mocassins, I suffered a great deal from the severity of the
cold; we had scarcely rode a mile before our hats, the bows of our
cravats, our hair, whiskers, eyebrows and eyelashes were covered with frost and icicles.
I actually found upon shutting my eyes for a little time that
my eyelashes were frozen to my cheek, we ascertain upon our arrival that the thermometer indicated the temperature at 4 degrees below 0, this is the coldest weather ever known in Virginia, (so we are told) it
has been a very fine day to-day, and although very cold has moderated some. We attended church to-day I heard Mr. Turner, an excellent sermon on the New Year, Mr. J. and his wife were at our house last summer if you recollect, I spoke to him after church and called upon him. Mr. James Dwight we found in this city also, endeavoring to establish himself in business here, he has closed his concern in Charleston: he was very glad to see me, and inquired particularly after you a gentleman by the name of Proctor, I also found here who travelled with us in the Steamboat from N. London to
New York last year, he also enquired after your ladyship.
I find contrary to my expectation a very fine hotel in
Richmond, Kept by Mr. Butler of Haven, where we are
very comfortably situated; we shall set out to-morrow
for Petersburg at 11 o'clock 25 miles, where I shall finish
my letter.— By careful nursing and precaution I have succeeded in throwing off my cold, which was a very severe
one, and I am now entirely well. I have now and then
a twinge of the defective tooth which gives me a gentle hint
that I shall soon have to throw that off also.—
I find it a great comfort having a companion with
me, especially such a man as Mr. Silliman, an intelligent
prious man, and one whose feelings and views are congenial
with my own; we are also similarly situated, both having
left wives whom we ardently love and sigh after, and children that make us long for home; he has the advantage however of one in Britain to my one; he sends his
compliments to you and says he hopes to see you one of these
days. 10 o'clock P.M.
I called and sat a little while this evening with
Mr. Turner & his wife & Mrs. Burd.
Petersburg Virginia, Jan'y. 4. 1820.
Thanks to a kind Providence, I have safely
advanced another step on my journey, and am comfortably housed
in a very fine hotel established since Mr. S. was last here, so that
we are agreeably disappointed again; we rest here till to-morrow
morning, when, at 3 o'clock in the morning, we set out again on the
most unpleasant part of our whole route, we shall not stop again
till we reach Raleigh N.C. where we shall probably arrive at
room on Thursday, riding all night, I find it very expensive
travelling on this route and I therefore doubt whether I shall
ever go to Charleston again by land; Richmond is a very
pleasant place, containing about 17,000 inhabitants, in sum-
mer I think it must be very beautiful in the vicinity, it is
on the banks of James river, this place is similarly situated it
contains about 10,000 inhabitants and is on the banks of the Appomat-
tox river, the scenery immediately in this vicinity is very
picturesque, we had quite a pleasant ride yesterday the week
or having moderated, it is a delightful day to-day and the
snow begins to disappear. We are favored with the moon
at night which we feel to be a great security.—
I shall write you next from Raleigh Friday.
at 11. I do long, my dear wife, to see you again, I miss
you more than you can imagine.— what do you think of
going with me to Boston next winter, if our lives should
be spared and we are all well? I cannot do without you
another season, I want my dear affectionate service to make
much of, and to make much of me, and dear little Susan to
May with; time will pass heavily till I see you again, dearest.
Don't forget to write me often, at least once a fortnight, wont
you dear? I forgot to tell you that I saw Dr. O'MeRl Wager
in N.York they had a fine little boy about a month
older than little Susan, they sent a great deal of love to
you and congratulations, until I reciprocated.— Good bye
my dearest wife. Have you any expectation of another Susan? I wish to

Suppose you are now left alone at home
as father is probably on his way to Washington, and Ed-
wards at Andover; I therefore sit down a few moments to
entertain you with the wanderings of your elder son, and to
congratulate you with the intelligence that he is thus far on
his journey (by the blessing of God) safe and well; I believe
I wrote you from Fredericksburg, Virginia, informing
you that I left Washington on the 29th day of December
in company with Mr. Silliman of N.York, brother to Professor
Silliman of N.Haven, an excellent, pious, intelligent
man, with whom I have travelled till now, we part at
this place, I shall set out to-morrow (Sunday) for Chas-
tor, and he next week for Augusta Geo. I have found
his society a great comfort and security throughout this
long, tedious, uncomfortable journey; and we now part
with mutual regret; I arrived here this morning at 3 o'clock
from Raleigh (N.C.) having rode all night, the place from which
I write is the best hotel in the city, but it is a miserable, dirty,
uncomfortable place; I find that the stage goes to-morrow for
Charleston, and then not till Tuesday again, so that I have
the choice of travelling on the Sabbath or staying in this
dirty hole 3 days doing nothing but spend in time & money.
in this predicament I have consulted with Mr. Silliman,
and we both think that it is best to choose the former
of these two evils; I have found this journey much more
expensive than I had imagined; I am under the necessity of
borrowing 10 doll. from Mr. Silliman which will leave
something over. I presume at the end of the journey.— I
set out to-morrow morning at 5 o'clock ride all day and the
night, the next day I next night and reach Charleston prob:
ably on Tuesday morning, at 10 o'clock, when I shall be
glad to rest in good earnest.—
I have written four letters to Lucretia on the
way and requested her to inform you as I proceeded; I
thought this was better than to write 2 letters each time
one to you & one to her each cost me 25 cents, when by writing
to her yours would cost but 10 cents, you see I understand
economy! "Have at the Spicket and let out at the Burg," I think
I hear you say, among other proverbs; Well I can't help
it; I hope soon to begin to fill the barrell at the burg, as
soon as I can get to Charleston.—
I shall write you again when I reach Charleston
in the mean time I must bid you adieu! give my love
to Edie? and the family Nancy, Betsey, & Sally if with you
and believe me as ever, your affectionate Son
Sam. F. P. Morie.
I always close without enquiring after the Charleston
herd of nobility; what are they doing now? have they turned
you into the streets yet? I see by the papers that Mr. Mead
is dead. I hope he has gone to a better place, I believe he
was a good man, though misled in his business. — I should
like to know a little of the state of affairs at home, or
your account and the family's; I hope by the blessing of
Providence we shall all be safely settled in N.Haven
next spring. — I long for the time, for I do miss my dear
wife and child and Parents & brothers very, very
much.
Again good bye, remembering me
who enquire after me.
Mr. E. A. Morse.

My dear Wife,
I had intended to have left
this City for N York this morning but am delayed
by the delay of the legislature in acting on my
Memorial. Presented on Saturday, I committed
the Com to report this morning favorably but
some objection to the acceptance of the Report
is made by two members of the Report, of course
must lie over till tomorrow, when it is believed
it will pass with much opposition. It is P also that it will pass the House
& then my object in coming here will be accomplished.
I have seen nothing of Williams
of Utica nor heard from him -- have written
him very plainly today -- I have rec'd 8 50
from Webster & Skinner, on acct of salary
which I shall send you by Mr Thurston
if I can get it changed into proper bills
to send you -- You may give it to my
Elberdsee if you don't want it for family
uses, I see that it is endorsed on my note
in his hands -- I think it probable I shall
be obliged to stay here till Wednesday as
I shall leave my letter open & close it
tomorrow for the 5 O' mail -- I am impatient to get away -- My health is
rather feeble, the cold affects me but
I shall soon be in a warmer climate.
I am anxious to hear from the family

My Dear Husband
This day and tomorrow I presume you will spend in New
York if nothing has intervened to delay your arrival there agreeable
to your letter of the 6th from Albany which was received last Monday.
We were much pleased to find you had succeeded agreeable to your
expectations and sincerely pray that if the Undertaking is calculated
to promote the Glory of God as we trust it is he will graciously smile
on it and bless it. – This day took up the Newspaper and the
first thing that caught my eye was the death of our much loved
and excellent Father Geer my dear Husband he has entered into
his rest with respect to him we may say He is well he hangs
above the wicked care from troubling and where the weary
are at rest may we be daily prospering to follow him and all
who through faith and patience are inheriting the Promises
the paper says he died the 29 of Decr aged 94, this was the third
week day before you left home why none of the family should
have let us know it is astonishing to us all I should have
thought they would have sent an purpose but perhaps they
are anxious to satisfy us when known. – We have not heard a word from Finley or Richard since you left
us but are expecting to soon I had a letter from Secretia last week
she and little Susan were well though the latter had been sick with
a cold I say they send a great deal of love to me all and Grandpa
in particular and that little Susan sends many kisses & that she
is the best company in the world they think in their family
Yesterday Edwards went to Dr. Worcester in the Street in Boston who told me
that the council had dismissed Mr. Jay from the ministry but said nothing
about Charlestonion, We presume that he will give his answer to
next Sabbath and have no doubt it will be in the Affirmative
We do most earnestly hope you will feel it to be in your own
duty to agreeably submit to & rejoice in it as ordered in Infinite Wisdom
and come home resolved to get away with your family as early as in the
Spring as possible this will be a real comfort to your family, and in order
to it will you enquire whether our goods can be transported direct to
Newhaven if it will be best to charter a vessel at Newhaven or here
and what the expence of transportation will probably be & where our
things can be stored and the expence of storage that we may
make our calculations accordingly also please to look out for good lodging
for us see if Mrs. Deforest can accommodate us all viz. Junius
and his wife & child till they get a house to their minds and
provision made & if we shall need three bedrooms & a Parlour &c &c. Mr. G.

My Dearest Ladies,
Through the blessing of a kind and indulgent Providence I have been kept from all harm and have
at length arrived safely in Charleston; I left Fayetteville the morning I mentioned in my last, it was a very disagreeable
day, rainy & foggy, the coaches were watched beyond description most ingeniously contrived for inconvenience, we were as
much exposed as if out doors, the seats were wet, and the top leaked through every crack, so that in a short time
we were wet through; as night approached, the stages grew worse, and the weather more unfavorable; no moon, and
the darkness so great as to prevent our seeing our white horses, we proceeded without accident till about midnight, when our
leaders took fright at something and started out of the road, and in a moment the stage struck against a tree and stopped
with such violence as to throw us from the backseat to the front seat, we found on examination that the swingletree
was lost and the tongue broken, this detained us half an hour in a hard rain; we had a sleepless night, a miserable break-
fast at a log hovel for which we had to pay 75 cents, all the next day was rainy till towards night, it then cleared off fine
we got to Georgetown at 5 o'clock and set out immediately again, rode all night, very cold, but clear & pleasant, and
arrived without accident or sickness safely in Charleston.
ton yesterday at 9 o’Clock.
I went immediately to Aunt Finley’s, the moment
they saw me they all burst into tears I were silent; I never felt
more depressed than at this time, jaded out by a long, fatiguing
steeples ride, finding Aunt and little cousin in a different
house; in black; Aunt so altered I should scarcely have
known her, every thing reminding me of Uncle’s absence, this
too combined with the absence of my dear Lucretia, at Mr.
Munro’s, the room where we slept, and dined, and supper
the places where we walked, all, all made me; dear wife,
feel most miserably, I felt by anticipation, what might
take place, were we taken from each other by death, Oh!
may this day be far removed in mercy, but especially
dearest may we prepare at any time to say, “the Lord save
and the Lord hath taken away, blessed be the name of the
Lord.” I went early to bed, slept soundly 12 hours &
waked entirely refreshed and well, every one says I have
grown more fleshy, I have not an ache or pain; what
shall we render to the Lord for all his benefits?”
I have got excellent rooms over Dr. Bux-
baum’s Apothecary shop, it is as we had heard, he lost
his wife and partner in business, and was at death’s door
himself with yellow fever; the rooms are very conven-
ient and large I pay 33 dollars for them – I am
very busy in getting all things ready, so dearest excuse
the brevity of this letter, I have every thing to say but
must defer till next letter.— Thank you dearest
for your good long letter of Christmas eve, it comforts
me much, I recieved it yesterday, I am glad to hear
of the health of you all; what grieved me most was
the loss of your hair, but it was necessary; will it grow
out pretty long before I come home? I regret I did
not paint you before I left home, if we live I
shall certainly do it when I return.—
Aunt and cousins & the Peronneaux send
love to you & a great deal of it, they say
you must come next winter, so I say, I
have very much to say but must defer till another
opportunity as I am in the greatest haste.
Henry is well. Rick? I have not seen.—
Give a great deal of love to all father mother sisters
& brothers; and kiss the dear child for me often; I
am glad to hear she grows; don't make any more
apologies for writing of her improvements, you are
not particular enough, I want to hear of everything
write often good bye — your most affectionate
Husband
Thirley

written you that you will it -- I think Mrs

request I send at the same time

I arrived here last evening 5.30
& this morning was handed me your acceptable
1 King letter of the 19th in the 18th in the 18th done
from Gen Warren, the 13th. The information contained
in these letters is interesting in no common degree.
The die is cast -- The will of the Lord be done &
acquiesce with cheerfulness. The consequences as
to us will be well & I earnestly hope, to the old
& congregation also -- As to the men engaged in
objecting this change & thin measures, my opinion
of them remains unaltered. -- I shall answer Gen W's letter this evening
My last was from Phila. I remained there a day longer than expected. The stage was

city 36 miles in what may be called the slow stage.

Munroe & opened to him my whole plan which has
his very cordial approbation in every part of it he
says, that Mr Baltimore, thinks with him I hope some
good plan will be ripened before I leave this
City— But as I may be disappointed, as at Albany,

is here (Mrs C, mother in law I believe) – & I am to drink tea with them this afternoon.

I have all the attentions here, that I could wish

with me is the want of a subject to write

the mortgage is sufficient seventy-half the

My Dear Sir,
It gives me great pleasure to hear of your safe
arrival in Charleston; the late storm made me somewhat
uneasy on your account. — The account you have been
pleased to give me of the superb Portrait of my Daughter
is more gratifying than you can imagine — It only remains
that you should be equally well satisfied with the price —
I will not say it is my wish — to compensate you
for your extra labour, but I shall take care that you
shall be satisfied — whatever sum we conclude you
shall receive, shall be immediately paid you upon your
answering this letter — You have tried your best to give
your opinion of the price extra price — My reply shall
be immediate. — If I could for a moment suppose that
you think me capable of imposing upon your delicacy,
I would instantly name the extra price, but I have too
high an opinion of you, to do you such injustice — My
object is merely to have some idea of what you suppose
is sufficient, it may not entirely govern my decision —
I will also thank you to let me know the price
of the frame. — I will then direct Messrs Kershaw
& Lewis to make you immediate payment. — One
of the Vessels that attend at my plantation, will in
eight or ten days call on Messrs Kershaw & Lewis for the
Picture — I am unwilling that so good an opportunity should
be lost, or I would cheerfully agree to its remaining longer
with you as the Vessel is now at my plantation, the time
of her calling may be sooner, perhaps a few days longer than
the time I have mentioned. — I was much disappointed the
last winter, in not obtaining the Portrait of my friend Mr. Benj.
Dunkin, will you be so obliging as to assure me in your answer
that you will immediately commence it — I wish this Portrait
made a very neat one — I lately saw a beautiful Portrait of that
gallant officer, Lieutenant James Dudley, represented in his regimen-
tals — I wish just such a one of Mr. Dunkin paint him in
dress'd in his regimentals, the Epaulette & sword to be exposed —
Lieutenant Dudley was a reduced half Portrait, or rather a little more
than a half Portrait, in order that the body should appear to advance,
the painting extended to about half way down the thighs, the
colour of the pantaloons being thus introduced, it afforded a hand-
-some contrast with the coat which was of a different colour —
he was in the act of walking, his left hand being entirely exposed
& the left hand with the glove on, resting on the hilt of the sword;
the coat was buttoned, no part of the right arm was seen but
the right hand was fully exposed, one of the buttons about the mid-
-dle of the breast of the coat, was unbuttoned & the right hand was
placed resting partly in it; the figure a little turned to the left
as if to observe one but the face fully exposed to you; but a
small part of the sword was seen, only the handle as the left hand
rested on the hilt of the sword, the left arm was consequently
nearly dropp'd, the sword being hung on the left side at the
usual place — It was as I have said of a reduced but beauti-
-ful size, for example had the whole figure been painted
I suppose it would have been thirty two inches, no hat was
seen; it was painted on a small piece of board, but I assure
you it was truly elegant — Let Mr. Dunkin's be of this size,
& a plain back will be sufficient — You will receive from
Mr. H. F. Hudson Lewis the two large Portraits of my sons which
have been injured from being kept from the air, please to repair
them as soon as possible so that they may have time to dry before
their removal, I shall insist upon making you full compensa-
-tion for this trouble — Is it your intention to go to the North next
spring, & to return to Charleston next Winter — I am thinking
of a New Portrait I wish you to execute for me which is
the reason of my enquiring –
With Respect & Esteem,
I am, Dear Sir,
Your Most Obt Servt
John H Alston

We received your letter of the 22 January this morning.

language. He says nothing which you want him to say. His

history at all. He says, moreover, that "The languages of the
"Delawards, in Pennsylvania, of the Penobscots bordering on

"Rible, are radically same with the Mohagan" (or Muhhekaneeuw)
"I abst from my own knowledge." -- You see, therefore, that

hand him the receipt of Mr L Dwight for the ten Dollars and

out the Incumbance of your Geographical Works and I think I can

Several days have elapsed since I have heard from you & I fear that I shall have
no more letters till I reach Phila as you will suppose that I shall have left this city in this
time but my business will keep me here probably the greater part perhaps all this week It is
going on as fast & with as much success as I could reasonably expect I trust will have
in all respects a favorable issue The President (with whom I dined in a large company,
on Friday) & the Secretary of War (with whom I dined the day before) are very kind, about
me more as a friend than as a man of business. Mr. Adams, too is very attentive & obliging,
as indeed are all with whom I have to transact my business. Mr. Mc Kinney, the Agent of
Indian Affairs, I have from & am to spend to morrow, the following night at his house in
Georgetown, 3 or 4 miles from this for the purpose of giving us the official talk over deliberately
& fully all our affairs I shall get obtain information of Indians to bring home with me which will facilitate my getting much more
trust in my contemplated tour I have nothing new to add to what I expect wrote on the subject of
my Commission. I intended to have written you
a line by Mr Goodwin, the only one of the Charles-
town expedition with whom I spoke, but he left the
city on Saturday morning without giving me notice.
It was no great disappointment to me -- A letter
from Dr. Quincy, of Alexandria, requests me simply
to spend a day with him before I leave this District.
I think I shall go -- It is only 4 miles
from here. I preached today, at the Capitol, & P. M. for
my friend Dr. Lawrick. You will infer from this
long letter after I that I am not very sick yet my
circulations in my system are very languid in my feet
& hands, especially what remains of them troublesome. The weather here is very changable, damp, & sultry, the
street very muddy, all which are very unhealthful
to health. I am most comfortable lodged &
as kindly treated by all the family as I were
of their near kin. Mrs L has a son twenty
old & died with us below for the first time to-
day -- we talk often & much of you -- Our dear child
Diego -- Dr. L. seems well acquainted with my trial
& feels as I could wish --
I think much of your trying situation, &
hope you will soon have release & be good
days, according to the days in which you are
afflicted. My own feelings were never so well,

Charleston S.C. Jan. 17th 1820-
Dear Mother,
I recd your good letter of 19th of 22nd ult. I
thank you for it; I wish I had time to give you a nar-
tative of my journey as you will but, you know "time is
money," and we must "make hay while the sun shines," and
"a penny saved is a penny got," and "least said soonest
maided," &c. &c. and a good many other wise sayings, which
would be quite fat, but I can't think of them; the fact is
I have scarcely time to say or write a word, I am busily
employed in getting the cash or else Meds almanac for
Marchill foretell falsely; I am doing well, although the
city literally swarms with painters I am the only one
that has as much as he can do; all the rest are complaining.
I wish I could divide with some of them, very clever
men who have families to support, and can get nothing
to do. -- I recd a letter from Father at Washington today,
but I suppose it contains no news to you, he had seen the
Pres. who spoke well of my picture of him &c. --
Richard came from Johns Island 2 days or two
since I spent 2 or 3 days in town, I was very glad to
see him and find him contented in good spirits.
he went back again yesterday.
Henry is well and doing well, he is of great service
to me, and is fast improving, he is industrious, and
steady, and I hope will turn out well in the end, I
think he discovers good talents.
I feel rejoiced that things have come to such a crisis
in Charlestown, that our family will be released from
that region of trouble so soon; keep up your spirits
Mother, the Lord will show you good days according to
those in which you have seen evil; I think of New-
Haven with very pleasant anticipations, but I hope
in such a manner as I brought, not setting my affec-
tions on any of the enjoyments of this world to such a
degree that when they are taken from me, I shall re-
ceive and not be in a frame to say the Lord gave God the Lord
hath taken away blessed be the name of the Lord. I am
glad Lucretia and the dear little Susan intend meeting me
at N'Haven, I think it by far the best plan it will save
me a great deal of time, which as I said before is money
I shall have to spend some time in N'Haven in getting settled,
and I wish to commence Painting as soon as possible, for I
have more than a summer's work before me in the Overs'ts
Portrait and Mrs Balls. As soon as the Cash comes
in, Mother, it shall all be remitted except what I
immediately want; you may depend upon it that nothing
shall be left undone on my part, to help you & the rest
of us from that hole of vipers; I think it very probable
I shall return by the middle of May; it will depend
much on circumstances, however; I wish very much to
be with my dear wife and daughter, I must contrive to
bring them with me next season to Charleston, though it may
be more expensive yet I do not think that should be a consideration,
for I think that a man should not be separated
from his family but very seldom, and then under cases of
absolute necessity, as I consider the case to be at present
with me; that is, I think they should not be separated
for a great length of time if I know my own
disposition I am of a domestic habit, formed to this habit probably
by the circumstances that have been so peculiar to our family
in Charleston, I by no means regret having such a habit
if it can be properly regulated, I think it may be carried to
excess, and shut us from the opportunities of doing good by mixing
with our fellow men.
I am trying to get you some sweet potatoes and will
send some as soon as I can get them ready.
Aunt Finley and Cousins are well and desire to be particularly
remembered. Remember me suitably to all the family and friends.
I hate your affections. Son Finley.
I have made some enquiries for Martha Eder, do not yet find an opening.
Wm E. A. Morse.

My Dear Sir
I did not receive yours of the 25th ulto until
yesterday. I reside ten Miles from Georgetown, my father's
servant receives my letters & newspapers from the
office there, he brings them across the river & delivers them to my
servant who conveys them to me -- Your letter covering the
extracts from the papers was mistaken by my father's servant
who thought it contained money; and according to his instruc-
tions, declined the delivery of such letters to any one but to myself.
I am duly acquainted me of his having a letter of this sort, but
being engaged with the Company of two gentlemen from the North
who did not leave my house until yesterday, I was unable to
receive your letter before then. -- I have been thus particular in
my apology for the delay of my answer as I would not have you
wait a moment for payment, even if I knew it a matter of no con-
sequence. -- Messrs Kershaw & Lewis will hand you this and will
pay you immediately $250. for the frame -- and $600 more
for the picture -- also $10. for the boxing freight -- I will then
have paid you for the picture but $800. two hundred dollars
having been already paid you in part for it -- I know that
$1000 -- is the least sum I ought to have paid for it, two hundred
dollars is too small a sum for your extra labour, it does not come
up to the spirit of my Voluntary observations on the subject
I would have made $400 the extra price did -- I not believe I
should have occasion for a picture from you, nor others. --
I shall always consider you engaged to me for such pictures as I may
annually want. -- We will now begin with one of them -- I wish
another small whole length portrait of my Daughter -- the face only,
to be finished in Charleston, all the rest to be painted at your leisure, next
Summer, at the North, to be delivered to me the next Winter -- half
of the price to be paid when the head is finished. The other half when
the picture is delivered -- What is your price? -- It must be nearly
the size of the little picture you first painted of her, but somewhat
bigger, perhaps the length of the figure maybe about thirty two inches.
I always objected to your first little portrait of her because it is
rather too small — The face is not sufficiently large to give a fair likeness — Make the next just sufficiently large to effect this purpose — I should suppose that a figure of thirty two inches would answer — Let the Landscape equal
any of the little pieces of Guido — I wait with impatience for your answer with this assurance — I want words to express my anxiety for the attitude of this portrait — It is the attitude which marks a great genius — by this Raphael became entitled to the
appellation of the "Devine" — and I confess I would sooner have a fine attitude than a fine painting — Do me the favor of making the attitude the subject of your profound study and you will give me some knowledge of it before you leave Charleston — it would be very acceptable. — I have a place quite sufficiently large to receive the large Portrait — It will be sent to a fine new dwelling house on one of my plantations that I have hitherto not frequented as often as my interest required — It will be therefore advantageously placed as my residence henceforth be more frequent. — At present I reside in my kitchen while my house at my residence is finishing, when finished it will be the permanent place of the picture — I lately had the misfortune to be burnt out. Have the goodness to say to Mr. Dunkin that I have not yet received his answer to my letter — I believe me to be, Sir
Most sincerely yours obliged & humble servt
John C. Alston
Sam'l F. B. Morse Esqre

My dear Son I have to-day visited the President's Office & my business is drawing to a favorable close. I have been treated by both with great confidence, kindness & familiarity. I have never transacted business more pleasantly with any persons. It will go strong. I hope to get away this the close of next week -- I have made as comfortable as kind hospitality can make me President Finley's friend is all attention to me -- physician & friend -- I have Finley's head & the President in a box, with I shall camp out have at New Haven -- Mr. Kalston writes me that Mrs Hazard & Mrs R. are in serious earnest about removing to N.Y. -- I am employed to look out for a house for them on my return.

My dear wife Washington City Feb. 9th 1820
Yesterday I received my comm-
mands & instructions of from the President
who are all that I wish The compensation
is not fully settled, but is in good train for
it. I will be done probably today or tomorrow
so that I shall leave the city on Saturday
to spend the sabbath in Baltimore. A theme
move on home as fast as my health &
business will allow. The weather, for several
days past, has been very mild &
pleasant, which has produced a good effect on
my health & encourages hope that warmer weather
& journeying will restore me & expect to
commence my journey some time in May. I
shall calculate to have the Company accompany me
in my Northern summer tour of about two months
& half a Tour on my Southern tour of three
or four months to commence in October.
I shall probably take a carriage & horse & driver
to be under my own control. I intend to take
the journey in the best manner to accomplish
my business & to secure my own health.
Hope you will consent to take a seat with us at
this, & Sackett Harbor, to remain among our friends
in that quarter, till our return -- This can be arranged
when I get home. We have much to do between
this & the middle of May -- May the Lord strengthen
us to fulfil it -- The Com m unity having given me
notice that they shall expect that we leave
the house the first of April -- I have written
them on the subject -- I think they are in
no great haste -- have little regard to our
feelings or accommodation -- All, however,
is of a piece -- They must have the credit
(so far as it is creditable) of acting consistently
with their conduct, in its kind, has been uniform for
the year past. I cannot help feeling very strongly
the ungrateful & unkind treatment I have received
from a part of the people & from some of my brethren.
But the Lord hath permitted it to take place
for our good & I pray for our good & as coming from
them, I desire to submit to it all without a murmur.
He is kindly telling over us all this at the moment
we need it -- my anchor here in the great object which
I have in view, & the pleasant prospects we have
before us of a quiet settlement in St. Haven -- Our
premian concerns are growing better & better
every day & I have no doubt of a full relief from
all solicitude on that head in many months. We
have many tokens that the Lord though severely
trusting us has not forsaken us. In him let us firmly
trust -- let us look above all things his continual
precence - I live always near to him by prayer.
I wish Edw'd to enclose to me to meet me at N.Y. in
immediately on receiving this, the first of the 2000
three bills - reserving the other two - I can displace
it in N.Y. better than in Boston. Write me, that
best. You have sent on to this city by my request,
I to whom sent - I expect no act. If my order does - I
with Edwards to get the first part of the new Bridge-
ment in readiness as soon as possible that it may
be put to use. I expect the whole finished, under our in-
spection before our removal - If you can see
Mr. Steepon & Capt. Spillet on the subject of the
sale of the house, I urge their assistance in
enabling us to sell it. If so, be glad. You will
of course be disposing of articles of our country
if you have opportunity to make your business
whatever you can sell for its value
you had better sell enough of our favorite articles - Probably Mr. Tracy can dispose of the
valuable furniture, stable and yard
with is better fitted to the house than his will be -
You will think of all these things.
I cannot exactly tell when I shall be at home, but
shall write you on my way - I shall come home with
a new set of feelings for the scene will be trying. I hope
I shall be enabled to bear it - I have written
instructions & advised to be ready to go with us on
our removal to N. Haven - there will be enough
of us to take a stage by ourselves. I shall write
to Mr. Spillett & Rich before I leave the city of Boston. Know
the fate of the family & of myself. I must stop. Remember my respects to all
my friends - Love to the family - I will bless you my dear wife & family at home

My beloved Husband,
It is with no small degree of pleasure that I sit
down at this time to write to my dear Tully; not however without feeling
a little something like compunction for not having written him one line in
nearby, a fortnight and for which offence I deserve a hearty pardon in his
next letter; but in excuse I plead a constant inability to write in the
day and night too, during a month past, and the days have been so
respectively cold, and short that one could scarcely look around, and perform
the ordinary duties of the day, before it was night. I received your dear
letter informing me of your safe arrival at Charleston, after the terrible
encounters on the way, and seeing the goodness of the Lord, which we
have experienced in such remarkable degree, make a suitable impression
upon our hearts, and lives, and may we with greater earnestness enquire
God what with them have us to do, and put in the way of his commandments
with enlarged hearts I look forward, dearest, with anticipation
of the most pleasing kind to your return, after a few short months
shall have passed away, how earnestly I long to see you, Tully, you
can never know how public expressions cannot give you an idea of my
love, nor of the continually increasing attachment I feel for my dear
Husband, little dear, your more interesting and intelligent every day,
and is the source of incessant pleasure to me, in the absence of her
dear father, in this, with peculiar pleasure, I trace the growth and
loving kindness of our heavenly Father who gives us all our blessings and
the capacity for enjoying them, and at times I should be too often to
give way to emotion. The trials I have experienced, were it not that
this article of interest, my feelings that I can neither feel dull or unhappy,
you never saw a little thing so full of life and spirit as she is
she is a very pleasant child, and does nothing but foolish from morning
to night, as my poor arms often testify, the dear babe gives
finely, and is very healthy -- you would smile, dear to see the police she
I am glad to hear, dear, you are accommodated with such excellent rooms but
the rent you give is a comfortable price, however every thing in Charleston
is dear
I hope to receive a good long letter from your dear husband
this evening, you must write me after love, my greatest earthly comfort
is to receive good tidings from my husband
I received a long letter from Philip State last
month he took a journey to Lexington during the Christmas holidays
and did not write for some time which caused us much anxiety
Mr Everett wrote a letter to Charles informing him he had some business
with a gentleman of L. who he was about to settle in the western style
that is to fight a duel, but added as Charles was a friend to both
parties perhaps his interference might produce an amicable adjustment
accordingly Charles took his leave, and proceeded seventy five long miles
in that uncomfortable season, to use his emotions with him sufficient
to prevent what all men of opinion would term him in blood
Everett but is a pretty choleric young man and often gets
into such a state of mind that he returns to Louisville. There has been
nothing new to say Mr. Charleston had been a widower almost one
whole year and to allay his inconstant sorrow for his first love, has
taken to himself another Uncle Joseph Walker is published and will
be married in the course of a few weeks, we always considered him
an inveterate old bachelor but Mr. Stegney's weighty charms have
melted his heart -- Mr. Chadbourne has a little daughter a few drops
of milk like some other he is very fond of -- you would think
he is married a few days before us -- Mrs. M. Garland has one
about the same age born September, baptized in the afternoon
Mary Green sends her love to you now together with my Parents, brothers
and sisters -- baby Susan sends Dear Papa a sweet kiss -- my health
has been very poor this even weather a constant feverish head ache all
the time, Mr. Bartlett encourages me in the hope that I had entirely got
rid of the feverish habit but I am very subject to such I think
I have not drank tea out been out a single evening since you left me
but good bye my precious husband your most affectionately

regret that you are so long detained at Washington which will prevent your

our letters at Philadelphia in which E has given his right
course to be pursued in this business I think you had better not get
home till the beginning of March, it would save you very materially
gaining to make E your agent to settle your pecuniary concerns
with them before you return and have nothing to do with them. I
have called on him to know when it would be convenient for
us to quit the house. told him by the first of May we had
made our arrangements to go and that he should wish to be left
to ourselves to pack up our things without the interunction of
a family with small children in the house at the time of so much
confusion as that would be to us and there could not accomodate
Mr. Fay with any convenience to ourselves he said he did not
think of it in that view before but thought it well enough &
he would mention it he believed some of the Comte was to call on
one of them here however for which I am glad. I hope we shall be
away long before then though I thought I would fix it to the last mo-
ment to give us time without being tormented with their knocking
Calvin has been to see us he came on Saturday and went away on
Monday he brought no money he will not take his house of 5 years
old he can have $120 for him hold him well I do not want him and Adam
to sell him and send us the cash he said he would in the spring if
he could his firm from his account of it is well stocked and get he does
not know when he shall be able to pay you he is a queer man I think out
you know pretty well what I think on that subject so no more. Old Deacon
Frothingham is quite feeble as is his wife Dr Porter of Andover is to sail
in a few Days for Charleston for her health he has deafness in forming
and offering to take anything for us to our sons I find that Lin
ly has all his pictures in Charleston and has a room where they are ex
hibited I presume he receives nothing for it and of course will have stren
gth of country to see them if it does not take up too much of his time

Edward is hard at work at the geography he wishes to see you before he is

Your kind letter of the 9th ult? was

to Mr Wilson I accept with many thanks. You have
liberty to open them though I am not ambitious to have
them seen in company with your own productions.
Knowing that the contrast will not be favourable to
my pictures so far as regards myself I am sorry
for I know that you look with charity on the
works of your inferiors but the Public are not
so tender in their feelings or charitable in their
expressions. I have as you advised written to Mr A.
and made known to him that I had forwarded the
Paintings to you, and also that you are authorized
to receive the pay for them. any expense which
you may be at in consequence, you will deduct
from the same I have enclosed in the
box two sketches in India Ink to serve as keys
to the Pictures with notes on the margin, pointing
out the most important parts of the Pictures
thus you will then to send with the Paintings
to Mr A. – The price of the paintings you will
collect was agreed upon – that is 200 each for the

making in all five hundred & fifty dollars for the pictures

My dear Parents;
I am happy in remitting you the above
sum, of 800 dollts. if Edw. is at home he had better
present this immediately, so that in case Papa is not at
home he may have the use of it immediately on his re-
turn; out of this sum I wish strictly paid the moment
it is rec'd. 259 dollts. to Mr Doggett for his frame bill the
rest 541 dollts. may be set down to my credit; this money
I have just rec'd from Mr John Alston who insisted that
I should receive 200 dollts. more than I asked; is he
not a liberal minded man? at the same time he has
given me a commission to paint his daughter again full
length, not so large as the last nor so small as the first
for which I shall charge him perhaps 400 doll. he intimates in his letter that he shall wish pictures of me
annually and that I must pledge myself always to him
for the pictures he will wish; which of course I shall do
without much hesitation.
Inc. a letter from my dear wif yesterday with
gave me much pleasure as it informed me of her health
and that of the dear baby's; also one from Father at
Washington directed to Richard wht I opened and
shall forward to him.

Charleston Feb 15th 1821.
My Dearest Wife,
I beg to feel a little anxious to hear from you
now, it is a fortnight since I heard by letter from you,
but the mails still continue so irregular that I attri-
bate the delay entirely to them. I am quite tired of
seeing before the Post Office door the mail north of Raleigh.
Raleigh seems to be the sticking place. I sent yester-
day, to father, the (Courier) Feb 17th in which you
will see the notice of our Academy of Arts, the mule
were drawn up by myself, it looks prosperous now
but I am not sanguine as to its success, still I mean
to act as if I was sure, whilst I am here, which
will be but a short time, my plan of a school of
painting in N-Haven strikes me as eligible the more I
think of it. Providence I think is indicating me a
removal from Charleston for the present, I find no increase

My Dearest Love
I did not begin my letter to you as usual
on Sunday, as yesterday was communion Sabbath;
and the intermission short, we had a very interesting
meeting, it will rejoice you to learn that even in
Charleston there is a revival of religion, my dear wife
The Lord has heard the prayers of his children in their
place, and is visiting them in mercy, Dr. Palmer has
been for some time much engaged, and the church also
has roused in some degree from her slumbers, the prayer
meetings, are well attended, solemn and impressive, and
some sinners are awakened, and anxiously enquiring, what
shall we do to be saved, it is "the day of small things," but
how thankful ought we to be for a single drop in such
a place as Charleston, God has not forsaken this city
great and crying as their sins are, he remembers that
there is a remnant of his children here, and for their
sake he will bless the place; Oh! that this work just
commenced may go on with power in this strong hold
of Satan, until the affection shall be proved, that the
word of God is mighty, to the pulling down of strong hills
and till the whole aspect of this city shall be changed
from blasphemy, and profanity, to prayer & praise.
Will not Mr. Pettleton now visit us? are there none of
his zeal and experience in revivals, that will come here
to the help of the Lord against the mighty if he will
come I will pay his expenses to Charleston, and I will
engage that he shall be at no loss in pecuniary affairs,
indeed, that cannot happen, five times the amount of his
expenses could be raised here in half an hour. I have
endeavored to be faithful to my dear cousin, but of what
need have I to apply the promise "in due time ye shall
reap if ye faint not," I have as yet discovered no
signs of good in them, gay, and frivolous, Volatile, and
now they almost wish (I judge from their conduct) that I
would not visit them if I took so much religion to
them; yet I know they love me, but they hate the
truth, pray for them, dear ducece, and for me.
As to my Profession, I am now fully employed
from morning till night, and shall be kept here prob-
ably longer than I expected, as this is the last season
in Charleston, I may as well make the most of it, Par-
ming other portraits, I am painting Bishop Bowen, as a
present from some of his people to him, which is also
to be engraved, it is as large as the one of Gen. Thos Pinckney
for which I shall get $300, this picture I shall take
home to finish, and exhibit in N.York when the Bishop is

Good bye dear wife business calls me.
Spring has opened delightfully, peach and plum trees

weather almost uncomfortably warm; I think you
will have an early spring at the North. In the
latter part of April or May you may expect me home
as soon as I can finish my press of business.

My dear son,
We all rejoice with you most joyfully
in the many goodness of our common Lord that
he has given you & your dear
Lucylin another healthy & lovely daughter, &
us another dear grandchild she was born
precisly at 9 o’ clock in the morning Dr. M rs
Evans only attended & was ill but a few
hours I had a good night & is very comfortable
this morning Susan was introduced to her
sister this morning she knows not what to
do with her, or to say other than “Baby,” first
The little stranger has black hair, is plump &
promising we bid her a hearty welcome into
the family We have an experience made
an attentive physician & good folks in door
& around us all together shall take good care
Syderia & the children We have love enough
for them to prompt to this We all want to
see you & shall rejoice in your return but
are willing you should remain while you
have lucrative business
We have on the whole had a com-
fortable winter The weather has been un-
usually severe, changeful & trying & we have
all had our hands full of business but we
have had no severe sickness & have been satis-
fied with our domestic enjoyment & the friendly
visit of our good neighbors
Our affairs are brightening I shall have
no more use for your fine Adams' cannon at
the Banks & live in hope of soon being free from
various pecuniary concerns.
I presume Kentucky has kept you in-
formed of all matters interesting to you relating
to the family & friends I have considered her
as writing for the half of all. I have been en-
gaged, since my return from Washington, in pre-
paring my Report -- which will be much longer than
expected -- it is not yet finished -- I have had
many interruptions by necessary attentions to my
business affairs -- many letters to write -- we were
very more busy -- the last is going forward rapidly -- will
be a very valuable & valuable work.
Some of us will write you as a Sign -- In the
mean time your dear wife, parents, & children will
the family send you much love. Susan thinks you
have kept up in abundance every day & talks much of
dear Papa -- Remember also Henry who I hope
is doing well for himself & for you.
The Revival continues, is increasing
in College -- The Pestilence spreading in 21 Parishes &
of Hartford in this State -- It is powerful in Hartford
opening Unitarianism has shown its genuine spirit in
the settlement of the Winner over the Ab. Chr -- but
I think, overacting & the consequence will be
reaction -- Zion is evidently rising in her strength,
& glory -- the glorious things spoken of her are
coming to pass -- At such a time it is expected
that Chr should do their duty.
Remember us very affectionately to Aunt
Finley's children, & to Mrs. Palmer's young
to 1800 -- to Miss' Lepers all friends.
Your ever affectionate
fellow & brother
Wm. H. More

I am still engaged in my 2d part, will we be more
longer than I had expected. I hope to finish it in all
this month -- About 1000 inst. page letter paper have
been sent to the President -- as much more is ready
I will be sent by next mail -- I then will probably
have 200 pages more -- I think it will be published
before you get home or soon after
Your bottling are to this in Ellis St. in the Gazetteer
which is far as it is finished (200 pages) I think, for them
credit, I will satisfy the public -- due prospects in various
respects are brightening -- It gives as pleasure to hear
that yours are also -- that you are likely to bring
home some business for the summer -- I have done
nothing about buying the house stand for another
reason I wish you to write us what you will have
us do -- Let think the rent too high, considering
the accommodation -- Probably they will lower the
rent, & let us have the land to cultivate, life she
want exercise -- If we could at all, I think
it must be postponed till the next season, propose
Longa -- It will depend on my success in disposing
of my property
I have received of President Day $20 for
John Tabbs, that I wish you to give to him -- It should
be passed to your credit -- I hope you will finish
in getting the $15 dollars from Mr Mitchell, or in
his absence, of his parents -- Let Henry carry the note
to him, in them -- There is a trifling one from Mr
Hoffman I believe some books to be returned, but am
not certain, others may call on him I know, I receive
the books, bring them with your baggage --
Mr Willinston mentioned a book seller, whom he
could recommend as an Agent for selling my books.
Ask him for his name -- Enquire as to his responsibility
& activity, & request the Bookeller to write me
on what terms he would be willing to take the
Agency of telling my public affairs in Charleston
I wish him to write me as soon as he can for special
particular reasons I shall wish some one there to whom
I may send my report when published.
I shall keep you informed concerning your dear
Lucretia, & little Susan & Elizabeth Ann, all the
family. Remember your mother & me very affectionately
to Mrs Palmer, John Todd, Mrs Little
Mess Mrs Legarees & families, Mrs Beach Jones Gilchrist
Miss Ramseys, Mrs & Miss Ford -- My social society
& as you have already forgotten Henry, who
is doing well for himself for you.
Your Wife, Mother, brother, Nancy Betsey
all join in sending you much love, with your
affectionate affectionate son
George
If you have money by you to the amount of $2
& $400 or more you had better purchase a dress
on N. York & send it on -- It will be better to
remit it in this way than to bring it with
you -- I have yet got your bill of the Pen. 1799
for it $150 cash & due bill on interest for 100 -- to be
p'd 10th Apr. -- I am not now in funds for payment yet.
Does Mrs Alston give you no Commission for
next summer?
We wish you would send or bring home with you some
rice & sweet potatoes -- If coffee is as low as 25 cents per pound
you had better purchase a bag & bring it with you -- It is 28 cents
here --

Charleston April 28th
1813
Dear Sir
About the commencement of your labour
in Charleston, Mrs Rebekah Stiles placed
in your hands an old portrait with a desire that
you would take this from a Copy, which was prom-
ised on your part, but either from the great press
of business which you had to go through in
some other cause, she has not heard whether you
have done any thing in it, and your departure
from this place without any communication (the
period of which was not known to her) gives room
to suppose you have not done so; By her request
therefore I have to beg you will be so good as to
inform me what arrangement you have made
respecting it, Should you have the original
with you, I must beg the favour of you to send
it me by an excellent opportunity which
into office at the return of
Bennett in June next -- Any communications
from you upon the subject will be thankfully
received by very respectfully
your obedient
Wm S Bennett
ST B Morse Esquire
Pittsfield (May 25. 1821
My Dearest Wife
We are thus far on our tour safe
and sound; Mr. Hillman's health is very per-
fectly better, delicate, last night lodged at
Litchfield, Mr. S. had an excellent night and
is in good spirits -- at Litchfield I called on
Judge Reeves and sat a little while, I found Mr.
Farrar there from Andover, they all remarked me
very cordially, thanked me for her present,
enquired after the family &c. I called at
Mr Beecher's with Mr Hillman, and Judge Gould
no one at home, called with Mr S. at Dr.
Shields and stayed a few moments; I sat
a few moments also at Judge Gould's; I was
much pleased with the exterior appearance of
Litchfield saw at a distance Edwards pick-
ered pond, we left at 5 this morning, breakfasted at Norfolk, dined at Stockbridge, we
then left the Stage, and have him a wagon to go
on to Middlebury St at our leisure, we lodge here
to night, and shall probably reach Bennington, Vt.
to-morrow night.—
I have made one slight sketch of the
Hoosac mountain, at Stockbridge we visited
the marble quarries, and to-morrow at Pans'-
borough shall visit the quarries of fine white
marble there.— I am much delighted with my
excursion thus far, to travel with such a com-
paigner as Mr Silliman I consider as highly ad-
vantageous, as well as gratifying.—
Give my love to all the family, keep
dear little Susan for me, and remember me kindly
to neighbors & friends.— W.S. wrote Mr Silliman
last week from Litchfield.— W.S. desires his
kind regards to you all,
With sincere affection and duty
Yr affectionate husband
Samuel P. Morrell

so profusely, that I instantly sent off for a surgeon, after
sending to 3 or 4 Drs. Beers at length came, and Dr. Fittsworth,
who after examining the wounds, found there was no glass in
any of them; they tied the artery and bound the hand up
with lint and bandages. The 3 first nights I scarcely slept
at all, the pain was so great; The latter night, so extreme
that 70 drops of laudanum produced no effect upon me;
about 3 o'clock in the morning after extreme pain, and no sleep,
I called Nancy to take the bandage off and put a fresh poultice
upon it; I found the hand very much swollen so that I
had a thumb but an inch long, I bathed the hand for some
time with laudanum, oil, camphor, & salt-petite, and on the
application of the fresh poultice felt so much relieved from
pain that I slept nearly all the day. The Doctor called in
the evening, and observed that the critical time was
past that every thing looked as favorable as possible the limb
was taken away and I had a good nights rest, free from pain,
I have had every attention and kindness from my dear wife,
and family from our excellent Nancy Shepherd, and from
kind neighbors and friends. My hand will not probably
be materially injured, at least not for the purposes
of my profession; the only use I make of it in painting is to
hold the Palette, mattstick, and Spare brushes, which it can do
as well with a stiff thumb and finger (if that should be
the case,) as before.— I have no apprehension, however, that
this will be the case, but am not yet able to say with cer-
tainty.— Dr. Buss thinks I can leave off the postices by
Monday, and can then go out where I please without danger.
I cushioned my hand and arm up to day and walked round
the gardens, where, you perceive, I can now do little good.
Wenvy set out yesterday for Oxford.— I shall be about again
I hope next week, perhaps be able to paint.— I am in
excellent health as are all the rest of the family.—
I have been thus particular in describing all the
minutiae of this accident, that mother may not have
the least chance for her imagination to supply any
irrealties; I have told you length and breadth, bound-
daries, situation, and extent, and No. of Sq. miles of
the whole affair, and hope you will consider it all as
past, and cause of great thankfulness with me that it
was not worse; I have felt I believe entire submis-
sion; knowing that I deserved far worse, that it was
ordered by a wise and good being, who orders all things
right, and will accordingly to his promise make it work
for his own glory and my eternal good.— We have rec'd
3 letters from you since you left, 2 from N.york, and 1 from
Albany, we were glad to hear of your safety thus far; we rec'd
the order for 300 you sent from N.york. and the books, you are, this
evening safe? Some of the family will write you more particularly
soon on business affairs, which as you may suppose, I am in no situation to know
much about.— all send love.—
Yr Aff. Son Finley.

do respecting it. in your first letter you took of

Concerned as our own, we would wish you to do
very thing towards it as far as practicable, for it would
be one of the extremest mortifications to us to have the
future fall short of your expectations, we hope that
you will be able to complete the Small one day in
30 days. As the post liberty will be of the most
importance in the future we would wish you to
be as patient as possible in the Small drawing, we shall
also be quieted by the large portrait in some wear
while we are enjoying it. -- I had an interview
with Mr. Ray previous to my leaving Charleston, he told
me that the large portrait would be at my service
while I would wish it, he beg me also to mention
to you that he did not wish you to procure a frame
but that he intended to have it done in Charleston
I suppose you intend to exhibit it in this
City during the exhibition, we shall be obliged to log on
it the plot at our own risque as Mr. Ray seems to
think that he has already been at expense deficient
for one individual, however I do not suppose it
but what we shall have sufficient patronage to
warrant the undertaking. - You may judge of our
feelings anxious, feeling anxiety feeling when we tell
you that we feel as if our reputation hung on the
succes of this portrait. independent of its good execute
we are subject to the whim & predudices of persons
who are not competent to judge of the merits or
dilements of any picture. who perhaps will explain
more against that which is truly excellent than that
which is more adapted to their own Contrarie understandings
and I have no doubt but that in the course of my
life you have seen the truth of my assertion
verified. frequently. -
I have examined these Beautiful Medallions
which have presented to us and feel under many obligations
for your politeness
With esteem very Respectfully

My Dear Parents,
I have been waiting some time for
your promised letter from Utica, we rec'd your
note from there, saying you would write again
to-morrow; In expectation of this letter I have
delayed longer than I otherwise should have done
as you will probably feel anxious to hear how
my hand is; I suffered a great deal of pain
from it at the commencement; for it was very
badly mangled, but it is now free from pain and
the wounds are all healing fast and properly;
I think I shall escape altogether a stiff joint,
all the inconvenience will probably be a large
unsightly scar between my thumb & forefinger;
perhaps another on my fourth finger; I have great
reason to be thankful that all has proceeded so
favorable; it was a fortnight yesterday since I
hurt it; and I left off the poultice only last
Friday, I have not been able toaint or draw at
all since; but hope to, in a week or two. — I
have thought it advisable to take this opportunity
of sending you a copy of the paper which I
have been writing for the last few days. It is
not a very important one, but I think it may
interest you. I am, dear Sirs, your most
affectionate son,
Samuel

My dear More/ I am in debt to you I don't
know how many letters & must throw myself
entirely on your good nature to pardon a long
silence for which I blame myself most severely.
The truth is I am the very worst of correspondents
& my aversion to writing a letter amounts almost
to honor. I hope when this reaches you
you will do me the justice to believe that
I am incapable of forgetting an old friend
with whom I have spent so many pleasant
hours. It is with the sincerest pleasure
I have heard of the domestic happiness you
are enjoying and the of your prosperity in
your profession. Will not the latter enable
you soon to come to Europe?
For my own part I have but little
hope of returning to America at present. My
lot has been of late to have gained by
my pictures more reputation & less money
than I think I deserve. I am therefore not
able to make pecuniary sacrifices, and could
not pursue the line of art I am fondest
of with any hope of success there. I confess
also that the advantages of study I propose here,
the galleries of pictures, & the society of artists
are strong inducements for me to remain where
I am. I have also some hopes that my
mother & sister will pay me a visit here.
Newton is rapidly improving & rising into notice
This last picture, the "Impertinent Author" was
sold to Mr Hope for 50 guineas; he has made one
copy of it for Lord Carlisle & is to make another for
Mr Murray. He is now painting "Love's quarrelling"
from Moliere which promises to surpass the other.
I am still living with the Bridgens in
the old quarters. Harriet is not yet married
to Brock, (they are both too poor). Betty is
grown a shipping wench & is in good natured
as ever. I have just received a letter from
Carle who is at Rio Janeiro. He has been
sailing all about the coast of South America
& seems to have had his Robinson Crusoe propensities
folly gratified, having been shipwrecked on the
island of Juan Fernandez. He was annoyed by
Lord Cochrane wherever he went & "finding all
that coast in a state of warfare," he determined
(as he says) "to leave the Pacific Ocean.
Brockdon is married & gone to Italy,
Waller is living at 22 Charlotte Street, where
Allston had his room. Martin is getting
money & children. His pictures have become
very popular, though they are not so much
liked by the artists. They
are about the same
comparision to Turner that
a splendid Melo-drama
does to a play of Shakespeare. Not that
I mean to compare Turner to Shakespeare.
The remark is only made to explain
why they strike the public more than the
judges.
Adieu my dear fellow & believe me
ever yours
C.R.Leslie.
P.S. The worthy folks below Stairs all
desire to be kindly remembered to you

Boston Sept. 11th 1821
Wednesday morning 6 o'clock
Dear Parents,
We all arrived safely in this place on
Friday evening. On the day we left you we rode as
far as Stafford springs and the next day to Boston;
Nancy went to Charlestown on Saturday morning and
Eden Jr. to Andover in the afternoon; we have been
staying at Aunt Bartlett's where every kindness and
attention that could be paid has been paid to
us. Sue is quite well and highly delighted
with every thing, she has not given us the least
trouble, she won the affections of all in the place;
every one says they never saw so well behaved a
child. We leave Boston in an hour for
Concord; we find the stage goes every day. I
did not see Eden Jr. after he left me on Saturday
morning so I cannot tell you what he did or to bring.
I suppose he will write you from Dover.
I will write again at Concord. Harriet Bee sends a great
deal of love, and little Sue sends a kiss for dear Grand-
Papa & Grand mama and Uncle. With suitable remem-
bance to all the family I am your aff. son Finley.
