Concord N.H. Sept. 13th 1821.
Dear Parents,
We arrived safe in this place on Tuesday
evening after a very quiet and pleasant ride; Lucien-
tia and Susan both bore the ride very well, and are
in good health; little Sue behaved with her usual
goodness all the way. I presented your order to
Mr Fulsom at Chester, he told me there was nothing
due on the Turnpike Shares; he would write you on
the subjects you requested. – As to the loan of $1000.
from this bank, this also is abortive, not from any
want of willingness on the part of all concerned
but from absolute inability to loan it; the details
of the situation of the bank &c. I must give you
when I see you; – I shall leave Concord on
Saturday morning for Boston spend a few days in
Boston & endeavor to be home by Saturday night
of next week. – Lucertia will return with her
mother probably (who is in bad health,) and perhaps Sis-
ter Susan too. – Lucertia, and Father & mother, and all
relation & friends send a great deal of love to you, and little Sue
a great many kisses & Grand Papa & Grand mama Uncle. –
In health your affectionate Son
Wm. Kelley.

Dearest Sister
I arrived safely in this morning at
noon, just in season to take dinner with Aunt & Uncle Salisbury; I had a very pleasant ride and
felt no inconvenience from my early rising; I should have been very glad to have had my dear Lucrce & little Sue with me, but all is as should be; this
line shall soon meet again in our own hired house at N-Haven, where I long to be; I shall leave here on Thursday morning, probably, so as to take the N.
London boat on Friday home.
I was charged 13c. in the mail stage from Concord so that you had better take the Accommodation when you come down. I suppose
you will hear from Father, at that time, you must be at Andover in order to return with him; Edward wished me to say you had better not be in Andover
be there, if Father should be there, if Father should be there, if Father should be there, if Father should be there, if Father should be there,
will inform you in due season. You had perhaps
better drop a line to him to meet him at Andover care
of Edw. to know when you must be there, and I
think I would write it immediately so that it may not
be delayed in reaching him. I am a little particular
on this subject, as I should not care to have you
disappointed in getting home.
I shall call on Uncle & Aunt Bartlett
to-morrow morning and see about the Porter Va. I
talked with Aunt about getting you a bonnet; she
says, that it is no time to get a fashionable winter
bonnet in Boston now & that it would be much better
if you could get it in New York as the Bostonians get
their fashions from New York and of course much later
than we should in N.Haven; she thinks that white is
better than blue, Va Va Va which she can explain to you
much better than I can; she is willing, however, to
get any you wish if you still request it; she thinks if
you cannot wait for the new fashion, that your black
bonnet put in to proper shape with black plumes would
be as tasteful and fashionable as any you could procure,
I think so too. You had better write Aunt particularly
about it.

which it had permitted me, some few years since
even before I ever had the happiness of being Queen
to you -- I went 20 miles beyond Lake George some of the
most romantic Wild Scenery ever seen by me --
visit the Uncle of Mr. Cadell -- who since together
with his Wife have paid the debt still due by us:
and at this moment while Sarah -- the second Son
of that family is residing at my house -- in his way
to enter into business as a Merchant in Chicago in
a very flourishing Town in the State of Georgia -- he
has all my Moses Mildness -- with his swarmer
in mode -- but not the sortler in the -- he is but

the expected, but afflicting intelligence of the
death of your very worthy & beloved Mother
in law, Mrs Walker. The event took place on Mon-
day last. We have had few particulars of the

of her sins through Jesus Christ. She requested
Dr. P. to be sent for -- He can safely leave her
in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who
doth right -- I pray that the very great loss with
the family has sustained may be made up by the
bestowal of spiritual blessings. Lavinia is very
tenderly afflicted but is supported. I trust, by
the religion she professes -- We are all very
well & comfortable -- I am engaged, to live in
illness, in finishing my report -- laying in winter
wood & provisions & my own hands -- I have
my hands full --

New Haven Nov 24th 1821.
My very dear Husband,
Since I last wrote you I have received
two very kind letters from you one on Monday and one
yesterday morning both of which afforded me the highest
gratification, indeed even it not for the pleasure of hearing
from you my dear Finley this frequently I could not feel as an
accused to these long, and to me, very painful separations.
The time appears long already since I saw you my dear Husband
and though you have been gone but three weeks it seems
more like three months you have probably heard of the death
of our dear Mother ere this – what a sad change will
be made in our dear family – I scarcely realize it; as I
shall when I visit Corona again – the care of my mother is
so intimately connected with every thing there, that I shall
always be painfully reminded of her absence – but it is the
Lords doing – and I not only submit, but acquiesce in the
will of him, who doth all things well – I hope God that energy
has been mingled with judgment, that my strength has been
according to the day of trial – Hope the Lord of my soul
and forget not all his benefits – my prayer and desire is
that the may indeed prove a sanctifier affliction
to me, and all our dear family -- I have not heard from Concord
since I received the letter informing me of my Mothers death.
I wrote Susan a long letter last evening I think it probable
Charles will return to N.York this winter -- I feel for
Susan, a great weight of care and responsibility has devolved
upon her -- but I hope she will be able to pay us the long
expected visit next Spring -- but every thing here seems is so
uncertain, that I make no future calculations of enjoyment.
I shall send this letter by Mr Edwards, whom you will
probably often see -- Tatchell expects to go on soon, but this
will be determined on the Presidents answer to your note --
I will send your Correspondent full of tea and the Camas, about a
lb. Father -- who has spoken to Mr Turner to procure the
Elms -- Mr Hillhouse is absent for the winter at Savannah
or somewher in that region -- James is here on a visit --
he and Mary were here yesterday they requested to be kindly
remembered to you, as do all our neighbors --
Little Sue was much pleased with Papa's pretty letter she talks
about you when she sits up in the morning and wants
to hear a story about good Papa's her hair growsaster --
and she has a sweet color in the cold weather -- She is more
fond of reading than of reading but knows seven letters --
whilst I write she has got a piece of charcoal, with
which she is making eyes, and nose on her baby's face --
I feel very glad to hear you are furnishing your studies under
circumstances so favorable, but do not like to hear of your deafness
grateful and sincere appreciation of it -- as it you will get upon them by such means
a severe application to study -- I shall feel anxious about you, dear Kinley --
shall fear the consequences as it respects your health— Our love to
King— accept a large share for yourself from all the family and much
very much from your most affectionate
dear papa
Lucas
Serve you all time I want to see
you— I am your loving son
Samuel

Mr Taylor sermon this afternoon was from 2d Kings 4, 26, and she
answered It is well -- occasioned by the death of his youngest child.
Society -- about a year and a half old, whom they buried last Tuesday
after a very short illness -- this was a very sudden stroke, the father
particularly seemed bowed down under the pressure of this heavy
affliction, and he was enabled to speak with great feeling from
the above text -- how often are we reminded by the word
and providence of God, to beseech our children with are the
dearest earthly objects of affection to a Christian parent's heart,
as though an appearance them not, We ought ever to remember
how frail is the tenure of all our earthly enjoyments,
and how liable we are to have them torn from us by
death -- affliction reaches us more, the vanity of world
and the uncertainty of every thing here below, than any
thing else -- this is not our rest, we need to be continually
reminded of it, for we are all prone to make the
worlds too much our home and lose sight of heaven --
I feel very anxious to make a slight improvement of the
late chastisement of our heavenly Father in bringing me
of a dear, very dear Parent, if the fruit of this affliction
is to make sin more bitter -- to make me more afraid
& committing it in thought, word, and deed, more
heavily minded, more conformed to Him who was made
perfect thus suffering -- how shall I bless his chastising
hands! I received a kind letter of condolence from
Mary Appleton a few days since -- she expresses the hope
that you have been with me in this trial, that I have
enjoyed the sympathy of an affectionate husband and not
had the trial of his absence, in addition to other sorrows
but the time is short and these light afflictions will are but
for a moment shall work out for us a far more enduring
and eternal weight of glory, while we look not to the things
seen and temporal but to things unseen and eternal -- this view
of the subject makes me suffer with patience the will of God --
Iain would write more to night, dear Finley but my head
begins to ache -- I was very unwell last week, with a diarrhoo
in my head, faintness & loss of appetite -- I thought I must give
up, and take my bed, but I got better, walked out, and
thought a great deal of my illness was only to not
take the air and exercise often enough, and to want of
a little change of scene having been confined to the house
for more than three weeks Monday morning father received your
letter about the canvas on Saturday -- Mr Brown is making a box

Dear Father,
I have been delayed in sending the enclosed
by not being able to see Mr. Dwight;
I have nothing new to add with respect
to my own affairs except that I am progressing as
fast as can possibly be expected.
The choice of Chaplain yesterday by the
House I think will create a general feeling of regret
& may I not say of humiliation among true Chris-
tians of all denominations; after a hard struggle
of 4 ballotings Rev. Jared Sparks of Baltimore
was chosen their chaplain; Unitarians will triumph,
no doubt, they are playing a deep game here,
as their arch-master, the Secy of State is wholly
in their interest. -- Something should be done to
stop their career, or infidelity, (the remains of it
in our country) will soon arrange itself under this
name of Christianity in order to wound it more readily,
I am convinced that Prayer, united special prayer for
their swift destruction, will be the most powerful
weapon to assail them with, (is a weapon they cannot
will not God hear the prayers of his People, and
for his own glory's sake, reveal himself, and show
who is God indeed, whether this Baal, or the God of
Israel:—
In haste;
Give my love to Wife to little
Susan, Mother, Brothers, and the family, not
forgetting the neighbors.—
Yr Aff. Son
Sam'l P. B. More

I hope before I receive this your good Father will have
arrived safe and well. Your Dear Wife & little girl are well
as are all the family We are all much pleased with your
prospect of success in your Undertaking and daily pray
that the best of heavens blessings may continually attend
you even the Spirit of Grace. – I enclose a letter from An
droos of Hartford which I will thank you to hand to your
Father tell him the Atlas that Edwards men
tioned sending and which was to be sent to forselyne
by you arrived to day and altho open at one end so as
to slip in and out it came charged $4-62 1/2 cents
I intend to send it to forselyne and let him look at it and
get them at the post office to let it remain in the office
till your Father returns it was marked 10 printed sheets
they weighed it and marked it 9 1/4 ounces – young Mr Gould
has just called on your Father to request for himself & a num
ber say three or four of the Students the privilege afforded the
others of having the Geography & Atlas at 40 1/2 cents Discount
I told him I knew your Father would grant it if he were here

this wayward heart feel more sensibly, and more constantly the gratitude due for this continued uninterrupted stream of blessings; Why
lot is cast in mercy, dearest Luciece, I cannot but wonder at the goodness of God, it is indeed, unfathomable, when
I consider the innumerable sins and follies of my youth, my past ingratitude, and present insensibility, and contrast
them, with the showers of blessings, the blessings of the gospel, the blessings of a pious ancestry, of a pious education, in
the most favored country on earth; the choicest of all earthly blessings my dearest wife, these, and ten thousand hours
mercies; when I make this contrast I am dumb with wonder. What shall I render for all these blessings,
In my last letter, dear Luciece, I submitted a question for your decision, which I have since decided in the way which I know will suit my dear wife
(best, I mean as to the time of my return, I shall
complete the 70 and then return home I hope
by the first of March. I find the picture is be-
coming the subject of much conversation, and every
day gives me greater encouragement to believe that it
will be more popular than any picture heretofore ex-
hibited; all that I have asked, apparently, is, in it a
high distinction and honor, and I am evidently courted by
some in hopes of an invitation to sit, I shall indulge
all I can, consistently with being at home the time I men-
tion. I shall paint it on part of the great canvas of
all when I return home, that is to say it will be 11 feet
by 7 and an half feet, that will divide the great Canvas
exactly into 2 equal Parts on one of which I paint the
House of Representatives and on the other the Senate.
I find great pleasure in the studies I am making, &
feel confident as to the issue, if you will have patience
with me at home; I expect it will take me till next Oct.
to complete, should my health and strength be continued.
I hope your health is good my dearst Louise, and
that of my dear little Sue's. I do long to see that little prati-
ter, and again to be at our comfortable fire side.
Last night and the night before was very severely
cold here, and I suffered considerably in the night, from the
hardness of the bed, and a rheumatic attack in my right
hip and knee, but I feel nothing of it in the day time; I
use a hard brush and have almost scrubbed the skin off
which has driven away the Rheumatick. I
have rec'd $300. from Chatto for the pay for the
Bishop's picture, and have one portrait engaged
already, and almost another; so that I am doing
very well, thanks to our Great Benefactor and friend.
Father preached to day for Mr Post; his health
is very good I never knew it better. Father sends
a great deal of love to you all, and many kisses for
little Grand-daughter. I wish the little Pussy for
her Father a great many times, and tell her that
Papa will come home by and by.
Good bye Dearest Wife
Write often of affectionate
Husband as ever
Finley.
The butter, Mr Hercules, and the sausages, are having
rare cold times, somewhere in the ice between this
and N-York.

Dear M r M r -
I arrived here a few
days since from Georgia where I
have been constantly employed
since I last wrote to you - I
was much pleased to find here
a letter from you - I did not send
you in the Price - because I did not
think you would remain long enough
to receive it, I will send it in time
with the Palmetto tree - which
I think - I can procure exactly as
you want it - I shall not have time
to attend to it sooner - I think it
would suit you better then, than
sooner - I have had some account
of your undertaking from the Papers
& I do most cordially wish you suc-
cess with it - I have now a joint
prospect of being able to float
in this miserable tide of life with
less difficulty than hitherto -- but as
my light may be only a blue light -
I will not be too languid -
I have business enough now on hand to
occupy me the remainder of the season
when I shall again open these in Charleston
Our Plans -- that even so nicely scientifically
Quid out on our walk from Whitney --
but occupy any of my time it is only when
in company with a friend like yourself --
that I like to canvass possibilities -- or impossibilities
if you choose -- however I did not pretend to
believe my own propositions in that instance so that I
think the Court is still on my side -- If you have license -- I wish you to ascertain
for me -- in what manner the specification of the Patent for what is called the
trumpeting Steam Boat -- is drawn up -- whether the patentee claimed
in inventorship of applying power -- or only the application of it
to boats -- for the same thing has been used in this state 30 years -- in Italy
as far back as 1620 -- for I have opinion of it at that date -- it was the application
to guiding cars -- I mean the horizontal wheel but the inclined plane -- I shall be
very glad to hear from you when you
have been sent to Philadelphia. It might be
interesting to me to know how many of them are at Charleston -- as I have a friend who
forwarded my letter -- unless I am mistaken -- I have no notice of any thing in
my own country of Notice -- do call
to mind -- Your sincere friend
Bryant

William Cannon of Co
Smith, who is in England when I was at Alexandria a few weeks ago I received
by his hands a parcel of letters from America & read them while I was present. He then
asked me if I knew you. The happened at that moment to be reading a letter from your
brother Richard. He seemed delighted at meeting with one of your friends & hearing
from you & immediately wrote still preceding notices that I might send
them to you. He said also that he wished very much you would come to the Mediterranean & wished me to
say to you that if you will mention the time & place he will take you up & give you a cruise wherever
you may wish to go. — Capt. Smith, as you probably know, is now comman=
der of the Adventure & is employ'd in making surveys of different
coasts in the Mediterranean. He talked of you as of a very particular friend.
Louis & Roger de Coverly & May day are pronounced
to be the best productions of two exhibitions -- the
beauty & convenience of the Costume particularly admired.
He is now engaged in making illustrations for some work
publishing by Mr. Murray -- he still lives in the old place
in Buckingham St.
Mr. Jennings was well when I left -- he is going to Phila-
delphia some day next spring -- he carries the views of
the Panorama with him --
Mr. Earl has been at Lima & is now at Buenos Ayres
he will call at Paxton premises to go to England --
Where is Mr. Alston?
It likely you will meet the Institution --
I intend writing to your Brother
Richard in answer to his, before long
you will hear before this which
orders all things wisely, to afflict me
& disappoint me in removing my
dearest friend & brother. I never knew
what affliction was before. My heart
now sometimes sinks & dies within
me when I think what has taken
place I knew he was mortal & we often
say often & sometimes on
the possibility that
death might soon
separate us. But the
anticipation of the
such an event is one
thing & realizing it is another.
You will mourn when you hear of it.
I trust you will pray that an event
apparently so inauspicious & afflictive
may be overruled for great good.
To remember me very affectionately
to Mrs. M. & to your Parents &
Brothers. May you grow in
grace & thus be happy. Yours S
P. Fisk
P. S. I ought to tell you that Capt. Smith
invited me & urged me very strongly
to take passage on board his vessel
for Tripoli in order to see that place
visit the forts there &c. Had my cir=
cumstances & arrangements at
the time been such as to admit it
I would have gone with great pleasure.

Our President returned in the last week of our

of your Paintings we had, your Portrait room done in

for a beginning and at 25 sec perhaps the Season
considered - this was pretty well, it has done

we can hear nothing of its arrival, I got

head have now separated that
his face could no longer carry
the marks of Dr. McCall.

My dear daughter,
I thank you for your good letter of the 12th for your goodness in that you have so justly fairly
supplied the neglect of your husband I brethren We are relieved by the recovery of Bethany
& the improving health of your husband but grief to hear of the affliction of Mrs. Green which
to Adam present our tender sympathies I arrived safely, I well I of Sabbath morning
your Mother was at Charleston town attending worship there in the Morning I came over to dine
with one at the Longtans We have been there at Charleston town & Mr. Vinalls successively fine
I have been closely engaged in settling my personal prospering business with Clark who succeeded in making an arrangement which is nearly completed, that in existing circumstances, I think the best all round, which could be made, & which I have reason to hope will save me from any great loss of property by Clark
The conduct of Converse is shameful, & incompatible with integrity. He knows that it is his duty, & that it was my full expectation, expressed to him, that he should take care of that matter. There was no thought at the time it was given that Andrews would fail but enough till I get home
I am glad none of the family but one of us are on this note late or any return
We expect Edw's Friday night & hope to go Saturday 6 o'clock & get to Pompey in season &
so over I spend Sabbath in Woodstock & can now fix no time to be home -- but it will
be as early next week as possible --
Edw's may expect funds here to settle his debt I had requested $175 from Mr O -- but am glad to get
any -- If you will after receiving this address it to Hartford, to the care of Henry Read on No 9 --
The storm prevents my going abroad today & may delay my return as I mean to stay &
finish the business with C -- as far as it can be done at this time --
We hope Finley will recover strength to work at his pictures I find high respect for
him from it here -- Rich must not apply himself so closely to injure his health & spirit -- Debby
must also be cautioned --
Our affectionate regards to yourself, Harriet, & brother love & many kisses to dear little Sue & kind
remembrance to the Tracy, Nancy, Betsey & Eliza

New Haven Conn. Nov 19th 1822.
My Dear Mother,
Your letter of yesterday we have just received which has given us a great shock; I need not tell you that we shall feel very anxious until we hear again from you, and the state of Father's health, we fear his sickness is more serious than his ordinary dispositions, but we will hope the best; we shall expect another letter from you to-morrow, and a line every day till Father is better. We are all pretty well, Lucretia has a little of the head ache from sitting all day in your room with a charcoal fire, but will doubtless feel better in the morning; Edwards left us this morning for Boston, and will probably be in Boston soon after you receive this; he was detained partly by business of his own, and partly on Mrs. Bobb's account, who was unwilling to go in the distressed state of her sister Goodrich's family, little Edward Goodrich that beautiful boy was taken suddenly sick, and died last Thursday he was buried on Saturday. Prof. Goodrich's family are of course in much affliction, but seem greatly supported under it. We have had a busy and very interesting time with the missionaries, who
sailed at 6 o'clock this afternoon with a fine wind,
may God prosper them! particulars you will learn
better hereafter. We feel much gratified that you
are under the hospitable roof of Uncle and Aunt Batt
lett, and Aunt Livemore, we can easily believe that
you receive every kindness and attention from them;
give Lucretia and my most sincere love and thanks
to them for their kindness to us and to you.
Little Susan is in fine health and sends many kisses
to dear Grandpa, and Grandma; she continually asks
why don't they come home?
I hope your next letter will relieve our anxiety
about Father's health, and that he will be able to reach
home soon.
Our money for family expenses is running
out, as Father has been gone so much longer than he
expected if you have 10 dollars to spare, it would relieve us,
if not I will try and borrow it.
My Picture proceeds rapidly to a close. I shall
complete it in all fancy if I have my health.
Nancy feels much concerned for Father and sends
a great deal of love to you, she says she will come
on immediately if you should wish it.
Quentin Richard, Nancy Henry, Betsy and all
are well and send love to you.
Good bye Y Affectionate Son
Saml. J.B.Morris

Boston Feb'y 21. 1823
Friday evening.
My Dearest Wife;
I suppose you are anxious to know
the result of the first day's exhibition of the
Pictures; information of its being open is not
generally spread, and will not probably be under
4 or 5 days. The day was fine over head & warm
so that the walking became very bad. The receipts
in all were $40.55 cents of which $11.80 went for keys
making 38 keys sold, leaving $35.75 as the receipts for the
first day, things look favorable & I think on the whole
we may anticipate something from Boston. -- The
season tickets seem to have sold well between 30 & 40 cents
I think the reduction in price from 1 doll to 50 cents
was wise, and that the entire advantages of it are
not yet experienced, all are for bringing others with
them, so that in a day or two I shall know something
of the effect. -- I have nothing new since yesterday
I have got rid of my cold I think entirely. I dine
to-day at Mr S. Foley's they inquire after you & send love
While & Aunt Salisbury are well, they came to see my pic-
ture to-day. Son Mason has been in twice to-day he
came in the 2 time with Mr. Leav & family, he is very
much pleased as he recognises nearly all in the house.
I do not know when to say I shall be at home
again, you may depend upon it is soon as I can. I think
I shall go down to Salem and arrange the business there
and then return to Boston and then home.
Good bye my Dearest Wife
Your little friend for her Father tells her she must
leave to read before I come home.
Love to all.
Your Husband
Finley

My Dear Sir.
As there was some uncertainty with respect to the
Bank business when you left me, I thought perhaps you might
feel some uneasiness about it, I therefore now inform you that
I went to the City Bank on Friday morning, & found Mr. Payson,
he said that the news had not arrived, & that when it was sent
he would take care of it in the way which you proposed --
Yesterday was a very bad day here & I suppose that you
found it so -- the receipts were as follows $23175 of which
$11 were Season Tickets -- They stood 13 -- $1.624 --
I went down today with $30 to deposit -- but could not
get the Exchange -- I could not find any less than 500 Dollars Notes
I went to the Bank 800 from here it was -- Now I hope I could
probably get the Boston money next week, but it makes no
difference to them, so I shall keep my money by me until
next week --
I hope that you have had a pleasant journey home
& found your Friends all well -- The Receipts for
this day only $15413 -- Keys & $1. The reason of this
I know not -- however I hope we shall see better days ere long
I have sent out aman today with 500 handbills, & I
hope will do some good -- I have just now laid for
hastling 400 Keys $400 four dollars -- I think we
shall not make our fortunes out of them!
Please give me love to all the Family, and others who may
enquire after me -- Your Obst Lentt H. C. Batt

My Dear Sir
I have just rec'd your letter, I am glad to hear
that you are safe home again, I also rec'd this morning a letter
from my Father, they are all well. The weather has been very
unfavorable most of the time since you left me, so that the
receipts have been small, I think nearly as good in proportion
to the weather as formerly. My Books stand thus. Receipts for
Monday 11.50 Tuesday 8.50 Wednesday 13.63
Reys 60 Pots 4 do Pots 4 do Pots 4
Mon. Blues. very wet and blustering. Wet, dull and heavy
Today, thus, it has rained all day & now continues to rain fast
with considerable wind -- The streets are running Brooks, with
glass ice beneath
I have paid your Note at Mass. Bank, and destroyed it,
also $250 for distributing small Hand Bills, also 3, for board
you probably recollect Daniel Lemonnier has established himself
in Charleston and is said to be an excellent workman -- As I think
it necessary to get a new R of Bret I will let him make
things he said that he had no leather good enough to make them,
so I'd him in advance $5: that being his price for the Brets --
I hope you will not disapprove of this measure, as I cannot
wear my present Boots more than 1 or 2 days at a time, on account
of tightness -- As to lighting the Fiction in the East
as you propose -- it will be attended with some evidence & trouble
but perhaps may be profitable -- with your leave however I should
not think it best to do it until the walking is a little better
I have made enquiry about Lamps. Mr Doggett says that former
Exhibitors brought them with them from E. York, I cannot get any one
indeed I buy them, and I conclude that as we shall want them somewh
it will be best to get some made, I have accordingly spoken for
6 to be made in all this week, they are to be made larger enough to
take nearly a pint of ale in the Liverpool fashion, only plain with
that which falls on one side (this is the Liverpool Directly down
upon it) & the apparent aim on one side is a piece of finished tin brush
the lamp is finished and which I expect every selection, I think that
6 will be enough, but if they should not I must get more --
This will cost each -- your direction, about the green baize
I will attend to, a lot to pay for Uncle's liberty --
I should like to know how wide you would have the barges?
My Receipt this day will not amt to a Dollar, nor is it to
be wondered at for I should think that all would stay at home, who
were not necessitate to go out --
Saturday -- Long
In the first part of this letter in was written on Thursday I mention that
the receipt for that day would not amt to $1.00 a few more however came
in the afternoon so that my account was Thurs. 3 -- Friday 9 -- Saturday
being a pleasant day $22.90 -- Thurs 10.8 -- 8 p.m.
I intend to have deposit $27.00 in the City Bank today, but midlock

I have thought Sir, that when I get ready to Exhibit in the Exposition will

"For 3 weeks Only -- " because that people are
under the impression that it will be here a long time, and therefore put

and in that way save time Responce -- If the people of Philadelphia
had known that they could have seen the Exhibition any time, we might
have spent the Exhibition for 3 months, and not collected much
more than we did in 4 days --
I don't know but I ought to make some reply to the closing part
of your letter, which I shall do by saying that I felt you were
dispensing great confidence in me when you put your Picture into
my hands. And I assure you Sir, that my honorable feelings, (solicited
from the debt of gratitude which I owe you) would naturally prompt
me to do the best for you which it is in my power, please to accept of
this assurance, I believe me to be humbly Servt
H. B. Pratt

Boston. March 12th 1823
My Dear Sir,
you will probably not be much gratified with the
account that I shall now give of the receipt of your Picture; but
we must try to look at the bright side of things. Hope for the best
If I recollect right I wrote you on Sat last. I gave you an account
up to that time. On Monday I deposited in the U. Bank $42
forty two dollars — The receipts of Monday were $50
of Tuesday $50 and this day they will probably amount to $300!!!
The Weather is warm, the walking bad, it rained fast last
night & is dark & cloudy now — M. L. Wells was here last
evening, on his way home he appeared pleased with the Painting.
H. G. Otis, & his Daughter were here yesterday also. They knew
nearly all the Portraits, without the Key — Some Charleston
people have been over, such as — Dr. Zufro & McIntire — Harris — Devers
Kettell, Robertson &c. — I am making preparations to light
the Picture, but dont know how it will succeed, I find it a
very difficult job, but I shall know soon, and will write you
on present employment, but as I have undertaken it I shall
do my best, I shall not make anything out of the Key, not even
enough to clothe me, but I do not wish to be anxious about that
knowing that I shall be provided for — I shall expect to hear from you
again soon — Please remember me to all Friends, I believe me
Yrs respectfully H. C. Pratt

Boston March 15th 1820
My Dear Sir.
I had almost concluded not to write you
today, as I have nothing to interest you, but as you have
given me directions to write twice a week, perhaps you
will expect to hear from me. I see your letter yesterday,
was glad to hear you were well, & your family,
I have not yet opened the Picture in the Box, but am
ready to do it on the 1st of next week, I find it very
difficult to light this Picture properly, the lights have
to be placed near the floor, and near the Picture, so that
you can easily conceive that it takes a great deal of
light to illuminate the upper part, but this I cannot
light it so equally as I could wish yet the lamp light
gives a very rich glow upon the Picture: besides the
Lamps for the Picture I must have 1 for the Door $1. for
the head of the stairs — The weather on Thursday was
pleasant—Receipts $9.62 1/2 Sep. 372 — On Friday it rained
very fast most of the day — Receipts 75 — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — —
In the Evening it snowed, and this morning was very slippery,
it has thawed today, and the wind is very high —
The receipt to this day are $9.60 —
I offered to pay Mr Salisbury the Postage as you directed, but he

I have now 24 dollars by me which I expect to deposit on Monday

My Dear Sir,
You are probably expecting to hear by this time that I have taken considerable money, by the Exhibition, if it was best for you, I trust it would be the case; but thus it is not at present –
was pleasant – Rec'd 87-67-60 Tuesday – I devote you in part why you have probably need – Monday brought with it a cold easterly rain storm, which effectually kept the Bostonians by their firesides – And $10 – Today is March, weather windy, squalls of rain pleasant sunshine, 80 80!! – On Monday Evening I slighted the Picture, & had one man come to see me on Tuesday Evening, it seems to me that I did not light at all, this Evening I propose to try my luck again but do not expect many will come until next week (which is the last of Exhibition) and then I shall send around notice –

My dear Friend.
I trust I need not say how gratified I am by the receipt
of your very interesting letter, and how much I regret that so few opportunities
of communicating from the port of the enemy for indeed, I have
but the moment had notice of the present occasion, and cannot therefore
enter into the long detail. I am about to trouble you with.
I rejoice extremely in the success you have already in the
beautiful Act you have adopted, and have no doubt that American sailors
will meet to your talent and exertion. Ruthy American engines, I
cannot but feel deeply anyone that has advance in Science, Literature
and Art should be commensurate with her power. Remembrance stipulation
desirable and that can only be attained by a diligent and persevering
application of Genius to immediate objects. I shall be much disappointed
if circumstances prevent any having at some time or other a tour through
the United States.
I cannot, for want of time, enter at present, on any views &
projects, but I am glad to inform you that I am rapidly completing,
after some years labour, a post public undertaking the first volume
of which has just been published by the Dominikty, but I doubt
from Malta, previous to any copy having arrived from England. It is
large & worthy work, of which I shall be proud to send over one of the
first impressions for your notice. The instrumental results are determined
by the finest instruments, & the whole detail is the fruit of much
laborious fatigue.
I return many thanks for your handsome by printed Gazetteer
and am highly delighted with the account of your machinery for sculpting groups
of Sculpture. I hope you will, at some future day, visit my little collection of
Antiques, Minerals, Medals, &c. Thank you for sending me
the pictures of your pictures. I am sorry to hear that you are in England. You will find my
wife and children remain at No 14 Horton Street, Kensington. With
diverse wishes for your continued health & welfare. I subscribe myself
My dear Friend

Dear Sir,
I received your letter of the 18th and heartily rejoice
with you in the goodness of God. I hope your Son may be permitted
to grow up to be a comfort and joy to its Parents —
Among those who have visited your Picture, yesterday, were
Gov. Philips, Judge Quincy, Mrs (old Nick) Fuller, &c —
The Weather on Thursday was very stormy, from Morning to
night, the snow fell 4 or 5 inches — Wednesday was quite
blustering — Friday was pleasant, and very
thawy. I have taken off today — I think it will be safest for me
to pay off my bills, now before I depart any more in the bank,
Owing to the badness of the weather. I think I had better stay
here next week, and week after —
I have sent home the Recorder, which contains a
notice of yr Picture — being the same as has been copied by me,
Mr Willis called and left it here, you will observe also
that he has copied the Advertisement. I gave him a Season
Ticket for himself and family — The cause of Religion (as far
as my limited means will allow me to know), is steadily prospering
but I cannot give you particulars — I was desired to go last S. Evening
to hear an Universalist — he was a young man in every Sense
and I was ready to say with Truseli a most extravagant bad Preacher
The greatest part of his sermon being made up of expressions like

Boston March 26th 1823
Dear Sir:
I received your letter of Monday, and am
glad to hear that you are not disappointed as to the
succes of your Picture – Among those who have been
here to see it: are Mrs. Foley and Family; Miss Mary
Payson came with them – Mrs B. Gorham – Dr Hodder
of Charleston, who desired a particular remembrance of you
and your family – Mr Fisher (the artist) was here
yesterday – just arrived from Charleston S.C. – he appears
in better health than I ever saw him before; they all seemed
well pleased with your Picture –
Lellys Picture arrived here 2 days since in 6 days
from Charleston – to be Exhibited after yours is gone –
Mr Dunlaps also came here the same day, but has since
gone to Providence, Mr Dorsey, who has the care of it,
is here yet, – appears to be a fine young man –
Monday of this week was fair Receipt 500 Reys "37 1/2
Tuesday also fair Receipt 900 "75 Reys 1"
Wednesday Snow Storm all day – Receipt 1000 "75 Reys "12 1/2
The Receipt of Wed. 19th was 400 Reys "25 –
I have lighted the Picture 5 Evening and have in that time
taken 1450 – I heard Mr. Corneille Beach last Sunday
in Charleston. He is affixing Mr Fry for 3 or 4 weeks
In answer to my inquiries respecting his Family, he told me
that he has had another son added to his Family, about the
same time as yours, he was greatly surprised when
I informed him that you was keeping them Company
he says it is an interesting time in Charleston especially
among the youth — I went to the Chapel on Sunday Evening
but could not get in Mr Fry informed me that
numbers often went away for want of room tho the Chapel
is full twice as large as formerly
Majors Evarts Day, Cornelius Humphries have all been
here — Mr Allison told me that he would get
some of his Friends to write for your Pictures
The most common fault that is found with your
Pictures is its small size — if you could only say
that you had 10,000 feet of canvas to show. I presume
it would satisfy them — As for me I intend my
leisure time in bidding; but propose by 12 by (with yr
leave) to get some water colors, and Paint some
little designs for my amusement and improvement
I dont know that I have anything more to say at present
so I will leave the rest till next time, for the present
bidding you forever
With Respect Hesteen Lt Col 6th Srt
H C Pratt

Boston April 10th 1828
My Dear Sir.
I rec'd your letter this morning, and am glad to find that you have directed me to go Eastward, as there is no vessel for Baltimore short of 8 or 10 days. I should have lost much time in waiting - Monday this week was Rainy. I rec'd only 125 on that day Tuesday, Fair Rec'd 7:75 Wednesday - Pleasant Rec'd 1362 This is more than I have taken any day before - since the 10th of March which is 1 month - According to my usual success I have another stormy day today, so that I do not expect any company - I have not deposited any intency in Bank except that I have given you notice of $13,742 at 20 cents & 26 at another - I have now with me 51-68 - I have yet to pay for the Advertising in Newspapers, wh I suppose will amount to 25 - besides the Room Rent and Board, and a former bill of Mr Doggett's wh you directed me to pay so that I dont expect that I shall collect enough, in the 2 remaining days in Boston, even should the weather be pleasant, and the only way that I know of, to do, is to engage to send Mr D. his money from Salem or elsewhere as soon as I can collect it - I am glad to hear you say that Mr Aston is coming to N.Haven think he will be pleased with the place, and cannot doubt that his company will be very beneficial and agreeable to us - On the 1st of next week I shall go to Salem, but will write you on Saturday - Please to remember me in love to your Family. I believe me. Your Most Obl Servt
Henry C. Pratt

My dear Sir,
I beg you to accept my best
thanks for your letter, and for your kind
attention to my commission. which I am
worrying however that, circumstanced as I am,
it is wholly out of my power to enter
at present into the engagement you
recommend. The situation of the proposed
house &c are every way what I could
wish, and I should not hesitate did
I feel certain of being able to fulfill
the engagement. But indeed the future
is, for one so slack in purpose as I am, very
uncertain ground to build on; and though
I may allow myself to build air castles
on it, I should not feel if I were
acting either prudently or honestly to
tempt another to erect any thing more
substantial for me on so precarious a
foundation. In short, though I still adhere
to my plan (much as talked over with
you) and apprehend no cause of change,
it is yet so dependent on contingencies
that I can neither naturally do more
now than arm me with patience or indulge
myself in wishes. I have been obliged to leave
Bilsharzer ever since you were here, in order
to raise the means where with to proceed with it.
I hope, however, to resume it in about ten days
and then to continue and to the end without any
interruption. This unwelcome delay will of
course protract its completion far beyond the
time I had calculated, and it was on that calculation I had formed the hope of returning
going to Newhaven in the Autumn. It is true
I may still finish Belshamster in time for
this; but I cannot be certain of it, especially
as I was never in my life right in gusts
at the day of finish, in my labours. So in
my safest course at present seems to be
defer all thought the engaging a house until
I shall feel that I am at least within a
month of completing the work that is to
supply me with the means of living in it.
You will therefore have the goodness to make this
known to Dr Jones, that I may be no impediment
to his engaging with the other gentlemen whom
you mentioned. At the same time I must beg you
to make my best acknowledgements to him for
his kindness and liberality – as also to Professor
Silliman, whom I must sincerely thank for
the friendly interest he has taken in my
behalf. – As soon as I shall feel myself on
some ground I will lose no time in letting you
know. Meanwhile I shall work hard to reach the
Terra firma – so long to me a terra incognita –
another word – for fear that I have not been sufficient explicit, I must add, that I would have you on no
account either engage a house or give any
encouragement to any one building one with the
view of my taking it – as in case of unforeseen cir
to occasion disappointment, would
give me more pain than I am willing to risk, and such
as I should not easily get over.
I am sorry to find that you are so low-spirited.
You should not give way to discouraging thoughts so
soon; for your Picture can hardly be said as yet
to have had a full trial. If its exhibition here has
not been profitable to your purse, it has gained you
a full harvest of praise. I believe all amongst the
higher classes have been to see it, and, as far as I can learn,
there is but one opinion concerning it -- that it does
you great honour. I have heard many praise it
highly, and not a single voice against it. It is
especially admired by the best judges -- such as Mr
Dutton, Mr Lodman, Dana, and others whose opinions go a great way in the circles where they move.
Indeed it is so popular amongst them that I cannot
account for its lack of profit in the circumstances that the lower classes must have been
gaining in curiosity, and as they make the
map of the town, if it does not attract them
the receipts must of course be small. But from
theodormen I do not think it likely that the same
result will happen in the other great towns -- New-
York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Charleston. The common
people there, if mistake not, are more accustomed to visit
places of public amusement; and those that are in the habit
of attending them, I should suppose, would find entertainment
in this Picture. Besides, its career is but just begun. Be
of good heart then -- I have no doubt of your success. -- I have
applied for several weeks past to various of my friends to write
about it but without success until to day, when Dr Channing
undertook it. He has written a very handsome notice, giving the
picture high praise, and speaking of it in a way that I
think will procure it a good reception in
the other Cities it will take in its tour through the States. But
he has not said more than it deserves -- so live upon price
for the present, and depend on it a little patience will bring
you more solid food for long. The price will appear
in a day or two in the Daily Advertiser. When it does I will send
it to you. My respects to your Mother and other Muses
and believe me ever yours sincerely
H. Allston.

My Dear Sir:
I have just received your letter of March 31st, and I suppose
you that I am not a little surprised to know that you are so
just now, you have probably received before this time my letter
of April 2d and I think if you are acquainted with all the
circumstances, you will permit me to stay here another week
The Snow that fell on Monday rendered the walking (and riding
too) quite intolerable, but there has been rain since and now
the Snow is almost gone -- So that it is probable that next
week will be more favorable than any yet. add it to this
that yesterday was last day so that I could not open
I concluded in the beginning of this week that I should
have to stay the next, and therefore have not sent
around my last week Handbills I have consulted
Mr Doggett he says that he would not have me lay
any stress on his opinion, contrary to your orders, but
thinks if I stay next week I shall stand a good chance
for success as in any former week. others are of the same
opinion all agree in saying that we came here in the
most unfavorable season -- that Boston people will not
not come out unless in pleasant weather -- &c &c
On the other hand I have your orders to leave this place
next week, what to do I know not. I wish to consult
your interest and am decidedly of opinion that I should
that most effectually by stopping at any rate I see no
mischiefs that can arise from such a course of conduct
State I am unwilling to disobey your orders respecting the
Pictum. And if any disadvantage should result from
such a course, hope you will attribute it to no bad motive
but to what under existing circumstances, I conceive to be my
duty. Besides your dispiriting letter, which I received this
morning. I have been visited with a violent toothache, which
still holds on to me, so that altogether I find I need a little
fortitude to keep up my spirits.
I have taken $8.50 today, and hope for more tomorrow
I have $22.50 in tax, -- have not paid the Advocting --
all other bills are paid I believe except the room --
I have not got the baize yet, the Scan did it at short
notice, and shall, unless I hear from you to contrary
on Monday, I wish to say however that it will
cost 14 or 16 doll., and I fear will not Panaway
so well as the gilt frame after all --
Do write me as soon as you receive this and
let me know if you approve the measures
I am taking --
With respect and affection
Yrs H. C. Pratt

Salem April 12th 1823
My Dear Sir,
I arrived here on Monday Evening, & the Picture, on Wednesday
morning, I have put it up in the Essex Coffee House, the Room is
small, but the bed that I could get in the place, I give 75 to day
for it at 44 pence week for Board. I have had the large Handbills
allied, & a 1000 small ones printed 300 of which were distributed
yesterday. I do not expect much from Salem, as I am tired they
do not take much interest in such things so that, if I
pay my expenses, and enough more to go on my way, I shall
be thankful. The Picture of France has received no injury in
moving and Putting up -- one of the Rose lovers is shot at
the carelessness of the driver -- the Printers here seem a
little more obligeing than in Boston. The Gazette (which I send
you) has just noticed it & says after he has seen the
Picture, he intends to give a more particular description
of it -- you will see by the Advertisement in this paper
that I have a cut to head it with -- it was done by Throck
in Boston -- I should have written you before that
it not best punctilily I had something to say --
It was a very unpleasant day yesterday, I slept 2-20 -- but
was not quite ready, and did not light in the Evening --
I have taken 5-12 today. The weather has been stormy more than
half of the day, but it is clear now and I intend to light this Evening
I wish you would write me immediately -- I am in haste
but with Affection and respect H. L. Platt

Salem May 3d 1823
My Dear Sir I have given above, an account of my Receipts
and expences and you will see by this that I have not cash
enough to meet my expenses by 3d 41, besides which it will
cost me for my passage to N York. In the Actin 11 or 12 dolls.
You, no doubt must be sensible of the mortification to
disappointment which this result has caused me, I know
not which way to turn, being a stranger here, and having no
credit with any one except Mr Cornelius, I went to
him this morning, and told him how I was situated, he
generously offered to let me have any amount that I wished,
and said he was glad to do anything that seemed like a
kindness to me, on account of his Friend Mr Morse,
he said. That he should have had me at his house while in
town, if it had been practicable, but he has the Crank boys
there, and a large Family. I expressd my gratitude to
him but told him that I could not have accepted such an offer
if he had made it He says his ashamed of Salem
people, for not giving more encouragement to the City
I shall borrow 220 of him, concluding that it will be the
best course that I can pursue I shall leave this ingenious
climate for N York, on Tuesday morning next in a Sloop for
New York, and I should rejoice to meet you there if it
is convenient, as you could probably be better able
than I to find a Room for the picture, but if you do not
go, please to send a line to meet me there informing me
of the fact I do not know that it will be
interesting or useful for me to say more at present,
Hoping that I may see you soon, I am Sir
Your Most Affy Servt H.B. Pratt

My Dear Sir
When I last wrote to you, I expected to have
sailed from here on Monday last, but the Vespett did not get ready
to go until Wednesday, and then we had an East wind, on Thursd
morning the Wind was rather N. East, and we sailed, but before
we passed the Light House, it veered round completely ahead, and
blowing very fresh, and looking likely to Storm, we thought best
to put back, which we have since found for our good, as it blew a
Gale and Storms all last night, and all day today -- but there
is a prospect of a fair wind now for tomorrow Morning, when I hope
we shall be able to get under way -- Fearing that you might
feel concerned about your Picture, myself on account of delay,
I thought best to send you a line informing you of its safety --
I hope to be in N.York as soon as Monday Evening, and
also sincerly hope to meet you there, and I think you will
consider it important that you should --
My health is good, and hope that you and your Family enjoy this
inestimable Blessing, hoping soon to see you. I am Sirs
Yr Affl Servt
H.b Pratt

before this I would request Mrs M. to inform him of the content of

New York June 132 1823
Dear Sir
The receipt of yesterday was $4122 in the
greater part of wt. was taken in the Evening
I have paid Mrs Richards 8 dolts and 4 dolts at the C. House
for my Taverns, also 1 to Mr Durand, also 3 dolts to the
carpenters $3.50 for the Sign — 3 pay 25 cts to Hunderd
for Distributing 16 Bills I have sent round 900 —
The Baize and other Drapery cost 6.372 — for bill I have
paid 3" besides a number of small things which you will
see in the Book — I have 30 dolts for Mr Boraitter
for the rent of room, which he has never yet called for
I have covered the Frame with Drapery, and think
it looks better, The Chandelier, now in the greatest light
which catches the eye in looking at the Picture, and it
seems as tho the Frame was needless — Mr Jarvis was
here today — spoke very highly of the Picture.
The times are very dull. Fine Exhibitions are complaining
that I believe the Court of Death is doing pretty well.
I walked at Platt's, in Broadway, where I saw some very
good French Brushes. In a good variety of sizes, the Price
is from 12 1/2 to 25 cts each, I should be glad to secure a set
for myself if I had the means to do so
I feel more & more determined in my plan of going into
the Country, to Paint Landscape & Portraits. There is here
in town a Mr Wallis who has taken 2 Views of P. York
and the surrounding Scenery, in Water colours, They are
to be engraved in Aquatint Price to be 12s in pairs
He has issued Proposal, and has already obtained 25 or 30
Subscribers. This I think shows that People are fond of Views.
I doubt not but you have thought from my former letters,
that I was impatient to get released from the care of your
Pictures. I confess I am somewhat so, because I find it
much more is known, and fear that so long an interval
from Painting will prove more injurious, than what I ever
anticipated, when I commenced the Exhibition, but notwithstanding
all this, I wish you to keep me here as long as you
consider it necessary for your convenience, and if my letters
are written in a moment of discontentment, you must not
think that I wish you to release me until it is convenient for
you to do so.
The receipt of this day is 3s 2½d
The 3 last days have averaged 1s 2s 5d about one half taken
in the evenings I have lighted every Evening in the week, so
that I am confined here from 7 o'clock A.M till after 10 P.M.
except the short time at my meals. You must excuse
this bad writing as my Pen is poor and I have for the present
lost my knife. Please give my love to your Family
I should be glad to hear often from you, you can be sure
by him down to the Packet now at them in the shortest letter.
I remain Yours &c H. C. Pratt
Sam C. F. B. Morse. Ege

I am sorry that Henry returns
to me without bringing to you what you anticipated when I saw you. However, your pictures have been praised by judges & amateurs, but yet this is not they only thing an artist thinks desirable. The want of success with the multitude is, that the figures are small, whereas they do not boast of taste, must be pleased with something that can be comprehended at once, with figures (course I badly proportioned if you please) larger than life, & should man
aspaint Hercules strangling serpents, the form as large as a steple, & the latter as immense as the size of the sea serpent, he would please New York. My Dear Mr. More
Your two letters (the first en-
closing 25 dollars) have been received by me
6 during my late absence. I should have

I expect to leave to Boston in will depart

I hope your beloved wife's parents a

head has been a season of affliction to me.

a, one who must get past through the

Will join with me in affectionate
and very cordial remembrances to your
Parents, wife, Brothers & little "pikamines"
while I can assure you

thirteen respects

THE NEW-YORK OBSERVER,
A RELIGIOUS NEWSPAPER,
Is published weekly in the city of New-York, on Saturday morning. The first number was issued on
the 17th May. The paper is principally devoted to Religious Intelligence, but contains also miscellaneous
articles and summaries of news and information on every subject, in which the community is interested. The
advantages enjoyed in the city of New-York for collecting the earliest intelligence from all parts of the
globe, and for diffusing it rapidly in this country, it is now well understood, are greatly superior to those of
any other city in the United States, and this pre-eminence is every year increasing. The conductors of
the Observer, by means of their correspondence with gentlemen in Europe, will be able to procure the
earliest information on all subjects interesting to the Religious community. The Observer will not be the
advocate of the peculiar opinions of any sect or denomination, religious or political.
RECOMMENDATIONS.
We regard the publication of a paper upon the plan exhibited in the Prospectus of the Observer, as an object of great importance.
The character and qualifications of the Editors, inspire the fullest confidence that it will be conducted in such a manner as to merit
the general patronage of the Christian community.
JAMES RICHARDS, Pastor of the first Presbyterian Church, Newark, N. J.
PHILIP HAY, Pastor of the Second Presbyterian Church, Newark, N. J.
ASA THILLYER, Pastor of the First Presbyterian Church, Orange, N. J.
SAMUEL FISHER, Pastor of the Presbyterian Church, Patterson, N. J.
It is with no common pleasure I have been made acquainted with the design of establishing a weekly religious paper in this city,
to be styled the "New-York Observer." Nothing has delayed the appearance of such a publication, and nothing has prevented
the combined patronage of the Christian community in its favour, but the difficulty of procuring men who are competent to the
editorial department. That difficulty is now removed. In the talents and acquisitions of the gentlemen who are to be the
Editors, I have high confidence ; and shall be much disappointed, if the Observer stands second to any paper of the kind in our country.
GARDINER SPRING, Pastor of the Brick Presbyterian Church.
New-York, April 1823.
The claims of the New-York Observer to public patronage are so clearly and forcibly stated in the Prospectus, that I find no-
thing to be added on the subject. I therefore simply express my satisfaction that such a paper is about to be established in this
city ; and may hope that it will meet with a liberal support. The character of the gentlemen who are to be the Editors, is an ample
pledge that it will be conducted with ability, and with advantage to the great interest of truth.
J. M. MATHEWS, Pastor of the Reformed Dutch Church, in Garden-street.
New-York, 27th-April, 1823.
I have carefully perused the prospectus of the "NEW-YORK OBSERVER," and am well assured at the capacity with which
its editorial concern will be conducted, and its evangelical character sustained. Of that capacity, as it respects intellectual re-
sources, religious principle, and the not less valuable quality of adaptiveness to the peculiar service, I entertain the highest opinion.
Such a weekly vehicle as the Observer proposes, and which is of religious and general intelligence, is eminently needed in this metropolis,
and will, I devoutly trust, receive a general and generous patronage from men, and the most primitively important successors of the
herradication of God.
SAMUEL H. COX, Pastor of the Spring-street Presbyterian Church.
New-York, April 29, 1823.
It has for many years been deemed of the last importance, that a religious newspaper be established in this city, upon some
plan of frequent and familiar communication with the middle section of our country ; and the partial supply of religious intelligence,
now afforded by one or two publications of this kind in New-England, does but increase the consideration of the necessity of obtaining
such a paper in New-York. The paper of the "NEW-YORK OBSERVER," proposes, as appears to me, the best of all methods
for distributing, cheaply and rapidly, the most valuable of information interesting to the church and the community at large.—
But what is of much greater concern, the Observer is to be edited with a knowledge of the subject, with a high degree of attention to the
object, with a liberal spirit, with a strong sense of the importance of the subject, and with a strong sense of the necessity of
promoting the great interests which are enlightened. It is, therefore, with less hesitation than I have ever felt before, and with
a stronger assurance of its success, that I recommend to the people of my charge, and to the Christian community generally, the
patronage of the "New-York Observer."
PH. M. WHELEPLEY, Pastor of the First Presbyterian Church.
We cheerfully recommend the general plan of the contemplated paper, and are persuaded that the Editors will conduct it to
public satisfaction.
JOHN B. BOMEYN, Pastor of the Presbyterian Church in Cedar-street.
JOHN WILLIAMS, Pastor of the Baptist Meeting in Oliver-street.
New-York, May 3d, 1823.
Having full confidence in the integrity and talents of the Editors of the above paper, I cheerfully concur in recommending it to
the patronage of my fellow-citizens.
PHILIP MILLEDOLER, Collegiate Pastor of the Reformed Dutch Church.
New-York, May 3d, 1823.

The plan of a weekly paper, such as proposed in the prospectus of the Observer, is one which promises much usefulness, and
which the best interests of our city particularly require. We, therefore, cheerfully concur in recommending it to the patronage of the
public.
WM. MCMURRAY, Pastor of the Reformed Dutch Church in Market-street.
THOS. McCALLISTER, Pastor of the Presbyterian Church in Rutger-street.
STEPHEN N. ROWAN, Pastor of the Presbyterian Church in Greenwich village.
New-York, May 3d, 1823.
The influence of New-York newspapers upon the sentiments of the community, is felt by all. Whatever serves as a pure vehicle for the
most seditious diffusions of religious prejudice, is most pressably acquainted with what is as given an intimate in the affairs of Christ's
kingdom, as they do in the concerns of the empire as they do, and must excel a salutary influence upon religious society. Such
a vehicle the "New-York Observer," from the object it proposes, and the character of its Editors, promises to be.
JOHN KNOX, Collegiate Pastor of the Reformed Dutch Church.
New-York, May 3d, 1823.
A religious newspaper, which, without respect of persons, names, or parties, gives correct intelligence of what is going on in
the peculiar kingdom of God our Saviour, is worthy of Christian patronage, and much needed in this city. Hoping that the Observer
will be conducted on truly Christian and liberal principles, we give it our recommendation.
ALEX. McLEOD, Pastor of the Reformed Presbyterian Church.
ROBERT MCCARTY, Pastor of the Orange-street Presbyterian Church.
New-York, May 5th, 1823.
I entirely concur in the opinion that a religious Newspaper, such as that proposed to be published under the title of the "New-
York Observer," may be made, if properly conducted, a means of circulating much valuable information, and of eminently promoting
the interest of peace and order in society. Having a very favourable opinion of the capacity of the gentlemen who are to be its
Editors, and relying upon their assurance of the Christian and liberal principles which are to be observed in the discharge of their duty, I
cannot but wish them success in so useful an undertaking.
JAMES MILNOR, Rector of St. George's Church.
New-York, May 20, 1823.
While all the friends of Christianity will readily admit the great importance of establishing a religious newspaper in this city,
those who are acquainted with the talents, the literary attainments, the successful experience, and the influence of the conductors
of the New-York Observer, cannot but feel assured that it will, in every respect, merit the general patronage of the community.
WARD STAFFORD, Pastor elect of the Bowery Presbyterian Church.
WILLIAM PATTON, Pastor of the Presbyterian Church in Elm-street.
New-York, May 5th, 1823.
Having had an opportunity to peruse the first number of the first volume of a weekly newspaper, entitled the New-York Observer,
contemplated for the future to be regularly issued forth from the press, as a vehicle of religious and other useful information: I
cannot but express my highest approbation of the same; and as, from the character and qualifications of the editors, I feel the fullest
confidence that it will be conducted in such a manner as to give general satisfaction, I do most cordially recommend it to the
most liberal and extensive patronage of the Christian community of the city of New-York.
CHRISTIAN BURK, Pastor of the North-West Reformed Dutch Church of the city of New-York.
I cordially concur in the above recommendation.
NICHOLAS J. MARSELUS, Pastor of the Reformed Dutch Church at Greenwich.
I approve of the plan contained in the Prospectus of the New-York Observer. If conducted as proposed, it will certainly be
a powerful instrument for the diffusion of religious knowledge—for the pulling down of the strong holds of ignorance and darkness,
and distributing for the world with the light of the truth of the Gospel of Christ, and also in disseminating useful information on other
subjects interesting to the public.
STEPHEN OSTRANDER, Present pastor of the newly organized Reformed Dutch Church in Greenwich-street.
New-York, May 22d, 1823.
The New-York Observer being on such a plan as will be eminently serviceable to the community in general, I cheerfully recommend it to public attention.
JAMES G. O'GILVIE, Pastor of the Fourteenth Presbyterian Church, in Proust-street.
New-York, May 30, 1823.
I am much pleased with the plan of the New-York Observer, and with the specimen of execution given in the numbers which
have been issued. In the abilities of the writers I have great confidence. I think the paper is calculated to do much good, and do

JOHN MCDOWELL, Pastor of the 1st Presbyterian Church, Elizabethtown.

My ever dear Wife,
I intended to have written you by
the boat on Saturday knowing you would feel anxious
to know how I got through my journey &c. but I
was prevented writing in season by being engaged in look-
ing out for lodgings; When I arrived in N.York I found
the packet had not arrived with my baggage, so that I
came away from N.York without even a change of any
thing, leaving Richard to send my baggage by the next
boat; Every thing arrived safely, and I have got
into my lodgings with which I am pleased, I have
a large front room on the second story 25 by 18 feet
and 12 feet high a very fine room for Painting, also a neat
little bed room with every convenience, and board &
lodging all for 6 dollars per Week which I think is
very reasonable; My landlord is an elderly Irish
gentleman with 3 daughters, once in independent
circumstances but now reduced, every thing bears the
appearance of old fashioned gentility which you
know I always liked; everything is neat and clean
and genteel; The name of the family is Carter No.
94 North Pearl St. They are well acquainted with
Bishop Brownell & his lady, and say that they always
call on them when they come to Albany.—
Col. Baldwin has been very kind and obligeing to me
he is in high estimation in this city, and deservedly so.
Gen. Van Rensselaer called on me yesterday and
invited me to call and see him. Elkanah Watson Esq.
is not in town. I called on Mr. Chester, he was not
at home, I heard him preach to day; Mr Robert
Kalston and his two daughters Elizabeth & Abby came
up in the boat from N.York with me, he is not in
good health; Bishop Hobart was also on board and
young Stephen Salisbury of Worcester & a great many
acquaintances; there were about 250 persons in the
boat.— Dr. Rice & lady of Richmond came up in the
Friday's boat, he is also in ill health;—
I presume I shall see Mr. Tittiman soon
on his return. and yet
I can form no idea of the prospect of success
in my profession here, I shall paint one or more
gratuitously, and shall soon know, If I get enough
to employ me I shall go no farther, if not I may
visit some of the smaller interior towns.—
I feel the absence from home more than I ever
did, nothing but a sense of duty, and a full persuasion
that it is, in God's wise providence, for the best, keeps me
from being downright low-spirited; I am too happy in
the Society of my dear wife & family, and it is right that
I should be made to feel that they are not pleasures, on
which I must fix my affections too strongly; there is
nothing permanent but God, and to have our pleasures
permanent they must centre in him; then wherever we
go, we find the object of our enjoyment always with us.
I feel anxious to hear from you, and to know how
dear little Charles gets along, I can't but hope he will
outgrow his present feebleness. Don't let Susan want
your superintending care, till her Papa expects she
will be a very good girl, and not give you any time
or any reason to write that she has not been got.
I wait with some anxiety the result of Mr. Steele's
experiments, I look forward with some hope that that
invention may enable me to remain at home; but
I would not take thought for the morrow, God's
ways and time are the best.
Tell Father I delivered his notes, Mr. Steele
objected to the charge of 4 dollars & said it ought
to be 3.50 I knew nothing about it, and therefore, could
not rectify it, I hope Father & Mother are well, give
my love to them & Edw. & the rest of the family; Kiss
the dear children for me & believe me as ever my dear
Lucyce. Your Aff. husband
S.J.B. Morse.

Albany August 16th 1823 in
My Dearest Wife,
It is now nearly two weeks since I left home
and I have not received a single word of intelligence
from you. I must say I was disapponted in not receiving
a letter from you this morning, as I wrote you more
than a week ago: but it is possible you may have missed
the mail. I feel anxious to hear from you, especially
as I left Charles in such feeble health; do write me at
least once a week whilst I am here. I have written
twice before this, this letter being the third, you will also
hear verbally by M. & M. Silliman. I find it more
and more trying to leave home; I do long for the time
when I shall no longer be under the necessity of having
it. I am as yet uncertain whether I shall do anything
here; I am painting the Patron (who is the way will be in
N. Haven at Commencement to enter another son) but, as you
have rec'd no application for a portrait, many tell me
I have come at the wrong time; the same time that has
been sung in my ears for so long a time; I hope the right
time will come by & by; the winter it is said is the proper season,
but as it is better at the South in that season, it will
be more profitable to me there than here. I shall give
Albany a thorough trial and do my best leaving all events
in the hands of him who always orders all things for the
best. I have been introduced into a pleasant family
of the name of Lovett, she was a Mrs. Sillman of Windisch
Dalton knows them very well. Mrs Lovett wishes I could obtain
for her some lines of Poetry which father introduced into a sermon
preached at Woodstock being the answer of a lady to the question
"What is religion?" I told her I would mention it when I went home;
perhaps father can recollect it; religion is described in it as cheerful
not forbidding & gloomy.
If Henry is in NewHaven ask him to measure the Statue of
the Venus de Medici in feet & inches very accurately and let me know
in your letter; I want two measurements 1. the height of a perpendicular
line from the top of the head to the sole of the foot, and 2. the height
along the figure from head to foot being the height if the figure stood straight.
I wish Henry also to make particular enquiry on board the
packets and in the storehouses at N. Haven for my Hercules, for I
forgot to tell you that Mr Robertson found me it was put on
board the same packet with the Congress Hall; if so, it is missing,
but it is a kind of thing not easily lost & if search is made
for it I have no doubt it will be found, at best if it is advertised.
My I am pleasantly situated as to family, rooms, and
board, I only want enough to do. If I should not find
enough to employ me here I seriously think I shall return to
New York and sit down there, this I had rather not do at present
but it will be cheaper, for travelling is expensive, and
business very uncertain. I hear very unfavorable accounts
as to prospects of success westward. Roaming becomes more
& more insome. imperious necessity alone drives me to this
course. Don't think, by this, I am fainthearted I shall persevere
in this course, painful as is the separation from my dear
wife & family until Providence clearly points out my duty to
return. — Do write often, my dear Lucrce, for next to seeing
you, hearing from you is my greatest comfort. I hope Susan
is a good girl and continues to improve; tell her that Papa
expects she will be a comfort to Mama & GrandPapa & Grand-
Mama while he is gone, and that she must get a great many
trickets to show him when he comes home; give her Papa's kiss
whenever she behaves well; Kiss dear little Charles too. I hope
he is better, write me full particulars about them all.
I hope Father & Mother are well and that their dark
days are becoming brighter, I shall do all in my power to com-
fort them in the decline of life; When you write again let me
know from Father what I shall do about the sale of Steele &c.
which he sent me, they said the charge of $4..00 was wrong
and ought to be $3..50. I hate any dealings with book-sellers
they are a class of men I have very little respect for, they
seem to be as a class a most impertinent race of beings, the
more I see of them, the more I am convinced of this, there are many
honorable exceptions but they only prove general rule.
How does Mr. Agar progress with the machine? tell me all about
it when you write. — Give my love to Father, Mother, Edwards &c
Nancy Shepard & Henry, and remember me to the rest of the
family and all N. Haven friends. — I see by the Papers that Uncle
Stout of Belleville is dead. I keep a little corner of this open
as I find the mail will not go till Tuesday morning.
Monday morning Aug. 18th I have this moment been notified by
receiving your dear letter of the 13th. note it has been delayed 2 days
Sam Grier & Smith has the care of Charles, as I believe he understands more of him than
any other, your letter serves all my yearnings for home, but God time is the proper time. I have nothing
to do but wait for the mail to return to Providence. I am your affectionate husband
& ever
Samuel B. Mason
war to tell you since Saturday, and Mr. T. Sullivan spent part of the evening with me
last evening he is going to N.Haven he will be one of the Canal Engineers. I hope
Edwards will become acquainted with him & draw him attention at our house.
Having your letter directed to the care of Dr. Chester, this delays it one day, direct
in future simply to me as I am within a few steps of the office and engage regulary. It rejoices me greatly to hear that dear Susan behaves so well, and
has got so many tickets, till her it comforts Papa very much. Do be careful
of your health and that of my dear wife; I am not sorry to meet the cavalry. You say
you cannot spare me to go to Europe, I have no idea of it at present, my plans for the
future are in much confusion I see present duty, and that is sufficient, I dream of
this plan & that, but I feel entirely willing that God should direct my course for
in reviewing all the way he has led me thus far, I cannot but say "duly goodness
and mercy have followed me all the days of my life". Dear trust him in all
things, and I am happy when I trust him; though clouds & darkness envelope the sun
yet I know that God is directing all things, and I have reason to praise him that he
gives me the grace of full confidence in him, for I find my mind in perfect peace
while my heart is stayed on him. Both the soul & all that is within my physical
