Albany, Aug. 21st 1853.
Dear Mrs. White
Your dear letter of the 17th inst. is before me, it gives me great pleasure to hear of dear little Charles' convalescence. I hope he will continue to grow better until he gets entirely well. I was sorry to hear that Father was so sick. I hope it is only a temporary indisposition, and that by rest and the approach of cooler weather he will grow stronger.
I am in the prospect of something to do, I have one Portrait besides the portraits in progress, and a promise of money for 3 months. I calculate that this will pay all my expenses here, so that the two I am now painting well clear me in that respect, all that comes after will be gain, I am therefore, easier in my mind as to risk, the Portrait painting is Judge Moody Kent the brother of the Chancellor, who says I shall paint the Chancellor when he returns to Albany, and his notice, from these particulars you may infer that I shall be here for some little time longer, just as long as my good prospects continue; but should they fail I am pretty much determined to try N-York city, and sit down there in my profession permanently, I believe I have now attained sufficient proficiency to venture there, and though my progress may be slow at first, yet I believe it will be sure, I do not like the idea of going South, and I have given up the idea of New Orleans or any Southern city at least for the present, circumstances may vary this determination, but I think the prospects of a settlement (in my opinion) in New York is more favorable now than ever before.
I shall be near you, and home, in cases of emergency, and
in the summer and sickly season can visit you at N.Haven while
you can do the same to me in N.York, until it may be advisable to
live again at N.Haven altogether. I have out of this calculation the
event of the Machine for Sculpture; if that should entirely succeed
my plans would be materially varied, but I speak of my present
plan, as if that had failed.— It is necessary for me to be either
at home, or so near, as to be at home at short notice, and I am
completely tired of roaming abroad.
I see by the Papers there is one case of Yellow fever
in N-York which seems to have excited some alarm, I think
needlessly, Richard G. Charles, however, I hope will be in their
quart.— We had a very sudden death here yesterday, Mr. John Cook,
the man who sneezed so singularly, Mr. Tilliman knows him,
he left the reading-room, he died of bilious colic, or in eating
imprudently. The city is very healthy, I hope N.Haven continues
to be so too; I read with much surprise in a N.York paper
the death of Lucius Monson in the West Indies, I recollect
warning him very seriously never to stay through a summer at
the South, but money tempted him probably to his death.
I hope Mr. August will not be discouraged by the little
minutia of the machine, but carry it through, I should like to have
a letter from him on the subject, putting down a list of questions
respecting marble and marble cutting which he wishes me to ask to
stone cutters, as there are some here I can put a good many letters
I approve of Mr. Whitney's idea and am glad Father
has put me down for my share in the Schoolhouse.—
With respect to young Longworth, I should have no objections
to take him as a pupil provided I go to New York; on what
terms I am hardly prepared now to say, but I will resolve the
subject in my mind, and see if I cannot mature a proper plan
so that I can take a number to advantage.
I am glad to hear good accounts of my dear daughter Susan
if she has been a good girl and has not grieved Mama & Grandpapa
and Grandmama by getting up "Humpys" give her papa's Kisses for he
loves good girls; if she is very good all the time Papa will bring
her something from Albany.
I am obliged to close this, as I have but
a few moments to run to the Office before the mail closes.
Good bye, I ought to tell you however I met Colonel
Wm. Allison the old gentleman from Chatham N.Y. he will
pass through N.Havens, I wish I was there to show
him some attention.
Good bye again
Your affectionate husband
Samuel B. Pynchon
Love to all at home, and neighbors.
The family where I board know Mrs Pynchon I believe,
they speak of her as being very beautiful and a belle in Schenectady
when she came from.
My health was never better.
Mr. Lucius P. Morde

people leave N.York, would be pleasantest in N.Haven.
Thursday morning Aug. 28th.

Dear Son
I am very glad to hear of your health & prosperity
We did not have you hastily give up of John of visit to N.Y. next
Winter We are sensible of the sacrifice it will be to you to leave
but it may be best in present circumstances, to make the separation
Our purpose, in the severance, is over. I trust will not
be repeated. Our contract with Cookes is completed. About 100000
rec'd (on 10th 21st Monday) this is a great relief to us, put on -- If responsible
liberty are fast leaping I would urge you no further trouble. Think
effectual arrangements are made to meet all payments as they will
become due -- The Angus will write you about the Machine he
seems to be in good spirits about it -- We miss you much for our
harmonies I wish you here, not only for the sake of my wife & children
who are dear to us all, but to share with us in the fruits of cares after
Garden -- We are now enjoying the peaches & melons -- If the garden not
& vegetables we have a great abundance. Many more than we can
use -- Grapes want your attention. do do the budding & grafting of trees
fragments -- The front of Cookes charmingly is much admired for its
beauty -- Alexander keeps it in good order -- Col. Doncker lately
called on us was highly gratified told our neighbors how satisfied
& pleased he was that his place had fallen into such good hands -- W.
Joubert has just returned from Anvers -- painted Dr. Peter Hurd -- the
State offering on the Hill not as it should be -- Dr. Mundyock preached on the
statement two formers -- who are going to print by subscription -- He
is receiving the Trusteed have filled the vacancy in the Board by
the death of Judge Phillips -- by electing Mr. Hubbard of Boston --
well about 30 only graduated at Cambridge -- 70 or 80 are
to be coming to Yale in May -- the student for this year used to
go generally to C. -- do things so -- all coming in due time, to
a right time --
My health is still poor -- my strength is feebleness --
I can do but little -- that time goes -- I live in hope
of being better -- but my expectations are not satisfied --
I am very strong -- I am thankful that I have
in Col. Gibson who are willing & able to take care of me --
things will in time pass & develop on my path are
necessary to be continued -- These things I think I shall
be able to commit myself to the less embarrassent & more advantage
than has been feared -- When your return we
will settle arrangements for the future -- As to the family &
estate -- I see in what ways our past trials are working for our good
We shall, I have no doubt, find it good for us to have been afflicted --
The afflictions & duties we feel personally on each other, in our
several relations, will, I trust, be in future, more faithfully
exercised & fulfilled than they have been & our love much
increased --

[Bristol Oct 5th]
My Dear Sir
I arrived here at 11 o'clock yesterday, and am in good health
I found my Uncle here, and stay at his house, but he goes on Monday
to Newport with his family in a visit 13 weeks, and as I prefer
visiting that place, we have concluded it best for me to go down
now with him as he is well acquainted there, and will be of
great advantage to me, and you soon come back here, after which
I do not expect very great things from either place, as they
are both very much deteriorated in business within a few years, there
are however several very rich Families among which, perhaps I may
find something to do. I do not intend to be discouraged until I have
reason to be so, and hope that will not be soon
It seems by advertisement that Strickley (the fine merchant
and painter) is now in Providence Painting Portraits and diverting
for scholars to learn Painting and Drawing
I shall finish this and send it you from Newport
[Newport Oct 9th 1823]
We came down from Bristol on Monday, and I
have (with the assistance of Uncle Mann) found a place to board
and a room to paint in, and have commenced his portrait
I expect to commence Aunt Mrs. Tommow's tomorrow. There are
2 Painters here now before me, but none that I fear
My Aunt Mann, is daughter to Mr Vernon of this place
My Aunt Mann is a wealthiest and most respectable man in town, so
that I shall be brought into notice by them, and if anything
can be done here, I shall probably stand a good chance
I have found something here, that I never heard of, this you probably have, it is
a collection of Pictures in possession of Mr Vernon, he is Uncle
to Aunt Mann, and lives with her father, and is an old bachelor
of the old Masters, and ever purchased in France
at the revolution of the Stuart and the Muster, have seen them sketched
and I believe there is no doubt as to their originality
Among them are a Portrait by Leonardo, de Vinci, —
Succa Dying by vandyk, — a Landscape by Veruet,
and one that Stuart pronounces to be an unfinished Claude
(They are certainly the best Pictures that Sever saw at far as I can
judge, and I hope to derive some benefit from the study of them
I think probable I shall stay here 4 or 5 weeks, and then
return to Bristol. There are several large towns around here
within 30 miles, and Ass, where there may be something done,
I understand that Stuart has Painted several Portraits in Bristol
he of Mrs. also Thompson, and others
I have seen the famous Tower, in this place, it is a remarkable
building, it is built entirely of Rough stones, of various kinds and
shapes, and it is curious to see how perfectly the arches are formed
out of such materials. The Pillars that support the arches
are round and not angular (as I had supposed) it is about 25ft.
high and has windows in it, also at the top of the arches on the
inside are the holes in the wall for beams, and a fireplace like
inside are the holes in the wall for beams, and a fireplace like
If you send to me from New York while I am in Newport, you
can send by Steam Boat, as that reaches here in passing to Providence
Please give my love to your Papa & Mama Mrs. M. Little
Susan & Charles, and all the Family May the Spirits of Providence
rest upon you all, and reward you for your disinterested benevolence
and Kindness to me.
I wish you would write me as often as you can find an opportunity
I shall always value your letters very highly, and feel that I can

Accept of my best wishes, and believe me

I expect you must be surprised at my long silence but trust you will excuse me when I say it has been because I had nothing pleasing to communicate but I trust I now have found a more favorable climate and one which will cause me to write in order that you may rejoice with me in the success which I hope to meet with. – The prospect is very flattering – the Editors of the Mirror called on me and tendered me his paper for the purpose of inserting any communication I might wish – if you see the Mirror for next month you will find in it what he says and that is but little of what I have heard – however next week will decide my destiny for this city. – I shall then go to Springfield and Northampton and on my return stop at Middletown.

New York. Nov. 15th 1823.
Saturday evening.
My Dear Wife,
After a tedious & unpleasant voyage
I arrived here at 12 o'clock to-day; just as we left
N.Havien harbor yesterday a sail from St.W began and con-
tinued without interruption till last night at 12. we made
Black rock harbor at 2 o'clock yesterday after toasting
about for 6 hours all on board deaf sick, we lay at an-
chor in B.Rock harbor till 2 o'clock this morning and ar-
rived at Byram cove at daylight, we had a pleasant ride
from there here; I feel very tired and can write but
little, I am in good spirits, have obtained a place to
day at friend Coolidge's at 2.25 and am in treaty for a fine
room in Broadway opposite Trinity Church yard for which
I shall have to pay 7 doll. P. M. but still I think
though the price is great, it is better to give it and go vig-
orously at work. but Mr. Tracy is waiting with Charles
who is well, and I can write no more, love to Father & Mother
Sister and Rip the dear Children. I want the family
picture he.
Good bye My Aff. husband
Finley.
Wm Lucretia P. Morse

are a great comfort to your exiled husband, write him
often. I began to feel a little settled, and have begun to
paint two portraits, Chancellor Hunt and Mr. Irving Denver
the latter a small portrait; I feel encouraged in thinking
I shall do very well here with patience & industry, and I
have determined on both. The bed clothes & screen came safe
to hand, and I am as comfortable as I can well be without
my dear wife and family. I have been obliged to go into some
expence to get established, there are a great many necessary
little articles which are indispensable in beginning an establishment
such as a stove, coal, tin pitcher, basin, soap, wood,
shovel & tongs, heart brush, and some Bed's and which run away
with the cash; my greatest expence has been for a green baize
carpet which I found absolutely necessary to make my room
comfortable, it is a very excellent stout piece of green baize
contains 40 square yards & cost me 30 doll. although this seems
a large expenditure at the present time yet on mature consideration
I do not regret it; I have borrowed 50 doll. of Mr.
Cobit which I hope to pay him by a Portrait but dont know
how that will be; I board at friend Boolidges for $2.25 per Week
and live very well, it is more than half a mile from my room
so that I am obliged to walk more than 3 miles every day
this is good exercise for me & I feel the better for it; I sleep
in my room on the floor, and put my bed & out of sight
at night as at Washington, I feel in the spirit of "buckling
down to it," and am determined to paint & study with all my might
this winter.—
In considering my future prospects I have been a good
deal perplexed to know how we shall manage to live with each
other at all; if I should have enough to do here I cannot leave
it without disadvantage, and if I should not I cannot live in
N. Haven. In either case the result is the same in keeping me se-
parate from my dear family; the idea is a very melancholy
one to me I suppose you. There seems to be only one way, and
since I have been here, it seems to have fewer difficulties
attending it than any other, I mean that of removing all together
to this city, for some years; with the view (Providence per-
mitting) of returning permanently to New-Haven after I
shall have acquired sufficient to live there without depend-
ing on my profession for support, if that shall ever be; There
are many things in favor which I could better tell you than
write you, but I will mention some; first & may I not say
chiefly with me, is the comfort of my dear family, in whose
society I might lose the remembrance of the cares & toils of
the day, and to whom I might impart that instruction which is
due from a parent & the head of a family; another reason is
that I should be in New-York while our children are very young
and should probably leave it before they are old enough to be
exposed to the temptations of the city.— The expenses of the
city are not great and I really think with Charles, & our
other brothers boarding with us we could get along even for
less than it now costs us; I mean too that Father & Mother
shall accompany us; The house in N-Haven might be let
until we want it again at a very good rent: I wish
the subject to be well thought of, nor do I wish that part
which relates to my comfort in the society of my dearest earthly
blessings to be lightly esteemed in the account; I have a wife
and never to see her, to have children and have no influence in
forming their early habits, are privations of no small magnitude
and such as I shall try every method to remedy.
But it grows late, my dear wife, and I am
fatigued and must retire to my lonesome bed; Give my
loves to Father & Mother to Sister Susan, and kiss dear Sam
& Charley for their father; How is Susan's face since her tooth has
been drawn? Remember me to Clover Nancy Shepard & the rest of
the family and to all dear friends & neighbors in N-Haven; The
idea of leaving them is one of the most staggering reasons for
not leaving N-Haven that occurs to me. -- but again goodbye
I will write again soon --
Your affectionate husband
Finley

New York Dec. 8th 1823
My Dear Wife,
You will probably feel anxious to know
what I am doing, the answer is very simple. Nothing.
I am waiting for applications but none offer. The
Chancellor's Picture & Mr. Breese's have been finished about
a week, and as far as painting is concerned I am almost
completely idle, and of course a little less spirited. I have
been active in calling on my friends and inviting them
to my room, they have promised but as yet few have
called; as far as human foresight can perceive my prospects
have been gloomy indeed, the only gleam of hope (and I
cannot underrate it) is from confidence in God; when I
look upward, it calms my fears, and apprehensions for the
future, and I seem to hear my Savior say "if I clothe the
lilies of the field, shall I not also clothe you I ye of little
faith," here is my strong confidence, and I will patiently
wait for the direction of Providence. I have seen many
of the artists, indeed most of them, they all agree that little
is doing in New York; This city seems given wholly to commerce
every man is driving at one object the making of money, not the
spending of it; New York is a very miserable place to live in
and I feel that even if my family were here, I never could
feel at home; New Haven of all places on earth is more
like home than any other. I have seen Mrs Kingsley
at Mr. Perits she is well and says she left you in good
health & spirits. What is Mr. August doing with the Machine?
Is he still danguine? I should be glad to hear from him.
8 o’Clock P.M. I have just seen Fatcher letter
and am glad to hear that little Charles has got a tooth
through, I hope the dear little fellow will be carried safe through
all his troubles both in infancy and manhood. I may have some
thing of an interesting nature to communicate to you in a
few days which concerns our future prospects in life but as
it is only in agitation now I shall leave you to your guesses
what it is; the only clue I will at present give you is, that it
may cause me to return to New Haven in a few weeks for a short
time. I have written Mr. Doolittle and advised him from
his obligations to finish the contract, as he has lost all his
time and he can afford to lose it less even than I can; that
rather suffer the burden of the failure of the picture alone.
The order I gave Fatcher on him is good against me, and neither
may put it down against me. The due bill of 7 dollars of
Mr. Doolittle’s he will pay.
If Fatcher has not sent to Auburn the books which
were to be given by me (Boccaccius,) I wish he would not send
them, if any excuse or apology is necessary to the gentlemen
there, it will be sufficient to say that the Institution intended
giving them to was that over which Dr. Rice presided,
and by some mistake I had thought it was Auburn, which
is all true; you know I never wished to send them there
and the gentlemen in that region have behaved so shabbily
to the Editors of the Observer that I shall regret ever sending
them anything, I hope they are not gone.
In the house in which is my room there is a family of 7
small children the oldest not 10 years old, the youngest cries so
much like Charles that I have waited in the night once or twice
thinking it was him, but when wide awake I am soon undelivered
he is now crying which brings it to my mind.
One thing that tends to make me feel more low-spirited
perhaps than I otherwise should is that I have had a constant
cold in my throat ever since I have been here, it still troubles
me and I think is a little worse this evening; I was perhaps
impudent in conforming to the fashion here in New York in having
my whiskers shaved off at this season, my neck has felt cold
ever since, and though I rub it with camphor & wrap it in flannel
it gives it only temporary relief.
I long to see you all again, but all in good time,
Give my love to Father & Mother & Sister Susan, and Nancy
and keep my dear Susan & Charles for me many times; I hope
they will be great comfort to their mother in the absence of their
Father. — Excuse this incoherent speech, dear Wife, as
it comes from your affectionate husband
Finley.
Mr Lucretia P. Morse.

Dear Parents,
The check for $10 which you sent down by Holland
Coit was destroyed the moment that it was received, we having
been fully supplied with money for all our immediate want
from other quarters.
We received your letter by Mr Hillhouse, and also
one for to be delivered to Mr Henry, which I have directed Mr
Tracy to keep in his possession, and not deliver till further
orders. I have given this direction on the supposition that
it relates to books to be sold at auction. This way of
managing the business is so complicated and so expensive
that it has become vexations to all concerned. You send
down books to Mr Henry, and request him to deliver
them over to an auctioneer; and then comes letter after
letter to me and Richard to request Mr Tracy to call on
Mr Henry to call on the auctioneer to write you or
send you five millions through half a dozen
different hands again; and then there is the passage of
the books from the vessel to our room, and
from our room to Mr Henry's, and from Mr Henry's
to the auctioneer's; and then there is a double course
to be paid, the auctioneer's commission & Mr Henry's
commission. The books must bring pretty good prices, if
all these expenses do not eat up a good slice of the
prospects profits. – My advice is that the books be
left out of the circle, and that the
books be sent direct to Mr Tracy (not to Mr Tracy, case of John P. Haven) and
that Mr Tracy receive all the instructions.
With respect to funds, I have in my
possession Gocelyn's & Stiles' notes for $400 due some time
hence; Collins' note for $100 at ten months; Lockwood's
for $127 at eleven months; There will be due me from
Gocelyn's for U States Atlas in February (you say) $250,
all together and something from Converse on
account of sales of geography. All these together, if
the notes could be cashed, would not amount to more
than enough to pay the $900 which will become due to
Mr Seymour on the 17th of February, 1821 and then I owe besides
$75 to Tanner, which must be paid in January, and all my
tailor's bills in New Haven, and in Boston; I have some small debts
at Andover, and the balance of the note at Bank on which
Converse is indessor. – To be sure, there is a good deal due us
from Subscribers to Observer, but that cannot be collected
immediately, and besides, I suspect is not more than enough to
pay for the second half of the year. –
After this full explanation of my financial
condition, you can judge whether it would be prudent for
me to make a large investment in dead stock; or, whether
I could safely loan where there would be no prospect of
repayment under two or three years. –
We have received a letter from Utica stating that
dated Decr 1st (six weeks after our second letter was sent) stating
that the Directors had concluded on the whole to establish a
paper of their own; that they had so many local purposes
to answer, that a paper at New York would not do, I call
this a shabby business. And I do not regret their decision
on our own account, for I had made up my mind when I
heard of Richard's success, that we would have done a very silly
thing in making them the offer, that we did; but I think
it is mean and dishonorable in the extreme to write to us
as they did, offering without any means to take our paper after spending
offering without any means to take our paper after spending
and sending us down to a dollar, and
and then, when we had accepted their offer, to go and establish them
a paper of their own and send some agents all over the Country
to get Subscribers, while we were from home in
profound ignorance of their plans, and prevented from getting
Subscribers in their region. Such manoeuvering will never
prosper, and I have not one doubt that when Dick gets up
into that part of the world he will get more Subscribers
for the Observer than they will get for their paper. We intend
that the Observer shall be supported on the ground of its decided
superiority to every other paper weekly paper in the United States.
We can say this without vanity, because our plan is to
procure the assistance of a great many different persons, each
taking a separate department, and being well paid for
executing his part faithfully. This plan cannot be fully executed
in a week or a year, but whereas at present I am compelled to
manage all the departments alone, and nothing great, therefore,
ought to be expected. The man who is compelled to read such a vast
mass of miscellaneous trash every week as I am obliged to do
to make interesting selections, is not in a very happy
state of mind for collecting the power of his mind for original
composition.— As we proceed, I shall throw off a great deal
of the most laborious part of the business on to Subs. I am
getting Mr Tracy into the way of collecting the Ordinations,
Marriages & Deaths, and arranging them for publication.
When he gets used to this, I shall set him to preparing tables
and Statistical statements for The Register, a head
which will hereafter uniformly appear in the paper, and
as it I shall give a vast variety of interesting statistical
is. I intend to give the the and complete and complete list of Ordinations & Deaths of clergymen, which can be found
any paper in the country; and at the end of every quarter
or every year, I shall make out an alphabetical list so
that any man can conveniently refer to it hereafter and instantly
find the information for information. This will give
the paper character.—
With the blessing of Providence, I have no doubt of
success. — Finley is in good spirits again; not because
he has any prospect of business here; but he is dreaming of
the gold mines of Mexico. S. F. M.
No more letters from Richard. Several names have

The associations are very pleasant.
Remember me affectionately to Lucelia, Susan Walker,
Danny & Rip little Sue and baby Charles for Uncle Eder. Hope Charlie
will get well through cutting his little tooth.
Your affectionate Son
Sidney Evrone.

My Dear Sir, I have to thank you for your acceptance
in favour of Nov. 25. 1822. I have not yet seen the Bravery
last March, I had the agreeable intelligence, three
weeks ago, of their arrival at San Francisco. Their
is with them a was well when I last heard
from him. Your letter gives me some
hope of seeing you one day in the East. We have
no apartments to which we can invite you in
Malta, Beyrouth & Jerusalem. Perhaps, before
you arrive, there will be also other stations.
Probably you will find some of us ready to
travel with you. I would be very glad that
some Christian travellers should pass through
this country, & it would give me practical pleasure
to see yourself. It seems to me now that
one might very well come from America to
Malta the latter part of summer, make
the tour of Egypt in the Spring winter
pass through Syria in the spring, then
visit Smyrna, Constantinople, Greece &
Italy, & return home. It is true it will require
some time & money & some patience
& perseverance, some courage & good health.
If you come to Turkey you must be ready
to travel as you can, i.e. to ride a camel, a
camel or an ass, to sleep in the dirt among
vermin & in apartments which a comfortable
farmer would scarcely consider fit for his
swine, to sit down quietly among loudly talking
& laudless Bedouins, to meet with with fatalism,
hypocrisy, ignorance, stupidity, folly united with
pride, vainness & meanness, to be cheated by almost
every man you meet, to eat & drink, not much
good things as you have been used to, but such
as you can find, to meet continually with
little vexations, & yet to go through the
country contented, cheerful, happy & without
any difficulty worth naming. But now formidable as some of these things may look, on
paper, one may still get along very well
by taking things quietly, watching favorable
opportunities & making the best of everything.
And when a journey is over it makes very
little difference whether it was performed in
a steam-boat or an Egyptian land-jay, on a
stage-coach or on a mule, whether one slept
in a palace or under a broach, on a soft feather-
bed, with clean sheets, & an elegant counterpane
& curtain or with only a coarse blanket spread
on the ground, whether you have dined at
a gentleman's table every day or joined an
Arab in putting a foret to pieces with your
do so, for our immemerable comforts, they
showing us, the condition of vast multitudes
of our fellow=creatures. Oh my dear Sir, how fine
are very few of all the millions that live on earths
are blessed with either the
temporal or spiritual blessings
which we enjoy! Are we duly
sensible of this & does it fill our
hearts, as it ought, with gratitude?
My often affects my heart, at least my sensi-
bilities are touched. O that a deeper & more practi-
cal effect were produced on my heart, rendering it
more compassionate, generous, & benevolent.
I hope you and your family & Parents &
Brothers are all well & happy & doing good.
Remember me to them all & believe me
ever your affectionate friend
& brother in Christ Jesus,
Pliny Fisk

Will Mr. Poinsett have the goodness to answer the
following questions relating to Mexico for the ratification of
Mr. Morse.
1 How soon is it perfectly safe for a stranger to the Southern
climate to be at Tampico on his way to Mexico?
Ans. Last of October or beginning of Nov. Bates is not safe to
triple duty on the coast.
2. What detention will he meet with at Tampico from
custom house forms, and other government restrictions?
Ans. None, a trifling present smooths all difficulties.
3 What is the distance from Tampico to Mexico, and how
many days are occupied in the journey, Ans. 300 miles
about ten to fifteen days.
4. What is the amount of expenses necessarily incurred
from the first landing till he reaches Mexico?
Ans. from $50 to $100
5. If property is acquired in Mexico, is there any facilities
for remittance?
Ans. Such opportunities are better to bring your dollars with you unless the minute gives
a discount for the U.S.
6. When can he return with safety to the coast?
Ans. any time before May, but not till a day longer than is
required in the specific country.
7. Is a minister to be sent out to Mexico this season?
Ans. I do not know.
8. If yes, is it possible for me to be so attached to the mission
as to be under its protection, and to whom must I apply for
this purpose?

when and how he can be appointed.

My Dearest Wife,
Charles has given up the idea of visiting New
Haven at present, as he has but a little time left to
prepare for his examination in May, he will then
come up he says and pay you a visit, he thinks Susan
had better stay till then, and then he will accompany
her home I think so too if Father can shan him so
long from Concord. I had made my arrange-
ments to come up to morrow to spend a few days
in hopes that he would accompany me, but since
he declines I shall defer it for the present, unless
you say at home "home," as far as my business is
concerned I might be at present in N. Haven quite as
well as in N.York. I am waiting for news from Wash-
ington which will decide whether I go to Mexico or not;
I have several things to way bow, when I come up to
N.Haven I shall see if I cannot make some connec-
tion with Mr. Augur so as to bring the marble machine
into profitable operation I think a company might
be formed to advantage and that I might be so con-
nected with it by allowing the sole rise of my invention
and by superintending the designing department
that I may be able after all to settle down quietly
in N.Haven; I read your letter yesterday on the envelop
of Col. Haynes letter and was glad, very glad, to hear
that Mr. Augur has come out clear from the Townsend
business, it removes one difficulty to the arrangement
just proposed. — I ought to take out a patent for it
immediately to prevent any difficulties, but I have not
the means and will therefore wait until the Apollo
is finished. I can then determine more decidedly;
I hope Mr. Augur will expedite the business and let
me know when I can come to superintend the finishing
of it. — Suppose I should come on Friday, shall
I come and will he have the head in such a state that
I can direct about it to advantage? I can leave my
room in the case of a very clever young man who
is well recommended and who wishes to be a pupil
of mine, he has kindly offered to take charge of it,
and receive any visitors that may come, (which
will not take up much of his time, if my experience
hitherto is any criterion,) so that I could spend a few
days in N. Haven and not be missed at all from the
city. — I want some mending up, my cloak, two coats,
some stockings, and 3 pair of boots all want more or less
patching or renewing. — Edw. D. says that he will give me
2 dollars if I will count the Geographical in sheets for him, which
are in the lumber room at N. Haven, this will dispense two things
of the expense to N. Haven. — If you say "come," write
me by the return of mail that I may make any arrange-
ments in season, I could not stay more than 3 or 4 days
You cannot complain I think of my not writing
often; indeed, I claim no merit for it, for I have scarcely
anything else to do, I wish I were so much engaged that
I could write you but once a week; but I wait, and
wait, and wait, and hope that I shall have some com-
mission soon to enable me at last to pay off my
N.York scores, they are not great to be sure except for
room rent; Kiss the dear children, for me and
give my love to Sister Susan, and to Father & Mother
& Nancy and kind regards to all the good neighbors
& Friends.
Your aff. husband as ever
Sant J B. Mason

Washington March 6. 1824
My nomination not having been
confirmed until the 4th inst. has prevented an
earlier answer to your letter of the 25th ult.
Previous to the receipt of your letter
I had agreed to accept the services of Mr. Hazard
as my private secretary.
It would certainly afford me great
pleasure to promote your other objects, as far
as it may be in my power to do so. I have not
yet received my Commission nor had any interview
with the President or Secretary of State on the subject, or
can not at this time say what facilities should
be authorized to afford you.
Gentlemen however come to this
Country as attached to Foreign legations, who
bear their own expenses, & are required to perform
no duty. Their only advantage is a free passage,
and being considered as a part of the legation.
As far as the Govt. may be at the expense
of sending me to Mexico, you of course would be
free from all charges, by being a member
of my family. The United States will
gratisably transport us from Orleans to New Orleans,
to Orleans, and from there bring, we shall have
to bear our own expenses.
If these advantages with any
attentions that I can pay you, will be a suffi-
cient acknowledgment with you. I intended to beg you
to have your company.
Very Respectfully
By
William Edward

Dear Sir,
I return you many thanks
for your polite favor of the 6th and
for your kindness in offering me a place in
the legation.
Under any other circumstances than
those in which I am unfortunately placed
I should esteem your polite offer as in the
highest degree eligible, and possessing me
the advantages which I could wish, and still
conceive the advantages for to overbalance
the disadvantages that I accept it with
many thanks.
I was under the impression that
the government bore the expenses of
the legation to & from the United States
in your letter that as you had not yet confirmed
with the Pres. & Secy of State you were unable to say what facilities you would be authorized to afford me;
The only drawback to my gratification
is the probable expense which I may incur; and this may probably be removed
by your next communication; as you observe
that so far as the Govt. may be at the option
of sending you to Mexico I of course
should be free from all charges by being
a member of your family; You add,
however, that to N. Orleans & from Vera
Cruz to Mexico we must bear our own exp=
ences; this point I had the im=

My Dear Sir, Wisen
I lose not a moment in informing you of
my safe arrival, with all my baggage in good order, last evening.
I was much fatigued, went to bed early, and this morning
feel perfectly refreshed, and much better for my journey.
after leaving you on Wednesday morning. I had but just time
to reach the boat, before it started, in the land carriage
we occupied 3 stages over a very rough road; in crossing
a small creek in a ferry boat the stage ahead of
ours left the boat a little too soon and came near up-
setting in the water which would have put the Passengers into
a dangerous situation, as it was, the water came into the
cargo and wet some of the baggage, it was about an hour
before they could get the stage out of the water; next
came our turn; after travelling a few miles the springs
on one side gave way and let us down, almost up-
setting us, we got out without difficulty and in a few
minutes by putting a rail under one side we proceeded
on again, joyously telling the Passengers in the 3 stage
that it was their turn next; when we arrived at the
boat in the Delaware, to our surprise the 3 stage came in
with a rail under one side having met with a similar
accident a few miles after we left them, so we all
had our turn, but no injury to any of us. – In fact
I called on Mr. Dully, & Mr. Ratston & Mr. Leslie, who
on D. Mc Lellan to whose brother in Mexico, Mr Lilliman
has given me a letter, he was not in town, so that I did not
see him; On board the boat to Baltimore, I fell in with cousin
Russel Finley, who was going with Capt. Bruce and several others
on board the Georgia Packet for Charleston, which vessel lay
down the river at New Castle; he had just received his diploma
of M. D. and was returning to practice in Charleston, he appeared
quite a different character, (no radical change that I know of) but
sobbed and very much of a gentleman; I rejoice very much on
Aunt's account. — If you recollect I paid half a seat for
my baggage to Phila. (a $2 extra,) and expected I should be at much
expence all the way on account of it, but I paid nothing extra
from Phila. to Balt. and in Balt. I found a return stage to
Washington, the driver of which offered to take me & all my
baggage for one dollar less than the stage fare, which I accepte
and arrived an hour sooner than the regular stages. I
made no stay in Baltimore, of course could neither see Mrs
Appleton nor Mr Bushing, the latter to the latter I left in the
office.
I saw accidentally Major A. Dix who is to call
on me tomorrow morning with Mr. Mason Sec. of Location
with whom he is intimate, he told me that the Parapise would
not be ready to sail under a fortnight if so I shall immediately
take lodgings where I shall be at as little expence as possible.
I am now at Brown's. I saw Charles King the painter,
last week he has built him a splendid house and Painting
and exhibition room, the finest Painters establishment in
Rememberance to all the well wishes & friends
the country. King told me that I should certainly succeed in
Mexico, that some years ago he had an invitation to go
there by the Mexican Agent who was then in Washington
who promised him a free passage to & from Mexico if
he would consent; the troubled political state of that coun-
try at that time prevented his acceptance.
I have just scratched this in great haste to re-
lieve the minds of my dear family, and will write as
often as I find anything to communicate; I shall go
to the Church in the Representatives chamber this morning
I cannot bear the total disregard of the Sabbath, and of
everything religious which is so apparent all around me
I long for the time to sit down in quiet N.Haven.
I tell father that what he heard with respect to Mr Adams
kindness to an orthodox Chr, cannot be correct, I had a conversa-
tion with Dr. Sevall; he informed me that W. A. owned a pew
in Mr. Baker's Chr and one in the Episcopal Chr, & one in the Unitarian, but he
uniformly attended the latter, and gave his support to that Chr, &
it was well known that he is a thorough Unitarian, no one
here pretends to contradict it, but I will write particularly
on this subject to Father before I leave Washington.
With my dear Susan & Charles for me, and give
my love to all at home, write me and let me know how you
all are; you will have time to write me here once or twice.
In haste but with undiminished affection my
dear wife your husband
Stiles.
Rememberance to all the neighbors & friends

Washington April 19th 1824
Monday.
My Dear Lucretia
I am at this moment put into a very
embarrassing state of suspense, by a political occa-
sion which has caused a great excitement here, and
will excite considerable interest no doubt throughout
the country; this morning a remonstrance was read
in the House of R. from Hon. Ninian Edwards against
Mr. Crawford which contains such charges, of so
serious a nature, as has led to the appointment of
a select committee with powers to send for Person
and papers in order to a full investigation, and I am
told by many members of Congress that Mr. Ed-
wards will undoubtedly be sent for and occasion
of course a great delay in his journey to Mexico,
if not cause a suspension of his going until the next
season; you can easily conceive in what a state of
anxiety I am placed, by this occurrence; I shall know
in the course of a day or two what will be the issue of
this, and will then write you a fuller account of myself. I am
obliged to close in consequence of the closing of the Mail
I give you the earliest information of this event that you may be
prepared for any future step arising out of it.— I feel at times quite
homesick; this delay and suspense tries me more than dis-
tance, or even absence from my dear family, if I could be
on my way, and pursuing my profession I should feel
much better, but all will be for the best, though things
look dark I can and will trust him who will make
my path of duty plain before me, this satisfies my
mind and does not allow a single dissenting thought.
My dearest children, dear father, mother, Nancy & all the
family & friends & neighbors.
If anything interesting occurs you shall
hear from me to-morrow.
In haste but as ever affectionately
Yours Finley

My Dear Wife,

subject about which I wrote yesterday, but shall
without doubt know definitely to-morrow; it makes
a great noise here, and I presume will cause much
excitement through the country; a motion was made
in the House this morning that the Pres.t be requested
to prevent Mr. Edwards from leaving the country,
until the issue of this investigation was known; but
it was lost by a considerable majority; a committee
has been appointed to consider Mr. Edwards Memorial

and will write you again; from the complexion of

Washington April 22d 1824.
Thursday
My Dearest Wife,
I hardly know what to say, or think, or do;
I went to the House this morning to hear the Committee's Report.
They made a few statements to the house, in which it was
served that it was necessary to a full investigation to have
Mr. Edwards present, (Mr. Randolph informed the house that
a warrant was already issued to detain him, and that a messenger
was on the way to serve it; thus am I placed in a
most embarrassing state, one that no human foresight could
predict or provide against; I have no misgivings, however, I
know in whom I have believed, and although my way at
present seems completely hedged up, yet I know assuredly
that all will eventually in good, I have been told thus far
by an Almighty and wise and merciful God, and I will not,
cannot doubt but all things are ordered right; I, not only, do
not feel responding, but I can truly say I rejoice in this
trial, the way will be made plain, I will keep you informed
of every movement. Some say I shall be detained more than
a month and advise me to go home to wait, others advise me
to give it up altogether till next fall, and others to go on
without the legation among the latter is Mr. Poinsett; I
went to see the Secy. of the Navy, but did not find him
in his Office, I shall go again to morrow, and can then perhaps
determine what course I shall pursue, if he says the vessel
will not be detained but proceed to N. Orleans, I think I shall
go there in her, and leave the location to follow & proceed by
myself to Mexico; this latter, however, will require consideration.
I shall take the best advice, and act according to the best of my
judgment; tell Mother she must not suffer any uneasy feelings
on this subject or on my account; leave it all to be directed by
him who has ordered all things well thus far, and will continue so
to do; although I see no way as yet that is not beset with difficulties
although to go back seems ruin, and forward hazard, yet I am certain
that I shall be led by an unweaving guide into the right way in his
own proper time, to him I leave it; to him let us all leave it.
Dec? your affectionate letter of the 16.th it gave me mingled
emotions of pleasure & pain, I cannot tell you all I feel in seeing
the handwriting of her I so dearly love, in reading her expression
of tender regard, and at the same time thinking how long a separation
we may be led to endure; it is a subject on which I dare not trust myself to think too minutely; I can only leave
you in the hands of our heavenly Father and look forward with
hope to the time of our meeting again when it shall please him
to grant it.
With my dear children for me, many, many times, I give
you love to Father, Mother, brothers & all neighbors & friends and
the family. I have rec'd fathers letters of 9.th 16.th & 18.th and
mothers for which I thank them, I will answer them more
fully in a short time the moment I can know what my future
course will be. As even dearest wife & Aff. husband
Finley.

New York, April 24. 1824
Dear Parents,
Letters from Richard have been received repeatedly,
since you were here, all in doing subscriptions as usual. The
number now, I presume, does not vary 20 from 2000. My
last letter was from Uncle Sidney's at Scandia dock. I wrote
to the Utica gentlemen, a fortnight ago, and told them
that I should wait a fortnight for an answer, and should
then feel at liberty to publish or to adopt any other course
which might seem just and expedient. I have as yet
received no answer. I will send you a copy of my letter
to them.
With respect to money matters, I have to pay one of my
carriers and agents $50 on the 1st of May, Mr Seymour $400 in cash and a note for
$1000 more on the 17th of May, rent & board for me
to Phyllis more than $50 on the 1st of May, besides some
smaller debts. To meet these demands I have only $40 in
hand, Bottling & Co's note at 12 months for $50 & your
check on the New Haven bank for $50. Where the rest is to
come from I do not know. We cannot collect from our
subscribers in the city, have nearly all paid and those in
the country are not acceptable. It is a great evil in commencing business -- I
am perfectly satisfied that if I had a capital of one or
two thousand dollars, I could make $600 or $700 a year if I
am now paying. -- I notice in your letter to Mr Tracy that
you give him a message to Mr Cord & Mr Pent on some
subject with you do not name. I do intimateat that you would
not publish any more pamphlets or books on Indian affairs at
your own risk. We shall never get rid of our embarrassments
97788 long as this is kept up. -- Mr Bell has 150 copies of my
Atlas pledged for to him on account of his note, and liable to be
told at the end of 40 days if not redeemed
by cash or other property. The 40 days will be out I believe
on Wednesday or Thursday, and I hope that some provision
has been made to prevent the sacrifice? Some of our
Pocket Gazetteers are in the same situation, but I am
willing that they should be sold, as we can't sell them
in any other way, Whiting having spent the market.
We are expecting to see mother here at the
meeting of the Bible Society. Richard will probably have
returned from the by that time. From Richard's last
letter I observe that he now collects the money in advance
at the time he obtains the subscriptions. He will probably
have a hundred or two of dollars by the time he gets back
which will come very seasonably for my relief. Hereafter
I shall enjoy it upon him to be rigid in enforcing
payment in advance, as we have well ascertained
that we can have as many subscriptions as we
want who are willing to comply with these
terms.
I am Love to Lucretia, little
Bee & Charity, Nancy & all the
Family I am your affectionate Son
Selling Emmons

New York, 19 May 1824.
Dear Brother,
I write in haste to state that I have
seen Mr. Morse of Cherry Valley. He says that he spoke
to a number of his friends, after seeing you at
Albany, & all to whom he mentioned the subject
expressed a cheerfulness to have their portraits taken,
should you visit the Western Country. He thinks in
some of the largest villages, a dozen might become
your sitters. There are wealthy men scattered
the whole of that country, & by frequenting
your residence, you would no doubt have constant
employment. Edw. asked him what price would
be most eligible. He said 30 or 40 dollars for his
portrait at Underthatch. This is the amount
I believe of what he said on the subject, which he in-
troduced, which was among other topics this evening.
I only add that if you will consent to
begin anew, as you did at Portsmouth Concord,
I think you will at least be in a fairer way
to discover what know if this the most eligible situation, than you are
at New Haven; & I hope, your success intended success might induce you to give
relinquish the plan of going to Mexico.
With love to Lucretia, & all the families
Your affectionate brother
Rich. C. Morse

New York July 15th 1824.
Dear Parents, I have no letters from Lucretia
except the one brought by Charles, which makes it that
there are 15 days without any news from her, I put
her letter to you in the Office which you have probably got by this time; I endorsed on the back that
Lucretia was probably in Portsmouth, she had though
of going with Mr Pickering Susan's beau to visit
her friends for a few days in Portsmouth, this may
account for her not answering my letter as she had
not probably received it. We are all well. I am
coming on successfully with Mr Lawrence portrait;
I find from Lucretia's letter that there
is a route from Concord to Albany lately established
fare 5 dollars, from Albany, here, 2 dollars, & 3
from here to N Haven, makes it 10 dollars from Con-
cord to N Haven, this is the cheapest route by one half
then, to return; and perhaps I shall go for them from
Albany if I should go to Utica & Coopers town.
Love to all, in Great haste
Yr Aff. Son

New-York July 24th 1824.
Saturday.
My Dear Parents.
I have rec'd no letters
from Lucretia since the 30th of last month
nor any news of her, except in a letter from
Susan Walker, which mentions that Lucretia
did not enjoy good health, but hoped that
"the jaunt to Portsmouth might do her good,"
this makes it more than three weeks since I
have had any intelligence of her; I have
nothing to do at present here, every body
leaving town and the weather excessively hot: I
have thought I would take my Painting ap-
paratus, and jump on board the Steamboat for
Providence this afternoon, go immediately to
Concord; if all are well, I can go to Albany,
or Portsmouth and pursue my profession, if
things are otherwise, as I cannot but fear, I
must act accordingly, at any rate, if all
are well there, they must pay my expenses
in coming on, (that is, if it has been through
neglect of writing:) I cannot account for
Lucretia's silence in any other way but that
of her being too unwell to write, and in that case
I cannot be away from her.
I will let you know if I go this after-
noon, before I close this letter.
2 o'Clock
I have concluded to go this after-
noon to Providence, and shall leave this
hot city at 3 o'Clock. I think I can
employ myself as profitably where I am
going, as elsewhere; I have no time for
more words: good bye, love to all,
Yr Aff Son Finley.
Rev. Jud. Morse D.D.

Concord N.H. July 25th 1824
Dear Parents.
I arrived safely here on Monday evening, and found them all well to my great joy, after 3 weeks of anxious suspense; Lucretia pleaded guilty in not writing to me, it arose from thoughtlessness, I told her that she could calculate the difference between 18 cents and 18 dollars and that a letter costing but 18 Cts postage would probably have saved 18 dollars to me. On the whole, however, I think I shall make it advantageous, by going to Portsmouth where they are anxious to have me home, and it is of little consequence whether I paint in Utica or Portsmouth until Octr which is the season to return to N.York. In N.York I am encouraged to think I shall do well, I had a Portrait (a full length of a child of Mr. Hone's of N.York) engaged to be painted while on the passage to Providence, I shall present it in N.York.
The children are healthy Susan is much sunburnt, and not so pretty as she was, her hair has been cut short and looks like a shoe brush made of a fox's tail, but will look better when it grows longer, and when she is confined to the house by the winter, Charles has the whooping cough very mildly and looks very well. Lucretia has been quite unwell with a cough and
gave her friends some alarm, but she is entirely free from it
now and I think in very good health. Sister Susan is as
hearty as ever, and will probably be married this fall, perhaps
while I am here, there is now no doubt of her engagement
to Mr. Pickering, they will live at Greenland near Ports-
mouth where Mr. P. will build him a handsome house, and
when he owns considerable property, he is considered a
wealthy man, and is certainly a very amiable, pleasant
man. I do not feel very well to-day, having a little of a
sore throat, and an inclination to diarrhoea; but hope I shall
be well to-morrow. I am looking for something to do
here, which if I find I shall stay a few days, if not, I shall
go to Portsmouth and Paint a while there and stay in this
region until it is time to return to N.York which I shall
probably do with Lucretia & the children by the way of
Albany. Please write to me in Concord and the letter
will reach me if I am in Portsmouth. All send a great deal of love in which I join
Yr Aff-son Finley

Portland (Me.) Aug. 10th 1824.
Dear Parents,
I arrived here on Saturday from Portsmouth bringing letters from gentlemen in Portsmouth to Gen. Wingate, Judge Mellen and Mr. Asa Clapp, the first and last I have delivered, and find that Gen. W.
and his lady leave town to-morrow for Boston, Judge Mellen and family are absent on a tour, and I find only Mr. Clapp, who has no more taste than a cow, and who thinks I shall do nothing in Portland, my reception by him I must leave relating till I see you.
Portland is very sickly, there were three funerals on Saturday; on Sunday there were 12 notes read from Mr. Payton's pulpit, 10 of which were on account of deaths: four funerals this afternoon, and in one quarter of the town it is very dangerous to pass; the disease is malignant bilious fever, which some say was introduced here by a vessel from the W. Indies.— I am in great doubt what to do, but at present think it will be best to return to Portsmouth and paint the Portrait of God.
Woodbury who has agreed to sit; and Uncle Pickering was order-
ing to procure me some others I had them better go to
Berwick and paint 2 engaged there, and them to Hartford to
paint those there, so as to be in N.York if possible by
Oct. 1st I know not where to tell you to direct to me
but will inform you in season. -- Whilst I am writing
the bell is tolling for a fifth funeral, a coffin has just
passed the door, and one of the boarders says he has this
moment met another coffin in another part of the
city; I shall set out for Portsmouth to-morrow.
Yr Aff Sow

Concord Monday August 16th 1824
My Dear Parents,
I wrote you a hasty line from Portland
just as I was leaving it; since then I have been quite sick
but have now recovered except that I am very thin and
somewhat weak; I will give you the whole history of my
diseases. The very afternoon that I wrote you at Portland
I was walking in the garden of the house where I boarded with a
gentleman an old school fellow of mine at Andover Academy; as
I passed through one of the alleys I picked a leaf from a plant
which they call the caper but which proved to be a poisonous veg-
etable and not the common caper, I observed a milky juice
run from the plant very copiously from the place where I stuck
the leaf, and having 5 or 6 ringworms on my face, my com-
panion said to me "Why don't you put that juice upon your
ringworms it will cure them," I accordingly without further con-
sideration applied it to all of them, in about half an hour
they began to smart, and gradually to burn so painfully that
I could not sleep, but rose in the night and walked the room
for some time, and in the morning the lower part of my face
was one mass of violent inflammation, studded with blisters
over the whole surface; I became alarmed and sent for Dr. Cum-
ming's the first physician in Portland, who seemed much surprised
at the effect of this poisonous plant and observed that my
blood must be in an inflamed state or such a result could
not have happened, and that I must be careful of myself,
I told him I had engaged my passage to Portsmouth, and if I was
going to be sick any time I wished to be among my friends
if possible; he said he did not think it would hurt me if
I was careful not to eat anything solid, and drink nothing heat-
ing. I according set out, and suffered great pain from the inflam-
mation which extended to my eyes, and before I got to Portsmouth
I was scarcely able to see, my face being much more swollen than
when I was in N.Haven, and the lower part of my face was one
blisters, I went to Uncle Jacob Pickering's where I was imme-
dately received with every attention; I went to bed and sent for Dr. Pierpoint, who confirmed Dr. Cummins
opinion that my blood was in a highly inflamed state, and that
I had a good deal of fever, and that in all probability I
had been saved a serious inflammatory fever, by having all
its virulence drawn out upon the face; I took an emetic, and
after 2 days confinement was able to set out for Concord where
I now am, and am recruiting fast; I began Gov. Woodbery's Portrait
to-day small $15., and begin Mr. Pickering's tomorrow same size
and price instead of 30.; I shall have 2 or 3 more probably here
and I shall then set out for Hartford where I hope to be in about
3 weeks; Shall you be ready to receive Lucretia and the chil-
ldren in that time say commencement; I wish to know this, for
you can easily see how circumstances have embarrassed my
movements, I ought to be in Hartford to execute the portraits
engaged, soon; if I go on in 3 weeks, I must either leave
Lucretia & the children, which is here, and let them come on with
out me, (which on many accounts will be very inconvenient
& troublesome to Lucretia,) or bring them on with me, which L.
desires, and then we may interfere with Mother's arrangements
for company, and we may not arrive when you will be glad
to see us; Now I wish to return to N-York the moment I
can after Oct. and establish myself without further concern,
if I am to live in poverty, it will be as well there
as any where, and if to make money, why there is the place;
I have run about long enough, I must settle down now.
Please write me, what your arrangements are, in regard to
our return, Lucretia and the children are well and send a great
deal of love. I leave a space for L. to complete this letter.
Dear Mother, I was much qualified to receive a letter from you
last week, and should have answered it had full, & not little
writing rendered it superfluous -- my friend here says, & that my visit
is likely to be shortened -- nothing could have happened more beneficially
than Shirley's return to Concord -- I am glad to find he has been
so well since the journey -- the country air seems to agree
so well with him as it does with the children and myself
as to our return, if Shirley must go to Hartford, it seems unavoidable,
as he has neither the time or money to expect an adequate
journey -- and it would be a source of unhappiness to him to be
again removed so great a distance from his family, with the
possight of their immediate return so uncertain -- I have not time
to add any more but will send love for you all I remain your affy
P.S. Lucretia feels very delicate about expressing a wish to return, lest
she should interfere with Mother's arrangements, knowing as we will do that mother
is pretty set, and a little nervous about her arrangements for company.
Now I think we can entertain company quite as well if we were all at
home, and I cant but think some of the company would like to see
us too. —
Yr aff. Son Finley

My dear Son
I have been here since Tuesday
I hope to return to N.Y. on Monday (my birth
day) having completed as far as it can be done,
my work for the Cooks -- It has been, as they
have conducted it, a perplexing business --
but -- I hope all will have a favorable issue.
This hope you know, is ever cherished by
Your father -- Miss Ceder with the three
Miss Matthews, Miss Adams left us for
N.Y. on Monday evening after a very
sant visit -- Your uncle Calvin paid us
a short visit on Saturday -- I may goe
back by the way of your uncle Jonathan,
New Habitation in Vermont -- To Fayette
they was to pass through N.Y. this morning on
his way, rapidly to Boston to be at Court
on Wednesday --
We long much to see you, Lucinda
& the Children -- You must be here as

you -- enough perhaps to take up all the
time you will have to spare -- There
are some you know at N.Y. -- The
fruit is now beginning to be ripe, so
we want you & the Children to enjoy
it.
My health is very good considering how much I am called to do

thankful.
Col. Trumbull is here with his

affectionately to my children, & to my father
Walker & the family -- Your affectionate Son

My Dear Parents,
Your letters have been duly rec'd. We are
all pretty well, the children complain a little, but we
attribute it to the weather, whooping cough, &c in Charles
to leething. We shall set out from here on Tuesday
afternoon for Londonderry in a wagon, so as to take
the stage to Boston as it passes us at a reasonable
hour on the next day, and expect to be in Boston on
Wednesday even'd. we shall probably remain there a
day, and then proceed to Hartford by the middle road,
and endeavor to be at home by Saturday night.
Fatter mentions that Fisher is in Hartford "taking
these portraits which I might have taken a month ago"
I don't exactly understand this; if 8 portraits were enga-
ged for me, and I have written to Mr. Ellsworth saying
I should be there on Commencement week, I don't
see how any of those engaged to me can employ Mr.
Fisher without violating their word & honor. If this
is the case, however I shall not be worried much, as
I have enough to do in N-York at a greater price, &
the sooner I can get there the better. I have
finished 2 here Mr. Pickering's & Mr. Bartlett's, each
30 dollars, and hope to finish another to-morrow &
a lady, which is nearly completed, for 30 more, So
that I have not been idle the last week; I have seven
more applications which I could answer if I could stay
but it is of more importance that I should not disappoint
my friends in N.York. If those are ready
in N.Haven I will begin as soon as I get home.
All send love, We shall all be glad to get
home again. I hope Nancy will not have
gone before we arrive.
In great haste
but with real affection
I am

I received your letter in due
season, and regretted by Mr. Field, to make some further enquiry.
Perhaps it would be no more that justice for me to state
he is a young man, that he appears to possess an uncommon
aptitude for landscape & portrait painting -- He has very
recently had an application to paint the scene at Betsy's brae
where the Indians massacred a company of our men, while
they were on the trees, plucking grapes from the vines.--
This piece of painting was executed with taste & elegance, considering
the advantages of the young man -- as a compensation
for which he received 10 dollars.-- He has recently
resided a few weeks in Boston this summer with a man
who carries on the business of painting.-- He could have
married there & had his board & clothes paid him, -- but he
wished to attend to a different branch.-- He wishes to attend
particularly to Portrait painting.--
It would be gratifying to Mr. Field to have you
write & give him definite information as you should
think expedient on the following subjects of enquiry:
1. In what particular branches of painting do you expect
most likely to be engaged? 2. Should he commence with you, can
he have the liberty of quitting, at any time he wishes? 3. Would
there not be some prospect, if he should prove tractable, that he
might pay his expenses, after some months had elapsed? or,
whether you could not, perhaps, afford to loan him, after some
months, by having his services? -- Will you be so good as to
state a little more definitely with respect to his finding his
own materials for printing -- what will probably be the
expense of these articles -- whether he will have any of his
time to paint for himself, &c.
Should Mr. Field commence his studies with
you, you will find him a young man, of rather retiring,
but amiable, modest deportment, correct in his habits, &
faithful & trusty in his business.
He is possessed of rather a slender constitution, &
perhaps, there may be some days that he will not be able
to attend to business.
Should we conclude to come, perhaps you may
wish to state more definitely than in your last letter,
the time you would like to have him arrive at N.Y.
& give some directions where he can find you after
he arrives & any further particulars, that you may think
of service to him &c.
Please to state also whether you wish for
a definite answer &c if so, where you wish it to be directed.
With respect, Sir,
Yrs. Mts: to yours, Servt.
Genus Calhoun.

Dear Sir
I called last evening at your house to
consult you on the expediency of addressing a line to Mr Heston
for the purpose of fixing him if possible, in our part of the
town, if he should remove here. The house which you
formerly occupied, together with the painting room, would
form, I should suppose, a very complete establishment for
him. The house, as you know, is as large and genteel
as the custom of the place requires, and the situation pleasant;
far preferable for a man of his taste and habits
in one nearer the scene of business. The painting room, which
I suppose you would be willing to rent or sell, would form
an important part of the establishment. If he with a
large garden than has hitherto belonged to the place,
I would willingly add to it the lot in front of Mr
Silliman thus extending the garden through to the Avenue.
If he would take the place in a house, even a short one,
I should be happy further to improve it, by any little
establishments which he may think desirable, such as
arding fruit trees & Thattbery -- enclosing the green space at
the north end of the house &c --
It appeared to me that you might, at my
request, suggest the situation to Mr. A. and, being perfectly
agreed with it, could perhaps give him to just an
idea of it as to determine him to fix there. I should
think $2000 as an exhibitent rent for the house & ground.
Now think of this, and if the idea pleases you, act to
him immediately -- Prof. Illman would be particularly
pleased at such an arrangement, and would be a good
assistant for Mr A. Yours truly
JD HICKS

My dear Henley
I have received but two letters from you
the last dated 17th Novr 1824. 13 long days have elapsed
since I last heard from my dear husband. I have been
in a state of almost constant suffering from
the ague and tooth-pain and full debilitation
from the pain in my husband's hand and not to receive
one comforting line from my beloved husband has
made me watch his death with despair. His description - do have
pity on me and write of him if it is but a line.
I wrote this to my dear husband, they had no
party there last night. I was confined to the house with
the ague and am still too weak to go out this
morning as the weather is damp. I regret very much that
I am so unfortunate as not to be able to see them
before they go. The ladies and Miss Fill, Charles grows pretty
every day - he is happy and soon he calls upon them
to come and keep his sick. Whenever I drop a word
he talks about the roughness of his father's face he
and seems to remember all about you.
If I do not hear from you I shall think
you have forgotten your promise to come to love him

New York Decr. 1. 1824.—
Dear Father,
On the subject of your letter I would say that Mr. M. Nutt might take the picture for 4 months from this date, allowing me one fourth part of its exhibition; but I must expressly and imperiously enjoin it on him and all who know the fact not to mention on any account whatever my being the painter of it; this I must solemnly promise.— The picture is in the Garrett of the house I believe.
As to sending $50. in a fortnight I can no more admit it than $50.000, my picture are not painted yet, nor shall I be at the receipt of any money under 6 weeks at least, indeed I have borrowed more than 50 dollars already to pay common every day expenses, and shall have to borrow more before I receive any of my own, you must not at all depend on me, for I cannot promise any thing.
In great haste but with much love to all, Lucretia children, mother &c. Your aff. son
Sam. P. B. More

Dear Edw
You do not answer my letters, I am
kept in suspense whether or not you have received them
Our affairs are now in a state to require frequent
intercourse. Beside the interest we feel in the success
of your paper concerning which we write frequently to hear,
it is important for me immediately to know what you
intend to do toward the new edition agreed to be printed by
Converse. I have not more than a day, let of the last
edition in hand except what are in the hands of the Auctioneers -- not a great matter -- There is nothing therefore
to hinder the putting a new edition immediately to press
The market -- will be quite clear by the time it could be
printed -- I have been busy to prepare the work, I shall soon
devote my time permanently to the revision is completed.
Write you to inform me immediately, whether you can
situate me any assistance, how much of what kind -- I
think there is a good prospect of a quick sale. You
do not answer me concerning the settlement of
the work -- with you were to have finished according to that
Lord told me in Septt before this time -- If you don't
prepare such a book I will do it -- Mr. Mutt wishes to
publish himself a book, I shall throw the country down
to his school -- I think he could do well for
himself with it -- Your Atlass complete so be ready
to accompany the new edition of the Georgian to be made
by his Agents to get his whole edition printed
for the time it is out -- he obtains worth, I Mutt
are in high spirits about it
I can get no answer to my letters to Cookes on the subject
of the Georgians -- what they intend to do -- I have my course with
them marked out with in due time. I shall make known to
them -- to you -- I shall take legal advice before I act, I know
what I can do
Offering has demanded the Am. of his due bill
in the new edition of the Georgians Atlass -- though the Judge decided
that this work was not demandable by him, in any one of the
other bills -- What be means I don't know unless I expect that
the whole Court will decide the question differently from Judging
the whole -- which is not probable -- have off him the Clerk of
the Court -- which is all that remains of my publications

My Dearest Husband,
I received your dear letters by Mr. Jackson with
much pleasure and should have written you last week if I could
have found a leisure moment. I have had a good deal to attend
to, of late, Caroline went to Stamford to keep Thanksgiving and was
about a week there. We should have been very glad to have had you with us
at the anniversary.asting, Penniman and Lincoln died with us. I
should have been glad to have asked more of our acquaintance among
the thrifty but my own situation and Caroline's absence rendered it
impossible -- We are all well, the children are in excellent health, but
many of our neighbors are sick, Chauncey Goodrich has been very
ill with the dropsy but is convalescent, and several more are sick
with the bronchial -- Little Charles talks a great deal about you, he always
every day new words. he says "New York, for the Mutt Doctor. House
make books," and many other words the children were delighted with
their Edwards present of books -- they have been lent to all the
children in the neighborhood -- Our society are much pleased with
Mr. Bacon, at their last meeting Father was present, 68 voted
in favor of giving him a call, 20 were opposed on the ground of
Mr. W's being only young not having reached his 28th year, and not
having had sufficient time to hear him -- the opposition is very
trifling -- it seems to be so -- he wrote the piece signed LL
in Christian Spectator on a Lady's Work Basket, all you can
please with -- it was addressed to Elizabeth Hooker -- Mr. Cornelius
who was here last week on his way to Somers informed me of
the fact -- so excuse this errand -- it will show you I have
not forgotten you -- I hear but seldom from your dear Kinley but
suppose you are much occupied, I look forward to next month
with the hope of seeing my dear husband for a little season --
we all rejoice in your success, and are much interested in
hearing of your progress -- and would like to see the picture
of the little girl -- I cannot find the White paint in
our closet, but do not give up the hope of
finding it elsewhere -- If I find it I shall send it
to Mr. Kitt who goes to Myak shortly --
In haste but with much affection I remain
your
Laetitia

My dear Vielgy
I am almost tempted to say, I do not know whether it
will give you any pleasure to hear from me; and, although I feel that
my absence is unworthy of attention, yet I cannot help feeling a
good deal disappointed that my dear husband does not write of himself.
It seems as if you had been absent an age and as if months had
intervened since I had heard from you -- I eagerly looked for a letter
from my dear Vielgy this morning but looked in vain; I hope to receive
one tomorrow -- I have not been so well of late, have been a little grieved
and restless at night and unable to sleep, in bed without a painful
effort -- I have felt rather distressed from wanting so indifferently and
have been too ready to indulge in groundless fears and apprehensions
of my situation -- I should feel better if I could have resolution to go
abroad and take exercise in the open air every day, but it is a hard
matter to quit the fine old little Charles every day, grown more attached
to me and does not feel happy at my sight. He sleeps with me,
he is so affectionate and pleasant in the morning that I cannot
consent to be parted from him, especially as my dear husband and confidence is
absent Thursday morning to my great joy heard from my dear Vielgy. I feel much better every
way I talk with them to the business with the High Court, only it could not have been
done to your satisfaction -- I talk here a good deal of care and perplexity, and is doing all he
can to extricate himself from his embarrassments -- you find us a good one night just
toward 10 o'clock a.m. a pleasant dinner -- I suppose you will come up the last week in January -- I want to see

My dear Son,
I write with difficulty, being almost
lost amidst the ruin which surrounds me – within one
short month I had been called upon to follow three of
our relatives to the silent grave & had scarcely received
from the shock when the appalling news of Lucius's
lamented death plunged me into the deepest sorrow.
Since that melancholy event I have scarcely known what
to do. My mind is constantly agitated with most melancholy
and pained emotions – Soon after you left us
I set about arranging my affairs here with intention
to visit you next spring & to remain a considerable
time; But the afflicting dispensation of Divine Providence
has dissipated all my plans & reduced me to the
lowest state of despondency – Our Loss is great & griefs
to be borne. She was a pleasant & a favorite child
with whom I entertained the fond expectation of spending
the residue of days, But the Almighty in his
Providence has seen fit to take her from us – and
we are left desolate to mourn her loss. We must bow
with submission to his holy will with a firm reliance on
his mercy & goodness. I feel for you, I feel for the dear
little children & I feel for myself – You are all near & dear
to me & whatever may happen in the course of Providence you
will almost find me an infidel in spirit
Chas Walker

which I hope you have received in good order

well she seems perfectly contented and happy
and grows more affectionate every day; I
stay altogether at Dr. Mathews, sleep and
have my meals there. — Dr. Mathews is
to be married again in June to a daughter
of John Hone, Esq. Sister of Mr. Hone whose
little girl I am painting, sister to Mr. Van Schaick
and sister of Mrs. S. Howland; her father
is a man of great wealth, and respectability
and it is altogether a very eligible connection
for Dr. M. I have taken a house $400 rent
of Mr. Isaac Lawrence, it is in the upper part
of the city, but is a very fine 3 story house which
will accommodate me in my profession handsomely.
There is a cellar and cellar kitchen, 2 rooms 18 by
12 feet on the first floor, 2 rooms on the second one of
which is 18 feet square, 2 rooms in the third, one in
the garret, beside a stove room and other garret rooms.
I shall occupy the house in the following manner;
