New York April 19th 1825.
My Dear Parents,
Your letter to Edw. & Rich and the
Bundle arrived safely by Miss Whittlesby; she left no
word where she stays in New-York so I cannot call on
her, — I don't understand mothers short and touchy
letter, as far as it concerns me. I wish mother would
not write when she is in such a mood, it is not right.
As to my coming to New Haven on the 25th inst.
I wrote the College Committee that it was absolutely im-
possible, and sent a verbal message to you by Mr. Joe-
clyn to the same effect, I am therefore at a loss to know
what you mean when you say that the Senior Class &
Mr. Silliman, and all will be disappointed if I don't
come, and that you will expect me certainly in
Saturday's boat; Now I understand my own business
best, and if they take the ground of being offended or
put out because I can't do impossibilities, then they may
find some one else to paint the picture, for my business
here is worth double what that picture will be to me in
New Haven, and if they take that ground, after what I have
stated to them, I shall have nothing to do with the thing.
I wrote them my reasons for not coming up before the 1st
I wish, when the blossoms begin to swell on the large
apple tree, just before they open into blow, that one or two
of the middling sized limbs might be carefully girdled
by taking out a ring of bark, completely round the limb,
a quarter of an inch in width; the ring should be made
on that part of the limb nearest the body of the tree; this
process performed at the time I mention (which is prob-
ably now,) will make those limbs bear larger fruit than
the rest of the tree and ripen sooner; I am anxious to pro-
duce this year the largest apple.—
Give my love to all friends and neighbors, and
many Kisses to the dear boys.—
Your affectionate Son
Sam'l L. V. Moss

When I see you which will probably be in a week from
next Tuesday night I will tell you more particularly.
I shall be able to stay with you but 2 or 3 days
for my business purposes. — I want several things from home.—
One of the darkest points in
my future prospects is the necessity of being absent so
much from my dear children, I want them round
me, but I do not see how it can be accomplished, a cloud
hangs over me in regard to them, but I will still trust a
wise and just God, I have no reason to distrust him,
he will make my way clear, and in this persuasion I
can patiently wait; his will be done — Present duty
seems plain, every thing in my profession here looks bright,
and it is clearly my duty to stay here at present. —

My Dear Parents,
I arrived safely with all my
furniture the morning after I left you, and what
is remarkable, have all the articles without an
injury to the value of 25 Cents, the sofa, the dining
table, and the breakfast table particularly are safely in
their places without the slightest new scratch upon them,
my cast also, are without a single new break, so
that I have every reason to be thankful.—
I should have written you before, but have had
no breathing time till now.—
I send this by Mr. Durand, firm of North
Kiss and Durand who has in charge the bandbox
containing little Charles' new hat, and some things
also I believe with Susan left.— Mrs Eder says
with respect to coming to N.Haven that she will
not be able certainly to come before the last
of June, so that your arrangements will probably
suit all round. they are all well at
Dr. Matthews and send love to little Susan &c.
The D was married on Monday night as was
expected -- I hope to send the money to pay
my bills soon, as soon as I can get a little
arranged and feel at home, which I am doing
fast, -- How are the little ones, has dear little Tim
ley yet broken out with the measles, I shall feel anxious
to hear from them till I know they have
gone through with that disease. -- Keep them
all for me, and do not let Susan run wild
without discipline and instruction; I do hope
Miss Peters will take her. --
In haste but with affection as ever yr Son
Sam: F: B: Morse

New York June 11. 1825.
My Dear Parents,
I write a line by Pick, who
goes to day to N-Haven; I am well as usual
and very busy, at least as much as the
weather will permit; I find I have not the
strength I had before I painted the Congr's
Hall, but still I think I am better than I
have been for a long time.— I long to
see my dear little ones, how do they do? Does
Susan improve, and does Charles continue
docile, and pleasant dispositioned? I shall
come and see them as soon as I can leave
my painting with advantage which I can
not possibly now do? As to sending money
I have been disappointed in receiving money
from those who owe me, or I should have
sent it long since, I shall have $150. due
for Mr. Silliman which I shall put into
mother's hands to pay the bills I have in New
Haven. — I close in haste
Yr Aff. Son
Saml. F. B. Morse

To Gen. Lafayette,
In asking your acceptance of the enclosed
Poetic tribute, I have not the vanity to suppose
It can contribute much gratification, but if it shall
be considered as an endeavor to show to you some
slight return of gratitude for the kind sympathy you
evinced towards me at a time of deep affliction, I shall
have attained my aim. Gladly would I offer to do
you any service but while a whole nation stands
waiting to answer the expression of your smallest
wish, my individual desire to serve you can only be
considered as contending for a portion of that kind honor
which all feel in deserving you.
Believe me with the highest consideration
Tho. O. Lentz

New York. July 13th 1825.
My Dear Parents,
I expect to finish Prof. Filliman's
picture this week so as to be able to bring it
with me to N.Haven on Saturday, and hope
to stay with you till Tuesday evening. I have
been wholly occupied in running after Lafayette,
have obtained two settings from him, and have
completed with him; as soon as this dread-
ful hot weather is over I shall commence
the large picture of him. – I long to see
my dear little ones, I hope they bear this
weather well, tell Nancy I shall bring the
comb & fan which she spoke of when I return.
Kindly bear the dear children for me, and remem-
ber me kindly to Miss Eder, and the young
ladies of der charge, and to all friends, in great
haste but with affection as ever
Yr obedient Servt
Sam. J.W. Mosse.

My Dear Parents,
I write a line just to say that I called
the day before yesterday on Uncle Arthur, I saw him
but he looked very ill, he had just been tapped
by Dr. Post, and many gallons of water taken from
him, he said he felt better; I called to-day and
learn that Dr. Post has given it as his opinion
that he cannot live the day out; he may live a
few days but the Dr. says he cannot survive; I don't
know whether mother or you can leave home
at this time but if you can I know it would be
a great gratification to them at Mrs. Stout's, I am
in hopes you will get this so early as to prepare to
come in the boat the even. you receive this. (In day)
I have concluded not to go to N.Haven
so soon as I had intended; I think I shall finish
the picture of the little girl here. — Rip the children
for me, and love to family & friends My Aff Son
In haste
Sam. F. B. Morse

New York Sep 10th 1825.
Dear Brother
I wrote you several days since saying that
I had received a letter from Professor John Maclean,
of Princeton N. T. requesting to know your
views for a portrait of the "head size" as he
terms it. - To day one of the tutors of the college
called on me to know why the letter had not been
answered. I told him that I had written you I was
waiting your answer, as I did not wish to
burden Mr Maclean with the portage of a letter
merely to say that I did not know. - I told him
further that I would write again to you &
request you to communicate directly with
Professor Maclean on the subject. He says that
it is a portrait of Dr Horack that they want,
for the college, as he has been a benefactor to
the institution. -
The prize essays have done coming in. I have
a small cart load of them. What shall I do with
them.
The letter by Mr Brinkerhoff came
but no peaches. He had carried them by mistake to his
house & forgotten to bring them in with him. Will
bring me a basket of fresh peaches from his own
Garden on Monday to pay for them.
I shall not come up to New Haven till
fortnight or three weeks from this. When I come, I want
to spend three or four weeks, & Mr Dodd is not yet
sufficiently initiated.
Richard sends in names continually. About 40 this week. The whole number since he commenced
this tour 184. He A letter received this morning says
Direct to me at Champlain, what I find by Morris gazetter,
the best authority, is in Clinton N.Y.
Love to all,
In haste
Your affeessed brother
S C More

Princeton Sept 26th 1825
My dear Sir
The Faculty of the College of New Jersey will thank you to furnish them with a portrait of Dr. David Horsack, on a canvas of 30 inches by 25 inches. – The head of the degree of Life. You will be pleased to be guided entirely by the Doctor's wishes in relation to introducing either on both hands. One reason for not furnishing a portrait of a larger size, is, that the Faculty desire that the Doctor's should be the first of a collection, whilst they hope will be made for the College. – You will do the Faculty a favour by furnishing for the portrait a handsome and suitable frame.
Very respectfully
Yours
Sam'l B. Monselelag

New York Nov. 3. 1825.
My Dear Parents,
You know just before I left you
I told you that I should be unable to write
you often, as every leisure moment must
be devoted to my lectures, which I hope to
complete by March if possible, but I have
made it conditional altogether whether I lecture
or not; I devote only my evenings to this
purpose and if I cannot complete them by
devoting this time to them I defer them until
another season. — My finger and leg are
(I may say) entirely well, they are a little tender
but give me no uneasiness; I am fainting
away with all my might; Our house keeper
is exactly what we could wish, a good econ-
omist and faithful in every thing; we are
getting along comfortably; I was professed
for money a few days since but have got through
the pressure for the present, by pumping hard
I expect to keep my head above water.
I was sorry to hear that mother is not well.
I hope she will regain her health, and long be
spared to be a blessing to her family who all
love her very, very much; I hope dear little
Finley has got over the difficulty with his
finger, and that the rest of the children are
well, I long to see them again but dare not think
of it at present. Give my love to Richard
to Nancy and all neighbors & friends.
Cousin Sarah Landing was on the point
of being with you with Richard, I arrived in
the carriage with her at the Steamboat wharf
just in time to see the boat clear from the
wharf. She hopes to be able to spend one day
with you yet. I wish you would invite her
in one of your letters to me, she will be here
about ten days longer.
In great haste, tomorrow being
Grand Canal celebration all is in confusion
Our love to mother
Yr Aff Son
Sam J. B. Mosse

New York Nov. 11th 1825.
My Dear Parents,
We are all well and pursuing our
avocations as usual; Cousin Sarah Lansing
leaves N.York for Utica tomorrow, she has
been so long from home that she feels that she
must not remain any longer absent, she wishes
me to thank you for your invitation to her, to
visit you, and regret exceedingly that she cannot
see you at N.Haven, and hopes to visit you per
haps another season. — She sends a little
present of various little things to Susan, Charles,
and Finley.— I like cousin Sarah very much
I think she is a fine woman, and has an amiable
and affectionate disposition.— Cousin Susan is
doing well, and her infant, she thanks you for your
congratulations, it was born on the Grand Canal
celebration day, and I tell her she must put Grand
canal in the name somewhere, perhaps call him Jacob
Grand Canal Stout but she calls him Edward Carpenter
Stout. — 97879 Kisses to the dear Children, I long to see them
and you all, but dare not think of it, Remember me to Nancy, to the
family, neighbors and friends in general. In haste but with affection as ever
Yr Son. S.F.B. Morse.

N.York Novr. 18, 1825.
My Dear Parents,
I received your letter by Mr. Goodsell;
I was very sorry to hear of dear mother's continued illness; I feel almost tempted to break away from New-York, and return to N.Haven if I thought by so doing I could be of the least service to her in relieving her cares; and Nancy too I feel exceedingly for her, she has been very kind to my dear little ones, and I can only pray, that, if it is not in my power to show her how much gratitude I feel towards her, by some more substantial token, than mere thanks, that He in whom is all fullness of blessing, will reward her abundantly here and hereafter;
I want not the inclination, you all well know to believe you all, but the way to do it is mysteriously hedged up; after weighing well my duty; it seems to be clearly pointed out that I remain where I am; reputation in abundance is flowing in upon me which in the end
will, with the blessing of Providence, be wealth; but
for the present I seem most peculiarly situated
as to commanding money; my great pictures, as I
have often told you are not profitable in com-
parison with smaller, they take much time and oblige
me to wait for my money till they are finished.— I am
industrious, and shall make sufficient to clear me from
debt and I hope transmit you something in the end;
but as for immediate cash I am upon the last
10 dollars also, and expect to be dunned for some
debts of long standing, but I must say to my creditors
have patience with me and I will pay you all; I
have almost completed Miss Horis picture for which
I shall receive $250.— but 100 must immediately be
transmitted to London to M. Bromfield, and the
other 150 will just about pay the greater debts I owe
in N-York; I am determined (Providence permitting)
to contract no new debts, but the most pressing domestic
necessary debts such as fuel & food, not even clothing
until I see every great debt paid that I now owe
and this I hope to accomplish this winter.— I am
paining Gov. Clinton for an engraver $60.— Lafayette
I shall soon commence and go directly through with
It mentioned that reputation was flowing
me. — The younger artists have formed a
association at the Academy and elected me
President, we meet in the evenings of 3 days
to draw, and it has been conducted thus
with such success, as to have trebled the number
of our association and excited the attention, and affection
of the community; there is a spirit of harmony
among the artists, every one says what never before
was said, and which augurs well for the success of
the artist. The artists are pleased to attribute it to
my exertions, and I find in them expressions and
feelings of respect which have been very
interesting to me. I have had, however, in producing
a pleasant state of things I think there was the preparation
to the state of mind of the artists themselves; I find a liberal
feeling in the younger part of them, and a refinement of
manners which will redeem the character of the art from the
degradation to which a few dissipated interlopers, have tamper
with it. A literary society, admission
to which must be by unanimous vote, and to which many
respectable literary characters of the city have been denied ad-
mission, have chosen me a member, together with W. Hillhouse
and W. Longfellow, poets. — these indicate good feeling towards me
to say the least and in the end will be of advantage. I have no doubt
God gloria! —
Yr Aff. Son Sam P. Mose

My Dear Mother,
By Mr. Converse who goes to New
Haven this afternoon I drop you this hasty
line, just to say that I received yours of the
2d of April yesterday. I immediately called
on Mr. Jappan as you requested; he took the
list which I made out, and said he would

down among the furniture to be disposed of, I
had rather not part with that, as I shall want

I cannot come to N.Haven, as I am to move myself

You ask for the bill of the sugar, you will please accept
the triple as a present from me, and if there is any
thing else you may at any time want, just inform me
and if I am in funds you shall have it. I was

My Dear Parents,
I have just heard from Mother and
feel anxious about Father; nothing but the most
imperious necessity prevents my coming immediately
to N.Haven; indeed as it is, I will try and break away
sometime next week if possible, and pass one
day with you, but how to do it without detriment
to my business I don't know; I am engaged on my
Lafayette which the Corporation are anxious to have
and in the prosecution of which picture I have met
and still meet with the most unexpected and con-
stant interruptions; I have many times resolved
to let every thing else suffer and finish it, but
some unforeseen event has from the very commen-
cement, constantly broken in, and obliged me to
delay it.— I am for a day or two now, enga-
ged in our first Exhibition of our new Academy
which is in a flourishing condition, and receives
the approbation, of most of the influential char-
acters in the city and State;— I have longed
for some time from a little respite, but like our
good Father all his sons seem destined for most
busy stations in Society, and constant exertion not
for themselves alone but for the public benefit.
I have not written you on account of such a
pressure of business in various ways, that I cannot
find a moment's leisure, I have just got settled
after moving, my No. is now 124 Broadway
corner of Cedar St. opposite City Hotel; I board at
the National Hotel. I am now called away
by 50 people. Rise my dear little ones, I feel
depressed often that I must spend so much of my
time from them; Love to all. —
I will write again soon
Y Affectionate Son as ever
Sam. J. S. Morgan

New Haven Sept. 20. 1826.
Dear Mother,
I arrived safely home after leaving you
yesterday, and found that neither the house nor the
folks had run away. Dear little Charles was taken
sick a few hours after we had left home, and
Nancy felt anxious about him; he complained of
his leg, which was swollen, and broke out with an
eczema which the doctor thought at first was Epi-
silis but afterwards thought it occasioned by rheu-
matism; he was confined to the bed all day last Sun-
day, and could not walk on Monday, but yesterday
he played about quite lively, and to-day is as great
a fly about as ever; he is now in bed fast asleep
after being well tired with his day's romping all over
the house. Little Finley is gaining very fast, he
begins to acquire his numerous little arts and tricks
which he had before his sickness; I can't but hope
he will yet be a well child. Susan is as usual,
occasionally has a little of humpee, but for the
most part a good girl.— All are well at home,
and I shall set out in the morning at 8 o’clock for
Wethersfield to Paint Judge Mitchell &c.— I heard
from N.York yesterday Edwards & Charles Walker
are well, all prosperous.—
Persevere in your travels, mother, as long as
you think it does you good, and tell Dick to
brush up his best bows and bring home some lady
to grace the now desolate mansion.—
I have no fears about home, I shall
let you know the worst always when I write,
so never think that matters are worse than I
represent; as to little Charles, once more, he is
as well as he ever was, or I should not leave home
as I shall to-morrow morning without the least fear
of any relapse.—
Nancy and all send love, Nancy says
she is glad you are gone, and shall be glad when
you come back again.—
Remember me very kindly to Aunt Salisbury and
thank her, for her generous hospitality to me when in
Boston; and give my love to my dear cousin Elizabeth
Weese, I shall soon forget her, I hope we shall
see her in NewHaven why can't you bring her on?
To cousin Hazard Sproudia if he is in Boston, give
my love, and to all kind friends in Boston or Casle-
town give my regards.
In haste but as ever
Your affectionate Son
Finley.
Mrs Eliz. Ann Morse.

and myself and landscapes of the Principal landscape
Painters, for a Gallery on board the boat, I consider

company I shall do my best. What do you
that of saying no son shall ever hear the word of God on

S. D. P. Morse Esqr
Dear Sir
On my return from
New York, I received the official notice of what you
had previously informed me had been done by the
Academy in regard to myself i.e. that I had been
elected an Artist of the Institution.
I did not think it worth while to express to you
my mind on this subject, at the time when I saw you
in New York, but after mature reflection, finding
my instinctive feelings confirmed by sober reason, I do
not hesitate, confidentially, to make them known to
you.
From the first I feared you would not easily
hit upon a plan in the organization of a
National Academy, by which you would enlist the
feelings and estimation of Artists generally, residing
out of the City of New York. The only mode of doing
this I take to be, a judicious conferment of the honours
of the Institution wherever they are merited. The difficulty
by which I apprehended, was, that you would confine
your election of Academicians and Associates to resident
Artists, and that, from a laudable desire to maintain
the importance of the Honorary Membership, none
but a few Artists in the country, of the highest standing,
could be consistently united with you as Members.—
This would many respectable Artists be excluded
from the only marks of honour or consideration, which
can be valuable as coming from a body of men devoted
to the same pursuits as themselves, some of whom
perhaps of no greater attainments, though adventitiously
advanced to the grade of Academicians.
I say these are the only grades which are objects
worthy of the consideration of a professional Artist
and why?— Because the customs of Society, and the
relations in which men exist to one another in the commu-
nity as men, are such, that no one whatever may, be
his attainments will consent to a connexion with an
Institution in which he is publicly classed in the lowest
of many grades as those you have established.—
However just the discrimination may possibly be,
it is a thing at which the self-love of every individual
will revolt.
97911
I might here allude to the usages of professional
men generally in support of the foregoing remarks,
but I shall pass on
The place of Academician, so far as the honour of
it may be properly esteemed, is worthy of the ambition
of all Artists, however eminent. The same may be said
of the Honorary membership. The Associate is in
a class very way inferior to these, and is elected from
among his fellow Artists, as a preparatory step to
the ultimate honour of the Academy. What remains
is the bulk of professional men, who will not feel them
selves complimented by any farther subdivision of
their ranks.
To be sure of having a compliment valued, it
should be seen that it is valued by those who
confer it. Now it seems to me that the Body of Artists
of your Academy, (I speak plainly) is a sort of
common receptacle, to be filled with those whom you
may think best to attach to the interests of the
Academy, and yet, in doing which you hazard
nothing of the dignity of the standing grades.
I make this remark, notwithstanding I know that
this body embraces some persons of talent, of whom
it is not worth while to speak lightly. How some
of them appreciate their rank may be easily imagined.
There seems to be the imprint of littleness on every
thing relating to this grade. All the other elections
are to be made with much circumspection, at particular times, by unanimous vote. The Artist may
be either professional or Amateur; he may be proposed
and voted for at any time, and elected by a bare
majority. And even in the Catalogue, his subordinate connexion to the Academy is significantly
hinted by a little A.
This grade, soutions, so indefinite, embracing
persons of so widely different views as must
respectively belong to Artists and Amateurs, appears
to me to be alike unfit for either.
To the one it is barely an acknowledgement of his
professional character as an Artist, as distinguished
from a Student or Copy-while the other is thereby
furnished with a technical character which he seldom
wishes to avow.
The remedy (if you should wish my opinion) would
be very simple, and most consistent with the proposed
design of the Academy -- It is thin -- The Academicians
possessing the whole Executive power, might be
resident Artists (though in London the Royal Academy
there was an exception in the case of Raeburn who never
lived in London) and their number ought to be limited.
The Associates might or might not be limited
and there cannot be the least inconvenience in leaving
the number of them unlimited. -- Now the very term,
Associate, is one peculiarly adapted to such a relation
as Artists, in various parts of the country ought to sustain,
in an Institution professibly national; and by conferring
this where you might not choose to confer the honorary
membership, you would find an opportunity of
discriminating, without belittling or offending any --
In this way, and by the Honorary membership, how resident
Artists would sustain a parallel standing with the
resident Academicians and Associates, subject, however,
to the rule which requires a residence of one year
in New York, before they would be eligible to an election
into the body of Academicians.
While on this subject I will just notice an improvement
which might be made in the initial letter of the
Associate membership. -- The N.A. is definite and will
be easily understood, but the more it is not intelligible
if used in any other place than in the Catalogue.
Why not A.R.A. as properly as A.R.A. -- I think the
initials should not only distinctly indicate the
particular membership, but should also convey
a positive idea of the Academy with which the Artist
is connected.
You will perhaps think I have enlarged beyond
all bounds in the remarks I have made. I certainly
should not have done so, but for the hope of promoting
the interests of the Academy; my personal wishes could
have been expressed in few words -- From what I have
already said, you will not be surprised when I tell you
that I cannot consistently return my thanks for the
vote of membership which has been announced. --
I would not think more highly of myself than I
ought to think -- and I submit my views on this
subject with full confidence in your candour
and brotherly feeling, and in the belief, that if you
do not agree with me in sentiment now, you will
one long be convinced of the soundness of the objections
I have urged.
If a reply from me to the letter of the Secretary is
essential to my being considered fully a member, my
purpose will be accomplished by silence. but if
that should be insufficient, then I would request
you to hint my wish to be left out in such
a manner as will excite the least remark.
I make this communication confidentially, and
should not be willing to have it seen by any
member, excepting Mr Towns & Mr Durand, if you
should have occasion to show it to them.
With sincere gratification at the success of
the Academy, and with hopes of its increasing
prosperity I am as ever
Truly Your Friend

I had the pleasure, to day, of receiving your
Circular communication to which, I must mention the
7th but dated on the 4th inst. under other circumstances
and considerations than those in which I am now
placed, I should have been pleased to contribute
to the support of your infant institution My
attention was directed towards it from its first
commencement, I watched its progress with
intense interest, and as I had been labouring
long on a similar project in this City which
I intended to establish with a view to an
improvement of the Public Taste and rendering the
artist independent of an arbitrary existing tax,
which it lays the least of it, stood in the way of improvement
and knew only to debate the profession with a
view to effect my purpose, I commenced a series of
communications in the United States Gazette under
the signature of Natural Truth, in which I endeavoured
to prove that the arts and Public Taste were
almost stationary, owing to the paralysing influence
of the Directors of the Pennsylvania Academy of the
fine Art, whose sole object was a Missionary one
in every sense of the word, arrogating to themselves
all the Prophets, and placing themselves first in
Public view, claimed and absorbed all the Honor,
too — The artist is considered as a wear
underling, a tool suited for their purposes —
However I did not succeed, and have been persecuted
for my good wishes, to the utmost of their police —
These Communications have to my knowledge
read by several artists in this State, as the Papers
containing them have sent for to your City, and
as they succeeded your formation into a society
I sometimes thought they were found in some
way or other useful — after your society was
formed I did it least expect some small
attention — They have paid to other artists of this
City, but not to me, not even a Circular till
now — It is true I am but an indifferent artist
and I neither wish nor expect your society
to alter its opinion of, or change its conduct
towards me — I wish the society all possible
success. It has done itself honor, and
will confirm, I am sure, what I predicted
would follow, if the same experiment had been
made in Philadelphia — I had therefore long since
come to the conclusion, that as I was not an object of
sufficient notice to warrant first attention, and
that at the time your respect was paid to my Friends in
this City — My Views would of course be but secondary
consideration, and therefore I did not send any
to you. Thank you for your kind and memorable
letter. I can only interpret it as a compliment, at least
for the present, I shall not, I hope, incur the displeasure
if I fail to send any of my works — I respect
its earnestness, and shall not fail to admire
the enterprise and talents of its Members
respectively and collectively, in all of which, you
will perceive that I also have some respect for myself
whatever may be the opinion entertained by others —
I am very respectfully yours at
Jascha Shaw.

My Dear Sir I am happy to congratulate you
on your safe return to your home and friends.
It is an event to which I have been looking
for many months with great satisfaction
and I hope before long to see you and
recount together some of the interesting
circumstances which have occurred since
our parting farewell in the Piazza Colonna.
Poor Cooper! it was a long farewell to him.
I at first intended to subjoin what I am now
saying to two sides of a letter which I began
May 2nd 1831 during an alarming attack of
inflammation of the lungs. I had begun
to recover after two months illness, the last of
which was severe and attended with very threatening
symptoms. I had made more exertions than I ought
to have done in riding out in a close carriage
the day before and I was compelled to break off
my letter abruptly and give up agains to a temporary
lapse from which I only escaped with great caution.
It was not until after six months that the symptoms
peculiar to that disorder entirely left me, since
then I have not been troubled with them at all.—
I have been glad that you prolonged your stay beyond
your first intention and should have received great
satisfaction if during this time you had just
written me a few lines.— Your opportunities
have been great and they will result in gain
to the public and I trust to yourself. — I must
express myself highly delighted with the copy of
the School of Athens. This carefully executed
and so happy in the tone of colour, as a copy in
oil, that it is a treasure to the art, in the sense
in which that copy in the Royal Academy (though
of inferior execution if I need not rightly) is
important to that institution. The copy also of
the Tintoretto which Mr Walker has is a capital
hit in colour and effect, reviving in my mind
the striking peculiarities of the great original.—
The small original pictures which were exhibited
in New York last summer (one a group of musicians
playing to the image of the virgin I believe) were
also very fine and delighted me much -- But I
must wait until I see you to say all I think
and feel -- only this adding that as a brother I
have been soliciting for your welfare and now
rejoice in your return -- Our friend Bob Loomis
happy to learn has returned, and if I could leave
home for a few days I should go and see you both.
Perhaps I shall be able to do so shortly --
I hope you have seen the August Sophia & Daughter
because I think you will be pleased with it, and
if you are, a favourable word dropped as occasion
may offer -- in conversation -- or otherwise, may prove
of great importance to him at this moment. --
From what he has done unaided by advantages
of foreign study or encouragement of almost any
kind, I think you will be glad to contribute
to his advancement by that countenance of his
pretensions which will operate favorably on public
sentiment -- in Boston an unlimited partiality for
Greenough as one of themselves, shut the door against
August -- and his exhibition did not do well --
I rejoice in Greenough's success -- he is worthy of it, but
it was ungenerous in the Bostonians to let August
98164
appeal to their taste and love for art result in
an unprofitable exhibition. -- It is doing better
in New York and it is from N.York and the
south or West that he must look for support
rather than from Boston. -- On his account I pay
the postage of this letter -- I should be glad
to receive one from you in return but knowing
how your time is taken up I shall not feel myself neglected
if you should find it inconvenient to write to me --
However of paper I must close and am with great regard
as ever sincerely yours
St. H. Torrey

My dear Mosso,
I saw the other day in the
National Intelligencer, a letter of Lafayette to an American on the way of quitting Europe, which was copied from the New York Observer. I conjectured that the letter was addressed to you, and consequently that you are returned home. Have I guessed right? Hoping that I have, I have determined to write you a letter. Do not think that I shall often trouble you in this way; for, living so remotely from most scenes of general interest, I do not feel myself entitled to do so. My apology at the present time must be found in my sharing largely in the extreme interest which all true Americans feel in the continuance of our glorious Union, the existence of which is at least jeopardized by the recent measures of a sister State.
The salvation of the Union consists with the North -- and it can be effected only in one way -- viz, by the repeal of the present high protective tariff -- or, a dissolution of the Union is absolutely inevitable. These are the only alternatives. The North must give up and
98165
denote the title which the South so frequently claims,
that of "generous." — The South will not yield on
such from the ground it has taken; unless the
tariff of protection is removed, and time should
convince our people that this has been wrongfully
accused as the source of Southern depression. —
Discrimination is quite out of the question. Were it not
extra-constitutional, it is impracticable. For, in
case of a resort to force on the part of the general
government — North Carolina, Georgia and Alabama would go with South Carolina by an
immense majorities of their respective populations,
and would take an active part on her side.
You may be perfectly assured of this — I know it
is so. Old sober North Carolina would give a
majority of ten to one in favor of resistance to
the tariff. — The hostility to a tariff of protection is
rooted — and whether right or wrong, cannot be destroyed by any form of reasoning, nor subdued by any
display or exertion of Force. And granting that a
tariff of protection is constitutional, and beneficial to
the nation at large, shall we hazard our national
existence to maintain it? — Profits at the North are
under a delusion in supposing that the enemies of the
tariff compose a small majority of S. Carolina only. —
That state is warmly unanimous — most of the Union
parties out of Charleston, say, "the nullifiers have acted free
citadelately — but the state itself committed itself and will support it, at all hazards!" — Is it fair to you that
the whole South has a deep and inconquerable hostility
to the present tariff — that S. C. is really unanimous in
herself and that she will be sustained by immense
majorities in the adjoining states; and that this hostility
will be pushed to a dissolution of our Union, or to
our mutual civil war, and that you may afford
your friends and thus of these facts, constitute my
object and apology for writing to you at this time. I
thought moreover that you will believe me—for some
of our Southern Friends say "Peace, Peace, where
there is none."—
Where is our friend—(am I not justified in saying our
friend?)—Peninsular Cooper? Where is his charming
daughter? I hardly should dare tell you what he
made of her portrait. I delivered the whole picture perfect
and unaltered in the smallest degree, to Miss Delaney.
Have you time to write me whether I must visit Miss
C. from my mind or rather heart—that is, if I shall be
interposed—it would be asking of her too
much, to have her father and mother's
conservatism and drawing-room to live in this remote
part of our country, to say nothing of the change from
Europe to North Carolina.—Or, shall I visit New York
province, than I felt that I did when in Paris?—I
always labored under a great constraint when conversing
with her father—I believe I trouble you with my
reasons for quitting St. Y. in a letter to you in London. My
reasons for quitting St. Y. in a village rather than second
on the rising tide of Chelsea, on which I cast my
pamphlet—if it be ever found I think it will
be after very many days.—Since my return my practice
has been very great. I am sorry however that the
Chelsea contained my stay in Paris by one year at least.—
I hope you receive the little sum which you so
kindly and opportunely loaned me, in reason for your
own use of it.—I sent morocco one of my pamphlets

in quest of you. – Where is Habenham? and how does
he get along in painting?
I have written a long letter, and have asked several
questions; I should hardly be surprised however if you
should not find leisure to write – though a letter from
you would give much pleasure to

most Abt & humble Servant

In the year 1832, having visited Paris for the purpose
of study, I became acquainted with Professor Morse
Lancry, American Cooper, the American novelist, Green
and the Englishman. The letters of introduction from the
Vaubanew, Secretary of State to our ministers and councils
in Europe of the recent visit to Lafayette, I did not use the
first year but three to private individuals, because I
worked as full time as I could, because I
was the subject of Mr. Morse & Cooper introduced out to
Lafayette during the summer of 1832, and indeed him
to invite me to join the three or a fourth in a committee
appointed by the purpose of discussing of a large sum
of money sent from America to aid the Poles in their
struggle with Russia. Poland having fallen, and duty
became to aid, with the commence of the French government,
the escape of Polish refugees, and to assist, we
met, at the house of Mr. Cooper once a week, on the rue
de l'Amirique, the leading, who had expressed, and were
qualified to advise us. This association gave me
certain position among the leaders, of the political
clubs & some consideration, with the opinion of order, and
through them acquaintances elsewhere, who furnished me
with ideas to which I shall refer hereafter.
Louis Philippe "the King of Republics," had disgraced
at the expiration of the French liberals, and there were
immensely in the streets, and violent debate, in the Chambers.
In all of these America her institution, and her progress was
under constant disquietions, On one occasion, the attempt
was made in debate to prove America the heaviest taxed and
least orderly land in the civilized world. To which this Lafayette
called on Cooper for statement, & Mr. Cooper came from saying
of Southern society and gives them as well as himself as
when Lafayette presented them in the Chamber, with the
98175
authenticity, a member replied that "Mr. Cooper was well
known in the world as a matter of romance," before
a demand for an explanation of his from Mr. the
amendable "was made to a duel avoided."
2 first met Prof. Morse in the Louvre, copying Renouard's
great picture of the Angel of the Louvre, with small copies
of the choicest pictures of the collection on eight. When the
cholera broke out, being unwilling to run away, and find
that Prof. Morse intended to remain in the house in the Rue
de Turenne, where he then was, and not liking that he
should remain alone there, for poor Americans, I
not speaking the language, I ventured to move to
the same house. He agreed & I did so. By my room,
near higher & more exposed than his, we made my two
rooms, one bedroom, and lost him as one setting
room, & studios. We lived together, & generally said
the same company. Our conversation, always turned upon subjects of importance to me, and I have
never forgotten the substance of many of them. He
told me of his experiments on light, & shade, in painting
of his studies in England with Leslie Washington
at Stony Washington Irving, & others under Berry West.
of his visits to Italy, and the political information
which he obtained there (afterwards published in book
from some the columns of the New York Observer) &c &c
The Louvre was always closed on Monday, to clean
up the galleries after the popular exhibition of the Patriotes,
on Tuesday, so that Monday was our day for visit
excursions, &c. On one occasion I was left alone
and two or three times, during the week, he was absent
this was unusual but I asked no question, and
made no remark. But on Saturday evening, sitting
by our evening lamp, he seemed lost in thought
till suddenly he remarked: "The mail, in one case
are too slow. This French Telegraph is better, and
comes do even better in our clear atmosphere than
mine, where half of the time fog obscures the wires;
But this will not be fast enough: The lightning would
serve us better. These may well be the exact words,
but they conveyed the desire -- and I laughing said,
what I see what you have seen after you have been
examining the French system of Telegraph my "He
admitted that he had taken advantage of the kind
offer of one in authority to do so. -- In after years Prof.
McCrady, of Charleston, having attacked Morse, claims
to the invention. I wrote to him on the subject, and
he replied -- that Cooper's family declared that he
had spoken frequently to them of it during the
summer of 1832, but the idea only occurred to him
on his way home at sea in the following October --
that he had never claimed but the method of
sounding the depth of the water of the ocean was of great value
to him, yet truth was not to be disregarded for
any profit, and therefore he could not say, &c.
I collect this very clearly because when the invention
was made public I told my father of the pressing
emergency and also of Prof. Mc's remark to me in
New York in 1834, when asked what had become of
his great picture. "I told it said he -- for $1000 -- but
I have heard promising to some types & fixtures in
his studio -- over the steam office in New York -- some
thing which I hope will give me both fame & wealth
if I succeed."
Prof. Morse, in the mid winter, often expressed indignation at the system pursued in Europe. If poured
into the United States, the result of their population
said it was "like pouring dirty water into clean"
was intended to destroy the character & influence
of our country abroad & its prosperity at home, and
must be arrested in some way or other.
after he left I stayed more with myself -- in Italy -- where I used my letters to a limited degree

got acquainted with laymen & clericals, and

In May, 1834, I returned to New York. I spent
the summer partly at the residence of Mr. Zell, son
a nephew of Edward Loring, on the banks of the Hudson,
in aideremain excursion to the coal mines of Penna.
at New Port R.I., etc. in New York city. In New York city,
I frequently visited Prof. More, and was with him on
one occasion when the advent of George Thompson, M.P.,
and the beginning of the abolition excitement in Massachusetts,
revived my recollection of what had been told me in
warning, some months since. About the same time
a Dr Cox, living at Elecker Street, I think, had married
a negro to a white woman, and the indignation caused
had gutted his home in revenge. I spoke to Cox, and
he repudiated the idea, especially of John Quincy Adams
having any thing to do with it, and invited me to attend
an abolition meeting that night. The miserable, derisive,
flying speech made on the occasion, disgusted all
moderate men, and my friend asked "are the northern
people such fools as to listen to such as that?" My
reply was, "if I have read history, eight out of ten
of the people are always right at first, but when
passion is aroused, they never reason." He then
heard, what I shall never forget "The Northern people
will never sacrifice Constitution & laws under the
lead of fools of fanaticism to stay the goad that lays the
golden egg." I resolved already, because I began to
rule & speak on these subjects, as soon as the English
action in the East Indies, in 1836, showed that
my instruments had either had the precision
of a prophet, or the certainty of those behind
the diplomatic curtain.
I have not to mention that one day, while
in the rue Burenne - I was studying from my
own face reflected in a glass - as is often done by
young artists, when I remarked, how grand
it would be if we could invent a method of
fixing the image on the mirror. Prof. M. replied
that he had thought of it, while a pupil at Yale
college & that Professor Schleman (I think) and
himself had tried it, with a dash of nitrate of
silver on a piece of paper - but that unfortunately
it made the light dark & the shadows light,
but that if they could to reverse, we should
have a fac simile like india ink drawings?
I had they thought of using glass, as, in doing
the Daguerreotype, he would have been perfectly
anticipated - certainly the Photograph.
When the Cholera Asiaticus - put his word in
Paris - there being some hesitation about directing
he dead - I offered to go, with Ashel Smith - at that
time interne in one of the hospitals, and examine
the dead. We did so, and on my return - I gave
such spinning as made the people in our house
use a teaspoonful of Charcoal every morning
before going out, as a preventative, and that also
we had had a premonitory case in our porter,
no one in our wall, - where our example
extended - had the Cholera - although it roared
madly around us.
These memorances are submitted to Peter
Morse - and I desire to use them to aid me in the
making of a work intended to open the eyes
of the American people as far as I can - to the
true nature of the present attempt to destroy
the Republic, & also to give authority to
these incidents connected with himself
therein mentioned.

James F. Cooper, Esqr.
My dear Sir,
Don't scold at me. I don't deserve a scolding if you knew
all, and I do if you don't know all, for I have not written you since
I landed in Novr. What with severe illness for several weeks after my
arrival, and the accumulation of cares consequent on so long an absence
from home, I have been overwhelmed and distracted by calls upon my time
for a thousand things that pressed upon me for immediate attention, and so
I have put off and put off what I have been longing, I am ashamed to say for
weeks, (if not months) to do, I mean, to write you. The truth is, my dear
Sir, I have so much to say, that I know not where to commence. I throw
myself on your indulgence, and believing you will forgive me, I commence
without further apology.
First, as to things at home: New York is improved, as the word
goes wonderfully, you will return to a strange city, you will not rec-
ognize many of your acquaintance among the old buildings; brawn new build-
ings, stores and houses, are taking the place of the good staid modest
houses of the early settlers. Improvement is all the rage, and houses
and churchyards must be overthrown and upturned, whenever the Corporation
plough is set to work for the widening of a narrow, or the making of a new
street.- I believe you sometimes have a fit of the blues, it is singular
if you do not, with your temperament; I confess to many fits of this dis-
agreeable disorder, and I know nothing so likely to induce one, as the
fading, after an absence of some years from home, the great hour hand of
life sensibly advanced on all your former friends. What will be your sen-
sations after 6 or 7 years, if mine are acute after 3 years absence?- I
have not been much in society as yet, I have many visitations, but until I
clear off the accumulated rubbish of 3 years, which lies upon my table, I
must decline seeing much of my friends.- I have seen twice your sisters the
98195
2
Misses Delancy and was prevented from being at their house last Friday
evening by the severest snow-storm we have had this season. Our friends
the Jays I have met several times and have had much conversation with
them about you and your delightful family. Mr. P. A. Jay is a member
of the Club so I see him every Friday evening. Chancellor Kent also is
a member, and both warm friends of yours. What shall I say now respecting
the popular feeling towards you. You are partly right and greatly wrong
in your supposition that you are not properly estimated by that country
whom you have honored and defended. You are right in supposing that you
have some envious and even malignant backbiters, who have till lately suc-
ceeded in injuring your fame, and who would delight to see you seduced
to their level, but they are very few, and what little influence they
may have had is fast diminishing; But you are greatly wrong in supposing
you have not multitudes of warm friends and admirers, and they are in-
creasing every day; that they estimate you as you deserve I do not say.
They will come to a juster estimate when you return, for, I speak from
the heart, they cannot know you as I do without having the highest re-
spect and esteem for you. I am sure you will be greeted by your country-
men on your return, and do let me beg you to come in the Spring as you
contemplated when I left you.— By the way, I have something to tell you
in relation to the Review in the American about which we had so much
conversation; I gave you the name of the writer in Paris, on the authority
of Lieutenant Payne; Since I have been at home, it has been declared to
me that the Review was written here by an obscure clerk in a counting
house and Verplanck was cited to me as having assured my informant of the
fact. Now notwithstanding the authority cited, I think the document
itself is proof against such an origin. My informers were silenced by
my exposè of the matter, and I have heard nothing of the subject for a
long time. There has been some trickery in this business you may depend
98196
3
upon it.— This clerk whoever he is, is made to father it, and he might
have been the translator. If you can ferret the truth out, and expose
this contemptible meanness by ascertaining, as I think you can, whether
Nizard actually wrote it, I should delight to see the authors arraigned
at the bar of public opinion for their tricks.
You will want to know about the picture. I have done nothing
to it as yet, for the want of proper accommodations. I am now in excel-
lent apartments over the bookstore of the Carvills, (the rooms formerly
the Athenæum,) I have them a year from May, and one of them will make
an excellent Exhibition room for the picture when it is finished.— My
time for 10 or 12 days past has been occupied in answering a pamphlet
of Col. Trumbull who came out for the purpose of justifying his opposi-
tion to measures which had been devised for uniting the two Academies.
I send you the first copy hot from the press. There is a great deal to
dishearten in the state of feeling, or rather state of no feeling on the
arts in this city. The only way I can keep up my spirits is by resolutely
resisting all disposition to repine, and by fighting perseveringly against
all the obstacles that hinder the progress of art. I have been told
several times since my return that I was born 100 years too soon for the
arts in our country. I have replied if that be the case, I will try and
make it but 50.— I am more and more persuaded that I have quite as much
to do with the pen for the arts as the pencil, and if I can, in my day,
so enlighten the public mind as to make the way easier for those that come
after me, I don't know that I shall not have served the cause of the fine
arts as effectively as by painting pictures which might be appreciated
100 years after I am gone. If I am to be the Pioneer, and am fitted
for it, why should I not glory as much in felling the trees and clearing
away the rubbish as in showing the decorations suited to a more advanced
state of cultivation? Do remember me with the greatest respect and esteem
to Mrs. Cooper and your family; I will be a better correspondent in future.—

Mr. Rogers having this moment called on me to say he

business is probably settled by this time by Mr. Clay's compromise bill, so
that the legitimates of Europe may stop blowing their twopenny trumpets
in triumph at our disunion; the same clashing of interests in Europe would

3 or 4 years of wordy war, and some hundreds of gallons of ink, but no
necks are broken, nor heads, all will be in statu ante bello in a few
days. Now Mr. Cooper don't swear, nor breathe hard words, at what I am

my

My Business is better now than it ever was
before in Boston -- plenty of Portraits & now and
then a Landscape, for variety, but as for Prices,
alas! "nothing to speak of" -- I am most sadly
in want of a Manakin: and Cannot afford to buy
one Should you know of any Chance to buy
one at second hand for a small price, will
you let me know of it? Mr Pendleton offers to
get me out one from Paris for 175 Dolls. But
I cannot raise so much money at present, so
unless I can find some old one. I shall still have
to guess at my draperies. -- You cannot imagine
how much I rejoice at your safe
return to your own Country. I have during your
absence watched for intelligence of you, I will not
say with a Brother's, but with a Lover's anxiety.
-- I wish to come & settle in N.York that I may

whose Parents & connections are all here, I prefer
Boston for the present. Still she is desirous of visiting
N.York & I think I shall spend some months there
in the course of this year -- I must not forget to
tell you we have a Splendid Boy just beginning

in May, or the last of April. and shall have a

will find time to write me a line soon just to

H. C. Pratt.

My dear Sir,
The packet will go in a few minutes so I must be brief.-
I recd. an impudent sort of a letter from Gould a day or two ago enclosing
me a paper the N. York Traveller, (as yet of limited circulation,) in
which was an article which he pretends to have come accidentally
yet it bears too strong internal evidence of his own pen for me to doubt
who is the author, he says he has sent a copy to you. He is too low in
every respect for your notice. I could wish that he might be treated with
the most persevering silence, for every breath of notoriety exalts him
if it does not detract from you.- I saw Stone yesterday he is going to
explain today; as I said before in a former letter, there is no malice in
his attack, and he regrets having wounded. You know Stone, he is not al-
ways most prudent, but he is at heart on your side and well disposed. We
will see, however, what he says. As for King he has overshot his mark.
He is hollow hearted and shallow, and it requires all the charity I pos-
sess to resist my propensity to despise him.- I have no time to speculate
at present. I wish you were at home. You would soon set matters right.
I spent the 4th inst. at Mr. Jay's at Rye in the old mansion. He in-
sists that you have the mass of the public on your side, and that you
are wrong in being so sensitive to these petty attacks.- I do think myself
that the character of those who delight to sting if they can demands that
they should be treated with silent contempt.-
I long to see you all back again. N. York is remarkably healthy,
and my own health was never better.-
The picture will be finished this week.
Yrs in great haste but with sincere esteem and respect
S. F. B. Morse.

that my reasons for declining the
proposed loan, though many, and

Newton has no intention of

thanks for all the kind things

Published every morning at No. 2 South Gay

MORSE'S MAGNETIC TELEGRAPH.—The
chamber in the Railroad depot, Pratt street, in which
is placed the eastern station of the Electro-Magnetic
Telegraph of Professor Morse, continues to be filled
throughout the day with wondering spectators; and
the same scene is also presented at the south-western
station in the Capitol at Washington. The Telegraph
is completely successful in its operations, and consti-
tutes one of the most remarkable and astonishing tri-
umphs which the science and ingenuity of man have
ever achieved. Communications are now made be-
tween the cities of Baltimore and Washington with
the rapidity of lightning, and with perfect clearness
and accuracy. The whole arrangement is one of
great simplicity, and when the spectator stands at the
telegraphic table and sees the operator transmit a mes-
sage by a wire forty miles in length and receive an
answer back through the same medium—all in the
space of a few seconds—he cannot but be struck with
wonder and admiration. Professor MORSE has gain-
ed for himself an imperishable name, and we doubt
not that in due time he will be called on by the Gov-
ernment to prolong his magical lines to the extent of
hundreds of miles.
The Washington Standard states that on Wednes-
day there was a large number of gentlemen assembled
at the Capitol to hear the Telegraphic despatches
from Baltimore, as they were successively received.—
It was proposed that the thanks of those present be
tendered to Professor Morse, which was concurred in
generally, and the following resolution was offered by
Mr. George B. Wallis, correspondent of the Ohio States-
men, which was unanimously adopted, and three cheers
given for the Professor and his invention, to which he
returned his sincere thanks for the compliment:
Resolved, That the thanks of this meeting be and
they are hereby tendered to Professor Morse, for the
promptitude with which he has reported, via his Elec-
tro Magnetic Telegraph, the proceedings of the several
Baltimore political Conventions; and that we consider
his invention as worthy the countenance and support
of the Government.

MORSE'S MAGNETIC TELEGRAPH.
This new invention is completed from Baltimore to
Washington. The wire, perfectly secured against the
weather by a covering of rope yarn and tar, is con-
ducted on the top of posts about 20 feet high, and 100
yards apart.
The nominations of the Convention on Monday were
to be conveyed to Washington by this Telegraph,
where they would arrive in a few seconds.
On Saturday morning the Batteries were charged,
and the regular transmission of intelligence between
Washington and Baltimore commenced, as we learn
from the Baltimore Patriot. A large number of gen-
tlemen were present to see the operations of this truly
astonishing contrivance. Many admitted to the room
had their names sent down, and in less than a second
the apparatus in Baltimore was put in operation by
the attendant in Washington, and before the lapse of
a half minute the same names were returned plainly
written. At half past 11 o'clock, A. M. the question
being asked “What the news was at Washington?”
the answer was almost instantaneously returned, “Van
Buren stock is rising”—meaning of course that his
chances were strengthening to receive the nomination
of Monday last. The time of day was also enquired
for, when the response was given from the capital—
“forty-nine minutes past eleven.” At this period it
was also asked how many persons were spectators to
the Telegraphic experiments in Washington—the an-
swer was “sixteen.” After which a variety of names
were sent up from Washington, some with their com-
pliments to friends in Baltimore, whose names had
just been transmitted to them. Several items of pri-
vate intelligence were also transmitted backwards and
forwards, one of which was an order to an agent in
Baltimore not to pay a certain bill. The electric fluid
proved too slow, for it had been paid a few minutes
before.
At half past 12 o'clock, the following was sent to
Washington—“Ask a reporter in Congress to send a
despatch to the Baltimore Patriot at 2 p. m.” In a-
bout a minute the answer came back thus, “It will be
attended to.”
2 o'clock, p. m.—The despatch has arrived, and is
as follows:—
One o'clock.—There has been a motion in the House
to go into Committee of the Whole on the Oregon
question. Rejected 2 aves 79, nays 86.
Half past one.—The House is now engaged on pri-
vate bills.
Quarter to two.—Mr. Atherton is now speaking in
the Senate.
Mr. S. will not be in Baltimore to-night.
So that Baltimore papers are thus enabled to give
their readers information from Washington up to the
very hour of going to press. This is indeed the anni-
hilation of space.
We had the pleasure of witnessing the wonderful
operation of this Telegraph two or three weeks ago,
and, in common with all others who have seen it, were
indeed astonished, delighted and intensely interested
by the results exhibited. At that time the communication was perfected twenty-two miles, and the experiments were performed over that distance. Since then the wires have been laid as far as Baltimore, 40 miles, and the operation, as appears above, is still completely successful. It seems hardly credible that, by means of this mysterious influence, one may converse with a person twenty, or forty, or a hundred, or a thousand miles off, with almost as much ease and rapidity as though the two were face to face, yet such is the fact! At least the conveyance of intelligence from one mind to the other requires little, if any, more time than would be necessary to write and read the information communicated. In the very valuable and interesting report of Mr. Ellsworth, the Commissioner of Patents, and the accompanying papers, lately published, there is a description of the electro-magnetic telegraph, illustrated by plates; and with the help of this we shall endeavor to give our readers some idea, imperfect though it may be, of one of the great improvements of the age, and destined, the Commissioner thinks, to exercise a vast, and, it is believed, happy effect in the transmission of intelligence from one section of the country to another.
The electro-magnet, says the Commissioner, is the basis upon which this whole invention rests. This magnet is produced by coiling around a bar of soft iron, made in the form of a horse-shoe, copper-wire previously covered, similar to hamlet-wire, and varnished to prevent metallic contact with each other and the iron. The two terminations of the wire thus surrounding the iron in a spiral form, are brought out at each end of the curved bar and are connected, one with the zinc pole of a galvanic battery, the other with the platinum; the battery being prepared in the usual manner with its corroding acid, produces galvanic electricity, which starts off from one pole of the battery, follows the wire around the soft iron, and returns to the other pole of the battery by the other wire—thus forming a complete circuit. The galvanic fluid is now passing the whole length of the wire, and, while thus passing, the curved iron becomes a strong magnet. By connecting the two ends of the bent iron with a bar of similar soft iron, it will support many pounds weight. If, while in this condition, one of the wires is removed from the battery, the cross bar falls, and with it its weights. The curved iron returns instantly to its original state. It is unmagnetized. Complete the circuit, as at first, and in an instant it is again a magnet. Break the circuit, and it ceases to be a magnet. If the battery is placed 100, or 2,000, or 10,000 feet from the magnet, yet, when the one is connected with the other by intervening wires, the effect upon the magnet is the same—making it a magnet when the circuit is complete, and vice versa when it is broken. In this way, power is produced at a point of considerable distance from the generating agent, and wholly at the command of the operator at the battery to make or destroy the power produced with the utmost possible rapidity."
These being the principles of the operation of the fluid, a very ingenious, yet simple machinery is constructed for their practical application, provided with a little clock work apparatus, by means of which arbitrary marks, representing letters and figures are indented on a strip of paper, in form of a ribbon, which is coiled up on a roller and unwinds by the action of the machinery. The precise process, of course, can hardly be intelligibly explained without the plates.—The telegraphic alphabet is merely a series of dots, short lines and long lines, impressed upon the paper like the raised letters used by the blind—the length of the indentations and the intervening spaces depending upon the rapidity with which the electric circuit is closed and broken by the operator, who has, as said above, the entire control of it. The paper to be imprinted, being fixed upon a revolving cylinder, records despatches day and night; and this without ink, as the impressions are easily read even by the blind.—The records of the night continue entered in the morning. The alphabet is easily learned.
The rapidity of communication is truly astonishing; it is instantaneous. The rate at which the electric magnetic fluid passes, according to Mr Wheatstone, is 388,000 miles, (equal to 111/2 times around the globe) in one second. The following experiment tried at Washington, related by Mr Ellsworth, shows the rapidity of transmission very forcibly. As the train of cars was coming from Baltimore, a person stationed 4 miles off, at the instant the locomotive was opposite to him, gave notice of the fact that the cars were coming; and this news was received, and the acknowledgment of its reception at Washington returned, before the last car of the train had passed.—As each circuit, to be complete, must, in both cases, reach from one end to the other, and back, the whole distance, thus traversed in the time mentioned above, must have been 16 miles, besides the stopping of the machinery. So whatever the distance, the communication would be apparently instantaneous. We saw repeated instances of this lightning-like passage and return over twenty-two miles. When the Professor at Washington wished to call the attention of the person at the other extremity of the wires, he would close the circuit and give the necessary signal, and would hardly have ceased the requisite motion before a reply was received from his attendant, 22 miles off, that he was ready to communicate. Distance is absolutely annihilated. Experiments have already been made in this country, with wires of 160 miles in length, insulated in ends, with perfect success. Professor Morse has also discovered the astonishing fact that two galvanic currents may be passed in the same wire, in opposite directions, without interference with their respective functions; that intelligence may thus be transmitted through a single wire, at the same time, from opposite points—the two currents passing each other without any detention.
Among the numerous great and obvious advantages mentioned as likely to result from this mode of communication, the most amusing is that criminals will be deterred from the commission of crimes, under the hope of escape upon the "iron horse;" for the mandate of justice, outrunning their flight, will greet their arrival at the first stopping place. Just imagine the astonishment of a criminal who fancies himself escaping from the clutches of the law with all the speed of steam, as some old Hays, scores of miles from the scene of the crime which he committed but an hour ago as it were, touches him on the shoulder and says "you're my customer," telling the rogue as much about his offence as he knows himself!

If anything could add to the intense interest with
which the proceedings of the late Baltimore Convention
were regarded, the triumphant success of such
an invention as Prof. Morse's telegraph, was an
event calculated to produce such effect. It is fortunate
indeed that this great experiment was first tried
at a time when all men's minds were fixed upon the
point at which its wonderful powers were at work.
Although for a moment the means by which the intelligence
of important transactions was communicated and in some degree
brought about were lost sight of in the more immediate consequence
of the transactions themselves, yet, when astonishment and
surprise at the result of the Baltimore Convention
shall have subsided and curiosity have become satisfied
as to the why and wherefore, and the whole affair
come to be looked at as not more strange than
a thousand other things that have happened, then
public attention will become concentrated upon a
discovery of more importance than the decisions of
innumerable conventions like that in which it bore
a subordinate part. It was a happy circumstance,
we repeat, that the new telegraph made its first appearance
on the stage of human affairs to take part
in a momentous scene. It was fit that an invention
destined probably to revolutionize all our modes and
systems of business and to exert an incalculable influence
upon the future destiny of the species, should
be ushered into notice dealing with principalities and
powers.
Nor was the part taken in these transactions by
this telegraph a mere display to gratify curiosity.
It performed an important duty, accomplishing that
which without its assistance would probably not
have been done at all. Had the telegraph not been
broken up on Wednesday evening and the decision
of Mr. Wright to be the candidate for the Vice
Presidency would have become known too late to
be remedied. But by means of this wonderful mes-
passenger, we are told information of his unexpected
nomination was conveyed to Mr. Wright, who was
at his lodgings in Washington, 40 miles distant, in
five minutes, and in an equally short space of time
Mr. Wright made up his mind and informed the
convention to what effect. Then word came that
Col. Young wished to have a few minutes private
conversation with Mr. Wright, and forthwith these
cautious old politicians, the one at Baltimore,
the other in Washington, were whispering in each
other's ears, with as much ease as if sitting together
in the same room! Perhaps the distance did dimin-
ish the potency of the Colonel's exhortations, for
Wright continued inflexible, "deaf to his entreaties,"
at least so far as granting them was concerned. He
was then told that a committee were starting to come
down to talk with him over night, and so they did
come, probably some two hours afterwards, by that
antiquated mode of conveyance once thought to be
rapid, the railroad! As the Washington Spectator has it, "the locomotive with the mail train has
just come thundering along, bearing the news of the
nominations received here two hours ago by the
lightning express." What a vivid conception of
the change does this single sentence present! The
resistless locomotive, clad like a war horse in pan-
oply of steel, cutting its way over hill and dale fast-
er than the wind and breathing fire and smoke in
giantlike respirations reverberating along the valleys, astonishing the natives, frightening the cattle,
and almost enough, one would think, to make the
dead rise on their elbows in their graves to see what
was passing, this mighty engine, but late the wonder of the world, the "observed of all observers,"
the theme of the poet and the philosopher, the proud-
est triumph of human skill, coming in, panting and
blowing with its vain exertions, infinitely worse
distanced than the sorriest nag it ever rushed proudly by and more insignificant than any yelping puppy that ever barked at its wheels.
There appears to have been some show of enthusiasm at the close of the proceedings of the convention on Wednesday afternoon. Were not the extraordinary events then occurring enough to have
a awakened enthusiasm in the dullest breast? Within ten minutes from the result of the final ballot for
President being made known, there came into the
room of the convention this message from the Capitol: "The Democracy of the Union to their democratic brethren at Baltimore: Three cheers for James
K. Polk!" Does any one wonder that such an occurrence produced an electrical effect upon the assembly?
There is no end to the conjectures that might be
made of the uses to which this invention, unquestionably the greatest of the present age, may be applied. Already it has been used to communicate
information to stop the passage of a check obtained
by fraudulent means and to ascertain the goodness
of another, even while the passer stood at the bank
counter. It must paralyze rogery. The police in
NEW-YORK:
THURSDAY, JUNE 29, 1826.
Morse's Lafayette.—The full length Portrait
of Gen. Lafayette, executed by this artist for
the Corporation of the City, is completed ; and
we understand is to form one of the decorations
of the Dining Room, in the City Hall, at the
coming jubilee. We have seen it, and will at-
tempt a description of it. The General is re-
presented in the plain dress in which he was
commonly seen among us ; a black coat, white
vest, and yellow pantaloons ; and to give pic-
turesqueness to the figure, the artist has added
a cloak of a negative colour, with a partial fa-
cing of crimson velvet, carelessly folded around
him. He is in the act of advancing, upon the
landing, or platform, of a high flight of steps,
which he is supposed to have just ascended.
The platform is a tessellated pavement of va-
riagated marble. The steps are not seen, but
are indicated by a massy balustrade upon his
left. On his right are three richly ornamented
ripii, or half columns, on two of which are the
busts of Washington and Franklin, while La-
fayette rests his right hand on the top of the
tuant cippus. In the background is a distant
country of woods, and plains and mountains,
while here and there, are seen the windings of
a river, now dark from the overshadowings of
the deep foliage on its borders, and now spark-
ling with the reflected light of the sky.
In the extreme distance is the calm ocean ;
the whole landscape lies in quiet, repose bask-
ing in the warm light of the setting sun. The sky
is in harmony with the landscape ; it is a gor-
geous sunset ; the stormy clouds are retiring and
melting away before the splendor of the sun's
beams, and tinged with their light, heighten ra-
ther than diminish the glory of his setting.—
The poetic allusion in the choice of such a back-
ground to the eventful life, and present quiet
situation of Lafayette, will strike every one.—
Upon the pannel of the lower part of the cip-
pus on which he is leaning, is a small bas-relief
consisting of five figures. It is Lafayette in the
prison of Olmutz, with his wife and two daugh-
ters ; these last seem wholly absorbed in grief,
while Lafayette is attending to the pronuncia-
tion of an ideal being (the Genius of Liberty)
who unfolds a scroll with these words : In splen-
dore occides. The introduction of this scene,
the darkest in the Life of Lafayette, in direct
contrast with the brightest in his, or any other's
history, is calculated to render it still brighter,
showing at one view what he was, and what he
is, or, (if we may so speak in allusion to the
ideal being in the bas-relief,) showing the pro-
phesy and the fulfilment in close union.
On the opposite side of the picture, upon the
end of the balustrade, is a rich vase, glowing
in the warm light of the sun, and containing a
flower, the 'Helianthus,' or 'tussol'
"That in its course still looks upon the sun."
The introduction of this flower, which is said
to turn its face to the sun whether in bright or
stormy weather, is here intended to allude to
the consistency of Lafayette ; for if there is
any trait of character more strongly marked
than another in this good man, it is that of stea-
dy, undeviating consistency ; a firm adherence
to his principles, whether tempted, as he was
at one time, by unexampled prosperity to seize
a throne, or at another, by the deepest adversity
to sacrifice but a portion of principle to gain
freedom and life.
Thus much for the conception of this pic-
ture ; and we here take leave to remark, that
success and eminence in the elegant art of paint-
ing, cannot be attained without the association
of discriminating taste and sound judgment,
with an eye that catches the forms and features
of men and things, and a pencil that can trans-
fer them to the canvass. Mr. Morse, in this,
the most successful effort of his genius, has hap-
pily illustrated the heroic career of our coun-
try's friend, by historical emblems and a glow-
ing picture of one of the most beautiful scenes
in nature—the sun sinking in the west, after a
storm, gilding the scattering clouds with golden
splendor and gladdening creation with his
smiles. The entire arrangement of the picture
is truly a delicate and beautiful compliment to
Lafayette.
In our estimation, the artist has been no less
successful in his likeness of the General than in
the arrangement of the whole picture. He ap-
pears in his natural, graceful, and dignified at-
titude. Every beholder, who has seen the
original, will immediately recognize his face,
form and features, and involuntarily recall to
his mind scenes of the past year, when the
great friend of liberty was receiving the free-
will homage of a grateful people.
In conclusion, we congratulate the city on
having the possession of so accurate a likeness
of the illustrious man who yet lives, and lives
in the heart of every American.
We have already extended this article over as much
space as we can well afford now, although much more
might be said. We can only add that the expense of
laying the wires on posts, as adopted by the Professor,
does not exceed $150 per mile. They may also be laid
beneath the ground, in pipes, as circumstances may
render advisable. Mr Morse is constantly making im-
provements and new discoveries which simplify the
process of transmission, and his efforts in the cause of
science deserve the profoundest gratitude of his coun-
trymen and of mankind. His room, where he oper-
ates, is in the Capitol; and it is very probable that,
at no distant day, the printers in Boston and New Or-
leans will be setting the types for the President's
Message and important public speeches, while they
are being delivered! Congress appropriated $30,000
at the last session to test the merits of the Telegraph,
and there is no reason why, if successful, it should
not be extended to Philadelphia, New York and Bos-
ton.
Dr. Page, of the Patent Office, to whom we are in-
debted for the document from which we have compiled
most of the above information, has paid much atten-
tion to the subject of electro-magnetism, and has con-
structed several beautiful and ingenious machines to
illustrate the application of the power. The Dr's re-
port is full of valuable and interesting scientific infor-
mation and we shall endeavor to recur to it, more at
length, hereafter.
