We find it impossible to make any correct estimate of the

Morse's Magnetic Telegraph.
It is a matter of pride to us, as Americans,
that Professor MORSE, whose achievements in
the world of Science will send his name to
posterity, even on the wings of the lightning, is
an American citizen—a New Yorker—but,
more than all, distinguished himself as one of
the earliest and most enthusiastic advocates of
American Republican principles Although it
may now well nigh have been forgotten—so
apathetic and indifferent was then public senti-
ment on this momentous subject—yet there are
some amongst us who still remember the name
of SAMUEL F. B. MORSE as identified with the
earliest movement and organization of the Na-
tive American party—that party which kindled
the holy flame that afterwards burned so
brightly in St. Louis and New Orleans, (where
it is now eclipsed but for a season) and, reflect-
ed back upon the Metropolis, burst out in a
streaming and triumphant blaze of glory here.
All these things make us proud and glad that
we can claim this great, this most estimable
man, as a fellow countryman, fellow citizen,
and elder brother in the cause of American
Republicanism. But more of this hereafter.
We are happy to learn that there is at least a
prospect that the wonderful Telegraph will ex-
tend one of its lightning-clad, nerves within a
twelvemonth or so, from Baltimore to New
York—thus embracing in a simultaneous in-
telligence—an omniscience of information—
the Commercial and Political Capitals of the
country. A writer in the Evening Post says:
He first proposes to sell out to the Govern-

Morse's ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH.—We have received the report of Mr. Ferris, of this city, concerning the electric telegraph invented by Mr. Morse, who is known to the public, not merely as an artist, but as one of the most ingenious mechanics of the age. We were about to make some mention of the subject, when we met with the following article in the Morning Post, which we transfer to our columns:
MORSE'S ELECTRO MAGNETIC TELEGRAPH.—
The Committee of Commerce, we are glad to see, have reported in favor of making a trial of the new telegraph invented by Professor Morse. They propose that the sum of thirty thousand dollars be appropriated, for the purpose of testing, under the direction of the Post Master General, the capacity and usefulness of the new system.
As this telegraph is one of the most curious inventions of the day, our readers will not regret the space which will be taken up in forming a short account of it. The instrument is founded upon the following scientific principles:
First. That a current of electricity will pass to any distance along a conductor connecting the two poles of a voltaic battery or generator of electricity, and produce visible effects at any desired points on that conductor.
Second. That magnetism is produced in a piece of soft iron (around which the conductor, in its progress is made to pass) when the electric current is permitted to flow, and that the magnetism ceases when the current of electricity is prevented from flowing. This current of electricity is produced and destroyed by breaking and closing the galvanic circuit at the pleasure of the operator of the telegraph, who, in this manner directs and controls the operation of a simple and compact piece of mechanism, styled the register, which, at the will of the operator at the point of communication, is made to record, at the point of reception, legible characters on a roll of paper put in motion at the same time with the writing instrument.— These characters the operator has arranged into a conventional alphabet, which is capable of being learned and used with very little practice.
Professor Morse has submitted his telegraphic plan to the severe scrutiny of European critics; and the Academy of Sciences, of Paris, the highest scientific tribunal in the world, hailed it with enthusiasm and approbation, when its operation was exhibited, and its principles explained by their distinguished perpetual secretary, M. Arago.
It appears, from documents produced by Professor Morse, that the thanks of savers! learned bodies in France were voted to him for his invention, and the large medal of honor was awarded to him by the Chamber of Industry; further appears, that several other systems of telegraphs, and the electric plant (among which were Watt's, Stephenson's, and Hume's, and Masson's, of Caen) had been submitted to the vote of the session, the consideration of the French Government, who appointed a commission to examine and report upon the merits of all. When this question was placed before the administrative chief of the telegraphs of France (M. Fey), who, in his note to Professor Morse, thus writes:
"I take your pleasure in confirming to you in writing that which I have already had the honor to say to you in your voice that I have prominently represented to the French Government, and to your electric magnetic telegraph, as being the system which presents the best chance of a practical application. I have declared to him that, if some trials are to be made with electric telegraphs, I do not hesitate to recommend that they should be made with your apparatus."
It is not too much to say that Professor Morse, of Princeton, the most profound and accomplished of our natural philosophers, has given warm approbation to Mr. Morse's plan, and has been succeeded by the American Institute of this country.
In his letter to the Committee of Congress, Morse shows in what way his telegraph may be made a source of revenue to the Government. He says:
"As a source of revenue, then, to the Government, few, I believe, have seriously contemplated such great profits to be derived from such a patent of telegraphs as I propose; and yet there is a surplus already obtained by which they can be demonstrated.
The first fact is, that every minute of the 24 hours is available to sent intelligence.

CELEBRATION IN PARIS FOR THE FOURTH OF JULY.—
The Americans in Paris, to the number of eighty,
sent out to a special dinner on the Fourth of
July, at Louis XV's Bay Richard's, to celebrate
the Anniversary of Independence. Samuel F. B. Morse,
the President of the Academy of Design, was the
President of the day and James Fenimore Cooper,
President Vice-Commander. Among the important guests were
General Lafayette, Mr. Rives, Mr. Enfield and Major
Isler; General Bernard, Adm to the King; Messrs.
C. W. Lafayette and Oscar Lafayette, son and
grandson of the late Lafayette, our Consul.
Citizens from almost every city were present.
The Editions of the Daily Advertiser have received
the following order of the proceedings from a friend
in Paris:
Gen. Lafayette was on the right, and Mr. Rives
on the left, of the President. Professor Horrey, of
Amherst College, invoked the blessing. The following
are the three regular texts that were drunk on the occasion:
1. The Festival we celebrate.—A beautiful memorial
of the origin and principles of the Government.
2. Before giving the address to the President, rose
and made the following observations:
"I cannot propose the next toast, Gentlemen, so
intimately connected with the last, without advert-
ing to the great and noble sentiments and measures we thus
day enjoy, above the thousands and millions of thousands of
thousands of our countrymen who are at this moment celebrating this great National Festival:
the honor and pleasure of being at our board our
venerable guest, my right hand, Mr. Horsey, whose
two words claim as their own. Yes, gentlemen, he belongs to America as well as to Europe. He is our
faithful citizen and his untiring voice in our
country would cry out against us, did he not manifest our nation's interest in his person and character.
With the masses of European politics we have
nothing to do; to the great general advances of good or bad government we cannot make satisfaction with
the success of one or that faction we can have no sympathy; but with the great principles of Republican Liberty, Civil and Religious Liberty, those
principles for which our fathers fought, the blessings of
our Fathers, and which he has steadily maintained for a long life, "through good reports and through evil reports," "through joy and sorrow," "We should not be
Amricans if we did not sympathize with them, we can
compromise one iota of these principles, and preserve our self-respect as loyal American citizens.
They are the principles of order and good government, of obedience to law; the principles under
Providence have made our country unparalleled in prosperity, principles which rest not in visionary theory, but are made palpable by the sure test of experiment and time.
But, gentlemen, we honor our guest as the staunch
unwavering defender of these principles, of our principles, of American principles. Has he ever deserted
them? Has he ever been known to abandon them,
there are some men, some toe who would
vish to direct public opinion, who are like the buoyy
on the river, who swing up and down in the current
setting this way and that way. If at an emergency,
there they are, we cannot tell you, we must consult the situation. We must know the quarter of
the day, the hour, the tide, the wind, the
tide, and they are, we may guess where they will find them. But, gentlemen, our guest is not of this
flaky character. He is a Tower amid the waters; his foundation is in the deep; his anchor is in
the flood and flow of the stream; the storm may gather
the waters may rise, and even dash above his head
but the flood subsides at last, and still he stands upon
ground. We have already arrived at the point where
the fullest confidence we point to where he stood six
and twenty years ago. He stands there now. The
water is still rising, but the waves have dashed
around him, the snow of the storm is lighted upon
him, but still he is there. I ask you there are lighted
up in his dark eyes, in his brightened eyes, unsullied
in its darkest—Lafayette!
This speech was interrupted with applause at almost every sentence, and the sentiments greeted by
noble cheers. The band played the Parisienne, after
which the General rose to reply.
After having expressed his acknowledgements for
the toast, and the manner in which it had been
received, he thus continued in a feeling manner:
"While on this happy occasion, I wish to commemorate of our great Fourth of July, I am delighted to
breathen among you, an American atmosphere; it
reminds me even to this mind the youthful recollection of a first, patriotic love, and the great occasion of
friendships formed in times of trial and danger.
It also retraces the subsequent forty years of
calamities, sacrifices, confusions, and solitude, be-
stowed by the American people upon a nation
adopted son, and more solely, an unparalleled, daily
holy welcome of more than thirteen months through two-four States of the Union, which in a continued series have come to me, and which I have
cherish a grateful heart. And, while I most feelingly
enjoy the marks of your approbation, expressed in
most flattering terms, to our honorable President,
am happy to acknowledge the proceeds of the
money I have been that day of my solemn reception in
the bosom of Congress, when their President, in the
sentence of the People of United States, did official-
ly declare that every sentiment, every act of every
long eventful life, has proved worthy of a disciple of
the American School."
Well may the people of the United States sympathize in the progressive liberties of Europe; well
may we, as American citizens, take a pride in the
endeavors in the several nations on this side of
the Atlantic to imitate, as far as their own circumstances can permit, the institutions which have
inspired to the United States a greater desire of practical liberty, legal order, public and individual security, and the improvement of industry, than has ever
been known in the history of mankind. I add to
those testimonies of sympathy, after I had formerly
opportunity to acknowledge the high and affectionate consideration for the great
work of July, 1860, so very recently displayed
throughout the United States; let us on this day
be justice to the generous interest they have taken in
the cause of liberty Poland, and particularly
express my gratitude for assistance I have received from the committee at Paris, in the appropria-
tions of American donations, and pay a tribute of
esteem to the late Daniel H. Houston, in execution
of the mission entrusted to him, when carrying
material and moral comfort into the heart of the
Centrals of the United States, and patriots of
Poland; he has caused high pride and warm blessings to be poured upon the American name. And
gentlemen, I shall give you a toast to Republicanism, to the bright daughters of American Independence."
Then followed the other regular toasts:
1. The People, the Institutions, and the President
of the United States. "Order is Heaven's first law."
2. The King of the French and the French nation.
3. The Union: we calculated its value till figures
fail us.
4. The memory of Washington. (Drank standing.)
5. The Army and Navy. Citizens doubly pledged
to Liberty and the Country.
6. To the memory of the dead of the Allied Army
of 1775, and to the health and happiness of the survivors.
7. The city of Paris; admiration for its courage,
respect for its arts, and thanks for its hospitality.
8. Person, Opinion, and Property. May our
Institutions ever respect the two first, and protect the last.
9. The three estates of the Republic; the Pul-
pit, the Schoolhouse, and the Press.
10. To the American art that of Nature, which
Art may supplant, may never survive.
11. The wedded interest of every really American
heart, Home, for better for worse.
After the regalia, the toast, the health of the other
guests, and successful drafts, and handsome replies
made by Mr. Rives, Gen. Bernard, Mr. G. W.
Lafayette, and Mr. Barnet.
The toast to the memory of the day was given:
"The worthy representative of the articles of the
country," Mr. Morse returned his thanks. The
President was then given; "James Fenimore
Coppock's stand," upon remembering the defender of
the distinctive principle of his country, which was
received with the greatest applause. To which Mr.
C. returned his thanks. The Committee of strangers
was also given, who deserved the greatest
credit for their services, and replied to Mr. Mc
Cranckan.
Many piquant Volunteers were given. The company separated at an early hour.

I have generally answered that I obtained what I asked which
ought to be satisfactory to me. The gentleman supposing I had sold it

meet in Oxford County, Maine, in which County is

1/5 is the Children, for he died without a will. Bonds

thy is administrator there & might as well be

& he is good & gives the Judge sentence, & acts for
all the rest of us - & therefore in this had better
act for the children - It is a small affair - but $50 or 600
in all for the time. I wish you, as you are first
entitled to be Guardian, to write to him that
you wish him to be guardian in Maine &
write a letter he can show the Judge.
I am administrator in U. C. & have received
the shares of the Infants cash there; about $8,800.
The total share will be about $18,5000 at
$4500 for each child. Is. Bet? some one must
be guardian there, for we sell the real estate, &
there must be a guardian to sign for them, but
of this here after. At present father will send your
letter to Timothy Walker in Russford, Oxford Co: Maine.

conduct & ever since Father killed him at Rumford he was perfectly satisfied. I was very much
pleased with all his acts at Concord -- He & Augustus took the furniture at Appomattox.

that the old place should go out of the family into the hands of strangers, but one wants it
at the price it will sell for. Mr. Pickering is quite out of health, Susan is large enough. They desire
Susan More to pass the winter there, but fear you will not permit it. All are well here.

Saturday Oct 3d 1834.
My dearest Father,
The book and your notes
arrived safely the morning of your departure,
and I wish you could have seen how pleased
I was. When I first looked at the book, I thought
it was from you, but on looking at the blank
leaf, I saw it was from the author, and I
assure you, father, I felt quite proud of it, because
I had it presented to me by the author,
which the girls told me was a great
honor. I cannot bear the thought of writing
him a note, dear father, for I have read
in his book what he says, about a young
ladies hand writing, and I am convinced
that he is very particular, therefore I shall
not like to have him scrutinize any of
my notes. I know it is proper that I should
address a line of thanks to him, and shall,
as soon as I have a good opportunity, as
I have not heard of one yet.
I wish, father, you would write, and tell me
how to commence the note, and end it. So, father
I have commenced my drawing, and taken
two lessons. The last time I began to draw a
pump, with a bucket. Miss Collis says, that I
have a great taste for drawing, and that she
never had a scholar learn the touch of lines so
readily as I have. I do not say this to boast,
dear father, but to let you know that I am
trying hard to improve. Another new scholar
has come to day. Mr Skinner's school began
Wednesday. Charles and Finley I suppose are
very much engaged in their studies.
The little girl that you came up from New York
with is here. Her name is Harriet Gordon, and she
is very accomplished for her age, although
quite rude. Our class in Logic, and in History,
are making great progress. In History we ask
each other questions, and that makes the
recitation very interesting. My health is
very good now. I have, the new Kalff, you
have me, and it is very pretty. I hope
to be surprised this month, father, in
seeing you, shall I not?
It is almost dinner time, so I must conclude
Please write soon, dear father. I am, as ever,
yours affectionate
daughter, Susan.

Grove Hall. Oct. 13th 1834.
My dear Father,
Your kind letters and present, around
safety. You do not know how surprised I was
when I opened the bundle, to find a nice
fur cape. I do not know how I shall ever repay
you for your kindness, dear father I mean to
try and please you in every thing, if it is in
my power, and I know I can, by being attentive
to my studies, and obedient to my teachers.
The fur cape is very comfortable this weather,
and will keep me warm this winter.
When do you intend going to Concord, father?
I wish I could go with you, and I know
it would do me good to take a journey I
remained stationary so long, besides I should
feel new energy to commence my studies for
the winter. I leave it to you dear father to
think about. If you should give your consent
I should be very glad, but if you do not I
know you would do it for my good.
I have four new boarders this term, Miss Pratt,
from Brooklyn, Miss Van Richten, from Albany, Miss
Shepherd, from Georgia, (Cruin to miss Mary Hillhouse)
and Harriet Goodwin. Nancy Shepherd that
lived with us, lived with her mother at Charlestown. Harriet said that she used to love Nancy
dearly, and Nancy would often tell her, how
she had the ear of a little Susan Moses.
Harriet and myself are both natives of Charlestown.
She resided in Charlestown until a year ago,
when her parents moved to New York.
I am coming along in my music very well. I have
commented the Caliph of Bagdat, and learned
three pages. We have got to Part Third in Logie.
I like the study very much. As for drawing I am
very fond of it next Tuesday I commence a large house.
Mrs Brick has not purchased my winter
dresses yet. She does not seem to be any pretty
calicoes in New Haven. Miss Catharine Brick
has not returned, she is sick in New York.
Charles came to see me Saturday, he is very
well, and says he studies hard and has
taken three drawing lessons. I love to have
him come and see me, he enjoys himself
so much. All the little girls like him, he is so
obliging. Finley says he does not like the girls
here, he had rather play at Mr Skinner's than
come and see Sister. My health is very good
except that I am troubled with the headache
especially if I do not exercise well.
I want to see you very much, dear father and wish
you would surprise me again.
Mrs Peters is going to walk with us to West Rock this
week, and after we have been all over the Rock, ride
home.
Sarah Gocelyn, Mr Greeley's eldest daughter who
is a day scholar here is dangerously ill. She
was prayed for in church last Sunday.
I must now go to my knitting, as it is the hour
for that branch. With love to Uncle, and Aunt,
I remain, as ever
Your affectionate daughter
Susan.
Mr Samuel H. P. Morse
New York

From Peter Taylor
Boston Feb. 20th 1835
Dear Sir.
The distress and oppression by
you in Mr Allston's situation gives you the
best claim to learn what we have accomplished.
Mr Dutton & Mr Doster entailed with me into the
labour, unprofitable as it was, of attempting his
release. We first learnt his debts, & then obtained
from him, the necessary text, permission to detain
prisoners to pay them. We have been successful,
fully, perfectly successful, and now his debts
are in payment to entire payment, we have
all that they require, & something more to
make him free from previous embarrass-
ment for a quarter more to come. One gentleman
advanced $1000, then other gentlemen
together advanced $1750, fine others together
$250 making a total of $3250. One note
of $2000 secured by Mortgage remains to be

An Exhibition of Paintings & other works of art
will be opened in this City early in June, to be
Conducted on a plan, which shall be more directly
Calculating to benefit the Exhibitors, than any
heretofore established here
The following inducements are offered for the Consideration
of Artists to exert their talent in favor
of this Exhibition. 1st It will be a favorable opportunity
to display their works as specimens, or
for Sale 2d There will be a Sale by Auction, at
the Galleries at some time during the Exhibition
on such Occasion the Exhibitors will have the
privilege of selling any of their Original works
contained in the Collection. 3d Each Artist whose
works make part of this Collection shall be
entitled of half the gross receipt, of certain
days or weeks of the Exhibition, the extent
of the Benefit to be regulated by the probable
value & importance of the works contributed. This,
Together with the time, selected for each contribution
Benefit shall be agreed upon (when practicable)
between the parties, at the time the pictures are
loaned, or at some time previous to the Opening of
the Galleries, in order that the time assigned to each
may be made public with the ensuing advertisement.
All Paintings to be included in the first Exhibition must be ready in Boston by the 20th May
and must be in gilt frames, unless they are of very large size, in which case frames
of some other material will be admitted. — It is intended to make this Exhibition
annual and to commence (after this season) on the first of May & continue 4 months, but
any pictures may be removed by the owners after 2 months from the opening of the Gallery.
The Establishment will be under the direction of the undersigned, he therefore invites
those Artists to whom this Circular is addressed to forward at the expense of the Exhibition
any works which they may think proper, and he engages to take special care that the
Paintings shall be returned without injury.
Those who propose sending pictures, are requested to give notice to the undersigned as soon as
convenient that he may make arrangements accordingly.

My dear Sir,
Your acceptable letter in answer to mine of the 13th April was
duey rec'd and should have been replied to by me before this time but for
the unusual pressure of duties connected with the Academy, which is
always greatest at the season for our Annual Exhibition.
With regard to the matter on which I felt that I ought to
address you, as the article in the Courier was editorial, as your
name alone is published at the head of the paper as editor, and
as I had presented a copy of my work to you as a friend and
not as editor, you can easily believe that my surprise was
great at the manner in which not only the matter of the book
was noticed, but at the use which was made of presenting to you
a copy with my respects. I was obliged to consider you as
the writer and yet the very first observation I made to my brother
when I had read it was "Mr. Willington never wrote that article,
I know him too well to believe that he would treat any one who
had made a compliment to him with so uncourteous a manner
yet it appeared on the face of it as if I could therefore be
no less than attribute it to him until I had written you an
explanation. Your letter my dear Sir, is entirely satisfactory
so far as regards yourself, and I am not disposed to cavil
at the editorial amende that I call it? I might with
justice, perhaps, ask Mr. Yeadon why he would have
said that a copy had been presented to him with the author's
respects, when the author had not the pleasure of his acquaintance

My dear Sir,
In looking over some old sketchbooks I
yesterday, accidentally found the enclosed slight outline
of M. P. V. R., which I hope Roger, and think, made at
Cooperstown, (I think in 1839 just before I left the country for
my late visit to Europe.) Your brother Stephen and himself
well remember the time. Thinking it might be pathetical to
you to have it, imperfect as it is, and perhaps possessing no
resemblance (of which you are of course the better judge,) I
have cut the leaf out of my book, and ask your acceptance
of it.—
Since I heard but a week or two since of your
severe affliction, and affliction, my dear Sir, in which I
know how to sympathize with you from the bottom of my
heart, I was upon the point of sitting down to write you
having experienced in my own case the influence of the kind
sympathy of friends in mitigating the danger of a trouble the latter
part of which must be felt in order to be understood. Yet you will
feel as I felt that the sympathy of those most dear
to us can only apply a healing touch to all the wounds which our
much beloved sends through all the affections of the heart. The heart
knows its own bitterness and alone who makes the heart can
real the wounds, which he in righteousness and in mercy too, has fit to inflict.
on his children, not for his pleasure but their profit. I hope
very decidedly, that you now in the time of your trouble have
the support of the religion of the gospel, those true substan-
tial supports arising from a firm and heartfelt conviction that
God is good when he takes away sin, as when he gives.
This is an indication of the fact that God has sent affliction and
trials to test and purify us, which is a matter of concern to the soul which
feels every disease however secret, and to none of which
is the heart pouring out God, may be satisfied by the least
admissions of affliction, unshaken and at peace.
That this peace may be yours, the nearest trial or the nearest danger of my dear
friend
Yr sincere friend

New York May 27th, 1836-
My dear Sir,
I send you for your perusal the second edition of Maria Monk's
disclosures. I think the additional matter is very important and con-
clusive of the truth of her story. The fact that she has accompanied
her volume with a plan of all the rooms in the Convent is very strong
in favor of her sincerity and integrity. Were she an impostor I cannot
believe she would have dared to put forth a document of this kind, which,
if materially incorrect, cannot fail in the course of a few days from
its publication of exposing the whole cheat. You will see in the papers
an announcement of her abduction. From a variety of secret and very
suspicious manoeuvres, there was every reason to believe that a plot was
ripened for the purpose of getting possession of her. She had had inter-
views with various persons from Canada, against whom she was warned by
her friends, and on Wednesday evening she was missing. Her guardian,
Mr. Slocum, was in much trouble about it, applied to the police and could
get no assistance, the only method left was to advise the public of the
state of the case and get the public eye directed to the matter. The next
day she returned, and her absence was satisfactorily explained. Would
you not write a short notice of the second edition (even two or three
lines would answer,) for one of the Cooperstown papers, sufficient to draw
attention to the subject of her book?-
I send you a little work for Master Paul which if you approve please
present him in my name, I find it has interested my own boys very much, and
I think it will him also.-
I also ask your acceptance of a work of one of Dr. Beecher's
daughters. It strikes me as possessing great originality and enlarge-
ment of thought, and she combats infidelity in a masterly manner. But
there is a vindication of New England character in it at page 14 and on-
ward which is so just that your candid mind I am sure will give it its just
98343
2
weight in removing some of your anti puritanic feelings.—
I want to come up and see you, but I don't know that I can force
myself away from New York. Our exhibition is yet doing bravely. We
have had a few wet days, and yet the average daily receipts is not greatly
lessened; we made a calculation that if we received 17.50 pr day for the
remaining days of Exhibition, (36 in number,) our receipts would be 3000
in all, but yesterday with unfavorable weather our receipts were 79
dollars.— Nothing yet from Horace.—
I am reading your Switzerland, I like it much, but this is doubtless
to be set down by the American et omne id genus as prejudice.— Please
present my best respects to Mrs. Cooper and the young ladies. In haste
but with real respect & esteem
Yr friend & servt.
Saml. F. B. Morse.
New York June 13th 1836-
Dr Sir,
Well, our friend Horace has come, and he looks in fine health
and spirits. He goes to Washington today and must see his mother in
Boston before he can come to Cooperstown. I have told him that when-
ever he is ready I will go to the Hall with him.-
I send you by Mr. Pratt a small parcel of books. I am inclined
to think you will be pleased with Mrs Beecher's book, there is such a
fairness and truly liberal spirit (and unaffected) throughout, at the
same time there is such a masculine character of reasoning, freed from
masculine asperity of manner, as I think will commend itself to you.
I confess myself so far sectarian as she is, and no farther, her last
chapter contains my own sentiments in regard to other denominations per-
fectly.- In great haste but with real esteem
Your friend and serv.
Saml. F. B. Morse.
Please present my kind regards to Mrs. Cooper and the young ladies.)
The strange coincidence of some, and the rapid succession of other quite striking circumstances, induces me to mention them to you by writing, as I was not so happy to find you at your residence:
1.) Ludwig enumerates, since a few weeks, among the names of subscribers to his paper that of a certain Merrick, Esq., in Columbian, Col. C. Ohio (if I am not mistaken) and of Anderson, Esq., editor in Ohio, both names of individuals that probably putted my ruin on board of the Hudson. Merrick brought my trunk to the Philadelphia Restaurant-Hotel, N.Y. the day after I had one on shore, for I was scarcely able to save my papers, and left trunk behind. I considered my help to Capt. Edis. Insurance.
2.) The "Allegemeine Zeitung" of to-morrow will contain an article on the Orange Party in Ireland, wherein the editor compares the English Protestants pretty hardy.
3.) A few days since I was requested by my landlord (bookbinder, Fred Kamp), a man who formerly belonged to the Church of the Jesuitical preacher (Rizzotto from Vienna, now in Philadelphia) to write his address on a small piece of paper, which I did, as he pretended to have no ink.
4.) Yesterday afternoon Mr. Ludwig retreated with his foreman (Westall) into a corner of the composing room, where he opened something like a respectable library of my maps of London, which I had left at home in my room, on the table.
5.) In the evening, when I went home, I found my map in its place, but missed several pages of extracts I lately made from the German "Lexicon" (Encyclopedia) for some literary purpose, and which I had likewise left on the table.
6.) Yesterday afternoon, the pressman Richards, who has quitted Ludwig's office, came there again with the singular intention to offer me a volume, entitled "the mutiny", which he recommended me to read. I positively declined it, telling him, I was too much engaged to squander my time away with such things.
7.) On Monday or on Tuesday evening I had met that young German, Stoller, out of whose hands I received, at 7 o'clock, $20, or account of the $100. D. Kaemmer in Pittsburgh. He surprised me with the news that he had quitted the company of Mrs. Mueller and Oppenheim. I returned, at the door of his house, a book (a vol. of the Engl.) which he had lent to me, cautiously avoiding seeing him in his room.
8.) To-day, Ludwig ordered me to hardly half a dollar he gave to me to his apprentice Theodore and tell him, it was for those newspapers (ports) which, to-morrow will have to be sent to Philadelphia. I objected, that I did not like
To Prof. S.F.B. Morse, N.Y.
98346
to speak to him, being on bad terms with him. He consented then, I should give it
to Mr. Angell, his proof reader and ask him to give it to the boy. Angell, as soon as he
had the 50 cents piece between his fingers, put on hat and coat and went off. —
Ludwig, as he several times had done before, ordered me illiterate to copy some
account in his book, on a piece of paper, I did so.
9.) This evening I was told Ludwig and his former partner, Packmann, book binder,
a very double-faced man, by whom I was introduced to my present lodgment, had
gone to Albany. The deaf man, with whom I quarrelled before, went yesterday
away to Connecticut.
10.) I heard, this afternoon, several of the composers, in a low voice, talk
about Ludwig's offering money for false reports against me. "But," said one
voice, "it is a considerable risk," in I would not open my mouth, said old
Mr. Westall, but for a --, I did not understand the rest. — One of them,
the man who was present when the deaf man and Ludwig depreciated and
assured me that they always liked and esteemed me, — showed to me an eagle
and a sample in gold, and asked me, if I ever had seen such money. I replied,
"Yes," but I never had any of them in my possession. — Afterwards I met
these two men with a third one, Ogg, in the street; they invited me friends,
to accept a glass of beer of them. I did not like to offend them, and therefore
did not decline; but went immediately thereafter up to the eating-house,
of --, where I took tea, whence directly to the university. — Some of the
composers had (in the office) spoken the words: "He won't carry it on further
than till the 4th of July. — If they can get him once to the State prison,
he'll never get off."
11.) A few weeks past, an unavoidable snare was laid to me. My land-
lord, Heikhamm, told me, that a young woman, of a very good family (!!),
and arrived in his neighbourhood (in Germany) had arrived here, and was wait-
ing for her uncle, a farmer in Lyons, N.Y. She was entirely unacquainted
with the English language, and, for this reason, would stay in his, not in a
boarding house. They more than once invited me to take a walk with them,
but I always refused. At last, however, I said that my refusals provoked
them very much, so that I was in real danger of losing my little room; this
would have been an extremely disagreeable occupation even a fatal thing
to me; — consequently, I chose, among two evils, the smallest, and accom-
panied them once to the battery, and once to Hoboken.
One of these little matters might, in their connection with others,
gradually become important; thus, I dare to take the liberty of making
you acquainted with them.
I see daily more that nothing is so dangerous as to be, among
r- s, an honest man. Yet, I solemnly assure you, Sir, that, with
the only exception of my affair against my officer in Heidelberg,
I never did, nor shall do, any thing of which I could have the remotest
reason to be ashamed.
With true admiration of your noble character,
I have the honour to be forever,
Sir,
Your most grateful and
obedient servant
L. C. Henninger-Kausing.
New-York, June 20th, 1836.
Sam. F. B. Morse, Esqre,
Director of the National
Academy

Dear Sir,
Your favor of Jul. 8, confirming a report, which I
had heard before, of Mr. Henniger's death, was received a few days
ago. The statement, contained in the Journal of Commerce, which you
had so kindly as sending to me, would certainly be curious and
interesting, if the matter communicated were real facts instead
of being, as I am inclined to think, a great measure of offspring
of poor Henniger's limited imagination. That you may not con-
sider this a mere assertion, I will point out some of the improbable lies,
anachronisms, exaggerations and erroneous statements.

Dear Sir,
I thank you for your kind letter of the 8th inst
which I received only three days ago, on my return from a journey
to the West, to this place which I have made my summer residence.
It was about ten days ago, at Pittsburgh, that I received the
sad information of the death of young Claving in whom you
have taken so generous an interest. My acquaintance with
him began last summer when he called upon me at
Watertown, near Boston. He told me his story, and handed
to me part of a manuscript work on the Jesuits which I
read with great interest and returned to him with some criticisms
which he thought just. I then endeavored to find a publisher
for him, but did not succeed. He left Boston in order to
return to Pittsburgh, as he told me, and since that time I
did not learn anything with regard to him, until my recent
visit to that town.
I know of no particulars of his history except those which
he undoubtedly made known to you, and which are summarily
mentioned in the newspaper which you sent me. His residence
at and near Pittsburgh I do not see mentioned in this account.
There are at Pittsburgh some persons who know Clavering
very well, and who probably are able to give you some
interesting information concerning him. I mention
particularly a German apothecary, I believe his name
is Braun though I do not feel quite sure. The person
I mean may however be easily ascertained by applying
to Mr Leo Wolf, a young merchant at Pittsburgh
who during my short residence in that town introduced
me to him for the purpose of giving me the information
I desired concerning Clavering. You have probably
acquaintances in Pittsburgh who could easily collect
what information may be obtained there.
The whole manner and appearance of this unfortunate
young man impressed me with a perfect faith in his
sincerity; and however extraordinary some of the
incidents in his life, I believe he told what he
conscionately believed true. Real persecutions, however,
had evidently so much affected his imagination that
he often saw secret plots and machinations in mere
accidents; and I thought it my duty to tell him so,
and to warn him against giving way to vague suspicions
which could not fail often to create the evil which he
apprehended, and must prove as injurious to the state
of his mind as to his prospects in the world.
I am very glad to learn from you that he left his
papers as a legacy in your hands. Whatever mistakes
of judgment there may be in them mixed up with important
truths, I think they ought to be made known as forming
a part of the moral portrait of a man who under different
circumstances would have taken a very different stand
in society, and whose example would probably be looked upon
as an encouragement rather than a warning to others.
Yours very respectfully & truly
C. Follen.

pain in one of my eyes, from over-use of
them; so that I do not intend to write

would come well in aid of what I had

spoke of you as you would wish, and
as I honestly think you deserve. He
was not here when I got the second
letter. But I have lately written to
him about you -- and the letter, though
not long, will, I think, carry some
weight with it. Among other things
I observed, "that much as I wish to speak
Morse as a friend whom I highly value,
I would not say a word in his favour,
had I any doubt of his competency;
but I can conscientiously say that I do
believe him competent to the task.” This is
plain language, and I think more to the
purpose than a whole sheet of flourishes;
and Jarvis, who has known me for forty
years, knows that I would not have risked
my own life to serve it my own brother, if he did not
deserve it. Keep a good heart, my friend,
at all events. God bless you.
Yours affectionately,
Wm. Allston.
I shall no doubt see Mr. J. again when
he returns to Boston.

in common with others the full power of your natural affection and esteem for me. I am sorry to notice the public opinion that I am a person who is always flatterer and

My dear Sir,
I have received your letter in reply
to my last, and thank you for the efforts which
you have so kindly made, at my suggestion, in
behalf of poor Stuart Wilson: on which subject
I shall say more at another time, my object now being
to say a few words concerning myself.
I find to my utter surprise a paragraph
giving the words of the Newspapers stating that I
had accepted the Commission, offered by the Committee
of Congress, for one of the pictures which they have
ordered for the Capitol; and moreover, that I had
accepted it under certain conditions namely, of
executing it at my own time &c. This statement
it seems appeared more than a month ago in the
New York Mirror; from which it has been copied
into the papers here. And it has worried me more
than you can imagine; and the more so that I
could not notice it at the time without delay
anticipating my answer to the Committee which
I did not send until the third of this Month (Feb.
1837). I had delayed my answer until this
time, as I observed in my letter to Mr Jarvis, in
order that I might give the subject the fullest
consideration. Now that the answer is at last
sent, it is proper that I correct the mistake. I
will therefore thank you to have the following
paragraphs, which are enclosed in brackets, inserted
in the New-York Mirror: First however, sparing
the Editor, that I have no ill feeling whatever
towards the writer of the paragraphs alluded to;
indeed I could not reasonably entertain any

much feeling (however the mistake might have troubled me ) since it was certainly couched
in very complimentary terms, harshly never doubted that it was written and was evidently written
with a very friendly motive or rather, I should say, in a very friendly spirit. — You need make
no other preface to the following than this: Extract
of a letter from Washington Allison to a Friend in

[There having appeared, nearly two months ago,
an article in the New-York Mirror, stating that I
had accepted a Commission for one of the National
Pictures, voted by Congress, I must request the
inserted in that journal.
When the article alluded to appeared in the
Mirror, I had not made up my mind on the subject
farther than that I would not, under any circumstances,
accept more than a commission for one picture,
should I conclude in the affirmative; and that I had
formed this impression (as is well known to my friends
here) so long ago as when Mr Vanplanck was in
Congress: that I did not send my answer to the
subject down to the Committee until the third of this
month [February]; and that, in that answer I have
altogether declined the proposed Commission:
that I did not rectify the article at the time it
first appeared, because I could not have done so
without anticipating my answer to the Committee
— which would have been, to say the least, not respect-
ful; finally, that I had delayed the answer
until the time above-mentioned in order to give the
subject the fullest consideration. My reasons for the
result being wholly of a private nature, I shall
not speak of them here. — I trust it is hardly necessary for me to add, that I duly appreciate the honour
which I have thus been obliged to decline. I shall ever gratefully remember it; nor shall I soon forget the peculiar favour with which the Committee have
honoured me on this occasion.]
I cannot imagine how the story should have taken the shape in which it appeared in the Mirror. Could it have grown out of what I requested you to say concerning my resolution (so long ago formed) on no account to accept more than one of the offered pictures? If so, it seems to me strange logic, that because I had resolved not to accept two, that people should conclude I must therefore have accepted one! When I made this request of yours, it was with reference to the artist, that they might know the kind of feeling which I had towards them: not that I wished to be commended for a "good" feeling, but to claim for myself what I considered a proper one. This was had been long made known by myself. — Do not suppose that I think the refusal came from you. I know it could not be what passed between us concerning the future was altogether contingent and hypothetical, and expressed merely my wishes, not my intentions, for the latter I did not know myself, as they would depend on future circumstances; and, besides, they took no definite shape, as I was merely building castles with you in private conversation. But now that I have sent my answer to the Committee, I have done with castle-building on public ground. In this matter my resolution is fixed; it is the only way in which I can hope to secure my peace. So there's an end on't.
The above was written (as you will have seen by a note on the first page) about more than a fortnight ago. I have now learned the disappointment of the "Pictures." I had hoped to have found your name amongst the commissioned Artists, but I was grieved to find that all my efforts in your behalf have proved fruitless. I know what your disappointment must have been at this result, and most sincerely do I sympathise with you. That my efforts were both sincere and conscientious I hope will be some consolation to you. But let not this disappointment cast you down, my friend. You have it still in your power to let the world know what you can do. I pray you to think from your mind, and determine to haunt all the better for it. God bless you. Your affectionate friend.
Washington Allston.

My dear Morse
I am glad to have an excuse for
writing to you and should not have allowed
the winter to pass without doing so if I could
have found a good one -- The Artists' Fund
Lieuteney of Philadelphia offers me one now
for it has elected me an honorary member
which honour I consider equivocal -- thin-
king the Society to be of a Puritanish genere
liberate in acknowledging the honor extended
now you have doubtless been equally
flattered -- tell me have you accepted the
favour? If you have let me know your
reasons for so doing they will most probably
be good for me as well as for you --
I do think the Artists of Philadelphia
have regarded themselves by forming them-
selves into a Charity Club -- their much
worth to their true interest it would have
been to appropriate their means to the alms
ment of the Art they profess instead of antici-
pating poverty & destitution by making provision
for poverty & destitution
Although I have given my excuse for writing I
have not let you have the benefit of my letter
I have learned with mortification & disappointment
that your name was not among the chosen --
I have feared that you would carry into effect
your resolution of abandoning the Art -- resigning
the presidency of our Academy -- I sincerely
hope you will have reason to cast aside that
resolution -- To your own Academy amidst existence & present prosperity -- if in after time
it should become a great Institution your name
will always be coupled with its greatness -- but
if you have no strong much fear that the Fabric
will crumble to pieces -- your are the Keystone
of the Arch -- If you remain with us (though
may furnish the Academy with black not
lockheed) I hope my fears may be main &
The circumstances will conspire to induce you

I await the opening of the river with impatience
Smith is here a Confess with you & to understand

I have it in my power to do as Council Man.
By the long letter you have read Mr. Jameson's

book - but having read it you will enjoy the
Prussian history - that we could have
some great work in which we could lay out
our whole mind.

monoy" No 1. Have read, it puts up - how

Write soon & let me know your mind &
bank the Artist Fund (Twist it had been fun)

believe me
Yours very truly
Thomas Cole

NEWLY INVENTED TELEGRAPH.—We take the following from a Washington letter in the Baltimore Patriot.
Mr. Gomon and his associate, Mr. Servell, have, after many years application to the subject, invented an important system of Telegraphs, which puts into the hands every one of the two kinds that has yet been attempted. By this admirable plan, they can communicate every kind of information, word by word, and punctuate the same, without using more signals than words, and with as much certainty as if they were written. The system of Mr. Gomon has received the most flattering encouragement from those literary and scientific gentlemen to whom they have explained the system, and it is not a doubt in their minds that it will accomplish the purpose of the invention, and realize all that has been anticipated from it. Mr. Gomon assures me that he will be able to communicate a despatch of one hundred words from New York to New Orleans in half an hour;—and those who are thoroughly acquainted with the system confirm his promises. How elementary does every other system appear in comparison of that which is described in the preceding paragraph. This system is so powerful in contemplating the consequences of such an achievement of human ingenuity. Distance is annihilated. Thousands of miles no longer divide us. We know on the instant what it is in the affairs of the world, and determination of our fellow citizens of other countries. Furthermore, it is that we live in an age for whose intellectual progress nothing is too ripe.
We know nothing of the telegraph of Messrs. Gomon and Servell except what is related in the above paragraph; but we do know that a gentleman of our acquaintance, several years since, suggested that intelligence might be communicated almost instantaneously, hundreds, if not thousands of miles, by means of very fine wires, properly coated to protect them from moisture, and extending between places thus widely separated. It is well known that the electric fluid occupies no perceptible time in passing many miles on a wire; and if it is possible, by connecting one end of the wire with an electrical or galvanic battery to produce any sensible effect whatever at the other, it is obvious that if there are twenty four wires, each representing a letter of the Alphabet they may be connected with the battery successively in any order; and if so connected in the order of the letters of any word or sentences, the word or sentences could be read at any station by a person standing at the other end of the wire. All the letters of a paragraph in a newspaper could thus be touched successively by a man in Philadelphia and the contents, verbatim et literatum, be conveyed to New York as fast as a composer could set up the type! It is not impossible that the time may be near when speeches in Congress taken down by reporters, and conveyed by these "electric telegraphs" to New York or New Orleans, may be in type, printed, circulated, and read, within a few hours after the voice of the speaker has ceased at Washington. The wire necessary for a distance of a hundred miles need not weigh many pounds, and if enclosed in an iron or rubber tube, and supported at high points along the route at intervals of 4 or 500 feet, could be extended through an immense distance at a trifling expense. The feasibility of the project depends entirely upon the practicability of producing any sensible effect at one end of a long wire by connecting the other and with an electrical or galvanic battery.
MORSE'S TELEGRAPH AND THE ENGLISH
TELEGRAPH.
MAGNIFICENT TELEGRAPH OFFICE,
Washington, February 9, 1848.
Editors: Your London correspondent in this
morning's Intelligence says: "The electric telegraph has
commenced operation in London, and transmits messages
to all parts of England. The price charged for sending a
message of one hundred words to Liverpool is £5. ($22.20.)
This is considered so high that great dissatisfaction is ex-
pressed. The time occupied in forwarding such a message
is about ten minutes. Do you not do this business quicker
and cheaper? The distance between London and Liverpool
is two hundred and twenty miles.
I can satisfactorily answer your correspondent's question.
The distance from Washington to New York is two hundred
and twenty-five miles, and a message of one hundred
words is transmitted ordinarily in five minutes, but sometimes
in three and a half minutes, at a charge of five dollars for the
first hundred words, but only three dollars and thirty-three
cents for the second and for each following hundred words.
The comparative efficiency of the American and English systems
of electric telegraphs is therefore easily stated and comprehended:
English telegraph, 100 words, 220 miles, 10 min. $22.20;
American telegraph, 100 words, 225 miles, 5 min. $25.00.
That England is not now reaping the vastly superior advantages
of the American telegraphic system is owing to the injustice of
her Attorney General, in 1838, in most unscrupulously refusing
to grant Professor Morse's application for a patent at that
time, on a plea false in fact, but, had it been a fact, illegal in
its application. An illustration of the old adage that "might
make might right" will now more forcibly exhibit than
its own force the counsel pursued by the English Attorney
General upon the application of Professor Morse at that time.
It is hoped for the credit of Great Britain, that she will yet
do that justice to the Professor which is due by all the
world to a public benefactor.
With high respect, your friend and obedient servant,
B. B. FRENCH,

TARIFF OF CHARGES BY THE WASHINGTON
AND NEW ORLEANS TELEGRAPH COMPANY.—We have received a tariff of charges by the
Washington and New Orleans Telegraph Company from the telegraph office in Washington,
and the respective intervening points. It is published by the company, and we find that for
the first ten words sent to the first nearest point, Georgetown, two miles from Washington,
the charge is fifteen cents for each additional word; to Alexandria, 10 miles,
16 cents for ten words; to Charleston, S. C. 644
miles, the charge is 79 cents for ten words, and
16 cents for each additional word; to Mobile,
1,262 miles, the charge is 16 cents for ten words, and
16 cents for each additional word; to New Orleans,
1,716 miles, the charge is $2, and 10 cents for
each additional word. Between Mobile and New
Orleans the charge is fifteen cents for ten words, and
16 cents for each additional word. From Charleston to New Orleans 110 miles. Editors
and proprietors of newspapers receiving news for
their own paper are only charged one quarter of
the above rates. All other communications are
written in our language and sent to us. No
charges are added for signature and date, and communications prepaid.
LINES OF ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH.—There are being erected two or three new lines of electric telegraph between Washington, New York and Boston,
by different companies and individuals. From the
abundance of things, there will, we fear, be a
great deal of quarrelling about these new lines. A
new enterprise of the same character in the West
has been stopped, and is now a subject of litigation, and we much fear that similar proceedings
will take place concerning the Atlantic lines, before
managers are settled down, and the companies or individuals who are contracting them will be permitted to enjoy their own rights or inventions.
Professor Morse certainly, thus far, has given good
work, and has been a model of industry. His patent
was the first to carry it into practical operation; and
although it might be advantageous to the public
to encourage rivalry in this business, still it ought
to be done with due regard to the rights of original inventors.

The Post-rule, is for the purpose of carrying the Rule when
prepared with its type, it consists of a small lever like the
lever to the key of a horse collar, but with a
shaping rule with its type at the intersection of single cogs.
The lever falls into a notch, and rises upon the
notch, and rises upon the type. The lever is a
portion of the circuit by affixing a portion of the conductor to it
with a point of the post-rule, and otherwise connected so that the circuit will close
at the end it always. The other end is at the end of
the lever which has the most motion, and is made to break or close
the circuit at the end of its motion. The point of the con-
ductor is connected by a turnbuckle to the post-rule, at
the other extremity of the circuit, or upon a plate of copper
silver or other metal attached to the said extremity.
2. The rule is made to pass with regularity as to space and time, beneath
the lever, by means of a pinion wheel fitting the cogs, which wheel
is made to revolve either by a crank moved by the hand, or by
other power in any of the usual methods.
3. The Rule is kept in its channel or way made for that purpose.
The Post-rule sends the intelligence.
Fourth; The Register.
The Register receives and records the intelligence, and is thus
constructed, 1st An Electro-magnet made in any of the usual modes
of forming it, such as winding insulated copper wire, or winding copper or tin
foil, or other metal, and in a form of circular form, has the two extremities of the coils connected
with the circuit or conductors, so that the coils around the magnet make
part of the circuit. The power of this magnet is applied, 2. To
a Lever or Pendulum by affixing to the lever or pendulum the Armature of
the magnet or short bar of iron, at such a distance that the Electro-magnet will readily
attract it, a small weight or spring keeps the armature from the magnet, when the
magnet is not in action.
to the Lever is attached a Pencil, or Fountain Pen, or Printing Wheel, or other

upon 4th. A Cylinder of a size to hold a convenient sheet of Paper which
is wrapped around it. The Pencil or other marking material is made to revolve slowly and regularly by means of
the shaft of a clock machinery and to advance a short distance every revolution
of a screw or screw line. The Pencil or other marking material is in contact with the surface of the Cylinder either by its own weight or by a small
magnet attached to it, or when the Printing wheel is moved into contact
with the magnet when required to mark. 5th. A Needle or other magnet is offered to the
register, and regulated by the movements of the lever. 6th. An alarm apparatus to give notice that
a communication is about to be made to the President and is made to

Dear Sir I received yours of
the 11th in the 10th and am much pleased to learn of the
succsess of a contract if our water experiment succeeds I presume nothing can be done in that way until we have made a trial. I regret much that you have as myself been disappointed in not obtaining the wine. I was fearful the reels would not be finished in time for you, and myself to use since the receipt of your favour, to retain the two that were finished until the remaining two were complete, which is now the case, and will be sent to you on Monday with direction for them to be left in the case of the Governor.
I have some directions to give you in regard to opening the boxes. You will find on the sides of the top cover four screens, two on each side by which the uppermost cover is fastened.
When they are taken out you can lift the top off, and you will find the reels in order for immediate use. I would suggest to you to have them remain in the lower story of the University (Perhaps you can obtain Prof. Beckers room) as they will be very heavy and difficult to take up and down from this Hall as soon after they are filled with wine. I am very busy with our Machines. I find there is considerable work to do upon them. But we have not got very well with them and I see nothing in the way of completing them next week
my father goes to the City next week and will stay but
a few days. However I hope, that will not deter you from
visiting us as early as possible. I have acquainted Mrs Rail
of your offered service and she regards me to say that she
will be happy to receive them, and that she will be greatly
obliged to you if you will purchase points. brushes for
her. I think that large boxes are to be had for the purpose of
containing paints and brushes if so, be kind enough to obtain
one.
I have disposed with the large spiral wheel, and have con-
cluded to use one smaller on the opposite end of the shaft. The
reason for doing so, was that three inches was not more than
enough for the magnet, and that the large spiral would be
in the way of the magnet. Now, the space between the drum
will be clear, and free. I think you will like the last plan
the best.
I have completed as far as head work is concerned my
letter Machine and shall make the pattern for it, as I have
leasure from the attention due the writing Machine. This is
not, I presume, objectionable, I should rejoice to try it a
well watered at Washington this winter, and produce an extra
astonishment, would it not be fine?
What has become of Mrs Patterson will the leave the City before
the wire is all wound? I hope not, or we will meet with further delay, which is horrible to think of just now, as I have
my eye still intently fixed upon Europe. I fear we shall lose
our advantage over European discoveries if there is much delay.
The secret shall be well kept.
I assume you will scarcely recognise me when you come
out. For you must know I have something else to do besides
ride clean my boots, and wear a clean face, and besides the
shop present a different scene from the Pastor or Study,
and wears a somewhat different appearance. However there
are some clean beds in Spedwell to which I sometime
resort, and which I hope you will be able to find on your
arrival. The remainder of the sheet I will serve for Monday
Monday morning.
I am inclined to think that my father will not visit
the City this week: -- I am think of nothing more to com
mandate. I shall wait with great interest to hear
from you by your next. Remember me of your
prof. gall.
I remain yours truly
Alfred Vail

My Dear Brother,
This will be handed you by Mr. Stephen
Vail the father of Mr. Vail who is engaged with me in the
Telegraph. He wishes to have some conversation with you on
the subject of Paper, as he has just become possessed of a
paper mill which is manufactured first rate paper. You
will of course know best whether it is desirable to make
a contract with him for a regular supply. Mr. Vail
is well known as a faithful man in his contracts and
entirely responsible.
You will perhaps be surprised to learn that I
came out here to be sick; I caught a severe cold the day
I left New York from the sudden change of temperature, and
was taken down with one of my bilious attacks, which under
other treatment and circumstances might have resulted seriously.
But through a kind providence, I have been thrown among
most attentive and kind and skillful friends, who have treated
me more like one of their own children than like a stranger.
Mr. Vail has been a perfect mother to me; our good Nancy
Thazard can alone compare with her. Through her nursing and
constant attention I am now able to leave my room and have
been down stairs to-day, and hope to be out in a few days. This
sickness well of course detain me a while longer than I intended,
for I must finish the portraits before I return. I may possibly, if
strong enough, come in on Saturday, and return here again on Tuesday
following. I have learned a good deal about a bilious habit by this sickness
so that I think I could now be a pretty good nurse to you if you
should have a serious attack. The truth is we are all of a bilious habit.
poor Richard seems to be the greatest sufferer from it, and I should like
to see him well through a good course of medical treatment. How is
he? I called to see him the evening before I left town, but could make
no one answer at the door, so I was obliged to go without laying good bye.
give my love to him and his family.
The machinery for the Telegraph goes forward daily; slowly
but well and through. You will be surprised at the strength and quantity
of machinery, greater doubtless than will eventually be necessary, yet
it gains the main points, certainty and accuracy.

if I should not come. I am sending Mr. Vail any letter from me at the
office. I wish you would write a line by McVail and tell me any
news for I surely the Journal of Commerce.
W. S. is of opposite politics to yourself.
Yours as ever
Y. A. H. Brothers

Spindletop Jan. 13th
Dear Brother,
Mr. Alfred Vail is just going in to N.York and will
return on Monday morning; The machinery is at length complete
and we have thrown it to the Missouri people with great
delight. It is the talk of all the people round, and the principal
inhabitants of Newark made a special expedition on Friday to
see it. The success is complete. We have tried the experiment of
sending a pretty full letter, which I got up from the members given
me, transmitted through two miles of wire and deciphered with but
a single unimportant error. — I am staying only to perfect a
modification of my fortune, and hope to see you on Saturday or
on the earliest on Wednesday when I shall tell you about it.
The matter looks well now, and I desire to feel grateful to him
who gives success, and he always surprised for any disappointment
which he in Infinite wisdom may have in store.—
I long to hear also about your doing in the upper story.
give my regards to them all. Love to Richard and family.
Your great brother & wife Brotten
Sam. P. Brotten

Your long silence with regard to my
letter to you, dated in May, but respecting the
National Academy of Design in connection
with myself, has been a matter of much concern
to me. I have been waiting patiently, though
anxiously, for many months, and it now seems
that you must altogether have forgotten it or
have decided to give me no answer. If the
former, I hope this note will prove salutary,
in reminding you of an answer naturally
expected; if the latter, you will much oblige me
by affording me of such conclusion.
Yours very respectfully
S. D. B. Morff Layton

My Dear Sir
During his final illness I find it my duty to inform you that the affair of Dr Jackson
is put in such condition that you have nothing to fear. I wrote you by yesterday's mail
a copy of Jackson's communication in the Boston Post and accompanying
this is a copy of the Ken containing your brother's reply which was also published
in the Courier of M.Y. - Mr. Spivak is now in town on the business of the
Board of Directors making investigations and I have communicated with
him in person today. He thinks we will have a good report from the Senate on
the Telegraph. I have sent in a petition to allow our Company to import
wire & rubbing duty free. Seguin says the rails are self sufficient
and I am sending to the Prosper Committee Mr. D. S. doing what he can at
the Government office. We are anxiously awaiting the results. What are you doing
& suppose you are as anxious as I am regarding the action of the French
Government and the St Germain Rail Road I am giving a course of lectures on Chemistry at
McKistock's office every day ever since the delay here for more lectures
given. The University is now at the Colonial etc.
public estimation. I sent you sometime since a pamphlet
containing the resignation of our Faculty, namely Professor Joseph
Patton, Hackley Norton Burt & Davis Linne which the Faculty
have now organized with new professors and one of these professors
namely Professor Dwight Rogers of the Chem. Dept. has since resigned
the Medical Faculty has been since you left appointed and cure
on the eve of being organized in all 18 professors but in consequence
of the game played by the Chancellor & some members of the Council
they have resigned in a body and are going to publish their
transactions and history in a pamphlet form stating they have kept together
and are now applying to the legislature for a charter under
the name of the Manhattan Medical College. I will thank you
to day to the Directors of the Garden of Plants that I shall forward to
them as soon as practicable a box of the Suspended Red cedar, Forsythia
& Chiltenango with American Ligustrum. Yours truly L.D. Spivak

The Sub-Committee, from the Committee of Science and Arts appointed
to examine the Electro-Magnetic Telegraph of Professor Samuel F.
B. Morse.
Report, That this instrument was exhibited to them in
the hall of the Institute, and every opportunity given by Mr. Morse
and his associate Mr Alfred Vail, to examine it carefully, and to
judge of its operation; and they now present the following as
the result of their observations. [The instrument is here described]
The instrument may be briefly described as follows;
1st There is a galvanic battery of sixty pairs of plates 7 by 8 1/2
inches each, arranged according to the very convenient plan
suggested by Prof. Howe, and set in action by a solution of sulphate
of copper
2d The poles of this battery can be connected at pleasure,
with a circuit of copper wires, which in the experiments with
ed was ten miles in length. The greater part of the wire was
wound round two cylinders, and the coils insulated from one
another, by being covered with cotton thread.
3d In the middle of this circuit of wire, that is, at what
was the Regulator. In this there is an electro-magnet, made
of a bar of soft iron bent in the form of a horse-shoe, and
surrounded by coils of the wire, which forms the circuit.
The keeper of this magnet is at the short arm of a bent
lever, at the end of the longer arm of which is a
fountain pen. When the keeper is drawn against the
magnet, the pen comes in contact with a roll of paper
wound round a cylinder, and makes a mark with
ink upon this paper. While the telegraph is in operation,
the cylinder which carries the paper is made to revolve
slowly upon its axis by an apparatus like the kitchen jack

It may be proper to state that the idea of using electro-
magnetism for telegraphic purposes has presented itself to sev-
eral different individuals, and that it may be difficult to
settle among them the question of their originality. Gauss has
a telegraph of this kind, in actual operation, for communicat-
ing signals between the University at Göttingen and his magnetic
Observatory in its vicinity. Mr. Wheatstone of London has
also been for some time engaged in experiments on an electro-
magnetic telegraph. But the plan of Professor Morse is, so
far as the Committee are informed, entirely different from
any of those devised by other individuals, all of which act
by giving different directions to a magnetic needle, and
would therefore require several circuits of wires between the
stations.
In conclusion, the Committee beg to state
their high gratification with the exhibition of Professor
Morse's telegraph, and their hope that means may begin
to him to subject it to the test of an actual experiment
made between stations at a considerable distance from each
other. The advantages, which this telegraph, would present
if successful, over every kind hitherto used, make it
worthy of the patronage of the Government. These are,
that the stations may be a distance asunder far exceeding
that to which all other telegraphs are limited, and that
the signals may be given at night and in rains, and
fogs, when other telegraphs fail.

Dr. Six,
Yours of the 4th came to hand
yesterday. A compliance with your proposal would be
exceedingly agreeable to me & my family, & since the re-
ception of your request we have talked it over & stuck
to make provision for it. On the whole, however,
we regret to say, it will not be convenient for us to
accommodate your daughter as a boarder. We
already have a young lady with us who rooms with
Harriet, & whom we have engaged to keep till the 1st
of May. If we could dispense of her, we would gladly
take Susan in her place, you are only sorry we can
not do so. But, as it is, we have only one spare
room & subject, as we are, to company which we
must accommodate, we think it our duty to deny
ourselves the pleasure of having your daughter with
us, as a boarder, which would be very agreeable to
us all. It is with reluctance on your account, as well
as our own that we decline, as it would afford us great
pleasure to do you the kindness which you request.
In account of the present of the times, we expect to
change our quarters on the 1st of May. After that, should
you desire the accommodation proposed, it may be
in our power to grant it. In the mean time, should
your daughter return to New York, we shall be happy
to see her often at our house, to cherish the intimacy
which already exists between her & our own daughter,
which, on her part, we regard as a privilege. There is

I hope you will bear with me a moment, while I take the liberty to address you
for a few lines. I have seen by your publication of the
Confessions of a French Catholic priest, that the author is now
in New York. I myself am a Frenchman ordained Priest
by Bishop Foleyt of Bardstown Ky. in 1830. I have
acted in the capacity of a Priest, nearly five years, on the
two most conspicuous stations of the Diocese. But in consequence of an injustice done me by theadjutor Bishop,
I have ceased to officiate, and, in all probability, I will never
officiate again — and because I suppose to be bullied — into
what I conceived to be a flagrant wrong, they have attempted
to injure me in public opinion. Still in the camp, I have
lettered the gaulet, and taught them with their own means
I have already published from members in the Western Protestant, a religious paper of this place, in which, I have
confuted their charges with their own official Documents.
I have in my possession, letters of five Bishops,
and two archbishops of the United States, and several love letters of the men to their Priest, which go to confirm the
Statements made in the "Confessions". The Catholic clergy
of this place, in a paper edited by them, have noticed the work
and, as a matter of course, denounce it as "a vile fabrication"
which they say "was never written even by an apostate priest" I am
perfectly content with the details made in the "Confessions", as
a recommendation from me might have some weight with the
public in this great Western region. I would, therefore, beg of
you, to consider me the bearer of the author, you may
say, by any word that he will never be betrayed. Your
disgraceful attempt to produce a reciprocal service
to each other -- and of a beneficial result to the public --
there is only one copy of the "Confessions" in this place -- a
number of strong words will very rarely.
The materials in my possession, could make a
handsome volume, and it has been my design for some
time past to undertake the task; but my constant engagement
for the last six months, has prevented me, for this, to do so; besides,
being a stranger, I feel the necessity of an experienced
hand. Your kind kindness to the French gentleman who
published the "Confessions" you have revived, has induced me to address
you, most humbly requesting, that you would be good
enough to extend the same favour to me -- and to
advise me of the best means to take, in my present
situation, to carry my contemplated work, successfully
to an end.
In the expectation of an answer, as speedy as
your communication will allow, I remain,
Respectfully yours
Birot

Since my return,
I have been very busily engaged in finishing
the machine, and have now got it so far com-
pleted, as to assure you of its being sent to the
City this week. I have been entirely "non plus" with
the battery, and how to remedy the evil I know
not. On my return, I procured more Sulphuric -- but
found that, although the action of the solution
on the plate was as good as ever -- that is, that
the Sulphate of Copper was as readily decomposed,
yet, the Magnetic effect was not so great, or which
is the same thing, the electric effect -- I washed the
plate, thoroughly cleaning them several times, and
renewed the solution, with no better effect -- then
I tried Sulphuric acid, both to try the effect of it
upon the magnet, and also to clean the copper
plates, but without success. -- There was however
on every trial a feeble effect upon the magnet, and
a very small spark visible on breaking the circuit.
After spending two days in this way, and using
almost 3 lbs of Sulphur -- I resolved to send it together
with the Machine to you, that you might with
the assistance of Dr. Gale discover the cause, and ap-
ply the remedy -- After all my experience of two days
the only cause I can assign for its acting thus, is that
the copper plate is covered with a minute film of copper
which I cannot get off. -- Perhaps it may be some
thing else -- Our large battery never served me this
time, and I am afraid it will not do so again. I am
your very obliged servant
Samuel F. B. Morse
