to remove any sinister impressions or misconstruction, with regard to our
motive and intentions; and at the same time, being actuated
by feelings of the greatest respect and regard, beg leave to address
you in this manner, for the purpose of expressing our regret, that we
should appear in so unfavorable a light.
We disclaim any intention of disrespect to yourself or to any of the gentlemen who were not
re-elected; on the contrary, we have the greatest regard for their
private characters, and are perfectly sensible of the services they have
done, and the great services they have rendered to the Academy.
Notwithstanding, we feel the impression, that it would better promote the welfare of the Institution, by having changes from
time to time in the Council, thereby encouraging the younger members,
by allowing them to participate in the management of the Academy, and
stimulating them to greater exertions for distinction.
It has been objected to our proceedings that we have removed
without giving them any intimation of what we were about to do.
In reply to this objection, we beg leave to state, that we have
removed no one; but merely elected some new members to
supply the places of those whose term of service expires in July.
And as for the manner, we had no precedent for doing otherwise.
It is foreign to our purpose, here to state, all
the reasons which have had an influence in bringing about
the change in Council; but merely to state in this manner, some
of the leading points, and to prove, by our sincere esteem and respect
not only for yourself, but for those who now give place for
others of our election.
If we have elected some new members, it
is only proof that we wished for change or rotation in
office; not to rebuke the President or those not reelected.
If it be doubted that we did not reelect the President, his in
firmness and the intention of the President to go abroad were
the reasons.
With regard to the members of Council, one of
them does not reside in New York and consequently cannot be
expected to perform all the necessary duties of his office; another
has been long in place, which was all that could be said against
Mr. Ingham; and (although it may not have been his fault) another
was blamed for allowing it out of 13 of his pictures to be placed
upon the line and in the best lights.
We are aware how difficult must be the task of pleasing
every one. We hope, Sir, that you will view what has been
done, more favorably, the disclaim any intention of creating
a party or any distinctions whatever, and with the best wishes
towards the members of the Academy, and yourself individually
We remain
Your humble
Saint F. Balloue Esqr.

ence in each of the modes or means in being susceptible
of, of course, that end. It will be seen.
Now I am not aware that there is any

relays employed in my invention, and for which

Some metallic wires - others do liberise - for

July 12. 1838 Thursday
Dear Brother,
I arrived here Tuesday morning, having spent Sabbath
at Bolbec, very agreeably, & passed Monday at the memorable city of
Rouen. The pleasure I anticipated from a personal acquaintance with
our respected Correspondent, W. de Felice, was fully realized. But
of him this interesting family I have not time now to speak. In
addition to the pleasure of this visit, I was most agreeably surprised
to find Mr. de Felice, just at the point of going to Switzerland, he
would have gone last week, but from a slight indisposition was in-
duced to defer it -- as if on purpose for me to accompany him.
He expects to be in Paris to day or tomorrow, & to leave on Saturday
or at farthest on Monday next (as he is impatient of longer delay)
for Lausanne and Geneva by way of Dijon. &c. Mr. H. Lutterott
to whom I had a letter, has given me the outline of a tour in Switzerland
which he says may be accomplished in 3 or 4 weeks. He advises my
visiting Carlsbad near Tiflitz in Bohemia, about two days journey bey-
ond Switzerland which I may do, if my health seems to require it.
Sir. Hottinger informs me that Cousin Edwin Salisbury's letters are
addressed to Interlaken on June, which I find is in my route, so
that I shall probably have the pleasure of seeing him there.
I have not yet called on Mr. Cap, but may, before I set off for Tiflitz?
My health continues to improve. I rode all night for 2 nights on
my way, I was also a night on board the steam-boat, yet until yester-
day, had not a tinge of my old complaint, that arising to imprudence
is walking in the hot sun. I am to-day well again, I shall not care
to see anything of Paris till my return here. But enough of myself.
My kind regards to Mr. Smith, Success to the Telegraph, for -- I shall
want money, if I prolong my stay in Europe. I have followed your
instructions to write on half a sheet of blotting paper. You will have

My dear brother.
It is a long time since I had written you
and in my last I led you to expect that about this
time both Richard and myself would be on the
water on our return. I have not wished to raise
expectations in regard to my Telegraphic
matters, for I felt and still feel in this this
world of disappointments, that flattering
appearances should not prevent us from
setting bounds to vainqueur expectations.
Perhaps I have erred on the other
side, and have fallen into distrust which
Providence in a thousand ways was calling
for my confidence and gratitude. Certainly,
now everything looks successful, yet as nothing
is consummated I hold myself loose and keep
prepared for disappointment. I will tell you
how matters stand. I have obtained a patent
in France, although Wheatstone has also here a
patent for his invention. They do not
interfere except that my invention is
pronounced far superior in simplicity and
practability. They are different inventions.
After waiting awhile it was safe to exhibit my
invention I was desirous that the King should
see it, and this would doubtless have been
affected before this, but for the birth of the Count

Opération
Avant de décrire les fonctions de l'appareil
ci-dessus, je crois devoir faire remarquer que pendant
qu'il est au repos, l'électro-magnétisme est en
circulation sur toute la ligne, et que c'est seulement
quand les circuits sont interrompus que
l'appareil est mis en activité. Ce qui constitue
une différence avec le mode décrit dans le premier
brevet, dans lequel l'appareil est en repos, quand
la circulation est interrompue, et ne marche que
quand la communication est rétablie.
On établit un appareil semblable à celui ci-
dessus décrit et représenté dans les dessins ci-joints
à tous les endroits de la ligne, avec lesquels on
désire établir communication. Quand le locomoteur
et son train ont refoulé la tige B, celle-ci
fait basculer le tiroir C, et éteint la tige F, qui
dans sa marche ascendante fait échapper la
distente G, alors la roue H n'étant plus retenue
ce déclenche le mouvement que lui impose la roue
I, et tourne sur son axe. Ses dents viennent
succesivement en contact avec le talon du levier
et s'abaissent.
Le levier I pivote alors sur son centre de
mouvement et la fourchette qu'il porte à son
extrémité opposée est retirée des vases de
mercurie, le courant galvanique cesse de passer
dans les conducteurs, l'électro aimant perd sa
force attractrice, et l'armature Q s'en éloigne
sollicitée par un repos. Le mouvement du
levier R rend toute liberté au marteau T qu'il
tenait soulevé, celui-ci retombe et coupe le timbre.
Chaque dent de la roue H fait ainsi échapper une
fois le marteau.
Chaque fois que la tige I3 est repoussée, la roue
H fait une révolution complète, alors la première
dent que porte cette roue détermine un coup de
marteau sur le timbre. Ce premier coup sera à
appeler l'attention de la personne chargée de
recevoir les renseignements ; un pistolet silencieux suit ce
premier coup, le coup ou les coups suivants déterminent le numéro de la station pour laquelle l'endroit de
la ligne où passe la locomotive.
En moyens du loqueteux M. on peut donner
autant de coups qu'on veut, et de tels endroits
qu'on le désire où se trouve placé un appareil
Semblable à celui ci depuis pour transmettre
tous les signaux que le besoin du service pourrait exiger.
Le même moyen pourrait être appliqué au système
décrit au bruit d'origine pour transmettre des signaux
représentés par des nombres divers de coups de marteau
sur un timbre sonore. Quand on désire garder les
traces des signaux transmis, on se sert du rapporteur
décrit au bruit d'origine. Dans ce cas, les conducteurs
sont disposés de maniere à mettre en mouvement le
dit rapporteur lors de l'échappement de la première
dent de la roue H, cette dent produit cet effet, en outre
de celui ci-dessus signalé.
On pourrait aussi transmettre des signaux en plongeant
avec la main le levier à fourchette dans les valves à
mercurie, et en le retirant des mêmes valves, mais la
préférence que je donne aux mécanismes que j'ai
décrits vient de ce que les mouvements sont plus réguliers

My very dear Arthur
Since to seeing you, the greatest pleasure I have ever a
day is, writing to you, and this morning, found a favorable opportunity for
holding a letter that will give you an idea how much I miss the great
Western littoral and amid the thousands of letters I received to Europe
there was a rare long one from a certain gentleman by the name of Spencer
found in these days for his Christian character.
I am becoming very impatient to see such a letter as I dare say it
will be the keel of at least a letter from your Mr. H. of Smith's
hear, has also your parole for me, but as he left the American Congress
is seated in the pocket ship Jefferson the 21st and I never yet enjoyed
the pleasure of seeing him yet a letter.
Since I last wrote you dear father, I have been quite ill, having
a severe cold which I think about a week since, and deal with
chills, & constipation, & lastly with typhus pitts produced by Dr. Baker, and
to say I was able to go out to watch against Mrs. Baker was very
kind to me during my short illness and every day I live for more
& more. Do you not think she is a lovely woman, father?
This Thursday (the 29th) was Thanksgiving day, to this day I am in
awe of the American states. It did not seem like Thanksgiving
to me, when I was unable to attend church or to eat much dinner
the old men's association to Mrs. Williams to deliver in Boston
then but only 2000. Mrs. Baker and little Mary, young, they had a
very pleasant time indeed, and in the evening the two families came over to
their office. Mrs. Medwin, when several of their relatives had assembled
there, and I, had quite heard ministers Baptistly to the pastor,
when we were agreeably surprised by a flying visit from my
pretty niece, during which she had not been home for a great while.
He seemed to be in very good health and would have been come to
our bed many times, but he had to go for business during the short
time long time. He sleeps upon the floor of the house now, and
though he had to come here, we never got him away to call on me.
The dear boys are yet at school, and I am sure they are compelled
to this work with them, they are very compelled
and send under, to stay in the house & keep warm by the fire.
Unfortunately, this nice new suit of clothes which they had made
before they went up there, paid them so much. Now they prefer
wearing their old clothes which by this time must be pretty well
ironed out. They have no mittens either to keep their hands warm, so
I have begun to send them some nice warm ones – Uncle Selmy
has considered, I believe, when Uncle Richard returns to send
them up to Mr. Wacklam's school at Manchester etc. It is an excellent
school I know but I cannot bear the thought of going so far away
from us all to look another home – As I do wish to be a very
colds & black fellow – I must be that they are warmly clad before
they go to Charleston must have a warm coat as his Clerk is all
done out – to be sure it is a very cold thing.
You do not know dear father how you about children long to see
you – and I do hope you will be able to come before April.
I am growing more and more impatient to see you again, and I hope
the good Jewish people will make haste and accept your telegraph,
and take your picture to reward you for it – as that seems to be
the most essential part, just now.
Yesterday, her was all bustle and Company for Mr. Joe R. Peters arrived
in the morning – with his bride, Mrs Smith from Albany. I was much
pleased with her though I think she better rather be married –
She told me that she used to know my grand father Marks – as well
as you – and that the name of Marks would be even dear when she has
you a little in her mouth from you – about the time in Mexico – which
she intends stopping one or two returns from Philadelphia.
This morning they left for that place. When it is to be for the
first time her three daughters – Abby, Mary & Caroline – she is
at a Jewish School in Philadelphia – I hope they will be pleased
with their new step mother.
I read, now, and practise every day dear father and cousin – me
to make myself useful to the members of the family. I am reading
now – Prescott's history of the Reign of Ferdinand & Isabella – which is in
its two large volumes & next, I am going to take up Roncquer's
history of the United States both of which Dr. Peters has lately been
purchased with – I have a fine opportunity of seeing all the new
publications as Dr. P is in town and has them sent to him.
I shall be in some new music, dear father, on your return -- and a few minutes
can be found for me, when I am doing -- that is if you can afford it.
The ships here crowded are playing about the room -- Many say I must have
come to you -- tell you that she is so concerned about your that you must return
to the Liverpool & bring her home cargo. -- I am firing to keep this letter open.
All that I can do is to send a letter to answer from you.

Mr. President,
Your welcome letter, also had the pleasure of his Company here to leave. He has
had a long voyage of it. Do you not think so? He really began to feel anxious
for his safety, as he has been out over two months, and the Ville de Lyon
which sailed from Havana Nov. reached New York before the Union.
However, he has at length arrived safely, and is improving health, or
at least feels thankful for that. They enclose a subscription of sales in
lead woods, but no stores. It is very pleasant to hear from your dear father
and to learn that every thing thus far, appeared so favorable. Dr. Dale has
done me the favor to allow me to send your letter to him, and I have
also been sending an account of the Telegraph in a French paper which
you sent him. Your letter found me as well as usual, and quite happy
in the society of my friends here: but every day is long for your return, &
to see you once more. Your fleet so swiftly, that ships will soon be here
now! We have not seen Mr. H. L. Smith yet, though he arrived the
week before last. If he has any letters for us, they have gone to the United,
as he started for Washington immediately on his arrival, leaving a note
for Dr. Dale saying, that he preferred to hear from you sooner in letter
than he would call the week, week on his return. As yet, we have seen
nothing of him.

Introduction,
Les Modifications apportées à l'appareil décrit au Bureau d'Orison ont pour
objet de supprimer au service des chemins de fer, de manière à faire connaître la position
de chaque locomotive et du train de wagons sur la voie de fer qu'ils parcourent,
a indiquer successivement les diverses stations auxquelles ils parviennent, &
à transmettre, dès avis & des ordres sur toute la longueur de la ligne, ou à toutes
les stations.
Dessins,
Figure 1, offre une situation verticale de l'appareil de télégraphie
par l'électricité magnétique pour transmettre des ordres &
des avis sur des chemins de fer.
Figure 2, est la vue d'ensemble du même appareil.
Figure 3, Situation verticale de l'appareil en lui opposé à celui
représenté figure 1.
Figure 4, Vue latérale du même Appareil prise du côté droit de la ligne.
Figure 5, Vue latérale du même Appareil prise du côté opposé à celui d'usage.
Figure 6, C'était à la détente.
Figures 7, 8, 9, 10, Représentes la première d'une dent, la seconde de
deux dents, la troisième de trois dents, la quatrième de quatre
dents, sans compter une dente de mise en ligne qui existe
sur toutes les Reprises.
Description,
A, C'est la borne d'un Rail auquel l'appareil communique.
B, C'est un fer traversant une meulaise pratiquée dans le Rail A, la dite ligne
infinitésimale par barre au levier horizontal C.
C, Levier horizontal ayant son centre de mouvement en D sur un boulon
en cheville réglable reposant dans des canneslets en bois ou en pierre. Ce levier est
chargé à son extrémité par un poids E, qui maintient avec force le levier
sur son appui F, de manière qu'une pression légère telle que celle causée
par le pied d'un homme puisse faire fléchir la ligne B, c'est à dire le levier
C mettre le mécanisme en marche comme nous le verrons ci après.
F, Levier vertical articulé à l'extrémité du levier C : le levier F joue dans des
guides fixés à la paroi de l'appareil.
98552
C, Détente touchant parfois le levier F, et portant une pièce d'électro Aimant à qui
soigne au passage d'une cheville que porte la borne H.
H, borne avec un nombre de dents égal au numéro de la station où elle sera
placée une première dent posée en avant des autres soit à mettre l'appareil
en marche et n'est pas complète pour l'indication.
I, Levier à fourchette déjà décrit dans l'appareil du Brevet précédent.
J J, Petits vases pour recevoir le mercure.
K K, Conducteur venant d'un des piliers du généralis et se terminant à un
des vases de mercure.
K', Conducteur partant de l'autre vase de mercure et communiquant avec
l'électro Aimant L.
L, Electro Aimant à un bout duquel communiqué le Conducteur K', dont
les hélices entendent tout le dit Electro Aimant; l'autre bout du dit
Conducteur K', reste ensuite de la même manière à un seul Electro-
Aimant L ainsi de suite jusqu'au dernier, alors le Conducteur retourne
en ligne droite et non interrompu vers le second des piliers du généralis
but avec lequel il s'inut en communication.
M, Télescope a l'onde suivant à interrupteur à détente le circuit à cet
effet en sentant le bouton du Conducteur qui alaise un bout et élève le
bout opposé du levier à fourchette 1 et interrompt la communication.
N N N', sort d'engrenages semblables à ceux d'une horloge, mis en marche
par un poids et une corde. On pourrait aussi employer le mouvement
à un ressort contenu dans un cartillet comme dans les pendules. La roue
N qui marche plus lentement que les autres mène la roue Hartmann
d'une roue à engrenage N' lié à N' et monté sur le même axe.
O O, Timbre sur lequel vient frapper le marteau P.
P, Armature d'électro Aimant montée sur un levier R qui a son
contre de mouvement sur la borne S.
Opération,
Avant de décider les fonctions de l'appareil ci-dessus je crois devoir
faire remarquer que pendant qu'il est au repos l'électro-Aimant est
en circulation sur toute la ligne, et que c'est seulement quand les circuits
sont interrompus que l'appareil est mis en activité. Ce qui constitue une
différence avec le mode décrit dans le premier Brevet, dans lequel l'appareil
est en repos quand la circulation est interrompue et ne marche que
quand la communication est rétablie.
En établit un Appareil semblable à celui ci-dessus décrit et représenté
dans les dessins ci-joints, à tous les endroits de la ligne avec lesquels en désire
établir communication.

An out-line of what Mr. Morse will propose
to do in relation to contracts for the use
of his Electric Telegraph.
1st. He will furnish the requisite wires for a direct
circuit -- that is, to communicate back and forth -- be-
tween any two distant points, not less than 20
miles distant, and between any more distant
points, prepaid for use -- for $500, or 2500 francs
per mile -- including therein every preparation of
wires for use and preservation, that is to say, covered with the requisite non-conductor, and encased
in iron, a lead tube, or other suitable composition
for their protection in the trench -- The trench is to
be dug at any depth that shall suit the contractor, and covered at his expense -- All other expenses

not will acknowledge that these principles were entirely
new to him. I also mention certain Electric Magnets
one of which I have placed in baggage in terms stiff

fundamental ancient, for in August Express the mail
circulates from L'Electricité et le Magnétisme, publication in

Dear Sir
I have been wholly occu-
pied for the last week in copying out the correspond-
ence, and other documents to defend myself against
the infamous attack of Dr Jackson, notice of which
my brother sent me. I have sent it this day by D-
Mitchell who sails in the Ville de Lyon on the 16th the
packet that takes this; I have sent a letter to Dr
Jackson calling on him to save his character by a
total disclaimer of his presumptuous claim, with
in one week from the receipt of the letter, and giving
him the plea of "mistake" and "misconception of my
invention" by which he may retreat. If he fails
to de thes I have requested my brother to put
lik immediately my defence, in which I give a
history of the invention, the correspondence between
Dr Jackson & Myself, and close with the letters of
Gen. M. Reeves, W. Fisher of Phila and Capt. Sill.
I cannot conceive of such infatuation as has pos-
sessed that man. He can scarcely be deceived; So
must be his consummate self conceit that deceives
him, if he is deceived. But this cannot be, he knows
he has no title whatever to a single unit of any
kind in the matter. It is pure wickedness.
The event will be favorable to the invention, it
will be for it one of the best advertisements, for
there are hundreds who will read controversy, who
will not take the pains to read a dispassionate des-
cription. – I received your 2nd letter authorizing me to
draw on you for such monies as I may want; a close
calculation will oblige me to draw for £200 in lieu
of £150, as I told you I should in my last, for it is
possible that I shall be compelled to stay a little
longer than I anticipated in consequence of some
prospects favorable from Russia. The Baron
Meyendorf, the Russian Government agent for
reporting to the Emperor all important discoveries
has been to see the Telegraph, he is very much
pleased with it; and says he shall report it to
his Government; He introduced to me M. Ameyet
who has proposed also an Electric Telegraph, but
upon seeing mine, he could not restrain his grati-
fication, and with his whole soul he is at work
to forward it with all who have influence. He is
the right hand man of the Baron Meyendorf, and he is
exerting all his powers to have the Russian Govern-
ment adopt my Telegraph. To the objections of the
various Savans who were present yesterday at the
experiment, that the great difficulty was with the
wires to prevent them being destroyed by malveillance,
he replied that even this which was the only plausible
objection which could be urged, was in reality nothing
that placed beneath a rail road they were perfectly
secure, for the men that watched the rail, would
also watch the wires. I go with him to-morrow to search
for the drawings of Sommering & Steinhil Telegraphs,
with a description of them, at the Institute. It is really
a noble-minded man. The Baron told me he had
a large soul, and I find he has. I have no claim
on him, and yet he seems to take as much interest in my
invention as if it were his own, from different con-
duct from Jacksons! In mentioning obligation I
ought to mention my room-mate Mr. McCull, I am
indebted to him, mediately for all the success I have
had among the Savans here. his acquaintance with
Mr. Fulleren de Paris and others, has been of great service
and then his knowledge of the language of which I am
ignorant, enabling him to explain the whole process
at my various experiments, has made him invaluable to me. Indeed I don't know what I should have
dune without him. You will have learned how the
dissolution of the Chamber has created further delay in my business; I was on the very point of having
a call to exhibit it to the Chamber, at the moment they
were dissolved. I learned through Amyet that the
Gouv. were seriously thinking of establishing a Telegraph
line on the electric principle between Paris and
Marne, but that such was the political state of affairs
that nothing would certainly be done this year. But
he thought it would eventually be done, and that
mine (if I understood him right) would be the
one adopted it to forming a company to take it up
If such it impracticable for the reason the Telegraph
is a Government monopoly and therefore I am
wholly dependent on it. The Government takes
no commercial or social use of the Telegraph and
the reason why the St. Leads have not taken hold is
that they have not decided whether it can be attended
to. I get no answer yet from the Minister of State. Do
you think your patience would hold out as long?
I begin to doubt whether I shall remain any. Indeed
but for the aspect of things at work, the sooner I return
home the better; I do not see that I can further benefit
the concern at present here except by making it
known to the various men; this obtains honor, and profit
its merits, and profit may be a consequence at some future time. I shall, if possible, make this sort of an arrangement with the Baron if he should propose anything from Russia, viz. that I should return to America immediately and visit Russia or send an agent in
the Summer, for I must return, and arrange my affairs for the change which this Telegraph has compelled me to make. He may require an answer from St. Petersburg, and that will delay me, but I had better return and come out again if necessary, with a more perfected and compact instrument which I cannot get here situated as I am.

duly received, and we both return answer by the same ship, which sail's tomorrow
I can easily conceive that your situation in Paris, away from friends & family,
must be a trying one, and am sorry that it has not often been cheered by
letters from those who cherish the recollection of you on this side of the water. I am
sensible that I am very deficient as a correspondent (or rather, am not
corresponding) with absent friends; but you must not lay all the fault
on me this time. When you went away, you expected to be absent but 3
or 4 months, & it seemed so uncertain whether a letter, if written would
reach Europe before you embarked that I had not much encouragement to write.
Afterwards, you announced that you would be on your return before
letters could reach you, & that we need not write. It was then several
weeks before we heard that you had changed your plans, & determined
to remain. During all this time, the suspense & uncertainty kept me
from writing. I have written, however, certainly two & I think three
if not four letters, this being either the fourth or fifth. Susan has written
quite a number, and has you so constantly in number mind, that I
am confident she has not been at all remorse; certainly not, since
you informed us that you were to remain in Paris during the
winter.
The boys are still at Hudson, with their uncle Richard, whose
health I suspect is somewhat improved, but not yet radically restored.
I have been full of cares & perplexities of late, and sometimes they
have been almost too much to bear. The new buildings on the corner have
been under roof the for three months, & during the winter, I have been slowly
finishing inside. The walls stand well, remarkably well, & Judicious building,
who have examined them carefully in every part, say the buildings are
firm & secure; but there has been a disquieting excitement from one
approbation that they were nuisance; and it was even carried so far
that the Grand Jury were requested to present the buildings as a nuisance;
and under a strange misapprehension respecting them, they were on the point
of doing so. Happily, however, they discovered before it was too late, that there
was not the least occasion for alarm, and disposed without any action on the matter.
I hear nothing from Dr. Jackson, since the articles which I wrote
vindicating you from his calumnies. It is well he came on & just as he did, as
your attempt is complete, & he is disabled that he now can do you no further
harm. I sent you both my articles, in former letters.
Geography has been much improved since you left, especially
in the style of lettering marks. We could not, if you recollected, give the body of the
letter without great difficulty, but wrote in handwriting; and the lower
can Roman letters had only the long stroke without the hair-stroke. I have now
invented a method of making both perfect, and equal to the handiwork of copper-
plate lettering. Munson has actually engraved in three days of hard work, nearly
equal to 300 words, on the model of Pennsylvania, equivalent to 2400 letters.
This, I promise, could not be done so handilyously on copper in double the time; &
then, you know, our plate will strike 300,000 copies, while the copper plate will
strike only 10,000, and we can print at least sixty times as fast.
Dr. Matthews has resigned the Chancellorship of the University, & Mr.
Flagglinghams is appointed to succeed him. He will accept, if the University is
freed from debt, and an effort is now making to accomplish this object.
Your room will not be disinterested, as the medical hall is not to be made.
Last year has been a year of very great expense, an immense sum
having been required for the new buildings; whilst it has been a year of little income,
from rents, & this year, if we meet with no disaster, the tide will begin to turn,
& it would not be surprising, if the income from rents & the paper in three years
enabled us to pay all debt & carry description, mortgages & floating debt, &
left us a property, (real estate & the paper) yielding an income of $20,000
per annum. I say this to encourage you when you feel distressed in view of pecuniary
matters, for if you fail to realize enough for your support from your own property
you may calculate confidently, if I am successful, that I will make up the deficiency of
I shall feel very poor & stingy while I am in debt, let my income be as so
large & prospects ever so good; but, if I know myself, I shall be very little
disposed to keep hold of money or to hoard or accumulate, after debts are paid.
It will go very freely for experiments, for public objects, & for the aid of
any who may need aid. It was never any part of my plan or wish to lay the
prosperity on the corner of Napan & Beckham, or to leave Mrs Drake's house & lot, although
I always thought it a property that would yield a large interest if properly improved;
but I would have preferred a less income with less care & less risk. See no
reason yet to change any views. -- There is great care, there is some risk; but
the prospect still is that it will yield a very handsome interest. If we had not
bought it, however, I should now be in a condition to settle down in the family state
& depend freely & liberally for my own support, for the prosecution of experiments, for
public objects &c. Perhaps, in a little time, I may do all these on a larger scale, in
consequence of working, but I do not like the delay. --
The more I think of your telegraph the more I advise it. I speak constantly as one of the most simple and beautiful inventions of any country
or any age. I do not wonder that the savans of the old world speak of it as
cruelty and brutality.
Since the first of January I have resumed the editing of the Observer,
We found that the list was diminishing very sadly under Mr Tracy, although
in some respects a first-rate editor. So much depreciation was felt, that I was under
the necessity of taking the chair again. The list is now going up again, & I am
in hope that Telegraphy will enable us to push it ahead gloriously. If you find
nothing else to do when you get back, we can no doubt make a berth
for you in connection with the paper.
After all, the longer I live, the more thoroughly satisfied I am that it
is of little consequence whether our lot here is marked by prosperity or adversity. The grand
thing is to have the talent, like the bee, of extracting honey from the thorn as well as the
flower. If we are the children of God we can do this, & there is no deprivation in
which we cannot be happy. I have little experience, thus far, of anything in this
life that deserves the name of trial, but I trust, I have in some measure been enabled
to make this improvement of the light afflictions which have fallen to my lot.
Hoping soon to see you, & commending you in my prayers meanwhile
constantly to the God, I am your affectionate brother
Sir Murray Evans

My dear Sir,
Iake the first mo-
ment of rest from the fatigues of my business engage
to apprize you of my arrival yesterday in the Hotel Weiler.
The day before I left Paris I concluded the arrange
ment with the Russian Government through the Baron
Meyen deff, so far as he had power, and shall expect
through the Russian Ministers the answer of Govt
at St. Petersburg by the 10th of May. There are some
points different from those I believe I sketched in
my letter to you of Feb 22d. The second interview the
Baron believed that he had limited the compensation
"half the economy," to 3 years, instead of 5, as both
Mr Amyot and myself understood him to say. He
seemed a little troubled at this, and reproached him
self for not pulling it down in writing at the time,
for he had written 3 years to his Govt and it was too
late to rectify the matter; but he observed that if I
was successful, I might safely rely on the liberal
disposition of the Emperor. It is limited also to the
route from St. Petersburg to Warsaw 800 Miles. I
wish much to see you and with as little delay as
possible, for the time is very limited on account of
the season of the year in which it is necessary to be
in St. Petersburg in order to labor at all. I
was so unfortunate as to miss Dr. Cole by a single
day, he left for the South on Saturday and I arrived
on Sunday night. I regret this extremely for I
wished much conversation with him on points con-
nected with the scientific part of the matter. I re-
ceived yours of the 7th inst. on my arrival. I am
ever exceedingly sorry that my draft should have caused
you any embarrassment. I could not have done
otherwise; the business of the Telegraph Board, the
close required more expenditure to bring it to a successful
issue than I could have anticipated when I gave you my estimate of "100 per month." Of this
I think you will be satisfied, when I shall have
the pleasure of seeing you.
I am quite disappointed
in finding nothing done by Congress, and nothing
accomplished in the way of Company, I had hoped
to find on my return some funds ready for
prosecuting with vigour the enterprise which
I fear will suffer for the want.
I think a moment of my situation, I left New
York for Europe to be gone 3 months, but have been
gone 11 months; my only means of support, which are
in my profession in which I have been compelled to abandon
entirely for the present, giving my undivided time and efforts to this enterprise. I return with not
a farthing in my pocket and have to borrow even for my
meals and even worse than this I have incurred a debt
of rent by my absence which I should have avoided if
98654
had been at home, or rather if I had been aware that
I should have been obliged to stay so long abroad.
I do not mention this in the way of complaint, but merely
to show that I also have been compelled to make great sacrifices
for the common good and am willing to make more
yet if necessary. If the enterprise is to be pursued, we must
all in our various ways put the shoulder to the wheel.
I wish much to see you and talk over all matters, for
it seems to me that the present state of the enterprise
in regard to Russia affects vitally the whole concern.
Excuse me at present for I have not recovered
from the effects of the voyage.
Truly your friend's Sust as ever
Sand J. B. Morse

Under date of August 12, Mr. Merse
New York August 15th 1839
again writes to Mr Smith:
My dear Sir
I received yours of the 2nd inst. and the
paper accompanying it containing the notice of Mr
Chamberlain. I had previously been assured that
my forebodings were true in regard to his fate. I
sent you a New York Observer a few days ago giving a
more full account of him which I hope you
have received.
We shall hear double lies from Mr
Brown, when he returns, what was done by Mr C.
in regard to the Telegraph in the East. Our enterprise
abroad is declined to give us anxiety if not to end in
disappointment. I have just received a letter from
Mr Amyott who was to have been my companion to Rus-
sia, and leave from him the unwelcome news that the
Emperor has decided against the Telegraph. I
have been expecting a letter from the Baron Meyen-
dorff every day, for Mr Amyot informs me that he in-
tended writing me. The Emperors objections are, it seems,
that "malveillance can easily interrupt the communica-
tion". Mr Amyot scouts the idea and writes that he
refuted the objection to the satisfaction of the Baron
who, indeed, did not need the reputation for himself for
that whole matter was fully discussed between us when
in Paris. The papers I should judge from the tone of
Mr. Amyck's letter was much disappoimented, yet as a
faithful and obedient subject of one whose may is
nay, I will be cautious in so expressing himself as to
be self committed. Thus, my dear Sir, prospects a
broad look dark; I turn with some faint to my own
Country again Will Congress do anything? or is my
time and your generous zeal and pecuniary sacri
fice to end only in disappointment? If so I can
bear it for myself but I feel it most keenly for those
who have been engaged with me, for you, for the Mail
Tails & Dr. Gale. But I will yet hope. I dont know
that our enterprise looks darker than Fulton's once
appeared. There is no intense difficulty, the de-
pressing causes are extinsic. I hope to see you soon
and talk over all our affairs. You wish me to bring
the Telegraph with me. In the hope of doing this I
have delayed my journey for some days, and shall
endeavour to bring the new instrument which has
been unavoidably delayed by the Mechanician.
My present purpose is to leave for the East on
this day week (Monday) and probably by Saturday,
or the Monday following may see you in Portland.
I have footed up my accounts abroad and find
a balance in my favor of about 200 francs. This
result may perhaps be varied in some slight degree as the
changing of pounds Sterling into francs and dollars may have
caused some error. – I hope to see Dr. Gale before I leave
he is daily expected from the South
Whistled with real esteem
Your friend and Servt
Sam'l C. J. Mare
Sam C J Mare

Master Wm. Lander came immediately to his
assistance, but not being a good swimmer
nor very strong, Charles carried him
under. Your Son Charles came immedi-
ately, so soon as he discovered their danger
related William & soon brought Master
Blake to a footing, while Wm. swam
out. But for the timely & efficient assistance
given by your Son there is reason to fear
that both boys would have perished.
We had contented to let them go to
this place, a Mill pond, only because
he had become weary of their impotency.
They will certainly never be allowed
to go again when they will be in
any sort of danger. It is a little
remarkable that, as the boys were
leaving home, help in earnest & half
in pleasantness I made your Son responsible
for the safety of his companions;
a responsibility which he very readily
accepted.
I am happy to be able to say that
Charles advances in arithmetic; We found
his deficiencies and that he thought
it advisable that besides the French
this should be his only study.
I shall probably be in your city
before many days and shall be pleased
to answer all the inquiries you will
naturally have to make.
With much esteem
Your Old Friend
P. De F. Elz

Dear Sir,
I cannot but express the high gratification with which I witnessed the operation of your
beautiful and ingenious Electro magnetic Engine. It performed more than promised. I was told
that it would raise 500 pounds of steel in one minute. It raised 523 pounds of steel in a minute. From these
data any one can calculate the power which an erection of machinery on this principle, can be able to avail
I have seen a number variety of electro magnetic engines in operation, among which I have also
had submitted to my inspection examination several plans not yet completed. Of these latter I need not speak, as trial
alone will test satisfactorily the principles on which they are constructed, but of the former I can say with truth
Yours is the most powerful, and contained within the smallest compass of any I have seen. The peculiarities
which pleased me in your engine, are the novel construction and arrangement of the magnets and armatures, and the
ingenious mode of breaking and closing the circuit.
and the individual connections of each Plate of the battery with its own conductor.

BE IT KNOWN, that I, Samuel F. B. Morse, now of Poughkeepsie, in the county of
Dutchess, in the State of New York, have invented a new and useful apparatus for, and
a system of transmitting intelligence between distant points, by means of Electro-Mag-
netism, which puts in motion machinery for producing sounds or signs, and recording
signs upon paper or other suitable material, which invention I denominate the Ame-
rican Electro-Magnetic Telegraph, and that the following is a full, clear and exact de-
scription of the principle or character thereof, which distinguishes it from all other Tele-
graphs previously known, and of the manner of making and constructing said apparatus
and applying said system, reference being had to the accompanying drawings, making
part of this specification in which Examples 1, 2, and 3, show my system of signs consisting
of a combination of dots and spaces, and of dots, spaces and horizontal lines intended to
represent—Example 1, signs for numbers; Example 2, signs for compound numbers; Example
3, signs for letters; all which signs may also represent words or sentences. Examples 4,
5 and 6, are specimens of the form of type used for regulating the imprinting of the signs.
Example 7, is the type rule; Example 8, apparatus for connecting and breaking the
Electrical or Galvanic circuit. Example 10, Fig. 1, is a perspective view of the regis-
tering apparatus, Fig. 2, a top plan, Fig. 3, a side elevation of the train of wheels moving
the paper and regulating its motion, Fig. 4, a sectional elevation of the Registering lever
and parts appended thereto, Fig. 5, alarm apparatus. Example 11, is a diagram, show-
ing the relative positions of the different parts of an approved form of apparatus, including
a combination of circuits.
Prior to my first application for a patent, it had been essayed to use the currents of
Electricity or Galvanism for Telegraphic purposes, either by decomposition or the action
or exercise of the deflective force of a current upon a magnetized bar or needle, which de-
composition or deflection required to be noted by ocular inspection at the instant the sign
was made.
By my invention the intelligence can be transmitted, and imprinted on paper or other
suitable substance, without requiring the aid of any person at the station to which the
communication is transmitted, so as to be read at any time thereafter.
My apparatus for this purpose consists of two principal parts or combinations.
The first part consists of a Galvanic Battery, or any known generator of Galvanism or
Electricity, a Galvanic or Electric circuit, composed of any known conductors of Electricity,
a port rule and signal lever or other contrivance for closing and breaking the circuit, all in
combination with an Electro-Magnet, or device by which the motive power of the Electric or
Galvanic current, which I call Electro-Magnetism, may be developed and applied to give
motion to other machinery for the purpose of marking or imprinting intelligible characters,
signs or letters at any distances; the conductors may be suspended in the air upon posts
or otherwise, or buried in the ground, being always well insulated at the posts or in the
ground. This combination is illustrated in the annexed drawings in Example 11, Fig. 2,
where D indicates the battery; a, a, the circuit; B, the signal lever; and
C the Electro-Magnet.
The new parts and the operation of this portion of my apparatus, I thus further
describe, viz: at any convenient point in the circuit, (generally near the generator) a
break is made in the conductor, and the two ends thereof are immersed in mercury cups
as shown in the drawings at E, E, Fig. 1, example S. To connect the circuit, I employ
an inverted V formed piece of metal or other proper connector A, suspended over the
mercury cups E, E, in the end of a horizontal lever denominated in said drawing the “signal
lever,” whose fulcrum is at a, so that when the connector A is dipt into the cups, the cir-
cuit is completed. Between the fulcrum and connector A, there is affixed to the under
side of the lever and projecting downward a triangular tooth b, which bears on the upper
surface of the types about to be described, and is raised or lowered by them.
The lever may be counter-balanced by a weight or its equivalent as at C, to make it
move easily. The types are composed of flat straight strips of metal, as shown in exam-
pies 4 and 5, of the drawings herunto annexed, having their upper edges indented to suit
the character to be represented, and which will be hereinafter more fully set forth in the
description of the operation of the machine. The indentations are made of sufficient
depth to allow the connector A to be plunged into the mercury cups, and the highest sur-
face raises it from them. It is obvious that the forms of the upper surface of the types
may be reversed, and the cog b placed on the other side of the fulcrum, and the same
effect would be produced. The types are set up and confined in a Rule to form any re-
quired sentences in one long line. This rule, denominated in the drawings, Example 8,
“Type Rule,” has on its under side a rack that gears into a pinion x, on a shaft under the
grooved railings D, of common construction, on which said rule slides, and is directed
under the cog b, on the lever; the types are advanced at a regular speed by the applica-
tion of any convenient power to the pinion x, and bring the notches, or raised and de-
pressed parts successively under the cog b.
The mercury cups may be dispensed with, and any other convenient metallic con-
98760
taet be made to accomplish the same end, and the closing and breaking of the circuit may
be effected by applying the hand or any other machinery to the signal lever, or by any
other mode adapted to the same end. The closing of the circuit by the depression of the
signal lever, causes the electric current to run upon the circuit a, a, Ex. 11, Fig. 2, and
through the helices of the Electro-Magnet C, which is thus charged with power to move
any machinery which may be connected with it in a proper manner.
The second part of my invention, consists of a Register for Recording the characters,
signs or letters transmitted from any distance, and is composed of the following parts in
combination, viz: a bent lever A, as shown most distinctly in example 10, Fig. 4. To
one arm of this lever there is attached one or more pencils, fountain pins, or other suit-
able marking instruments, B, directly under which is placed a suitable cylinder, D, over
which the paper passes on which the marking for signs are made.
This cylinder turns on its axis, and is connected by a train of wheels and pinions with
a barrel m, Fig. 3, example 10, of common construction which is driven by a weight and
cord wound thereon, and also with a fly K of same Fig. which regulates its motion. To
the other arm of the lever (which is also an armature) is affixed a spiral spring i, as seen
in Example 10, Figs. 1 and 4.
Near the cylinder D, a reel or spool, d, is placed, on which a strip of paper or other
markable material is wound, the end of which is carried over the cylinder D, and is confined
thereon by means of two tapes and endless bands or their equivalents, one at each edge
which pass around two pulleys b, b, one on each side of cylinder D. This is clearly
represented in Figures 2 and 4, Example 10. The clock work is kept at rest by a detent
g, in contact with the fly wheel k, in Fig. 3, and connected with the lever as shown in
Figure 5.
To the Register may be attached an alarm bell as shown in Example 10, Fig. 5, the
machinery for striking which may be variously modified and therefore need not to be
described.
The Register, or second part of my Invention, is operated upon by the first part, in the
following manner, viz: the short end of the pen lever in the second part as seen in example
10, Fig. 4, is an armature f, which is brought in proximity to the Electro-Magnet C, in
the circuit a, a, as shown in Example 11, Fig. 2, and in Example 10, Fig. 4. The Electro-
Magnet C, being charged by closing the circuit, attracts the armature, bringing it nearly
in contact, thus imparting a movement to the lever A. By this movement of the lever,
the detent, Fig. 5, Example 10, is removed from the fly wheel, and the clock work begins
to move, carrying the paper over the cylinder D, and at the same time the fountain pen,
pencil, or other marking instrument is, by the action of the lever, set in motion.
The circuit being broken, the lever is brought back to its position by the spiral spring
i, and by the closing and breaking of the circuit, more or less rapidly, dots and spaces and
marks of any required length are made upon the paper and in any required combinations.
My system of characters consists of dots, spaces and lines, variously combined, to form
letters and other characters, a specimen of which is represented in Examples 1, 2, and 3.
To make a dot, a notch or indentation is required in the types, into which the cog or
tooth on the "signal lever" will fall and instantly rise from, as the types move onward and
when a line is to be formed on the paper at the Register as a sign, the notch in the type is
extended, so that the lever will remain down for a space of time, sufficient to make the
line required.
The alarm bell shown at A, Example 10, Fig. 5, may be struck by means of a ham-
mer, actuated by a supplementary Electro-Magnet placed in the same circuit as that first
named. Any convenient number of Registers and Registering stations, may be connected
with the same circuit, all constructed and operating as above described.
To extend more effectually the communication by my apparatus, I adopt the following
arrangement, whereby I can use any number of additional batteries or generators of Elec-
tricity, and by which I can connect progressively any number of consecutive circuits,
viz: I place at any point in the first circuit an Electro-Magnet, and opposite its poles I
place an armature on a lever, like that described for Registering, but instead of using the
said lever to mark with, I use it to close and break a second circuit, precisely as the
signal lever is used to close and break the first circuit.
The second circuit has an independent battery, and may be used to work a Register
or other apparatus for Registering, or to close and break a third circuit or both, and thus
by a combination of circuits the requisite power can be obtained at any distances, ad-infi-
num. This combination is shown in Example 11, Fig. 1.
It will be observed that my vocabulary system of signs or secret writing by cypher
can be conveniently used in communicating by this Telegraph, and any mode of closing
and breaking a circuit may be adopted, the object being to do so at proper intervals.
CLAIMS.
First. Having thus fully described my Invention, I wish it to be understood that I
do not claim the use of the Galvanic current or currents of Electricity, for the purpose of
Telegraphic communications generally, but what I specially claim as my Invention and
Improvement, is making use of the motive power of magnetism, when developed by the
action of such current or currents, substantially, as set forth in the foregoing description of
the first principal part of my Invention, as means of operating or giving motion to machi-
nery, which may be used to imprint signals upon paper or other suitable material, or to
produce sounds in any desired manner for the purpose of Telegraphic communication at
any distances. The only ways in which the Galvanic current has been proposed to be
used prior to my Invention and Improvement, were by bubbles resulting from decomposi-
tion, and the action or exercise of Electrical power upon a magnetized bar or needle, and
the bubbles, and the deflections of the needles thus produced, were the subjects of in-
spection and had no power, or were not applied to record the communication. I there-
fore, characterize my Invention as the first Recording or Printing Telegraph by means of
Electro-Magnetism.
There are various known modes of producing motions by Electro-Magnetism, but
none of these had been applied, prior to my Invention and Improvement, to actuate or
give motion to printing or recording machinery, which is the chief point of my Invention
and Improvement.
Second. I also claim, as my Invention and Improvement, the employment of the
machinery called the Register or Recording instrument, composed of the train of clock
wheels, cylinders and other apparatus or their equivalents, for moving the material upon
which the characters are to be imprinted, and for imprinting said characters substantially,
as set forth in the foregoing description of the second principal part of my Invention.
Third. I also claim as my Invention and Improvement, the combination of machinery
herein described, consisting of the generator of Electricity, the circuit of conductors, the
contrivance for closing and breaking the circuit, the Electro-Magnet, the pen or contri-
vance for marking, and the machinery for sustaining and moving the paper all together,
constituting one apparatus or Telegraphic machine, which I denominate the American
Electro-Magnetic Telegraph.
Fourth. I also claim as my Invention, the combination of two or more Galvanic or
Electric circuits, with independent batteries substantially by the means herein described,
for the purpose of obviating the diminished force of Electro-Magnetism in long circuits, and
enabling me to command sufficient power to put in motion registering or recording ma-
chinery at any distances.
Fifth. I claim as my Invention, the system of signs consisting of dots and spaces,
and of dots, spaces, and horizontal lines, for numerals, letters, words, or sentences sub-
stantially, as herein set forth and illustrated, for Telegraphic purposes.
Sixth. I also claim as my Invention, the system of signs, consisting of dots and
spaces, and of dots, spaces and horizontal lines substantially, as herein set forth and
illustrated, in combination with machinery, for recording them as signals for Telegraphic
purposes.
Seventh. I also claim as my Invention, the types, or their equivalent, and the type
Rule, and Port Rule, in combination with the signal lever or its equivalent, as herein des-
cribed, for the purpose of closing and breaking the circuit of Galvanic or Electric con-
ductors.
Eighth. I do not propose to limit myself to the specific machinery, or parts of ma-
chinery described in the foregoing specification and claims, the essence of my Invention
being the use of the motive power of the Electric or Galvanic current, which I call Elec-
tro-Magnetism, however developed, for marking or printing intelligible characters, signs
of letters at any distances, being a new application of that power, of which I claim to be
the first Inventor or discoverer.

New Haven, June 31st 1840.
My dear Father,
I suppose you would like to be informed of your
news. I suppose my daughter Susan's safe arrival, is it down to
write you the very next day after I arrived. -- We had a delightful
passage up the Sound. -- Mr. Luelton introduced another lady,
who was placed in his care, with three little boys. Her name
is Mrs. Richards, a very sweet lady from this city, and I became
quite well acquainted with her, before we reached N.Y. Heaven.
The sun came out quite bright, when we were about half way
here, so after all we had a delightful day. -- Mr. Luelton rode
up with me to Mrs. Deverson's, when we arrived about half past
one, and found a warm welcome. I am sure I thought to be
very thankful that I found such good company, for Mr. L.
was very attentive to me, and I felt as if I was well provided
for. The family were at dinner when I arrived -- they said
they had quite given up in despair of seeing me, but were very
glad to see me. The father, you do not know how beautiful
New Haven looks, from an unvarnished view, and the fine elm
trees in their glory; the new houses that have been erected since
I was here, are very handsome. Give me N.Y. Haven for my home.
After dinner I laid down & took a short nap, and
towards nine -- Henrietta Silliman called in. She came to see
98767
Maria, not knowing that I was here, but seemed very glad to
see me. She does not expect to go West in four or five days
as she is waiting for her brother in law, Mr Currah. After
Maria and myself took a stroll up in the avenue and as we
were coming back met Hemmen, who insisted upon our calling
us, a few moments, so we went in, and saw Mrs Fillman,
and Julia. They enquired particularly after you, & Uncle
We have came back and stopped in to Dr Taylor, a few
moments found them & her mother he only said now at
Home. They gave me a warm welcome, and wanted to hear
all about your mission, and the rest of the Morris. Mrs Taylor
says, I must write Uncle Sidney, that she wishes him to come
back and make her a visit this Summer, for she longs to see him
again & hopes he will not fail to accept her invitation.
The boys, she has thought for some time of writing him a
letter, especially to invite him, and hopes to hear that he has
accepted it. - Mrs Bethany Whittlesey was over there, and told
me I must come over and see her.
I am going over to see about Salisbury this morning.
should have gone yesterday, but heard Mr Elias Edwards I
was going to visit on a journey that afternoon, and concluded
I would wait till after the trouble of departure was over,
before I went.
Every thing looks so delightful to me, father, the streets are

the Division has just put her head in, & says I must give

it looks very much like rain, this morning, and is quite

New Haven July 20th 1840.
My Dearest Father,
Your letter dated the 9th only reached me, if you
will believe it, last Sunday eve; and to day, upon returning from a
delightful ride to East Rock I was rather very happy by the receipt
of another epistle from you, which was delivered by Mr Davis, during
my absence. I have been wondering for a long long while, why
your father did not write me, but presumed it was owing to your
being so busy. While I thought Charley might have at least sent me a
few lines, to let me know you had not quite forgotten your runaway
daughter. I was so disappointed in the other day in regard to sending you, in
several of my friends, a letter. My package was all in readiness to be
sent by Boston Edward Salisbury and Cally, who were going to the
city, I shall very probably appeared to take letters, when they went.
They were entertained for a three days on account of the illness of two
Worleys little daughter Agnes - do I keep my package for them when to
my surprise and disappointment on calling the same day, I found
they had gone. It seems Captain C. Hall sent me word by his man, that
he should go on the morrow - but the servant says it to the men - as
thus they were all written for nothing. - I wrote Charley until
you a letter together - but as it was full of inquiries why you did
not write etc. I understand upon receiving yours of the 9th not to
send it, but write another - so here I am at my third epistle.
I mean to send this in the office to make sure sending it.
Genius or Catty went to Morris Corn for a little while -- and then returned
to their house -- when I had the pleasure of seeing them very often. They
sent in for me twice to dine with them -- the first time I was engaged
to spend the day at Mr. Thalledens' Hermitage, and the second
I went -- and had a very pleasant visit -- They think your
letters an excellent one & consider he hopes to see you if he
stays long enough in the city. They have now gone to Princeton
in N. Jersey to stay some length of time, as the physicians think
sea bathing will be good for his Catty.-- About Calisburg is very
much taken up in attending to Cadie Martha who is now able to
talk out -- I am in their glee, & she is very kind to me, -- always
ingenuous when I have heard from you -- & it was not three
evenings to tea sociably, last week -- to the Taylor -- Prof. Filliman
& a Mrs Hotchkiss -- a cousin of the Denisons. -- We met Mrs Hubbard,
her daughter (Faith that was) and she is very pleasant to have me come
and visit her in Hanover, another season -- Her husband is Josephus
Van. Do she used to be a dear friend of my mother's? I should be
delighted to go -- and old
time friends to have me come and visit her in Hanover, another
season -- I am very happy here, dear father -- and friends are around
me -- and my home at Olds Denisons is delightful. The tall stately
Elms -- despite it quite cool, even during the vexing weather we
have had for a week past -- I hardly trust, I shall not in the
mildest of terms complain, forget the quiet of home -- and trust I may
use them right. -- I attend the Center Church & sit with Aunt
Lucy's family morning -- & in the afternoon go with Miss Susan Taylor to
the Village Chapel to hear Prof. Ficker -- sometimes attend the Episcopal
with the Miss Denisons.--
Now give it was in Uncle Charles to send me your
money -- was he not, dear father -- how can I ever repay him
for his many kindnesses to me -- I was thinking how would
it do to let it remain in the Bank, and then, as I wantell
it -- Can any one do so? Then when I want any little
article a little out of the common line -- it can suit for the most -- or if I
wish to contribute to Benevolent Soc. can draw from that. If you
think however father, that it would do better in Harriet's hands -- I
will abide by your opinion -- I have wanted for some time past
one of those large black red Skirts with fringe -- that the Ladies wear
so much in their cloys. Almost every young lady has one been, & I
find they are very convenient indeed -- still as it was more a luxury
I concluded I would do without one -- seeing I must draw up on Harriet's
liberty for the Unit. I think now I can afford to get one, and dear
father, if it is not too much to ask -- some day when you are going down town
with you get one one -- I should like to have Harriet Pitts judgement
about that dress -- not so much if you would call on her -- she would
accompany you, & know with pleasure. -- I do not wish one over
seven or eight dollars -- and please take the money from Harriet. Much will
& Charles would take it to Albany -- she would send it next day by Mr
Tucker -- I feel very to trouble you -- perhaps if you give the money to Harriet,
she would give it to some one, and purchase it, without troubling you to ask
-- pay her -- I must write Harriet Charles again -- and thank her for
this very pleasant & unexpectative present -- You speak of a letter you
have sent me -- I have not yet it yet, but presume I shall be informed
when the penny post comes -- We have had very hot weather here for
a week past, but last Sunday there was a Local Thunder Showers -- & the
day the air is cool & invigorating -- Early this morning Miss O's cousin called
in a carriage & took us all out to the Rocks we rolled half way up the
Mr -- then got out & walked up to the top, & the little house there is built
then for the recreation of visitors -- We came back, Branch pleased with
our game -- The Taylors say, after I have done here -- I must come &
make them a visit & then Margaret Sherman wants me to visit her,
do you must not expect, dear father -- that Miss Davis will be ready
to return quite so soon, as part often commerce -- You had better
let me remain till cool weather -- for my health is so good here --
But we will talk about that, when you come up -- We have plenty
of fine tea -- & flowers as Mrs J. has a fine garden --
do not, think I forget you, dear father, Annie so many friends. Do you
still think of letting me keep house for you in the University? I like the
plan - provide me & can have a female companion there. - Why is Charley
so silent - do ask him a copy of the Mrs - weekly - but he must not write
on them, tell him - I am glad to hear such good accounts of dear
little Sue - also of Charley - as it is so evil his affection. I must go out to
return some of my calls - for last week I did not make any. It was so hot.
I hope Mr. Gourand will be put down, finally - I have seen several proofs
in the U. of Conn. relative to it - on your letter. Every one thinks you
likeness excellent - that has been put to the Hill House, but they were all out, & should so again soon. Mrs Demer de-
liver her best regards to you - says she hopes to see you Commencement.
Write much love to Uncle - Cousin & brother for me - dear father - and accept
a great deal for yourself - from J. ran as I depart
your

Monsieur et Ami,
La personne qui vous remettra cette lettre est un jeune homme
que j'ose prendre la liberté de vous recommander avec la
plus vive inttance & à qui je vous prie de rendre tous les
services qu'il vous sera possible comme s'il s'agissait de moi-même.
Je le connais depuis son enfance; la famille est presque la
mienne tant je lui suis lié d'amitié et constante amitié.
Il est très instruit & plein de moyens intellectuels: c'est ce qu'on
peut appeler un excellent & honnête jeune homme. Une longue
maladie lui a fait perdre la carrière de notariat qu'il avait
embrassée d'abord & c'est par une vocation particuliere qu'il
porte maintenant à courir les chances du commerce au delà
des mers. Veuillez donc le recevoir, je vous en prie, avec la
vonté que je vous connais si bien & le recommander de votre
cote, si cela est possible, à tous ceux qui pourront lui être
utiles: je me porte pour son répondant pour tous les
rapports.
Parlons maintenant un peu de nos affaires. Vous savez
que j'ai livré fin janvier dernier a M. le baron de
Meyerndorff un télégraphe électrique pour lequel il m'a
payé seulement mes déboursés, la somme de Deux cent trente
francs. Il était si pressé pour cette livraison que je n'ai
pas eu le temps peut être de lui donner la dernière main;
j'aurais voulu le faire fonctionner plus longtemps sous mes yeux,

attache aucune importance car je ne doute pas que votre

capable de faire; je vous prierai seulement de vouloir bien me

Saint Petersbourg presque immédiatement après mon livraison

parler de lui. Vu où il est de même de vous? Je l'ignore.
Quand recevrai-je de vos nouvelles? je n'en sais pas
défendant. Les rapports actuels de notre gouvernement avec

Dear Father
It was very fortunate that we decided going
home by the way of Baltimore, else I should not have been
master so happy by the receipt of your kind letter.
We were all glad to hear New York friends were well, and it
will not be long now before we are in the city again, as Uncle
has decided to return either on the ensuing Monday or
Tuesday - and Mrs. Hooker will probably go with us, and
perhaps Mrs. Littman. It was quite a surprise to me, when
Mark said he thought he should return to Iowa, however
I expect you, dear father, that for my part I shall be
very glad to get back again - although I have enjoyed
the journey exceedingly. - But I want to see you
again, and I am tired of living in a trunk, of packing
and un packing - & so is Aunt Kate - I often think - if I
get weary now, that will it be when I get abroad - but
I do not mean to borrow trouble - I know I shall have
many home sick hours, when separated so widely from you,
dear father - for even now there are times when I get home
sick, and feel as if I could not hear the thought of leaving
friends - and country. I know it will be for my good,
and I shall cheer myself up by thinking that perhaps
you, write some over and join us, and thank Charles too. I see
by a few ink papers that this has a vital just arrived
from Guayama and I do hope it has brought me a letter
from Uncle - for it seems as if I could not give up his accom-
panying us.
And now I suppose you would like to know when we have
been wandering and what we have seen and heard in the
course of our travels. Last Saturday morning we left Philadel-
phia for Baltimore and took rooms at the Exchange Hotel,
but I must say it is the best house I ever saw in; every-
thing is so neat, and the table so fine, that we are all quite
in love with it. I have a pleasant little chamber at the
door that leads into Wales, so it is very pleasant for such a
scramble as I am. We took a walk out to see the Lewis-

old school-mate married aettached here but as her name was
Mrs Smith, our beach of converse proved fruitless. As you see

Dear Father,
I was just going to put a letter in the office
saying you might expect me in the city on Tuesday morning
next, with Linlin Joe when your truly welcome letter
arrived, and changed all my plans completely.
Sincerely do I hope you will come on -- and let it
be, your father as near the 28th as possible, because
Charles' vacation is only Wednesday, and it will be keeping
him from College. I am really sorry that I cannot
return with you for I shall have to go with
any opportunity that presents itself -- as Cousin Joe will return
on Monday, because his vacation is out on Wednesday.
I should like to return at least two days before
he will go. I have many little things to do -- and
arrange, that can only be done in the city --
you know I can stay at the Kittilans, who
now live in Grand St -- and they will be very
happy to have me too.
By the way, dear father - there has a poor woman been
making me some under garments, and I was to pay
her Wistham. & she would see to it. Will you let Charity
take them 1s 70d - and say it was for the place?
It will oblige me much if you will.
I have a flying report that my friend & school mate
Sam Shepherd of Bengal, thinks of accompanying me to
Bordeaux - so if there has a letter come to the office post marked
Washingtoon, Co - I shall begin to think it true. Please bring
on all letters that may have come - dear father. I hope
the will go - and am very anxious to ascertain the truth
of such a report. As to Lord Charles, I fear I shall
have to give him up. It seems very strange that he
has not wrote.
I shall not engage myself dear father, and indeed
he does not seem to think I would be doing myself
justice to do so. I have always been strongly opposed
to long engagements - especially of such a length as one
would necessarily be - four and even five years.
Though I think now my affection for him would not
change, by a voyage across the ocean - still I think
you engaging myself - but some improvement change
my feelings entirely, for I know I am rather fickle.
He has sent me a long letter for you, this morning
under the belief that I was to leave on the morning
but as that plan is changed I presume he will
prefer taking it back & waiting to see you himself.
The family have been very polite to me. Still they discourage
him, by telling him he stands but a poor chance -- so long
an interval must elapse before we can be united -- and I
Shall be placed soon, in such different circumstances.
I know that he loves me truly -- and would be willing to
make any sacrifice for me. Lewis he wrote that letter, I
have received some more notes from him -- and he is willing
to have me go abroad free, and if my affection does not
change, to be engaged on my return.
Then is brother Charles? Why will you not let him come
to us with you, dear father, and leave me home to
see him? His friends and relatives would be delighted
to have him. -- So bring on your Daguerreotype -- for

taken, by you. -- I hope you will at last call
Mell Balliett at No 4 Howard St on your way here

Your petition in relation to the Electro-Magnetic Telegraph having been before Congress for many Long Years and no final action
having been had thereon, I thought I would write you on the subject and inform you that nothing had ever been done by Congress at any of the subsequent Sessions and propose to obtain this claim for you for the Patent Right as I am confident I could render you services of great
value towards obtaining it. The Printed Journals of the House of Representatives show that nothing has transpired on the subject. The opposition that will be made on account of the great expense attendant on laying down the wire and constructing the appurtenances of the Telegraph is the greatest difficulty that will have to be contended with. It appears by the newspapers (some time since) that an Association was about to be formed for the purpose of establishing a line of Electrics Magnetic Telegraph, but as I have never heard that this Association was formed or effected anything which if they had would have been known, I presume there was not a sufficient subscription for the effectuation of the design of forming a Company. The Committee of Commerce of the Senate last Session reported a Bill for $50000 to make an experimental test of Genon's plan of Telegraphs. This Telegraph of Genon's being on the Semaphoric plan can be established with much greater economy than yours, which may cause much opposition from that score, to yours, and a preference for Genon's with many members and no doubt there will be a hard struggle by the friends of that plan in Congress in favor of that. There is so possibility that this claim can be obtained, although it would be an extremely difficult task, from the very low state of the Treasury which causes a severe scrutiny of claims, and from the struggle of both parties to cut down all expenditures to the lowest possible point, and from the fact that so great is the delay that any claim which is admitted on all hands to be perfectly just has very little chance of passing, so great are the delays so very numerous the forms which a claim has to go through -- first through one House and then through the other, and only on Sundays and Saturdays are claims taken up, and very often they are passed aside even on three days by the press of the National business. Also the immense amount of the National business and the great press by claimants to draw the attention of Members to their respective matters so completely absorbs their whole time that it is very difficult to get a claim of any kind through.
I think having to pass both Houses it is with difficulty that it can be procured to be reported from the Committees in time to pass one House before the close of a Session, much less to go through the Committees and the Senate's forms and pass the other before its close: as Committees will only take up claims in the order in which they were referred to them, the Chairman divides the

PRIVATE CIRCULAR
To the Members of the Association for procuring from me an Historical Painting.
New York, Nov. 30. 1841.
Dear Sir,—In the year 1837, an Association was formed, of which you were a member, for the purpose of commissioning
me to execute a large Historical picture. Forty-five shares, of $50 each share, were subscribed, payable by $5 per share
quarterly, making a total of $2250, or $225 per quarter.
On calling for the first instalment from the subscribers, there were but.............. $205
dollars collected, leaving a deficit for the first quarter of......................... 20 dollars.
On the second instalment but...................................................... 170
dollars were collected, leaving a deficit on the second quarter of.................... 55 dollars
On the third instalment but...................................................... 135
dollars were collected, leaving a deficit on the third quarter of.................... 90 dollars.
thus making on the three installments a Total deficit of...................... 165 dollars!!
This diminution in such a rapid ratio of the collections of a quarterly sum, small at most, alarmed me, and I found it ne-
cessary seriously to calculate the cost of the enterprise in which I had embarked. Having no means aside from this subscrip-
tion, it was indispensably necessary to be assured of sufficient capital before I could advance another step. At this junc-
ture, my attention was directed by a letter from the Secretary of the Treasury at Washington, to my invention of the Electro-
magnetic Telegraph, made several years before. The attention of the government being directed to this subject, the Telegraph
offered in the opinion of my friends, the readiest and quickest mode of supplying myself with means for a future prosecution of
my commission. Accordingly at once requested the Secretary to give me an order for a loan of $5000 to be applied to the
three installments, until I had ascertain the proceeds with the Telegraph. I need not give the details of more than three years
labors, hopes, and disappointments, in waiting for the action of our own and foreign governments. It is sufficient to say that my
expectations, or rather those of my friends, so far as pecuniary profit is concerned, have been vain. I have as yet not realized
one cent, and I thus find myself farther from my object than ever. Upon deliberately considering the matter, the late winter and
spring, I came to the determination, in the first place, to free myself from the pecuniary obligations under which I had long
lain to my friends of the Association, and I commenced a systematic economy and penchance by which I had gradually to
amass the money for that purpose, which sum it would have been impossible for me to raise to $510. Three hundred dollars
of this sum I had already laid down when an article in the N. York Mirror of the 16th Oct. determined me at once to commence
the refunding of the funds received. In compliance with this determination, I have the pleasure herewith to send you
five dollars being the amount collected from you for one instalment on one share according to the
Treasurer's account rendered to me.
I return this sum with many thanks for your kind intentions, sincerely regretting that circumstances beyond my control should
have prevented the accomplishment of my wishes and those of my friends. Although as yet frustrated, I do not entirely
despair; a system of financial obligation is of all things to me most fatal to that independence of mind which is absolutely
necessary to a free exercise of its higher powers, and in thus freeing myself from this obligation, I hope you will see in it the
evidence, not that I abandon my enterprise, nor that I am insensible to those other obligations which gratitude towards each, and
all of the Association imposes, but, (as matters now stand,) that I have taken the first necessary step to the final accomplish-
ment of my design.
With sincere respect, your most obedient servant,
Samuel F. B. Morse.
