My dear Sir.
I have just received another letter from Mr. Isaac
A. Coffin from Washington in relation to the Telegraph.
I gave him to understand last Summer that it was
favorable to his proposition but that I could do nothing
without consulting the other proprietors. From you I
received a definite answer and power to propose certain
terms, but not from Mr. Alfred Vail who wished to con
sult his brother. It is perhaps my fault that he has
not answered definitely as I penciled on recently read
ing his letter he waited for a reply to my letter, so that
I have not a power of Attorney to act for him. From Mr.
Galt I expect one in a few days. Indeed my dear Sir
Something ought to be done to carry forward this enterprise
that we may all receive what I think we all deserve. The
whole labor and expense of moving at all, devolves on me,
and I have nothing in the world (completely crippled
in means, I have scarcely, (indeed I have not at all,) the
means even to pay the postage of letters on the subject.
I feel it most tantalizing to find that there is a move
ment in Washington on the subject to know that the Telegraph
will be before Congress this session and from the means
possessed by Lord & Wheatstone (yes Wheatstone who
successfully headed us in England) one or the other of
their two plans will probably be adopted Wheatstone
Samprase you know has a patent here and has expended
$1000. to get every thing prepared for a campaign to carry
his project into operation, and more than this his patent
is dated before mine! My dear Sir to speak as I feel,
I am sick at heart to perceive how easily others, foreign
ers can manage our Congress and can contrive to cheat
our Country out of the honor of a discovery of which the
Country boasts, and our countrymen out of the profit, which
are our due; to perceive how easily they can find men
and means to help them in their plans, and how difficult, may
impossible for us to find either Is it really so?
or am I deceived. What can be done? Do write immediately
and propose something. Will you not be in Washington
this Winter? Will you not call on me as you pass
through New York if you do go?
Genox has his Telegraph on
the Capitol, and a Committee of the Senate reported in
favor of trying him for a short distance, and will pass a
bill this Session if we are not doing something. Some means
some how must be raised. I have been compelled to stop
my machine just at the moment of completion. I cannot
move a step without running in debt, and that I cannot
do.
As to the Company that was thought of to carry the Telegraph
into operation here, it is another of those ignes fatui
that have just led me on to waste a little more time,
money and patience. The gentleman who proposed the matter
was doubtless friendly disposed, but he lacks judgement and perseverance in
98873
a matter of this sort.
If Congress could but pass the bill of 300000 before
them there would be no difficulty. There is no difficulty
in the scientific or mechanical part of the matter,
that is a problem solved. The only difficulty that
remains is obtaining funds which Congress can furnish
to carry it into execution. I have a great deal to
say, but must stop for want of time to write more.
Everything done by me in regard to the Telegraph
is at arms length. I can do nothing without consultation,
and when I wish to consult on the most trivial
thing, I have three letters to write, and a week or ten
days to wait before I can receive an answer. I feel,
at times, almost ready to cast the whole matter to the
winds, and turn my attention forever from the subject.
Indeed I feel almost inclined at times to destroy
the evidences of priority of invention in my possession,
and let Wheatstone and England take the credit of it.
For it is tantalizing in the highest degree to find the
papers and the lecturers boasting of the invention as
one of the greatest of the age, and as an honor to America,
and yet to have the nation by its representatives,
leave the inventor without either the means to fruit
his invention fairly before his Countrymen, or to defend
himself against foreign attack. If I had the means
in any way of support in Washington this winter, I would
go on in the middle of Jan st and push the matter

Dear Sir
Your letter of the 3d inst. was received,
in which you offer me five per cent commission to attend to your claim before Congress.
As from the extreme uncertainty of a claim ever passing Congress after years of
immense labor trouble anxiety variation; it is common to allow even one half, but even the
lowest commission is twenty per cent. But I will vigorously attend to the claim for only
one half of the lowest amount given for ten per cent if it is ever obtained, and if not
obtained after years of trouble, time, labour, expense and fatigue nothing. This certainty
is low enough most especially as I have to take the risk after infinite labor of having no
renumeration. As the appropriation reported by the Committee was much lower than your
estimate which was $20,000, as contained in printed document No 153, and the estimate of
$26,000 comprised compensation for the services of yourself, Mr. Galt & Mr. Vail the
larger sum of $30,000, will, even deducting my commission in case of success leave more than
a full remuneration according to the estimate for yourself and Mr. Galt & Vail, as you
will have a right to apply the additional $4,000 to the contingency of increased payment for the
services of the experiment, as well as to any other item in the estimate; and it being the application
of principles of profound science, you have a right to charge a much higher remuneration than
that in the estimate. Therefore you can afford to allow this commission out of the $30,000
appropriation, but even supposing for a moment that which will not be the case, that it did
not leave enough to compensate the proprietors, you should waive compensation for the present
for services in the experiment, until the Government purchase the Invention, which its
testing it will be a strong step towards. The obtaining the appropriation is Herculean
(and the risk of not doing it after next elections great) compared to the trouble of the experiment
and the undying honor and eternal applause which will be your lot in case it being carried
into effect will alone be a glorious reward for you for the trouble of the experiment. five
per cent as a contingent commission is too little and after spending years of effort might not
succeed: there are hundreds of kinds of businesses where there is no contingency where five per cent
is allowed, but nothing on earth so extremely contingent or uncertain as the passage of a claim
before Congress. Congress being the Legislature of a Nation of over 17,000,000 of population
with a Republican form of Government causes an enormous and unparalleled amount of
business of a National character to be constantly before it. Every Session therefore, it
necessarily leaves an extremely long Calender of unfinished business. The thing is new
untried, and being a matter dependent on the principles of profound Science, it will be
extremely difficult to impress members with its principles. This is a claim, too, more than
ordinarily difficult, in consequence of the rivalry of other plans, and the very powerful in
and influence and headway which those plans have already gained, thus generating
and violent opposition to this. If it should ever get to pass the House, it would meet
the most powerful opposition from the Committee of Commerce of the Senate a Committee
of surpassing talent and energy, who would contend that it was wrong at a time when the
Government was borrowing money, to attempt the most expensive plan, and which was untried, when
this plan was economical and for all practical purposes unsufficient; that their was a plan that
had been demonstrated, and would ridicule this plan as visionary and theoretical; -- and their powerful
opposition is seriously apprehended as an insuperable obstacle to the passage of this
Bill. Therefore, in addition to the two Houses being generally disposed to all claims, and the
State of the Treasury, here is all this tremendous influence which will be directed against
it, which adds infinitely to the difficulty and vastly lessen the chance of obtaining it. I ought in
fair justice if I undertake it, to have the chance of at least ten percent, after many years
of intense labor, many nights during which I shall set up all night relative to this claim,
always laboring days, to advance it, and writing very late at night to promote it -- it may
be obtained -- there being indisputable claims which have been pending for twenty years, is the vast amount and great pressure of the National business. Or claims about which
is no hesitation twenty per cent is allowed, and ten percent on one half the lowest amount
allowed, or a claim to which there is such powerful opposition is certainly low and rarer
and as I should, necessarily from the fact of the favour with which Governor's plan has been
by the Senate (one of its most powerful Committees having made a formal Official Report
strongly in favour of it) be compelled to make every far greater election than usual in relation
to this claim, it would be very hard that I should not have that per centage, and I can
undertake to make the immense exertion, which I know are absolutely necessary for even a
remote possibility to get this claim through, at the risk of obtaining nothing -- and not have
the chance of one half the amount that those do where the amount is admitted by Congress
be due and only awaits legislative authority to settle it. Congress are fearful to allow a
claims from the precedents they set, -- and this will be most violently opposed from the precedents
that it will set -- will be objected that this precedent will draw a large amount from the
Treasury in future to purchase future Patents, for Public Improvements for the Army or Sea
-- and object that it will be quoted as a justification of intolerable appropriation for such purposes
From the very low state of the Treasury from the Tariff coming down to the lowest
state at this time -- and as the Government have confessed their Estimates into the narrowest
profitable limits, and have come into power with the pledge of Reform of expenditure, and the
other party violently oppose all expenditures for fear of consequence of a high Tariff, -- these facts
show that both parties are striving every nerve to cut off expenditures, which will naturally give
the opposition to the claim from both parties, and difficulty of obtaining it. Under all the
circumstances if the above remuneration will be allowed only in case the claim is obtained, and if
not obtained, notwithstanding whatever trouble, time, expense or fatigue, -- it will
make the greatest exertions possible to procure the passage of a Law for the claim, through all
the Committees and all the Stages of both Houses -- infinitely greater exertions I am sure than
any other person whatever ever has, but otherwise I cannot go on, for it is useless for me to
wear out my life on the mere chance for a claim to which there must be the most powerful opposition,
and which therefore whatever may be the efforts, is highly probable to fail
of passing. Please reply immediately on the reception of this on the
above subject of the per-centage, as if I go on with it I wish to state
to you immediately at great length the systematic mode, method, and
exertions which I should adopt to forward it in the most efficient manner
-- that I may know whether I am to go on or not as if I go with this
claim, I wish to commence immediately to make every arrangement necessary to
promote it: and your courtesies in so doing will be at all times reciprocated.
I am With the Highest Esteem & Regard
Your Obd Servt
Isaac N Cofflin

By S.F. B. Morse,
Dear Sir:
Having recently returned to this
City after an absence of nine months, I deem it a duty
I should have discharged longer than this, to inform you of
the reasons why I have not fulfilled the pecuniary
obligation I am under to you for instructing me in the
use of the Daguerreotype. Notwithstanding all my efforts
I found the constant humidity of the atmosphere counter-
quent on incessant rains, baffled all my attempts
to succeed. I then relinquished that employment and
took a small school in the County which has furnished
me with a bare subsistence till now. My prospects,
however, are brightening somewhat as I have recently been
elected Classical teacher in the Cokesburg Manual
School School in this State. My labor in that Insti-
tution will commence with the 1st of February next, and
as soon as I receive the first payment of my Salary I will
forward the amount due you.
Yours with sincere regard and esteem
Charles Taylor

"The diff erence between practical knowledge and theoretical
knowledge is this. The
one contains the elements of an immediate
application, the other not. The one asks what
use can be made of this truth? The other,
what is this truth? Wherein does it consist?
"The former seeks truth on account of the ben e
efit to be derived from it, the latter desires it
on its own account, and not for the sake of
something else, which it is to serve as means.
"In the one case truth is rendered subservient
to selfish interests, in the other it is consid er
ered more valuable than any thing else, the
supreme good. Practical knowledge having only
usefulness in view, must spread itself over a
large field; it thus becomes superficial. But true
knowledge is less practical than that which does
not exhaust its subjects. Truly practical know l
ledge is solid and thorough; but all solid kno w
ledge must be theoretical, must be acquired for its
own sake, and as it is in itself since every relation to something else renders it impure. We will exhibit in a few words two kinds of theory.
Both are united in having the same principles but they differ in the manner of representing them.
The one begins with single facts, observes and examines them, unites such as exhibit essential affinities under a common head, and as those excluded will show something common with each other new classes will be formed, and a number of classes more allied to each other than other will again become subordinate to a higher one. Every day adds new facts, and as the whole exists in its parts, this cannot be seen until all the latter have been collected. No one can say when this will be effected. According to this theory all heads & classes, or rather principles seem to have been gained by observation and by uniting those facts, that show similarity. Yet unless man had formed an idea of union previous to his making experiments, he would I could not think of investigating single cases, since his investigations could not have any Scientific object. This object is the union sought for. The other theory begins, therefore, with the principle of Science, and experience is to corroborate & prove it. It has not suffered itself to be drowned in the constantly increasing number
80
"number of facts, nor to become confused by them. The principle
"is the life of all experiments, and is the same to Science, that the
"centre is to a periphery. All the parts of Science are organized
"by it, and filled with it, as every member of the body indicates
"the presence of the soul. It attracts, what belongs to Science
"and arranges it, and excludes what is foreign to it. This principle
"giving Science a systematical character, throws light
"upon all its parts by the mutual support, they afford to each
"other and which proceeds from their position & relation to each
"other. This theory it cannot be denied, has little reference
"to practice; it will exhaust truth, it will exhibit Science
"as a whole; it does not deduce its rules for action.
"What then is its value? The former theory is engaged with single
"actions, for which it gives the rules, the latter examines the
"general nature of these rules. The former theory reduces
"the many instances of language to general rules,
"the latter unfolds before us the principles of grammar, gives
"us the philosophy of it, and shows the necessity & connexion
"of the many single rules. Both kinds of grammar are necessary.
"They are related to each other as History & the Philosophy of History,
"the latter cannot be written without the former; yet the former
"is a mere collection of dry bones without the latter. The one de-
"mands exact discrimination, and penetrating acuteness; the other
"a productive genius. The one makes fine distinctions in given
"facts; the other derives deep & fruitful ideas from them."

The Geological survey of this state has been completed, and the
final report is in proof. The first volume will appear on the 16th of August.
It has been thought very desirable to give an introduction setting forth the
history of the progress and present condition of literature, science and the arts
in the State of New York. May I duly give to furnish you with notes for a memoir
of this undertaking as relative to the arts of design? The more full the notes
should be, the more useful; yet it is my opinion that such notes as shall be
submitted by the Scientific and literary Gentlemen throughout the state,
shall render it into a brief compendious article. The magnitude of the final
report of the Survey and the interest it is expected to excite seem to favor the
design of making better known to the world the scientific and literary
achievements of the citizens of this State.
Sam. Sis. with my high respect.
Your humble servant.

My Dear Sir,
In reply to your letter of the 17th of
which I have just received, I have the
honor to transmit to you the Catalogues of the Academy of Design for
the years 1841 & 1842, from the files of
which, especially that of the present year
you will learn the general plan, character, &
condition of the National Academy of Design in addition to this information in relation to the
state of the fine arts in this city. It gives me pleasure to state that it is desirous of
giving notice on the introduction to the Academy of several years since Philadelphia took the lead in the encouragement of the Fine Arts; her Academy of Fine
Arts was the first established in the U.S. and for several years the spirit which animated some of her citizens gave her the name of the Athens of America.
BCA
New York soon after established the American Academy of Fine Arts, which has successfully competed with Philadelphia and Baltimore in the taste and zeal for the fine arts. But since the formation of the Academy of Design, however, a manifest revolution has taken place. New York now takes precedence of all cities in the country, in furnishing the simplest means of study to the artist or amateur. There are about 100 artists in the different cities of the United States, and about 70 artists in this city. While in Boston or Baltimore I was in Paris the Arts languish, in New York they flourish; and although they suffer individually with the rest of the cities in the general absurdity, yet they are able to live. The Academy (as is shewn in the Preface of the Catalogue of 1842) has created an embarrassment, and while the effect of the general admiration in diminishing the receipts this present season, gives them some consolation, it amounts to about $10000, while the receipts of the Exhibition at Philadelphia have amounted to $8000. Our Schools of Fine Art are scattered over the country, and if managed with the prudence of real artists have not distinguished themselves. The Academy of Design, if its founders will be accomplished, in making New York the central point of the Arts as it has been of the Common Schools of the country.
thus one of the great designs of the founders of
the Academy, is in a fair way of accomplishment
that of making New-York the great centre
of the Fine Arts, as it has long been of the
Commerce of the country.
Without it ought to be stated, that the Acad-
emy has not received from the city or state, a
single cent, while all its labors from its found-
ation to the present moment have been entirely
for the public benefit. When it is considered
that in all civilized countries the Fine Arts
are fostered by the various governments with
at great cost, from the beneficial effect, not increased merely value of manufactures on which their cultivation
is brought to bear, the achievement
of the artists will be more properly appreciated
I have the honor to be Sir
With the highest respect
Yours respectfully

My dear Sir, I have received your letter of the 13th ult. and am much obliged for your kindness in sending me a copy of the telegraphic instrument which you will receive notice of my Telegraph, I showed it to a few friends
occasionally within a few weeks, among others to Prof. Henry of Princeton (a copy of whose letter I have sent you some time since) he had never seen it in operation but had only heard of it from description the principle on which it is founded. He is not of an enthusiastic temperament but exceedingly critical of giving an opinion on Scientific inventions, yet in this case he expressed himself in the warmest terms and the telegraphic Telegraph (who informed me) that he had found it the most beautiful and ingenious instrument he had ever seen. Indeed since I last wrote you I have been wholly occupied in perfecting its details and something with the whole system. There is not a shadow of doubt as to its performing all that I have promised in regard to it and indeed all that has been conceived of it. You can understand the difficulty arising from want of means that I have had to encourage, I had hoped to be able to show my perfects instrument in Washington last before this and was sent to this morning contemplating its perfection last week. The result of the proposed arrangement of Congress has stopped my preparations and introduces I fear another year of hardships and anxieties.

Dear Father,
As I have an opportunity of writing you again to
town by Mr. Munson, I will not lose it. My stove & fixtures came safe
I will have to get a model to put it up for me, that is break up a
small part of the fire place. I am comfortabley situated for the winter
now or will be as soon as I get my stove up & coal which last I
will obtain from the Treasurer there is charged in any item bill.
I will give you below a list of my further expenses, $10 would not
have fitted me out quite, one of my companions from Mr. Jones
has given $15 for his fit-out and thinks it quite reasonable I believe
to have made the best use I could of my money, but let you
judge I here subscribe those occurred since my last.

anywhere obtain, and cheaper than I might get one at another time.
My lessons are very long and hard, I have to study all the time I
am up till past 10 o clock. Aunt Salisbury & cousin Martin are so
very kind to me, I have taken my meals there ever since I
have been here, waiting for Uncle Richard, where can he be?
I have but one vest which is rather dirty, I cannot be wasted

Charles

Charles

Dear Father
Necessity once more compels me to write
you for the means to make a few more necessary purchases
in the first place they board, according to the rules of the
club ought to be paid weekly $25.00 at the entrance into
it I have now been there a week & have not yet arrived to
pay next day washerman's bill $21.36 to. Then my society
for $12,000 & I have been shunned for that. I was told
I need not pay till next term but am misinformed; then
I want oil, a pair of scissors,reek Testament (about 75 cents),
an Election book (25 cents) some blanks for compositions &
Translations, and $2.50 to pay for what I borrowed; before
I could find any club to board, I was obliged to take
4 meals at an eating house, Uncle R came here & told me
he could not take me for something of at all, so I told
he came nothing so that I had found a club, for I had
then, but going around there I found my vacancy in
it (the club) had been filled by another member of it
who had been absent, so I determined to go to another
at last I succeeded in finding Mr Akeman who has one
vacancy, which I took $1.75 for week in the price of board &
very good board it is most of the members are church
members & the strictest order is observed at table.
I had to borrow 25cts yesterday to pay postage. I don't like
to borrow farther, if you or Uncle R's did would place $10,00
in Uncle R's hands I would give you an account how
I spent it, though I have been aware that it costs a
good deal to furnish a room & I think I have not spent
too much for it. I will soon have to get a Table &
looking glass as Mrs Whitspley will want hers soon,
I thought they to go with the room, but it was the
bureau & chairs. If you could come up here & see how
I am situated you could judge of what I needed.
Prof Worley says it is not necessary to have guardrooms
as customary except when coming from a great distance
I write in haste as I have but little time. If you
should send me any money please pay postage for I
have not got one cent. The books I use every day viz First
Testament & Eulatations, I have borrowed so get, but it is not
likely I can for much longer. Has Mr Frisby made me
a meal I really want one I have but one & that
is not over clean.
Write soon as possible
Your affectionate Son
Charlotte W Mason

New Haven Nov 28th 1847
Dear Father,
I have asked Prof Goodrich concerning my
guardianship & he says he would rather have me put one who
has little more to do with college than he. Prof Olmstead
no doubt would take that charge as he is the guardian of
one of my class now. Prof $200 should be sent by Truck R
is gone $25 for board $29.57 for coal $1 for oil, candles, a
few medicines postage etc. All that I owe now in New Haven is my
stock bill $3.25 & the washerwoman $1.18.74. I purchased a necktie for
$1.50 to the one I got in NY being rather too much worn. I
received a vest from Bridgeport one that I thought I had lost.
My overcoat that you purchased for me in Madison this last
fall is in want of repairs the cloth is very weak & the velveteen
collar has split & worn in several places. It will cost me
$2 or 3 dol. to get it fixed over re buttoned etc. I really want
a new one but will wait till next winter, I can make
this one last through this winter. I am well situated for the winter now and
only want a little money to keep me in coal, oil, & clean clothes.
This finding a guardian is a new business to me & I hardly know
how to go to work, I am sorry it has given you so much
concern & yet the matter is just where it was at first. Prof
Woolley told me he would not like the charge & Prof Goodrich
98970
-rich does not seem to like to undertake it, what now shall
I do? I can ask Prof. Chas. H. he is the only one I know
who would be likely to become my guardian.
I am now in want of a little to keep me
in comfort & will have to pay a little charge for postage if
Uncle Sid will come up here soon perhaps he can arrange
all matters satisfactorily, Uncle Richard is expecting him.
I see by Aunt Selina's letter that Sister & Mrs. Ford have
arrived in Sanit, & that Sister is well pleased.
I have been quite unwell, I did not go out for
2 or 3 days & stood at Uncle R where Charity was very kind
& kind, I am now pretty well though at times feel rather
weak, I should like to have a high desk to stand up &
study, the Best in his lecture & as recommended from
them are in pretty general use throughout college, he states
that was hurtful to lean over a low table for any length of
time.
Our vacation will be in about 5 weeks, then I
hope to see you in New York. My studies are all easy
except Mathematics I wished I had paid more attention to
that while at Mr. Jones but he advised me not to do so
there would be time enough at college.
We are all well here in N Haven & would
like to see you but I suppose you are pretty busy now
preparing for Christmas. When you write please tell us when
Sidie did is coming. Love to Mr Uncle & Aunt State
all friends.
Yours affectionately Son
Charles (over)

willing I will ask him, I suppose they would require to
be furnished with the means before giving out money.
Charles

Washington Dec. 18. 1842.—
Dear Sidney:
I have not written you since my arrival
as I had nothing special to say, nor have I now any-
thing very decided to communicate in relation to my
enterprise, except that it is in a very favorable train.
The Telegraph as you will see by Thursdays or Fridays
Intelligence of last week is established between two of
the Comtesse rooms in the Capitol, and excites universal
admiration. I am told from all quarters that there is
but one sentiment in Congress respecting it, and that
the appropriation will unquestionably pass. The discovery
I made just before leaving N.York of the fact that two or
more circuits will pass without interference at the same
time on the same wire, excites the wonder of all the scienti-
fic in & out of Congress here, and when I show them
the certainty of it, in the practical application of it to
simplify my Telegraph, their admiration is loudly expressed
and it has created a feeling highly advantageous to me.
I believe I drew for you a method by which I thought
I could pass rivers without any wires through the water,
I tried the experiment across the Canal here on Friday
afternoon with perfect success; this also has added a
fresh interest to my favor, and I beg you to hope that I am
on the eve of realizing something in the shape of Compen-
sation for my time and means expended in bringing my in-
vention to its present state. It does not be sougains,
however,
however, for I have had too much experience of destructive
hopes to indulge in any premature expectation. Now there
is no opposition, but it may spring up unexpectedly and
defeat all. I am pleasantly and economically situatd.
At first I took board and lodgings at the Amer. Hotel at Penns-
ylvania house, where however they charged me & that is to say
16 dollars p r week, so after one week, I found a private
boarding house, (Mr. Hatcher Missouri Avenue,) for 6
that is 12 dollars p r week, where I am better accommodated
in a pleasant family and at a cheaper rate. To-morrow I
shall further reduce my expenditure, as Dr Fisher is invited
to pass the rest of his time here, at the house of Rev. W.
Rich who is his relative, and my expenses are therefore,
reduced to 6 dollars p r week. This reduction will enable
me to stay until my bill is carried through. I am told
by some members of the Senate, that it will go through the
Senate without the least delay or hesitation, and some
members of the House are declared it should pass in the
House by acclamation, and this may possibly be the case.
I find every where the most kindly feelings, and in
view of it all I cannot but recognize the special goodness
& mercy of our Heavenly Father. In his hands are all hearts,
he turns and can turn them as it pleases him, and to him
from the heart I would give all the praise and all the
glory.
I find Dr Fisher a great help, he is acquainted with
a great many of the members, and he found among them an
creating an interest for the Telegraph. — Mr Smith has not
yet made his appearance, and if he does not come soon
every thing will be accomplished without him. — My
Associates proprietors are at present broken reeds, yet I am
aware they are disabled in various ways, and I ought to
remember that their help in the commencement of the
enterprise was essential in putting the Telegraph into the
position it now is, therefore, although they give me no aid,
it is not from unwillingness but from inability, and I
shall not grudge them their proportion of its profits, nor
do I believe they will be unwilling to reimburse me my
expenses, should the Telegraph eventually be purchased by the
Government.—
Mr. Ferris our representative is very much interested
in understanding the scientific principles on which
my Telegraph is based, and has exerted himself very strongly
on my behalf; so has Mr. Boardman, and in a special manner
Dr. Ayrigg of N. Jersey the latter of whom is determined the
bills shall pass by declaration. — Mr. Huntington of the Senate
Mr. Woodbury, and Mr. Wright are also very strongly friendly to the
Telegraph.—
Write me to the care of Mr. Boardman or rather under
cover to him.— Give much love to Sister, to boys in Jail,
and all at the Telegraphic rooms.— I hope Splendifera
is well, I think I shall be here till after the holidays.—
July 2d Off. brother S. D. B. Morse.

New Haven Thursday 18th 42
I am happy to inform you that I have
arrived safely in this delightful city, after a passage of
forty-one days. I was doing to leave before receiving your letter
from father -- and as he died just expect to remain in
to the longer than I pass our baggage throug the Custom
house, I took the liberty to go to the Printing office, where
always gives me a hearty welcome -- especially as I
supposed much only in fulfilling for him the duties of
station in Europe. My friend Miss Laurence came
with me this morning all called at doubt if there I
had the pleasure of seeing you there -- whose contents are
very pleasing to me. I shall now remain till your coming
on, which I hope will be very soon, dearest father, I
want to tell you so much, and I hope I can finish
up to the last part of this letter -- I have returned quite
very strong -- and am desirous of getting up for Spring as
soon as possible -- Uncle Chris will give you all
(particulars concerning the Civil, by the division of
the United States) -- and all his family are knowing --
to Philadelphia in 21st times -- I think you will be pleased
with him. He said if you will favorably he should come
on by the first of July -- hoped I should be really -- to be
married or that he would not go with him a tour
to Magarita & of I rushed to New Orleans in October.
I want to be in New York when he arrives if possible,
and miss July with him there with him on board
of. So the father comes on soon as possible -- my clothes
is all for Summer, and the weather is quite cool yet --
about will tell me on arrangements, I suspect, when I
get time to talk with her alone -- I write now in great
haste by such we leave with Miss Cannon in the
night boat -- I almost wish you were going here
so much do I long to see my dear father. why nature
have deemed it wise to move, and I feel as well
as I ever am making a great sacrifice to leave on
to him in Birmingham -- but I hope in a few years he will
come home to live here -- We must all persuade
him when he comes in -- But I have not time to
write more -- I am now at the Printing, but go over to
lunch in a few moments to stay until you arrive.
Do dear father come up very soon -- and see
the rain off daughter
Ever to mother & family
Yours
Julia

In compliance with your request I beg
have to submit my opinion in relation to the electric Mayne-
rie Telegraph of Joseph Morse.
I have examined its scientific principles and the mechanism
of its construction, and am satisfied that the first are correct
and the latter well combined for the purpose of obtaining the
desired results. I have also been a frequent witness of its practical
operation, and am happy to the vastity with which it writes down alone
station the words and sentences intended to be conveyed from the other.
In the transmission of intelligence through great distances physical
difficulties will probably exist with some of which any one at present
is unacquainted that any of these can be found inconvenient.
The advantage of this mode of communication over all others is, that while
its indications are transmitted with a certainty equal to that of light in
many cases between points so far separated as to be invisible from
each other; by night as well as by day; and in most gloomy as well
as in bright sunlight.

Dear Father,
You see I continue to improve every opportunity
I have of addressing you I would like to introduce you to
the bearer, Mr. Melanathon Wholply, son of the lady who has rented me
my room. He has kindly offered to be the bearer if any letter
or small parcel you may see fit to send me, my post if you
think of getting me would be very conveniently placed by this means
he returns Saturday at 4pm.
Mr. Richard arrived here yesterday to take possession of his house in the morning
I have joined the Unionian Society.
I will have to pay a tax of $2.00 every 3 months for which I am at liberty to draw 4 books from the library, and attend
their meetings every 3rd night to hear debates, speeches & orations
and can also debate do if I wish. Every one in Col is a member
of 1 of 3 societies, Brothers, Catholics, Unionians the Catholics
is composed almost entirely of Gentlemen, the Unionian is the
largest has consequently the greatest power & their laws are
the sweetest in the world for they require the labor to be paid
on entering, but in the Union when it is convenient but before
or at the commencement of the next term. I have had no time
to draw a book out of its library, as my studies require all my attention
I am out of money now, and will have to
remain some time from you, to pay my little debts as postage, wishing
to $5.00 would be sufficient I think. I hope you don't think
that I have laid out my money foolishly, I am sure I
have done the best I could, it cost me quite a good deal for outfits
for 4 years, hereafter I will not have so many recessions
to please as I am pretty well settled, and will have only
a few minor wants.
I wish you would come up to see me some
time -- Prof. Hooker, Wilson, Harman & family are all well, they
are a very very kind & nice family. Selecting a very well India
late Draper's son.
Your lessons are long and hard and require nearly all my
time. Algebra especially is rather difficult to me a new beginning.
I lost to get a catalog, forget any code in as there is no calendar
as yet in the house it cost me 10 cents, raise a board for a book
for effects.
Uncle Richard cannot take me this winter very well
he would have to look out for board for myself and a young man
from the Jones' school by name gets hard in a private family at
$2.50 for week and there are others of my class board there all in
very gentlemanly set, I shall take ten here tonight and if I like it
will remain till I hear from you, I know a place where
I could board for 1.50 but there are some hard cases as
they are called, there, perhaps Uncle R. may find it convenient
after he is settled, to take me, but he can not tell how it
will be. Prof. Hooker advised me if I could reasonably obtain
board where Jackson did, to do it, as he was very likely to go
into associations of good characters. Benson has been very kind to
me indeed I have regularly taken my meals there since I came
to be has told me every thing I have wanted to know.
Having I have just seen reason to Walker who said that he
only pays 12 1/2 p. per week at $2, so in to much, & I have convinced
to wait till tomorrow to find some good club, his club is full. As it was past Benson Montgomery's supper time I borrowed
one of my companions, for 25 cts I asked him, but he presented
on me a $2.00 bill, which I have laid out as follows I am
paid 3 cents oil 1/2 pt 28 Benjwich Cuts (Candles are too expensive) 1/4 for 10 candles
for soap 2 cents in 10 cts Total $1.03. Some my washerwoman
for 2 weeks wash about 9 shillings, if I were to pay with that remains
of the $2.00, I would still owe for 6 cts, so if you sent me $3 I would
have $3 left. etc for my board I suppose they would not require me
to pay weekly, if they should I would let you know I have borrowed
an oil can, but will have to get one tomorrow or next day they
come to 25 cts. I will also have to purchase a Greek Testament.
My time for writing here is very limited, and therefore you must excuse
all mistakes, in consistances, as I have no time to write deeply or clearly
to think.
Yours to all
From your affectionate Son
Charles

Dear Sidney,
I sent you a copy of the Report on
the Telegraph a day or two since. — I was in hopes of
having it called up to-day but the House refused to go
into Com'tte of the whole on the State of the Union so it is
deferred, the first time they go into Com'tte of the whole on
The S. of Union it will probably be called up and be decided
upon. Every thing looks favorable, but I do not discount
myself to beanguine, for I know not what may be done
secretly against it. I shall believe it passed when the six-
signature of the Pres't is affixed to it and not before.—
I meant to have asked you in my last to send me
the Observer and a copy of your last maps; send me them
under cover to Genl. W. W. Boardman, or to Genl. C. G. Ferris. I
wish to show them as specimens of Georgraphy.—
Are there any letters from Susan for me? if so
send them also.—
I have no news to give you.—
Truly J. A. F. Brethec

Washington Jan. 16. 1843.
Dear Sidney, I snatch the moments of waiting for
company in the Com'te Room of Commerce to write
a few lines. Patience is a virtue much needed
and much tried here. So far as opinion goes every
thing is favorable to my bill. I hear of no opposition
but should not be surprised if it met with some.
The great difficulty is to get it up before the house; there
are so many who must "define their position" as the
term is, so many who must say something to Buchanan
that a great deal of the people's time is wasted in
mere idle unprofitable speculifying. -- I hope something
may be done this week that shall be decisive
so that I may know what to do.
I have received all your letters I believe except
one that you say was sent me from Susan
soon after I came. I have not none from her
since I have been here. Let me know about it
for I am anxious to hear about her. -- I am attending
to your request concerning Nicolet's map and you shall
hear from me in a day or two respecting it.
I am fully persuaded that if you were on here and
could inquire around a little, there would be found
a most lucrative business under government for your
heroic efforts in proving. I have shown it to many, and
they are without exception astonished at its beauty.
By the by let me know if the Observer has an
Agent here. I have been asked by one or two who have
seen the Atlas, and wish to subscribe. I could not tell
them the conditions of the Atlas.
You speak of Richard and his occasional turn
of low spirits, and think his suspicion that you
have a little tendency that way, is unfounded. I
rather agree with him and think you have of late
manifested a little of the Morse or Breese (don't
tell Cousin Sam,) disposition. I have lately had a
turn of it myself. This waiting at so much risk,
makes me question myself, am I in the path of duty?
When I think that the little money I brought with
me is nearly gone, that if nothing should be done by
Congress, I shall be in a destitute state, that perhaps
I shall have again to be a burden to friends, until I
know to what to turn my hands, I feel low-spirited. I
am only relieved by naked trust in God, and it is right
that this should be so.
Give love to all; I write in great haste for I
must be in the House, and stir up my friends to
propose the bill as soon as possible.
Yr Aff. Crotter
Finley.
Sidney E. Morse Esq.

My dear friend Cogdell,
Inc'd your welcome letter today, by which
I learned with pleasure that you had received the Report
on my Telegraph which I sent you. I shall not allow you
to forget me, for I do not forget my
friends, however circumstances may seem to favor that idea;
I have not been upon a bed of roses I assure you, for many
years past, My history would present a curious series
of disappointments, trials, and successes, and yet who am
you and other faithful friends in your own hospitable city
but there is no prospect of it that I can see, I often wish
you and talk of you too when I see your busts of Mac
and Hotchkiss in our collection of Statuary in NY k . If
you visit us in NY k , we have now an Academy of which
you need not be ashamed of being a member. We have been
the largest and choicest collection of models in the country, and
a fine body of artists, who, although depressed by the financial state of things
still continue to live, and to produce their annual fruit upon
the walls of our Exhibition room. In our new rooms we have one
devoted to sculpture, and I need not say that your works in
that art or in painting will be welcomed by all your associates
in the Academy.
I confess to being a bad correspondent; for as my
associations of late years have enlarged, my correspondence also
has enlarged, and I find it impossible to avoid the imputation of
neglecting my friends, without neglecting parties that I am compelled
by necessity to perform. I am waiting the passage of my
bill that I may know how to shape my future course. If it passes
as I am encouraged to think it will, I have a work to
perform in organizing my Telegraphic system for the country
which may employ me for the rest of my life (over)

Dear Sidney,
I send you Susan's letter which
I will thank you to take care of for
me. I will you would write her a line
and Catherine too occasionally, for she
will prize them very much. —
I am still in suspense, and it is
painful and trying to me, but there is no
help for it but patience. —
You can help me if a few lines
were inserted in the Journal of Commerce
and Evening Post or in the latter only,
simply stating the fact that the press
throughout the country supports the views
of the Report, and that it is evidently
the popular wish that the bill recom-
mended should pass. — If inserted send
me a copy. — In looking over the papers
with which you exchange, you will perceive
the case to be so, and if the fact be stated
in a single paragraph, it will be read here
and produce an effect.
I have been talking with some of
the Senators, and if my bill is not taken
up in the House soon, I think it will
be moved as an amendment to the Military
appropriation bill when the comes from
the House to the Senate, and so be bought
before the House for concurrence in this
way I am told I can get it before
the House if they continue to neglect
a direct action upon it. —
I have the promise of Dr. Linn
of the Senate of a copy of the maps
you wrote for, of the Oregon so soon as
they are published and laid on the
Senators desks, but they have not yet
been published. —
Thanks Cousin Samuel from me
for sending me the Observer. I hope
he will send me one every week.
Send one to Susan also, if it is not al-
ready done. —
I sent you Mr Cathoun's speech a
day or two ago, and remarked on a
note of a singular character and of
some importance. I learn since
that Mr. Benton in reply showed
that the true map referred to by
Dr. Franklin was in our own Archives
and a late letter, the last Dr. Franklin
ever wrote, as I understand, confirms
the U. States claim of boundary line.
To be sure this is of little consequence now since the
matter is settled. Write me occasionally if but a
word or two.
Love to all,
Do you hear from Mr
of Charles?
Y aff. hotly ever
Finley
New Haven, Conn. July 1848.
Dear Doctor,
Your letter was received yesterday and as it
was most convenient for me to write to day, I did not exactly
comply with your request to write immediately. Our studies this term
are very hard, and they continually grow harder. I must say I
am not very fond of Algebra, we are hurried on so fast that I
have hardly time to understand it, in many places I do not under-
stand. Most of my class have been through the Algebra
before and even they sometimes flunk one or two. If the class went
off of their own accord because the lessons were too hard for them.
My other studies are easy, of the two Latin & Greek I like Greek
the best. I have changed my room and got a room mate. Boston
is my room mate the one that was examined with me we pay
$11.50 per week for our rooms and it is a week of peace to have them
gone. I have been at Mrs. Wilhelly's not more than 10 days and I paid for
them in vacation as an arm ame but now we are not charged for
vacation. I had to get some new furniture chairs, tables, etc. as
I had none of my own. I received the Public Document you sent
me, you must write when you have complete success. Nothing of any
interest has taken place here, our friends are all well. One of my
old schoolmates who was a V.P. in Kentucky, I knew him till he died, he
was very much liked by his class, and a good scholar.
I stayed here during vacation, as Uncle R thought
it would not be worth while to go to New York for so short
a time as two weeks, the fare being $10 down I have
been quite well, last term I was sick once or twice.
I like to be where I can get plenty of exercise, I intend to
be a farmer if possible, nothing would be better than
to be in possession of a good farm and have plenty of work.
Fin it seems is now a printer Uncle Sid wrote last week
that I am set up a column & a half of last week's Observer
From your affectionate Son
Charles

Under standing that it is a desideratum
in relation to your Telegraph that it should be capable of
transmitting dispatches public & private that can be read only
by the person to whom addressed, I take the liberty to in-
form you that I am in possession of an instrument for
writing in cipher any communication whatsoever, in such
manner that it can be read only by means of a similar instru-
ment, similarly adjusted.— The changes of adjustment of which
it is susceptible are almost infinite in number.— So that
every person on the Globe may have a different key by which
to adjust the instrument.— To transmit communications
thus written, the Telegraph needs only to possess the power to make
35 distinct characters or signs which may be readily distingu-
ished from each other.— Single instruments at each Tele-
graph Station, to which correspondents may have access will
be sufficient.— The Instrument is not very expensive; & any
person may be taught to use it in five minutes.—
The Instrument is constructed ready for exhibition; &
should you think such a device would be available for
your purposes, I shall be happy to show it to you
at any time.— Both the instrument & the device are
my property though not my invention.— I would dispose
of it to you for a moderate consideration in money, or on
some terms conditioned on its being ultimately adopted & made
available.—
Very Respectfully Yours
Eli W. Blake

Washington March 14th 1843.
Sir
I have received your communication of the 10th inst.
stating the plan of operations you propose for fulfilling the object of the act of congress to test the practicability of establishing a system of electric-magnetic telegraphy in the United States.
In general, I approve the plan proposed by you. The appropriation of the two assistants whom you propose to employ, ought however to be fixed before they are engaged, and you will report to the Department the amount or rate which you deem reasonable. Some arrangement in respect to your own transportation should also be made, and you will state the item which you expect, either in reference to the whole undertaking, or to the time which may be devoted to it.
In order to preserve a proper check over the expenditures, and to conform to the established practice of the Department, specifying to the conclusion of any contract for materials, or for any work by the job, you will submit the same to this Department for its approval, and no contract will be recognised as valid without such approval. Of course this remonstrance does not apply to the hiring of labourers by the day or the month, although the rate of wages proposed to be paid in such cases should be submitted to the Department.
An advance of a remunerable sum to enable you to commence your operations will be made on your requisition, stating
the Amount and object, and designating the place at which you desire
the Same to be paid or transmitted by you. And at the operations
proceed, such Sum will be paid, from time to time, as may be re-
quired on similar requisitions.
If you will be held accountable for all moneys
paid on your application, you will find it necessary, to be ex-
ceedingly careful to take vouchers in duplicate for all sums
expended by you. You will be required to account month-
by at least for the Amounts received, and no advances or
payments will be made while there shall remain any Undis-
creetable Sum unaccounted for. It may be well for you
to devote one of your assistants, the duties of a disburting
agent, and of keeping the accounts of the Experiment.
Very Respectfully,
Your obedient servant
J. C. Danver

March 26. 1843.
My dearest Sir.
State the liberty of sending a letter for my
friend Brown, which I beg of you to forward to his Excellency.
I desire to trouble you with these little commissions, but the
truth is that you have so benedicted a disposition that you
must not marvel that it is likely to be seriously taxed.
When you have occasion to expedite letters to the Rocky
Mountains you must use my services in a similar way.
I send you a daily Gazette of yesterday Containing
an article published over the actual W. which you
have probably noticed – The article was written by one
to assist the Community of a great fraud upon their
Common Sense, which has been attempted by a travelling
picture exhibited in Advertising for exhibition the
original picture painted by Mr. Clark for the British
Institution in 1846 or 1847. The article has drawn out
a reply in which the picture is unblushingly
claimed as the original painted by Mr. Clark. I
think I never knew a case of such unparalleled
impudence – The picture is certainly the oldest I
can saw, for a picture of any pretension. It is
absolutely beneath Criticism – The owner of the
picture is in Mr. Clark of your City the same I
premise, who admits the stories of Conspicuous Persons
The photograph in his Catalogue – If you have any acquaintance
who have been in London for the past year and
have given the original petition let me know the fact
This will settle the point of its originality for the proprietor
says that the picket was purchased in land on I brought
to this County more than two years since -
Such proof wasacity deserving exposure -
Your letter to Mrs Walton was received last week
and I am fully quite jealous of Sarah Anna, that
her letter should have been answered first - So you
are in for another letter you deserve - Your gallantry
will of course prompt you to lose no time in replying
to your fair Cousin -
I feel a strong desire that you should be successful
in your electric-magnetic project, and I think you
have acted wisely in selecting the cities of Baltimore
& Washington for the termini of your lightning
Course -
With kind remembrances from all
at Utica I remain
Most Truly
P. R. Walton

telegraph upon the mail road to Washington; requiring

Engineers in such manner as not to interfere with our
operations; and requesting from you the concurrence,
especially the recommendation of Mr. Latrobe, of the
use of the Telegraph for the benefit of the country, but
under stipulation which dispermised you may readily
grant. Have only to add, therefore, that it will give me
pleasure to confer with you upon the subject when ever
you please.
Yours

The greatest practical difficulty you will
ever to contend with, I should think, will
be the insulation of the wires. Twine is a
partial conductor and by making the surface
of contact sufficiently extended lateral trans-
mission will take place to some extent. The
loop however on this account can only be determined
by direct experiment with extended wires. It will
probably increase with an increasing ratio; first an
amount of the greater surface of contact and secondly
because electricity of greater tension will be required
to send the current through the longer wire.
In order to diminish the number of points of
contact it might perhaps be well to wrap around
each wire besides its continuous covering an extra
strand of copper twine with the several turns at
a distance from each other thus
of the two wires the contact instead of being
continuous will only exist at the points where the outer
strands of twin trench meet other.
Jalvanic electricity has never been made to project
itself through a stratum of air of the ordinary density so
as to exhibit a spark, although the experiment has been
tried with a battery of several hundred plates and with
the holes approached within the 1000 part of an inch.
I should therefore conclude that that it would be of
little importance to fill the spaces with cement provided
the metal can be as well secured from contact by less expensive
means.
I shall probably visit New York sometime
during the present college vacation and shall not
fail to accept the kind invitation of Professor More
to visit your establishment and perhaps make
some experiments with your long wires.
Respectfully yours,
Joseph Henry

New York, May 17th 1843
Copy to F.O.J Smith,
Dear Sir:-
I have this morning received enclosing the
contract for treading. I have examined
the contract and I must say I am not
exactly pleased with the terms. If I un-
derstood you right before you left for
Boston, you were confident a contract
could be made for within the estimates
given in to the Govt, and I had hoped
that something could be saved from
that estimate as from the others, so as to
present the experiment before the country
in as cheap a form as possible. I have
taken a pride in showing to Govt how
cheap the Telegraph can be laid, since
the main objection, and the one most
likely to defeat our uttermost plans, is its
great expense. I have in my other con-
tracts been able to be far within my esti-
mates to Govt and I had hoped to be
able to present to the Sec'y the contract
for treading likewise reduced. There are
plenty of applicants here who will do
it for much less and one even said he
might let for one half. I shall do nothing
in regard to the matter until I see you.

My dear Sir
The present serves to introduce my
friend, Mr Joseph Ames, the young artist whose
pictures you saw at my house. his pictures I am
convinced, are a better recommendation to your favor
than any I can give him.
As Mr Ames visits your city for
the purpose of seeing new works of art, I hope it
will be in your power to show him some of
your pictures. I should be particularly pleased if
he could see the copies you made of the portraits
of Rembrandt and Titian, while in Florence. —
Having never seen any genuine specimens
of the old masters, I think it would be very
gratifying to him to see them so well repeated
As my friend is a disciple of Alston I hope
you will consider him entitled to your best
commend & encouragement. I am assure you that
he is capable of appreciating and improving by them
I am your Sir, with great
regards. Truly Yours
Henry Greenough

To Hon. John C. Spencer,
Sec'y of Treasury.
In the letter
to the Hon. Sec'y dated March 10th/1843,
in which I proposed my general plan,
I leave this remark, speaking of the
wire after its insulating preparation
should be completed: - "Many inter-
esting experiments bearing upon the gen-
eral result can then be tried before the
wire is enclosed." The experiments alluded
to were tried on Tuesday with perfect
success. I had prepared a galvanic
battery of 300 pairs in order to have
ample power at command, but, to my
great gratification, I found that 100
pairs were sufficient to produce (through
the whole distance of 160 miles) all the
effects I desired.
Some careful experiments on the de-
composing power at various distances
were made, from which the law of
propulsion has been deduced, verifying
the results of Ohm, and those which
I made (in) the summer of 1842, and
alluded to in my letter to the Hon.
C. G. Ferris, published in the House
Report No. 17 of the last Congress.
The practical inference from this
law is that a telegraphic commu-
nication on any plan may with certainty
be established across the Atlantic!
Startling as this may seem now, the
time will come when this project will
be realized.

mentioned at all, neither as Bartlett agent, nor
as the recipient of the money, but all payments

authorised vouchers. It is to you immaterial who

that they are authorised.

with the lead pipe embraced by my contract with him
reasonably to fulfill that contract you will oblige me if

ance within the contract price at the rate of seven and

contract and this shall be your authority therefor.

H. O. J. Smith Esq

Sir,
An arrangement has been made with Messrs.
Tatham and Brothers for from 25 to 30 miles of lead pipe
of 3/8ths of an inch bore and weighing one pound to the yard;
the wires four in number of the four diff. colors they are to have
placed within the pipe. The pipe is to be in lengths of
from 450 to 600 feet, to be wound upon a drum of from
6 to 8 inches diameter, and six inches wide, the whole well packed in cases or
boxes for transportation; the delivery to be on board of packet
(for Baltimore,) (a canal boat) at their expense. Ten miles
are to be delivered thus prepared perfectly sound on or before
the 10th Novr. 1843. Ten miles more on or before the 15th Novr.
and the whole of the remainder on or before the 20th Novr.
The wire prepared for induction, is to be delivered by us at
Phi ca or New York at the option of the Messrs. Tatham.
All is submitted for my approval.
You will therefore proceed immediately to inspect and prove the lengths of pipe, by the air pump on
forcing pump or both, and perfecting the installation of the wire installation of the wire in their occupation
by a battery. You will remain until the 20th instant or until the pipe shall have been completely, and
successfully sent off to Baltimore to the care of D. Burkett
of 14 Commerce St. You will keep an exact account
of the property submitted for your inspection, taking the
proper receipts & memoranda for securing it from depu
dation or injury, and report to me at the office of the
Respective Commissioners

Patents. On the other side of this letter and enclosed are orders

Prof Morse,

Sir,
Yours of the 27th ult also yours of the 5th inst
were duly received. The first gave me great joy that
I had thus far met your approbation. Though in an
exceedingly debilitated state I was so much elated that it
seemed I was able to start off on the next passage of
The boat of Cox but my told me it was a piece of pre-
sumption that would very likely lay me in my grave
I was forced, though much against my will, to yield
I am now rapidly improving and hope to be able to leave
here on Monday 11th for the line of work -- God has been
exceedingly merciful in raising me from the gates of the grave
My bones pricked through my shirt in almost every direction
But it is most true to close the mail and I am
nearly to quit from the office --
Cock F. I think will close up his work tomorrow
and then of course will leave immediately for B. order
Jetham has been delayed by the giving away of parts of the
Engine Machinery. I shall go to Seattle and look into the
matter of the Pipe line report without delay. I
I believe I have all the bills of Lading but I have
not the time to look them over before we mail
many close but all shall be attended to im-
mEDIATELY
Write Salem pay the bill for porous cases
In haste yours
S D Gale

New York Oct 8 1840
Prof Morex
My Dear Sir
Although I wrote you yesterday, and commu-
nicated what information I had at the time; yet I was not at
all satisfied with what I had communicated. We had a great
snow storm here, Snow fell 7 or 8 inches, but a large portion
of it has already been reduced to a liquefying state (I am)
Jackson finished his contract of drawing fire last night, there
is about 1 mile to from and pack they expect to finish the work
tomorrow (Saturday) evening and all of us to come on the first
of the week. My health is daily improving. It seems to
have followed every thing connected with service work, and
his works -- I have never seen a well dug mine but it is
intended the night work in that damp cellar of a place.
Oh! that you had never known that man but it is
to late to lament.
I have examined the Bills of Lading of the Boxes sent by the steam-
boat packet to Baltimore from Durrell's factory -- the following is a correct
copy
Packet Clyde Recd Oct 17 3 Boxes Oct 25 6 B
Schooner Roe Oct 26 3 B
Schooner Michigan " 30 7 B
Schooner Maria Nov 12 6 B Nov 18 6 B
Schooner Milesent " 16 " 6 B + 3 B Nov 17 " 2 B

42 Boxes
The Error was with Mr. Loring in writing Mr. Barback, 14 Boxes by
the Illinois, when the Bills of Lading make it 11
I should not have permitted Mr. Loring to write Mr. B. at all but
for my extreme dexterity at the time. I took my pen to write
but felt so much exhausted I was obliged to lay it down
again. I dictated writing but Mr. Loring obtained that
he had sent 14 Boxes by this vessel – I know the bills of
Lading would tell a being only much enfeebled did examine the subject any farther.
My mind has been on you & the work, daily and hourly, and
trust with the permission of Divine Providence to be able to transport my body there also. I suppose we should from your last
letter but one find you in Washington and after that I shall
enquire at the Whitmans Eagle Tavern and suppose we have come on
direct to Washington, shall we get our passage free from Bto W. – shall
we say nothing about it and pay a dear mileage? If you have
any directions to give you might leave a note for me at the Eagle
Tavern with the clerk or Bar keeper where I shall inquire.
I will try to do up your business to make it acceptable –
I cannot close without expressing my gratitude for your
many acts of kindness. Our Heavenly Father will reward you
I will try to do my duty.
I trust you will excuse this wandering from Bassinck
and believe me
Your Obd. Servt
L.D. Gale

New York Dec. 9th 1843.
Prof Morse, Superintendent of U.S. Telegraphs
Sir I have the honor to report to you that
Mr. Falkam here made & delivered on board ship (39) thirty
nine casks of Lead pipe with the wires enclosed in them
which after faithfully proving, according to your instructions,
I have accepted & approved, the net weight of which is 57,534 lbs
including the wires. They have also made about 12,600 lbs
including the wires, of which about half has been proved & accepted
but is not yet packed & delivered, but will be in the course of the
day. The proving & accepting, packing & delivery will be completed
in the first part of the week. According to your instructions I will
have the wire not yet enclosed amounting to about 525 lbs, weighed
packed & prepared for shipping to Washington I will deposit it here
subject to your order. As soon as we can complete all that is now
here on hand I weigh the spools & I will transmit to you a schedule
containing on exact account of every reel of wire & pipe with
the weight of each & the times of shipment & also on account of
all that remains on hand. I am very sorry to hear from De Gole that
Schell's pipe is so very worthless but it is no more than I was
afraid would be the case. He is all well, but has left in hourly
expectation of her confinement. I shall hurry the business here
as rapidly as is consistent with perfection so that if my come on
at the earliest possible moment I will write to you some week or two
weeks since but not having heard from you of the receipt of the letter I
suppose it has misrendered, terms of payment would be paid to receive a
draft if not inconvenient to you for the 25 miles not yet paid for on
the contract with Mr Smith leaving the balance till the final adjustment
De Gole is improving in health slowly. I trust will recover perfectly
to the month of April to morrow I should be glad if you would give him
authority to let me have some money to have with my wife return home on
I remain very respectfully
Your Obt Servt
James C Fisher Jr. S.S.P.
P.S. Would it not be well to try to see who or whose boxes will have before putting them down De Gole & I
bott fear on reflection that will be too weak.

The delay here in the completion of the contract could
not be attributed to Messrs. Fathams as they were always
in advance of us with the pipe except for two days, but

according to your instructions any faster. We intended
to prove it faithfully and could not hurry it any
faster with safety to the success of the enterprise which
I thought of paramount importance.—

receipt for the last month to Messrs. Thomas bill on Ben Smith
for the pipe concerning which they would like to hear from you
at your earliest convenience
I remain very respectfully
your Hts Servt

Washington D.C. Dec. 16th 1843.
Dear Sidney,
I write a hearty line just to say that
after the payment of $5.00 each to the wives of Batting
and Taylor, up to this date, you need pay no more
as I have discharged both from pay & service after date,
in consequence of my preparing to go into winter quarters.
The season is against all my operations and I expect to
resume in the spring.
I have difficulties and trouble in my work
but none of a nature as yet to discourage, they arise
from neglect and unfaithfulness, (alter has) on the part
of Fisher, whom I shall probably dismiss, although on
many accounts I shall do it reluctantly. — I shall give
him an opportunity to excuse himself, if he ever gets here.
I have been expecting both him and Gale for 3 weeks, and neither
but without bringing either of them. They may have a good excuse
we shall see.
I am uneasy respecting 2 drafts sent to Fisher
to pay Jathams on their order, amounting $273.20. One
drawn by Bank of Wash. on National Bank New York
for $273.20 and one by myself on Bk of America for
$400.00. The package was directed to Fisher, and painted
by Mr Ellsworth at Patent Office on 2 Dec. 1843.—
When you go to Wall St. please ask at the Banks
respecting them, although I may find letters before this
reach you which may relieve my mind. I have received
letters in answer from Fisher to letters subsequently written, and
He does not allude to them. —
Where is Edward? I had hoped to see him, and
should have written him. I do hope he will not leave
the country without my seeing him. When does he think
of going? and how is his health.—
Love to all. In greatest haste
Yr truly as ever
Colt. brother
Sam: P: B: Morry.

Sir.
I have the honor to report that from my inability
to supply to the Contractor for trenching for the Tele-
graphic wires, at the stipulated time a sufficient quan-
tity of suitable pipe to enable him to fulfill the contract
on his part to the full extent of the proposed line, I am
under the necessity of leaving a portion of that work
unfinished until spring. But as this postponement
necessarily violates the contract on the part of the
Government I have made an arrangement with
the Contractor for trenching to postpone his further
operation which I herewith submit for the Honora-
ble Secretary's approval. The Contractor has been
prompt and efficient to fulfill his undertaking so
far as I have been able to supply pipe, and has also
been subjected to much loss of time and extra expense
in consequence. I have therefore entered into such an
agreement as I believe to be just towards him, and under
the circumstances most for the interest of the Government
and the enterprise, hoping it may meet with the ap-
probation of the Department.
With great respect
Y. Ob Servt.

Prof. S.F.B. Morse Superintendent of Telegraph
Sir
I was this morning informed by the
means Fothams that you had written to me on the 1st of
December enclosing two drafts for $7500 made payable from
the Hon H.L. Ellsworth, & also 3 other letters in reference to
them I had yet received no answer from me, Immediately
on receiving this information I requested Mr Wm Fothams to
go with to the Post office to made search for them, as I had
repeatedly made inquiries for letters before without success
on inquiring we were informed that there were none, insisted
on or examination I after some time your letter of the 12th inst
from Baltimore was found. I then collated with Mr Fothams in the
Postmaster & after a long search I must questioning it was found
that your letter of the 10th enclosing the drafts & your letter of
the 11th inst finding fault with me for not answering the letter
& not reporting the progress of the work had been sent to
the Observer office where we proceeded to found them.
The letters were all directed to me without any specified place,
Had they been directed to me, at Messrs Fothams or at my residence
I should probably have received them without fail & much misunderstanding
being saved to all, Your instructions to me were to direct to
the case of D. Buford 14 Commerce St Baltimore, to whom I reported
wrote for you & to whose case I directed several letters for you which
were put in the office here by Messrs Fothams Clerk.
not having received or you will perceive by what I have written
above my instructions to write to you at my other place. succeeding
no answer I could not tell to what the delay in your writing was
owing. It is now explained, The delay here in the completion of
the contract could not be attributed to my being in Athens as they were
always in advance of us with the paper, but our face here was not
sufficient to prove the paper according to your instructions my
forter. We endeavored to provide it. faithfully I could not trust it
our forter with safety to the success of the enterprise which I
thought of paramount importance. I had received no intimations
from you that I must come immediately on to your written instructions
directed me to remain till the last coils of paper were shipped
to Baltimore & I had no choice in the matter. I trust that this will
suffice to explain my conduct which you say in your letter of the 4th
just needs explanation. I forwarded by the Gole a receipt for the
month of November for 40000. I shall enclose with this letter
the receipts of the means Athens, the schedule of the weights
& the duplicate bills of lading, which I have retained. That they
may be compared in Baltimore with the paper received from home
expecting Mr Fisher's confinement I now write in more of a
hurry than I otherwise should have expressed on her account
I remain very respectfully
your Old Servt
James Fisher
