My Dear Sir
It is now something since I have heard from
you directly though I hear from your works through the public
prints that you are pushing the Telegraph more vigorously.
The impression in N.Y. is very strong that it will be extended until
it shall spread every important key town in the U.S. My Brother
has just returned from Boston and tells me that it was the most
frequent topic of conversation wherever he went.
It seems you have finally got to Baltimore. Did the appropriation
hold out and what is the condition of the enterprise before Congress?
that is, what sort of a proposition have you made, and what pro-
gress has it made in Congress? I am the more anxious to know as
I have recently received a lengthy communication from Mr. Riggs
attempting to vindicate his own acts relative to the Telegraph and
showing wherein he blames you. I at first thought I would include
to you the communication but on reflection decided otherwise. I will give
in brief his complaint. It is that 1. you will not come to any terms
to settle his claim against the government in the trenching contracts
2. you will not determine even on the mode by which you may
ascertain the amount of any payment which he the contractor ought to
receive and which you as Superintendent ought to apply for
3d. that you have referred him over to the Sec'y of the Treasury for
payment and he cannot to his fault – that the Secretary, without notifying
Mr S. had decided on the case and reported it to government.
Mr S. goes on to say that in consequence of this state of affairs
Can any one blame me for refusing to enter into any new engage-
ments concerning the Telegraph until the old claim is secured?
He also states that he has proposed to leave the whole subject
to the 3 Lieutenants Avery Cornell Tail and himself
to abide by their decision.
May I ask how far will his opposition under present 400
flagrants influence government's action in the funding application,
and whether his refusal to participate in such application can
be legal course put on injunction on the proceedings.
May I ask what is the substance of your application, to what dis-
tract does it extend and what amount is asked for from government?
Have you in case an appropriation should be made fixed on your
assistant or assistant? Do you suppose I should be needed,
I do not make application to influence your mind in this matter
in any manner. I know all your kindness of heart to do favors
for others has resulted in personal demeriture to yourself, I wish
you to understand I do not desire to come into the Telegraph to turn
ear of employment away one you already have, nor to come
under any circumstances unless I can be of as much benefit
to the Telegraph as the Telegraph is to me.
I am still engaged in my Sugar of Lead works at present very
much enlarged. I have my brother with me who acts as foreman
We have 2 Buildings 100ft by 25., one 70 by 25., one 30 by 25, besides a
shed or two and are making 800 lbs of lead and shall soon make 1400-
suppose you should need me what salary would you think of giving
and how long would it continue?
I ask these things that I may better understand your views.
One thing I will add while it is on my mind, Mr. S. says he thinks
"I feel that under the impressions which a reliance on Prof. Hordis's
supposed knowledge of Electic Currents gave rise to great injustice was done to Prof. Simon in accusing him of negligence in attempting the wire line and laid upon their failure to work satisfactorily in fields & I design so far as I have been thus made
the instrument of injustice by reliance upon erroneous theories, to make ample amends to him whenever an opportunity shall offer" &c. &c.
I do not write these things to find fault but to let you know what is going on - I have the same confidence in your sense of justice that I have always had.
Dr F has behaved very badly towards me, not only has he robbed me of all my plans & continuances for the manufacture of Sugar of Lead but in order to justify his glaring and palpable misconduct he has represented to his friends that I had promised him a partnership in the manufacture for the aid and improvements he had afforded and the only hold he had on me was to rob me of my improvements to build up himself.
The first and only time I ever said anything about this to Fraternal relation to my factory or business was when I learned you had discharged him and then I wrote F stating that it was possible I might be able to make some arrangement with him to take charge of my factory and accordingly when I reached home last Christmas I went directly to see Dr F to profess an arrangement when I was repulsed with a "Much obliged I can do better"
I shall be glad to hear from you soon
Respectfully
Ed Lisle

Dr. C. J. Smith Esq.
Dear Sir,
Mr. Vail and myself as proprietors of
the Telegraph in common with yourself have given to
the Memoranda of agreement which you handed in yesterday,
such consideration as the limited time we had at command
would allow. And the better to understand its legal
bearings, we took council of a legal gentleman in Baltimore
M. Latrobe, who has promised to send down by the
morning train a draft of such a memorandum as will
embody our views. A transaction of this kind we do not wish
to act upon hastily, and the press of other engagements at a time
when what we have to do must be done quickly, compels us to
propose some simple mode of promoting our general interests
without interfering more than is necessary with our individual
preferences. I have a great repugnance to the management of
such a contract as is proposed, even in its most unobjectionable
form, and while I would accord to enter into such contracts
with the Govt. as you and it can for the mutual benefit of the
proprietors arrange, we wish ourselves to be free from its
moral and as well as pecuniary responsibilities. Now can not this be brought about by the adoption of one
of the following propositions.
1st We propose to sell to the Government the whole
Patent, for a definite sum.
2d We will sell to Genl. the use of the Telegraph
for its own purposes, leaving to us the right to
sell rights to others.
3d We will sell rights at so much per mile,
4th Let Government go on and construct, and
leave it to Genl. to say what compensation shall be given
us for the use of it.
Very Respectfully
Yr Obser
S.J. Morse

Dear Sir,
The bill you drew, I find is liable to
the following objections, and therefore a different
bill had better be drawn, and I am willing that
Mr. Choate or any other Honorable Member should
draft a bill to be presented, against which I
will state no objections.
I am advised by my Counsel at Baltimore
that each Proprietor becomes liable under the
contract you have drawn as a Partner, and
therefore, as I am not willing to assume the
such an obligations I am opposed to signing the
Contract.
I am willing to sell the whole right of the
Telegraph, or I am willing to sell the right
to construct and use it for a given distance
at a certain rate per mile and as the Govt. are not
likely in your opinion now to pay us the full
value this last may be the best.
1. It compels the Govt. to contract with the
Proprietors of Telegraphs for the Construction
of the Telegraph, as well as for the use of
the right (of the proprietors) -
2. It makes one Superintendent, while he is
also Contractor, and owns one half of the Telegraph.
3. No sum is definitly appropriated from the
hearing, but the P.M. General is authorized
to take money ad libitum for the object.
4. No sum is fixed for the right to use the
Telegraph.
5. The proprietors may sell to companies & individuals
viduals, and yet a penalty of imprisonment for
years is annexed for a slight damage to private
property by enacting that the penalty shall attach
to all times of Telegraph hereafter made in the U.S. §
6. To prevent all competition arising from bids and
while the work may be done as appears by the estimate
of Mr. Cornell for $192. per mile the proprietors
might demand a much larger sum over and above
a liberal compensation for the right.
Now, however, objecting you may have sufficient
reason to satisfy your own mind in relation
to the soundness of your own views, you cannot expect
that they will be placed before Congress and not
undergo the most rigid scrutiny. You know
I objected in the outset to any such proposition as
would in the short time in which Congress now
have at Command, lead to discussion, and so defeat the
bill. The straight forward simple way is undoubtedly
best for all concerned.

Respectfully yours,

Professor F B Morse
Lincoln
I have been writing to
hear of the intention of the Telegraphic association
as regards the disposal of the funds to the government
from Alfred. But have been disappointed and
I would therefore desire you to inform me if it is
consistent with your feelings and the interest
of all concerned. (not without) that project is now
on foot and if its ultimate success is more possible
you may rest assured that although apparently
not with you my heart is there -- In my presence
at Philadelphia I lost all of my available property
and I have lifted up a pretty good heart until this year
when and other circumstances have broken up for me
to such an extent that sometimes I feel I would rather
not have been born -- The connection with the Telegraph
now is my only hope -- and hence the intense anxiety
I feel is occasioned -- You will please excuse me for saying
so much of myself -- and please do not mention it
to anyone except to and to him I have never told so
much as is contained in this letter --
I would add that although I feel reluctant to mention it
that if nothing but an appropriation is made
of a situation could be given to me for the purpose
of laying it down I would be very glad to have
the offer of it. if in your opinion I could perform the duties required.
I am through the Journal of Commerce heard somewhat
of the general operation of the Telegraph but not enough
to satisfy. I would have written it but want of funds prevented me. I would there take the opportunity to express
to you my gratitude for the kindnesses which you have
extended to me in way of employment and I hope
that he has not been backward in doing his part
in the laborious task which you have had to endure.
I know that as to honesty he knows nothing else.
and from what I have heard from him. I know
his whole existence was in the object which you have
attained.
I am the Servt

I have but a moment to say that your faith as
a Christian will be tried as well as my own, in the blow

ate letter accusing my friend Mr. Ellsworth in the most

cover any but the darkest designs upon us all. I am
sick at heart and can only find relief in that refuge,
which in the hour of seeming hopelessness, has appeared
so often to turn sorrow to joy. Let Him be your hope
and trust, and all will come right. I have no fear
for the result. No time to add

The proprietors of Morse's Electric Mag-
netic Telegraph feel grateful to bankers
for its past liberality in testing the practi-
cability to the satisfaction of the public.
The proprietors did not need such
a test to satisfy themselves merely.
In consideration of that liberality, they
have felt under obligations to tender the
right of extending the Telegraph to NewYork,
to the Government, before yielding to any
of the opportunities offered of placing it
in the charge of private associations.
But many years of expense and
toil have been spent in perfecting it, and
the proprietors cannot afford to suffer
a year to be lost for the decision of Congress
on its acceptance or non-acceptance
by the Government, to the exclusion of
private associations.
Their motto is obscure obscure . If
bankers is not prepared to extend it, by
advancing only the means of construction, the
proprietors cannot be blamed for suffer-
ing the enterprise of individuals to die
to, though its effect upon the revenues
of the P. O Department, be disastrous.
It requires no argument, nor complication
of facts, to demonstrate, that for the purposes
of carrying intelligence, neither horse power,
nor steam power, nor the enterprise of private
express riders, nor the best efforts of the
P. O Department, cannot compete
99666
with the powers and advantages of
the Telegraph.
If the Telegraph is calculated
to enrich itself upon the perquisites of the
P. O. Department, and accomplish
in the great productive lines of business
about even private expenses
cannot be the damage of the P. O.
system; surely the government
should have the control of it, and
not suffer it to pass into hands that
it control it only for purposes of
speculation, & monopoly the means
of instantaneous intercourse between
the principal points of political &
commercial news.
The proprietors have no other
alternative but to seek their reward
in the enthusiasm of the Government, or in
that of individuals.
If Congress shall elect to make
the necessary appropriation at the
present session, the Government will retain
its control over the Telegraph.
If Congress is either undisposed
to do this, or refuses it to be omitted,
the proprietors will have discharged
their obligations in making the offer
they have, and must be considered as
at liberty to accomplish such their
damages they desire in the enterprise
of private individuals & capitalists.

Dear Prof. Thomson
I arrived safely this
morning and in about 2 hours after had
the car unloaded and Mr. Avery is now
cleaning up the dirty sines and putting
them in order (all that were dirty) -- While
I was very much engaged this morning I got
Mr Burbank to inquire about the copper dies
Mr. McKin will furnish the dies at 50cts
per lb. cut out, which is 5 cts advance on
sheet copper. This would make a great saving.
The holes in the centre Mr. McKin cannot do
But Mr Burbank can punch the holes at
a cost of $2 per day & $1.00 for a tool to punch the
holes. -- The labour will not I think exceed much
of over a day -- The acids is with Stabler & Lanby
and they will do what they can with it. Mr B
will take the acid elsewhere if SL & C will not do
the thing that's nice -- Mr Burbank has balls of
cotton thread and will do the best he can.
Mr Avery is extremely anxious to see his family
and would receive as a great favour of you
would grant him a furlough -- will you
be kind enough to drop a line as soon
as you can. I trust your leg is fast
improving and that soon I shall see
you hoping about as brisk as usual
I remain yours affectiony
Alfred Vail

S. S. B. Morse Esq
Dear Sir
I have been expecting you
in the City, but learned yesterday from
your British Sidney that you might not be
here for some time -- I have witnessed the
succes of your Telegraph with great gratifica-
tions, and most heartily congratulate you
on your perfect triumph -- It has secured
to you as much fame as you could de-
rive, and will bring you as much money
as will make you independent for
the rest of life -- I am domiciled with
my family in the family of your friend Doctor
Gale, and so far am only pleasantly situated -- I have conversed with him much
about the Telegraph, and he informs me
that he has a small interest in it, but
has given you a Carl Blanch for any arrangement for its disposal Which you may
think proper to make -- I did suppose
that your proposals to Congress would have received a final action, notwithstanding
ing the influence of the Evil genius, which
has presided over the Nation the State system.
But since it has failed for the time being,
it has thrust me that possibly you would
like to sell it, or the right to use it between
Baltimore and New York, and would construct
the same between the places for fair
consideration -- If you would do so, I
heard of some parties to whom I should
like to apply for the means, and if you
will give me terms, I will make the application
in such a way that if nothing comes
of it the matter shall not be known.
I suppose that the mail road companies would
allow it to be constructed through their lines
for moderate compensation. Had the Congress
voted it, construction that day, your calculation
as to procuring the right of way for
it -- If you would like to do any thing in
the premises, please say so by early mail
that you will construct the telegraph for
between the two places including or excluding
the expense of the right of way, and dilate it in
complette order for operation making the suitable
number of stations between the two places -- and
had much you will charge in
additional for an absolute and exclusive
right to use it between said places for the
term of the patent - My impression is, that
I could secure a company in a short time,
and have it completed before Congress
shall meet again - The money being
raised, how long would it take you
to complete the structure through the Ohio
distance? Please address me at 215-8th and
11th St.
I am very sincerely

Washington June 23, 1844
My dear brother,
I am still in the bed, and from appearances I
am likely to be held here for many days, perhaps weeks. The
wound on the leg was worse than I at first supposed. It seems
slow in healing and has been much inflamed although now
yielding to remedies. My hope was to have spent some weeks
in New York, but it will now depend on the time of the healing
of my leg. The ways of God are mysterious, and I find prayer
answered in a way not at all anticipated. This accident as
we are apt to call it, I can plainly see is calculated to effect
many salutary objects. I needed rest of body and mind, after
my intense anxieties and excitations, and I might have neglected
it and so perhaps brought on prematurely disacle of both, but
I am involuntarily laid up, so that I must keep quiet, and
although the fall that caused my wound was painful at first
yet I have no severe pain with it now. But the principal
effect is doubtless intended to be of a spiritual character, and
I am afforded an opportunity of quiet reflection, on the wonderful
dealings of God with me. I cannot but constantly exclaim
What hath God wrought? When I look back upon the darkness
of the last winter, and reflect how at one time every thing seemed
hopeless, when I remember that all my associates in the enter-
prise of the Telegraph had either deserted me or were discouraged
and even Mr. Vail who has held fast to me from the beginning
felt like giving up, just in the deepest darkness of all, when I
remember that giving up all hope myself from any other
source that than his right arm, which brings Salvation, his salvation did
come in answer to prayer, Faith is strengthened, and did I not know
by too sad experience the deceitfulness of the heart, I should say that
it was impossible for me again to distrust or feel anxiety, and due anxiety
for the future. But he who knows the heart, knows its diseased, and
as the Good Physician, if we give ourselves unreservedly into his hands
to be cured, he will give that medicine which his perfect knowledge
of our case prescribes. - I am well aware that just now my principles
ring from one end of the country to the other, I cannot take up a paper
in which I do not find something to flatter the natural pride of the
heart. I have prayed, indeed, against it, I have asked for a right
spirit under a trial of a new character, for prosperity is a
trial, and our Saviour has denounced a woe on us "when all
men speak well of us," may it not then be in answer to this
prayer, that he shoots me up, to strengthen me against the temptations
which the praises of the world present, and so by meditation
on his dealings with me, and reviewing the way in which he has led
me, showing me my perfect helplessness without him, is preparing
to bless me with stronger Faith, and more unreserved trust in Him.
To Him, indeed belongs all the glory. I have had evidence enough
that without Christ I could do nothing, all my strength is there,
and I fervently desire to ascribe to him all the praise. -
I know not what is before me, nor would I feel any
joy for He who hath led me thus far will not now desert me. If
I am to have influence, increased influence, I desire to have it for
Christ, to use it for his cause; if wealth, for Christ, if more
knowledge, for Christ. I speak sincerely when I say, I fear pros-
perity, lest I should be proud and forget, whence it comes.
I send you a copy of Niles' Register which has a good
account of Telegraphs and of mine, but containing some errors
which ought to be corrected if unpublished.—
Give much love to my dear Susan, and her fine boy,
and to Catherine with her fine boy, & dear little Lucretia;—
I hope Charles is settled, and determined to exert all his
abilities to be useful in an honorable business.—
I think of you and your difficulties with Cousin Samuel
I wish that you could see Uncle Sidney, perhaps
a free conversation with him would set matters
right, at present, I fear an unpleasant family
breach. Uncle Sidney is a man of strict integrity and I
think when your representations are made to him, he will
perceive how unjustly and improperly you have been treated.
As it now stands Cousin has had the whole telling of the story
and with the natural bias of parents towards their children
they will think of course that you have wronged him.—
Love to Finley and to Richard & family
Truly your affectionate brother
Sam. F. B. Morse

Dear Sir;
Your of the 25th inst. is received and in reply I would say that I have not from the
part with the Government, without leave of the Department; I shall be in NewYork in a week or two
probably and can perhaps span you the quantity you want from some of my own which is stored there.—
In regard to my opinion of the failure of the first trial lead pipe I think the failure due to the
injury the insulation received in putting it into the pipe, such was the injury that not a single coil that I tried was
free from the fatal defect of having the electricity cross from wire to wire and to the pipe, so that my pipe has turned out
a dead loss, and has been sold for simple lead. It is its being tested before it left your premises; if it is true, it was my
misfortune to have trusted this testing to an unfaithful assistant, who passed it all as sound, leaving it to me to discover
when too late to remedy the evil, the fatal defect I have mentioned.
I congratulate you on your safe return, and thank you for the information respecting the extent of the English
Telegraph; The extent in pipe is or was greater than you mention. From London to Dayton on the G. Western R. way 13 miles
was laid down two or three years since. I am very respectfully

Dear Sir,
In the other letter I have copied a letter just received from Phila. What can we say in answer? I have expressed
that if we gave permission to construct the line for $10,000, or say $100,000 mile that sum to be secured and
paid to us six months after the work is commenced that this would be a simple and easy mode of arranging the
whole matter. Please give me your own views of what you think best. I think myself if we at once
fix the rate at 100 cents as our price for the construction of the line, we shall soon have orders from all parts of the Country, and our profits
will come in rapidly, and sure. If you think any of us should desire further to increase our own profits by contracting with any company or companies this might
be done without embarrassment to the rest. I think that $100 per mile might be substituted for $50 in forming a
company for the N.York & Boston line. I am still confined by my leg, but hope to be able to go out in a few days.
Respectfuly, J. Mose
By granting a privilege on a particular line we do not have ourselves from granting a privilege on another line between two points, so that unless we sell right in states (which we ought to avoid)
we can have a good profit from God at the same time that we accommodate private companies.

Baltimore July 1st 1844
Dear Sir, In reply to your query for what
sum I would sell my share of the patent right
in the Telegraph, which amounts to one half,
frankly say that if One hundred and ten thous-
and dollars shall be secured to me in cash or
current funds in the United States or stocks at cash
value, so that I may be disposed to accept of present
value, I will assign over all my rights and
privileges in the Telegraph in the U. States.
offer it at this price, not that I estimate
the value of the invention so low, for it is perfectly demonstrable that it is not half its value,
but that I may have my own mind to be
occupied in perfecting the system, and in a
general superintendance of it, unembarrassed
by the business arrangements necessary to
secure its utmost usefulness and value.
If you are disposed to negotiate this
matter, and find me susceptible at that
price, I will give you the refusal of this offer
for four months from date, that is to say till
the 1st of November 1844, and will make
over to you the said ten thousand dollars, for
Your services in negotiating the business, provided
of course, the sum designated, One hundred and ten
thousand dollars, be duly paid over and secured

Philadelphia July 1, 1844
Dear Sir,
As soon as you hear from your partner
I would be obliged to you to let me have answer
to the queries contained in my brother's letter, as well as
to those I made verbally when I saw you.
From what I have done since I returned I am sanguine of success in establishing
a telegraphic line between here and New York, but
I cannot consent to put the means I have for the
purpose into operation without some guarantee that
I shall not waste money and time in the attempt.
Within thirty or forty days I think with the peculiar
means in my power I can doubtless obtain the
Capital, provided it is not a greater sum than
that you mentioned to me. Therefore I would be
obliged to you if you would give me in legal form
the right to purchase if I choose to do so within
say forty days, for the sum you and your partners
agree upon an electro magnetic telegraph to be
erected between this city and New York upon the
line of the rail road, and the patent right to the
exclusive use of the telegraph to erected by you
and to any number of additional wires or additional telegraphs hereafter erected on the same
route, or between the cities of Philadelphia and
New York. The consent of the rail road Company
to the erection of the Telegraph to be obtained and
paid for by me in addition to the sum to
be paid to you.
I make as I explained to you this proposition,
in order that I may secure for myself the
office of agent or director of the line, as there will
be such a person needed to superintend the
postage arrangements &c as well as the
working of the telegraph, -- and I wish par-
ticularly to make such an agreement with you
in order that after I have obtained for you
the means of erecting the line, (a service worthy
of done acknowledgment) I may not, by parties
who may become interested be put aside and
the office bestowed on another.
If you agree to my proposition I would
be glad if you would write to me imme-
diately, and I will set to work without delay
With great respect
From ofst Servt
Edward P. Fry

Dear Prof. Moone
I wrote to you this morning
stating that I would be ready tomorrow for
experiment. I however shall not be ready
so early as I contemplated in consequence
of all the stores being shut up, and I have
not been able to get the acid I want for
the experiments, I shall however be early at
7 in the morning and as your east &
Ground circuit is closed you will know
when I am ready by the ringing of the bell
if it is in a condition to be rung when I am
ready — If at 11 o'clock no action takes place
send to the cars for a letter, as I will write
if any thing is wrong — wire broken &c — and
at 11 o'clock I will change to West & Ground.
Then after we get started you can order the
experiments to suit yourself — write if you can
not attend yourself by tomorrow mornings train
I do hope that no impediment will be put in
our way towards continuing the Telegraph in
operation during the Summer & Fall, by stopping
the appropriation — I presume Sec. Babb will
leave it to the discretion of Mr. Young who will
I feel assured yield to the wishes of several here
% whom he is indebted for his place, and who will
see him whenever you desire it. Mr. Rogers tells me
this — The wires which were broken at Bladenburg
were untwisted. The ends of her with and you
the breaks which Cleveland mended on Tuesday,
were occasioned by lightning he says
as the two posts on either side of the break were
marked along the bark with the streak or cut
made by the fluid descending to the ground, as
I also the trees in the immediate neighborhood
The breaks were not at any joint, but of whole
cloth as he says, -- between the same posts
but not directly opposite each other. They were
6 or 8 feet apart, one on each wire, and about
3 miles beyond Beltsville toward Washington.
I hope your leg has entirely healed and that
you have had a long siege, but I trust
it is all for the best although it does not
appear so -- Will you leave for New York
soon? -- Cleveland is now cleaning up the old
vine's -- and Brown may send me the other
which he has cast. -- I have not yet got from
Dr Page the thinktop of the Copper state for the
Dixie's, and I can therefore do nothing until
he sends me a sample of the thinktop.
Your Most Obest Servt
Alfred Bait

Dear Sir,
Yours of July 1st & 2 I have duly
received; I have written in the language suggested to you to the day of this.
In answer to your query respecting the wire, I would say that the Benedict & Burnham
Manufacturing Co. at Waterbury Conn. furnished me my wire, and as excellent an article as
was ever made; I found them faithful and prompt Messrs. Brown & Elton of the same place also made
proposals; they furnished Colt with his wire.
I have on hand a quantity of wire all prepared which I am authorized to dispose of
by the Department; you can have it at a sacrifice.
You kindly propose to dedicate the vocabularies to me and ask my permission to do. I certainly grant it with pleasure, and hail your
proposal as an evidence that our intercourse in future will be established of a more amicable character.
I have consulted with Mr. Vail, and I have written to Mr. in the language suggested by you to Mr. Fry adding only the following
paragraph: "The contract will be entered into on his own responsibility and will contain a
provision that will secure to you the rights of all the proprietors in the patent." For it will be received
by you as such.
Very respectfully yours
Samuel D. Slocum
Secretary of War

upon consulting Dr.
1 have made a proposition to Mr. Burbank
to sell out my share of the Patent right for the unexpended time of the Patent for One hundred & ten
thousand Dollars, to be paid over & secured to me in 6
months from the date of proposition. I am fully aware
that this is not half what I should get, but for
the sake of having my mind free for a general supervision
of the system and to perfect it, I will face
so the prospects of greater remuneration.
You will see by the Batt. Pat. of yesterday which I sent
you, an article which will be favorable to your plans. The
feeling at the Department as regard to the Telegraph is
more enthusiastic than ever. They say God must have it.
You will be satisfied to learn the result of some experiments
made yesterday. We determined to try how few caps
of the Batteries would operate the line through the 40 miles. —
We had been using 80, 70, and at one time 48 caps. Will you
believe it 10 pairs actually operated the Telegraph perfectly well
and these 10 12 caps which had been in constant action for
more than 36 hours. You will see the importance of this result
in its bearing on the expence of maintenance of Batteries in the article
of consumption of materials and care of Batteries. I have batteries
all enough to operate my Telegraph from Wash. to Boston. —
I have given Fry 20 days to consider proposals
to his 1st Augt. —

Baltimore July 10, 1844.
Dear Sir,
I have this moment received
advices from my partners in the Telegraph,
and I am able to say, that one of the proprietors
will contract to put up a line complete from Philad o
to New York (reserving intermediate lines, but with
the limitation that they shall at no time be con-
verted into a continuous line so as to conflict with
or prejudice the main and direct line,) for Sixty
thousand dollars which shall include two circuits,
one for simultaneous use each way and instruments
at each end of each, and deliver it completed by 1st
Jan 7 1845 including the right to use the same ex-
clusively – reserving the right to use the same posts
for the construction of the intermediate lines but
never to the prejudice or injury of the main line – The
payments to be one quarter as the contracts for ma-
terials shall become due, or within thirty days after
signing of the contract: One quarter when one half
of the line shall be completed, and the remainder
when the whole line shall be delivered on the 1st day of
January next. –
The proposition above is to deliver the Telegraph
ready for use between Philadelphia & New York or such
point opposite the cities as shall be nearest & most
feasible in case difficulty be found in cropping to the
city at this time -- and without extra charge -- and in-
cluding the exclusive right to use the same -- promising
that you procure the Railroad Company's assent to
erect the posts on their line.
The total expense of sustaining it in operation day &
night between those two points will not exceed as near
as I can now estimate $2,500. per annum for each sta-
-tion. Superintending the construction is
included in the above proposition. But superintending
the use of the Telegraph will be only such an expense
as will procure the services of young men who can be
instructed at a trifling cost in all the essential of
the business in a few days all which I will attend to
for a fair compensation. --
The right to use the Telegraph is put at a small
sum in the above proportion in order to enable it
to be in hands that will teach the public and the
Government how mighty an engine the Telegraph
is. -- In case the proposal is acceded
to one of the proprietors ready to contract, will im-
-mediately visit your city and enter at once upon
all necessary arrangements for the earliest pro-
gress of the work.
The contract will be entered into by him on
his own responsibility and will contain a provision
that will secure to you the rights of all the proprietors
in the Patent.
I cannot well accede to the request for forty
days consideration whether to accept the terms now
offered, as there are applications from Newyork of
such a nature as to make it necessary to have your
decision in 20 days from date, that is to say by
the 1st of August next.
Although I shall probably be in Newyork
for some days to come, yet address me at Wash-
-ington under cover to Hon. H. L. Ellsworth
Commissioner of Patents.
I am very respectfully
Yr Obt Servant
(Signed) Saml. F. B. Morse

By the experiments made today
There must be some wrong connection at your
end — For strange as it is — The East & ground
worked well. & West & Ground & East & West
but when the two independent

register. — If you will take your time to
just trace out the wires tomorrow I think
all will come right — I could not get a
spark from the west wire when in the double
circuit showing conclusively some wrong
connection. It is not here for I have proved
it — By the last experiment I proved it to
my satisfaction — I presume you either soldered
wrong wires together, or there is some misunderstanding at the box of the big magnet — Let us
try it again tomorrow and patienty work it
out. When we can get 8 & 7 at 5 and 13 & 14
at 11 at your end all right so that you will
be able only to receive and not to write the
thing will be OK and then we can go on
Yours in haste
Alfred Vail

Dear Sir:
A letter from Mr. Fry of Phila. in
disfavor to the proposals, which you sent, I have
just received. I wish much to see you, as I can
not move in this matter until I know your views.
I am here for about a fortnight, and wish
some arrangements made by which our business
can be transacted without the necessity of so much
waiting and so much writing. I have an excellent
office here which might be used for an Agency
for the Telegraph; but we must settle terms for
such an Agent first. When will you be here?
How are matters in relation to the New York &
Boston line? -- Mr. Fry objects to our reservation
of the way lines, and finds it an objection
in the minds of Capitalists to whom he has
applied. He also makes this proposition, that
money shall be raised to defray the cost of the
construction, and then this sum shall be doubled
as the amount of stock, this sum shall be doubled of which stock
we shall take in payment of our right. --
This strikes me favorably, for it would serve
all round; it appears to me that we might then
give up the intermediate lines, for we should at
least be interested to the use of one half of its
value; you could contract to construct, and avail
yourself of the profits of contract, while you would
also divide your portion of the sum paid for patent
right, and I should be content with this arrange-
ment, as I could undoubtedly sell my stock to
advantage. - Please think of this and let me
know what are your views as soon as possible. -
Mr. Fry is here and I am here, and other applica-
tions are also expected, so that I wish you were
here to settle terms. -
I have mentioned George Vail, he is, as a
proprietor under Alfred, very desirous of engaging in
the contract between Phil. & N York, and is an
efficient and driving man, and I believe all con-
cerned will be benefited by his exertions, and experi-
ence. - I have a letter from him on the subject. If
you can be here, I can send for him, and we can
talk over the matter. -
In haste Yr Ob Servt
Sam: F: B: mose

Dear Sir
I have not the pleasure of seeing from
you a line since you left us here, — In relation
to the refusal of your half which you gave me, I
find the enquiry made can you not content more
of your desires therefore if Mr Gale will do so,
that he will, or if you please give me a refusal
for the purchase of his 18th also — I have not heard
from Mr Smith yet, but should suppose him
willing enough to do as you have. Mr Cornell
has not yet made his appearance — How will it do for
me to employ help to take up the lead? by having
Mr Avery with me a day or two, so as to have it
done as it should be could it not be done to
your will? In such case I would give it all the
personal attendance possible, and in my absence
would have one equally as good on the spot, as
to play let my play be left to Cornell, say 150,
or any way that you might deem best. All is if
you think my position requiring, which command him
as I presume you are anxious to have it so.
Again if in the construction of a line of telegraph you
may be desired to represent it — and prefer to continue
as to the basis & connecting part of it, would it be agreeable
in such case, still to accept with the view of my taking
your plan so far as you might deem it practicable, &
and for this favour if time is something to be made
on such construction between the cost of materials
labour & price of contract - let us divide what can
be thus obtained - although I am inclined somewhat
to believe that I may depend in the sale of the company
I shall be glad to hear from you on the
position owned by the Gall - and any thing else
you may please to communicate
Your affectionately truly
David Burkitt.
* On this score I see at once that there would be responsibility
on your part as to advancement -- & made to
carry it out -- yet allow me to say, that if the enemy's
troops in such case come up in your mind, what are
the circumstances of Mr B. so that you might know
that hands might or might not be applied to the right
purpose -- I would in that case remark that I do
not owe the amount of $100000 in the world -- I
only mention this, as sometimes in our business way
of affairs -- a person speaks for favor or credit,
the question comes up, is he honest, & not how
much is he worth, but how much does he owe,
& what are his liabilities
Your in honest feeling
AB

Dear Prof Morse
Your letter has just been
received, and I hasten to say that I cannot
consent to part with my share on the same
terms that you do. At all events it would
be wrong for me to decide a matter which
is of so much importance to me and without
well weighing the matter. — You are aware
that it has already slipped from my hands
by being so hasty and I must be more deliberate
now.
Mr Rogers and myself are telegraphing now
but are not open to the public, your experiment

I have not ascertained the amount which I could

correct data, when the register is perfect I have
proof of the fact that it may be very much
increased.
Dr Page is waiting your return to experiment
with his machine.
The magazine you sent cannot be found.
I have been telegraphing at the same time that
Mr Rogers has been writing with but one
battery, and that consisted of 20 cups, —
I did not try less though 6s would have

Thankful that I might not have expressed myself
with sufficient clearness while in conversation with you this afternoon,
having been somewhat embarrassed, I beg leave to repeat what I then
stated.
I suppose the earth to be a battery, having its concentrated force
of attraction at the magnetic pole; if this be so, the fluid will rush from
all parts of the surface towards that point; the reacting force of which
will produce a motion to the earth equal to its diurnal motion on it
axis: when the fluid becomes too abundant it will be discharged
at the magnetic pole, producing the "Northern Lights" which are
known to be most brilliant after a long period of dry and stormy weather
when the atmosphere is the least charged with electricity, hence acting
as a safety valve.
If this be so, the needle of the compass must be attracted towards that
point, and it will have precisely that "disp" which observation
proves it to possess. — Should the magnetic pole (about 11º from the
pole of the earth) be retratory, or have a certain motion round its own
centre, it would be "the regulating power", to keep the earth steady in
its motion. These are the prominent points in this theory, and I
have an sufficient to entitle it to investigation.
Very respectfully
Robert Leslie
P.S. I may add that your investigations as far as they have come to
my knowledge all tend to establish in my mind the truth of the theory

The Syro-Egyptian Society of London
Aug 30th 1860
Sir I am requested by the Council of the Syro-Egyptian
Society to forward you a Copy of their Prospectus, and
to state that they will feel their hands much strengthened
if you will kindly permit them to appoint you their
Agent and Referee for New York. You will perceive
that the Society are anxious to avail themselves of
every opportunity of obtaining authentic information
from the Orient, and of rendering facilities to gentlemen
who may be travelling or residing abroad to uphold
the objects which they have in view, by becoming
Non-Resident Members (See page 8) – It is obvious
that this can only be accomplished by appointing
Agents in the Capital Towns, & in other important
Localities. You will therefore greatly oblige
the Council by affording them the advantage of
your influence and valuable co-operation – It is
of course necessary that their Agents should satisfy
themselves of the respectability of the parties they may
recommend to the Council for election (See page 12)
and I send you herewith a Form which can, at
any time, be copied, filled up, and transmitted to
me as the Honorary Secretary, when any gentlemen
devise to be proposed as Members. Suffice it
to say that great exertions are making in various
quarters - new members are elected at every meeting,
several valuable papers have already been received, and
we have two works of interest now in the press -
A Society like this, recommends itself; as it has nothing
to do with Politics, and must tend to the improvement of
Asia Minor, Egypt, Palestine & Syria, as well as to the
advancements of Literature, Science, and the Arts - it only
requires to be made known.
Anticipating the favor of an early communication
from you I remain Sir
Very faithfully Yours
H Holt Gates Esq
Hon: Sec.

proportion to the size of the copper plates at the extremities of the Conductors. The number of cups of the battery

other on the same side also affects the result.

Friend Mose
Dear Sir It is now almost
two week since you left us and I have had the
gratification to learn by others that you are busy
in Boston, with the Telegraph. I presume you
have been so engage as not to find time to
write. Yet a letter from you would be very
welcome. — We have got underway at the Post
office although our room is not finished yet.
after Mr Cornell left the man he engage would
do no more and we were a week relying upon
the false promises of Carpenters and had again
to move our stuff to another shop — From last
Saturday until Tuesday I was very sick, but
have now got pretty well, yet not entirely. I
have every thing ready for the Election which
comes of next Wednesday, and we intend to keep
it up late on that night, very much interest is
manifested to have all the Baltimore City returns
as soon as possible, and I trust none will be dis-
appointed — In selecting the main wires at the
post office, from the wires that run from P O to
Capitol I had some difficulty — There seemed to
be no difference by the galvanometer which two of
the four I took, all deflected the needle alike
99848
So that in using the two lateral wires for telegraphic
purposes between the P O & E I presume we may
have difficulty. If so, I will abandon them, and
use the main wires for that purpose, which I
can readily do, — I fear that they (the two lateral
wires) may have to come down. For during a heavy
rain storm on Tuesday last, all at once we
could not work, and Rogers says his pen was
kept up against the paper the whole time, I also
experienced much difficulty with my big magnet,
But the next morning every thing went off well
again. The storm being over. There is no doubt
that it will not do to put up the wires in a
bundle unless much better insulated.
Mr Ellsworth has returned. I have not seen
him. — I have not been able to get the line ready
between the capitol and post office yet. But if
I am not to buy next week telegraphing, I will
have it done. I want to see how it will go.
If you do not return soon will you send me
some more money if you please — I have not
heard from home since you left. Mr Burbank
is making a rush in Philadelphia. How does
the matter look in Boston? I guess the telegraph will
not be up by the 1st of February. Please write
as soon as you can.
Yours obet Bert
Alfred Pail

Is the Assistant Superintendent of the Telegraph
Washington: Alfred Vail, Esg.
Washington D.C., Oct 11th 1844.
Sir,
As there are so great interest taken, by
the citizens generally of both political parties, in
the results of the various elections occurring at
this season, you will be specially careful not to give
a partisan character to any information you
may transmit.
If you give a result, note the source
from which you obtain it. If such, you may
anyone let it be touched by a respectable
name, and preserve a record of the same.
Send no mere rumors, and as far as
practicable give only official results, or such
as both parties agree in.
Let no one announce from the
wires any intelligence as sent by Telegraph,
except such as one as you shall duly
authorize.
Very Respectfully
Yr. Ob Servt
Sam'l C.D. Mosse
Superintendent of the Electric
Telegraphs of the United States.

Dear Sir.
Inclosed is a letter which I received, will
be obliged if you will hand it to Mr Vaid.
On calling at the Telegraph Office this fore noon
I learned from Mr Rogers that Mr V. resigned, who was
on the instrument up stairs? Mr R. replaced Mr B. this
Son - Mr Strong this brother. To which Mr V. orders perfectly,
"take it down & box it up" -
I thought I would explain to you, so far as I
know, and for my own part, I had an inclination to learn
if you were willing - And as for my son, he did accompany
me occasion ally but not with a view to learn neither is he
qualified for it. but no one else has attended with me. &
I was about to have a key & fasten myself in when I practised
Mr Strong does not wish, he says to learn, only to read
as there was an opportunity, he would be able to answer
when alone, or rather to signify that the attendant was absent.
Mr Rogers & I presume did it by the permission of his brother
and there can be no doubt of the best of situation or the fact
of either. being a young man, clock in the Mechanics Bank, and
of the first respectable and I learn from his brother that character
he has no particular desire, other than curiosity, as he has a very
good situation when he will be. If however you have
objections to my speaking, & such as you did not think of when you con
sented, I will say no more, but if you are willing, I would be
pleased to continue. Yours respectfully Truly
David Barback.
If it be given permission that I may continue my
practise, I will in all case, have it look
myself in if this is what is wanted - for I had no
desire to make it public.
Professor S.F.B. Morse

Washington Octr. 20th 1844
Sir,
Your letter of the 30th of August 1844 forwarded
to me by my friend the Rev. D. Savers, and enclosing
the Prospectus of the plan & objects of the Pyro Egypt-
ian Society of London, I have just received, and I
thank you for the confidence bestowed upon me by the
Iron Society of which you are the Secretary, in appoint-
ing me agent of its Agents in N.York. I must nevertheless
decline the honor in consequence of the reasons
that, My important duties as the Superintendent of Telegraphs
for the U. State, make it necessary that I should pass
the principal part of my time in this City and not in
N. York.
I have, there are other doublets in N. York whose services
in Gunfiring the projectiles of your Society would be far more efficient than mine
can possibly be, from their more direct interest in them.
But while I decline the Agency of the Society for the
City of N.York, it will give me pleasure if I can render
it any service.
I remain Sir
Very Respectfully
Yr Ob. Servt
Sam. F. B. Morse
Pres. of the National Academy

Sunday evening.
I am sorry to see you on a subject of great
importance to mention morning at 9 1/2 o'clock at the
Telegraph Office. Some circumstances totally affecting
our whole interest in the Telegraph have been communi-
cated to me the last evening by a friend which re-
quires our immediate attention. I write this that
you may not leave in the morning before I see you.
Truly your friend & Servt
Samuel F. B. Morse

dollars per mile between Albany and the

My dear Sir
Baltimore October 28th 1844
I thought of writing a line to you while in Wash
ington but had not time — I feel anxious to effect
something with you & the then proprietor in regard to the
privilege of constituting your line of Telegraph — I could not
arrange any terms with Mr Smith as respecting the right
to use it into a Company, — But I think he would
be willing to sell the right of building, apart from the right
of using, either for a sum out right, or for a percentage
on the contents, or a fix Cottage on the profits — if he and
the other proprietor could agree on the terms, I wish you would
talk with him on the subject now, to ascertain if any thing can be
done advantageously to all concerned, in this way, I don't wish
to interfere with the right which Congress will want to use the
invention, but only the right of contracting for building the
line — I did not name any rate. Would be willing to give
to either of you when I was in Washington — but will name
the sum of ten thousands dollars for the right of building
lines, to be paid as you & Mr Smith & the U. S. may think
should be from earnings.
I have written Mr Smith in the letter which we
refer to, another proposal — If he does not show it to you,
I wish you would ask to see it, that you may judge
whether it is not for the interest of all parties to do what
I then propose about the route to Buffalo — I think if I
could get him to agree to it, if you think favorably enough
of it, to encourage it. He professes to be willing to assist me
and more so, because he is not willing to accede to the

Yours respectfully & truly
David Barback.

Very Respectfully

Paris Nov 12. 1844
My dear Sir
I should write to you occasionally did
not the newspapers furnish promptly and in detail
all news from this side of the Atlantic indeed from
every corner of the world. I now write lest by
chance a matter which concerns yourself, and the
United States too, should escape your observation.
I saw in the Journal des Debats of yesterday that
the Minister of the Interior has appointed a
Commission to report on Electrical Telegraphy
telegraphie electrique: I think your invention
ought on this occasion to be duly presented to
the notice of Europe. Independently of the discovery
of this application of electric galvanism, I am
persuaded your apparatus for transmitting it,
etc., is much superior to any employed here;
unless perhaps some great improvements may have
been recently introduced of which I am ignorant.
I saw Prof. Wheatstone's apparatus at King's College
London: -- You may remember I saw yours at
Washington in the Capitol before any time was laid
down, and I have seen subsequently in the
American newspapers notices of it working between
Washington and Baltimore. One account of it
was published in several European newspapers
but it has not appeared to me that your
discouraging and manner of application have yet received
here the attention they are entitled to. The names of
Wheatstone, Faraday and others are often mentioned in
connection with this subject. I once spoke of your
Teligraph to Mr Wheatstone, but my remarks resulted
in no conversation.
The Minister of the Interior is himself president
of the Commission, M Arago is one of the members.
I would gladly take charge of any communication,
but I hope soon to return to America. Besides it
would be better perhaps to send through M. Payet at
Washington, or the American Minister or some
of your scientific friends at Paris.
I hear of McCloskey through his new publications,
and I should add, through the frequent notices and
advertisements of his old ones in the French Newspaper.
His high reputation on the Continent is undiminished.
France in my opinion enjoys a solid material
prosperity. The active strife waged here between Roman
Catholicism or Ultramontanism and the moral
and intellectual independence of France cannot
have escaped your attention. The party which bows
to Rome seems to be adding most to its numbers;
seems boldly, even themselves. Liberty of instruction which
this party claims, it is asserted means the right to
teach blind submission to Rome in matters of religion,
and political opinions subordinate of the present dynasty;
and further that the perfect organization of the Roman
stry would soon render such instruction exclusive of
all others. — It is I think quite true that religion
and morality have been making much progress for
many years in France. This I attribute in a very
great degree to the peace it enjoys and the
consequent absence of the demoralizing influences of
war. — When in Rome last spring I had a long
interview with the Pope who said to me he was
satisfied with the condition and prospect of the Catholic
Church in America. To me at a distance, the public
mind in America appears to be in a strongly unformed
state—what with Millenium, Mormonism, etc., and
ought I not to add Presyison? it would not
suffice me if the Pope should come to possess so
authority among you. Where are the three Powers
the school though, the printing press and the Pulpit?
On my way through the United States to Texas
I hope to see you—I want to confer with you on a
topic too extensive to be introduced into the door of a
rambling letter.
Truly and sincerely
Your
Ashbel Smith

Dear Sir,

In relation to my movement as to the formation of a company I can see no difficulty in doing it if the proprietor will come in. – And since I left you here, I have seen others that will like an interest in it.
Your respectfully & truly
David Burbank.

New York Nov. 13th 1844.
Dear Sir.
I have received yours of the 4th & 5th inst. and
reply in relation to the several subjects you mention in
that order.
I like very well the suggestion in regard to the pre
sentation of a set of the Telegraphic Dictionary, you are
publishing to each member of Congress, and when I return to
Washington will see the Secretary and let if he will about it.
As to the dedication to me, since you have asked
my opinion, I must say, I should prefer to have it much
curtailed, and less laudatory; I must refer it entirely to
you, however, as it is not for me to say what others should
write or think of me.
In regard to the Bartlett claim, and your
plan for settling it, I cannot admit that as proprietors
of the Telegraph we have any thing to do with it. I
regret that there has been any mention of it, and I had
hoped that you yourself would have come to the deter
mination to leave that matter altogether, or at least
until the Telegraph bill had been definitely settled in
Congress. However much I regret the determination made
to man and probably to defeat all our progress in
the Senate, it is a matter over which I have no control
and therefore in the aspect that has been given to it, the suppression of
details which had better not be pushed to a decision, does
not rest with me. -- In regard, however, to such a Division
of the property of the Telegraph as shall enable each of
us to labor for the general benefit without embarrass
ment from each other, I think it worthy of consideration
and the principle on which such a division is proposed to
might be extended to embrace the entire property. The subject
however, requires mature deliberation, and I am not now
prepared to present the plan but will think it over, and
consult with Vail & Galt and arrange it, perhaps, definitively
when I see you again in Washington.
I have letters from Vail at Wash & Rogers at Balt.
stating the fact that complete success has attended all the trans
missions of results by Telegraph, thus not having failed in
a single instance, and to the satisfaction of both political
parties in the transmission execution of the Telegraph.
to F.O.J. Smith Esq.
Chilly Yglesias
Sam. P. M'Nary.

My dear Sir
Your returned favor of yesterday includes a check on the Bank of Washington is part of it
and I might not perhaps have written to day, would not put me right with you as to what I said to my last
about the proposition coming in. I addressed to Mr Smith not coming in to the proposition which I then gave you
1217 tails approbation. although I had Mr Smith's letter to that effect, and after I left you room in Washington
I spent most of the evening with him to accomplish it still I did not refuse to the letter he sent me, suggesting he concluded
it was for some wise purpose he felt just then did not like to come in to it, it might be to suit his will
alter his plan with his Boston concern, but when he left me at the Boat he seemed to think something may
get be done to suit all. The amount of it is, President, your enterprise Stuart will not gain reward
did it begin to be appreciated in a small degree does not The Pres without distinction of party run in Baltimore
have promised to advocate its construction throughout the Union. The attention & kindness of Major Rogers
& Tait and their concern in due course I think give a favorable impression who I do hope that the "American"
will act with discretion & dignity, then they will prevail they need more than present counsel.
I am yours truly in haste
David Burnside

Dear Sir
I have read with great admiration and delight, the various accounts which have been published of your wonderful discoveries in the magnetic telegraph, enabling you to annihilate time and space, and giving to the people of this great Country, the means of leaving, instantly, at the two extremities of the Union, all the important transactions at the seat of government, enabling the merchant to transmit with perfect accuracy and at trifling expense, important intelligence from Boston to New Orleans, with the rapidity of lightning. I saw an exhibit ion , on a limited scale, of your telegraph by E. Cornell at this place last summer, and was delighted with the simplicity and rapidity with which letters could be made, and I am astonished that scientific men in Europe should not have seen the best advantages of your telegraph, over any of the plans now in use either in England, France, or Russia. As an American, I rejoice that you met with no better reception when abroad,
as the honor now belongs exclusively
to our own Country, and I parti
cipate in the glory, in common with
every other American. I think the time
is not distant when the people will
require our government to extend your
telegraph from Washington to New Orleans,
and from Washington to Boston, enabling
the daily papers in all of our Atlantic cities,
to publish the proceedings of Congress, as
soon as they are now published at
the Capitol. My object in writing to you
is to know whether you would have
any objection to my exhibiting your
telegraphs, in the principal towns in
this, and the Western States, in connection
with experiments in Galvanism, and
electro magnetism. I propose obtaining one
of Professor Locke's "Organised batteries," and
to exhibit your telegraphs, I would only
require your apparatus for marking, or
recording the communications if you
have no objection to my making such
use of your invention, please let me
know where I could obtain such
machinery as I would require, and the
cost of it.
I beg leave to refer you, for any
information respecting me, to
The Honl Amasa Dana of this district,
(an uncompromising bitter foe of) or
to Honl Silas Wright Hon. H.L. Ellsworth
William Grindlage Esq of George Town
or Richard Boyer Esq of Washington.
Respectfully
Yr Odt Servt
J. Speer Jr
Professor More
Washington
P.S. Please direct to me at Bridge, care of
C. H. Johnson Esqr

Washington Dec. 6th 1844.
Sir, I have the honor to state that in the
letter I had the honor to address to the Depart-
ment under date Sept. 27th 1837 in reply to
queries addressed me by the Department respect-
ing Telegraphs I have this passage, "The cost of
"printing, in the first instance, of a Telegraphic Dic-
"tionary, should also be taken into the account, as
"each Officer of the Government as well as many
"others would require a copy should this mode of
"Telegraphic Communication go into effect. This Dic-
"tionary would contain a full vocabulary of all
"the words in common use in the English language
"with the numbers regularly affixed to each
"word." — One of the proprietors of the Elec-
tric magnetic telegraph has now in the press a
Telegraphic Vocabular, or Dictionary of this
character, printing at his own cost, and he has
proposed to distribute a copy of his Dictionary
containing of two copies to each of the members of
Congress at the cost price of one dollar & twenty-five
cents each copy , and to take in payment a quan-
tity of the surplus wire which remains on hand
from the experimental essay with the Telegraph &
at the market valuation.
The expense of the number of copies necessary
to supply the members of Congress as proposed
will not exceed Five hundred dollars, and the
one on hand will not probably fall short
in value of One thousand dollars.
I would respectfully request to make
the arrangement proposed by exchanging
the necessary quantity of wire for the requisite
number of copies of the Dictionary to be distrib-
uted among the members of Congress as pro-
posed.
Very Respectfully Sir
Y. M. O. H. Servt.
Sam'l F. B. Morse

My dear Sir
Baltimore Oct 7th 1844,
In addition to what I have written respecting the Telegraph Office here, I thought it proper that I should again intimate with the observation and remarks now being made respecting the Games of Chess, at the Telegraph Office here. As perhaps without explanation the fact may seem to prejudice the public mind, I own this is somewhat difficult especially when they do not listen to explanation.
I have been enquired of several times if such was the fact, I replied I believe something of the kind was done & merely to test the capacity of the Telegraph -- but it doesn't seem to satisfy their curiosity so long as it exists, especially when strangers seize the Office to use, as in the case may be, to find they may not be admitted to witness its function for the reason of it being thus occupied, or even if admitted then, an impression unfavorable is carried with them.
It is the susceptibility of the people, perhaps more one now so, I know of nothing to the contrary but others equally so, I stand in this kind of sentence (of that the word) and would like to participate, but find them seldom included by previous complaint; And thus in fact may be the only to cause the doubt does not rest solely by the ear, and the most thing the feared, is some foolish spirit in the papers proposing to the contrary. The Roger Button with whom I made you acquainted when you were here, I by the way, a valuable young man a member of one of the Chambers here, spoke to his brother Henry, as to what he had been enquired of H.R. -- I think the anxiety of Mr. Roger as he enquired of me, if I had heard much said of this? -- No man could be better qualified to fill the Station he occupies, always prompt, vigilant, attentive to the true interests of the Telegraph.
I have written this with fondness, and
and in confidence to the Professor, that he may deduce from
it, what in his good judgment may be deemed best and
expedient in relation to the purpose — And would simply
suggest, that the illustration may well apply here; that
an ounce of prevention is worth as much as a pound
of cure —
I am yours truly
David Barbour

present controversy to seem to sustain his argument that
I had not at that time a Telegraph prepared for use and ex-
hibition in the U. States. The passage is this "Can you tell
"me at what expense you can have a Telegraph made
"for me with your improvements at N.York? If you should
"leave of a sudden we should have a perfect instrument
"to operate with at home. That Deficiency was alone
"what delayed our whole wishes through the last win-
"ter - A perfect instrument should be exhibited at the
"earliest opening of Congress & by it an appropriation
"will be rendered certain. The proprietors must Con-
"tribute pro rata and have one at best made off hand
"for home use, under your own eye Direction. Will
"you write me the probable expense, and propose it to the
"Messrs. Rails I will contribute my proportion." -
On this I remark that the inquiry respecting the expense at
which a Telegraph could be made in N.York, was not of such a Telegraph
as had already been made, a set of which I had already made
"a Telegraph with your improvements." I had made some improvements
while studying upon it in Paris, reducing it in size, and making it of
brass instead of wood, and adding the necessary for a London Telegraph
with various other modifications. Mr. Smith was desirous of obtaining
these improvements, and it is evident from what he says after, that
the instruments he speaks of could not be doing which I was to procure without "charge or expense to Mr. Smith" for they were to be procured
by contribution from the Proprietors pro rata.

Washington Jan. 3. 1845
Sir,
I have the honor to enclose Copies of
a letter published by order of Congress, on the
subject of my Electric Magnetic Telegraph which accompanies it.
By the Report No. 17, it will be seen that the
system which I have now in successful operation
was examined in 1838 by a Commission appointed
by the Minister of the Interior, and the preference
given to mine over all others.
Precisely that the French Government are
examining the subject of Electric Telegraphs with
reference to the establishment of some one of the
systems offered to the public, I am desirous of
having the facts in regard to mine placed before the
Commission. I shall be exceedingly happy to show
to you the operation of my Telegraph, and to explain
it in all its details.
I leave the city for New York to day, to be about
a week. On my return I will have the honor of
approving your visit, and should it be agreeable to
you to witness the operation of the Telegraph I will
hold myself in readiness at any moment to do so, but you
may have the honor to visit my residence at
your convenience.
I have the honor to be with great respect
Y. M. Alphonse Praets

My Dear Sir
Yours of the 20th reached here while I was from
home. sickness or death has been our constant companion since your life
until within the last few days.
I have just returned from New York where I went to aid in
the last kind offices to the late Mrs Conner who died at our
house on Sunday morning last and was buried at N.Y.
on Wednesday
Thus am my apology for not answering, or rather writing you
before. I shall probably write again in a day or two –
I enclose to you a fifty doll. or note, No 143 Sent to, on
The Seventh Ward Bank. I regret that I have left you out
of the use of it so long – Mr Brown on whom I depended told me
sometime since he could give it me any day when I must have
it, but he has been unexpectedly delayed by the Insurance Company
in obtaining his losses so when I first applied to him he found
more difficulties than were anticipated – I beg you to accept my
thanks for the favor conferred.
Now for the petition. The day after your left for W– I
called on Mr Dudley, of the firm, (J. H. Hennion to consult
about the business of the petition. Mr C. said Mr Chepkin
was the man to draw it up and he would see him and
hasten the thing – so let it rest two days when I again
see Mr J– to know what progress had been made. I found the
gentleman had very considerable work done – He rather
Three obstacles in the way he said the petition ought to be printed
and he did not know who should pay for it -- He said the printing
would cost $150 -- We cannot charge that to proof of Honor -- very
well I replied I will pay that and remove that objection if you
will get the signatures -- In the mean time Mrs Louisa Sisson did
did -- On my return from M.S.B. I called this morning on my
Merchant for the list of petitioners to my great vexation
and notification I found the gentleman Mr C. who accorded
me in this manner, "Your fellow sum to be very dilatory
in forwarding that petition" and took from his desk the
draft of a petition so badly drawn up as in my opinion to
render it objectionable. It had 3 names on it at the head of which
stood Loring C. Chapin a large letter. After some remarks he
(Mr Godling) urged the necessity of my taking the paper to the Mayor
to get his signature first -- Having removed the names from
the first of the paper I supplied him with a obtainable letter
of introduction I went to the Mayor who recognized this paper
which had been presented by the said Chapin on (Bulley)
before. He said Mr Haspin said he had no objection to
put his name to the paper but he would not have it -- So you see I have written all this mass of detail
that you may know how the matter has been conducted ab initio. It has been an utter failure from
being put into bad hands -- Chapin has not brains enough
to do his own business -- Godling complains he has so much
business that he has no time to give it -- Notwithstanding all
he said to you he says a different song when you are away
I shall go to see your brother in the morning and take
conseel as to the best course to be pursued.
In the mean time I will send to you this communication
Mrs G. desires to be remembered
Prof S.F. Morse
Respectfully your Friend & Servt
S.C. Gale

In reply to your request that I would give you
my views on the subject of taking the Years & Keys in the
House of Representatives. I would observe that the present
mode seems to be generally admitted to be defective, especially
from the circumstance of it consuming so much valuable
time, and it is by no means a new thought that another
and better plan could be desired. American
The time consumed in taking the Years & Keys, even
with the experience & admirable tact of the present
Clerk of the House is however less than a quarter of an
hour, and more often 20 minutes. When it is considered
that the Years & Keys are called in an average
times in a day, some estimate may be formed of the
consumption of time during a Session of Congress.
While so much important public business is done over
from Session to Session in the plea of want of time, or
is hurried defectively, through for the same reason,
I think that any mechanical plan to prevent a needless
waste of time must meet with public favor. I have several mechanical modes which I think
would be effective in reducing the time to 3 minutes
which includes of course the reading off the names
by the Clerk if that should be deemed necessary.
One mode is by the use of a Gatunie balloting, to
electing a needle bearing a card, which according as the
current is directed turns to the right or left, the
right hand being Yes & the left Nay, these cards are then
instantly and simultaneously displayed upon a light frame
erected in the centre of the floor, and each Senator's vote
is cast in the same way as in the House of Commons, and the
result stands thus: Right hand stands for Yes, Left hand for Nay, and the
columns can be counted, and the vote recorded at leisure.
This effect can be produced by the simple
turning of a small hand at each desk to the Yes or Nay marked
on the plate, and which is further locked by each member.
Then is also a mechanical mode of producing
the same effect, which would require which would require
another feature. A
The experiment could be made for about $1500
and should it be desired I will undertake to that sum
to construct the necessary fighting and have an experimental
essay ready for the next session of Congress.
Very Respectfully, I am,

Dear Sir,
I do not think I could purchase a final
purchase for your interest in the Telegraph in the terms men-
tioned in your letter of the 17th inst. Men may be found who will
risk $30,000 as the matter stands before the public; but if made
aware that Professor Morse himself declined taking a lien on
the whole interest sold as security for the balance of the purchase
money, they would be likely to lose all confidence in the invention.
The first of June next is too soon for the advance payment;
it allows too little time for making arrangements a finding a
purchase. It should not be sooner than the first of July.
It should interest commence until at least a reason-
able time has been given to make the enterprise productive, say the
first of January next.
It is understood of course, that all the risks of the
enterprise are to fall on the purchaser while the patent is
to be guaranteed by you, and the purchaser is to have
the benefit of all discoveries and improvements hereafter
made by you pertaining to the subject matter.
The increased price beyond what I understand it
to be and the heavy advance required, diminishes both my ability
and inclination to become a purchaser; but I would like to
have terms which, in case of incapacity, I could show to this and

Dear Professor Morse
San Francisco, January 24th 1847.
I saw a few days ago in the Newspapers it announced that the Union Government has gone in
violation of establishing a magnetic Telegraph, and an Effect of the Government of Union forbidding
all from putting up a Telegraph of any kind. These and other news led me to believe that
Casper is now thinking really about the erection of telegraph lines along her railroads, &
that other Former Friends will soonen, or later to the same.
I read also somewhere that the Telegraph in use now in France has been by its inventor, improved, &
that it is much better of it continental Europe. I know however that whatever
may be this Telegraph improved, it will always be inferior to yours Professor, on every account,
& consequently, that if your Telegraph were better than in Europe, and especially in France,
it would be preferred above all others. It seems, therefore, to me quite plain, that you
would advance your interest and reputation by presenting your invention to the Union Government,
& thereby secure to yourselves an exclusive privilege for the Russian Warpath, not
only, but also for the whole extent of the Russian Confederacy. And if you had no business
to do this, yourself or other persons to do it by, I would most cheerfully undertake this business
myself as your agent, against a remuneration to be granted only, when your own Telegraph
should effectually be adopted by Russia, or any other German Power at your own
discretion.
A West Engineer of Paris has lately invented a Machine for Building Mountains &c., boring
Tunnels in the Alps for oil-roads. You know there is a project of opening a Railroad
from Savoy to Constance through the Alps, & property through Val de Blanio, in this case
and the Mountain Inclination, which must have a tunnel about four miles long to
reach the Rhine on the northern side, otherwise through Sover, & another more general
scheme of opening a Railroad from Paris to Lyons, & Savoy through the Alps
between Perdonnette on this side, & Bardane on the Savoy side. To bore the former
it will take 10 years, the latter 25 or 30, they say. I have invented, in any
hand, another contrivance to pass over, not through the Mountains, A locomotive of so

Joseph Morse My Dear Sir
Yours of the 3d ult came to hand
yester eve, giving me information of the arrival of my papers
of power of attorney in due time, and of the manner in which
Mr K. is occupying himself. Thank you for the report of Prof.
Johnson; it is a most valuable document.
I am still unemployed except for a few days hence, and
should the enterprise of forming private companies for extend-
ing the Telegraph be successful, I should be glad to be a-
gain employed in it, and am confident you will do
all in your power to accomplish my desire, you will oblige
me very much if you will consult with Mr Findall if you
deem it proper to do so, and write me at your earliest convenience what
are the probabilities in my favor supposing the Telegraph be extended
by private companies.
I see it announced in the daily papers that subscription books
are to be opened in Baltimore, Phila & in N.Y. to make up a stock
company &c but I am not informed as to anything further -- I would not
willingly absorb your time, but as I have been idle most of the time since
Oct last, I find it necessary to look for some point or prominence
not very far ahead on which I may rest my hopes. I am not willing
to enter again into the business of manufacturing for a length of years
&c, expecting to be re-called to Jefferson College in about 2 years
to take my old station again; thus, in my anxiety to make provision for myself and family, I have ventured to lay the whole
matter before you. If there is to be no tolerable prospect for me
please let me know the worst of it. In addition I would
say, I have understood, or rather inferred, from the language of the
newspapers that you or Mr. Kindall would have the immediate su-
pervision of the whole line should such an enterprise be undertaken.
Hoping to hear from you soon I have the honor to be
Very respectfully yours
A. H. Gall
Samuel F. P. Morse Esq.
P.S. Please make my respects to Hon. Mr. Ellsworth and say to him
I thank him for the copy of his last annual report
