My dear Sir
We expect to close tomorrow an arrangement
for the construction of a line of telegraph from
Washington to this place. The substantial terms
are the same as in the project I proposed at
Washington: viz. one half of the stock to the subscri-
bers. But some changes in the details are agreed
upon, such as limiting the amount of stock from
$300,000 to $400,000, naming the Trustees in the
article of agreement and leaving them to raise the
subscription, and some other immaterial points whether
the stock will be raised at once or some time
will be taken up in the operation, I am not yet informed.
This operation will yield us cash to you or me
for some time to come; yet I am desirous if practicable to make the purchase of you to raise the
$20,000 will require probably a pledge of my entire interest with other security: Would you
have any objection to this -- say the payment of $10,000 in hand and the other $10,000 to come and
let you run out the money at any time after the 1st July that you may want it, to bear interest from that date. If it be the same to you
I should be glad of the accommodation, and should you go to Europe I will arrange that your
drafts shall be paid to the extent of the
$20,000 and will myself meet any losses con-
sequent upon the exchange.
Amxious to see things moving I shall probably remain here a few days after the signing of the
paper if I can in the least expedite the raising
of the stock and also to see to my own arrangement. If the arrangement I suggest would be
acceptable please inform me by return mail.
With high regard
Your friend
Amos Kendall

Dear Sir.
I have not written to
you before this, but have been so busy that I had
no time to gather up anything with writing.
Hearing some news yesterday, I visited the
Telegraphic office, where I remained in conversation
with the director during the afternoon. The Telegraph
(Wheatstone's) is really as pretty a failure as ever in
law. Potentially it requires an hour for them to transmit a sentence which you could do with speed in
five minutes. The Telegraph works by the deflection of two needles, and they deflect so slowly, that they
can scarcely read the letters at all. They use five wires, each wire being composed of three smaller wires twisted together. Has I cannot see what is gained by this? In my opinion there is a lot. I gave
the man that fiddling you gave me -- also a bill of
your alphabet, and honest report; but I gave him no information in respect to the manner in which yours was made. You manifest a
great wish that your Telegraph would transmit as rapidly as we could talk -- which the poem I gave
you proved -- and still more wish that it would do it, for their does not exist. In a word, I consider Wheatstone's Telegraph without any comparison with Morse's; and you may congratulate
yourself upon having got far the best Telegraph in the world. The English are a bloating
mind, people, puffed up with an idea of their own importance, and depreciating the value of all other
people -- particularly the Americans, of whom they are jealous enough. The agent of the Telegraph
new, told me that he thought we had introduced
Wheatstone's Telegraph in our Country! And you
may be sure he was justified in when he saw
that we had surpassed them. Bain's Telegraph
is better than Wheatstone's, but it puts confusion into
your mind, because it does not work so well, and is very
complicated. I am convinced now that no Telegraph
can be made to do duty well, unless it is made on
the plan of yours. We have applied for a

so that we may consider ourselves safe. It has come out favorable in our experiment, and

Dear Sir.
Prof. Baker of this city wishes to procure a Correspondent
for the benefit of his Chemistry class, as also does a gentleman from Boston, connected
as I was given to understand, with one of the Universities there. I agreed with them
to write you to secure your consent to their correspondence either here, or wherever you may direct.
While writing to you, I cannot help supposing as much that you
would give the making of your instruments to Mr Clark, who has done himself much
Credit by the correct workmanship on the one he made for me.
When I returned from the line, a week after putting one of your
new instruments up, I found the standard covered with brass jingles, and the wheels
making a noise like a circular saw. Whether it was from trial treatment or original
defect I am not positive, but I feel certain that Mr Clark would execute your orders to
much better purpose, and with satisfaction to all interested. The line home to Mr. Clark is stopped.
Where we shall resume I know not.
Very respectfully yours
James H. Dick.

Ref Samuel F. B. Morse
Sir
At sufficient time has now elapsed,
for any feelings of invitation arising from the conduct of either of us,
to have subsided, I have taken the liberty of calling your attention to a
subject in which I am somewhat interested, I have written to you before
on the subject but no answer has been received, I suppose that my
letters have either not been received, or you have from some cause or other
been prevented from replying, when I went on to Washington with
you in December 1842. there was an understanding between us that
you were to bear all my expenses, in going, staying, returning therefrom.
The second week after our arrival at Washington, as you will short of funds
it was uncertain how long you might have to remain in order to save you
from paying out money for me I accepted the invitation of a relative I resided
with him during my stay in Washington, you told me then, respecting the
assurance to me afterwards, that if the bill passed for the trial of the Telegraph
you would pay to me the money which you would otherwise have had to
pay for my board, Confiding in this assurance, & feeling sure of the passage
of the bill, I borrowed money of a friend which has since been repaid to him,
I am now, very much in want of money for the support of my family &
would feel much obliged to you, if you would remit to me in accordance
with your promise, the amount ($51.60 two years interest being added).
which you were thus relieved from paying at that time. I am glad for your
sake that your prospects are so good for the extension of the telegraph, though I
have no store in the benefits, which I shall always feel glad to think I stepped
in some degree to assist you to, I hope to have an answer at your earliest convenience
Please direct to 38 Sansom St. Philadelphia I remain very respectfully
Yours to
James Fisher M.D.

Professor Morse,
Dear Sir,
Ever since you have
established the Telegraph, I have been very desirous
to know whether it had been used on the Sabbath.
Having no evidence that it has been so used, I
will take it for granted that it has not been so em-
ployed under your special direction.
But as the Government are to become interest-
ed in it (if they have not altogether become so,) I feel
peculiarly anxious that you should insist, in your
contest with them, as well as with individuals, who
may purchase or become interested in it, that it
should not be used on the Lord's Day, except in
cases of emergency say necessity or mercy—in which
instances there would be comparative speed.
I have, for many years, been using every means
in my power to prevent the desecration of that holy
day, in various ways—particularly by Mail, Steamboat,
canal Boats, Rail Roads &c. If I succeeded, I gave
you a paper relative to our K. Road being used on that
day. If not I send you one by mail.
I have spent much time, and money, for printing
postage, & traveling expenses relative to it, and I sometimes
hear that all my efforts will be lost.
the Telegraphs are to be used on the Lord's
Day, I think we may well despair of making any
greater advances for the preservation of the day to be
kept holy throughout these United States.
May I not hope that you have had the
subject under serious consideration, and at the earliest
placed a BARRIER to prevent its use on the
first day of the week.
Yours, very respectfully,
William G. Hooker.

My dear Sir –
I received last Steamers a
letter from one of the principal London Publishers
requesting me to procure from you a description of your

Yours ever true

Chayama May 22 1860.
My dearasher
I have been sadly disappointed
this Winter Spring in receiving so few letters from my
friends & relations truly they seem to have had
enough of me in my last visit, and I am quite
forgetten. - From your dearest father, I have
received but two or at the most three letters,
a from brother thom - from aunts or uncles
not a line. By God's light I certainly expect
letters & it was a bitter disappointment, but
Charles was to blame in putting off letters, late
sending the things. I wrote for, & forwarding
letters (if there were any) - But I will not
take up the whole of this sheet in grumbling -
but tell you that we are all quite well in
old Suayama. I am thin having lost ten pounds since my arrival but nothing seems
to be the matter with me except debility.
Little Charles is very well - He sits by my
side at the table playing & has just scribbled
you -- give my proof -- as I held his little finger.
He sends a little lock of his hair -- one of the
dear curls I have been cutting off to make
his hair grown thick. The other day a dentist
here from N. York extracted two of his front teeth,
from were quite decayed, and the other two he
thinks will come out themselves. He talks a
great deal now, but several letters he cannot
pronounce distinctly -- how he beguises the a great
deal of company for me, as I am so much
alone in the day.
I long to hear from you again, dear father,
and I know how the Telegraph comes on,
as I seldom see a newspaper to learn of
its progress. I sent your poetry (or rather
the poetry upon an invention) to Dr Thomas
Findlay -- They were all well except Mother
Laid when I heard from them. She never
enjoys very good health. Mrs. Mrs. Lundt
& the children have all sailed for Germany
to spend the Summer. Mrs. Lundt is one of Mrs
Obermann's daughters -- a fine girl -- Mrs O.
is also in Germany yet. The Minister in
St. Thomas I believe has been dismissed for
a season, at least. He was engaged to Maria
Travati from St Croix one of my old school
mates. The reports are so various I hardly know
yet what was the cause of his dismissal.
We have had a visit from the Genl. General
of Price in his annual tour round the
Isles of France and I am sending for a
look of my hair & a kiss - Ioppel grandson
Island - I did not get a peek at his kindness.
The home very pleasant weather yet, and
he continues healthy - I believe. - How are
the Heaviside friends when you heard from there
I wrote Aunt Salisbury by the return of a N. House
& sent her a pet of Tamaraide. I wonder when
I am, dear father, in N.Y. a walk or flying
all about. Have the Ellsworths moved well?
I shall look for letters by the Seiden on her
return and if I do not get any, shall be sad
enough, for it is such a hint to receive long
letters from the absent one love. - This letter will
get by Capt Curtis now of the Boston Courier - Edward
is very well study, I send much love to
you as does also Sophia daughter

My Dear Sir,
We have not yet effected any arrangement
with the New Jersey Railroad; but we think
they will come to terms in a few days. It
is so clearly their interest that the Telegraphs
will be associated with them, I am satisfied
we have but to be patient and firm to ac-
complish all we ask.
With Mr. Butterfield we have made a
written contract and he has gone home to
organize his company.
Mr. Henry O'Keiley, who went up in the
Steamboat with Butterfield, has come back
full of the telegraphs, that he has pro-
pounded to get up the line from Philadel-
phia west to St Louis & Lake City. Mr.
Smith coming with me in recommending
that he be allowed three fourths of any
line he may cause to be built in that
direction in case our company decline fur-
ishing the fund on those terms.
Gen. Armstrong, our consul at Liverpool
is here. I have been conversing with him
about attempting to make something out
of your Telegraph in England. It has permitted
me my profressing to advise you to come
on here as soon as possible. He expects to sail
next Thursday. He will not
I hope to be able at the same time to return
to you, and if not to devote some other way
of raising funds to enable you to visit Europe.
By the mail which brings this, I shall write
to my Sister in the Washington City Post
office to forward a packet of papers by you
and beg that you will inform him where
to leave them.
Please consult Mr. Neil as to the Western line
and see whether he objects to the terms proposed,
and also whether he is willing to offer
other lines of secondary importance, such as
Boston to Portland, to be built on the same
terms. In these cases it is proposed that the
amount to be refunded to subscribers in
case of a call to the government, shall
be 20 per cent over the cost instead of two
for one as with our Washington Co.
With great consideration
Your friend
Amos Kendall

not engaged, or I should have suffered of it.
You must indeed feel desolate with the family
removed, & in a new boarding house, & I wish
I could be near your dearest father at this
time with ye little grandson, & cheer you up.
He is a sweet little fellow if I do say it, this
he cannot boast of much beauty -- I would
like to come on this season -- perhaps all you
feel a reluctance to cross the ocean, for
I cannot forget that fearful storm at sea,
when our ship's mind blew hard upon her, I
feel extremely nervous -- For from a few days
past I have had a house full -- five children
Counting mine, under six yrs of age -- two ladies
one English one German and a nurse -- then
we all going to Germany & as there are no
boats they depend upon the kindness of friends --
the vessel is leaking here & I think I find from
the German lady a letter to Edward so we
entertain by many as we could.
They have now gone on board, & I feel
begin to feel better again.
We have high winds now, quite like spring hurricans
and squalls of rain= I did at the same time
with up letter on for Charlie a month old & one
from Aunt Kate two months old. Where they remain
I cannot imagine – Well my dear father
I must close as I expect the vessel will sail
to day. Edward made a great deal of money by
the advance of the price in Bengal, but by sub-
sequent speculations finds fair to lose every
bit of it. The life of a merchant is very changable
These losses quite depress him at times – I fear this
far distant when we can come to America
again to live. Charlie sends you a kiss, and
wants to cut off another lock of hair, not thinking
one sufficient. All well in St Thomas & often
enquire after you – they send me many little
tokens of their affection. On his birth day his aunt
Helena made a pretty little pocket scarf & his aunt
Mann a little dress. They are very kind people.
I shall write by every vessel dear father – &
hope soon hear from you again. Edward desires
to remain with me as he has a little daughter
Samuel H B Moser, Esq.

The main object of the Transatlantic
Submarine Telegraph Company is by a main
Submarine line stretching across the Atlantic
(from either Milford Haven or the Western
Coast of Ireland to the point of the American
Coast of Nova Scotia or the Canadas, for
uniting on the most liberal basis all the
various Electric Telegraph Companies of
America (already stretching over some 40,000
Miles of territory) with all the various telegraph
Companies in Europe, either belonging to the
several Governments, or private Companies,
extending from Great Britain across the
Continent of Europe to the East & India,
The more fully to ensure this object the
Projectors in Europe & America engage
(apart from all special or private interest
as original Inventors or projectors of the
various Electric Submarine Telegraphs
which they have executed or are engaged
in carrying out under concessions of the
diver Governments in America stretching
from Canada on the North East
to the extremes of America on the South
and West, and from Great Britain
across Europe to the Mediterranean,
India & the Pacific Ocean.)
They have determined & do determine,
that this great link of communication
between the old & new world shall be
freely opened in Europe to all Companies
equally & without partiality or preference.
The works will be proceeded with
so soon as the various arrangements are completed with the Governments of Europe
& the United States, and it is calculated
that the line might be opened for
communication within 2 years from
the present date.
Careful soundings have been made
for this purpose by the able Nautical
Surveyor Lieut. Many of the U.S. Navy
& preparations & Studies are in progress for
putting the Company into active Operation
during the ensuing year.

Dear Sir.
I promised to write to you, and you promised to take
the trouble to decipher my style of writing, a task not
so easy as you perhaps imagined at the time.
After a journey of 14 days & 18 hours, the old Great
Western, which is getting really old & fatigued in comparison
with her younger sister Midmounts Cunardia, which made her trip
in 10 days, I was safely landed at Liverpool, and after five hours'
rest I hastened on to London, the City of all cities!
After delivering the Dispatches to our Minister, my first inquiry
was for the Telegraph; a considerable risk brought me to the Depot
of the great Western Railway, where I found the office of the electric
magnetic Wheatstone Telegraph; -- a small room containing many
magic looking boxes, enough in number to bring a man to the state in the
time of holy inquisition, and crammed in all directions with mysterious wires
coming from these boxes and from a battery of 12 small caps (stuck off hands)
leading out to a slender pole towards the other station. -- The assistant
was just engaged over one of these boxes to move two handles rapidly
to the right a left at his option, whereby a pair of magnetic needles moved
with them and pointing to signs & few letters, after having despatched
his ideas upon electrical wings towards the west I paid my admission fee
of one shilling, a thing so very natural in England, for which he very
politely explained the operation of the apparatus just mentioned. --
My first question was a natural one, "What is the Telegraph?" -- I told him that I had seen your Telegraph on the other side of the ocean,
and anxious to learn the difference between both. -- He informed me it was true that your Telegraph is allowed in operation
between New York & Boston; in respect to the I gave him as a correct
information as I thought it true. -- He showed me a large roll of your telegraphic Dispatches in Alphabet

when I assured him of the authority of said slips paper, he

Washington Tuesday eve. Feb. 15. 45
My dear Sir
The enclosed two letters were handed me
by Daniel Campbell who said he found them in the pocket
of a trunk he had by exchange from Henry. I send them to
you supposing that you will be going out with him and
being uncertain whether if preceded to New Haven if they would
reach him. Will you be kind as to charge of them.
The weather for some days has been turning, melting killing
the thermometer this afternoon at 7 past 5 in Mr Wood's room
stood at 100º and nearly to 100. In the Patent office in the
space way between the rooms it stood at 86 and on being
carried into the library mounted up to 92. Isa you have it
not much less in New York than we have it here. 8 persons
died sunstroke today here – nothing new – I see the Commis-
sioner is not strongly for House Telegraph – I hope they will let us
know a little more about it after such pretensions.
I meant my dear Sir to have spoken to you respecting the
amount which I am indebted to you before you left, but it
exceeds
my mind at the time as you went off so suddenly to me.
Grateful as I feel for your kindness I have also wished when in my
power to repay the obligation. You recollect perhaps I mentioned to you
professing if it suited your views discharging it so far as I could by
translating various documents, and I believe you expressed your willingness
to do it. If I may mention that I have translated about
30 or 35 pages of German and perhaps some 20 or 25 of French delinued
to yourself by Mr. Vaill. I suppose that a fair rate of compensation would
be at 30 or 40 dollars If you think this would be right you will
allow me to consider so much of my debt discharged. If too much
allow what you think proper -- It is not improbable Mr. Vaill may need
some nine translations from German or French and it would agreeable
to me to do them and apply it as he sees fit. -- Write if it meets your views.
And shall I trouble you my dear Sir with a little communication
As you will be in Paris which is so famed for its pretty things -- will
you with your well known taste select for me some little articles suitable
and agreeable to a lady say $5 or 6 wont for me to make a new Gen's
present to my wife -- and let her know it -- I don't care about trunkets
as she does not wear them -- but some real pretty adornage of furniture
and case -- memorandums book etc -- that may strike your fancy and
I know it will suit me. I suppose two or three small articles might be
got which would not hinder your progress -- if you think best put it
in one. -- If I had the gold with me now I would enclose the money
and I hope I may be able to do so by some opportunity before you
leave, but I shall not promptly part. It may be I shall press upon
you much on your kindness as you have expressed your willingness to continue
your business of books before you return. Will you let me know your address in London or Paris both if I should write
and now may dear constantly bearing in mind the many favors you
have shown, the pleasant hours in your private society and the useful
information derived from your converse with sincere wishes for your
best welfare I commit you to the grace of our God and Redeemer
hoping for you that He will grant you a prosperous way & when
you stand princes and kings a to indicate your right to your family
honored fame may He be with you and while His smiles lighten
your heart you are honored instruments of His own in sustaining &
diffusing the truth that you and all your talents and prosperity
may be regarded ever as His who has permitted to meet on earth
but if not here in your bright and glorious work where faith
shall be swallowed up in vision
Affectionately & gratefully
Your friend Goodrich Sutt
Prof. J. F. B. Morse

On my return on Saturday from Washington I found
your note containing proposals for purchasing my portion
of the Patent right of the Telegraph. I have taken them into
consideration, and would say in reply that the only terms
at the present time that would tempt me to part with my
right is a realization in cash or notes at 3 & 6 months
for $100,000, for 8/16th of the patent right. Should such an
offer be made within, 10 days from date I think I would part
with this much, the Telegraph stock as I have stated
as I find myself practically doubling that amount as my share, and the only
inducement, therefore, that I could have, is the sure realization
of a certain sum, free from all contingencies.
If you cannot renew the offer of your 7/16th of the Patent
right in all countries out of the U. States, for the sum you men-
tioned which was the sum you had extended in writing Europe amounting to about $6,000, and give me the refusal of it till 1 Dec.
I should like it otherwise next, I do not dare to have it. Such an offer on your part would
induce me to make exertions to procure you that sum, in the
hope that I might make something myself, but as it is more
than doubtful whether I shall make anything, I have no particu-
lar inducement to enter into the enterprise. What I do
in Europe at the present time is to effect favorably our enterprise at home
for the purpose of preventing the Printing Office into words
you may have no fear of it. It is mathematically demonstrable that it is
of no consequence with mine.
Respectfully.
J.B. Morse

Dear Sir,
W. S. Colt has
a model of the "American Semaphore"
which I should like you to get and pre-
sent to His Majesty Louis Phillip, in my
behalf; if you think it not too trouble-
some and worthy of such notice by you;
(or make any disposition of it you please.)
I have learned that he is constantly adding
to his collection of models, and I should
like to throw in my invention.
If you will pay the expense attending
its shipment &c. I will remit you the
amount to New York, or refund you,
on your return to the U. S.
The Semaphore tower is a new style
of architecture termed the Chrystalline by
the inventor Mr. George Hayden a worthy
mechanic of this city.
If you conclude to take the Semaphore
with you; upon your arrival in Europe
have it put in good order and handsomey
painted.
I will forward you a Chart explanatory
of my system.
I am just this moment in receipt of your
letter of 14th inst. and feel very thankful
for your kind testimonial in favor of my
Dictionary.
The more I operate with your Telegraph
the better I am convinced of its superiority
over any improvement that has been men-
tioned; and I am fully convinced satisfied
that we can, & will outstrip all Competitors.
The article enclosed by you will appear
in the American if occasion requires.
A certain James O. Connor has been out
in the American with a description of a
printing Telegraph, which, he claims as
original, I have told all my friends, if
he had been posted on Electric Telegraphy,
he would have made a much greater
discovery, by finding out, that, what
he claims as new, is nothing more than
the Telegraph used by Mr Bain in
England? I did not think it worthy
of further notice.
Your faithful servant
Henny J Rogers

be so steady as if the shaft (which should be

Yrs Truly
Chas. G. Page

What am I to do for funds to meet my
engagements? This is a serious and troublesome
question with me. If you will relinquish your
portion (one quarter) I can get assistance elsewhere,
or if you will remit me $150 (which, when you
come to see the state of the account on your action
will be found to be less than the amount of your
portion of the expenses). The book may go out of
of my hands, by the process of law, if I
cannot meet my engagements, which have
been predicated upon the sale of the book.
Mr Rogers tell me he has written to you,
and given an account of the number of
letters which we have been able to write
per minute.
Every thing moves on as usual. There
is nothing new. Let us hear from you often.
Any new works upon telegraphs would be of
no service to me in this work, so that you
need not purchase any on my account.
I remain yours sincerely
Alfred Vail.

Professor Samuel F. B. Morse
Dear Sir, It may be satisfactory to you prior
to your departure for Europe to learn what progress I have made as your agent in arrangements
to bring Morse electric Magnetic Telegraph into
general use.
My agreement with you was closed on the 1st of
March last. Within a few days thereafter a
contract was formed for building a line from
New Orleans to Mobile; but I never had much
confidence in its performance and am not likely
to be agreeably disappointed.
Having failed in an attempt at New York to
run means to commissary operations on a large
scale, your co-proprietor Mr Smith and myself,
after overcoming many difficulties succeeded in
organizing a joint stock company at Washington
to build a line from that place to New York.
This began with a subscription of $15,000 required
to be sufficient to build a line of two
rivers from New York to Philadelphia. In consequence
of the exertant demands of the New
York and Camden & Atlantic Railroad companies
for the right of way and their control over
the Susquehaha and other improvements on the
direct line, much time has been occupied
in discovering some other practicable route.
These difficulties, I trust, are on the point
of being overcome, and it is expected that the
two great cities will be connected by Telegraph
in October next.
A company has been organized with a
subscription of $40,500 to build a line from
the city of New York through Albany to the
100230
city of Buffalo. By the liberal legislation of New
York, all difficulties as to right of way in that
State are abated, and this Company have a clear
field on the common roads throughout their en-
tire line. This fact influences the Railroad
companies to concede the privilege of erecting
the posts on their property. A large portion
of the stock of this line will undoubtedly
be constructed before next January.
A contract has been made with George
De Someroy Esq. by which he has undertaken
to get up a Company to construct the line
from New York to Boston. Much confidence
is felt in his ability and disposition to
effect the object, and it is expected that
a portion if not the whole of this line
will also be built before next January.
An arrangement has been made with Har-
ry Ridley Esqr. by which he has undertaken to
get up a western line through Pennsylvania
to St Louis bringing to St Louis and the Lakes.
Double can entertain no better he will accomplish
any thing; but more efficient men
Morgan Livingston & Wells of this City are suf-
ficient for the contract in case of this failure.
The lines to Washington and to Buffalo from
this City are virtually built upon shares. But
as the value of the lines is estimated at more
than four times the cost, stock to four times
the cost is to be issued, one have to the
jurors of the patent right and one have
to the subscribers. Thus the $15,000 subscribed
to the Washington line will produce $60,000
of stock and the $40,500 to the Buffalo
line will produce $162,000 of stock. The
stock annexing to the extent of the interest from
the present subscriptions will be $111,000. That
to make complete lines on these routes will
cost about $200,000, giving a stock of $800,000,
half of which or $400,000 will belong to the
grantee of the patent right.
On the Boston line the grantor of the patent
right can to receive half the stock on the three
first wires and two thirds of that issued upon
each additional wire. The effect will be to
give them about three fifths of the stock
when the line is completed which cannot be
less than $200,000.
On the line from Washington to New Orleans
they may expect to get half the stock and on
the western line one fourth and the same
rate on many short lines.
I will not undertake to estimate the value
of these stocks; but there is no good reason
to doubt that those issued on the great lines
from Boston to New Orleans and from
New York to Buffalo will be worth, at
least
With great esteem

Exeter, Monday May 6th 1845
Dear Sir,
Mr S. W. Chick, a manufacturer of Philosophical
instruments in this village, has had his attention turned
particularly to the phenomena of Electric Magnetism and
among other curiosities of the science, has constructed the
Telegraph. He is in the habit occasionally of giving lectures
and experiments in a humble way in the same village
around me, when sometimes the exhibition of the Telegraph
is called for. He is unwilling to do anything destructive
or the proprietor of that ingenious instrument should think
a truce upon ground rights, and no desire to put it to
any other use than as agent in duty. As such it would
in this neighborhood increase the popularity of his
institutions. I have examined the paper on the subject and
in your answer while you expressed an individual
opinion, he received no official assurance that others
would be satisfied. It would do him a favor could you
afford to drop from a line telling him whether he may
or may not exercise his discretion with an assurance
on his part, that he will never intentionally invade
these rights to which he justly belongs to the inventor of
that wonderful machine. As a man and a minister
of the gospel I would not even at this urgent business to
aid him if I suspected he had any other than honorable
designs, and if you think them will be any thing improper
in consenting or that this suggestion is out of place you
will have the goodness to tell me frankly.
With great respect
Your Washington Thacker

Dear Sir.
I just met a gentleman from Philadelphia
Mr Ch. Rath, who returns with the great
Victory, and promised to forward your enclosed
lines. I sent you yesterday a Mr. Cooper from Brussels
containing some account of my expedition of your Telegraph.
It was generally admired, and if that had been from
Mr. Wheaton, who came before me, I am sure
our management could have been used with the Belgian
Government, but I explained the necessity of
your invention, a hope when I return that, in
obtainable change to make experiments on some road. --
I am on my way to Leipzig & from there to Vienna, from
which I shall give you a long account of my
doings. --
I find a Selective Telegraph near Sir la Chapelle,
on near Mayence & Wiesbaden, all on the principles
of reading Discs, like those of Wheaton. --
The Ambassador of Austria at Brussels gave
me letters to Mitherniet, I stopped at Johannisburg
on the Rhine where I passed by, but I was not
there, and had only the pleasure to drink in his
chateau a real glass of Johannisburg. --
I find Prince Metternich at Vienna. —
I invited the principal officer of the government of
the Ambassadress to see your Telegraph, all when
delighted, but as I said Wheatstone was before me, &
through the influence of the English Ambassadress
& the royal family he will probably establish his Telegraph there.—
This journey is highly interesting. I have access to
all Richard Establishment & Manufactories, &
when I return I will have Council in every
whole Europe.—
I send you the alphabet which I got in
at Rome.—
as soon as I hope to hear from you
Yours
Stollmann.

months hard labour and great expense been
getting up, namely, "Has the receiving magnet
and its necessity yet been published in any book
or paper"? I can unhesitatingly answer this
question by saying that "the receiving magnet
and its necessity" is no where described or alluded
to in the work. I studiously avoided it, and
I may repeat here what I stated in a former
letter that the description contains nothing more
than has been already published in an hundred
thousand prints of various kinds, Publications from
which extracts have been made by English periodicals,
It has been explained unreservedly to persons visiting
the Telegraph office and some of them going directly
to Europe.
Feeling an interest in the success of your visit abroad as well as a desire to do consistently what I can to forward your (to me erroneous) views, I stated the facts of the case to a number of persons whose judgement I know you to respect, among them the Hon Amos Kendall and Dr Page, the latter having read the proof sheet. They have stated to me that they cannot see what possible harm there is in its immediate publication -- Mr K in my conference with him thought it might be an advantage to publish it.
The work is not yet published and I cannot tell when it will be, I cannot accede to your proposition which a moment's reflection will convince you as impossible.
Mr Rogers and our whole force wish to be remembered to you. I trust your visit to Europe will be every way beneficial to you and our interests but knowing something of the English character & the French situation of things, I shall not be disappointed if you return as you left without accomplishing your object. I understand the Emperor of
Russia has refused to adopt your plan of the
Electro Magnetic Telegraph, it comes from Mr
Bodiseo, so I presume you will not visit St
Petersburg— The fact is, Europe will not acknowledge
America in this case out of pride, I fear it, but
we shall see. It would give me pleasure to
learn of your whereabouts and what prospects you
see in the present or future. If any thing of interest
transpires I will write. You will probably be
informed of the unfortunate death of Mr Kendall
son's William by the papers, He was shot by John
C Keives brother in law in the street. The affair happened
about 6 P.M. Mr K was in N.Y. so the Telegraph
announced it to Mr Rogers who wrote the letter to
K which announced to him the melancholy news.
Wishing you intense uninterrupted enjoyment &
abundant success believe me to be your friend
and Servt
Alfred Vail

I guarantee the following results. 1st. My instruments one
at each extremity, each with one conductor shall give the same
quantity of intelligence in a shorter time than any other system of

easily legible. — 3d. My instruments shall cost less than those
of any other system in use. — 4th. I will teach the use of my

Hamburg.
Called by appointment on Mr Arneumann
at the R. R. Depot, in Altona; found
that the plan of Wheatstone was not much
in favor although the King of Denmark saw
it in operation and was pleased, as one naturally
would be even at the most indifferent kind of Telegraph on the Electric principle.
They consider it too expensive & not efficient. Four wires run from the Depot down to the river, by means of which information was given from river to Depot a distance of less than
a fourth of a mile. I went into the room where the instrument had been, (it was now removed and is not used,) the woman who occupied the room on being asked where it was said "God be thanked it was taken away," What the precise cause of the good woman's joy was, I could not say.
I was recommended to ascertain from Copenhagen, from the Director Bluhme; & Herr Conferenz Rath Garlieb
and Francke at Copenhagen, General Zoll Kammer.
If anything is done in the way of Telegraphs, I think them in little doubt mine will be adopted, for I learned for the first time that Wheatstone's cannot be multiplied on a route, while mine may be multiplied every foot of the way. — I mean to examine this critically. I have to Mr. J. Brun,
Kammerjunker 42 Nørgade Copenhagen,
copies of documents, and alphabet, and
also specimens of telegraph writing. He will
show them to the King, and correspond
with me on the subject.

ment which make Morses so preferable, they will experiment a few miles distance only, and no

Gentlemen. I would call your attention to the fact that
my stay in London is necessarily very limited, and
the negotiation with the Gen. Com. Telegraph company
in relation to my system of Electro Magnetic Telegraphs
must, therefore, be brought to a conclusion, one way or
the other, speedily.
I would not, however, have the Company hasten in
their decision, and if they are desirous of more time
to consider the matter, I would request them to
say so, and to name a time when they can give
me a definite answer to the proposals I made before
I left London for the North of Europe.
I have engagements in Paris which require me
to visit France as soon as possible, and if it will be
any accommodation to the Company in regard to
time, I will at once proceed to visit that country,
and await their answer till my return, although
such a course will materially affect that part
of the arrangements I had proposed, namely,
to initiate such person or persons, as the Com-
pany may designate, into the arcania of my whole
system. This will require a little time and as
my absence from my Official duties in the United
States
States is limited, and is fast drawing to a close,

to me, and may be also to the Company, if they
wish to avail themselves of the advantages I offer
them, particularly more those of a personal
tution in the operations of the mean time, Gentlemen,
my, Relinquish.

My Dear Sir,
London Oct. 26th 1845.
I write a hastily line just to say that I
have learned from Galjnnani's messenger of Saturday, last
that there is a commission of the French Govt. examining the various systems of Electric Telegraphs, and
that they have not yet reported. I have my telegraphs
with me, and intend visiting Paris with it, within a fortnight.
I have just written a line to M. Arago on the subject, and
I have told him that you have him a copy of my
letter to the Jos. J. of the Treasury, duplicate of which I
send you; asking you to send him one. They oppose
attending to it, which I am persuaded from personal examination
of Wheatstone's system that my system has the advantage not
only in simplicity but efficiency, and this I hope to prove
before the commission. I am prepared to prove priority
whenever that my telegraphs in extending in the U. States
and already contracts are in process of execution, from

Paris Nov. 1. 1845
Dear Sidney,
Hotel Wagram
Rue Rivoli
I should have written you before
but my time has been so occupied that I have not
had the least time to write. — I arrived at Rouen
on Saturday evening of the day I left you,
after a delightful calm passage. We stayed over
Sunday at Boulogne and on Monday set out for
Paris in the Diligence, and riding all night
arrived here on Tuesday at 9 A.M. Finding
Maurice's hotel full, I came here, where I
found Cousin Woolsey, Louis Martha is well,
and so strong that she can bear the fatigue of
sightseeing, all day. They leave to-day for Nice.
I am still satisfied in verifying the fact
that my Telegraph is ahead of all the other
systens proposed. Wheatstone's is not adopted
here. The line from Paris to Rouen is not on
this plan but is an experimental line of the
Gov. Commission. I went to see it yesterday
with my old friend the Administrator in Chief
of the Telegraphs of France, M. Foy, who
is one of the Comt. to decide on the best
made for France. The system on this line in its
modification, I cannot spare time to describe it.
He shows on a dial plate by arms like the common
Telegraph the same signals as are now in use. He
requires 2 wires, and can give but 12 signs in a
minute!! At once divine one. He uses the magnet
(my basis) as Wheatstone uses it to move a watchwheel.
I have had a long interview with M. Arago, he is the
same affable and polite man as in 1839, he is a
warm friend of mine, and contends for priority in my
favor, and is also partial to my Telegraphic system as the
best. He is President of the Commission, and is going to
writ e e the History of Electric Telegraphy, I shall give
him the facts concerning mine. The day after tomorrow
I exhibit my Telegraphic system again to the Academy of
Sciences, and am in the midst of preparations for
a day important to me. I have strong hopes that
mine will be the system adopted, but there may
be obstacles, I do not see. Wheatstone at any
rate is not in favor here. He may crow on his
own dunghill, but the French cock crows here.
Edward has not yet arrived but I expect
fact he will be here in a day or two. I must
close to be in time for the Ambassador bag.
Being Porteur des Depeches cleared me
from all difficulty in bringing my instruments.
In great haste, but with affectionate regards
to all, to Sister Catherine, Elizabeth, and the
precious babies, and kind remembrances to Mary.
I remain affectionately yours ever
Yr brother
Sam. F. B. Morse.
Sidney Morse.
I like the French; every nation has
its defects, and I could wish many changes here
but the French are a fine people. I receive a wel-
come here to which I was a perfect stranger in
England. How deep this welcome may be I cannot
say but if one must be cheated, I like to have it
done in a civil and polite way.

Washington Nov 2d 1845
My Dear Sir,
Your invaluable favor of the 18th ult. is at
hand, and I hope your views in England may
on this matter you, be fully realized.
Our progress on this side of the Atlantic is as
follows:
The entire line from Albany to Buffalo, a
distance of 224 miles, is under contract, and will
probably be finished in 60 to 90 days.
The line from Boston to New York is in the
same condition.
A line from Boston to Lowell and another from
Buffalo to Lockport, are nearly or quite com-
pleted.
A line is building from Louisville to Harv-
ings to be carried westwardly to Petersburg
and Wheeling.
The line from New York to Philadelphia is
already finished. House has obstructed us in
getting funds to bring it on to Baltimore;
but a letter from New York by the last
mail informs me that $700000 have been
subscribed, and it may expected the balance
would be made up by this day.
Bolt is building from New York to Long
Island.
100284
A line from Syracuse to Syracuse has been
disturbed by us, but I have not heard of any
thing done upon it. Some New Yorkers have undertaken to raise
funds for the entire line from New Orleans
to the first of next April.
The Buffalo line is to be extended to New York
or connect with the New York & Boston line.
From New Orleans to Buffalo, the telegraph is
to be built upon shares, one half to the owners of
the patent and the other to the capitalists. On
the Louisville and Western line, we have a joint
on the minor lines, we are to have half the
profits, if any, after deducting the expenses and
reserving with legal interest on the original cost.
I have had some disagreement with my associate,
but all is now going on smoothly.
I omitted the copy above, that on the New York
& Boston line we get half the stock issued
on the posts and three first wires, and two
thousands on all additional wires.
I think the operations of the season are satisfactory,
and that we will come to Congress with an imposing front.
It is deemed necessary to surrender your first
patent and take out a new one. From Page it
is the opinion that it would not be maintained
in court on account of the vagueness of
its description, and that it may be made
to cover ample ground. We must fortify ourselves
on every point, for we may expect attacks
from every quarter, as soon as it is ascertained
that we have treasure in our fortress. Hope
Newspaper will allow of your
immediate return.

Dear Sir.
I received yesterday a letter from Mr. Clarenbach dated
17 Octob. Stockholm, stating that you had not gone to
St Petersburg as you intended, but returned to London.
In every moment I saw in Galibierne's message of
today, that three three Kings ready papers to the Academy
of Science concerning your Telegraph, which induced
me to believe that you are still in Paris -- and I should
have the opportunity to give you a short account before you
leave this Continent.
You keep my things in Brussels; -- from there I went to
Berlin when I arrived at the port, where many influential
offices were absent, and pushed for time I started for this
Place. The subject of Telegraph was then just before
the government and with the letters of introduction
to Prince Metternich I obtained immediately audience,
and he appointed a day to see the Telegraph; he was
exceedingly pleased, and requested me to show it to the
Minister of Finance Baron Hucholz; from that
quarter, had a long Conversation, in that subject with
him, and in few days afterwards I exhibited it to him, he
was like Prince Metternich very much pleased, and I did not
fail to show him the advantages of your own others.
several days after that, I received a note from Baron Kuntzeck
requesting to bring the Telegraph to the Palace, where his
Highness the archduke Louis and Count Colonnat
Minister of the Interior wish to see it. — I did not
fail to be there at the appointed hour, both examined it
for 1/2 of an hour, and expressed their satisfaction in
regard to its simplicity & compactness of government
building, —
I had reason to expect an audience by the Emperor,
and in few days, I received a note stating the desire of
the Emperor to see the Telegraph was made known to me
I went to the Palace, and experienced before the Imperial
Empress & all the members of the Imperial house
the apparatus worked well, and every one was delighted
with its performance. Prince Muthernet who was present
explained it in strange terms in regard to its usefulness
for governmental purposes; and if I was sagacious I would
deceiveable to believe that there is no doubt of my success.
But how like every other scientific men, who think to
know every thing better, and experiment on a small scale
and interested in certain plans,
and many other invisible subterranean currents are the obstacles
which I have to encounter. If the Committee appointed by the
French government should make a favorable report on your
system, the matter would be easy here, but if the report should
be against you, it will influence the committee here.
A gentleman with whom I have had an interview with Bain
has been sent by this government to France & England to advocate the electric
magnetic Telegraph, he brought with him Bain's, and seems to
be very much in favor of it; but since he saw yours I have
seen the interest which it excited, he proposes to employ them
both grounds the principal stations, and Bain's at the
intermediate stations for Railroad purposes: -- he says that
Bain's works will & is exclusively simple & practical. I
have not seen it yet.
I wish you would write me all about that matter, and give
me your views how I shall proceed in case they ask for the
price, -- must can not be hoped in this part of the world. --
tells me if you make improvements. -- I shall remain here
until something positive is decided -- I intend to visit
Italy & return by the way of Paris to America, which
will not be before next spring.
Mr. Mills with whom I live altogether is exceedingly kind
& invites me in every way to further your interest.
When you Come to Washington tell my wife, that I am well
and that I try to be with her, as soon my business will
allow me, to set sail.
I wish you would request Mr Smith to write out an
article in my exhibit in of your Telegraph before the
Emperor des St. of Austria, he will find in the letter
to Mrs. Fleickmann a full account, and I am sure
it would interest our Americans, and reminds them that

I hope you will answer this letter, I would you

I promised our Consul him Mr. Schwarz to have

I shall be the most influential man of the railroad
companies.
Your advice, success to you, and a happy journey
from the King's ditch. -- Thousand compliments
to all my friends here & there, and in reminding you
once more to write me I sign myself

12 o'clock, M.
Dear Sidney,
In the hope of being in Halifax
this evening, and in time for the Britannia
which left Boston for Liverpool yesterday, I
write you a hearty line to inform you of our
progress and safety thus far. We came
out of Liverpool in a hurricane, and until
yesterday we have encountered only bad gales
and yet this morning we made the land, about
80 miles from Halifax. Our ship is a noble
sea boat, and all things considered we have had
a delightful passage, for although, it has been
as tempestuous as I ever knew it at sea, yet
the perfect ease with which our Steamer braved
the waves, and made headway against the most
violent storms, calmed all uneasy fears. The
least distance we have made in any 24 hours
is 101 miles. Yesterday we made 257 miles
and today 286 miles, up to 12 o'clock. We ex-
pect to be in Halifax about 5 o'clock this if
afternoon, where we remain about 3 hours, and
then proceed to Boston 36 hours distant. We
hope, therefore, to be in Boston on Thursday morning
the 4th. Edward is well, and we shall both

My dear Brother
Until this moment I have not had
a moment's time to write you since my return home.
I wrote you by the Britannia, however, from Halifax
so that you knew of my safe arrival there far in
a short time after I left you. I found all well in
N.York, and came on here with a little delay as
possible. Telegraph matters look very well, I can
hardly go into detail further than to say that, the
line from N.York to Phila. will probably go into operation
in a few days, and before many week the
entire line from N.Y. to Wash. will be complete.
The line from Buffalo to Lockport is in successful
operation, and the Posts from Buffalo to Albany
are all planted, they are nearly up all the distance
from Boston to N.York. – There are many other
lines all ready for operation for short distances. The
Post Master Genl. has recommended the purchase by Govt.
and before the Session is out I think some money will
be made and perhaps consummated before its close.
There are of course some crosses & difficulties, but
none of a serious character. Accounts from Austria
are most flattering; I think that Govt. is prepared
to adopt it. You will see in the Intelligence
of the 23d Inst. (I think) two columns of Mr. Gleirsch-
man's doing with the Telegraph in Vienna, which will
precisely interest you.
Mr. Lind has sailed for Porto Rico; he learned just
after we arrived that his Manager on the estate was dead, and
he felt very desirous of reaching home as soon as possible. Susan
is in New York for the winter & little Charley, she is in better
health. Charley is well and I am glad to think doing well.
Our political horizon looks somewhat dark, but I still
hope that war may be avoided, I do not think it depends
on us. If war should take place, England will find it a
very difficult affair from the Chinese war, and notwithstanding
all the lamentations that "we are not prepared," we are better pre-
pared than they have any idea of.
I have so many interruptions, and so many letters to
write that I am compelled to cut short my letter or run
the risk of missing the Steam. Therefore, I must say
good bye after saying give my love to Katherine & Eliza-
beth and kiss the 'babies' for me. Write me how you
are doing. I will write you longer & better soon.
Affectionately as ever
Your brother
Finley

Dear Vail
I am here at Newark at the Court House. There
was a strong defection of the militia last night about
10 o'clock; but this morning the arms must be broken
somewhere, as Bailey & Coulson have been waiting all
day without effect. Mr. Joel went about 11 o'clock in
a buggy towards Louisville to look after the difficulty.
It is an anxious time, & I have had so much of anxiety
from various causes, that I am almost sick. But I
shall rally I hope, after to-morrow. Keep up battery in
good order. Tell me if you tried the little magnet, &
with what effect. I have no time to add, it is so
dark, & I must go. I hope all will be right for the
news by Steamer. Efforts will be made to get it here
to transmit, to you, but we have great opposition all
round, the Government the press, & certain Speculators.
It will be almost a miracle if we succeed. But
if the wires are whole, we will try. I put up two letters.
You must be very anxious what you say & do about
C. You must restrain your feelings. It is impossible
to get along just at present, without him, & the
violence of your opposition will only create sympathy for
him, she can do us a great deal of injury. I have
no more favorable opinion of his proceedings than
I ever have, but we must wait a proper opportunity, for
freeing ourselves from him. I cannot write more now
but had hoped to converse with you by telegraph. Goodby
till Monday. In instant haste - S.B. Morley.

Dear Vail.
I have just received the extract from your letter
to Mrs Vail, & I will gladly return to N.York tomorrow
with Mr Kendall, as I intended if I could leave; but I
cannot, & shall therefore intend to leave as the
in N.York by Monday night, or at earliest Tuesday night
In the meantime you will see Mr Kendall, & can prepare the
preliminaries of some arrangement, by which our actions
ments shall have my, on your stamp & approval. All will
work right with a little consultation, after throwing overboard
that mapplot, who has confused all our arrangements.
There is one thing in respect to Lowell, in which you are
in error. You say he has thrown aside my magnets
"& substituted his". He never put mine in use at all, &
what he calls his, is but a clumpingification of mine, that is
I say, he has simply multiplied the parts, having 4
magnets instead of one, requiring 4 times the work &
multiplying four times the chances of derangement, chances
which his magnets oppose to a chance -- if they who
have used them are correct in their reports of them.
And for this thing he expects to take out a patent. He
cannot get it. Let us I am not right, & if he could, he will
not use it without my permission. Measures shall be
taken to stop his further interference on my ground.
You have tested me more than you are aware of in asking
me to take charge of the books from Gideons & the cost will
be heavy (taken in the case) of such a quantity. There are
several hundred weights. You ask further that I will bring
in wire from Phila. If time permits me to stop & get it, I
will endeavors to do it. Perhaps Mr Kendall will take it
when he passes this town next -- I will write about it. I
have much to say to you. I have just put in action
one of my little magnets, substituting it for the big magnet
in the Office. It works very strong & beautifully. I want
to try some experiments with you up the River. Put me in
mind when I see you. I speak hastily but truly as ever
Yours Fred L. Co.

is working to Springfield -- The people are getting
outrageous in reference to the way in which that
unenterprising thing is conducted, and I am asked
daily, why is it that the Patents to not look
into the matter. Where is Mr Kendall, and when
will he let us know what the state of things is
in regard to the line. Where is our interest? Where
is our stock? Have we any property in that line?
I should like to know. Is it not too bad.
I have not been able to look over the files of the
Evening Post but will do so, and if your correction
is noticed send you a copy.
In regard to Mr K. I think I can tell you
wherein he has been playing since I have long
had suspicion in regard to his conduct in that
quarter, but I will defer it till I reach home. I
shall start as soon as I can get two instruments
finished, which will not be until the end of next
week. I hope Mr Kent will get Mr Chubbuck
a somebody who can be a little ambitious and
work steadily and hurry if need be, --
I have yet to learn whether there is up a
foot of wire on the southern line -- Perhaps all
my hurry and care and anxiety is for nothing.
I should be glad to have some light upon
that subject, and would thank you to let me
know what is going on in regard to the line on
receipt of this -- Please say also to Mr Kendall
that if any sum is to be asked for the
entire right of way condition the Gov purchase, I desire
to be consulted. You will find the things
belonging to the lathe in your cupboard -- The
stocks do not belong to it, nor the Vice. I
Believe me to be ever sincere

Improvement in the Electric Magnetic Telegraph
by means of which more than one pen can operate through one circuit.
A 1 , A 2 , A 3 , A 4 are magnets of different sizes with
their coils a helices also of different sizes. The poles of
the helices are connected with a battery in the following
manner. A 1 , the smallest magnet is connected with the whole
number of cups (say 12) in number of the battery, being the weakest
magnet from its fewer coils in the helix, or more
coils to give power enough to move the Respec attached to the lever
of my Register. A 2 , the next larger has more coils in the helix
and will require a less number of cups in the battery to move
the lever of the Register (say 9 cups) A 3 still larger requires
still fewer (say 6 cups) and A 4 still larger, requires still fewer
(say 3 cups) and so on for more magnets. The principle
of this arrangement is that an electric magnet is (within certain limits,) made more powerful in proportion to the addition of turns of wire or coils in the helix, and is operated upon at a distance in proportion to the number of cups or elements in the battery. By this arrangement I intend to add more than one lever for recording on my paper at the Register, each lever being moved by its own magnet, acting as the battery, more or less in number, are applied to the movement of the several magnets. And this arrangement is intended to operate several magnets at pleasure by one circuit only of wire. (See over leaf.)
I wish to enter a Caveat for this arrangement made in June of 1845, that I may have time to complete the necessary apparatus for the Specification of Letters Patent.

Dear Sidney,
I find I have but a single
half hour in which to write you, and I must
therefore be short. I thank you for your
letter and advice respecting Jackson, although
I think there will be no necessity for it.
He is very quiet, and makes light of the
whole matter as one of no consequence. He
will not trouble me any more.
Do you remember some little time
before we left for Europe, I was conversing
with you, (it was in June I think,) on a method
of using different batteries & magnets, both of
different strength in order to multiply the means
of writing with more rapidity, for example
a battery of 3 cups will not give magnetism
enough to operate a magnet and pen, when
the magnet has few coils, and is small, but
6 cups will move that magnet, and so on. This
method you will remember I think, was
suggested in order to provide against any supposed
improvement on my mode of writing by Hesse
I have drawn out a plan, and prepared a
caveat for that mode, on that principle
as I think something may be made of it.
I am the more induced to this as in conversation
with Prof. Twining a day or two ago, he thinks
he has made an improvement but is dark upon
the means he adopts, but I had the impression
it was something of this kind, and I therefore
at once told him that you and I had talked
over this method many months ago, and that
it was my intention to try it.— What I
wish of you is that in your next letter to me
you would give me such a course for its sub-
ject, that I may be prepared against any attempt
from that quarter should they be made. I don't
know that I shall be troubled with it, but I
wish to be prepared.—
Telegraph matters are looking very well
we are operating between Newark and Phila, and
the point is decided that the stock is a divided
paying stock; the stockholders are in good spirits
and prepared to push forward. We are troubled
with the river, and that is the reason we cannot
communicate direct to N.York, but hope to be
able in a few weeks.— Buffalo & Lockport

prevent any unpleasant feeling on

in obtaining the means for completion, that line.

would be somewhat longer; but it is not

to despatch an Agent to pay for timbers long
delivered along the line; and I have to request,
under these circumstances, that you will en-
cuse me for about one week, when I will
remit to the artist you allude to. If it
causes any inconvenience, I will see it re-
solved.

You may be sure that no time will now

Before the 2nd of March, you will have the

hundreds of miles of continuous or connected routes.

There are several reasons why the wire
should consist at least of four strands, and
thoroughly covered. In the first place,
one wire would not be sufficient to
conduct well or in other words, a very

the next place strength and durability is
wanted. An anchor might bring up most

should prefer Sweet battery for the

think that four square feet of wire
would be adequate to operate a mile
with ease. The receiving magnet for the

evening. I truly regret that business
which I cannot forego, compels me to be
absent in New York at the time.
But while absent in person I
trust I shall be with you in spirit, and
I wish sincerly pray that the Lord of the
Sabbath may preside at the deliberations of
the Convention, and direct it to measures
which shall result to his own glory
and the best interests of those for whom
the Sabbath was made.
I have felt much anxiety in relation
to the influence of the Telegraph which
the Magnetic Telegraph when extended them
out the land, and a desire to ascertain
from the Telegraph Bureau
on the general principles which should govern
its operation on that day. Although in
many respects it is a mail, yet there are
striking and palpable differences in its labor.
Its operations are noisy, and all within doors
and the agents are few, but these few are occupied
in a business which must depend upon
the opportunities of public worship and, if that sacred
rest is designed for them as well as for universal
animal nature, bases of necessity and of mercy.
I know are not breaches of the Sabbath

Dear Sir: On your return through
this city, I hope you will delay over
one train to examine the instruments
I am having made for our West End Line,
from drawings made for me by Mr.
Reid, & apparently well liked by Mr.
Vail. I think they will not fall
far short of your wishes; & that they
will not be unworthy of the name
which I propose to engrave on
them, in regard to the Inventor.
I expect that two of them will
be ready over in about 7 or 10 days. —
I have frequently expressed the
opinion to Mr Kendall, Mr Vail Potter,
in reference to Cornell & other inventors,
that no instruments should be used
that were not approved by the Patentees,
on any time; and hence, though
I have affixed your Mail fully
of my two endeavors to get instruments
made for our line, of better form
& character than now used, I deem
it proper to report to you when they
will be ready for inspection by you.
I am now personally attending to
cording the line to Baltimore, with
the iron four-strand cord, which I
have had made for the purpose.
It has required considerable trouble
to get the article all right to begin
with; but, now that we are fairly on the
route, we will make short work of the
line. We are able to make it (the end)
look more uniform than the co light
Copper wire could lie. As to the power
of transmitting the fluid, you would not
have doubted it (if you did at all
doubt) had you been with us when
a shock was sent through. I am
perfectly satisfied that it is needless
to coat with Gun, to preserve from
rust; but, as some think it best to do
so, for the sake of greater security, the iron
car is coated with coal-tar, the
best article I have found after
many trials. On line between
Lancaster & Hainslight working ele-
gantly, & the main local batteries are

New Haven March 14th 1846.
My dear Sir.
Your favor of the 12th just came to
hand last evening. I think my letter led you to infer
that I considered the plan I proposed for communicating
by Telegraph as entitled to more originality than I claimed.
The principal features of my plan which I thought now
was, to have a book such as proposed, for general circulation
whence I had supposed that the words of the kind herefore used
were on a comparatively small scale, & designed only for
the Telegraph offices or for private use. The Kind Report limited Report
I had not seen; I borrowed it of a friend today, & find, much in
it that is new & interesting.
The plan of having a book of numbered phrases & for gen-
eral use, appears to me more important as I contemplate
it, (among other reasons, besides those already suggested,) it affords
so great facilities for private or secret correspondence. It will
only be necessary for persons to agree previously upon certain letters
of the alphabet to represent the digits, after the manner in which
merchants mark their goods, & no persons should should where hands the cor-
respondence might pass, would be any the wiser for it. Something of the
kind is suggested on one of the pages of the report to which you re-
fere, though not exactly the same as the plan I have in my mind.
Will you have the kindness to inform me how large a work
Mr Rogers is preparing, & also whether in your opinion
an additional work by another hand would be useful?
I should by no means expect or wish to publish any thing
that would interfere with the usefulness of his. It may be that
the field opens is so ample that several works of the kind are
desirable I would not interfere essentially with each other. It would
afford me pleasure to do anything in my power to facilitate this
great public improvement, but I should by no means think of
attempting any thing of the kind proposed without your advised
cordial approbation.
I will thank you to let me hear from you once more on
this subject. I trust you will pardon me for the trouble
I give you.
With sentiments of great respect
I am Yours etc
A.C.R. Baldwin

Washington March 28th 1826
Dear Sidney. I am just reminded that this is the last day
for writing by the Steamer, and I therefore, take a moment to write
you a hasty line. I was much gratified at receiving a letter from
you by the last arrival. I thank you for your evidence on the fact
of inventing the mode of making one circuit operate more than one
pen. Since I wrote, Prof. Tannin has explained more at large his plan of
writing and it is only a modification of my keyed instrument offering no
advantage but on the contrary having more disadvantages. It will not amount
to anything. If you see the American paper as I suppose you do, you
will see how the Telegraph is going ahead. In a few weeks we
shall hear direct from Washington to Boston 430 miles! We have
some difficulties with the New York & Philadelphia line on account of
the North River, but we shall surmount them soon. In regard to
the Rotundo Picture, I learn that my friends are quite zealous, and
it is not improbable that it may be given me to execute. If so what
should you say to seeing me in Paris? However, this is but Castlebuilding.
I am quite indifferent as to the result, except that in case it is given me, I shall
be restored to my position as an artist by the same power that prostrated me, and
then shall I not more than ever have cause to explain, "Surely your heart led
me in a way which I know not." -- I have already, in looking back
seen enough of the dealings of Providence with me, to excite
my wonder, and gratitude. How singularly has my way been hedged
up in my profession, at the very moment when human appearance
every thing seemed prosperously tending to the accomplishment of
my desire in painting a National Picture. The language of Poor
idence in all his dealings with me has been almost like that to
Abraham "Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac whom thou
lovest, -- and offer him for a burnt offering ye." -- It has always
seemed a mystery to me, how I should have been led on to the ac-
quiescence of the knowledge of Painting, with so much
sacrifice of time, and money, and though so many anxieties & per-
plexities, and then suddenly be stopped, as if a wall were built
across my path, so that I could pursue my profession no longer.
But I believe, I had grace to trust in God, persuaded that he
could and would clear up, in his own time and manner, all
the mystery that surrounded me, and now, if not greatly deceived
I have a glimpse of his wonderful, truly wonderful mercy towards
me. He has chosen thus to order events, that one mind might be
concentrated upon that intention, which he has permitted to be
born for the blessing, I trust, of the world. And he has chosen me
as the instrument, and given me the honor, and at the moment
when all has been accomplished which is essential to its success
he is ordering events as again to turn my thoughts to my almost
sacrificed Isaac, At times I am almost overwhelmed with the
thoughts of God's goodness, in making privations and affliction
the means of palpable blessings. It seems at such times that I
could never again distrust God, however incomprehensible his
dispensation towards me, and yet the heart is so deceitful I
trouble in the very exercise of faith lest it fail in the hour of
trial, and it would fail but for the gift of spiritual strength.

Dear Sir,
In looking over Bob an old account book I found within
the leaves the enclosed note of yours for $149.00 dollars. My memory
in such matters is very treacherous, and I have been puzzled to know
whether it has been paid or not. I have an indistinct recollection of some money
leaving about the date of the note, and a vague impression that the
note has been paid, but why it in my possession rests is the mystery. If
it has been paid, you ought to have it. If not you can probably solve
the mystery by reference to your own accounts, and will let me know
I am the more inclined to think it has been paid, from the fact that I
had not charged my memory with it. But if not you will make it all
right.
I regard to the line from Boston to Norfolk I should
like to hear from you its condition. When all the way through
should delight to have you in the Exchange in Boston,
while I shall be here, and hold the first telegraphic inter-
course from Washington to Boston. We ought to have some
plan of operation concerted against the completion of the entire
line. If instruments shall be ready at intermediate stations
say at Worcester, Springfield, Hartford, New Haven, Philadelphia,
Philadelphia, Wilmington, and Baltimore, you can conceive
the effect when it is announced that each of these places
received the same intelligence at the same moment. Let
me hear from you on this subject.
There are already indications of attempts to impress
the enemy with the idea that we are making preparations for
an attack upon their communications.
Ever affy

Professor Morse
Sir
Your letter of the 13th
just has just come to hand, and I hasten to
answer it. I cannot describe the surprise,
mortification and regret which the contents and
tone of your letter occasioned me.
I will tell you plainly all I have
done, together with my motives. I think I shall
be able to convince you that I intended right, and
therefore not blamable.
The paragraph you speak of, in the Daily
Courant did receive my "approbation" but the
error shall be as promptly and fully corrected
as you desire.
I did believe there was a "U.S. Telegraphic Comp-
any" that Prof. Morse, Mr. Vail, Dr. Gale and Mr.
Smith formed that Company. and I supposed
that all the other companies were subordinates.
I also supposed that the two works, by Mr.
Vail, of which I have the agency, belonged to this
Company -- or that they had an interest in them. I
do not remember that I was told so, in so many
words -- although I have the impression that Mr
Vail said something to that effect. At any rate,
I believed such to be the fact, and I acted upon it.
I was anxious to sell these works, -- both on
my own account, and on Mr. Rail's and Yours.
I had the Agency of them -- and in some slight
sense I might call myself (as I believed) the
( humble) Agent of the U.S. Telegraphic Company.
Under this belief, that I was acting for the interest
of the Company, (although as much, as more for
my own interest) I pursued the course you
see. I was aware of the fact that the success
of my exhibitions -- as well as the sale of these
works, depended very much upon the authority
by which I came before the public. I think
I was actuated as much by me, as the other.
It is true, it seemed rather a stretch
of propriety to call myself an "Agent of the
U.S. Telegraphic Company" or to allow an editor
to do so, simply because I had these works for
sale. -- but in doing so, I did not claim that
I was transcending any privilege you had given
me, -- or that I was claiming an authority which
you would not sanction. Believe me, Sir, this
is true.
I have felt proud and humbly grateful for
the attention and kindness you have shown me;
and I hope most sincerely that I shall so
manage that, you shall not regret the Certifi-
cate you gave me.
I regret exceedingly that I have done that which
should occasion such a censure. I have done
wrong -- but it was under a mistaken impression
My explanations of the Telegraph have been
well patronized -- the first night receipts in New
Haven were $88.00. Every Professor except two, I
believe, in Yale College were present. -- Many of
them flattered me by personal commendations.
My success in the sale of this work
has not not been as great as I could be think, principally to the fact, that nearly my
whole time has been occupied with the painting.
I trust it will be different in a few days,
when I arrive in Boston.
In all my future operations with
the Telegraph, I would pursue just that course
which you desire. I would not represent myself
other than I am. Suppose I adopt the course I
purposed in New York -- "Mr. Colton, by the permission
of Prof. Morse" -- This will give me, apparently,
some authority -- and yet will not make you, or
any one else, my backer.
The "Annexed" -- I have prepared in such a
manner as I think will meet your wishes, and at
the same time, will not be a direct confession
to the public that I have used unwarranted authority.
It will have its effect upon those interested.
I should be pleased to know your feelings upon the
subject. I enclose $20.00 (which is more than
I have received) for Mr. Bail. Yours humbled Friend. G.R. Colton
(Professor Morse)
If you prefer, I will not publish your certificate

your bill. You were correct in supposing your letter to Mr. Green had probably not reached him.
I hope it will not be long before your country and mine will be more immediately connected by steam packets dependent on England for communication.

should have had two or more receiving magnets for you
long since had you ordered them. But you only made
inquiries respecting them without ordering any.
I have no means of having them made here in Washington
But if you desire me to obtain two or more, I will procure them to be made here in Washington
for you in a very short time if the funds are advanced for the
purpose. (You have been so far ahead of my time in supplying me with
the necessary magnets, and satisfy yourself respecting them if you have any doubts, I have never heard of any
fault found with them, notwithstanding I have them in operation here and at Baltimore, at Phila. & Wilmington,
and they work admirably, I am perfectly satisfied of their immense excellence, I am not in a situation to take upon myself any
financial risk in supplying them. I have done already, to the full extent of my means in
advancing money for instruments to the N.Y. & Wash. Cts. and I cannot
advance any more. I can furnish you with money as you desire it
for 10 dollars at once if you pay for it immediately. If you pay for it
France specially for this purpose in this will be required for us 18 dollars a piece. If you
pay for it immediately and they will be paid for them every day. I
have already paid for them which are nearly completed. They can be finished
you will find them in a few days after you give the order,
and remit me the money.
The Condition of the N.Y. & Wash. Cts. I regret quite as
much as any one, but I have had nothing to do with
nothing to do with
its management, and no responsibility rests with me. The wire
is bad, and has been badly put up in some parts of the line. Who
is to blame? I do not pretend to say. But much more is
made of these difficulties by some persons, principal to the whole
enterprise than is necessary. Just. Perhaps stock-jobsitions
are at the bottom of the difficulties. All difficulties will be surmounted in
good time, as all scientific difficulties have already been.
The lines agree with you, ought to have been more
substantially built. I hope your line from Atlanta to Atlanta
will be built. It cannot do was to urge the necessity of this course but cheaper
circuits prevailed. In regard to intermediate Stations I believe
I gave you a slight sketch of the mode of
arranging them. These arrangements will depend
much on the quantity of business required at each
station. If with which you enter into such have little
business, a single instrument truly will be necessary at the
intermediate Station, if you wish to communicate each way
to and from an intermediate at the same time, then two sets will be
required. I will write you again on this subject.
Our line here is in perfect order, and is kept so with no
little trouble; there was but one day during all the last
year in which it was not in a condition to communicate at
any moment, and that was from an accident by lightning.
My own wish, from the beginning ever since the experiment of
this line proved successful, was to have stout posts
from 15 or 16 inches at the bottom to 1 foot at top, and capable
of holding 30 or 40 wires if necessary.

I have this day sent on to you
Susan's picture. I followed get the man to pack
