The Schooner will sail from here on Monday next
the Captain says he will be in Washington by Thursday
or Friday next I directed the box to you and send
you here enclosed the receipt of the Captain of the
Schooner returns to day from Bridgeport.

little sketch you wrote me about, I have looked on everywhere
I could think of, are you sure you have not put it away?

you are getting on. Don't you want me to volunteer for Mexico to get a little
Glory!
From your affectionate Son
Charles W. Morse

Dear Sir,
About 2 years ago I
made an invention for protecting the wires of
your Telegraph from injury from the passing
of discharges of the electric fluid from the
atmosphere, along the wire, to the earth, at
the points where the wire passes through or
near the post; or from the earth upward,
through the same channel, to the atmos-
phere. Probably the discharges go would
mostly be from the atmosphere downwards,
My plan is to have a suitable point, coat-
ed with Platinum, attached to the Tel-
egraph wire near the post (at many posts
as may be found necessary probably one
in each quarter of a mile) & another point
of the same kind, attached to a lightning rod
which I propose should be erected on the
post for the purpose of forming a channel
for the fluid between the Telegraph wire
& the earth. The point on the Telegraph
wire, & that on the lightning rod attached
to the post, must be placed at such dis-
tance from each other as to allow the fluid
when your wire is operating to continue along the Telegraph
wire from end to end; but when the wire
receiving a charge from the atmosphere, the
same distance from each other
allowing the fluid to leap from the point on
the wire to that on the lightning rod attached
to the post, & in short any wire which
from its charge pass to the earth. This is
the general feature of my arrangement. Details I need not give. It would to the
wide is always sufficient.
I am led to make this communication to
you, at this time, from seeing in the Morning Telegraph, of this city, a notice of the
destruction of the wire of the Telegraph,
recently, in New Jersey, by the passing of the
electric fluid from the circuit-jacket,
contiguous, at most here through the wire
to the post, to the earth. The wire was broken
& the post was destroyed. The conduct of
the electric current, interruptions of the
kind, I think, could be very easily prevented in future.
Pardon me Sir, for indicating in plain
terms my estimate of your
incomparable invention. For you Fame
will build a new Pillar in her Temple,
higher & more magnificent than
all of the others, & on the top of it inscribe the name of Morse.
I am very respectfully yours
AB Quincy.

May 24, 1846.
Dear Sir:
Your kind letter came to me like
a stream of water in a dry and parched land. It
whispered to my heart the sweet secret of Christian con-
centration. I cannot be mistaken. The words seemed to
come from the same spring whereon I have drawn in
other days long draughts of that peace which passeth
all understanding. It is an additional token of Hearer's
goodness for which I flow now tears of sincere gratitude.
The Board here will not allow me to stay,
and my dear Mother also objects to my relinquishing
my pursuits in Philadelphia. I hurried here to be
guardians, and watch over her until her final steps
found her long last home; but after making every
arrangement filial affection could desire, and finding
her anxious to have me return to my associations, I
shall leave for Philadelphia in a few days. Of course
a new appointment has been made on the strength
of my letter to Mr Kendall, circumstributing my sphere
to the operations of the Western line; but even in this
relation I may have it in my power to reply in some
degree, and at some times, the kind confidence reposed
in me by myself and associates, I have wedded my
heart too much to the Telegraph, and given up too often
quiet communion with my Maker and family altar.
Struck down in a moment with no previous intimations of
his departure, just risen from his knees and family worship,
repose and sighing for his everlasting rest my father's death
recalled my sense of duty to him, who balances the
electric power that sustains - animates - governs all. - His
loving Kindness never changes. The conductors of his love
never break, and the communications it bears are all
without money and without price. I shall, I trust, never
again break the circuit - or leave my wedge neglected
from the Key -
Convey, if convenient, my respectful remembrance to
Mr. Kendall & Mr. Vail and trusting that he may always
impart to you and yours the consolations with which you
have delaced me - believe me
Yours respectfully and sincerely
James D. Perkins.

of it and from Havre are to be paid by you. According to our account,
we have paid Messr. Bouquet the amount of this bill, say $1450,
which bill accompanied the package, and in virtue of the order you sent
us, we have drawn upon Geo. Peabody, of London for $181.6 which balance
the account at you will provide by the annexed statement.

that we may have other and frequent opportunities of being useful to you,
we remain
Sam'l G. P. Breckinridge

Having the honor to submit a sketch
of a machine I have devised for the purpose of cut-
ting into strips the paper used for the Telegraph, I think
it will cut fast and lose no paper in the operation.
The mode of operation is this, A Roll of paper is put
in its place as at R, the end is then carried through the
rollers C, C, & after passing the knives K an inch or two
(they being previously adjusted) they are let down upon it,
it is then drawn as far as the farther set of spokes, the
end is then cut & the strips attached in due order to the
spokes of the naked shaft, if it is desirable to have but a small
hole in the roll.
The machine is then ready for operation and may be
moved by a crank attached to either set of spokes. I
judged it best to place the spokes alternately one beyond the
other that the strips may not interfere with each other
& that each roll may be easier regulated should they get
loose, or wind crooked or any other accident befall them.
I think this machine will cut the paper smooth &
without waste, and wind it tight and even.
I know not what experience you possess for effecting this
object but should the above meet your wishes better
I trust I may not to forgetter in its application.
Yours respectfully
J. F. B. Post Exp.

Washington, 22 August, 1840.
My Dear Sir:
Some few days since, I received a letter
from Mr Wood, who is now stationed at Buffalo,
informing me that the line of Telegraph would
soon be completed through to New-York, and that
the Company would like to secure the services
of a competent person to take charge of the New
York terminus. He wrote at the request of the
President of the Company, Mr Inston, who wished
to ascertain if I would be willing to leave my
present station and assume the duties of that
post.
I replied to Mr Wood immediately, and re-
fired the President of the Company to you; as I
understood from him that you were expected at
Buffalo, stating that I should be pleased to go
to New-York, provided the compensation would justify
me in going there.
You know that my present compen-
sation is very small, and much less that the
Company's operations receive at this terminus. My
request is that you will give me an opportunity of
expressing to the President of the Company
my willingness to accept the position of
Superintendent of the New-York terminus.
I am, Sir, your obedient Servant,
George W. McClellan.

take yours first.
My cellar experiment was not so unsuccessful
as you imagine. I succeeded to my entire satisfaction in
taking 3 inches of skin, a little of the flesh, & a trifle of bone
from the front of my left leg, & so the result, for one week's
entire leisure with my leg in a chair: The experiment was
to satisfy myself that I deem it needless to try it again,
having established beyond a doubt, that Skin flesh alone
are no match against wood, iron, &c &c. I am entirely
well of it, & enjoyed my visit to the Western States very

I have just tried an experiment
upon un soldered joints of Copper wire. I cut
up into a 1000 pieces copper wire of the kind we use, and
then put them all together myself that I might
be confident of them being done well. Every joint
was made by twisting the end of one wire around
the body of the other with the pincher and the
contact perfect and clean. These I have hung up
at the ceiling running back & forth over my head
in length about 150 feet and this morning I tested
it by putting the wire in the circuit from here to
Baltimore, and also put in the circuit our old
Galvanometer, and what do you think was the
result? Give a guess before I tell you. The galvama-
ter stood the same with the 1000 joints in the
circuit, as it did when out of the circuit, I am
much surprised at it but so it is -- The wire is bright
at the joints and I presume the difference should
not have been much, but still I thought there would
be some. I dont think it worth while to mention
this to any Contractors or other for there is no much
neglect in putting up the telegraphic wires that
it is necessary to insist upon their doing more to get
done even what is absolutely necessary. I desire to
make the same experiment with iron wire and with
you could get for that purpose 1000 pieces 4 1/2 inches
long & bring them on with you. I should prefer
annealed wire of the same number as this. Will
you also bring with you 10 or 15 pounds of the
fine shot we used for testing the strength of magnet
I want it for the same purpose.

Is not this the feature of the age? The
visitor to Lake Erie holding confidential converse with his friend in New York! The very annihilation of distance! Time and space will become mere nihilities. We stand amazed at the gigantic power displayed by man when, he grapples with the mysteries of Nature. Twas well done for old Yale, to call the magician naturae legum doctor—we omit the rest As New Yorkers, we are proud of the Doctor, and we are proud too, of that classic pile, in whose silent halls this beautiful philosophical mechanism was arranged and perfected. The University has much to boast of. Nor is this her only original performance; it is not generally known that the first Daguerriian portrait was taken by Dr. Draper, though such is the fact. How great individual is over corporate capacity, is here strikingly shown. The very elements which form the Anglo-Saxon character are brought out in wonderful development in the Anglo-American. While England, by her government, has got with great labor 175 miles of telegraph into operation, and then compelled to abandon it, the United States with her individual enterprise, has now in successful operation 1269 miles. This is American enterprise! But it is citizen enterprise. We must yield the palm to England in some matters. When as a government she undertakes a matter, she very seldom fails. Her public men are held responsible It is not the plan to let a ship of war lie on the stocks 20 years before it is completed. How desirable it is, that some of our citizen enterprise should enter our government councils.

Washington Sept 13th 1844
Dear Morre
I have permission of the department
to spend a few days at the North, for which I
shall leave here on Wednesday morning, and proceed
directly for your city, provided Mrs Bail is there,
and if so I should be glad to see you on Thursday
morning at the Observer Buildings, when I will
tell you more about the experiment of the joints.
I shall spend only a day or so in the City, &
return soon to Washington. I heard a powerful
funeral sermon from Mr Spole today on the
occasion of Mr Speir, a member of his Church
who died after a short illness in the hope of a
blessed immortality. I had the pleasure of Mr
Speir's acquaintance, who was a member of our
Lodge. The character of Mr Speir and his happy
death exhibited a striking, though silent contrast
with the melancholy death of Mr Connell, and
must have struck every hearer, though Mr Spole
did not attend to him (Mr Connell). I presume
you have learned of Mr Stone's death. Dr Pages
opinion: There have been many sudden deaths
all around us, and many are still sick. I
have however been well, for which I am very
thankful. I hope you are in the enjoyment of
perfect health, and will long remain so. I
learn by Tel from Phila that Mr Kendall is
better and has been out today. Hoping to see
you soon I remain yours friend as ever
Alfred Bail

Washington, Sept. 15th 1846.
My Dear Sir:
It is extremely painful for me to inform you, that a serious
misunderstanding took place yesterday,
between my brother Louis, and Genl. Vail;
brought about by, (as I am indeed to
believe, from other sources than Louis),
the overbearing conduct of Genl. Vail,
because Louis was somewhat over his
time at dinner. Louis says, that,
he has borne with this ill-treatment
from Genl. Vail long enough, - and he
appeals to your protection, against
a repetition of it.
This difficulty is rendered
still more painful to me, because
I am on the eve of departure, on a
visit to our widowed mother; and
instead of giving her every satis-
164
-faction with regard to Louis, and his
future prospects, I shall have but
a mournful story to tell her.
I consider that it is my duty,
as the guardian of my brother, to drop
you these hasty lines, with the fervent
hope that you will be able to set
the matter right.
Mr. Vail is gone away, and has
taken Louis away from the instrument
altogether, putting Mr. Clark there,
until he returns. This is, doubtless,
intended to degrade Louis. I hardly
thought that Mr. Vail would have
carried his feelings thus far; but
I have relied upon Louis to remain
perfectly quiet; and quiet his indis-
tant feelings, until he hears from
you.
Louis has settled his accounts
with Mr. Vail, agreeably to the
order of the latter.
I invoke, my dear Sir, your
prompt attention to this matter.
Please direct your reply, and advice,
to Louis. My direction, until the
22nd instant, will be at "Belvidere,
Warren Co., New-Jersey".
In great haste,
with high regard,
Sincerely, Your's,
Wm C. Huntziger.

N York Oct 7 1846
Dear Vail
Ex of 3d have just wd on my return from
Utica I am sorry that Louis Charles b show such a
temper. He stands in his own light. I had just procured
for him at Utica the appointment to the N York office
under Mr Wood at a salary of $500. but if it is
correct, what you report, & he shows such a distrustful
& sulky disposition, I fear it will so far towards mod-
ifying the wish of the Directors to have him in their em-
ployment. I regret it exceedingly as I had every disposition
to befriend him, & to advance him as far as his own
interest & the proper claims of older persons will permit.
I shall still endeavor to have the appointment for
him, hoping that this temper will be corrected, or him
by proper reflection. If it is not, he must pursue
his own course, without any interference of mine, for
I have too much on my mind, & weightier concerns
I think of, than to study the means of curing a bad temper,
in him. I have written to your brother George to procure
the stone for you, as I have as much as I can do, to
get ready for a visit to Wash n . I wish to see you, &
Mr Kendall on matters of importance to all concerned.
I have just ordered of Stockell, 4 Registers & he has
promised me he will so on with them, with delay I
cannot say when he will have them done. Keep this
private for reasons I will tell you when I see you. Our
receipts on the Buffalo line for 23 days only (all
one month) were $2940 in odd dollars!!
that is at the rate after expenses all paid of 14 p cent!
Cornell is app'd Superintendent of the line that is of our
door operations to keep the line in order. Those who
speculate are preparing to come out. We must be prepared
to meet them. It is an attempt doubled to frighten, &
to get some money from us, to purchase him out.
I guess he will be mistaken. But we shall have the
spec's against us, because they will hope to bring us to
lower terms, if they can get up a competition therefor
will be foughted if considerable of a puffing is
forthcoming. Good bye for the present. I do hope Louis for
his own & Mother's sake will not fight against his own
interest.

Washington, Oct 8th 1876.
Dear Sir:
I have received your letter of yesterday's date, and
passed its contents with the greatest pain, because I am
sure that the grossest misrepresentations, in every respect,
have been made to you respecting my conduct. I have
never received any message from you to the effect that
it was "your request that I should be reinstated in
my office", and, that, it is declined on my part! Your
name has never been mentioned to me, in any way
by Mr Bail, since his return!
I should deeply regret if any impression,
calculated to change your good opinion of me, could, for
a single moment, find a resting place within your
breast; and I have, therefore, to request that you will
suspend your judgment until you should hear further
from me. My brother, to whom I have shown your
letter, is much pained at its content; and requests me to
say, that he would not, on any account, have me to
accept of a situation from the Company, with the present
unkind impressions towards me, and my family resting upon
your mind, conveyed, doubtless, for the purpose of injuring
me in your estimation; for he well knows my attachment to you, personally, and

with great respect

Washington Oct. 9th 1846
Prof. S. F. B. Morse.
My dear Sir, urgent business called me
home; but had I been apprized of the extreme
danger division of the Board of the N.Y. M.L.
R.R. Co. I should have gone over from Phila-
delphia.
It is strange ground in this country that those
interested shall not decide important questions for
themselves and the directors will not be sustained.
We cannot in justice to ourselves or the country
agrimence in this division. It is a fatal injury to
a large mass of our property and denying to us
in part the consideration of our contract. But
worse than that -- it is the breaking down of
the system we had projected to give the bene-
fits of the Telegraph to every village and prevent
the Telegraph to the country as practically on unit,
upon whose wires messages would travel from
one end of the country to the other immediately.
I propose, however, before resorting to other remedies
to propose selling to the company our interest
in all the side lines and take payment in stock.
I have no doubt I can bring the company
to a connection or to a proprietor.
When shall we see you?
Most truly yours
Amos Kendall

My Dear Sir, By a pamphlet I have recently received
through the Penny post I see that an agreement has
been entered into with John J. Haley Esq to construct
a line of Telegraph from Petersburg to New Albany
Not having any acquaintance with
Mr Haley I am induced to apply to you asking the
favor to give me a letter of introduction to that
gentleman, with a view of obtaining from him the
situation of canvassing agent throughout the
entire extent of the line for subscriptions to the stock.
My large acquaintance throughout the whole
extent of the line and my intimate intimate knowledge of
the habits and manners of the inhabitants of the
Eastern section of the Country would enable me,
I flatter myself, to place the matter before them
in such a manner as to induce an immediate
subscription to the stock.
While writing allows me to take the liberty
of saying a word in reference to the route chosen.
See you go by the way of Wilmington to Charleston.
This I look upon as a bad arranged and ill
selected route for various reasons. Wilmington
is a very sickly place, hardly any Commercial
importance, besides in passing from Wilmington
to Charleston you have to pass the swamps as well as
as the rivers of the Great Little Pee Dee and the
Dantee with other smaller streams. These rivers
when full discharge themselves into the swamps
making them rise sometimes 15 or 20 feet and
passenger and wagon coaches carried through the
swamps by flatboats being at times
unmanageable by the force of the current would
be carried against the posts of the Telegraph
and they be destroyed.
Another objection against laying through the
low Country is the sparseness of the population
which will lead to difficulties in obtaining
subscription along the line and likewise the
low character of the resident whites in that section
who could and would destroy the line for a few
dollars without the slightest chance of being
detected. Again should the line break or get
out of order there would be great difficulties in
fixing it during the summer season the fever
of that country being fatal even to the inhabitants
should they remain out during the night.
These objections do not apply to the upper route.
The Country is remarkably healthy and by taking
what is termed the up-Country route and passing
through Raleigh R.C.A. to which there is now a
Rail road, from there to Camden Columbia S.C.
to which place a rail road is now in process of
construction and to or to Aiken which intersect the
Charleston and Hamburg Railroad and from Aiken a branch
to Charleston, you pass through a section of country
where inhabitants are over of character, intelligence
and wealth, and who would by taking subscriptions
to the stock feel an interest in the line and
be safeguards for its protection
We are aware a line of Mail Road exists from
Augusta 165 miles to West point from which
place a rail road is already constructed to
Montgomery. Now it appears to me that from
Montgomery you should go to Pensacola that being
a naval depot where vessels are continually
coming in with dispatches for government, and to
which place the government will be sending dispatches
which business alone do you as the Telegraph is
concerned will be more lucrative than the whole
Commercial Correspondence particularly during
the Continental of the Mexican war -
From Pensacola to Mobile and Mobile and New
Orleans with sentiments of the highest
Consideration and esteem
Your obedient Servant
John M. Leitch
Very respectfully
President Saml F B More

right to the right wire. A plate of copper is also
buried in the earth and a wire or wires attached to the
instrument as in the diagram. A small battery of

the emergency requires it.

Dear Sir
Having an engagement to
lecture before a Literary Association of young
men (called the Young Men's Institute)
in this place, and in several other places in this
region, upon the subject of the Magnetic Telegraph
I am desirous of getting in possession of as many
interesting and useful facts relating to the
subject as possible; and as I know of no better
source to which to apply for such information,
I take the liberty of addressing you.
I have been engaged in lecturing
upon Electricity and kindred subjects, more or
less, for ten years past; but within two years
have lectured more particularly upon the Magnetic Telegraph. Two years ago I gave three
lectures before the B.M. Institute of this
place, upon the latter subject, and they in desire
ous, with other Associations in this vicinity,
of having this same subject presented to them
again -- which I have consented to do.
To illustrate the subject I have
two recording Instruments, one of which I
make myself; (and I think it works as neatly
as any, that I have ever seen) the other is like
those which have been in use on the New York
& Buffalo line, which I have remodeled so
that it works very well indeed. -- So that with
230 the assistance of another operator I am able to
represent two termini of a line by stationing the
Instruments at the two extremities of the room —
and messages are transmitted to and fro before the
audience, and the whole operation explained.
Now if you will favour me with
a synopsis of some incidents, (humorous or otherwise
for the sake of variety) or facts which might be
interesting to a promising audience, and would
serve to illustrate the utility of the invention
and the importance of its general adoption thro-
ughout the country, you will greatly oblige
me. In order to convince the community in
this region of the ultimate success and utility of the
telegraph there is a very strong prejudice to contend
with, which has been irrevocably fixed upon
their minds in consequence of the ill success,
this day, of the New York & Boston line.
(But the object is worthy of a higher standard of judgment than this
line affords.) Please answer this as soon as
convenient and oblige
Your humble Servt
Prof S. F. B. Morse
New York
G. C. Strong
P.S. You are probably aware that I have
been in the employ of the New York & Boston
Tel. Company, but resigned my office on account
of the insufficiency of the salary. — I am now out
of employment. If you should know of a situation
on any Tel. line where I could serve to advan-
tage, either as an operator or in any other capacity,
and will inform me of it, you will do me
a great favour. I hope however that other
lines, as well as the New York to Buffalo
line, have a better set of Registers than this
line has. The instruments in this line and the
manner in which they are worked are certainly
not decent -- they are a disservice to the enterprise.
I do not believe anything is lost in the
end, in having things done well.
I clip an article from a paper
published here which I inclose.
Yours,
J. C. S.
J. E. Strong,

Dear Sir.
As I am preparing for publication
descriptions of many of the Electric Magnetic mach-
ines which I have arranged and constructed since
the spring of 1833, being the most important portion of my experiments, before me since I obtained my patents, and as I wish to make
some statements in regard to the Electric Telegraph, I intend upon you at this time, to learn of you the state of your first experiments
in applying Electric magnetism to Telegraphic
purposes. I am aware of your investigations on board
the Packet ship in 1832, and I recollect having a
conversation with you on the subject of using
galvanic electricity for the Telegraph, at 42 Stamford
Street, of Paris in the spring of 1831, but do not
recollect that you mentioned any experiments
that you had then made in galvanic or Electric
magnetism. Please forgive me with the state of
your first experiments in Electric magnetism for
Telegraphic purposes at your earliest convenience.
I am anxious to obtain a small battery of the
kind used for the Telegraph, consisting of two
porous cups and platinum plates. If you can
get them here and send them to me, with your
bill, I will remit you the money for the same
I cannot procure the materials in Liverpool and
I wish to obtain them soon, in order to complete
some certain experiments.
Respectfully yours
Thomas Tannish

Dear Sir,
In answer to your question respecting the
cause of the diminution of power which your bay has
experienced in working the line, it formerly required but
70 CUPS and now requires 200 and yet apparently
with less power, I have done more data before I can form
a sound judgment. It may be owing to a deterioration of
the zincs or acids employed. I should wish to know the
condition of the zincs, and whether they have been much corroded,
whether this has produced so much corroded, the batteries
too long in use, for either case there would be a cause for the
difficulty you mention. Another cause may be, a want of
care in making perfect connections in the various Offices or in
some of them. – Still another cause may be the increase
in the number of receiving magnets on the line, the receiving
magnets are made of finer wire than the main conductors, and
although a certain number may not sensible on the current in
the main conductors, yet when this fine wire is multiplied beyond a certain
quantity the diminution of current may become quite
sensible, and require greater power of battery to overcome it.
If this should be so, the subject of sufficient current

to do this in the course of the Spring if possible. A free line
in any experiment might be made by concert of your offices,
by taking some time after business hours, and cutting off
successively the various offices receiving magnets at the various
stations and connecting the main line through the remaining
without passing through the magnets offices, and ascertaining how few cups will operate through
as each is cut off. This will show if the diminution of power is owing to the magnets or to some hid-
den defect in the main line. I hope it will prove that the

I think I have a remedy in some modification of the magnets.
I am glad that you have dismissed Cornell from his position as

LETTER PRINTING TELEGRAPH.—Figure 2.
EXPLANATION OF FIGURE 2.—The telegraph circuit passes through this machine, being received by the wire Z, and passing through the coil of the magnet A, passes off by the wire B. The electric current in the telegraph circuit is supposed to be suspended, and consequently the armature C is elevated from the magnet by the spring D applied to the armature helve. To the upper side of this helve, immediately over the armature, is attached a wedge shaped projection, which is also nominated a stop, because it stops the motion of the cylinder F, by coming in contact with a series of 28 teeth or cogs which project from the periphery of the cylinder.— These teeth as well as the stop, are wedge-shaped, and being sharp at the ends, the stop when it rises is very certain to pass between some two of the teeth. The type cylinder is about two inches in diameter, mounted on a horizontal shaft G, and contains 28 types, two only of which are represented by the dotted lines H and I; these types are arranged circularly, just inside the periphery of the cylinder, and with sufficient space between them for the arm to connect the periphery to the shaft. A wire spring, represented by dotted lines J, extends from the shaft to each of the types, and serves to return it to its position when it has been pressed forward. The cylinder, when not restrained by the stop, is put in motion by a belt K, which communicates with another wheel impelled by a weight or spring. The motion of the cylinder is regulated by means of a verge L, which plays into a scape ment wheel M, which has 28 teeth, and revolves at the rate of 130 times per minute.— The strip of paper N O, is drawn from a roll not represented, and passes over the register, roller P, passing between that and the friction roller Q. A horizontal punch R, is attached to a pivot at the end of the punch shaft S, a little below the centre, and extends to the type cylinder and nearly in contact with the horizontal blade and of the type (This punch may be connected to a central crane between the bearings of the punch shaft.) This shaft, when not restrained, is put in quick motion by means of the belt T T, which connects with a wheel driven by a weight or spring— This punch shaft is restrained by an elastic hook U, which takes to a horn projecting from the helve of the armature; and when released from this horn by the depression of the armature, it is restrained by another horn V, which takes to a tooth projecting from the side of the horn V. An ink-roller W, is mounted in front of the types, and distributes a very soft printing ink to the faces thereof as they pass around. A ratchet X, is attached to the end of the register roller, and a hood spring Y, projects forward from a cross-bar which is attached to the punch shaft, and takes to the teeth of the ratchet near P. We shall now describe its operation.—When a key of fig. 1 is depressed, the telegraph circuit is closed as before described, and at the same instant the armature of fig. 2 is attracted to the magnet, and the type cylinder is put in motion with a velocity precisely equal to that of the stop-wheel, fig. 1. When the stop strikes the key, the telegraph circuit being broken, the stop of fig. 2 stops the type cylinder, and the punch shaft being liberated, revolves at the same instant, by which the punch forces one of the types against the paper, and the spring hook taking to the teeth of the ratchet draws forward the register roller with the paper, and the punch shaft is stopped by the hook taking to the horn V. It will be understood that the types are so arranged that the punch will invariably project the same letter which is on the depressed key: for by means of the wedge shape of the stop and the teeth, any variation of the motion of the scapement wheels of the two machines, less than half a tooth in a single revolution, will be adjusted when the wheels stop. The type which answers to the blank key, is a blank too short to reach the paper, and is used to space between the letters. The star is used to designate the letters which are used for numerals; also interrogation and when placed after a space, it signifies a change or a final class of subject. These types are mounted somewhat very light, so it is important that the inertia of the stop-wheel and the type cylinder should be exactly equal, that equal times may be occupied in moving equal distances: but if any error occurs, the attendant will readily right it. We shall put these machines in progress of construction immediately.—En. SCL. AMER.

delighted to welcome you home again. Telegraph matters are becoming
more & more interesting, the people of the country every where desirous of availing
themselves of its facilities and the lines are being extended in all directions. As might be expected then, I have my plans interlaced with
the telegraph project, which I have been trying to put up real telegraphs
and contest my patent. I am ready for them. We have had to apply
for an injunction on the Phil. d Pittsburg line, the case is an approximate
one and will be decided on Monday or Tuesday at Phila in C. Court
of U. States. I have no anxiety at the result, there are more
F. Als than one, yet not one quite so bad. I think amid all the
scramble, I shall probably have enough come to my share, and
it does not matter by what means but Heavenly Father chooses
to control my receipts, for I shall have just what he pleases,
none can hinder it, and more I do not want.
We have just received sad news from the West. Mr Ellsworth,
had a fall which broke his leg badly, and is terminiated fatally
on the 14th inst. The loss of his mother is a sad blow to poor
Annie, and must greatly shock Henry in Stockholm when he
hears the melancholy tidings.
Richard will doubtless write you by Steamer from N.York
and give you all news from that quarter. I have just got a letter
from Susan at Syracuse, all well and in good spirit, and sends
much love to you and all. Charles is well and passing the winter
at Newburg, &c. is Finley at Bladewack.
If it comes in your way I should be glad if you could send
me immediately some account of the operations of letter printing
Telegraphs, if any are in use. Houses & their Associates are
making most strenuous efforts to interfere, and embarrass me
by playing on the ignorance of the public, and the natural tim-
idity of Capitalists. I shall probably have to lay the law
upon him, and make an example, before my patent is
confirmed in the minds of the public. It is the course
I am told of every substantial Patent. It has to undergo
the ordeal of one trial in the Courts. As I said before I
am ready for them. But to make assurance doubly sure
I should be glad to have such accounts of the failure of
Common letter printing Telegraphs in Europe, as would con-
firm the timid who have embarked in my Patent, and
alarm the timid who think embarking in Houses, and
I believe that a true account of the operation of Bain's
will furnish me with that desideratum. You know how
much more weight is given to any opinion from abroad than
from even the highest sources at home. If, therefore, I can pub-
lish "An extract from a highly respectable Scientific Gentle-
man in England," it will tend to dispel effectually the delu-
sion on this subject.
Although I thus write you need have no fear that my
operations will be seriously affected by any schemes of Common
letter printing Telegraphs. I have just filed a Caveat for
one which I have invented, which as far transcends in sim-
plicity and efficiency, any previous plan for the purpose
as my Telegraphic system is superior to the old visual telegraph
I will have it in operation by the time you return.
I have been longing to publish your masterly pamphlet on
American Slavery, but have been deterred by your request
that if one should arrive in the country, not to publish till
we got your revised edition. So I have waited till now, I
have today sent it to the Union, and Richard writes that it
will appear in the Observer also this week. I had read it to
several Members of Congress, and they were so desirous of
having it published that I have been for some time tempted
to publish notwithstanding your request to the contrary. I have
taken care that proper credit should be given to you, and
have not hesitated to give your name in full. I
believe it will be read with equal interest in every
part of the country. I think you have most effect-
ually closed the mouths of English men on that subject,
and in so doing have paved the way for a peaceful, and
proper abolition of the evil as fast as providential circum-
stances will allow. No foreign interference. Especially
we will allow no interference from England. We can do
without her help. Indeed her help is hindrance. The
odium of Slavery recoils upon her tenfold from her arrogant
and officious, and impertinent interference in the matter, after
the centuries of wrong she has inflicted upon us, in forcing it
originally upon us. You say right that she must approach us
in the attitude of penitence. Yes upon her knees.
I hope you will pursue the subject. You will be listened to
at the South, when others will not be heard.
Good night, I almost fear I have missed the mail.
Truly Your Aff. brother as ever
Sam. P. B. M'Nary.
Sidney L. More Esq.

Yours of the 15th inst. has just been received

Freeman Dana at the New York Athenaeum. Professor Dana is now Professor of Chemistry in the University of
Washington. When in 1832 I conceived the plan of my Magnetic Telegraph, the information received from
Prof. Dana in relation to the Electric magnet, furnished me with the ready conception of applying its force to printing my signs
in letters. The more important of my experiments however, in applying the magnet, were not made until the latter part of
1835. At the New York City University, the essential parts of my invention were then proved, and during the year 1836, were
occasionally modified as I had leisure from other duties to make experiments. My object was not to obtain any great power, but any
power however small with the magnet, a magnetism, at a distance, that I had obtained for short distances of a few hundred feet, but I had

with which my experiments were performed publicly at the University and afterwards in Washington. I recollect contrasting the operation
of your ingenious magnetic engine in Stanton Street and also I think in Cedar St near Broadway; there was one experiment you had

made which interested me more than your engine forthwith upon doing
of my own researches. You had a long frame with perhaps a dozen

your object is to understand the person right who showed it to me, (it was

was to know if the same power was given to each of the magnets by the

I reflected suggesting to him that an intensity battery would probably give
a better result, as I had found diminution of magnetic power from a

Y. C. Servt.

Dear Sidney, I have this moment received yours by the
Cambria, and am rejoiced to learn that you are all so
well in health. You do not say a word about your return in
the probable time we may expect you. I hope you will in
your next that we may know whether to write you or not.
In regard to Telegraph improvements, I would say that I
have intended a caveat for two methods of recording, one of
them by printing from ordinary type, but although simpler
and more efficient than any other plan for the same object it
cannot compete with my present plan, I shall proceed to
make it for curiosity sake, and to defeat these insinuations
on their own ground. But I have no apprehensions whatever
from House or any other. They are mere bubbles which
will burst in their proper time.
I have a carried time of it with the Telegraph, adverse
and successful results, I have just received my first divi-
idend on the N.Y. Alb. and Buffalo line, 3 P.C.'s for 5 months,
$1393,,00. This is a good beginning. We shall make a
dividend on the N.Y. Wash. line soon, we have had extra
expenses on this line but our receipts for several
weeks have averaged $200,,000 per day! Boston line
is managed by Smith, I need not say to you what the
result is except that it is so badly managed that it is
odious everywhere, and there is no doubt that it is in-
tentional on his part that he may get the stock at
a depreciated value, and so obtain the control and
use it as a monopoly for speculation. A more perfect
specimen of satanic possession, I do not believe
exists. I have to keep appearances with him; but
100390
as soon as I can cut adrift from him I mean to, even
at great sacrifice.
We have just had a lawsuit in Phila. before Judge
Kane; we applied for an injunction, to stay irregular
and injurious proceedings on the part of Western (Pitts-
burg, & Cincinnati Company,) and our application
has been refused on technical grounds. I know
not what will be the issue. I am trying to have matters
compromised but do not know if it can be done, and we
may have to contest it in law. Our application was in
court of equity. — A movement of Smith was the cause of all!
I called on Mr. WM. Beeckman last evening. I
found them well and in good spirits, although you are
perhaps aware that, he has met with losses, which
make it necessary for him to despoil of his house
in Wash. Place and procure a humble residence.—
All well at Richard's, he will write and let you
know how Obewer matters go. I am glad to have
had it in my power to loan him $3000 at 6 percent interest to pay off
a sum, which was called for. We have great cause
of gratitude for the prosperity which seems to be
flowing in upon us. Let us consult how we can
use it for the glory of Him who purchased all our
blessings for us by his own sufferings.
I received yesterday letters from Susan & Edward in
Michigan. They were well and in good spirits; Edw.
writes that his business last year after deducting losses
and expenses left him clear gain $900000
I made arrangements sometime ago with a gentleman in Washington
Jacob Bigelow Esq. to procure me a special act of Parliament

action. Your plan if I write very
impious, and would be well

I have left Wash t altogether, and am settling in

My dear Sir.
Now what Mr. Danforth told me I hoped
that we might have the pleasure of seeing you about
this time but I suppose you did not choose to mingle
in the turmoil of a closing season.
You have probably heard that Mr. Spole is to leave
us for West Point - of course our post fit will be vacant.
As an individual I wish to ask you if there would be
a possibility in your opinion of obtaining Mr. Hill-
might not his views of duty lead him to consider this
city a good field of labor. - nothing but duty could in-
duce him - but it seems to me that he could exercise
a commanding influence here who knows what jewels of
the brightest water God might allow him to find here
to give the Redmen's curse - You could you, as you know
him so well, ask him by a line if there might be such
a possibility - I have heard his name mentioned by a man
here - and some have asked me unofficially to ascertain -
Your intimacy with him might allow you to ask the ques-
tion - you could say that some who felt deeply for the welfare
of this place had ventured to utter his name, if you then put
it was deserving of knowing for them if they might turn their thoughts
to him. If you could be in any way instrumental of obtaining
a favorable response I am convinced you would do us great good.
Mr. Ellsworth will look out as he goes on to New England
& the members of the Church Congregation are of consequence
in that God may fill the vacancy which will soon be
made.
The House had a few days of painful & pleasantable interest
with Mr. Exchequer -- I wish it could have been prolonged
especially for Annie as many would have been grateful to
touch her kind attention & sympathy. Poor Annie seems to
feel desolate indeed -- I fear lest she may, without her
feelings around herself too much exhausted from the great duties
of life -- in which God is discriminating her -- next to
Lafayette there is no place where she could spend
some time less sadly than at Washington -- I trust that
Heaven will grant her strength to bear her trials & make
her to come forth brighter from his furnace of affliction.
I have just learned today that with their usual disavowal
inaction & justice! Congress have voted $60000 to have the
House filled by young Powell -- He enlisted all Ohio's
strength to vote up -- New York I understand
will vote for you -- I hope however you may yet yourself
resume the need & furnish the public the most striking
commentary on their utter disregard of justice -- by
placing somewhere the "Genius of the Republic" in such
colors that shall make them blush & hang their heads to
think themselves such men --
I have had your the cast which you gave me of the
Tying Hercules put together all but the big toe which
I shall leave till you come on as we cannot tell precisely
by its appearance. It is much a mist and I think you
need for it. I hope we shall see you here this spring
at all events come see us when you visit us.
We are going to give up the house to the Depes P.O.
& shall take a small house in about a month
boarding with them till then. But I must stop
If you think you can write to Mr. Kirk will you do
so soon I let me know what he says. We all unite in
a kind remembrance to you.
Affectionately Yours
Prof. S. F. B. Morse

Mered Vail Eng
Dear Sir Yours of the 3d inst
was received this morning and in answer thereto
I have to say, the whole amount of money paid
the Patentees on the Canada line is some $4500

paid Prof Morse and with the exception of the
$300 paid you the balance has been received by
Mr Smith

500 mile; the cost of construction is about 75 to
80 doll$ per mile. As soon as we can get a settle-
ment with the Montreal Company we shall be
ready to close the business with the Patentees. This
will not likely be before May next
Yours with respect
Wells & Co

clear up my account and I must say he
does not take that interest in affording me

stand my account – I hope you reach

tainty – I wish I could take a ride with them
this fine day. My best regards to Mrs Morris
Yours now as ever
Alfred Bail

Have you indeed succeeded in realizing true pecuniary advantage from the Telegraph? I am glad to be disappointed. You cannot need my suggestions that your attention must be strongly turned to two points—the securing the wires against the attacks of parties interested in intercepting information; and the importance of securing accurate and authentic information through them. Charles Frederick Johnson Esq
Dear Sir: My absence for the week past
attending a court at Norwich has prevented an earlier answer to the questions proposed by you for my consideration and opinion. The first question is as follows; "Can the claim for the use of the motive power of magnetism when developed &c. as the means of operating a printing mechanism which may be used to imprint signals upon paper or to produce sounds for telegraphic communications be sustained in this general form; or would his claim be limited to his (Morse's) method of applying this power for this purpose. In connection with this question you refer to the fact that Steinhil in Germany in 1838 applied this motive power to imprint signals upon paper & to produce sounds. His method of operating was described in a public work published in London in 1839 - Sa Surgeons annual of Electricity, and also Vail's work.
Second Question. Supposing Mr. Moris claim is to be limited to his method of imprinting signals or producing sounds what is regarded as his method? The suggestion he is entitled to hold his specific machinery with which he operates to make dots and lines - do he also entitled to - or can he hold the system of signs consisting of dots and lines for this purpose Steinhil recorded by means of dots alone upon two lines and vary by combination of marks upon different divisions of the Paper. Then would it be an infringement of Mr. Moris rights to make signs consisting of dots and lines by the motive power of magnetism in a manner different from his? For example by the deflection of the needle applied to press the paper against a stationary pen or pencil or by demagnetizing a permanent magnet by passing the current around it.
2
Third Question Would it be an infringement of (Mr. Morse claims
Rights) to apply the motive power of magnetism to dry balls
of different colors and thus forming signs for telegraphic
communication? The sign thus formed being retained any length
of time for the convenience of reading off.
These questions arise upon the Patent granted
to S. F. B. Morse, dated 15th June 1840. At the commencement
of his specification Mr. Morse declares that he has invented
a new and useful apparatus & system of transmitting intelligence
between distant points by means of Electric magnets which
put in Motion Machinery for producing sounds, or signs and
recording the signs upon paper or other suitable material. I
see nothing further in the Specification bearing on the questions
proposed till we come to the claim which is as follows: "Having
this fully described my invention, I wish it to be understood
that I do not claim the use of galvanic current or currents of
electricity for the purpose of telegraphic communication, but
what I especially claim as my invention and improvement is
making use of the motive power of magnetism when developed by
the action of such current or currents as a means of operating
or giving motion to machinery which may be used to imprint
signs upon paper or other suitable material or to produce
sounds in any desired manner for the purpose of telegraphic
communication. The only ways in which the galvanic current
has heretofore been proposed to be used is by decomposition
and the action or exercise of the deflective force of a current
upon a magnetized bar or needle and the decompositions
and deflections thus produced were the subject of no
section and had no power of recording the communication.
I therefore characterize my invention as the first recording or
printing Telegraph by means of Electric Magnetism. There
are various known modes of producing motions by Electric
magnetism, but none of these have hitherto been applied to
3. Quentin Quinlans should it be an infringement to use this motive power of magnetism to make dots alone
to indicate letters by their position upon the paper.
actuate or give motion to printing or recording machinery which
is the chief point of my invention and improvement. I also
claim the system of signs consisting of dots and lines substantially
as herein set forth and illustrated in combination with the key
for recording signals. I also claim the types and rule in combi-
nation with the signal levers as herein described for the
purpose of connecting and breaking the circuit of galvanism
and electricity. I also claim in combination with an electric
magnet used for telegraphic purposes the time of clock work
actuated by a weight or spring for the purpose of carrying the
material on which the record is to be made under the registering
pin substantially in the manner specified. I also claim the
combination of two or more circuits of galvanism or electricity
generated by independent batteries by means of electromagnets
as above described."
This claim is not expressed in as concise and clear
language as it might have been. If I understand the claim
it is the application of the Power of Magnetism to move ma-
chinery to make sounds and record signs for telegraphic com-
munications. This is the idea expressed in a few words. The
making use of the power of magnetism when developed is
making use of the magnetic power and nothing more. The means
of operating or giving Motion to Machinery is briefly applying the Power
of Magnetism to that purpose. In the next sentence of this claim
the Patentee states that the only way in which the galvanic
current has heretofore been professed to be used is by decompositio
and the action or exercise of the deflective force of a current
upon a magnetized bar or needle; and he states that the decompo-
sitions and deflections thus produced were the subject of inspection
and had no power of recording any communication. This sentence
was intended to show that the Patentee did not claim the
Galvanic current for all and every purpose; and in all its
properties; for he states how its deflective force had been used
before and immediately adds "I therefore characterize my Telegraph
as the first recording or printing Telegraph by means of Electromagnetism"
3
4
The Patentee further states, that there are various known
modes of producing motion by Electro-Magnetism; but none
of them, he says, have been before applied to give motion to
printing or recording machinery; which he says is the chief
point of my invention -- what then is this claim, when extracted from the words in which it is expressed? It appears to me that this is a claim to the exclusive right of the use of the Electro-Magnetic Power to move machinery of all kinds and descriptions for recording sounds or signs for telegraphic communication -- The Patentee does not claim to be the inventor of the machinery used to record the sounds and signs but in this item of his claim, simply the application of the Power of Propulsion to the use of which he expects an ever-increasing demand. The Examiner stated that the only requisite of his claim is that he should state that the exclusive right of the application of the Electro-Magnetic power to move machinery. Can a man by a Patent gain an exclusive right to use for a particular purpose the expansive power of Steam? Can a man gain the exclusive Right to the use of any of the laws of Nature for any particular purpose however new? Such as the attraction of gravitation Repulsion -- The expansive power of Steam! The incompressibility of water or any of the elements of nature, The machinery by which any of these principles are used may be patented; but the principles themselves can not be the subject of a Patent -- they must always remain open and free for every one to experiment upon. Otherwise the Patent Law instead of promoting the improvement of the useful art would be a bar to such improvements. The Authorities fully sustain these positions. Philips on Patents chap. 7. § 1. p. 95 de Judson on Patents, 4th Edition & cases there cited Bentham & Waller Bull Dr. Henry Blood 485 by Spence C. J. "It is the better opinion that the Patent for the application of a principle must be as bad as one for the principle itself." Also in Kings Whaler End Barns 350 By Affolot C. J. "But no
merely philosophical or abstract principle can answer the
word manufacture" By the English Patent Law nothing can be
the subject of a patent that can not be brought under the head
of some new manufacture and our law in principle is the same.
It seems to me that if Mr Morse can patent the exclusive use of
the motive power of Electro magnetism to move machinery to
record sounds or signs for telegraphic communications, Fulton
might well have patented the propelling power of steam when
used to drive certain Machinery to propel a boat thru the
water. Now can the two cases be distinguished? Had Mr
Morse been advised to put his invention in the construction
of the Machinery to be operated upon by the Electromagnetical
power and taken a patent for that, it would have
been for quite a different thing. But it may be said that
the word application as used in Mr Morser's Patent is to have
the same meaning as the word combination; and that the Patent
is to be used as though the Patent had claimed the use
of his Machinery in Combination with Electro Magnetism. To
which I reply that had the patent been so expressed it would
have read very differently from what it does now. Application
and Combination are words of very different meaning.
Combination cannot here be used in place of application without
changing very materially the meaning of the Patent.
But suppose we substitute the word combination. The Patent
would be for a Combination of elements and not for the
elements themselves. These elements would be certain specific
items of Machinery in Combination with Electro magnetism.
If any of the essential parts of this Machinery should be
changed then the identity of the Combination would be destroyed
and the patent would not cover the new Combination. Patents
336 Party & Supplies. My answer, therefore to the first question
proposed, is that the claim for the use of the motive power of
magnetism as made is in form too general and cannot
in my judgment be sustained. In this answer I allow Mr Morse
to be the first and original inventor of all he claims; and that it was
not in print in any Public work before he applied for his
first patent and this is granting probably more than can be
proved. From the short time I have had to examine books on
this subject it appears to me that Mr. Morse's plan excepting
the idea of making on paper his signs was in print and published
in the periodicals of the day a year or two before the date of his
first patent and some time before he made application for
a patent. His Plan for marking by a system of signs on paper
or some other substance appears to be found in no publication;
and as the evidence now stands before me, I should think that
would be considered as his invention.
The second question proposed involves this considera-
tion of the remaining claims made in this patent, which
are combinations merely and without any claim to be the in-
ventor of any of the elements of these combinations. These combinations
claimed are the combinations of the system of dots and
lines with the telegraph for recording signals. 2d. The combination
of the types and rule with the signal lever as therein described
3. The combination of the clock work with an Electro magnet
for Telegraphic purposes as stated. 4th. The combination of two
or more circuits of Galvanism or electricity generated by independent
batteries by means of electro-magnets as above described, making
in the whole form, combinations which are separately claimed as
independent combinations. This second question proposed really
involves several questions; First what is to be regarded as
Mr. Morse's method of imprinting or recording signals? In
answer I remark that I suppose it is the method or plan by
him specified consisting of a system of dots and lines made by
pens or pencils on paper when moved by the Galvanic power
and if the claim is good, any other combination
this is claimed as a combination, substantially the same, moved
by the same power and for the same purpose, would be an infringement of the patent. The most essential parts of the combination are the dots and lines. If another combination should be
used, when dots only were used or when lines only were used, it
would in my judgment according to the case of Smith v. Fols Pugge
to 16 Peters 336, be an infringement of Mr. Morse's Patent.
But those changes in the combination must not be mere
formal change without any real or improved improvement.
They must be something more than the mere substituting one
Mechanical Equivalent for another, showing that the change
is really colorable, and for the purpose of avoiding the patent.
Mr Mordes claim is for a system of dots and lines, any use of
dots and lines not coming within the Mr Mordes system of
dots and lines would not be an infringement of his patent.
Whether a specific case would be an infringement cannot be
determined till the case is stated.
Second. Would it be an infringement of Mr Mordes Patent to
make signs consisting of dots and lines by the action power of
magnetism different from his namely by the deflective power of
magnetism applied to press the paper by the use of the needle
or by de-magnetizing a permanent magnet? To answer to
this inquiry I remark that if Mr Mordes first claim is
good, he holds the the exclusive right to the power of Electro
magnetism, whether deflective or negative when applied to
machinery to mark or imprint a system of dots and lines
on paper or other like substance for telegraphic purposes.
But I have herebefore said I thought that claim too broad, I
do not think that either of the instances supposed of deflective
or negative power, as stated, would be or could be,
awarding to the settled principles of Law considered
as an infringement of Mr Mordes Patent, but as there is
not any adjudicated case within my knowledge
directly in point, and as this is a point not very clear
to my own mind I speak with some hesitation, not
knowing exactly how it might strike the mind of a Judge.
Mr Mordes does not claim simply the system of dots and
lines in combination with the Electro magnetic power, or with
the use of that power, but he claims the system of dots and
lines, that is, I suppose, the system specified of dots and
lines substantially as stated in combination with the Telegraph
for sending signals. It is not easy to state exactly
7
what the Patentee here means to claim when he says he claims the system of dots and lines in combination with the recording telegraph. What are the elements of this combination? It is not dots and lines in combination but the system that is the Patentee's system of dots and lines in combination with the magnetic telegraph, that is with all the other apparatus of the Telegraph for recording signals. Did the Patentee mean to claim such a combination as this and what is his language seems to import? If so any essential change in any part of the Machinery would break the combination. This part of the patentee's claim is so broad and so general that it is impossible to come to any certain definite result concerning it. I should think it pretty clear that the use of dots alone or lines alone however varied in their positions to indicate ideas or degrees of ideas would be no infringement of this patent. The answer to the third question has already been to a great extent given. But I will add I have no doubt in answering this question in the negative as I have before remarked the use of dots alone or of lines alone, would be no infringement of this patent.
In answer to the fourth question; I remark that in any judgment the use of Balls as the question supposes, would be no violation of Mr. Morse's patent. The Balls can in no sense be considered as a system of digits consisting of dots and lines although they may be used to accomplish the same object. It is not the object that is patented but the means of accomplishing that object. The means may be various; and if always and means of accomplishing the object are patented, then the door is closed against all future improvement by any one else. In conclusion I remark that on some points I have not arrived at that clearness and certainty which is always desirable and most satisfactory.
The subject of this patent is almost entirely new and we are in the out precedents in point. We are obliged to apply as far as applicable the general principles of the Patent law. Your friend with much esteem

Dear Sir,
I am very much obliged to you for your answer, that I have little or nothing to say
to reply to your letter, as I am so much occupied in making my life comfortable that I
have little time to spend in correspondence. I prefer to have the papers

to petitions, and prefer that others should feel the facts
into form. In regard to my life as a Sainte, Dunbar
History of the Arts of Design, Vol. 2. page 308, gives a
true account. So also does the writer (M. Trickman
Philadelphia) in his notice in Godey's Lady's book published
in Philadelphia Nov. 1846.
In relation to my invention of the Telegraph, the facts are
mostly given in Mr. Vails larger work entitled the American Electric
Magnetic Telegraph published in Philadelphia by Lea & Blanchard.
Mr. Vail was only Assistant Superintendent of the Government line, and
I gave him the many of the materials for his work. I am at present
collecting some more minute details of the invention, at the request
of the Committee of the NY Historical Society, who wish to preserve
them, and who will report on the subject. When finished
I will take pleasure in forwarding you a copy.
In the mean time please subscribe to your work, and say to whom I shall pay
even the subscription money.
Very Respectfully
Yours

Dear Sir,
Yours of the 15 inst. is hand, contents
received.
I see, by the reading of it, that you think
all is fair, as to Mr. Wood's leaving. -- Allow me to
give you one or two Extracts from his two notes which I
received at two different times on Sunday, without
going much into detail, as my time is very much
overfilled at present.
Mr. Wood says "I have this morning received
"by mail wholly unsought for and unexpectedly to
"myself a proposition for my services" so much for
that fact.
In a personal Conversation with Mr. Wood he
gave me to understand that he had been a constant
protest going on for some weeks; he parted, and
after I had gone to bed, about 11 p.m. a Boy brought
a letter from Mr. Wood, which I got up and read,
in which amongst other things, he remarks "L.O.W.
"named 3 persons as suitors and one of them name
"we mine" (Wood).
Now I would ask any man of common sense
why L.O.W have done this, unless it is because they
have more interest in Canada than in the New York
A & Puff Telegraph; and here allow me to remark,
100431
that L&W have a large amount of money to disburse
in Canada, and my opinion is that this is to be a
part of Wood's employment, and to watch the Canadian,
whilst at the same time he is to be teaching some young
men to become operators.
You say we ought to raise operator's wages; I
intend, to give more than any other line
in the United States, and more than any of them
ever got for their services, and if we had not
snakes in the grass they would all be satisfied.
I employed Mr. Backus at Syracuse and paid
him at the rate of $500 a year, with the understanding
that if all was right he was to be paid $100 more
at the end of the year. He was highly recommended
by a gentleman in New York; I found him unfit to
do as he had undertaken to do, sufficient his place
with a young man for little over half the salary,
and he is one of the best we have on the line.
You call my attention to what was said at
one of our meetings about high salaries; allow me
to remind you of some part of the conversation,
which was that "Girl or Women" could manage
most of our Side Office.
I have never failed to encourage responsible
young men to qualify themselves for the duties of the
office, and after trying many of them I find they
they are not all of them competent to do what they have
undertaken, any more than all who try can make
first rate artist or invent something to compare with
the one invention, of which you, at an all other
men have created the proof.
There is no new idea in what is said about
our liability; it was submitted to the Board, and
has been to good counsel, and there is no difference
of opinion; the Company is liable, and so it was
stated at the meeting; and one of the biggest
mistakes was made by Mr. Barton at Buffalo, last
July, after being in daily practice for almost a
year, and he called one of our best operators in
all this firm, what I have no doubt you knew
before, that all men kind are liable to
mistake.
The error at Rome was committed by a
man who had been under the tutelage of Mr. Wood,
and influenced of Mr. Curtis; it was merely in the
spelling of a word, but sufficient to make as
liable and as shall have to pay about $500.
Now if you can tell me how to make better
perfect, then I can tell you how to prevent mistake
in Telegraphing.
I shall send Mr. Barton to New York to take
charge of that Office; I cannot consent to put
100432
any man into the irresponsible situation of running clerk
without personal interview and becoming fully
satisfied that he is just what he ought to be.
I see no necessity for calling the Board together
because Mr. Wood is going away, this is all a
matter of detail which a Board of Directors cannot
change the position of; -- I think, as you do, that
it is not worth making a fuss about Mr. Wood
leaving. I regret it, but do not feel as if
the line would have to be discontinued in conse-
=quence of it. -- I wish you not to understand
me as being opposed to calling a meeting of
the Board, but I see nothing for them to do
that will warrant the expense.
The question of liability is well settled,
if we never pay for doing business, which is
what the line is built for.
I return one of your Sense for your endorsement
authorizing me to transfer 12 shares of it to A Hindlely
as the balance is for yourself it is not necessary on the
others, or for any more than 12 shares.
I am very respectfully your

Boston, Mar. 19. 1847.
Dear Sir:
This morning returned from Washington, where I hoped to see you respecting the subject of my former letter. And on my arrival here, I found your kind favor of the 13th arresting me. You will have already seen by an article of mine in the Boston Daily Advertiser sent you, which I asked the correspondence. At the time I wrote you, however, I supposed the article of it had been published. I regret would I could not have seen you, as I have many things to say, which I cannot do on paper.
But to be brief, Dr Jackson has set up claims to an alluvial discovery that of Dr W.F. G. Morton, having pledged himself not to do so, as you will see by my paper in the Advertiser.
From Mr. Eddy, a friend of mine in this city, I hear that while he was in Paris in 1839, Dr J. favored him the very paper in which he lays claim to your invention; then paper was directed to M. Eilie de Grammont & by him copied before the French Acad. Mr E. being present at M.
Beaumont. In like manner, in a discovery made by Dr Morton to which Dr J. has not better claim, he wrote this same Eilie de Grammont in November last, in which case he claims to be the sole discoverer! Now this is a mania of the doctor's must be met promptly. Even under that of your
call the matter one letter. Not so, however, for Dr. J.
still claims all the merit of your invention. For more
than a year I have worried in the family of a poor
medical friend of Dr. J's family; & while there
often has been stated that he had been unjustly
dealt with. On some, & I confess regretted as
I am, on my own, these statements, no official re-
putation had thus wrought. And it was not
the last winter in Washington that I observed
it a true state of the case.
Had such being the facts -- I have to request
that you will allow me to publish your letter to
me. I have shown it to Mr. Eddy, father of
the gentleman before mentioned, & one of the most respectable citizens. He saw all Jackson's letters to your
& yours to him & particularly the last which I
asked him what he should do with, & when
Mr. Eddy advised him to hide it in his book-
case! His opinion is that it will do you no harm & even
causes much good to publish it in a paper I am
trusting up. If, also, you will allow some truly private
to occupy the entire correspondence, I will cheerfully
refuse the appeal. They can next Summer, I will
transmit such documents to Europe & particu-
larly to France, or will have a tendency to
give out only ourselves but you also. But what
ever be your decision, I shall in no wise draw
you into the controversy. Were you to visit Boston
room I shall be happy to know it, as I am so
your. My office is 19 Tremont Row: or should
I be in N.Y. again I beg to be allowed to introduce
myself.
You will, I trust, give the liberty I am
taking & believe me
Respectfully
Yours etc
Edw. Warren

I do not wish my letter to you published. I wish not to
attack Dr Jackson nor even defend myself in public from his
private attacks. If in any of his publications he
attacks the constitutionality of his claim, which I consider settled by default, then it will be time, and proper for me to notice
it him. If on looking over back numbers of the Boston
Post any one should notice that my challenge was never
never answered by Jackson, and the question should be
put to him in a public journal why did he never reply? He
wanted either to be silent or to reopen the subject. If he
chose to be silent, you might make your own inference
and the public would also make the same. If he wanted
to reopen the subject, he would have to admit that he
had prepared to defend himself, but I wish not to be instrumental in reopening a controversy
which is settled in the public mind. The most charitable construction of the Dr's conduct, as a monomania induced by excessive vanity.
I enclose you an article in the Herald of this morning from Paris, which shows the matter of the Lethon in a new and to you certainly an interesting light. Please send me any publications respecting the Dr which may appear. If you visit New York I shall be happy to see you.

Washington March 24th 1847
Friend Mosse your Tel despatch of the 19th &
letter of 16th both reached me late last week while
at Richmond and consequently I could not reply to
them until my return. he have had an anxious time
of it at Richmond, and a glorious result. we have defeated a man who is feared not esteemed by the people
of Virginia. and he is Monroe Robinson, a bosom
friend of Mr H Rogers. Mr Robinson object was
to pass a bill through the Va Legislature compelling
us to sell the Tel. right to him for a 1/4 proportion or
the deny us the right to put it up any where East
of the Blue Ridge. The injustice of such an act
became palpable to the members of the Legislature
through papers drawn up & printed by Mr Kendall
with which the members were furnished, The consequence
was, our substitute, for the Robinson bill (which had
already passed the house) was agreed to by the Senate
13 to 7 and the House by 44 to 27. Thus
has justice triumphed over despotism & inveterate
meanness. The line will be immediately built.
I have this morning taken a hasty inspection of
Thurber's machine, and see no advantage which
we may derive from its application to the Telegraph.
To work it would require some fixtures similar to
letter printing Telegraphs and a great deal of other
machinery. I at present think it is of no account.
Enclosed you will find a Check on the Bank
of America, New York, signed Corcoran & Riggs
for two hundred & ten dollars. — drawn in your

stated as due to him in a previous letter to you
& which I think is 1137. — To Mr Kent the

New York March 29th 1847
Dear Sidney, We received your letter by the Hibernia which
would have been more grateful had they been longer. We are glad to hear of
your continued health, but should have been more rejoiced to know that
you were soon coming home, for we want to see you, we get no clue
to the time we may expect you. Yet you need not return on account
of the suffering of any interest, I believe all is going on well in Ohio
on matters. I suppose that Emoryphy would take a less fine and more
magetic position if you were here, as Mr. Thomson when I see him says,
"I wish your brother would come back again soon," not that there is any
particular difficulty, but that he needs some one to lean upon.--
Your letter on Slavery has been published not only in Ohio but in the
Journal of Commerce, and has made a very favorable impression. I think
you have shut them mouths completely in Britain, and it appears to me
that they are much quieter since, or I hear less of their doings. Richard
& I are having an edition published in pamphlet form for distribution. I
hope you will continue to write on this and kindred subjects with your strong
pen. Have you ever thought of collecting while you are in England the
materials for writing the life of Tomwell? His life should be written by
an American, not by a Churchman of the English monarchical stamp.
He has never had justice done to him, for he has been in the hands of his
enemies. You could do him justice.--
I am now in New York permanently; that is, I have no longer any official
connection with Washington, and am thinking of flying down here
so soon as I can get my Telegraphic matters into such a state as to warrant
it, but my patience is still much tried, although the enterprise looks well,
and is prospering, yet somehow I do not command the cast, as some business
men would, if they were in the same situation. The property is doubtless
good, and is increasing, but I cannot use it, as I could the money, for while
every body seems to think I have the wealth of John Jacob, the only sum
100450
I have actually realized in my first dividend on one line about 1400 dollars, and
with this I cannot purchase a house, but time will perhaps enable me to do so,
if it is well that I should have one. I think if probable that Jacob Big-
elow Esq. of Washington will soon visit England for the purpose of getting a
special act granting me a Patent. My case is certainly a strong one, for there
was not a shadow of justice in refusing my application in 1838. Every system
that I have seen in hand ofad Europe is fair inferior to mine, and totally
different. I give you a list of lines of my Telegraph in North America;
for the Canadas are all alive in regard to it, and they are putting up
mine in preference to any other.

This is exclusive of many branch lines and several contracts
for new lines under consideration. I have had some pretty threat-
ning obstacles, but they as yet are summer clouds, which seem to be
6302
disputing through the smiles of our Heavenly Father. — Houses affair I
think is dead, I believe it has been held up by speculators to drive a better
bargain with me, thinking to scan me, but they don't find me so easily fixed
on it. — In Virginia I had to oppose a most bigoted narrow liberal clique
in a Rail road company, who had the address to get a bill through the House
of Delegates, giving them actually the monopoly of Telegraphs, and attempting
to hallo before they were out of the woods, Mckindell went post haste to Richmond,
met the bill and its supporters before the Committee of the Senate, and after
a sharp contest, procured its rejection in the Senate and the adoption by a vote of 13 to 7 of a substitute granting me right
of way and corporate powers, which bill after violent opposition in the House
was finally passed 44 to 27. So a mean intrigue was defeated
most dismally, and I came off triumphant.
I had also as you know some difficulties at the West; there
is a prospect of a fair adjustment of them.
We are at this moment in a good deal of excitement
with the rumours from the Rio Grande. Santa Anna
has an overwhelming force of some 30,000 men, while
Taylor has but about 6,000, yet it is evident that
Santa Anna has been discomfited. Authentic accounts may
arrive to give you details by this Steamer. If they arrive after

gale, worthy of March, has temporarily stopped the Telegraphs

of the Telegraph, yet he may have more claim to the Lethon
for ought that I know. I have some reputation, his vanity will
tempt him to open the controversy again on the Telegraph, if

he does, I think I shall shut him up effectually —
