History of proceedings in England to procure a
Patent for my Telegraph.
In the Spring of 1838 I left the United
States and arrived in London in June, for the purpose
of obtaining letters Patent for my Electro-magnetic
Telegraph system which had been publicly exhibited in the
New York City University on the Spring, and before
the Congress of the United States at Washington, on the
Summer of the year 1837-1838
I had learned before leaving the United States
that Professor Wheatstone and Mr Cooke of London had
obtained letters Patent in England for a "magnetic needle
Telegraph", based on the name implies on the deflection
of the Needle. Their Telegraph at that time required
Six Conductors between the two points of intercommuni-
cation, for a single instrument at each of the two points.
Their mode of indicating signs was by deflecting
Three needles in various ways, so as to
point to the required letter upon a diamond shaped
dial plate. It was necessary that the signal should
be observed at the instant, or it was lost, and vanished
forever.
I applied for letters Patent for my mode of giving
intelligence at a distance by electricity, differing in
all respects from Messrs Wheatstone and Cooke's mode,
having nothing in common on the whole system,
but the use of Electricity on Metallic Conductors, for
which use no one could obtain an exclusive privilege,
since this had been used for nearly One hundred Years.
My system was based on the attractive power of the
Electro-Magnet, or magnetic power by Electricity, and
applied to impart permanent signs at a distance.
I made no use of the magnetic needle, I required
but one Conductor between the two points, or any
number of intermediate points of intercommunication.
I used paper, moved by clock machinery, upon
which I caused the lever moved by the magnet to
imprint the letters and words of any required despatch,
having also invented and adapted a new and
peculiar Alphabetic Character for that purpose, a
conventional Alphabet easily recognised, and easily
made and read by the operator
It is obvious at once from a simple statement of
these facts that the system of Messrs. Wheatstone and
Cooke, and my system were wholly unlike each other.
As I have just observed, there was nothing in common
in the two systems, but the use of electricity upon
metallic conductors, for which no one could obtain
an exclusive privilege.
The various steps required by law, were taken by me
to procure a patent for my mode, and the fees were
paid at the Clerks Office June 22nd, and at Home
Department June 25th 1838*, and I had reached that
part of the process which required the sanction of the
Attorney General. At this point I met the opposition of
Messrs Cooke and Wheatstone, and also of a Mr. Darcy,
and a hearing was ordered before the Attorney General
at John Campbell's on July 12th 1838. I attended at the
Attorney General's residence on the morning of that
day, carrying with me my Telegraphic apparatus for
the purpose of explaining to him the difference between
my system and those of my opponents. But contrary
to my expectations the similarity or dissimilarity
of my mode of operation was not considered by
the Attorney General. He neither examined my
instrument, which I had brought for that purpose,
nor did he ask any question bearing upon it.

was met by the declaration that my method had been
published, and in proof of a copy of the (London) Mechanics
Magazine, No 757 for February 10th 1838, was produced;
and I was told that in consequence I could not
proceed
At this summary decision I was certainly
surprised, being conscious that there had been no
such publication of my method as the law required
to invalidate a patent, and even if there had been,
I ventured to hint to the Attorney General, that, if I
was rightly informed on regard to the British law,
it was the province of a jury, and not of the Attorney
General to decide that point. I conceived that if
I had offered a substantially different mode of
doing the same thing, this was sufficient to entitle
me to a patent. But if after having obtained a patent,
my opponents could choose before a Court and Jury,
that my mode had been previously published, then
it was for that Court and Jury to declare my Patent
void. I therefore considered myself unjustly
dealt with by the Attorney General, who it appeared
to me, had stepped out of the sphere of his duties,
assuming the power of a Court and Jury, to
forbid me to proceed.
Unwilling to submit to such manifest injustice
without attempting to correct what might possibly
be mere misapprehensions, I immediately on my
return to my lodgings, with the assistance of a
legal friend, drew up and sent the following letter
to the Attorney General
In consequence of my request for this letter I was
allowed a second hearing. I attended accordingly
but as my charge, the Attorney General had not
himself even read the letter. He carelessly took it up,
and turned over the leaves without reading it, and then
asked me if I had not taken measures for a patent in
my own country, and upon my reply, on the affirmative,
he remarked that "America was a large country, and I
ought to be satisfied with a patent there" I replied
that, with all due deference, I did not consider that
as a point submitted for the Hon. Attorney General's
decision. That the question submitted was, whether
there were any legal obstacles on the way of my obtain-
ing Letters Patent for my Telegraph on England?
He observed he considered my invention as having
been published, and that he must therefore forbid
me to proceed.
Francis O.J. Smith Esq. was present at the latter part
of this interview and can testify that the ground of
refusal taken by the Attorney General was "that my
invention had been published"
Thus forbidden to proceed by an authority from
which there was no appeal, as I learned, but to
Parliament, and this at great cost of time and money
I immediately left England for France, where I found no
difficulty in securing a Patent. My invention there not only
in conversation with the Earl of Lincoln just previous to the
assembling of the company at his house on March 1839, to
witness the operation of my Telegraph, he observed to me
that he had just met Sir John Campbell and had
invited him to be present, but he declined. At the
same time asked Sir John on what ground he had refused
my application for a Patent. In which Sir John gave the
same reason, to wit "that my invention had been published"
the noble Earl may perfectly recollect this circumstance

attracted the regards of the distinguished squavans of
Paris but in a marked degree the admiration of many
of the English nobility and gentry at that time on
the French Capitol. So several of these while explaining
the operation of my Telegraphic system, related
the history of my treatment by the English Attorney
General. The celebrated Earl of Elgin took a deep interest
in the matter, and was intent on my obtaining a special
act of Parliament to secure to me my just rights as
the inventor of the Electro-Magnetic Telegraph. He repeatedly visited me, bringing with him many of his
distinguished friends, and among them on one occasion
the noble Earl of Lincoln, since, one of her Majesty's
Privy Council. The Hon. Henry Drummond also
interested himself for me, and through his kindness
and Lord Elgin's, I received letters of introduction to
Lord Brougham, and the Marquis of Northampton,
the President of the Royal Society, and several
other distinguished persons in England, the Earl
of Lincoln pledged me special kindness. On taking
leave of me in Paris he gave me his card, and requesting to bring my Telegraphic instruments, with me
to London, pressed me to give him the earliest
notice of my arrival in London.
I must here say that for weeks I had been engaged
in negotiations with the Russian Consul in
State the Baron Alexandre de Meyerdorff, arranging
measures for putting the Telegraph in operation in
Russia. The terms of a contract had been mutually
agreed upon, and all was concluded but the signature
of the Emperor to legalize it. In order to take advantage
of the ensuing summer season for my operations in
Russia, I determined to proceed immediately to the
United States to make some necessary preparations
for the enterprise, and thus awaiting for the formal com-
pletion of the contract papers, being led to conclude that
the signature of the Emperor was there, being a matter
of mere form. Under these circumstances I left Paris
on the 13th March 1839, and arrived in London on the
15th of the same month. The next day I sent my card
to the Earl of Lincoln, and my letter and card to the
Marquis of Northampton, and in two or three hours re-
ceived a visit from both. By Lord Lincoln I was at
once invited to send my telegrams to his house in
Park Lane, and on the 19th of March, suppressed its
operation to Members of both Houses of Parliament, of
the Royal Society and Lords of the Admiralty. From
the circumstances mentioned, my time in London
was necessarily short, my passage having been secured
on the Great Western to sail on the 23rd of March.
Although solicited to remain awhile in London both
by the Earl of Lincoln, and the Hon. Henry Drummond,
with a view to obtaining a special Act of Parliament
for a patent, I was compelled by the circumstances of
the case to defer till some more favorable opportunity,
on my expected return to England, any attempt
of the kind. The Emperor of Russia, however, refused
to ratify the contract made with me by his Counsellor
of State, and my design of returning to Europe was
frustrated, and I have not to this hour had the
means to prosecute this enterprise to a result in
England. All my exertions were needed to establish
my Telegraphic system on my own country.
Time has shown conclusively the essential difference
of my Telegraphic system from those of my opponents.
Time has also shown that my system was not published
in England as alleged by the Attorney General, for to
this day, no Professor Wheatstone in England has published any
thing that does not show that as yet it is perfectly mis-
understood. Professor Wheatstone has even pronounced
lately (within 3 Years) in Paris my system useless and
unpracticable, as I learn from the highest authority.
Surely after the results before the world of the practical
operation of my system for so long a time, and over 1,000
miles of country, furnishing daily to the press, in cities
5 or 600 miles apart, whole columns of news simultaneously,
Prof. Wheatstone could not have understood my system,
and thus risk his reputation as a man of science, by
such a hasty opinion, if my system had been published
in England, Prof. Wheatstones sagacity would certainly
have comprehended the superior simplicity and efficiency
of my system, and he never would have hazarded
such a remark, I consider this fact conclusive on
the point of publication. But as this was the ground,
the sole ground, of not allowing me to proceed in taking
out letters Patent, I will not leave the settlement of
the question to inference, I will state that there was
not even the shadow of a publication, in the legal
sense of the term. The sole document upon which my
opponents rested to prove a publication is that referred
to in the Mechanics Magazine page 332. Let any one
read that paper and see whether my invention is
there anywhere described. It is there stated that
"five years before (in 1832) I had invented an Electro
Telegraph", that the distinguishing features of my
Telegraph are "a Register which permanently records
in characters easily legible, the fullest communication,
and the use of but one wire as a conductor". It will
scarcely be believed, and yet it is true, that this is
all the description or publication of my invention at
that time made in England, or known to my opponents,
and yet on such a pretended publication as this, was
I forbidden to proceed to obtain letters Patent
At that time I had with me the drawing of an
instrument called the Receiving-Magnet, connected
with a Relay or local Battery, a provision against the
reduction of the magnetic power of the main Battery, as
the length of the conductors increased. By means of a
fresh Battery and magnet, any quantity of power could
be obtained, according to the size of the said magnet
or local Battery. This instrument has never to my knowledge
been described up to this date (1847) in any public
Journal either in America or in Europe. The receiving
magnet was a provision devised for an exigency,
which, at that time, I conceived only to be possible,
but was to be used and would be effectual in case
such exigency occurred. This instrument was unnecessary
in any of the then attempted systems of Electric Telegraphs,
nor was it then necessary, nor is it now necessary, in
the exhibition of my main instrument called the
Register, which is confined to a few miles of conductors.
But it is essential to the efficiency of my whole system
when a circuit connects two points at a great distance
from each other. Although devised sometime in the
year 1835 while contemplating this possible exigency
it was not necessary to bring it into use till the first
line of conductors for my Telegraph was prepared.
This exigency occurred in trying the power of the
Register magnet through a circuit of one hundred
and sixty miles of wire, the magnetism even from
a powerful Battery was found to be too feeble for my
purpose, but the application of the Receiving magnet
100457
which had been prepared in reserve, and was at hand
effectually and immediately relieved the difficulty.
Now, under what pretence of justice was I denied
a Patent for this instrument? It was secured to me in
France but a few weeks after the rejection of my applica-
tion in England. No description of the receiving
magnet can be found in any book published in
England or America, or, so far as I have learned in
any other country up to this hour!
This is the statement of my case. The
refusal to grant me a Patent was at that time
very disastrous. It was, especially discouraging to
have made a long voyage across the Atlantic in
vain, incurring great expense and loss of time,
which in their consequences produced years of
delay on the prosecution of my enterprise.
Is it asking or expecting too much, that a
special Act of Parliament should be granted me
to protect me in rights so long and so wrongfully
withheld from me?
(Signed) Samuel F.B. Morse

Mr Rogers was here last week and could not
help asking him why he passed such a singular
course of conduct toward the Magnetic Telegraph
interest. He evinced considerable equivocation and
at last stated that you had cast him overboard and
had not acted in his behalf as he thought you should
I asked him what he had expected you to do -- this he
could not answer satisfactorily -- to that it appeared
to me that he had conjured up his imagination to think
that he had a right to expect you would run yourself
to the death to get him a handsome place and salary
on some of the Telegraph lines -- I told him you did
not and would not interest yourself for any one
more than what was in accordance with the wishes
of the various Directors of Telegraph Companies —
I told him, still more that instead of Prof Morses
mind being prejudiced against him, that when
your first suspicions were excited in reference to
his conduct you received it with reluctance and
when those suspicions were confirmed, that you
were grieved and perplexed — He admitted that
he had spoken unadvisedly, and stated that your
plan was superior to any other — I told him that
in conversation with me personally and through
the telegraph with me and other his language
and general tenor of his letter was meant
as to induce the belief that he was not what
he formerly was and professed to be our friend —
I did not spare him — and told him that if
he chose to pursue such an equivocal course
that I wish him to consider my confidence in
him at an end. That he might go and do
what he could to the injury of our common potent
interests all I wished was to know how we were
to consider each other hereafter. At times he
was brave — Then again cut down and at
last said, He thought as much of you and me
as ever, and said "we will fall out" —
I fear that his expectation have been raised very
high, and although by the expedience of a little
patience might have been realized, But he could
not wait, and therefore he has been trying all
acts of ways to obtain something, be it from
our friend or foe to our interest -- He has not
yet accepted the office of Chief Operator at
Baltimore at $600 -- and constant service --
Louis is out of employment. Mr Kendall promised
him a place at Baltimore if Mr Rogers does not
accept, -- I hope Louis may have some situation,
But his mother seemed to express no thanks for

Your friend as ever

I have nothing else to do, than to find them places, & not

entirely benevolent Friend & Father. It is this reflection
alone, that takes out the sting who in gratitude has planted
in the heart, & wages on in the state of him who makes
his sun to shine on the unjust as well as the Just, &
the rain to fall on the thankful as well as the
unthankful.

its incipient stage.
In thus handing over to you the Line, I deem it
proper that I should establish a basis upon which
it is satisfactory condition, wherever it may be deemed advisable to construct, and will cheerfully consent to submit it from your Board or
from your Superintendent, for their review if it
satisfactory, in every reasonable manner, as my
earlier communications with the whole line to the
Mississippi and the Lakes, proved every thing of
it, in the best practicable order for the business of
the public and the interests of all concerned. Indeed, it is
my intention to make complete survey of the line,
I have now engaged a suitable party to proceed immediately with some of the improvements.
It of all things, I desire to impress upon the
line useful and profitable, and in any way that my
assistance can be rendered beneficial, assistance will
be on every hand given to you for that purpose.
In every arrangement made by myself and
my associates for extending Lines of Telegraph between the Atlantic and Lakes, and Mississippi, you
may rest assured that the most seriouscious care
will be taken to consult and defend the interests of all
who have invested in the line, the Atlantic and
Ohio section, which I now deliver over to your
possession; and I confidently assert that the results
upon this line will more simply realize all reasonable
attentions of those who will invest in the new
enterprise.
With my hearty thanks for the confidence and
friendship I have experienced from the stockholders
generally, during the construction of this important
section of Telegraph, I conclude with the assurance
that if with your permission I may use
their courtesy by always endeavoring to render to
this line every aid in my power, while carrying out
the construction of the new and important Atlantic Telegraph System towards the Lakes and the Mississippi, and in other sections of the United States.
Respectfully yours,
HENRY O'RIELLY.

New York May 8th 1847
Dear Sidney,
We received your letter by the Caladenia, with its enclosure cut from the Morning Chronicle respecting the Telegraph of Houses.
Was there ever such aubfaced fraud! I wait to see your note to the Editor exposing it. There is not a mile of Houses Telegraph in operation or likely to be in operation in this country! Messrs. Livingston & Roberts are constructing the Telegraph under my Patent and immediately commenced with me the 8th letter in minute work performed by my Telegraph instruments. House has only exhibited his machine in a room. It is a perfect humbug. He could not put it in operation even if he were allowed by me liberty to try. He cannot use it in a room without using parts which are covered by my Patent. The whole article which has been palmed off on the Chronicle is doubtless from inherent marks which I see in it. It is the product of the same hand that wrote the ephemeral abortive proofs in this country, for example, in both are the constant repetition of the word "treating" as though it were impossible for any mistake to be committed by his machine. The object of these innocent expedited means is undoubtedly to deceive the English if they can into a belief that it is Houses system which is so successful here in order that they may get some return for their expenses on their abortive breathing which could not be obtained here. I shall expose them here and perhaps send you a copy in the papers by this opportunity. It is an attempt at deliberate fraud, and as such the English public ought to be put on their guard against it.
While on this subject I must also say that on Monday next May 10th the Northumberland Packet sails for England, and in her will go a party consisting of Mr. Wilson Robertson, his son, and a son of my former friend Chaplin of Native American territory. They have had my instruments made, and are going to try their fortune with them in Europe. Their first attempt was to do entirely without me or consulting with me, and the elder Robertson was an enemy of Houses, and while there was any prospect of doing anything with that humbug, upballed it against me, thinking it a faction with me and got my sanction. This I have not given, for Smith refuses to have any thing to do with him, and I have totally learned that he is wholly devoid of principle, his only object being to get money, any how, and any where. I regret this much because the son is an adept at the manipulation of my system, understands it perfectly, and young Chaplin as far as I can learn is also a clever young man, and I should be glad to support the latter if I could consistently. As it is I cannot, I know not how to act in regard to the matter. I only wish it known, say to Mr Bancroft and others that they do not go out with my sanction, but it is in consequence of the character of the elder Robertson rather than of the other two. You may at your discretion say this to Mr. Bancroft from me -- My agent in London to procure for me a special act of Parliament will be Jacob Bigelow, Esq. of Washington, who either by himself or by Mr Greenough Patent Agent of Washington will proceed to England very shortly for the purpose. Any attempt to use my name by any others, or my instruments, is without my sanction and wholly unauthorized by me.
May 13th. Since writing the previous part of my letter I have no
thought is best to write to all our Govt Agents in the principal
countries of Europe, advising them of the state of things in regard
to Robinson's operations; this I do in self defence lest it be supposed
that any trick of his, or unfair dealing has my sanction, and
so bring discredit on the country and on me.
Telegraph matters on the large scale are doing well. The
line to New Orleans is in rapid progress of construction. The money
receivabty is subscribed, and the Contractor thinks it will be in operation
by the time Congress comes together. If it is ready by the 1st of January
next it will be well. Our Western line difficulties are not yet settled.
But on the extended scale of our operations, that line is comparatively
insignificant, and we can wait our time. My system is in rapid
progress in Canada, although with trifling benefit pecuniarily to myself, still
the becoming the adoption of my system is something. A line from Toronto
to Louisville already connects with our Buffalo line. Another from Toronto to
Montreal is building, all the posts being on the ground (400 miles). From
Montreal to Quebec 150 miles contracted for; from Quebec to Halifax 700 miles
fully contracted for. On these I (or rather the Patents) get 10 p.c. on cost of construction.
I think there will be a dividend on the Southern line, as well as Buffalo
Madigan line in July or August. Our receipts (gross) on each of the two lines
W.Y.-Buffalo & N.Y.- Wash. are about $800,000 p'c week and on the increase.
I have made arrangements with F.A.J.S. to exchange all my interest in Boston
line for an equal amount of his interest on the Southern line, so as to withdraw
all responsibility from me on Boston line, which is in debt and will not work out
probably under a year. Smith is Smith's pet, and so likely to be, but I have become
used to him, and you would be surprised to find how well oil & water of
year to year. There must be Croesus, and the aim should be rather to bear them
peacefully, graciously, and patiently than to have them removed.
May 14th. I must close my letter today for fear of accidents in time to
tomorrow's mail, I shall send you Saturday's Herald which will
contain a notice of the scandalous piece in the Lon. Morning Chronicle which
you sent me, and also the statistics of my Telegraph lines by which
you will see that there are in actual operation, contracted for, and in
process of construction not less than 9,300 miles of my Telegraph
in the U.S. States and Canada.
You will see by the papers the unparalleled success of our gallant
army in Mexico, the Battle of Buena Vista, Vera Cruz, Cerro Gordo,
probably (Sierra Gorda), and Scott still advancing on Mexico. I hope you
have seen enough of English mistification to believe all that is said
against your country, by her Tory spirits. When all the circumstances
of this war are well weighed, you will not join the cry, against the Adminis-
tration, of those who for mere party ends lose sight of their country's greater interests.
In forming an opinion of the action of the Government, one consideration seems to
be wholly lost sight of by the unpopulated cartilages of the Tribune & Express
school. They forget that our Government is from its very nature, susceptible
of information known only to itself. Every resolution of inquiry, in Congress,
is based on this fact, and supposes that government has secret information, of the designs
of other governments, which to divulge before the world would be detrimental to the public
interests." If the more than hints given out of foreign influence of European powers with
our Concerns are well considered, our difficulties with Mexico are deeper than can be
futilely shorn by Government authority. The hints and not hints merely of putting a
French or Spanish Monarch on the Mexican Throne, which for years have been false,
will furnish some clue to what I mean. The inordinate hostility of the Mexican
Hierarchy, who cannot but foresee the downfall of their power if we should come
into the door to all our offers of negotiation for peace, though that
war has marred all their designs, and how far these designs are
connected with the Leopold operations in our own country, may be judged of
if not positively known. Dreadful as war is, and to be deprecated when it can
possibly be avoided, I am not a non-resistant under all circumstances, but
believe that the Armies of a nation are to be looked upon in the light of a Sheriff's
Armed Process which at the bidding of the nation must execute the law, responsible
only to God for its right use or abuse. Our Government has allowed the
Sheriff to execute the law on Mexico, and in view of the above considerations
my leanings are with the Government of my country; I do not hold to the false
axiom "My Country Right or Wrong," but my Country is the right, and I believe her.
If your position in regard to the slavery question had been maintained here
in the formation of our branch of Evangelical Alliance, the Alliance
would probably have been popular and large, but as it is I consider it
a perfect failure. I signed my name previous to the discussion of the
basis; I have serious thoughts of with drawing it, with my reasons if
thought necessary. Your ground is the only true ground here, and
the disgust and indifference manifested, will show these rabid Ab-
olitionists that they have mistaken their ground. I have no idea of
taking a false step, out of courtesy to the narrow-minded, illiberal prejudices
of British Tories.
We are all well, except little Willy, the youngest of Richards'
who is teething, we hope nothing serious though he is feeble. I had
letter from Susan a few days ago, I think she may be here in
July, witte little Charley whom she lays is growing finely, and is truly
a smart boy. I long to be in a condition to have them return and
live with me. Perhaps it is nearer, than they imagine, that is

Y. Olb Servt

Dear More
Your Telegraph despatch reached
here at 11h 40 AM and I hentaled some time
to send the Book since I have here not over
10 copies left while I presume Mr Kent has 15
or 20. Supposing however that he may have with
them I concluded to send you the half dozen by
express. I will send them to Adams & Co
This afternoon.
Mr Haley passed through here a few
days since and I had a brief talk with
him about getting Register for Southern Line
I proposed to him to give me their construction
principally in order to give me an opportunity
to spend the summer north with my family
who are going on in a few days. I should
like very much if the arrangement could
be made; -- But I cannot do it, unless per
mitted to make such instrument as I can
warrant and that will be perfect and also
at most prices as will pay me for the time
spent in superintending them
Mr Kendall is again back. The line
south works very well so far but is not
long enough to show a closer foot if it has
any which I have no doubt it has
In haste I remain yours now
and ever
Alfred Vail

Washington, May 14th 1847
at Mills. Warren's
My dear Sir,
Your Chief Engineer in Holland,
Conrad, asks me to furnish him, if possible, with
the signs used for communication by the
Electro Magnetic Telegraphs in the United States.
My personal acquaintance with you enables
me to make an appeal to your kindness in
favour of my countryman. Would you be so
kind to point out to me the best way I can
take to get what could satisfy to his affectionate
demands? Please accept in advance my
thanks to any answer to this question, which
I hope will not cause any great trouble to you.
With sentiments of respect,
S. F. P. More, Brig. Genl.

Dear Morse
I had hope on Mr Kendall's
return he could tell me something of the progress
you had made with your printing Telegraph
But all he knew about it was that you were
working at something - I hope to see you very
soon and see it work. Of Mr Houses I hear
nothing and guess a little that he can find no
one advance money for such visionary operations.
To me and no doubt to it will be a cause
of grief to learn a little incident which has occurred
with in a few days passed - You are
well aware that the Corner Stone of the Smithsonian
Institute was laid a few days since - On the
announcement that such would be the case, I
addressed a note to B B French Esq inquiring of him
If a copy of my work on the American Telegraph could
would be worth depositing, To which he replied
"certainly" and stated that Mr Mill Atchelert was
the proper person to address upon that subject - I
accordingly addressed Mr Mills a note upon the
subject and he at once called upon me &
stated it was both novel and very desirable to
deposit a copy describing an invention so
purely american and so astonishing and beneficial
in its results. & he cheerfully and thankfully
received at my hands a copy without any
inscription in it of any kind and told me
it should be deposited provided there was room
for it. I informed it would accordingly have
been done yesterday I met Mr Mill as asked
him what disposition had been made of the
Book - when to my surprise he informed me
that Mr Leaton and others were very desirous
of having it deposited and contended that it
should, But that Prof Henry refused
to let it be put with the other articles to be
deposited and consequently it is thrown out -
I requested Mr Mill to state to Prof Henry
that I considered myself injured and stated
to him also that I had long since heard
of charges which Prof Henry had made &
had also written to him - To which he had
made no reply and yet was still making
charges against me which was beneath an
honorable man - I shall now take pains
to have an understanding with him - I
will vindicate myself let what will
happen - His course is insulting and
he chooses to consider me beneath his
notice, inasmuch as he pays no regard
to my letter requesting to know wherein I
have offended -
I am sorry to learn that he has the prospect
of troubles at the very onset of his career
as Sec. He has bid defiance to a portion
of the Building Committee, who want to
spend money rather faster than is agreeable
to Prof H. who says he will not certify
to Contractors bills without which they are void.
The other portion of Building Committee wear
vengence and say they will make it too
hot for him in Washington. So far has
it gone that Prof Henry was not even
invited by Building Committee to be present
at the laying of the Corner Stone and came
on and witnessed it, in the capacity of a
"looper" as one of his friends terms it. He
has therefore the prospect of a long war
during which, I venture to say, electricity
will not be thought of.
I have nothing new to say. Fred's
line is working well and doing well.
I remain Your esteemed
friend & etc
Wfred Vail

Dear Sir:
I promised when I left
you in New York I would write
in regard to the interview I proposed
having with, & at the solicitation of
Mr Robinson. Before doing so I hope
you will not suppose, as Mr Kendall
has done heretofore, that I am aiding
others in driving the owners of your
Patent into terms; but view it as you
would have done before Mr Kendall was
your Agent, that is, fair and
candid statement of facts made by
a man of honour.
Mr Robinson is decided upon
the construction of a line of telegraph
on the Richle Rail Road, and also
its extension to Washington city, I
think he has interested other parties
in the matter, and I have no doubt
but he will be able to extend it
beyond those places. The article in
the Rail Road Journal seems to
be a popular subject with many
persons interested in Rail Roads
and expressed pretty generally
their views.
Indeed so sanguine and desirous
are Mr Robinson and his friends,
that I have been solicited to aid
them in their designs of making
telegraphs a part of the Rail road
system. I have informed these gentle
men of the claim your invention en
tilles you to, but find they will em
bark in any other, that seems likely
to succeed without infringing on your
rights.
I have been informed that if I
omit this opportunity of placing my
self at the head of this movement,
which I can realize a handsome income,
that they will invite others who
are ready & willing to embark in
it. This puts me in an un
enviable position, as I dislike do
ing any thing contrary to the interest
of my friends, but at the same
time some of these very friends
advise me to be governed by
my own interest without regard
to theirs. To be candid, it is the
opinion of these gentlemen, that
I do not occupy the position in
regard to your Telegraph, that I
am entitled to, and that I have
nothing to expect from any party
where Mr. K is the counsellor,
and that they are ready to sustain
me in any efforts I may make
for the support of my family.
I have told Mr Robinson and
others, to show me as good a
telegraph as yours; and on more
favorable terms; and not interfering with yours, and that they
I might be disposed to join in
their enterprise, if I could not
do any better. These remarks
are not made to influence you
in any way, but merely to apprise
you that I am the one I ought
to support my family
after
feet of
expectancies.
Very respectfully
Your obedient Servt
Henry J Rogers

Dear Sir
Yours of 17th I have received. I am not
surprized at the proceeding of Mr. Robinson, after
his attempts to annoy and embarrass the operation
of the Telegraph, in Richmond last winter, but
I have no belief in his ability, much as he may
vault it, to seriously, to injure , the public convenience,
add to his own selfishness, and not the public good,
I regret to see, seems to be his impelling motive.
I have too much confidence in an enlightened
public opinion especially in the chivalrous
South and among the principle-loving Virginians,
to believe for a moment that his schemes
will succeed, even should he temporarily deceive

New York May 28th 1847.
Dear Sidney, I am obliged to write you a more hurried
letter than I intended, as I am unexpectedly called to
Washington this afternoon on business, and so shall not
have time to write the last days of the month and I
cannot let our first splendid steamer the Washington
on the 1st June go without taking you a letter. I expect you will receive
this on the 12th of June, let me know how near I am to
the mark. We are looking with a good deal of gratification
to the latter part of July in the hope of seeing you all safe
home again. Susan and Edward Hope will also be here
with dear little Charley, and then we shall have such a lot
of little cousins, the whole city will not be able to contain us.
My Telegraph affairs present both prosperous and adverse
phases. South & North they look well, but in the Valley
and West from Phila I have dishonest men to deal with,
and shall have much trouble to put things right. But I
am not distressed about it. The same wise hand still
directs and I know all will work well if the heart
only reposes on him with unshaken faith.
I shall have a somewhat romantic story to tell
you when you arrive respecting my foreign Telegraph
prospects, at present I must be mum. It may result
in advantage to me. I am still writing you from the
old office in your buildings, where you left me, and
I lodge in Bank St. at Richards. When you return
100524
I hope to make some arrangements for a home, if that
be best. Perhaps we may get a house together in some
sort, so as to be at much together as possible. There are
not many years before us at best, and therefore, I want
we should make the best use of time that is left, there
is a great deal to do yet to benefit the world, and with
God's help I will yet do more than I have done.
Of your affairs here, Richard and Mcminson keep
you advised. They seem prosperous.
The papers will tell you of the aspect of our political
relations; I presume you will feel much of the same disgust
that I feel at the party distortion of all representations
of our national measures. It seems to be a principle with
some to represent every thing done or proposed by the
opposite party as of course wrong, and they according denounced
and attribute all sorts of bad motives to their opponents.
It has never shown itself more strongly than in the conduct
of such preachers as the "Express," which I think pure excellence
at the head of the unprincipled, Mexico I have ever considered
as the aggressor in the present war, and our government as
compelled to proceed against her as they have done. And now
what else can we do, after repeated offers to negotiate, which
offers are as repeatedly treated with disdain, what else can
be done but to hold the Country in Subjection until the
people have got rid of their military and clerical
tyrants, and have learned to govern themselves? Looking upon
the affair in the light of a Providential interference, it strikes
me that the time had fully come when that rotten hierarchy
and corrupt and feeble political system, was to be over
thrown. I doubt, however, if there was at first the least
idea of such a result by those who ordered the order;
yet this seems to be the process that is going on, and in all
probability will be consummated.
But I must abruptly stop as I find it is
time for me to be going down to the boat.
Give much love to Catherine Elizabeth the Chicks
and believe me as ever Your Aff. brother
S.D. Morse.
Sidney E. Morse, Esq

My dear sir
Mr. Miller has been about two days not returned last
week. He has been disappointed in obtaining the money when
he expected it but in still desiring to complete the arrangement
I suggested to him that I would quite agree to an interim
but in it would assume your purpose to secure a bond
of his matters or a bond & mortgage for the money portion
of the arrangement stating that if it could be paid in
payment if you agreed to provide that it was
permissible for myself to take it, although I could not
undertake to say that it would be agreeable.
Mr Miller would like to give a bond & mortgage
which should be approved by you, for $3500 (the cash
portion) and complete the real estate portion of the bargain
$3500- and to retain the privilege of completing the
remainder $3000 by paying 1/2 cash & then making
next spring - if he can obtain satisfactory agreement to make
An addition to the first part of the proposition the
question is whether an approved bond & mortgage could
be equal to cash to you. If so there would be
no objection to you concluding the arrangement as
Miller can furnish such a security - I think unless
you might realize the money on such a security arrangement
difficultly though of this you must judge - I do not
think that it would be prudent on your part to agree to
the latter part of the proposition since much as Miller would
take no risk and it would all be on your side -
after consideration please write me with your views
and think me as to your wishes -- which I am alluded
to with the greatest pleasure.
Since your return you have undoubtedly read
the intelligence of the accident -- Deming of Dear Fancy
She died in the bed blind sustained by light regimen
faith and fully prepared to meet the dread change
from life to eternity -- It is a severe affliction to
us all yet our loss is eminently her great gain --
Reason perfectly consigns them to the great
last -- We looked to you during the tumult.
Yours Truly
W. Walker

Dear Sir:
Your favor of 15th is now before me,
and I am not surprised to hear of the opposi-
tion made to my being brought forwards as
a candidate for the Presidency of the Magnetic
Telegraph Company, after the misrepresentation,
and false accusations made when I was not
present to refute them. In justice to myself
and friends I am determined to have these
things cleared up. I am now satisfied why
so little estimate was placed upon the service
I was willingly rendering others, when their
aim has been to lessen me in the estimation
of my fellow citizens who hold stock in the
M. Telegraph Co. I have however the proud
satisfaction of knowing, that instead of depreciating me, it has had the contrary effect
of elevating, and strengthening their confidence
in me. Let my chance be but upon the
hazard of a die, and I will risk it, and
neither yielding to Mr. Trimble nor Mr Fuller,
the last gentleman, I feel assured by letters
from Capt. Black will support me, and Mr
Trimble has already admitted that I am
competent to fill the Station. I learn today
there is another "Richmond in the field" in the
person of Mr. Hart. It may turn out that
you will have to take part in this election, and
I should you do so, probably you may be inclined
to think more favorable of me than others, and
find it to your interest to support me, as
that alone influences mankind nowadays.
As for the numerous "Richmonds in the field"
they will find it plain as good a right to
wear the "Red Rose" as any of them, and that
I am as able to defend it.
You say when "I suggested your name
they rejected the idea as preposterous", this of
course might be expected from those who have
their own ends to accomplish, I presume the
parties who are against the Patents are
the persons who think it so preposterous in
me to endeavour to elevate myself to the
Presidency. I am convinced of one thing, that
it is more difficult to obtain a preposterous
prominent position, than it is to fill it.
I now occupy a prominent position
before the public and the government, as any
of my opponents, and having gained it
solely by my own perseverance and indi-
stry, it is not likely that I will yield
it to mortal man. I know this much,
that prominent men throughout the
Country are willing, and are assisting me

his improvements there to, not heretofore sold or placed
under contract, within the following Territory, land
in all of the territory of the United States bounded
in the south by the route extending from Baltimore
to St. Louis via Wheeling, Columbus, Cincinnati

Wheeling- Also all within the boundaries of New York
and the New England States- And that said Kendall,
in like manner, shall have full and exclusive power
for and in behalf of the first party, to bargain sell
and convey any and all other rights for the construction
and use of said Moses Patent not heretofore sold or
placed under contract within all the remaining territory
of the several States of the Union now existing-
And the sales of each party within his said territory,
made pursuant to the provision of these presents shall
be satisfied and concurred in by the other party, from
time to time, as may be required, and by due and legal
process of Conveyance.
The manner of disposing of
such lines and realising Cash therefor shall be such as
the respective parties shall in their discretion think best
for the Common Interest; and each shall account to the
other for monies realised by him, whether from absolute
sales or participation in the profit of Construction
or in any other mode out of the Common property;
provided that neither shall be bound to account to
the other for more than fifty dollars per mile on any
route as the aggregate belonging to the owners of the
Patents.
The terms of payment for sales made shall
be twenty five per cent of the amount that shall
be raised and paid as the first installment for
Construction purposes on the route sold, and a like
proportion of every succeeding installment until the
aggregate shall have been paid. And no Contract or
sale shall be made to extend the omission of the first
payment longer than nine months from the date of the Contract,
or to delay any succeeding installment beyond the period of sixty
days from the prior one; and no Conveyance of the Patents
for any route shall be made until the entire
price of purchase has been paid.
Neither of said parties
shall charge for his personal services or expenses of
himself or of any agent he may employ, nor incur
any liability in behalf of the other party in effecting
such sales beyond the requisite terms of Conveyance.

Your letters of the 31st of July & 15th of June have been forwarded

Cathleen with the children Elizabeth & Mary, and myself in the Sir Robert
Reid on Sunday the 13th ult. as informed you in my last. I trust they will

I received Mr. Munson's letter and am glad to hear that he intends
writing me by every steamer, and giving the particulars of the Congregational
operations. I must am utterly at a loss to know how I stand with the Hopkins
story book dollars & have been expended since my left America, & I am
anxious to know how much of this I am entitled to draw upon the
Harper's. Mr. Munson says that the Elizabeth City letters are now all expired
& wishes to know whether they shall be finished & if any one. By all means, let

to America in purpose of making arrangements with Mr Tracy to superintend
the work. I am to expect from Hermitage & I cannot do it. I cannot
do not know what he has done, or left under & but wish that the work may come out

and whatever else is necessary for the may be prepared by Mr Tracy. Let
this name, if he is willing, be omitted as the Author. If he is not willing,
let him prepare such brief preface or advertisement as will be suitable. In
the utter ignorance of the manner in which the work has been executed I cannot

From the National Intelligence of the 7th inst.
The Electric Telegraph, which now, in its combination with magnetism, is in such
successful operation, was previously supposed to be chemical, and 20 years ago. The following extract
from the American Mechanics Magazine for 1825 shows the weakness of the best authority, and
the necessity of depending upon experiments for success.
"Motion of the Electric Fluid. It has long been received as a fact that an electrical discharge
was capable of being transmitted through a very considerable distance, say two or three miles,
instantaneously, and without any considerable diminution of its intensity. M. Barlow,
however, by employing wires of various lengths up to 840 feet, and measuring the energy
of the actual action by a reflection produced in a magnetic needle, has found that
the intensity diminishes very rapidly and very nearly in the inverse ratio of the distance;
hence the idea of constructing electric telegraphs is quite chemical. * over.
Mr. H. Edelton. Permit me to add to the above interesting statement a fact worthy of
notice publication as a just tribute to a distinguished philosopher. The discovery of Prof.
Henry, as related by him in Silliman's Journal for 1831 was the first to prove the
feasibility of telegraphing by galvanic power; and while to him belongs the credit
of inventing the first electric magnetic engine, and the suggestion of its applicability
as a mechanical agent, to him also we are indebted for a most valuable discovery
without which the electric magnetic telegraph would have remained utterly
impracticable in the present state of our knowledge. It will not be worth while
at this time to attempt to explain its particular features, but suppose it to say that Prof.
Henry discovered a mode by which magnets of considerable power could be made
through very great lengths of wire, or at a great distance; and seeing at once the practical value of this discovery he remarked that "this" (that is the above discovery)
is directly applicable to M. W. Barlow's project of forming an electric magnetic telegraph.
The English journals have given the credit of this discovery to M. Wheatstone, but Henry's discovery
was announced many years before Wheatstone's telegraph involved this principle of action, or
was even conceived. I think I speak without national prejudice when I say that in the
scale of merit the balance is decidedly in favor of our own countrymen Henry & Morse
in developing this invention, of such vast utility & interest.
O. S. P.

My dear Friend
I have just returned from Hamburg
to which place I accompanied my dear wife and child
on their way to the United States, and where they left
me for London nearly three weeks since
It was in lieu of remain sometime after their
departure, in consequence of repeated attacks of the fever
and ague, with which complaint I have suffered since
last fall, at rather frequent interval, proving that Sweden
needs an accommodation in itself, as well as peace and quiet
as any nation of the United States, and that the climate
of our Western State, are found all over the world, even
in latitudes as high as this.
It would be quite a surprise to the
mother of those who assume that their and our relations
exclusive, to certain conditions and situations, like to be
that I brought the seed of the discord with me from
my former residence, for it happens in fact, that
almost every other person in Stockholm, has been similarly
affected, during the past six months.
While at Hamburg, I made the acquaintance
of Messrs. William & C. B. Robinson, who give encouragement
to introduce your excellent telegraph into Germany, and
I think with Considerable prospect of success. For the purpose
of aiding its future introduction into Sweden, I give the
form of a short telegraphic despatch, in my Majesty's
king of Sweden and Norway, which I have this day,
sent for his inspection, addressing the following communication
to the Minister of Their Affairs.

The undersigned has the honor to incline to Her

and also the Alphabet employed in the transmission
of communication.
The specimen mentioned was executed at the
understated by the American Telegraph, located at Hamburg
for the purpose of superseding the construction of
telegraphic lines, should occasion offer, from that city
to Berlin, Bremen and other places -- with a report that
it might be transmitted to His Majesty the King of Sweden
and Norway, both as a testimonial of respect, and an
evidence of the results, accomplished by an invention which
may, in truth, save to his Excellency, Anchalated time and
distance.
The undersigned embraces, on occasion to
mention, that there are now more than 300 miles, in
the United States, for which the power of this Telegraph
are in hourly operation. Fifteen hundred miles more
now under contract, will it is understood be finished
during the present year, and there is no doubt that before
long Boston and New Orleans, situated almost at
extreme points of the Union, will be brought by telegraphic
communication within a few moments of each other.
The passage of the Electric fluid, between points
however distant, is almost instantaneous, and the only
relation of the Telegraph in use with which the idea of time
can be properly connected, is the short period employed
in mailing down repeated intelligence at one end of a line
and receiving the same at the other. It is computed by
Prof. Hamady, and the gentlemen of his Scientific department
that a single moment would be sufficient for the passage
of the Electric current many times around the circumference
of the Earth.
The Telegraph in question, was invented by Prof.
S. A. B. Eldridge, a distinguished Citizen of the United States,
who it is well ascertained has the first to arrange and
apply, an apparatus, actually producing results, which the
eng. division, were regarded as almost impracticable.
The instrument employed in the formation
of the telegraphic letters, is simple in its parts, cheap, and
easy of construction, lasting down the character required
with equal facility, by night or day, and wholly unaffected
by any atmospheric changes or cold climates. The cost of Establishing telegraphic Communications, as proved by experience
in the United States, may be estimated at from 1500 to 2000
for each English mile, the pressure amount depending on the
nature of the ground, over which the insulated line is to be
constructed -- the readiness of a cup to materials, and the
price of labor.

To the Descendants of the early Planters of New England by the name of Morse, and
Morss, and Mors, and Mosse:—
GENTS,—
The subject of Genealogy is awakening
much attention; and whoever considers its
civil, scientific and moral bearings, must acknowledge its importance. Though the laws
of the older states have required the registration
of births, marriages, &c., yet these have been
neglected, and claims to enormous estates, it is
believed, have consequently been lost by the
rightful heirs. Nor is it certain that similar
forfeitures may not hereafter occur from the
same cause; for so long as the law of entailments shall continue in the mother country,
none can foresee what contingencies may
occur to furnish other claims which some one
of our name or race may recover, not perhaps through his descent from a Morse, but through
some one of his 20 or 40 grandmothers, who
might have been from as many distinct families.*
The evils of interalliances between those of
common blood are deplored; nor can these be prevented without complete family Registers,
which often show, in the parents, more common blood than is inherited by first cousins;
and sometimes nearly as much where the parties contemplating marriage have no suspicion of the slightest degree of relationship. Surely,
if the rising generations can be induced to give half the attention to pedigree bestowed by gentlemen of the Turf, imbeciles will diminish,
almshouses and asylums be less crowded, and posterity become more like the occupants of
New England in her days of physical energy and moral glory. Until this is done, the short-
ening of the average period of life, the effects of
different geological formations, climates, callings
and modes of living, will be rarely perceived,
and few know where and by what means the
greatest prosperity is to be sought.
But these are light reasons compared with
the moral. To presuming man, it is good to inquire where are the Fathers? and see how
soon his name also must be starred; and to a refined, pious mind, it is sweet to hold communion with departed worth; delightful to remember our sainted ancestors, to whom we are so indebted, and with whom we shall so soon be united.
God has formed man capable of happiness in his present and future state, and made
that course of life, which brings most enjoyment here, and fits him for immortal happiness, to be the very course to secure him a posthumous character, honorable and useful to his descendants; and he has endowed him with a principle of curiosity to know the history of those through whom he has derived his being, that he may learn and treasure it up, for his own admonition, warning and encouragement in well-doing. To preserve, then, the history of our ancestors, is to obey a law of our nature and second the benevolent design of the Creator. Most men seem to be conscious of the obligation; for those who have kept it, manifest a pleasure and feeling of self-approbation; while of such as have not, some are mortified, and blame parents or guardians; others are taking or resolved to take pains to recover their lost history; others less cultivated and scrupulous, as if ashamed of their ignorance and wishing to keep up appearances, or afraid of an humble origin, resort to fabulous traditions, without thinking that the absurdity and falsehood can and will be detected. But the Morses can be rescued from such temptations, and their origin proved to have been respectable, and in the best sense noble; and most of the name can be furnished, either with a complete Family Register of 7, 8 and 9 generations, or the means of rendering it so.
* In tracing the descent of a child of the 8th generation, I found, that while he inherited the name of one family he had on his father's side the blood of 20; and if he shall be found to have descended from as many through his mother, he can reckon 40 grandmothers. I also found him, through 2 of his grandmothers, heir in common with those prosecuting or preparing to prosecute claims in England, either of which, recovered and divided according to our laws, would relieve him from poverty. Such claims often rest on marriages solemnized hundreds of years ago.

With a view to the history of my Family, I,
30 years ago, began to examine and transcribe
ancient Records and MSS; and to write down
the reminiscences of the oldest persons of in-
telligence then living. As I progressed, it be-
came necessary to bring down the history of
all other families of similar but in reality of the
same name. Most who spell their names in
either of the above written forms, are the de-
scendants of 6 Puritans, whose birth and em-
barkation in England, I have ascertained.
These I have traced in their emigrations, settle-
ments and descendants from 1580 down to
1750, and in many instances, to 1847: and
have written biographical sketches of about 20
of their race. The names of 4,000 of their
descendants have been arranged in a Catalogue
with double indices, rendering it available in
tracing. The births, marriages, residences, and
deaths stand opposite the names. This I pro-
pose to publish at $2 per copy, so soon as suf-
ficient patronage can be obtained. The work
will be neatly bound, and entitled Memorial of
the Morses, and contain at least 250 pages, per-
haps 400. The names of all subscribers, with
their descent, if reported, will be added, with
blank leaves for continuing their genealogy.
The portraits of John Morse, commissary in
Philip's war; of Rev. Joseph M. of Derby,
Conn.; of Joseph M. of Nova Scotia, commis-
sary in the French war; of Ephraim M. of
New York, Captain in do.; of Doct. Samuel

of Boylston; of Doct. Isaac M. of Elisabeth-
town, N. J.; of Rev. John M. of Huntsville,
N. Y.; of Chancellor Kent of New York; of
Rev. Dr. Jedediah M. of Charlestown; of
James O. M., Esq., of Cherry Valley, N. Y., are

The portraits of Hon. Isaac E. M. of New Or-
leans; of Hon. Freeman H. M. of Bath, Me.;
of Abbot Lawrence, Esq., of Boston; of Prof.

Yours most respectfully,
ABNER MORSE.

Washington July 28th 1847
Prof. S. F. B. Morse
My Dear Sir
Mr. A. Reebe has sent me what
purports to be a copy of a letter from you
to him dated the 3d inst. in which you propose
the boundary arrangement of 10 per cent upon the cost with him in case
he will get up a company to build a line
of your telegraph in Texas. This he calls a
contract and from our refusal of a
connecting line from the Sabine to the Mississippe.
This proposal seems to be based on the assumption
that Texas is to be considered in relation to the
telegraph a foreign country. I do not understand
it to be so in point of fact. Upon the annexation
of a new state to the Union, I take it that the exclusive
rights of all patents are ipso facto extended
over its territory in the same manner and to
the same extent as they previously existed within
the former limits of the United States. If I am right
in this, Texas need not and should not be separated
from the rest of the Union in our telegraphic
operations. It may raise troublesome questions between
youself and corporations in the patents, besides
which (though I should make no difficulty about
it) I consider Texas as brought by annexation
within the scope of my contract with you as
well as of your patent.
It seems to me, therefore, the better way would be to
sell to Ohio and its associates the patent rights from
the Mississippi to any point named in Texas at an
agreed rate per mile. If your present to Texas is
of any avail (and I presume it is not) it would for-
tify either of these arrangements.
I shall promise nothing positively until I hear
from you on this subject.
I have nothing yet from Smith or Bass as to our
Western concerns
Sincerely
Your friend
Amos Kendall

29 July 1847
Dear Brother,
Speaking with Mr Davis, my brother-in law, he told
me quite how he would proceed, if he were in your case, as follows so far
as I can recollect: He would after examining the premises sufficiently
& ascertaining from the neighbors (such as Mr Hooker) the value of farms
in the vicinity request Mr D. to make you his lowest offer. Then
I say to him that if you have other places in view, I cannot decide at present;
that you will be that way in two or three weeks, till which time
you will have the proposition under consideration. When you come
at the end of that time, according to your price, if you find his price is exorbitant, tell him so;
& what you will give; and the result will probably be he will come
to your terms, or so nearly that you can close the bargain.
A transaction of such moment should not be done hurriedly,
at any disposition on the part of the seller to hurry it, I should construe
as a reason for declining to buy. I should ascertain how long it has been
for sale & if there are a have been any offers for it.
Mr Davis seems to think, as I believe Mr Cuming does, 100
100 acres is enough, & that the other 100 need not be stipulated for
conditionally. Yet I see no objection to such a clause.
As to stock, forming part of it, both Mr C. & Mr D. say
Be careful about buying. If you buy stock, you must buy proceeds
for the winter, during which time, you will have no use for your
stock. Second hand utterly, will be perhaps, of little worth to you.
A general consideration which influences me in the
choice of the region where I would settle is this: Whatever
we settle ourselves, obligations of a social & religious character
will be insisted upon us. Educated as we have been, these are
of a high order. Our children must enjoy as good institutions as
we have done. Our standard of religious habits & conduct must
be as high as in the best part of New England. Now it is easier
to reach these ends in N. England than elsewhere; and it is
proper to ask if we are called to make the sacrifice of going
elsewhere. I am willing to admit it, if it is made plain to
me (but this I must require) wherever we do settle, I hope
we shall go trusting in Divine strength to accomplish what
is reasonably to be expected of us.
I find all well & made happy as you may believe
by Elizabeth's return. We join in love to you all
Your affectionate brother
R. C. Morse

Poughkeepsie, North river July 30th 1847.
Dear Sidney: This is a day to be remembered, as you will learn in
the sequel. In the first place I congratulate you on the safe arrival of
your dear family, Catherine, Elizabeth, the children & nurse, all arrived
safely on Sunday last at 1 o'clock, I was in NewYork at the Astor house
with Susan little Charley, Mr. Overman & her son Henry, who had arrived
a few days before from the West Indies after a short and pleasant voyage
Richard with part of his family were at Saratoga, and the Telegraph told
him in a few minutes of the arrivals, Elizabeth accompanied her father
(who came down for her) to Saratoga, and I left Catherine and your children with
Dr. Livingston who were all to proceed for Williamsburg in a day or two and
where I suppose they now are. I was delighted to see Catherine and the children
looking so well; But & Lucence were pretty well browned, but looking very
hearty.— In my last I wrote you that I had been looking out for a farm in
this region, and gave you a diagram of a place which I fancied. Since then I
was informed of a place for sale South of this village 2 miles, on the banks of
the river, part of the old Livingston manor, and for superint. I have this day
concluded a bargain for it. There are about 100 acres. I pay for it $17,500.
I am almost afraid to tell you of its beauties and advantages. It is just such
a place as in England could not be purchased for double the number of pounds
sterling. Its "capabilities" as the landscape gardener would say, are unequalled. There
is every variety of surface, plain, hill, dale, glens, running streams, and fine fruit
and every variety of distant prospect, the Catskill mountains towards the South
and the Catskill towards the North, the Hudson with its variety of water craft,
Steamboats of all kinds, Sloops &c. constantly showing a varied scene.— I will not enlarge, I am congratulated by all in having made an
excellent purchase, and I find a most delightful neighborhood. Within a
few miles around, approaching by excellent roads, are Mr. Lenox, Gen. Talmadge,
Philip Van Rensselaer, &c. on one side; on the other Harry Livingston, Mr. Smith
Thomson, (judge Thomson's widow) and Sister to the first Mr. Arthur Breede, Mr.
Crosby, Mr. Boorman, Ve. Ie. -- The new railroad will run at the foot of the
ground (probably,) on the river and bring New York within 2 hours of us.
There is every facility for residence, good markets, churches, schools, take
it all in all I think it just the place for us all. If you should fancy
a spot on it for building, I can accomodate you; and Richard wants
20 acres reserved for him. Singular enough, this was the very spot where
Uncle Arthur found his wife; the trees are pointed out where he and
she used to ramble during their courtship. -- How are you going to
pay for it? I think I hear you ask. I pay of my own funds $10,000
cash, which is 6,500 of which I have in Bank, down on the stipings
of the papers, the rest remains on bond & mortgage, to be liquidated by
me at pleasure. I have $3,000 in real estate in Utica, guaranteed to yield
8 p. cent, and $23,000 Selby stock which Mr. Kendall says will yield
in a few months 12 p. cent. and by the first of Jan'y some $60,000 more
in Southern Selby stock which will be at par. Besides these there
are payments outright in cash for short lines, which are daily
called for, and in the month of Sept. I shall be in the receipt
of some $5 or $6,000, more, so that all things well weighed I
left safe in vesting the price of this estate in such a place, since
at worst I can get what I have agreed to pay for it, any moment,
for property is rising, and must rise on the river.
I wished much to have had you here to have your cool
judgement; but in your absence I have taken Mr. Burnings who
thinks I have a bargain. Your little son Newark lake came
at the moment I was deliberating. I was wishing you were here,
and the views you express in that letter of the kind of place that would
take your fancy, coincided so exactly with ours, that we conceived it
as a presidential intimation to go forward. I think I have not
moved in this matter without asking counsel of the great Counsellor,
and the way seems to have been made so plain, that I have no mis-
givings in the matter. In regard to the farm part for Charles Finley
I have wished their funds, in your hands, to rest for them in part pay-
ment, and for their sake I wish you were here at this time, as Charles
does not know exactly what the condition of his affairs is with you.
I think as you have the kedge anchors well fixed on this side, we
shall see you warping yourself up to this side of the Atlantic
soon. Do come soon, but come in a Steamer, a Burard Steam
so as not to be forever on the voyage.—
I forgot to say that Susan, and the Overmanns were
delighted with the place.
I have much more to say but must close to be in time
for the mail to Boston & the Steamer.—
In haste but affectionately as ever
Yr Brother
Sam Finer morden

Sharon Springs 6th September 1847
Dear Brother,
I received your letter of 29 ult. and the Telegraph
despatch announcing it, and was highly gratified with its contents.
I should have answered sooner, but have been occupied as I will proceed to state.
I came here with Sidney, leaving his mother & the younger children at Saratoga
to return to NYork this week, in company with Rev. Wm. Nathan Hanisly, Elizabeth
& Charlotte went ten days ago to Hadley, I am to go by way of Albany
& NYork. I remain here till Monday, 13th inst. when I must hasten home,
having been absent about 7 weeks. Sid's sore head is not easily cured. His general
health requires attention & I think of nothing less than taking him from
school for the present, hoping by care in his diet & exercise that he may
soon resume his studies.
In rejoice in your prosperity. I congratulate you on Hall, Mr Lind
Husman, Charles & Sidney & little Charles, & especially, that you are
all met under your own roof. I am above all pleased with your acknowledgment
of God's hand in all his dealings with you. If your readiness to bless them
whether be gives or takes away, You say well that you expect trials they will always
come, I be as great perhaps in prosperity as at any time. One source of
trial for you, indeed, will be the unwavering attempt to detract from your reputation
& your income. But you have already been not to be sensitive in these
maters. I believe your knowledge of human nature from too correct a source
to expect to gather grapes from thorns, a figs from thistles. As an offset to
this evil, you have the sympathy of the good who are glad of your success.
Dr. Bronson, Dr. Arthur Bronson & not a few others have strongly expressed their
selves to me.
I have much to say when we meet again, and Ianticipate
your reply.

late calling on you as early as practicable; but must first return

I cordially reciprocate your wish that Sidney himself may find a

Indeed I may as well say it, ever since Charles proposed buying a farm, I
have had a feeling of personal interest, & this is not so inaccouttable as it
might at first seem to be. For I have always hoped to live in the country,
& have seen fifty places that in themselves would suit me, indeed have
hardly seen the place that would not, in this fair creation. But how to
choose? Something was wanting to justify my preference of one place before
the rest. Hudson was Louis's native place, & this alone satisfied me
to live there as I did for 5 years, I had it been practicable, I could have
always lived there. Charles's settlement, even a better tie would satisfy
me to live in Potshessie, rather than elsewhere. But more when we
meet. You might think I was quite at leisure here I could entirely
communiqué any time; but if ever you should travel with a boy of 11
years old, you would find your mistake. Sid has no soul to commu-
nicate with but his father; unless I would see him restless &
unkindly, I must be devoted to all his wishes: play marbles, shoot
bore & armos, play checkers, & I expect soon to push pins. While
I am writing, he makes me impatient to be done, so that by stop-
ping now, I shall relieve him as well as you.
He joins me in love to you all.
Your affectionate brother
Richard Clapp

Dear Sidney,
A rainy day confines me to the house
this afternoon from Church, having been this morning.
So I improve the occasion I quiet to write you
from my new home, and home it seems truly as
far as we are permitted to call any place this side
heaven home. From the beginning of my search for
a place, till now, I have felt God directed; indeed,
if I had any misgivings that I had not the light of
his Countenance to direct and sustain, I should
not be happy with millions at my control. The
farm gains upon my affections at every day's residence,
I am now within 24 or 5 hours of New York; shall be
within 2 1/2 hours when the R.R. is completed. I am
within 15 minutes of the village. Am so far from
the road as to be away from Stragglers and dust
and yet conveniently near for all necessary pur-
poses. – The house has no pretensions to taste, but
is substantially built, and will answer well for a
point d'appui, and with the grounds can be prac-
tically improved as means and inclination dictate.
I have furnished it substantially and neatly, so that
I can see you and yours and give you a bed, when
you visit me which I hope will be before the winter
winter sets in. I am getting my domestic establishment
settled; trying my domestics; my farmer &c. shall
make some changes. I do not look for perfection in
them, nor do I expect to be free from trials. These I
shall undoubtedly have, but I look for grace to sur-
tain me in bearing any that may be affronted to me,
as yet my comforts & enjoyments far transcend all
discomforts. I am more and more persuaded God in-
tends to bless us here.
I have roughly calculated my expenses, and
my means to meet them, and allowing largely for
the former, and all reasonable uncertainties for
the latter, see my way clear.
I have some clouds and mutterings of thunder
in the horizon, (the necessary attendants I suppose
of a lightning project,) which I trust will give
no more of storm than will suffice, under him
who directs the elements, to clear the air and
make a severe and calm sunset. There are
attempts at infringement by the abettors of that
House humbug; but Smith has been put on their
trail, and he and they will fight it out.
Our line to Buffalo is doing well. At a meeting

Spedwell October 5th 1847
Friend More
I reached home the day following
my leave of you, found all my friends well. Father
& George made many enquiries respecting your elegant
seat on the Hudson, concerning which I satisfied them
as well as I was able. All are gratified to learn that
you have a home, a sweet home.
I enquired in New York concerning the port auger
and found that there were none to be had. But that
A Betten & Co 187 water St who keeps an agricultural
ware House has ordered a number of all sizes from the
Patentee 110 Stage of Baltimore and expects them every
day. Pieces $4.30. to $5.30 for auger 9 & 10 inches in diameter
with length of Shank 4 to 6 feet. You had better order
them from him and say how long you wish the
handle or Shank.
I could not learn anything about the traps. But
my Brother says that the plumbers make them of
lead and that the plumber in Park Roe near St
Spring's Church can make them for you. When I
go in again which will be the last of this week I
will make enquiries again and inform you.
I met Mr Cornell at New York St off who paid
me $150 dollars the 1st Instalment. He desired me to
give him permission to my signature thereto to allow
100625
him to alter the time of paying the instalments. But
I told him I could not do it myself but was perfectly
willing that Mr Kendall should Mr Smith had done
so he said. He wished it altered to coincide with the
time which had been advertised that the first
installment would become due from subscribers, as the
payments could not well be made to the hat-lees until
the money was paid in. I presume there will be no
difficulty in allowing him what he desires but I am not
familiar with the contract with him I could not consent
to do what I thought was Mr Kendall's duty.
Mr C told me that he learned that Hewes machine would
not register well and was constantly getting out of order
The papers state now that it can write as fast as yours
which if even true is a great falling off from 3000 I
do not believe that they can send a message of 10 words
without deranging the register and at a rate not exceeding
20 letters per minute of even that I believe if we could
let them alone and do justice to ourselves, the thing would
be abandoned in less than a month. It would not be
well to begin the prosecution too soon. Time it may die
of natural death.
Thistle told Cornell that he was going to use your
whether he had a right or not and put up lines just
where he pleased I think he will find that there is
some justice left yet when we come to submit it to the
Courts. I think of returning to Washington next week
the latter part. Mr Cornell had $800 for you I think
and wished I believe to pay it to you in person. When I
saw him he had not received your Tel me? as he had
been to Boston & just returned. Let me hear from you
if there is any thing special. Please present my
regards to Mrs & Miss Morse and Mr Morse.
I remain yours ever
Alfred Vail
Dr Samuel F B Morse
Poughkeepsie
