get it for me. I have Whately and Loudon already.
Oct. 14th I must close in haste, I kept this open till the last
moment to add any thing of interest. I have this moment
received from Smith some of the proceedings against O'Reilly
House &c. Their career is shot if justice has its course, but
I don't know how far injustice may be permitted to prevail,
My refuge is strong & sure, it will not further
than He permits.
Good bye. Your affectionate brother
Hinley.
Louisville Ky Oct 13th 1847
Samuel J B Moore Esq
Dear Sir
We have recently contracted
for a line or the night of the Mare's Telegraph, to be run
into the Great Monuments Cave in Ky, and I am anxious
to know from you what will be necessary to enable us to
succeed. It is a matter more for my own taste than otherwise
In order that you may the better informed me I will mention
the character of the Cave. In some parts of the cave it is
50 to 100 in width and the same in height. In other parts it
is very narrow, About 5 miles from the mouth the river often
fills the entire Cave for about 1 mile, beyond which opens
atend of about 50 ft and then you get into the most
beautiful part of the cave. It is dry, large and the crystalliza-
tions are beyond description in beauty. At the end of the
main Avenue (9 miles from mouth) there is the most often-
ed Chambers that I ever saw. It is about 10 ft in diameter
15 ft high, with large formations like the rocks above
ice at the end of houses making a connection between the
ceiling and the floor. I want an instrument in that
place, the wide running out the cave to the House about
300 Yds from its mouth. Much anxiety is often experienced
by persons going beyond the river, fearing that it might
not and fill up the Cave for that distance (1 mile) and
lyricly they have to stay in & beyond the river until
it falls. A Telegraph would remedy this danger as persons
could immediately be informed of the progress of a bearer
as soon after a storm the river rises and messengers have to be despatched, to inform them of the
fact.
What size wire will it take? Would it have to
be wrought with lead or something else? Would the rocks along
the side of the cave near which the wires would run, would
they effect the galvanic current? Please give me all
this information as I want to carry out the plan. Will
our instrument at both ends require a relay Magnet?
Please do not fail to answer this in full and
tell me all that I must do to succeed.
We expect to go to work very soon now and
build the lines which we have recently contracted
for. The O'Neelly are alert and doing all they can
to arrest our progress.
Mr F.G. Smith is at Baltimore Ohio, & Mr Kendall
has returned to Washington
Yours Truly
Jul. P. Shaffner

Utica Nov. 10, 1837.
Dear Sir-
On the day before yesterday the gentlemen for
whom I made the application for the loan of
$1000, informed me that Mr. Matteson whom he
offered as endorser refused to do so from some dis-
satisfaction in relation to the matter, and that he should
thence be obliged to abandon it. I have delayed
writing in hopes that they would bring it about.
In the meantime I shall receive interest on the
amount from the 3d instant. I have spoken
to two other gentlemen to take the money, and
have had one answer as early as Friday
who will be equally satisfactory, and I think
the offer of $1000 will cause it to take place. I desire until
you are satisfied as to the amount of the interest I will
not take it. I will write to you on Friday as soon as I see them.
I am required to leave the Cincinnati
on Monday morning. I am satisfied of the bankruptcy of
the House patent and seriously hope that
you will have no more trouble about it.
I speak to Mr. Willm about the Wall
street notes and he will take it to tomorrow.
Next day when I will depart the contract
to you in credit.
I will defer executing the contract about
the hours as you suggest until after the
15th January. The heavy rain now being com-
pleted. Our friend Calhoun is in Albany fully
engaged. He proposes to go to New York in
December or January. He has executed a
beautiful Cencliglin of Annie, and has informed
you carefully -- I shall send you a cast of it
by first opportunity.
Have you read the book -- I am anxious
to hear that it has arrived in good order.
I am happy to hear that Charles is about
coming to America to write. I am so glad that
if he has no more difficulty please to stay
that we shall be very happy to welcome
him at our house.
My wife's letter today. The happiness of
Charles has been lucky to become a father
and a mother -- I am sure he will make
an excellent one and I have no doubt that
Charles will make a good husband --
May this happiness be perpetual.
We are all well and with
the usual expressions of esteem and
affection I am
your affectionate
friend
Thomas N. Blanchard

My dear sir
I waited until to day to answer your
letter from Wood, or Mr Barrock to whom I had
assisted and made the 1000 for a sum or not - but
as they have neither of them called I suppose that
they committed it - I have enclosed Pomeroy
Walker 1000 note for 1000 on cit. at eight months
interest or a sum paid at United Bank - As I
am my self one of the partners of that house it does
not become me perhaps to trumpet our own
impossibility - But suppose it to say "entre nous"
that we have not got a solitary discountable
note in any Bank, and that our business produces
the comfortable revenue of $6.000 and an per annum -
My partners did not want to list it and only con-
cluded to do so at my solicitation -
As it is not very business like to make one's business public please to consider the above statement as to the establish-
ment confidential - It is not worth while in these
days of compulsion to invest it -
Should you at any time wish to realize the sum
on the note I will cash it for you on a weekly notice
Miller has paid his note $139.47 which I
shall deposit to your credit at United Bank and for
which you can immediately draw if you wish -
The interest on the $1000. from 3d to 13th int.
$1.92 I have given you credit for in my absence
you
Somuch for business
I will give you examination yesterday from
Palmer a condescension of a demand lady
in Alabama taken from a silhouette and from
the Dempster, which is certainly one of the
most perfectly beautiful specimens of art
I have ever seen. He is returning more
order in Albany. It will be our pleasure to
present the intimation to leave for New York
I believe in a few weeks
When shall we see you at this
All must and will always remember
I remain
Faithfully yours
W Witten

Dear Father,
Your very kind letter of the 25th inst.
has just come to hand, though I regret that I can
not be in Africa on the day I have so long wished, yet
I am very happy to say that my disappointment is very early
done, when by remaining here I oblige my best of fathers.
I would not have you, my dear father, think you are at
all on my account, I should think that I should have
been passed much more pleasantly by you in the City.
Everything is going on very well here, the two Patricks, for
themselves are engaged in getting out the rocks that include
the flough in the lower lot bordering on the James' bluff
and I think the time I have profitably employed Charles
hers himself employed. To day I have engaged a carpenter
to fix his (Charles) house at 100s for doing he will do it
all in one day, I am to get the materials. Our stable
floor wants repairing which I will let remain till you
come. I have several letters here for you, one of which is
from Sirs. We have indeed much to be thankful for, we
have at least for I am that among many in having
such a kind and affectionate father as you have always
been to me.
Ever your affectionate son
Charles

Dear Sidney, I am here for a few days, I called on the Harpens
yesterday to select an altar, and had some conversation, of so important a
nature to your interest, with James Harper that I cannot leave for P.
leisure without writing you on the subject. They seem very sure in regard
to the Primary Geography they say that it was promised by you long ago
that inquiries are respectfully and urgently made from Schools in all parts of
the country for it that they had promised it as being in preparation and
that for nearly two years they had repeatedly pledged their word that it should
be forthcoming soon, which now they are ashamed to say anything on the
subject. In the mean time it is stopping the sale of your school texts
that many Schools have thrown it out, acknowledging at the same time
that it was best not needed a preparatory book for it; that in case
of Eugene Smith, although inferior was taking the place of yours. It
was also stated that a gentleman after repeated disappointments had
determined to wait no longer but propose one himself which
could be got up in 60 days. They also said that it was through
this great exertion and those of Mr. Poison that your Geography
was not thrown out of the public Schools, and was retained
only on the ground of the Common School being in preparation.
That now a feeling hostile to your interests was getting up
&c. &c. much more in the same strain. Mr. Manson was
with me, and I asked him about it when we left. He says
they attack him on the subject every time he goes there and
wishes if you can expedite the matter to do so. I have told
you this just as it happened that you may pass your own judgment
on what is best to be done. I think your interests are suffering
by your absence, and really wish you were at home
on more accounts than one.
My own affairs are at this moment floundering. My opponents
O'Kelly & Co by their outraging efforts in misrepresentation and
inversion, have created a hostile feeling throughout the whole
West towards me, there is the Ante-rent principle with all
though the West of this state and I am looked upon as an obvious
monopolizer endeavors to monopolize the use of one of God's
elements 'electricity' for my own benefit, and ridiculous as is this
idea, it is working great mischief to me. The House humbug is
held up as a stalking horse to terrify, and to entitle Opposition
and opposition companies are organizing and find no difficulty,
it is said in finding capitalists to help them, and to oppose me,
and what they may effect it is impossible for me to say. The
most annoying part of the matter to me is, that notwithstanding
my matters are all in the hands of agents, and I have nothing to
do with any of the arrangements I am held up by name to
the odium of the public. — Lawsuits are commenced against
them at Cincinnati, and will be in Indiana & Illinois
as well as here, and so notwithstanding all my efforts to get
along peaceably, I find the fate of Whitney before me.
I think I may be able to secure my farm, and so have a place
to retire to for the evening of my days, but even this may be de-
nied me. A few months will decide. I know where my help
is and who controls all, and rest calmly in the persuasion
that his will is best and should be done. Were you here I
could tell you a great deal I cannot write. You have
before you the fate of an inventor, and take as much pains as
you will to secure to yourself your valuable invention, make up
your mind from my experience now in addition to others that you
will be robbed of it and abused into the bargain. This is the lot
of a successful inventor or discoverer, and no precautions I believe
will save him from it, he will meet with a mixed estimate , the
enlightened, the liberal will applaud him, and respect him
the ignorant, the sordid, the unprincipled will hate him, and
detract from his reputation, to compose their own contemptible selfish ends.
I don't know that you are so ignorant of the characters of the editors of the
Journal of Commerce as to be surprised that they should take ground against
me and with those that oppose me. The secret of their opposition is that many
of their subscribers dropped their paper, assigning as a reason that they obtained
through the Telegraph the news so long in advance of the mail that their paper was
considerably useless. They encourage opposition to the hope to get telegraphic news
at a cheaper rate, and to put people to death from the causes of invention, and
throw doubt on its originality with me, to accomplish their selfish ends.
I keep entirely aloof from them, for such means is so disagreeable I should
feel for my temper if I came in contact with it.
Smith behaves well now, and he is a good fighter, he and W. Kendall have just put out for the seat of war
at Cincinnati determined to bring the matter to an issue. We have good counsel
from Mr. Ewing, Secy. of Treasury under Gen. Harrison, is our counsel and has given his
written opinion that we are not only, right but have exercised the greatest
generosity and forbearance towards OR & his associates. The opposition to
me is two-fold, and it has colored at the West, OR endeavors to break down
my patent, that he may use parts of my invention without which he cannot use his old
and thus cause him to attack the originality of it, and having sold an interest in the Telegraph
they unite their forces to embarrass. An opposition line is building between N.Y. & Ohio
and so soon as Houses instruments are used successfully, if they should be, thus will the
case be tried here, P.R. Staple & Grant Lloyd my counsel. The press at the West as well
as here are prejudiced against me, because they have to pay a certain price, a mere statement about
its value is considered as for their news. They wish it cheap, competition they think will give
it to them, therefore, regardless of all things else whether I have rights or whether my opponents
have none, they join in the cry of "monopoly," a profit by the competition
I wish you could join with your invention, and fight down this most contemptible spirit I will give
you a hint of my plan, I believe it could be done taking hold of the Telegraph papers as "the
public good," that was ever cried with truth. With a press, (a newspaper, at every station
under the control of the Telegraph, a press with your invention, we could soon throw
overboard these two penny scribblers, who would lord it over the public, deceiving
them with the cry of public good only that they may put more pennies in their own pockets
I wish to take the largest view of the public benefit not only because it is right and noble
in itself but to show them up to the public the prof. hypocrisy of these men.
Think over some plan that will swallow up in great results for the public benefit
the narrow schemes of these selfish wretches -- I close in great haste Truly of the best
as ever
S. D. Morse

My dear Sir
You may recollect when I met you in Phila. on the unpleasant
bussiness of attending in a Court to arbitrate the contest of two parties for their
rights, you informed me of the Disturbing condition of O'Kelly's family. At that
moment I was led to believe from consultation with the Counsel for the
Patients that the case would undoubtedly go in their (the Patients) favor. Your
Statement touched me, and I could not bear to think that an innocent
wife, and offensive children should suffer, even from the wrong doing
of their proper protector, Should this prove to be the case. You re-
member, I authorized you to draw on me for Twenty dollars to be
remitted to M. O'Kelly's family, and to keep the source from them it was
desired secret. My object in writing is to ask if this was done, and in
case it was to request you to draw on me for that amount.
I see by the papers your admirable skill and tact with
your associate operator in transmitting the late Message of the
President. The performance reflects the highest credit on you
and them.
Truly wishing you all prosperity
remain Your friend
Sams S. B. Morse

My Dear Sir
your letter of 21 last this morning reached me and shall be promptly
answered.
A caveat can be renewed at the end of the year for another year
and so on, by renewing the caveat fee at the end of each year.
All caveat papers are retained continually in the secret archives
whether the caveat term has expired or not.
If you were to make application for a patent at this time it
would be probably 8 mos. before it would come up for examination
and in the mean time should you wish to have it delayed longer
than its term for the examination you could have it filed as a caveat
in the secret archives, and when you were ready (any time within the
year after it was so filed in the secret archives) you could call it up
to be examined as an application.
As you cannot conveniently attend to the construction of the instruments
I would by all means renew the caveat which is done by
sending a new fee to the office stating what is for
Mr Kendall is expected home in Christmas but may be obtained
until New Year.
With regard to the subject of your second page I will say I am willing
to hasten you will deal mercifully and kindly with me. You have been
strengthened to resist temptation in the hour of adversity and I can
surely trust you now in truth I do not suppose it best for the future
of the Telegraph that I should acquire an interest in it and hence
I am willing to be a user as it is.
Should you require my testimony in House's case I must be forbidding
to meet the requisition. You will again on that occasion the assignment
to be produced whereby the interest I once held was transferred to you.
Can we not to expect you in W. this winter? When you last wrote
me you obtained you would probably be here in January and
I would say we have an extra bed room which will be of your
service when you are disposed to use it. Send your trunk
to our house without ceremony when you arrive, it will please
us to have you do so.
I received your previous letter with the account of through
my friend Mr. Pisson of N.Y. all was right.
When you may have funds in hand for me you will please transfer
them to Mr. Pisson and at the same time send me the substance of
the transaction by mail -- let the moved transaction only be
communicated to him and whatever of explanation there may be, in the
case it is to be entertained.
With the highest esteem
Your truly
L. D. Gale

Dear Sir
I write to inform you that
Mr Kendall is now in Nashville and will return
again in a few days. Your letter awaits his return.
Your letter to the Herald will appear in one of our
daily papers tomorrow. It tells more than we in
this locality. We are going ahead with the line
to New Orleans. I have 25 hands on the road to
Nashville and will put on more next week. I have
10 on the road to Frankfurt, and my associate has
gangs at other parts. O'Kelly has 15 hands on the
Nashville part and I confidently expect a few
fight. My men are well armed and I think they
can do their duty. I shall be with them when the
parties get together and if any thing does occur, the
use of experts best will be appreciated by me. This
is to be lamented but if it comes we shall not back
out. I wrote a letter to you several weeks ago
relative to telegraphs in the great Manomouth levee, Please answer
me in detail, and tell me if you could not make
it convenient to be present at the levee when it
is carried in. Do say yes if you can it will be
about August
Yours as
S.F.S. Hartfurd

Dear Sidney
You perceive by the date that I am now in Washington, where I shall
be for a few weeks probably, I write you rather briefly and in haste, as I have much to
do and this is the last day for the steamer from Boston. I send you with this, which
I hope will reach you safely, two copies of the New York Herald, which will be ordered
to you in speaking of the efficiency of my Telegraph. Although noticed by the Friends
with his peculiar Whodomontade, there are the facts which are so plain, that one
can yesterday in the Herald of the 5th inst. gives nearly ten columns of Telegraphic
intelligence, transmitted without any extraordinary effort, among which is the Governor's
message of five columns, the Caledonian news of three columns, and Mr. Cat-
horne's speech and Congress news of more than three columns. I challenge any other
system than mine to equal this. — I see the English prints are blazing a part
of their Telegraph in telegraphing 700 words the Queen's speech in 15 minutes
and on halfphones while the Governor's message from Albany containing 5000!
words was telegraphed to NewYork, and at all the Stations on the line, in two and on halfphones
the same time. This gives a comparison of 5000 to 700.—
I see nothing in any of the efforts at improvement abroad that can compete
with mine. Bain's is mine made complicated, I could send with mine what he
is preparing his paper to send his 1000 in a minute, double if not triple
the amount. I reason in this way, if, as it is said, a boy can punch the holes
in his paper as fast as a compositor can set up type, then as I can make with my
key my letters, at the faithful extensivity of my time, at the rate of an expert penman
writing, and as a penman can write three times as fast as a compositor can set
up type than it follows, that while he is simply preparing his paper, I can have
transmitted three times the amount of matter that he has but prepared to send.
My type first excused on board ship and cast the first week on my arrival at
100691
and afterwards, more abundantly prepared for exhibiting the Telegraph in the
University and at Washington, can be better used for the purpose desired than Bainis.
When the time of preparation is of no consequence, such as an long public document,
my original type, and particulars and other machinery for regulating the transmission
might be of service, and they accomplish the purpose as well as if not better than
Bainis. Had it not been for that most ingenious invention of Sir John Campbell, England
would have had throughout all her borders, the most efficient system yet devised; (I
think I can say this without boasting, since facts support my assertion;) and it would have
been far more probable to have adopted my system when I offered it and to have compensated me for it, and then used it for her own advantage than to take the course
as yet pursued, of unjustly and illegally denying me a Patent, and then undertaking to falsify
from the honor, while in a covert and sound about way Britain imitating my
plans, and adopting the essential and peculiar features of my Telegraph. History
has a page for this Conduct, and Truth may be silenced for a while, she will at
length speak out in this case as in others and by another hand. If unjust piracy
on England's already blackened brow. However self-complacent her men of scientific
renown may be in their subject appropriation to themselves of American thought and labor
the time will come when Truth will show to the world the meanness as well as the injustice of their thefts, and the world's scorn will be their reward. -- I await, however,
for justice may yet be done, and when I recollect the interest excited by the very
injustice in the minds of some of England's true noblemen, the Earl of Elgin, the
Earl of Lincoln &c others, I cannot but think some movement self suggested may
be made to expunge from the record, the disgraceful act of one Attorney General.
I have had a Map of the Telegraph routes prepared and be-
graphed for the Herald. This Paper had uniformly been friendly to
me and to the enterprise, while every other paper in New York has seemed
to take a peculiar delight in detracting and crying down, and raising
up rivals, and blazing mistakes, and printing falsehoods, and
magnifying troubles. The motive of the Herald's course, so different
from all the rest, is not for me to condemnize. Under the editorship of Mr.
Hudson, it was an excellent paper having abandoned its objectionable features.
Since Mr. Bennett's return, there is also a return to some features quite objectionable.
But a kind office requires no justice a kind return, and I therefore, give him the
publication of the Telegraph Map. He will speak also of Cerography (the
old Cerography of course,) I employed Galway to plan it for me.
All was well in New York, I left the city on Thursday evening
to see you and shall welcome your home, not here, but in Europe.
My affairs at the West are in an unsettled state as yet. Mr. Kendall
is there, (at Louisville,) and writes enviously. Mr. O'Reilly and his associates
have conducted in a most outrageous manner, and have created a widespread
misconception by their machinations which it will take time and labor to dispel,
but the tide is turned I learn, and I hope soon that a step will
be put to their injurious proceedings.
As to the House affair, the rival lines to Phila have
got their posts up, but as yet they are under 'here poles.'
no wire upon them. I am preparing to contest the matter
as soon as any demonstration really injurious shall take place.
I doubt whether I shall be compelled to try the case, for as you say of the
English edition of it, it has not life enough in it to oppose against us.
The more I think of your discovery the more I admire it. I see that
it must revolutionize printing & engraving.
Good bye. Truly as ever your affectionate brother
Finley.
Sidney E. Morse, Esq.
Please continue sending me books, papers &c. on Telegraphy
which you think may be of service. I sent you a history of my case with
the Attorney General by a former Steamer. I hope you got it.

Dear Sir
Yours I received some time since and
what you designated in its pages I freely acknowledge. Although
the plan of two cylinders was new to me at the time. I was perfectly
aware that House's or any other Telegraph machine must be
operated by exact motions dependent on each other at each
Station. Although, if the apparatus I have devised (not calling
the uniform cylinder motion a new improvement) had been
what you most desired, I would willingly part with it
(which I hold is more simple and complete than any other
which has been invented) if it would place the original
inventor beyond the reach of competition of those (House to)
who would willingly, yet, gainingly blot his name from the
world and reap for themselves the benefit of what has probably
cost yourself many sleepless nights (like when your experiments
were defeated on Sommons-Island). I write not thus because
I despise or have the least grudge against House, for I know
him not. not even his residence. But I know men inventors of useful inventions, that would undoubtedly have been
made independent thereof from had it not been for like compulsion. Although you are probably reaping rich rewards
from your invention, it matters not the man or his circumstances. Of course I have some object and pride in
accomplishing what I have devised: But what I write below
me sincere. What I further devise is arranging the mac-
hine (Vig. Cut. No. 1.) so as to print your alphabet with equal
celerity with your apparatus. or if the operator shoots the common
alphabet The last which I send you is indeed a poor one and I fear you will be troubled to make it out, but it was
drawn according to my abilities and when suffering greatly
from the effects of an extracted tooth. I much wish I could
show to you the apparatus itself and thoroughly describe it.
that I might make it plain. But I will rest satisfied
by describing it as well as possible on paper. The draft
may seem to you greatly defective. and is indeed so. In the
explanation I forgot to say (and perhaps some others) when
receiving despatches the wire must be constantly connected
which may be done by an extra wire. Now being convinced
that the Printing Telegraph is inferior to yours I have but
to say, that if you like my plan (which like yours can
be varied in form) and you should ever have a cause to
use or dispose of the kind please remember since
I will here embrace the opportunity to inquire
to what extent you suppose the Oxide Hydrogen Bow
pipe can be used, or how many lbs of iron or other
metal it could be constructed to melt at a time
Excuse all defects, and answer me at your
leasure or in my time
Yours Truely from
Wm S Page

Dear Sir-
The Telegraphic Map is done - I am on the point of sending it to the United States Office when I received yours of the 12th inst.
The excessive cold weather at the commencement of the week prevented me from finishing it earlier, as I thought the risk of taking it through some of the operations, with the temperature 20 degrees below freezing, would be greater than them the delay would be injurious to you.
On Wednesday I will purchase some paper, and employ Mr. Almond who has just printed the Missionary Octavo, to strike off the 200 impressions which you have directed.
The proofs have yet been taken, I will send the first one I get by mail to you.
Yours with great regard
Prof. S.F.B. Morse

When I, in October of the year eighteen hundred, I thirtysix years
old, was on board the packet ship Sally on her voyage from France
to New-York, I conceived the idea of marking the telegraphic
signs, I had invented, (being dots, spaces to signify
numerals, by electrical decomposition of certain salts
and chemical compounds; and whereas the application
of the proper means for producing a successful result
of this thought, was soon after superseded in my mind
by another method, at the same time conceived of
marking the said signs, to wit, by magnetism produced
by electricity, which in the successful method was
in use, and having recently returned to my original
thought of applying decomposition by electricity through
a single circuit of Conductors, and discovered a means

to the marking of the French signs for numerals and
letters, and of any desired characters, I will here describe
the nature of my invention and the method by

The nature of my invention consists,
First, in the application of the decomposing effects of
Electricity, produced from any known generator
of Electricity to the marking Alphabetic or other signs
for numerals a letters, a words or sentences, though a simple
circuit of Electric conductors, by which intelligence may
be communicated, marked on cloth, metals or other

Thirdly, in the application of the bleaching qualities

In applying the decomposing effects of Electricity upon
any known salts that leave a mark as the result
of the said decomposition, I use
Class. A
A class of salts that produce a colored mark upon
cloth, paper thread or other material, under the action
of Electricity.
First: Sodide of tin in solution.
Second: Extract of Natgalls, and sulphate of iron in solution
making an ink which colors white canvas cloth of
a uniform grey.
Third: Acetate of lead, and nitrate of potash in solution.
Fourth: Iodide of potassium in solution.
Into either of these I dip a strip of cloth or thread
which is kept properly moistened, will there give a black
mark upon the cloth thread or other material, under the
action of Electricity.
Class B.
A class of salts, which color the cloth paper thread or other
material, and are bleached by the action of Electricity.
First: Iodide of tin in solution.
Second: Iodine digested in Alcohol.
Into either of these I dip a strip of cloth, paper thread
or other material; and if in solution Second I also dip
them into a solution of sulphate of Soda. The cloth or other
material in these cases becomes of a people color and
a bit dark. The electricity in these cases when a material
points a type is passed upon or comes in contact with
the moist cloth or other material bleaches it, and leaves
the print or the type impressed in white characters upon
the material.
Class. C.
A class of salts that produces a mark upon metal though
the intervening cloth or other material, and not upon
the material, under the action of Electricity.

Dear Sir,
Your of the 9th inst. forwarded from St. Louis
I have this moment received. It gives me real pain to learn
that there is any prospect of physical collision between the
Reilly party and ours, and I trust that this may arrive in time
to prevent any movement of those friendly to me which shall
provoke so sad a result. I emphatically say that if the law cannot
protect me in your region, I shall never sanction the appeal to
force to sustain myself, however, conscious of being in the right.
I infinitely prefer to suffer still more from the proscriptions
of these unprincipled men, than to gain my rights by a single
illegal step. Law and justice move slower than violence, but
their triumphs are more enduring. And I must have success through them
and my right.
I have great confidence in the high sense of right contained
in your region, despite the misinformations of those who would deceive them, and when the truth returns
to them their demands will be strong for the right, and I can trust them.
I hope you will do all in your power to prevent collision. If
the parties meet in putting up posts and wires, let them have their way
and opponents of my party will have no patent for putting up posts or wires, the men are not to blame, let no
feeling be entertained between them no rivalry, let friends, feeling as between

The above table shows daily receipts at the 7 offices, amounting to $18.10, or $5,647.20 for a year of 32 days. From which deduct the expenses, and 7 per cent. on the capital for one year, which is $3,625, and we have a surplus of $2,022.20, or about 14 per cent. on the capital, making in all, 21 per cent. profit on the business of the Line. Now this may appear like a large estimate, to those persons who have given but little attention to the subject of this new and extraordinary mode of conveying intelligence. But my experience, based upon the operations of other similar lines of Telegraph, justify me in expressing the opinion, that the estimate will be fully realized, the moment the Line is put in operation.
Many persons entertain the opinion that the business for a Telegraph is confined to a few individuals, who are styled as business men; this is an error. All classes of society contribute more or less business to the Telegraph. Merchants use it to order goods, make inquiries respecting the markets and negotiate sales of produce. The Lawyer uses the Telegraph to keep himself informed of the progress of business in Court, that he may know when his own cause is likely to be reached, without the expense and loss of time incident to waiting in person on the slow progress of justice. The Banker has frequent and important uses for the Telegraph. With its aid he can so regulate his affairs, as to preserve for his customers a sound and uniform currency.
The farmer uses the Telegraph to inquire the price in market of such articles of produce as he has to sell whenever he suspects the purchaser of offering too low a price, and while he is feeding his team, he is also preparing himself to meet his customer on equal footing. The Hotel Keeper uses the Telegraph in giving and receiving information respecting the movement of travelers. Physicians have occasional use for the Telegraph in consulting distant Physicians, or inviting them to attend some obstinate case as counsel. Stage proprietors find the Telegraph very convenient to regulate their business in ordering horses, inquiring after their teams during bad state of the roads, giving directions on the brack down occurs, &c., &c. Travelers have very frequent use for the Telegraph, and always give preference to routes having such accommodations, other things being equal. They keep their friends at home advised of the progress of their journey, the state of their health, giving directions and making requests about their business at home. &c., &c. Persons about leaving home on business will first inquire if the persons are at home with whom they have business and inform them of the time of their visit so as to ensure a meeting. Parties of pleasure visiting neighboring villages use the Telegraph to announce their intended visit, and order such accommodations as the nature of the case may demand. And all persons use the Telegraph more or less for social purposes—inquiring after the health of distant friends, giving information of the state of their own health, informing of deaths, marriages, births, &c. Communications of all these different characters I have seen presented at the office of Telegraph Stations.
The prices I have named in the estimated receipts are, in some instances, lower than is charged on any Line of Telegraph now in operation; in others, the same. As Telegraphs become better known they will be more used, and the prices charged will be reduced.
With these remarks I will submit the question to your consideration, whether the interests of your several villages, would not be advanced by erecting a Line of Telegraph from Troy to Whitehall, by which they would be connected at two points, with the great American Telegraph system.
E. CORNELL.

I have been with much regret the tone of your journal
in regard to the unpleasant controversy which, though
no seeking of mine, has grown out of a contract made
in 1865 by my agents with Mr. O'Kelly. I regret it
the more because I have been long led to entertain
admiration for your talents, and a high personal regard
for your character as represented to me by friends who know
you. If these representations are correct, you cannot know-
ingly give countenance to such desperate attempts to injure
me, as have been made by certain parties, not merely in
my legal rights, in denouncing my talent as an odious
monopoly, but through every kind of obstruction from the
merits of my inventions, thereby distorting upon it in such
a way as to rob me of the fruits of years of arduous toil, at
the moment when these seemed to be a prospect of my
reaping some reward. I believe you have been impressed
upon by wicked men, who have not hesitated to use false
blood and money to compass their selfish ends. These are
strong things but they are weighed and carefully selected.

inventions, rightfully belonging to our own country (as in
this present case) is given to other nations. They who are
